AP.B.2.5.A.4: Small nonpolar molecules, including `text(N)_2`, `text(O)_2`, and `text(CO)_2`, freely pass across the membrane. Hydrophilic substances, such as large polar molecules and ions, move across the membrane through embedded channel and transport proteins.
AP.B.2.5.A.5: Polar uncharged molecules, including `text(H)_2text(O)`, pass through the membrane in small amounts.
AP.B.2.5.B: Describe the role of the cell wall in maintaining cell structure and function.
AP.B.2.5.B.1: Cell walls provide a structural boundary, as well as a permeability barrier for some substances to the internal environments.
AP.B.2.5.B.2: Cell walls of plants, prokaryotes, and fungi are composed of complex carbohydrates.
AP.B.2.6.A: Describe the mechanisms that organisms use to maintain solute and water balance.
AP.B.2.6.A.1: Passive transport is the net movement of molecules from high concentration to low concentration without the direct input of metabolic energy.
AP.B.2.6.A.2: Passive transport plays a primary role in the import of materials and the export of wastes.
AP.B.2.6.A.3: Active transport requires the direct input of energy to move molecules from regions of low concentration to regions of high concentration.
AP.B.2.6.B: Describe the mechanisms that organisms use to transport large molecules across the plasma membrane.
AP.B.2.6.B.1: The selective permeability of membranes allows for the formation of concentration gradients of solutes across the membrane.
AP.B.2.6.B.2: The processes of endocytosis and exocytosis require energy to move large molecules into and out of cells.
AP.B.2.6.B.2.a: In exocytosis, internal vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and secrete large macromolecules out of the cell.
AP.B.2.6.B.2.b: In endocytosis, the cell takes in macromolecules and particulate matter by forming new vesicles derived from the plasma membrane.
AP.B.2.7.A: Explain how the structure of a molecule affects its ability to pass through the plasma membrane.
AP.B.2.7.A.1: Membrane proteins are required for facilitated diffusion of charged and large polar molecules through a membrane.
AP.B.2.7.A.1.a: Large quantities of water pass through aquaporins.
AP.B.2.7.A.1.b: Charged ions, including `Na^+` and `K^+`, require channel proteins to move through the membrane.
AP.B.2.7.A.1.c: Membranes may become polarized by movement of ions across the membrane.
AP.B.2.7.A.2: Membrane proteins are necessary for active transport.
AP.B.2.7.A.3: Metabolic energy (such as from ATP) is required for active transport of molecules and/or ions across the membrane and to establish and maintain concentration gradients.
AP.B.2.7.A.4: The `Na^+//K^+` ATPase contributes to the maintenance of the membrane potential.
AP.B.2.8.A: Explain how concentration gradients affect the movement of molecules across membranes.
AP.B.2.8.A.1: External environments can be hypotonic, hypertonic or isotonic to internal environments of cells.
AP.B.2.8.A.1.a: Water moves by osmosis from areas of high water potential/low osmolarity/low solute concentration to areas of low water potential/high osmolarity/high solute concentration.
AP.B.2.8.B: Explain how osmoregulatory mechanisms contribute to the health and survival of organisms.
AP.B.2.8.B.1: Growth and homeostasis are maintained by the constant movement of molecules across membranes.
AP.B.2.8.B.2: Osmoregulation maintains water balance and allows organisms to control their internal solute composition/water potential.
AP.B.2.9.A: Describe the processes that allow ions and other molecules to move across membranes.
AP.B.2.9.A.1: A variety of processes allow for the movement of ions and other molecules across membranes, including passive and active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis.
AP.B.2.10.A: Describe the membrane-bound structures of the eukaryotic cell.
AP.B.2.10.A.1: Membranes and membrane-bound organelles in eukaryotic cells compartmentalize intracellular metabolic processes and specific enzymatic reactions.
AP.B.2.10.B: Explain how internal membranes and membrane-bound organelles contribute to compartmentalization of eukaryotic cell functions.
AP.B.2.10.B.1: Internal membranes facilitate cellular processes by minimizing competing interactions and by increasing surface areas where reactions can occur.
AP.B.2.11.A: Describe similarities and/or differences in compartmentalization between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
AP.B.2.11.A.1: Membrane-bound organelles evolved from once free-living prokaryotic cells via endosymbiosis.
AP.B.2.11.A.2: Prokaryotes generally lack internal membrane- bound organelles but have internal regions with specialized structures and functions.
AP.B.2.11.A.3: Eukaryotic cells maintain internal membranes that partition the cell into specialized regions.
AP.B.2.11.B: Describe the relationship between the functions of endosymbiotic organelles and their free-living ancestral counterparts.
AP.B.2.11.B.1: Membrane-bound organelles evolved from previously free-living prokaryotic cells via endosymbiosis.
AP.B.3.1.A.1: The structure of enzymes includes the active site that specifically interacts with substrate molecules.
AP.B.3.1.A.2: For an enzyme-mediated chemical reaction to occur, the shape and charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site of the enzyme.
AP.B.3.2.A: Explain how enzymes affect the rate of biological reactions.
AP.B.3.2.A.1: The structure and function of enzymes contribute to the regulation of biological processes.
AP.B.3.2.A.1.a: Enzymes are biological catalysts that facilitate chemical reactions in cells by lowering the activation energy.
AP.B.3.3.A: Explain how changes to the structure of an enzyme may affect its function.
AP.B.3.3.A.1: Change to the molecular structure of a component in an enzymatic system may result in a change of the function or efficiency of the system.
AP.B.3.3.A.1.a: Denaturation of an enzyme occurs when the protein structure is disrupted, eliminating the ability to catalyze reactions.
AP.B.3.3.A.1.b: Environmental temperatures and pH outside the optimal range for a given enzyme will cause changes to its structure, altering the efficiency with which it catalyzes reactions.
AP.B.3.3.A.2: In some cases, enzyme denaturation is reversible, allowing the enzyme to regain activity.
AP.B.3.3.B: Explain how the cellular environment affects enzyme activity.
AP.B.3.3.B.1: Environmental pH can alter the efficiency of enzyme activity, including through disruption of hydrogen bonds that provide enzyme structure.
AP.B.3.3.B.2: The relative concentrations of substrates and products determine how efficiently an enzymatic reaction proceeds.
AP.B.3.3.B.3: Higher environmental temperatures increase the speed of movement of molecules in a solution, increasing the frequency of collisions between enzymes and substrates and therefore increasing the rate of reaction.
AP.B.3.3.B.4: Competitive inhibitor molecules can bind reversibly or irreversibly to the active site of the enzyme. Noncompetitive inhibitors can bind allosteric sites, changing the activity of the enzyme.
AP.B.3.4.A: Describe the role of energy in living organisms.
AP.B.3.4.A.1: All living systems require constant input of energy.
AP.B.3.4.A.2: Life requires a highly ordered system and does not violate the second law of thermodynamics.
AP.B.3.4.A.2.a: Energy input must exceed energy loss to maintain order and to power cellular processes.
AP.B.3.4.A.2.b: Cellular processes that release energy may be coupled with cellular processes that require energy.
AP.B.3.4.A.2.c: Loss of order or energy flow results in death.
AP.B.3.4.A.3: Energy-related pathways in biological systems are sequential to allow for a more controlled and efficient transfer of energy. A product of a reaction in a metabolic pathway is generally the reactant for the subsequent step in the pathway.
AP.B.3.5.A: Describe the photosynthetic processes that allow organisms to capture and store energy.
AP.B.3.5.A.1: Organisms capture and store energy for use in biological processes.
AP.B.3.5.A.1.a: Photosynthesis captures energy from the sun and produces sugars.
AP.B.3.5.A.1.a.i: Photosynthesis first evolved in prokaryotic organisms.
AP.B.3.5.A.1.a.ii: Scientific evidence supports the claim that prokaryotic (cyanobacterial) photosynthesis was responsible for the production of an oxygenated atmosphere.
AP.B.3.5.A.1.a.iii: Prokaryotic photosynthetic pathways were the foundation of eukaryotic photosynthesis.
AP.B.3.5.A.2: The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis in eukaryotes involve a series of coordinated reaction pathways that capture energy present in light to yield ATP and `text(NADPH)`, which power the production of organic molecules.
AP.B.3.5.B: Explain how cells capture energy from light and transfer it to biological molecules for storage and use.
AP.B.3.5.B.1: During photosynthesis, chlorophylls absorb energy from light, boosting electrons to a higher energy level in photosystems I and II.
AP.B.3.5.B.2: Photosystems I and II are embedded in the internal membranes of chloroplasts and are connected by the transfer of higher energy electrons through an electron transport chain (ETC).
AP.B.3.5.B.3: When electrons are transferred between molecules in a sequence of reactions as they pass through the ETC, an electrochemical gradient of protons (hydrogen ions) is established across the internal membrane.
AP.B.3.5.B.4: The formation of the proton gradient is linked to the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate via ATP synthase.
AP.B.3.5.B.5: The energy captured in the light reactions and transferred to ATP and `text(NADPH)` powers the production of carbohydrates from carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, which occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast.
AP.B.3.6.A: Describe the processes that allow organisms to use energy stored in biological macromolecules.
AP.B.3.6.A.1: Fermentation and cellular respiration use energy from biological macromolecules to produce ATP. Respiration and fermentation are characteristic of all forms of life.
AP.B.3.6.A.2: Cellular respiration in eukaryotes involves a series of coordinated enzyme-catalyzed reactions that capture energy from biological macromolecules.
AP.B.3.6.A.3: The electron transport chain transfers energy from electrons in a series of coupled reactions that establish an electrochemical gradient across membranes.
AP.B.3.6.A.3.a: Electron transport chain reactions occur in chloroplasts, mitochondria, and prokaryotic plasma membranes.
AP.B.3.6.A.3.b: In cellular respiration, electrons delivered by `text(NADH)` and `text(FADH)_2` are passed to a series of electron acceptor s as they move toward the terminal electron acceptor, oxygen. In photosynthesis, the terminal electron acceptor is `text(NADP)^+`. Aerobic prokaryotes use oxygen as a terminal electron acceptor, while anaerobic prokaryotes use other molecules.
AP.B.3.6.A.3.c: The transfer of electrons is accompanied by the formation of a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane or the internal membrane of chloroplasts, with the membrane(s) separating a region of high proton concentration from a region of low proton concentration. In prokaryotes, the passage of electrons is accompanied by the movement of protons across the plasma membrane.
AP.B.3.6.A.3.d: The flow of protons back through membrane-bound ATP synthase by chemiosmosis drives the formation of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This is known as oxidative phosphorylation in cellular respiration, and photophosphorylation in photosynthesis.
AP.B.3.6.A.3.e: n cellular respiration, decoupling oxidative phosphorylation from electron transport generates heat. This heat can be used by endothermic organisms to regulate body temperature.
AP.B.3.6.B: Explain how cells obtain energy from biological macromolecules in order to power cellular functions.
AP.B.3.6.B.1: Glycolysis is a biochemical pathway that releases energy in glucose to form ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate, `text(NADH)` from `text(NAD)^+`, and pyruvate.
AP.B.3.6.B.2: Pyruvate is transported from the cytosol to the mitochondrion, where further oxidation occurs.
AP.B.3.6.B.3: In the Krebs cycle, carbon dioxide is released from organic intermediates, ATP is synthesized from ADP and inorganic phosphate, and electrons are transferred to the coenzymes `text(NADH)` and `text(FADH)_2`.
AP.B.3.6.B.4: Electrons extracted in glycolysis and Krebs cycle reactions are transferred by `text(NADH)` and `text(FADH)_2` to the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
AP.B.3.6.B.5: When electrons are transferred between molecules in a sequence of reactions as they pass through the ETC, an electrochemical gradient of protons (hydrogen ions) across the inner mitochondrial membrane is established.
AP.B.3.6.B.6: Fermentation allows glycolysis to proceed in the absence of oxygen and produces organic molecules, including alcohol and lactic acid, as waste products.
AP.B.3.6.B.7: The conversion of ATP to ADP releases energy, which is used to power many metabolic processes.
AP.B.3.7.A: Explain the connection between variation in the number and types of molecules within cells to the ability of the organism to survive and/or reproduce in different environments.
AP.B.3.7.A.1: Variation at the molecular level provides organisms with the ability to respond to a variety of environmental stimuli.
AP.B.3.7.A.2: Variation in the number and types of molecules within cells provides organisms a greater ability to survive and/or reproduce in different environments.
AP.B.4.1.A: Describe the ways that cells can communicate with one another.
AP.B.4.1.A.1: Cells communicate with one another through direct contact with other cells or from a distance via chemical signaling.
AP.B.4.1.B: Explain how cells communicate with one another over short and long distances.
AP.B.4.1.B.1: Cells communicate over short distances by using local regulators that target cells in the vicinity of the signal-emitting cell.
AP.B.4.1.B.1.a: Signals released by one cell type can travel long distances to target cells of another cell type.
AP.B.4.2.A: Describe the components of a signal transduction pathway.
AP.B.4.2.A.1: Signal transduction pathways link signal reception with cellular responses.
AP.B.4.2.A.2: Many signal transduction pathways include protein modification and phosphorylation cascades.
AP.B.4.2.B: Describe the role of components of a signal transduction pathway in producing a cellular response.
AP.B.4.2.B.1: Signaling begins with the recognition of a chemical messenger-a ligand-by a receptor protein in a target cell.
AP.B.4.2.B.1.a: The ligand-binding domain of a receptor recognizes a specific chemical messenger, which can be a peptide, a small chemical, or protein, in a specific one-to-one relationship.
AP.B.4.2.B.1.b: G protein-coupled receptors are an example of a receptor protein in eukaryotes.
AP.B.4.2.B.2: Signaling cascades relay signals from receptors to cell targets, often amplifying the incoming signals, resulting in the appropriate responses by the cell, which could include cell growth, secretion of molecules, or gene expression.
AP.B.4.2.B.2.a: After the ligand binds, the intracellular domain of a receptor protein changes shape, initiating transduction of the signal.
AP.B.4.2.B.2.b: Second messengers (such as cyclic AMP) are molecules that relay and amplify the intracellular signal.
AP.B.4.2.B.2.c: Binding of ligand-to-ligand-gated channels can cause the channel to open or close.
AP.B.4.3.A: Describe the role of the environment in eliciting a cellular response.
AP.B.4.3.A.1: Signal transduction pathways influence how the cell responds to its environment.
AP.B.4.3.B: Describe the different types of cellular responses elicited by a signal transduction pathway.
AP.B.4.3.B.1: Signal transduction may result in changes in gene expression and cell function, which may alter phenotype or result in programmed cell death (apoptosis).
AP.B.4.4.A: Explain how a change in the structure of any signaling molecule affects the activity of the signaling pathway.
AP.B.4.4.A.1: Changes in signal transduction pathways can alter cellular response.
AP.B.4.4.A.1.a: Mutations in any domain of the receptor protein or in any component of the signaling pathway may affect the downstream components by altering the subsequent transduction of the signal.
AP.B.4.4.A.2: Chemicals that interfere with any component of the signaling pathway may activate or inhibit the pathway.
AP.B.4.5.A: Describe positive and/or negative feedback mechanisms.
AP.B.4.5.A.1: Organisms use feedback mechanisms to maintain their internal environments and respond to internal and external environmental changes.
AP.B.4.5.B: Explain how negative feedback helps to maintain homeostasis.
AP.B.4.5.B.1: Negative feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis for a particular condition by regulating physiological processes. If a system is perturbed, negative feedback mechanisms return the system back to its target set point. These processes operate at the molecular and cellular levels.
AP.B.4.5.C: Explain how positive feedback affects homeostasis.
AP.B.4.5.C.1: Positive feedback mechanisms amplify responses and processes in biological organisms. The variable initiating the response is moved farther away from the initial set point. Amplification occurs when the stimulus is further activated, which, in turn, initiates an additional response that produces system change.
AP.B.4.6.A: Describe the events that occur in the cell cycle.
AP.B.4.6.A.1: In eukaryotes, cells divide and transmit genetic information via two highly regulated processes.
AP.B.4.6.A.2: The cell cycle is a highly regulated series of events for the growth and reproduction of cells.
AP.B.4.6.A.2.a: The cell cycle consists of sequential stages of interphase (G1, S, G2), mitosis, and cytokinesis.
AP.B.4.6.A.2.b: A cell can enter a stage (G0) where it no longer divides, but it can reenter the cell cycle in response to appropriate cues. Nondividing cells may exit the cell cycle or be held at a particular stage in the cell cycle.
AP.B.4.6.B: Explain how mitosis results in the transmission of chromosomes from one generation to the next.
AP.B.4.6.B.1: Mitosis is a process that ensures the transfer of a complete genome from a parent cell to two genetically identical daughter cells.
AP.B.4.6.B.1.a: Mitosis plays a role in growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction.
AP.B.4.6.B.1.b: Mitosis alternates with interphase in the cell cycle.
AP.B.4.6.B.1.c: Mitosis occurs in a sequential series of steps (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase).
AP.B.4.7.A: Describe the role of checkpoints in regulating the cell cycle.
AP.B.4.7.A.1: A number of internal controls or checkpoints regulate progression through the cycle.
AP.B.4.7.A.2: Interactions between cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases control the cell cycle.
AP.B.4.7.B: Describe the effects of disruptions to the cell cycle on the cell or organism.
AP.B.4.7.B.1: Disruptions to the cell cycle may result in cancer and/or programmed cell death (apoptosis).
AP.B.5.1.A: Explain how meiosis results in the transmission of chromosomes from one generation to the next.
AP.B.5.1.A.1: Meiosis is a process that ensures the formation of haploid gamete cells in sexually reproducing diploid organisms.
AP.B.5.1.A.1.a: Meiosis results in daughter cells with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell.
AP.B.5.1.A.1.b: Meiosis involves two rounds of a sequential series of steps (meiosis I and meiosis II).
AP.B.5.1.B: Describe similarities and/ or differences between the phases and outcomes of mitosis and meiosis.
AP.B.5.1.B.1: Mitosis and meiosis are similar in the way chromosomes segregate but differ in the number of cells produced and the genetic content of the daughter cells.
AP.B.5.2.A: Explain how the process of meiosis generates genetic diversity.
AP.B.5.2.A.1: Separation of the homologous chromosomes in meiosis I ensures that each gamete receives a haploid (1n) set of chromosomes that comprises both maternal and paternal chromosomes.
AP.B.5.2.A.2: During meiosis I, homologous chromatids exchange genetic material via a process called “crossing over” (recombination), which increases genetic diversity among the resultant gametes.
AP.B.5.2.A.3: Sexual reproduction in eukaryotes involving gamete formation - including crossing over, the random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, and subsequent fertilization of gametes - serves to increase variation.
AP.B.5.3.A: Explain how shared, conserved, fundamental processes and features support the concept of common ancestry for all organisms.
AP.B.5.3.A.1: DNA and RNA are carriers of genetic information.
AP.B.5.3.A.2: Ribosomes are found in all forms of life.
AP.B.5.3.A.3: Major features of the genetic code are shared by all modern living systems.
AP.B.5.3.A.4: Core metabolic pathways are conserved across all currently recognized domains.
AP.B.5.3.B: Explain the inheritance of genes and traits as described by Mendel's laws.
AP.B.5.3.B.1: Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment can be applied to genes that are on different chromosomes.
AP.B.5.3.B.2: Fertilization involves the fusion of two haploid gametes, restoring the diploid number of chromosomes and increasing genetic variation in populations by creating new combinations of alleles in the zygote.
AP.B.5.3.B.2.a: Rules of probability can be applied to analyze passage of single-gene traits from parent to offspring.
AP.B.5.3.B.2.b: The pattern of inheritance (monohybrid, dihybrid, sex-linked, and genetically linked genes) can often be predicted from data, including pedigree, that give the parent genotype/phenotype and the offspring genotypes/phenotypes.
AP.B.5.4.A: Explain deviations from Mendel's model of the inheritance of traits.
AP.B.5.4.A.1: Patterns of inheritance of many traits do not follow ratios predicted by Mendel's laws and can be identified by quantitative analysis, where observed phenotypic ratios statistically differ from the predicted ratios.
AP.B.5.4.A.1.a: Genes that are adjacent and close to one another on the same chromosome may appear to be genetically linked; the probability that genetically linked genes will segregate as a unit can be used to calculate the map distance between them.
AP.B.5.4.A.2: Some traits are determined by genes on sex chromosomes and are known as sex-linked traits. The pattern of inheritance of sex-linked traits can often be predicted from data, including pedigree, indicating the parent genotype/phenotype and the offspring genotypes/phenotypes.
AP.B.5.4.A.3: Many traits are the product of multiple genes and/or physiological processes acting in combination; these traits therefore do not segregate in Mendelian patterns.
AP.B.5.4.A.4: Some traits result from non-nuclear inheritance.
AP.B.5.4.A.4.a: Chloroplasts and mitochondria are randomly assorted to gametes and daughter cells; thus, traits determined by chloroplast and mitochondrial DNA do not follow simple Mendelian rules.
AP.B.5.4.A.4.b: In animals, mitochondria are transmitted by the egg and not by sperm; as such, traits determined by the mitochondrial DNA are maternally inherited.
AP.B.5.4.A.4.c: In plants, mitochondria and chloroplasts are transmitted in the ovule and not in the pollen; as such, mitochondria-determined and chloroplast-determined traits are maternally inherited.
AP.B.5.5.A: Explain how the same genotype can result in multiple phenotypes under different environmental conditions.
AP.B.5.5.A.1: Environmental factors influence gene expression and can lead to phenotypic plasticity. Phenotypic plasticity occurs when individuals with the same genotype exhibit different phenotypes in different environments.
AP.B.5.6.A: Explain how chromosomal inheritance generates genetic variation in sexual reproduction.
AP.B.5.6.A.1: Segregation, independent assortment of chromosomes, and fertilization result in genetic variation in populations.
AP.B.5.6.A.2: The chromosomal basis of inheritance provides an understanding of the pattern of transmission of genes from parent to offspring.
AP.B.5.6.A.3: Certain human genetic disorders can be attributed to the inheritance of a single affected or mutated allele or specific chromosomal changes, such as nondisjunction.
AP.B.6.1.A: Describe the structures involved in passing hereditary information from one generation to the next.
AP.B.6.1.A.1: DNA, and in some cases RNA, is the primary source of heritable information.
AP.B.6.1.A.2: Genetic information is transmitted from one generation to the next through DNA or RNA.
AP.B.6.1.A.2.a: Genetic information is stored in and passed to subsequent generations through DNA molecules and, in some cases, RNA molecules.
AP.B.6.1.A.2.b: Prokaryotic organisms typically have circular chromosomes, while eukaryotic organisms typically have multiple linear chromosomes.
AP.B.6.1.A.3: Prokaryotes and eukaryotes can contain plasmids, which are small extra-chromosomal, double-stranded, circular DNA molecules.
AP.B.6.1.B: Describe the characteristics of DNA that allow it to be used as the hereditary material.
AP.B.6.1.B.1: DNA, and sometimes RNA, exhibits specific nucleotide base pairing that is conserved through evolution: adenine pairs with thymine or uracil (A-T or A-U) and cytosine pairs with guanine (C-G).
AP.B.6.1.B.1.a: Purines (G and A) have a double ring structure.
AP.B.6.1.B.1.b: Pyrimidines (C, T, and U) have a single ring structure.
AP.B.6.2.A: Describe the mechanisms by which genetic information is copied for transmission between generations.
AP.B.6.2.A.1: DNA replication ensures continuity of hereditary information.
AP.B.6.2.A.1.a: DNA is synthesized in the `5'` to `3'` direction.
AP.B.6.2.A.1.b: Replication is a semiconservative process-that is, one strand of DNA serves as the template for a new strand of complementary DNA.
AP.B.6.2.A.1.d: Topoisomerase relaxes supercoiling in front of the replication fork.
AP.B.6.2.A.1.e: DNA polymerase requires RNA primers to initiate DNA synthesis.
AP.B.6.2.A.1.f: DNA polymerase synthesizes new strands of DNA continuously on the leading strand and discontinuously on the lagging strand.
AP.B.6.2.A.1.g: Ligase joins the fragments on the lagging strand.
AP.B.6.3.A: Describe the mechanisms by which genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein.
AP.B.6.3.A.1: The sequence of the RNA bases, together with the structure of the RNA molecule, determines RNA function.
AP.B.6.3.A.1.a: mRNA molecules carry information from DNA to the ribosome.
AP.B.6.3.A.1.b: Distinct tRNA molecules bind specific amino acids and have anti-codon sequences that base pair with the mRNA. tRNA is recruited to the ribosome during translation to generate the primary peptide sequence based on the mRNA sequence.
AP.B.6.3.A.1.c: rRNA molecules are functional building blocks of ribosomes.
AP.B.6.3.A.2: Genetic information flows from a sequence of nucleotides in DNA to a sequence of bases in an mRNA molecule to a sequence of amino acids in a protein.
AP.B.6.3.A.3: RNA polymerases use a single template strand of DNA to direct the inclusion of bases in the newly formed RNA molecule. This process is known as transcription.
AP.B.6.3.A.4: The DNA strand acting as the template strand is also referred to as the noncoding strand, minus strand, or antisense strand. Selection of which DNA strand serves as the template strand depends on the gene being transcribed.
AP.B.6.3.A.5: The enzyme RNA polymerase synthesizes mRNA molecules in the `5'` to `3'` direction by reading the template DNA strand in the `3'` to `5'` direction.
AP.B.6.3.A.6: In eukaryotic cells the mRNA transcript undergoes a series of enzyme-regulated modifications.
AP.B.6.3.A.6.c: Excision of introns and splicing and retention of exons.
AP.B.6.3.A.6.d: Excision of introns and splicing and retention of exons can generate different versions of the resulting mRNA molecule; this is known as alternative splicing.
AP.B.6.4.A: Explain how the phenotype of an organism is determined by its genotype.
AP.B.6.4.A.1: Translation of the mRNA to generate a polypeptide occurs on ribosomes that are present in the cytoplasm of both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and on the rough endoplasmic reticulum of eukaryotic cells.
AP.B.6.4.A.2: In prokaryotic organisms, translation of the mRNA molecule occurs while it is being transcribed.
AP.B.6.4.A.3: Translation involves energy and many sequential steps, including initiation, elongation, and termination.
AP.B.6.4.A.4: The salient features of translation include.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.a: Translation is initiated when the rRNA in the ribosome interacts with the mRNA at the start codon.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.b: The sequence of nucleotides on the mRNA is read in triplets called codons.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.c: Each codon encodes a specific amino acid, which can be deduced by using a genetic code chart. Many amino acids are encoded by more than one codon.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.d: Nearly all living organisms use the same genetic code, which is evidence for the common ancestry of all living organisms.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.e: tRNA brings the correct amino acid to the correct place specified by the codon on the mRNA.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.f: The amino acid is transferred to the growing polypeptide chain.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.g: The process continues along the mRNA until a stop codon is reached.
AP.B.6.4.A.4.h: The process terminates by release of the newly synthesized polypeptide/protein.
AP.B.6.4.A.5: Genetic information in retroviruses is a special case and has an alternate flow of information: from RNA to DNA, made possible by reverse transcriptase, an enzyme that copies the viral RNA genome into DNA. This DNA integrates into the host genome and becomes transcribed and translated for the assembly of new viral progeny.
AP.B.6.5.A: Describe the types of interactions that regulate gene expression.
AP.B.6.5.A.1: Regulatory sequences are stretches of DNA that interact with regulatory proteins to control transcription.
AP.B.6.5.A.2: Epigenetic changes can affect gene expression through reversible modifications of DNA or histones.
AP.B.6.5.A.3: The phenotype of a cell or organism is determined by the combination of genes that are expressed and the levels at which they are expressed.
AP.B.6.5.A.3.a: Observable cell differentiation results from the expression of genes for tissue-specific proteins.
AP.B.6.5.A.3.b: INduction of transcription factors during development results in sequential gene expression.
AP.B.6.5.B: Explain how the location of regulatory sequences relates to their function.
AP.B.6.5.B.1: Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes have groups of genes that are coordinately regulated.
AP.B.6.5.B.1.a: In prokaryotes, groups of genes called operons are transcribed in a single mRNA molecule. The lac operon is an example of an inducible system.
AP.B.6.5.B.1.b: In eukaryotes, groups of genes may be influenced by the same transcription factors to coordinately regulate expression.
AP.B.6.6.A: Explain how the binding of transcription factors to promoter regions affects gene expression and/or the phenotype of the organism.
AP.B.6.6.A.1: Promoters are DNA sequences upstream of the transcription start site where RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind to initiate transcription.
AP.B.6.6.A.2: Negative regulatory molecules inhibit gene expression by binding to DNA and blocking transcription.
AP.B.6.6.B: Explain the connection between the regulation of gene expression and phenotypic differences in cells and organisms.
AP.B.6.6.B.1: Gene regulation results in differential gene expression and influences cell products and function.
AP.B.6.6.B.2: Certain small RNA molecules have roles in regulating gene expression.
AP.B.6.7.A: Describe the various types of mutation.
AP.B.6.7.A.1: Changes in genotype can result in changes in phenotype.
AP.B.6.7.A.1.a: The function and amount of gene products determine the phenotype of organisms.
AP.B.6.7.A.1.a.i: The normal function of the genes and gene products collectively comprises the normal function of organisms.
AP.B.6.7.A.1.a.ii: Disruptions in genes and gene products cause new phenotypes.
AP.B.6.7.A.2: Alterations in a DNA sequence can lead to changes in the type or amount of the protein produced and the consequent phenotype. DNA mutations can be positive, negative, or neutral based on the effect or the lack of effect they have on the resulting nucleic acid or protein and the phenotypes that are conferred by the protein.
AP.B.6.7.B: Explain how changes in genotype may result in changes in phenotype.
AP.B.6.7.B.1: Errors in DNA replication or DNA repair mechanisms, and external factors, including radiation and reactive chemicals, can cause random mutations in the DNA.
AP.B.6.7.B.1.a: Whether a mutation is detrimental, beneficial, or neutral depends on the environmental context.
AP.B.6.7.B.1.b: Mutations are the primary source of genetic variation.
AP.B.6.7.B.2: Errors in mitosis or meiosis can result in changes in phenotype.
AP.B.6.7.B.2.a: Changes in chromosome number often result in new phenotypes, including sterility caused by triploidy, and increased vigor of other polyploids.
AP.B.6.7.B.2.b: Changes in chromosome number often result in human disorders with developmental limitations, including Down syndrome/Trisomy 21 and Turner syndrome.
AP.B.6.7.C: Explain how alterations in DNA sequences contribute to variation that can be subject to natural selection.
AP.B.6.7.C.1: Changes in genotype may affect phenotypes that are subject to natural selection. Genetic changes that enhance survival and reproduction can be selected for by environmental conditions.
AP.B.6.7.C.1.a: The horizontal acquisitions of genetic information primarily in prokaryotes via transformation (uptake of naked DNA), transduction (viral transmission of genetic information), conjugation (cell-to-cell transfer of DNA), and transposition (movement of DNA segments within and between DNA molecules) increase variation.
AP.B.6.7.C.1.b: Related viruses can combine/recombine genetic information if they infect the same host cell.
AP.B.6.7.C.1.c: Reproduction processes that increase genetic variation are evolutionarily conserved and are shared by various organisms.
AP.B.6.8.A: Explain the use of genetic engineering techniques in analyzing or manipulating DNA.
AP.B.6.8.A.1: Genetic engineering techniques can be used to analyze and manipulate DNA and RNA.
AP.B.6.8.A.1.a: Electrophoresis separates molecules according to size and charge.
AP.B.6.8.A.1.b: During polymerase chain reaction (PCR), DNA fragments are amplified.
AP.B.6.8.A.1.c: Bacterial transformation introduces DNA into bacterial cells.
AP.B.6.8.A.1.d: DNA sequencing determines the order of nucleotides in a DNA molecule.
AP.B.7.1.A: Describe the causes of natural selection.
AP.B.7.1.A.1: Natural selection is a major mechanism of evolution.
AP.B.7.1.A.2: According to Darwin's theory of natural selection, competition for limited resources results in differential survival. Individuals with more favorable phenotypes are more likely to survive and produce more offspring, thus passing traits to subsequent generations.
AP.B.7.1.B: Explain how natural selection affects populations.
AP.B.7.1.B.1: Evolutionary fitness is measured by reproductive success.
AP.B.7.1.B.2: Biotic and abiotic environments can be more or less stable/fluctuating, and this affects the rate and direction of evolution; different genetic variations can be selected in each generation.
AP.B.7.2.A: Describe the importance of phenotypic variation in a population.
AP.B.7.2.A.1: Natural selection acts on phenotypic variations in populations.
AP.B.7.2.A.2: Environments change and apply selective pressures to populations.
AP.B.7.2.A.3: Some phenotypic variations significantly increase or decrease fitness of the organism in particular environments.
AP.B.7.3.A: Explain how humans can affect diversity within a population.
AP.B.7.3.A.1: Through artificial selection, humans affect variation in other species.
AP.B.7.3.B: Explain the relationship between changes in the environment and evolutionary changes in the population.
AP.B.7.3.B.1: Convergent evolution occurs when similar selective pressures result in similar phenotypic adaptations in different populations or species.
AP.B.7.4.A: Explain how random occurrences affect the genetic makeup of a population.
AP.B.7.4.A.1: Evolution is also driven by random occurrences.
AP.B.7.4.A.1.a: Mutation is a random process that contributes to evolution.
AP.B.7.4.A.1.b: Genetic drift is a nonselective process occurring in small populations.
AP.B.7.4.B: Describe the role of random processes in the evolution of specific populations.
AP.B.7.4.B.1: Reduction of genetic variation within a given population can increase the differences between populations of the same species.
AP.B.7.4.C: Describe the change in the genetic makeup of a population over time.
AP.B.7.4.C.1: Mutation results in genetic variation, which provides phenotypes on which natural selection acts.
AP.B.7.5.A: Describe the conditions under which allele and genotype frequencies will change in populations.
AP.B.7.5.A.1: Hardy-Weinberg is a model for describing and predicting allele frequencies in a nonevolving population. Conditions for a population or an allele to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium are-(1) a large population size, (2) absence of migration, (3) no net mutations, (4) random mating, and (5) absence of selection. These conditions are seldom met, but they provide a valuable null hypothesis.
AP.B.7.5.A.2: Allele frequencies in a population can be calculated from genotype frequencies.
AP.B.7.5.B: Explain the impacts on the population if any of the conditions of Hardy-Weinberg are not met.
AP.B.7.5.B.1: Changes in allele frequencies provide evidence for the occurrence of evolution in a population.
AP.B.7.5.B.2: Small populations are more susceptible to random environmental impact than large populations.
AP.B.7.6.A: Describe the types of data that provide evidence for evolution.
AP.B.7.6.A.1: Evolution is supported by scientific evidence from many disciplines (geographical, geological, physical, biochemical, and mathematical data).
AP.B.7.6.B: Explain how morphological, biochemical, and geological data provide evidence that organisms have changed over time.
AP.B.7.6.B.1: Molecular, morphological, and genetic evidence from extant and extinct organisms adds to our understanding of evolution.
AP.B.7.6.B.1.a: a. Fossils can be dated by a variety of methods. These include:
AP.B.7.6.B.1.a.i: The age of the rocks where a fossil is found.
AP.B.7.6.B.1.a.ii: The rate of decay of isotopes including carbon-14.
AP.B.7.6.B.1.b: Morphological homologies, including vestigial structures, represent features shared by common ancestry.
AP.B.7.6.B.2: A comparison of DNA nucleotide sequences and/or protein amino acid sequences provides evidence for evolution and common ancestry.
AP.B.7.6.C: Describe the fundamental molecular and cellular features shared across all domains of life, which provide evidence of common ancestry.
AP.B.7.6.C.1: Many fundamental molecular and cellular features and processes are conserved across organisms.
AP.B.7.6.C.2: Structural and functional evidence supports the relatedness of organisms in all domains.
AP.B.7.7.A: Describe structural and functional evidence on cellular and molecular levels that provides evidence for the common ancestry of all eukaryotes.
AP.B.7.7.A.1: Structural evidence indicates common ancestry of all eukaryotes.
AP.B.7.8.A: Explain how evolution is an ongoing process in all living organisms.
AP.B.7.8.A.1: Populations of organisms continue to evolve.
AP.B.7.8.A.2: All species have evolved and continue to evolve.
AP.B.7.8.A.2.b: Continuous change in the fossil record.
AP.B.7.8.A.2.c: Evolution of resistance to antibiotics, pesticides, herbicides, or chemotherapy drugs.
AP.B.7.8.A.2.d: Pathogens evolve and cause emergent diseases.
AP.B.7.9.A: Describe the types of evidence that can be used to infer an evolutionary relationship.
AP.B.7.9.A.1: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms show evolutionary relationships among lineages.
AP.B.7.9.A.1.a: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms both show relationships between lineages, but phylogenetic trees show the amount of change over time calibrated by fossils or a molecular clock.
AP.B.7.9.A.1.b: Traits that are either gained or lost during evolution can be used to construct phylogenetic trees and cladograms.
AP.B.7.9.A.1.b.i: Shared characters are present in more than one lineage.
AP.B.7.9.A.1.b.ii: Shared, derived characters indicate common ancestry and are informative for the construction of phylogenetic trees and cladograms.
AP.B.7.9.A.1.b.iii: The out-group represents the lineage that is least closely related to the remainder of the organisms in the phylogenetic tree or cladogram.
AP.B.7.9.A.1.c: Molecular data typically provide more accurate and reliable evidence than morphological traits in the construction of phylogenetic trees or cladograms.
AP.B.7.9.B: Explain how a phylogenetic tree and/or cladogram can be used to infer evolutionary relatedness.
AP.B.7.9.B.1: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms can be used to illustrate speciation that has occurred. The nodes on a tree represent the most recent common ancestor of any two groups or lineages.
AP.B.7.9.B.2: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms can be constructed from morphological similarities of living or fossil species and from DNA and protein sequence similarities.
AP.B.7.9.B.3: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms represent hypotheses and are constantly being revised, based on evidence.
AP.B.7.10.A: Describe the conditions under which new species may arise.
AP.B.7.10.A.1: Speciation may occur when two populations become reproductively isolated from each other.
AP.B.7.10.A.2: The biological species concept provides a commonly used definition of species for sexually reproducing organisms. It states that species can be defined as a group capable of interbreeding and exchanging genetic information to produce viable, fertile offspring.
AP.B.7.10.B: Describe the rate of evolution and speciation under different ecological conditions.
AP.B.7.10.B.1: Punctuated equilibrium is when evolution occurs rapidly after a long period of stasis. Gradualism is when evolution occurs slowly over hundreds of thousands or millions of years.
AP.B.7.10.B.2: Divergent evolution occurs when adaptation to new habitats results in phenotypic diversification. Speciation rates can be especially rapid during times of adaptive radiation as new habitats become available.
AP.B.7.10.C: Explain the processes and mechanisms that drive speciation.
AP.B.7.10.C.1: Speciation results in diversity of life forms.
AP.B.7.10.C.2: Speciation may be sympatric or allopatric.
AP.B.7.10.C.3: Various prezygotic and postzygotic mechanisms can maintain reproductive isolation and prevent gene flow between populations.
AP.B.7.11.A: Describe factors that lead to the extinction of a population.
AP.B.7.11.A.1: Extinctions have occurred throughout Earth's history.
AP.B.7.11.A.2: Extinction rates can be rapid during times of ecological stress.
AP.B.7.11.B: Explain how the risk of extinction is affected by changes in the environment.
AP.B.7.11.B.1: Human activity can drive changes in ecosystems that cause extinctions.
AP.B.7.11.C: Explain species diversity in an ecosystem as a function of speciation and extinction rates.
AP.B.7.11.C.1: The amount of diversity in an ecosystem can be determined by the rate of speciation and the rate of extinction.
AP.B.7.11.D: Explain how extinction can make new environments available for adaptive radiation.
AP.B.7.11.D.1: Extinction provides newly available niches that can then be exploited by different species.
AP.B.7.12.A: Explain how the genetic diversity of a species or population affects its ability to withstand environmental pressures.
AP.B.7.12.A.1: The level of variation in a population affects population dynamics.
AP.B.7.12.A.1.a: Population ability to respond to changes in the environment is influenced by genetic diversity. Species and populations with little genetic diversity are at risk of decline or extinction.
AP.B.7.12.A.1.b: Genetically diverse populations are more resilient to environmental perturbation because they are more likely to contain individuals who can withstand the environmental pressure.
AP.B.7.12.A.1.c: Alleles that are adaptive in one environmental condition may be deleterious in another because of different selective pressures.
AP.B.7.13.A: Describe the scientific evidence that provides support for models of the origin of life on Earth.
AP.B.7.13.A.1: Several hypotheses about the origin of life on Earth are supported with scientific evidence.
AP.B.7.13.A.1.a: Geological evidence provides support for models of the origin of life on Earth.
AP.B.7.13.A.1.a.i: Earth formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago (bya). The environment was too hostile for life until 3.9 bya, and the earliest fossil evidence for life dates to 3.5 bya. Taken together, this evidence provides a plausible range of dates when the origin of life could have occurred.
AP.B.7.13.A.1.b: There are several models about the origin of life on Earth.
AP.B.7.13.A.1.b.i: Primitive Earth provided inorganic precursors from which organic molecules could have been synthesized because of the presence of available free energy and the absence of a significant quantity of atmospheric oxygen (`text(O)_2`).
AP.B.7.13.A.1.b.ii: Organic molecules could have been transported to Earth by a meteorite or other celestial event.
AP.B.7.13.A.1.c: Chemical experiments have shown that it is possible to form complex organic molecules from inorganic molecules in the absence of life.
AP.B.7.13.A.1.c.i: Organic molecules/monomers served as building blocks for the formation of more complex molecules, including amino acids and nucleotides.
AP.B.7.13.A.1.c.ii: The joining of these monomers produced polymers with the ability to replicate, store, and transfer information.
AP.B.7.13.A.2: The RNA World Hypothesis proposes that RNA could have been the earliest genetic material.
AP.B.8.1.A: Explain how the behavioral and/or physiological response of an organism is related to changes in internal or external environment.
AP.B.8.1.A.1: Organisms respond to changes in their environment through behavioral and physiological mechanisms.
AP.B.8.1.A.2: Organisms exchange information with one another in response to internal changes and external cues, which can change behavior.
AP.B.8.1.B: Explain how the behavioral responses of organisms affect their overall fitness and may contribute to the success of the population.
AP.B.8.1.B.1: Individuals can act on information and communicate it to others.
AP.B.8.1.B.2.a: Organisms have a variety of signaling behaviors that produce changes in the behavior of other organisms and can result in differential reproductive success.
AP.B.8.1.B.2.b: Animals use visual, audible, tactile, electrical, and chemical signals to indicate dominance, find food, establish territory, and ensure reproductive success.
AP.B.8.1.B.3: Responses to information and communication of information are vital to natural selection and evolution.
AP.B.8.1.B.3.a: Natural selection favors innate and learned behaviors that increase survival and reproductive fitness.
AP.B.8.1.B.3.b: Cooperative behavior tends to increase the fitness of the individual and the survival of the population.
AP.B.8.2.A: Describe the strategies organisms use to acquire and use energy.
AP.B.8.2.A.1: Organisms use energy to maintain organization, grow, and reproduce.
AP.B.8.2.A.1.a: Organisms use different strategies to regulate body temperature and metabolism.
AP.B.8.2.A.1.a.i: Endotherms use thermal energy generated by metabolism to maintain homeostatic body temperatures.
AP.B.8.2.A.1.a.ii: Ectotherms lack efficient internal mechanisms for maintaining body temperature, though they may regulate their temperature behaviorally by moving into the sun or shade or by aggregating with other individuals.
AP.B.8.2.A.1.b: Different organisms use various reproductive strategies in response to energy availability.
AP.B.8.2.A.1.c: There is a relationship between metabolic rate per unit body mass and the size of multicellular organisms-generally, the smaller the organism, the higher the metabolic rate.
AP.B.8.2.A.1.d: A net gain in energy results in energy storage or the growth of an organism.
AP.B.8.2.A.1.e: A net loss of energy results in loss of mass and, ultimately, the death of an organism.
AP.B.8.2.B: Explain how changes in energy availability affect populations and ecosystems.
AP.B.8.2.B.1: Changes in energy availability can result in changes in population size.
AP.B.8.2.B.2: Changes in energy availability can result in disruptions to an ecosystem.
AP.B.8.2.B.2.a: A change in energy resources such as sunlight can affect the number and size ofthe trophic levels.
AP.B.8.2.B.2.b: A change in the producer level can affect the number and size of other trophic levels.
AP.B.8.2.C: Explain how the activities of autotrophs and heterotrophs enable the flow of energy within an ecosystem.
AP.B.8.2.C.1: Autotrophs capture energy from physical or chemical sources in the environment.
AP.B.8.2.C.1.a: Photosynthetic organisms capture energy present in sunlight.
AP.B.8.2.C.1.b: Chemosynthetic organisms capture energy from small inorganic molecules present in their environment, and this process can occur in the absence of oxygen.
AP.B.8.2.C.2: Heterotrophs capture energy present in carbon compounds produced by other organisms.
AP.B.8.2.C.2.a: Heterotrophs may metabolize carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins as sources of energy by hydrolysis.
AP.B.8.3.A: Describe factors that influence growth dynamics of populations.
AP.B.8.3.A.1: Populations comprise individual organisms that interact with one another and with the environment in complex ways.
AP.B.8.3.A.2: Many adaptations in organisms are related to obtaining and using energy and matter in a particular environment.
AP.B.8.3.A.2.a: Population growth dynamics depend on a number of factors.
AP.B.8.4.A: Explain how the density of a population affects and is determined by resource availability in the environment.
AP.B.8.4.A.1: A population can produce a density of individuals that exceeds the system's resource availability.
AP.B.8.4.A.2: As limits to growth due to density-dependent and density-independent factors are imposed, a logistic growth model generally ensues.
AP.B.8.5.A: Describe the structure of a community according to its species composition and diversity.
AP.B.8.5.A.1: The structure of a community is measured and described in terms of species composition and species diversity.
AP.B.8.5.B: Explain how interactions within and among populations influence community structure.
AP.B.8.5.B.1: Communities change over time depending on interactions between populations.
AP.B.8.5.B.2: Interactions among populations determine how they access energy and matter within a community.
AP.B.8.5.B.3: Relationships among interacting populations can be characterized by positive and negative effects and can be modeled. Examples include predator/prey interactions, trophic cascades, and niche partitioning.
AP.B.8.5.B.4: Competition, predation, and symbioses, including parasitism, mutualism, and commensalism, can drive population dynamics.
AP.B.8.5.C: Explain how community structure is related to energy availability in the environment.
AP.B.8.5.C.1: Cooperation or coordination between organisms, populations, and species can result in enhanced movement of, or access to, matter and energy.
AP.B.8.6.A: Describe the relationship between ecosystem diversity and its resilience to changes in the environment.
AP.B.8.6.A.1: Natural and artificial ecosystems with fewer component parts and with little diversity among the parts are often less resilient to changes in the environment.
AP.B.8.6.A.2: Keystone species, producers, and essential abiotic and biotic factors contribute to maintaining the diversity of an ecosystem.
AP.B.8.6.B: Explain how the addition or removal of any component of an ecosystem will affect its overall short-term and long-term structure.
AP.B.8.6.B.1: The diversity of species within an ecosystem may influence the organization of the ecosystem.
AP.B.8.6.B.2: The effects of keystone species on the ecosystem are disproportionate relative to their abundance in the ecosystem, and when they are removed from the ecosystem, the ecosystem often collapses.
AP.B.8.7.A: Explain the interaction between the environment and random or preexisting variations in populations.
AP.B.8.7.A.1: An adaptation is a genetic variation that is favored by selection and is manifested as a trait that provides an advantage to an organism in a particular environment.
AP.B.8.7.A.2: Mutations are random and are not directed by specific environmental pressures.
AP.B.8.7.B: Explain how invasive species affect ecosystem dynamics.
AP.B.8.7.B.1: The intentional or unintentional introduction of an invasive species can allow the species to exploit a new niche free of predators or competitors or to outcompete other organisms for resources.
AP.B.8.7.B.2: The availability of resources can result in uncontrolled population growth and ecological changes.
AP.B.8.7.C: Describe human activities that lead to changes in ecosystem structure and/or dynamics.
AP.B.8.7.C.1: The distribution of local and global ecosystems changes over time.
AP.B.8.7.C.2: Human impact accelerates change at local and global levels.
AP.B.8.7.C.2.a: The introduction of new diseases can devastate native species.
AP.B.8.7.C.2.b: Habitat change can occur because of human activity.
AP.B.8.7.D: Explain how geological and meteorological activity leads to changes in ecosystem structure and/or dynamics.
AP.B.8.7.D.1: Geological and meteorological events affect habitat change and ecosystem distribution. Biogeographical studies illustrate these changes.
AP.Ca.1.1: Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur At An Instant?
AP.Ca.1.1.A: Interpret the rate of change at an instant in terms of average rates of change over intervals containing that instant.
AP.Ca.1.1.A.1: Calculus uses limits to understand and model dynamic change.
AP.Ca.1.1.A.2: Because an average rate of change divides the change in one variable by the change in another, the average rate of change is undefined at a point where the change in the independent variable would be zero.
AP.Ca.1.1.A.3: The limit concept allows us to define instantaneous rate of change in terms of average rates of change.
AP.Ca.1.2.A: Represent limits analytically using correct notation.
AP.Ca.1.2.A.1: Given a function `f`, the limit of `f(x)` as `x` approaches `c` is a real number `R` if `f(x)` can be made arbitrarily close to `R` by taking `x` sufficiently close to `c` (but not equal to `c`). If the limit exists and is a real number, then the common notation is `lim_(x->c)f(x)=R`.
AP.Ca.1.2.B: Interpret limits expressed in analytic notation.
AP.Ca.1.2.B.1: A limit can be expressed in multiple ways, including graphically, numerically, and analytically.
AP.Ca.1.3.A.1: The concept of a limit includes one sided limits.
AP.Ca.1.3.A.2: Graphical information about a function can be used to estimate limits.
AP.Ca.1.3.A.3: Because of issues of scale, graphical representations of functions may miss important function behavior.
AP.Ca.1.3.A.4: A limit might not exist for some functions at particular values of `x`. Some ways that the limit might not exist are if the function is unbounded, if the function is oscillating near this value, or if the limit from the left does not equal the limit from the right.
AP.Ca.1.4.A.1: Numerical information can be used to estimate limits.
AP.Ca.1.5: Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties Of Limits
AP.Ca.1.5.A: Determine the limits of functions using limit theorems.
AP.Ca.1.5.A.1: One-sided limits can be determined analytically or graphically.
AP.Ca.1.5.A.2: Limits of sums, differences, products, quotients, and composite functions can be found using limit theorems.
AP.Ca.1.6.A: Determine the limits of functions using equivalent expressions for the function or the squeeze theorem.
AP.Ca.1.6.A.1: It may be necessary or helpful to rearrange expressions into equivalent forms before evaluating limits.
AP.Ca.1.8: Determining Limits Using The Squeeze Theorem
AP.Ca.1.8.A: Determine the limits of functions using equivalent expressions for the function or the squeeze theorem.
AP.Ca.1.8.A.1: The limit of a function may be found by using the squeeze theorem.
AP.Ca.1.10.A: Justify conclusions about continuity at a point using the definition.
AP.Ca.1.10.A.1: Types of discontinuities include removable discontinuities, jump discontinuities, and discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes.
AP.Ca.1.11.A: Justify conclusions about continuity at a point using the definition.
AP.Ca.1.11.A.1: A function `f` is continuous at `x=c` provided that `f(c)` exists, `lim_(x->c)f(x)` exists, and `lim_(x->c)f(x)=f(c)`.
AP.Ca.1.12.A: Determine intervals over which a function is continuous.
AP.Ca.1.12.A.1: A function is continuous on an interval if the function is continuous at each point in the interval.
AP.Ca.1.12.A.2: Polynomial, rational, power, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous on all points in their domains.
AP.Ca.1.13.A: Determine values of `x` or solve for parameters that make discontinuous functions continuous, if possible.
AP.Ca.1.13.A.1: If the limit of a function exists at a discontinuity in its graph, then it is possible to remove the discontinuity by defining or redefining the value of the function at that point, so it equals the value of the limit of the function as `x` approaches that point.
AP.Ca.1.13.A.2: In order for a piecewise-defined function to be continuous at a boundary to the partition of its domain, the value of the expression defining the function on one side of the boundary must equal the value of the expression defining the other side of the boundary, as well as the value of the function at the boundary.
AP.Ca.1.14.A: Interpret the behavior of functions using limits involving infinity.
AP.Ca.1.14.A.1: The concept of a limit can be extended to include infinite limits.
AP.Ca.1.14.A.2: Asymptotic and unbounded behavior of functions can be described and explained using limits.
AP.Ca.1.15: Connecting Limits At Infinity & Horizontal Asymptotes
AP.Ca.1.15.A: Interpret the behavior of functions using limits involving infinity.
AP.Ca.1.15.A.1: The concept of a limit can be extended to include limits at infinity.
AP.Ca.1.15.A.2: Limits at infinity describe end behavior.
AP.Ca.1.15.A.3: Relative magnitudes of functions and their rates of change can be compared using limits.
AP.Ca.1.16: Working With The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
AP.Ca.1.16.A: Explain the behavior of a function on an interval using the Intermediate Value Theorem.
AP.Ca.1.16.A.1: If `f` is a continuous function on the closed interval `[a,b]` and `d` is a number between `f(a)` and `f(b)`, then the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that there is at least one number `c` between `a` and `b`, such that `f(c)=d`.
AP.Ca.2.1: Defining Average & Instantaneous Rates Of Change At A Point
AP.Ca.2.1.A: Determine average rates of change using difference quotients.
AP.Ca.2.1.A.1: The difference quotients `(f(a+h)-f(a))/h` and `(f(x)-f(a))/(x-a)` express the average rate change of a function over an interval.
AP.Ca.2.1.B: Represent the derivative of a function as the limit of a difference quotient.
AP.Ca.2.1.B.1: The instantaneous rate of change of a function at `x=a` can be expressed by `lim_(h->0)(f(a+h)-f(a))/h` or `lim_(x->a)(f(x)-f(a))/(x-a)`, provided the limit exists. These are equivalent forms of the definition of the derivative and are denoted `f'(a)`.
AP.Ca.2.2: Defining The Derivative Of A Function & Using Derivative Notation
AP.Ca.2.2.A: Represent the derivative of a function as the limit of a difference quotient.
AP.Ca.2.2.A.1: The derivative of `f` is the function whose value at `x` is `lim_(h->0)(f(x+h)-f(x))/h`, provided this limit exists.
AP.Ca.2.2.A.2: For `y=f(x)`, notations for the derivative include `dy/dx`, `f'(x)`, and `y'`.
AP.Ca.2.2.A.3: The derivative can be represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally.
AP.Ca.2.2.B: Determine the equation of a line tangent to a curve at a given point.
AP.Ca.2.2.B.1: The derivative of a function at a point is the slope of the line tangent to a graph of the function at that point.
AP.Ca.2.3: Estimating Derivatives Of A Function At A Point
AP.Ca.2.3.A.1: The derivative at a point can be estimated from information given in tables or graphs.
AP.Ca.2.3.A.2: Technology can be used to calculate or estimate the value of a derivative of a function at a point.
AP.Ca.2.4: Connecting Differentiability & Continuity: Determining When Derivatives Do & Do Not Exist
AP.Ca.2.4.A: Explain the relationship between differentiability and continuity.
AP.Ca.2.4.A.1: If a function is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point. In particular, if a point is not in the domain of `f`, then it is not in the domain of `f'`.
AP.Ca.2.4.A.2: A continuous function may fail to be differentiable at a point in its domain.
AP.Ca.2.5.A.1: Direct application of the definition of the derivative and specific rules can be used to calculate the derivative for functions of the form `f(x)=x'`.
AP.Ca.2.6: Derivative Rules: Constant, Sum, Difference & Constant Multiple
AP.Ca.2.6.A.1: Sums, differences, and constant multiples of functions can be differentiated using derivative rules.
AP.Ca.2.6.A.2: The power rule combined with sum, difference, and constant multiple properties can be used to find the derivatives for polynomial functions.
AP.Ca.2.7.A.1: Specific rules can be used to find the derivatives for sine, cosine, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
AP.Ca.2.7.B: Interpret a limit as a definition of a derivative.
AP.Ca.2.7.B.1: In some cases, recognizing an expression for the definition of the derivative of a function whose derivative is known offers a strategy for determining a limit.
AP.Ca.2.8.A: Calculate derivatives of products and quotients of differentiable functions.
AP.Ca.2.8.A.1: Derivatives of products of differentiable functions can be found using the product rule.
AP.Ca.2.9.A: Calculate derivatives of products and quotients of differentiable functions.
AP.Ca.2.9.A.1: Derivatives of quotients of differentiable functions can be found using the quotient rule.
AP.Ca.2.10: Finding The Derivatives of Tangent, Cotangent, Secant & Cosecant Functions
AP.Ca.2.10.A: Calculate derivatives of products and quotients of differentiable functions.
AP.Ca.2.10.A.1: Rearranging tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant functions using identities allows differentiation using derivative rules.
AP.Ca.3.1.A: Calculate derivatives of compositions of differentiable functions.
AP.Ca.3.1.A.1: The chain rule provides a way to differentiate composite functions.
AP.Ca.3.2.A: Calculate derivatives of implicitly defined functions.
AP.Ca.3.2.A.1: The chain rule is the basis for implicit differentiation.
AP.Ca.3.3.A: Calculate derivatives of inverse and inverse trigonometric functions.
AP.Ca.3.3.A.1: The chain rule and definition of an inverse function can be used to find the derivative of an inverse function, provided the derivative exists.
AP.Ca.3.4.A: Calculate derivatives of inverse and inverse trigonometric functions.
AP.Ca.3.4.A.1: The chain rule applied with the definition of an inverse function, or the formula for the derivative of an inverse function, can be used to find the derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions.
AP.Ca.3.6.A: Determine higher order derivatives of a function.
AP.Ca.3.6.A.1: Differentiating `f'` produces the second derivative `f''`, provided the derivative of `f'` exists; repeating this process produces higher-order derivatives of `f'`.
AP.Ca.3.6.A.2: Higher-order derivatives are represented with a variety of notations. For `y=f(x)`, notations for the second derivative include `(d^2y)/(dx^2)`, `f''(x)`, and `y''`. Higher-order derivatives can be denoted `(d''y)/(dx'')` or `f^((n))(x)`.
AP.Ca.4.1: Interpreting The Meaning Of The Derivative In Context
AP.Ca.4.1.A: Interpret the meaning of a derivative in context.
AP.Ca.4.1.A.1: The derivative of a function can be interpreted as the instantaneous rate of change with respect to its independent variable.
AP.Ca.4.1.A.2: The derivative can be used to express information about rates of change in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.4.1.A.3: The unit for `f'(x)` is the unit for `f` divided by the unit for `x`.
AP.Ca.4.2: Straight-Line Motion: Connecting Position, Velocity & Acceleration
AP.Ca.4.2.A: Calculate rates of change in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.4.2.A.1: The derivative can be used to solve rectilinear motion problems involving position, speed, velocity, and acceleration.
AP.Ca.4.3: Rates of Change In Applied Contexts Other Than Motion
AP.Ca.4.3.A: Interpret rates of change in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.4.3.A.1: The derivative can be used to solve problems involving rates of change in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.4.4.A: Calculate related rates in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.4.4.A.1: The chain rule is the basis for differentiating variables in a related rates problem with respect to the same independent variable.
AP.Ca.4.4.A.2: Other differentiation rules, such as the product rule and the quotient rule, may also be necessary to differentiate all variables with respect to the same independent variable.
AP.Ca.4.5.A: Interpret related rates in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.4.5.A.1: The derivative can be used to solve related rates problems; that is, finding a rate at which one quantity is changing by relating it to other quantities whose rates of change are known.
AP.Ca.4.6: Approximating Values Of A Function Using Local Linearity & Linearization
AP.Ca.4.6.A: Approximate a value on a curve using the equation of a tangent line.
AP.Ca.4.6.A.1: The tangent line is the graph of a locally linear approximation of the function near the point of tangency.
AP.Ca.4.6.A.2: For a tangent line approximation, the function's behavior near the point of tangency may determine whether a tangent line value is an underestimate or an overestimate of the corresponding function value.
AP.Ca.4.7: Using L'Hospital's Rule For Determining Limits Of Indeterminate Forms
AP.Ca.4.7.A: Determine limits of functions that result in indeterminate forms.
AP.Ca.4.7.A.1: When the ratio of two functions tends to `0/0` or `oo/oo` in the limit, such forms are said to be indeterminate.
AP.Ca.4.7.A.2: Limits of the indeterminate forms `0/0` or `oo/oo` may be evaluated using L'Hospital's Rule.
AP.Ca.5.1.A: Justify conclusions about functions by applying the Mean Value Theorem over an interval.
AP.Ca.5.1.A.1: If a function `f` is continuous over the interval `[a,b]` and differentiable over the interval `(a,b)`, then the Mean Value Theorem guarantees a point within that open interval where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change over the interval.
AP.Ca.5.2: Extreme Value Theorem, Global Versus Local Extrema & Critical Points
AP.Ca.5.2.A: Justify conclusions about functions by applying the Extreme Value Theorem.
AP.Ca.5.2.A.1: If a function `f` is continuous over the interval `(a,b)`, then the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that `f` has at least one minimum value and at least one maximum value on `[a,b]`.
AP.Ca.5.2.A.2: A point on a function where the first derivative equals zero or fails to exist is a critical point of the function.
AP.Ca.5.2.A.3: All local (relative) extrema occur at critical points of a function, though not all critical points are local extrema.
AP.Ca.5.3: Determining Intervals On Which A Function Is Increasing Or Decreasing
AP.Ca.5.3.A: Justify conclusions about the behavior of a function based on the behavior of its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.3.A.1: The first derivative of a function can provide information about the function and its graph, including intervals where the function is increasing or decreasing.
AP.Ca.5.4: Using The First Derivative Test To Determine Relative (Local) Extrema
AP.Ca.5.4.A: Justify conclusions about the behavior of a function based on the behavior of its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.4.A.1: The first derivative of a function can determine the location of relative (local) extrema of the function.
AP.Ca.5.5: Using The Candidates Test To Determine Absolute (Global) Extrema
AP.Ca.5.5.A: Justify conclusions about the behavior of a function based on the behavior of its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.5.A.1: Absolute (global) extrema of a function on a closed interval can only occur at critical points or at endpoints.
AP.Ca.5.6: Determining Concavity Of Functions Over Their Domains
AP.Ca.5.6.A: Justify conclusions about the behavior of a function based on the behavior of its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.6.A.1: The graph of a function is concave up (down) on an open interval if the function's derivative is increasing (decreasing) on that interval.
AP.Ca.5.6.A.2: The second derivative of a function provides information about the function and its graph, including intervals of upward or downward concavity.
AP.Ca.5.6.A.3: The second derivative of a function may be used to locate points of inflection for the graph of the original function.
AP.Ca.5.7: Using The Second Derivative Test To Determine Extrema
AP.Ca.5.7.A: Justify conclusions about the behavior of a function based on the behavior of its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.7.A.1: The second derivative of a function may determine whether a critical point is the location of a relative (local) maximum or minimum.
AP.Ca.5.7.A.2: When a continuous function has only one critical point on an interval on its domain and the critical point corresponds to a relative (local) extremum of the function on the interval, then that critical point also corresponds to the absolute (global) extremum of the function on the interval.
AP.Ca.5.8: Sketching Graphs Of Functions & Their Derivatives
AP.Ca.5.8.A: Justify conclusions about the behavior of a function based on the behavior of its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.8.A.1: Key features of functions and their derivatives can be identified and related to their graphical, numerical, and analytical representations.
AP.Ca.5.8.A.2: Graphical, numerical, and analytical information from `f'` and `f''` can be used to predict and explain the behavior of `f`.
AP.Ca.5.9: Connecting A Function, Its First Derivative & Its Second Derivative
AP.Ca.5.9.A: Justify conclusions about the behavior of a function based on the behavior of its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.9.A.1: Key features of the graphs of `f`, `f'`, and `f''` are related to one another.
AP.Ca.5.10.A: Calculate minimum and maximum values in applied contexts or analysis of functions.
AP.Ca.5.10.A.1: The derivative can be used to solve optimization problems; that is, finding a minimum or maximum value of a function on a given interval.
AP.Ca.5.11.A: Interpret minimum and maximum values calculated in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.5.11.A.1: Minimum and maximum values of a function take on specific meanings in applied contexts.
AP.Ca.5.12.A: Determine critical points of implicit relations.
AP.Ca.5.12.A.1: A point on an implicit relation where the first derivative equals zero or does not exist is a critical point of the function.
AP.Ca.5.12.B: Justify conclusions about the behavior of an implicitly defined function based on evidence from its derivatives.
AP.Ca.5.12.B.1: Applications of derivatives can be extended to implicitly defined functions.
AP.Ca.5.12.B.2: Second derivatives involving implicit differentiation may be relations of `x`, `y`, and `dy/dx`.
AP.Ca.6.1.A: Interpret the meaning of areas associated with the graph of a rate of change in context.
AP.Ca.6.1.A.1: The area of the region between the graph of a rate of change function and the x axis gives the accumulation of change.
AP.Ca.6.1.A.2: In some cases, accumulation of change can be evaluated by using geometry.
AP.Ca.6.1.A.3: If a rate of change is positive (negative) over an interval, then the accumulated change is positive (negative).
AP.Ca.6.1.A.4: The unit for the area of a region defined by rate of change is the unit for the rate of change multiplied by the unit for the independent variable.
AP.Ca.6.2.A: Approximate a definite integral using geometric and numerical methods.
AP.Ca.6.2.A.1: Definite integrals can be approximated for functions that are represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally.
AP.Ca.6.2.A.2: Definite integrals can be approximated using a left Riemann sum, a right Riemann sum, a midpoint Riemann sum, or a trapezoidal sum; approximations can be computed using either uniform or nonuniform partitions.
AP.Ca.6.2.A.3: Definite integrals can be approximated using numerical methods, with or without technology.
AP.Ca.6.2.A.4: Depending on the behavior of a function, it may be possible to determine whether an approximation for a definite integral is an underestimate or overestimate for the value of the definite integral.
AP.Ca.6.3: Riemann Sums, Summation Notation & Definite Integral Notation
AP.Ca.6.3.A: Interpret the limiting case of the Riemann sum as a definite integral.
AP.Ca.6.3.A.1: The limit of an approximating Riemann sum can be interpreted as a definite integral.
AP.Ca.6.3.A.2: A Riemann sum, which requires a partition of an interval I, is the sum of products, each of which is the value of the function at a point in a subinterval multiplied by the length of that subinterval of the partition.
AP.Ca.6.3.B: Represent the limiting case of the Riemann sum as a definite integral.
AP.Ca.6.3.B.1: The definite integral of a continuous function `f` over the interval `[a,b]`, denoted by `int_a^bf(x)dx`, is the limit of Riemann sums as the widths of the subintervals approach `0`. That is, `int_a^bf(x)dx=lim_(text(max)Deltax_i->0)sum_(i=1)^nf(x_i^(**))Deltax_i`, where `n` is the number of subintervals, `Deltax_i` is the width of the `i^text(th)` subinterval, and `x_i^(**)` is a value in the `i^text(th)` subinterval.
AP.Ca.6.3.B.2: A definite integral can be translated into the limit of a related Riemann sum, and the limit of a Riemann sum can be written as a definite integral.
AP.Ca.6.4: The Fundamental Theorem Of Calculus & Accumulation Functions
AP.Ca.6.4.A: Represent accumulation functions using definite integrals.
AP.Ca.6.4.A.1: The definite integral can be used to define new functions.
AP.Ca.6.4.A.2: If f is a continuous function on an interval containing `a`, then `d/dx(int_a^xf(t)dt)=f(x)`, where `x` is in the interval.
AP.Ca.6.5: Interpreting The Behavior Of Accumulation Functions Involving Area
AP.Ca.6.5.A: Represent accumulation functions using definite integrals.
AP.Ca.6.5.A.1: Graphical, numerical, analytical, and verbal representations of a function `f` provide information about the function `g` defined as `g(x)=int_a^xf(t)dt`.
AP.Ca.6.6.A: Calculate a definite integral using areas and properties of definite integrals.
AP.Ca.6.6.A.1: In some cases, a definite integral can be evaluated by using geometry and the connection between the definite integral and area.
AP.Ca.6.6.A.2: Properties of definite integrals include the integral of a constant times a function, the integral of the sum of two functions, reversal of limits of integration, and the integral of a function over adjacent intervals.
AP.Ca.6.6.A.3: The definition of the definite integral may be extended to functions with removable or jump discontinuities.
AP.Ca.6.7: The Fundamental Theorem Of Calculus & Definite Integrals
AP.Ca.6.7.A: Evaluate definite integrals analytically using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
AP.Ca.6.7.A.1: An antiderivative of a function `f` is a function `g` whose derivative is `f`.
AP.Ca.6.7.A.2: If a function `f` is continuous on an interval containing `a`, the function defined by `F(x)=int_a^xf(t)dt` is an antiderivative of `f` for `x` in the interval.
AP.Ca.6.7.A.3: If `f` is continuous on the interval `[a,b]` and `F` is an antiderivative of `f`, then `int_a^bf(x)dx=F(b)-F(a)`.
AP.Ca.6.8: Finding Antiderivatives & Indefinite Integrals: Basic Rules & Notation
AP.Ca.6.8.A: Determine antiderivatives of functions and indefinite integrals, using knowledge of derivatives.
AP.Ca.6.8.A.1: `intf(x)dx` is an indefinite integral of the function `f` and can be expressed as `intf(x)dx=F(x)+C`, where `F'(x)=f(x)` and `C` is any constant.
AP.Ca.6.8.A.2: Differentiation rules provide the foundation for finding antiderivatives.
AP.Ca.6.8.A.3: Many functions do not have closed-form antiderivatives.
AP.Ca.6.9.A: For integrands requiring substitution or rearrangements into equivalent forms, determine indefinite integrals and evaluate definite integrals.
AP.Ca.6.9.A.1: Substitution of variables is a technique for finding antiderivatives.
AP.Ca.6.9.A.2: For a definite integral, substitution of variables requires corresponding changes to the limits of integration.
AP.Ca.6.10: Integrating Functions Using Long Division & Completing The Square
AP.Ca.6.10.A: For integrands requiring substitution or rearrangements into equivalent forms, determine indefinite integrals and evaluate definite integrals.
AP.Ca.6.10.A.1: Techniques for finding antiderivatives include rearrangements into equivalent forms, such as long division and completing the square.
AP.Ca.6.11.A: For integrands requiring integration by parts, determine indefinite integrals and evaluate definite integrals.
AP.Ca.6.11.A.1: Integration by parts is a technique for finding antiderivatives.
AP.Ca.6.12.A: For integrands requiring integration by linear partial fractions, determine indefinite integrals and evaluate definite integrals.
AP.Ca.6.12.A.1: Some rational functions can be decomposed into sums of ratios of linear, nonrepeating factors to which basic integration techniques can be applied.
AP.Ca.6.13.A: Evaluate an improper integral or determine that the integral diverges.
AP.Ca.6.13.A.1: An improper integral is an integral that has one or both limits infinite or has an integrand that is unbounded in the interval of integration.
AP.Ca.6.13.A.2: Improper integrals can be determined using limits of definite integrals.
AP.Ca.7.1.A: Interpret verbal statements of problems as differential equations involving a derivative expression.
AP.Ca.7.1.A.1: Differential equations relate a function of an independent variable and the function's derivatives.
AP.Ca.7.2.A.1: Derivatives can be used to verify that a function is a solution to a given differential equation.
AP.Ca.7.2.A.2: There may be infinitely many general solutions to a differential equation.
AP.Ca.7.3.A.1: A slope field is a graphical representation of a differential equation on a finite set of points in the plane.
AP.Ca.7.3.A.2: Slope fields provide information about the behavior of solutions to first-order differential equations.
AP.Ca.7.4.A.1: Solutions to differential equations are functions or families of functions.
AP.Ca.7.5.A.1: Euler's method provides a procedure for approximating a solution to a differential equation or a point on a solution curve.
AP.Ca.7.6: Finding General Solutions Using Separation Of Variables
AP.Ca.7.6.A: Determine general solutions to differential equations.
AP.Ca.7.6.A.1: Some differential equations can be solved by separation of variables.
AP.Ca.7.6.A.2: Antidifferentiation can be used to find general solutions to differential equations.
AP.Ca.7.7: Finding Particular Solutions Using Initial Conditions & Separation of Variables
AP.Ca.7.7.A: Determine particular solutions to differential equations.
AP.Ca.7.7.A.1: A general solution may describe infinitely many solutions to a differential equation. There is only one particular solution passing through a given point.
AP.Ca.7.7.A.2: The function `F` defined by `F(x)=y_0+int_a^xf(t)dt` is a particular solution to the differential equation `dy/dx=f(x)`, satisfying `F(a)=y_0`.
AP.Ca.7.7.A.3: Solutions to differential equations may be subject to domain restrictions.
AP.Ca.7.8.A: Interpret the meaning of a differential equation and its variables in context.
