AP.CSA.1.3.A.2: Arithmetic expressions include expressions of type `tttext(int)` and `tttext(double)`.
AP.CSA.1.3.A.3: The arithmetic operators consist of `tt(+)`, `tt(-)`, `tt(**)`, `tt(//)`, and `tt(%)`.
AP.CSA.1.3.A.4: An arithmetic operation that uses two `tttext(int)` values will evaluate to an `tttext(int)` value.
AP.CSA.1.3.A.5: An arithmetic operation that uses a `tttext(double)` value will evaluate to a `tttext(double)` value.
AP.CSA.1.3.A.6: Operators can be used to construct compound expressions.
AP.CSA.1.3.A.7: During evaluation, operands are associated with operators according to operator precedence to determine how they are grouped.
AP.CSA.1.3.A.8: An attempt to divide an integer by zero will result in an `tttext(ArithmeticException)` to occur.
AP.CSA.1.3.B: Evaluate what is stored in a variable as a result of an expression with an assignment statement.
AP.CSA.1.3.B.1: The assignment operator (`tt(=)`) allows a program to initialize or change the value stored in a variable. The value of the expression on the right is stored in the variable on the left.
AP.CSA.1.3.B.2: During execution, expressions are evaluated to produce a single value.
AP.CSA.1.3.B.3: The value of an expression has a type based on the evaluation of the expression.
AP.CSA.1.4.A: Evaluate what is stored in a variable as a result of an expression with an assignment statement.
AP.CSA.1.4.A.1: Compound assignment operators (`tt(+=)`, `tt(- =)`, `tt(**=,)` `tt(//=)`, `tt(%=)`) can be used in place of the assignment operator.
AP.CSA.1.4.A.2: The increment operator (`tt(++)`) and decrement operator (`tt(--)`) are used to add `1` or subtract `1` from the stored value of a variable or an array element. The new value is assigned to the variable or array element.
AP.CSA.1.5.A: Evaluate arithmetic expressions that use casting.
AP.CSA.1.5.A.1: The casting operators (`tttext(int)`) and (`tttext(double)`) can be used to create a temporary value converted to a different data type.
AP.CSA.1.5.A.2: Casting a `tttext(double)` value to an `tttext(int)` causes the digits to the right of the decimal point to be truncated.
AP.CSA.1.5.A.3: Some programming code causes `tttext(int)` values to be automatically cast (widened) to `tttext(double)` values.
AP.CSA.1.5.A.4: Values of type `tttext(double)` can be rounded to the nearest integer by `tt((text(int))(x+0.5))` or `tt((text(int))(x-0.5))` for negative numbers.
AP.CSA.1.5.A.5: Integer values in Java are represented by values of type `tttext(int)`, which are stored using a finite amount (`4` bytes) of memory. Therefore, an `tttext(int)` value must be in the range from `tttext(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` to `tttext(Integer.MAX_VALUE)` inclusive.
AP.CSA.1.5.A.6: If an expression would evaluate to an `tttext(int)` value outside of the allowed range, an integer overflow occurs. This could result in an incorrect value within the allowed range.
AP.CSA.2.1.A: Explain the relationship between a class and an object.
AP.CSA.2.1.A.1: An object is a specific instance of a class with defined attributes.
AP.CSA.2.1.A.2: A class is the formal implementation, or blueprint, of the attributes and behaviors of an object.
AP.CSA.2.2.A: Identify, using its signature, the correct constructor being called.
AP.CSA.2.2.A.1: A signature consists of the constructor name and the parameter list.
AP.CSA.2.2.A.2: The parameter list, in the header of a constructor, lists the types of the values that are passed and their variable names. These are often referred to as formal parameters.
AP.CSA.2.2.A.3: A parameter is a value that is passed into a constructor. These are often referred to as actual parameters.
AP.CSA.2.2.A.4: Constructors are said to be overloaded when there are multiple constructors with the same name but a different signature.
AP.CSA.2.2.A.5: The actual parameters passed to a constructor must be compatible with the types identified in the formal parameter list.
AP.CSA.2.2.A.6: Parameters are passed using call by value. Call by value initializes the formal parameters with copies of the actual parameters.
AP.CSA.2.2.B: For creating objects, create objects by calling constructors without parameters and create objects by calling constructors with parameters.
AP.CSA.2.2.B.1: Every object is created using the keyword `tttext(new)` followed by a call to one of the class's constructors.
AP.CSA.2.2.B.2: A class contains constructors that are invoked to create objects. They have the same name as the class.
AP.CSA.2.2.B.3: Existing classes and class libraries can be utilized as appropriate to create objects.
AP.CSA.2.2.B.4: Parameters allow values to be passed to the constructor to establish the initial state of the object.
AP.CSA.2.2.C: Define variables of the correct types to represent reference data.
AP.CSA.2.2.C.1: The keyword `tttext(null)` is a special value used to indicate that a reference is not associated with any object.
AP.CSA.2.2.C.2: The memory associated with a variable of a reference type holds an object reference value or, if there is no object, `tttext(null)`. This value is the memory address of the referenced object.
AP.CSA.2.3.A: Call non-static void methods without parameters.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.1: An object's behavior refers to what the object can do (or what can be done to it) and is defined by methods.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.2: Procedural abstraction allows a programmer to use a method by knowing what the method does even if they do not know how the method was written.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.3: A method signature for a method without parameters consists of the method name and an empty parameter list.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.4: A method or constructor call interrupts the sequential execution of statements, causing the program to first execute the statements in the method or constructor before continuing. Once the last statement in the method or constructor has executed or a return statement is executed, flow of control is returned to the point immediately following where the method or constructor was called.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.5: Non-static methods are called through objects of the class.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.6: The dot operator is used along with the object name to call non-static methods.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.7: Void methods do not have return values and are therefore not called as part of an expression.
AP.CSA.2.3.A.8: Using a `tttext(null)` reference to call a method or access an instance variable causes a `tttext(NullPointerException)` to be thrown.
AP.CSA.2.4: Calling A Void Method With Parameters
AP.CSA.2.4.A: Call non-static void methods with parameters.
AP.CSA.2.4.A.1: A method signature for a method with parameters consists of the method name and the ordered list of parameter types.
AP.CSA.2.4.A.2: Values provided in the parameter list need to correspond to the order and type in the method signature.
AP.CSA.2.4.A.3: Methods are said to be overloaded when there are multiple methods with the same name but a different signature.
AP.CSA.2.5.A: Call non-static non-void methods with or without parameters.
AP.CSA.2.5.A.1: Non-void methods return a value that is the same type as the return type in the signature. To use the return value when calling a non-void method, it must be stored in a variable or used as part of an expression.
AP.CSA.2.6.A: For `tttext(String)` class, create `tttext(String)` objects and call `tttext(String)` methods.
AP.CSA.2.6.A.1: `tttext(String)` objects can be created by using string literals or by calling the `tttext(String)` class constructor.
AP.CSA.2.6.A.2: `tttext(String)` objects are immutable, meaning that `tttext(String)` methods do not change the `tttext(String)` object.
AP.CSA.2.6.A.3: `tttext(String)` objects can be concatenated using the `tttext(+)` or `tttext(+=)` operator, resulting in a new `tttext(String)` object.
AP.CSA.2.6.A.4: Primitive values can be concatenated with a `tttext(String)` object. This causes implicit conversion of the values to `tttext(String)` objects.
AP.CSA.2.6.A.5: Escape sequences start with a `tttext(\)` and have a special meaning in Java. Escape sequences used in this course include `tttext(\”)`, `tttext(\\)`, and `tttext(\n)`.
AP.CSA.2.7.A: For `tttext(String)` class, create `tttext(String)` objects and call `tttext(String)` methods.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.1: Application program interfaces (APIs) and libraries simplify complex programming tasks.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.2: Documentation for APIs and libraries are essential to understanding the attributes and behaviors of an object of a class.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.3: Classes in the APIs and libraries are grouped into packages.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.4: The `tttext(String)` class is part of the `tttext(java.lang)` package. Classes in the `tttext(java.lang)` package are available by default.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.5: A `tttext(String)` object has index values from `tt(0)` to `tt(text(length)-1)`. Attempting to access indices outside this range will result in an `tttext(IndexOutOfBoundsException)`.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.6: A `tttext(String)` object can be concatenated with an object reference, which implicitly calls the referenced object's `tttext(toString)` method.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.7: The following `tttext(String)` methods and constructors - including what they do and when they are used-are part of the Java Quick Reference:
AP.CSA.2.7.A.7.a: `tt(text(String)(text(String str)))` - Constructs a new `tttext(String)` object that represents the same sequence of characters as `tttext(str)`.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.7.b: `tt(text(int length)())` - Returns the number of characters in a `tttext(String)` object.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.7.c: `tt(text(String substring)(text(int from),text(int to)))` - Returns the substring beginning at index `tttext(from)` and ending at index `tt(text(to)-1)`.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.7.e: `tt(text(int indexOf)(text(String str)))` - Returns the index of the first occurrence of `tttext(str)`; returns `tt(-1)` if not found.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.7.f: `tt(text(boolean equals)(text(String other)))` - Returns `tttext(true)` if `tttext(this)` is equal to other; returns `tttext(false)` otherwise.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.7.g: `tt(text(int compareTo)(text(String other)))` - Returns a value `tt(<0)` if `tttext(this)` is less than `tttext(other)`; returns zero if `tttext(this)` is equal to `tttext(other)`; returns a value `tt(>0)` if `tttext(this)` is greater than `tttext(other)`.
AP.CSA.2.7.A.8: A string identical to the single element substring at position `tttext(index)` can be created by calling `tt(text(substring)(text(index),text(index)+1))`.
AP.CSA.2.8.A: For wrapper classes, create `tttext(Integer)` objects, call `tttext(Integer)` methods, create `tttext(Double)` objects, and call `tttext(Double)` methods.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.1: The `tttext(Integer)` class and `tttext(Double)` class are part of the `tttext(java.lang)` package.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.2: The following `tttext(Integer)` methods and constructors-including what they do and when they are used-are part of the Java Quick Reference:
AP.CSA.2.8.A.2.a: `tt(text(Integer)(text(int value)))` - Constructs a new `tttext(Integer)` object that represents the specified `tttext(int)` value.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.2.b: `tttext(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` - The minimum value represented by an `tttext(int)` or `tttext(Integer)`.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.2.c: `tttext(Integer.MAX_VALUE)` - The maximum value represented by an `tttext(int)` or `tttext(Integer)`.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.2.d: `tt(text(int intValue)())` - Returns the value of this `tttext(Integer)` as an `tttext(int)`.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.3: The following `tttext(Double)` methods and constructors-including what they do and when they are used - are part of the Java Quick Reference:
AP.CSA.2.8.A.3.a: `tt(text(Double)(text(double value)))` - Constructs a new `tttext(Double)` object that represents the specified `tttext(double)` value.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.3.b: `tt(text(double doubleValue)())` - Returns the value of this `tttext(Double)` as a `tttext(double)`.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.4: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes between primitive types and their corresponding object wrapper classes. This includes converting an `tttext(int)` to an `tttext(Integer)` and a `tttext(double)` to a `tttext(Double)`.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.5: The Java compiler applies autoboxing when a primitive value is passed as a parameter to a method that expects an object of the corresponding wrapper class and assigned to a variable of the corresponding wrapper class.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.6: Unboxing is the automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes from the wrapper class to the primitive type. This includes converting an `tttext(Integer)` to an `tttext(int)` and a `tttext(Double)` to a `tttext(double)`.
AP.CSA.2.8.A.7: The Java compiler applies unboxing when a wrapper class object is passed as a parameter to a method that expects a value of the corresponding primitive type and assigned to a variable of the corresponding primitive type.
AP.CSA.2.9.A.1: Static methods are called using the dot operator along with the class name unless they are defined in the enclosing class.
AP.CSA.2.9.B: Evaluate expressions that use the `tttext(Math)` class methods.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.1: The `tttext(Math)` class is part of the `tttext(java.lang)` package.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.2: The `tttext(Math)` class contains only static methods.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.3: The following static `tttext(Math)` methods-including what they do and when they are used-are part of the Java Quick Reference:
AP.CSA.2.9.B.3.a: `tt(text(int abs)(text(int x)))` - Returns the absolute value of an `tttext(int)` value.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.3.b: `tt(text(double abs)(text(double x)))` - Returns the absolute value of a `tttext(double)` value.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.3.c: `tt(text(double pow)(text(double base),text(double exponent)))` - Returns the value of the first parameter raised to the power of the second parameter.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.3.d: `tt(text(double sqrt)(text(double x)))` - Returns the positive square root of a `tttext(double)` value.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.3.e: `tt(text(double random)())` - Returns a `tttext(double)` value greater than or equal to `0.0` and less than `1.0`.
AP.CSA.2.9.B.4: The values returned from `tttext(Math.random)` can be manipulated to produce a random `tttext(int)` or `tttext(double)` in a defined range.
AP.CSA.3.1.A: Evaluate Boolean expressions that use relational operators in program code.
AP.CSA.3.1.A.1: Primitive values and reference values can be compared using relational operators (i.e., `tt(==)` and `tt(! =)`).
AP.CSA.3.1.A.2: Arithmetic expression values can be compared using relational operators (i.e., `tt(<)`, `tt(>)`, `tt(< =)`, `tt(> =)`).
AP.CSA.3.1.A.3: An expression involving relational operators evaluates to a Boolean value.
AP.CSA.3.2.A: Represent branching logical processes by using conditional statements.
AP.CSA.3.2.A.1: Conditional statements interrupt the sequential execution of statements.
AP.CSA.3.2.A.2: `tttext(if)` statements affect the flow of control by executing different statements based on the value of a Boolean expression.
AP.CSA.3.2.A.3: A one-way selection (`tttext(if)` statement) is written when there is a set of statements to execute under a certain condition. In this case, the body is executed only when the Boolean condition is `tttext(true)`.
AP.CSA.3.3.A: Represent branching logical processes by using conditional statements.
AP.CSA.3.3.A.1: A two-way selection is written when there are two sets of statements- one to be executed when the Boolean condition is `tttext(true)`, and another set for when the Boolean condition is `tttext(false)`. In this case, the body of the “if” is executed when the Boolean condition is `tttext(true)`, and the body of the “else” is executed when the Boolean condition is `tttext(false)`.
AP.CSA.3.4.A: Represent branching logical processes by using conditional statements.
AP.CSA.3.4.A.1: A multi-way selection is written when there are a series of conditions with different statements for each condition. Multi-way selection is performed using `tttext(if-else-if)` statements such that exactly one section of code is executed based on the first condition that evaluates to true.
AP.CSA.3.5.A: Represent branching logical processes by using nested conditional statements.
AP.CSA.3.5.A.1: Nested `tttext(if)` statements consist of `tttext(if)` statements within `tttext(if)` statements.
AP.CSA.3.5.B: Evaluate compound Boolean expressions in program code.
AP.CSA.3.5.B.1: Logical operators `tt(!)`(not), `tt(&&)`(and), and `tt(||)`(or) are used with Boolean values. This represents the order these operators will be evaluated.
AP.CSA.3.5.B.2: An expression involving logical operators evaluates to a Boolean value.
AP.CSA.3.5.B.3: When the result of a logical expression using `tt(&&)` or `tt(||)` can be determined by evaluating only the first Boolean operand, the second is not evaluated. This is known as short-circuited evaluation.
AP.CSA.3.6.A: Compare and contrast equivalent Boolean expressions.
AP.CSA.3.6.A.1: De Morgan's Laws can be applied to Boolean expressions.
AP.CSA.3.6.A.2: Truth tables can be used to prove Boolean identities.
AP.CSA.3.6.A.3: Equivalent Boolean expressions will evaluate to the same value in all cases.
AP.CSA.3.7.A: Compare object references using Boolean expressions in program code.
AP.CSA.3.7.A.1: Two object references are considered aliases when they both reference the same object.
AP.CSA.3.7.A.2: Object reference values can be compared, using `tt(==)` and `tt(! =)`, to identify aliases.
AP.CSA.3.7.A.3: A reference value can be compared with `tttext(null)`, using `tt(==)` or `tt(! =)`, to determine if the reference actually references an object.
AP.CSA.3.7.A.4: Often classes have their own `tttext(equals)` method, which can be used to determine whether two objects of the class are equivalent.
AP.CSA.4.1.A: Represent iterative processes using a `tttext(while)` loop.
AP.CSA.4.1.A.1: Iteration statements change the flow of control by repeating a set of statements zero or more times until a condition is met.
AP.CSA.4.1.A.2: In loops, the Boolean expression is evaluated before each iteration of the loop body,including the first. When the expression evaluates to `tttext(true)`, the loop body is executed.This continues until the expression evaluates to `tttext(false)`, whereupon the iteration ceases.
AP.CSA.4.1.A.3: A loop is an infinite loop when the Boolean expression always evaluates to `tttext(true)`.
AP.CSA.4.1.A.4: If the Boolean expression evaluates to `tttext(false)` initially, the loop body is not executed at all.
AP.CSA.4.1.A.5: Executing a return statement inside an iteration statement will halt the loop and exit the method or constructor.
AP.CSA.4.1.B: For algorithms in the context of a particular specification that does not require the use of traversals, identify standard algorithms, modify standard algorithms, and develop an algorithm.
AP.CSA.4.1.B.1: There are standard algorithms to identify if an integer is or is not evenly divisible by another integer,identify the individual digits in an integer, and determine the frequency with which a specific criterion is met.
AP.CSA.4.1.B.2: There are standard algorithms to determine a minimum or maximum value and compute a sum, average, or mode.
AP.CSA.4.2.A: Represent iterative processes using a `tttext(for)` loop.
AP.CSA.4.2.A.1: There are three parts in a `tttext(for)` loop header: the initialization, the Boolean expression, and the increment. The increment statement can also be a decrement statement.
AP.CSA.4.2.A.2: In a `tttext(for)` loop, the initialization statement is only executed once before the first Boolean expression evaluation. The variable being initialized is referred to as a loop control variable.
AP.CSA.4.2.A.3: In each iteration of a `tttext(for)` loop, the increment statement is executed after the entire loop body is executed and before the Boolean expression is evaluated again.
AP.CSA.4.2.A.4: A `tttext(for)` loop can be rewritten into an equivalent `tttext(while)` loop and vice versa.
AP.CSA.4.2.A.5: “Off by one” errors occur when the iteration statement loops one time too many or one time too few.
AP.CSA.4.3.A: For algorithms in the context of a particular specification that involves `tttext(String)` objects, identify standard algorithms, modify standard algorithms, and develop an algorithm.
AP.CSA.4.3.A.1: There are standard algorithms that utilize String traversals to, find if one or more substrings has a particular property, determine the number of substrings that meet specific criteria, and create a new string with the characters reversed.
AP.CSA.4.4.A.1: Nested iteration statements are iteration statements that appear in the body of another iteration statement.
AP.CSA.4.4.A.2: When a loop is nested inside another loop, the inner loop must complete all its iterations before the outer loop can continue.
AP.CSA.4.5.A: Compute statement execution counts and informal run-time comparison of iterative statements.
AP.CSA.4.5.A.1: A statement execution count indicates the number of times a statement is executed by the program.
AP.CSA.5.1.A: Designate access and visibility constraints to classes, data, constructors, and methods.
AP.CSA.5.1.A.1: The keywords `tttext(public)` and `tttext(private)` affect the access of classes, data, constructors, and methods.
AP.CSA.5.1.A.2: The keyword `tttext(private)` restricts access to the declaring class, while the keyword `tttext(public)` allows access from classes outside the declaring class.
AP.CSA.5.1.A.4: Access to attributes should be kept internal to the class. Therefore, instance variables are designated as `tttext(private)`.
AP.CSA.5.1.A.6: Access to behaviors can be internal or external to the class. Therefore, methods can be designated as either `tttext(public)` or `tttext(private)`.
AP.CSA.5.1.B: Designate private visibility of instance variables to encapsulate the attributes of an object.
AP.CSA.5.1.B.1: Data encapsulation is a technique in which the implementation details of a class are kept hidden from the user.
AP.CSA.5.1.B.2: When designing a class, programmers make decisions about what data to make accessible and modifiable from an external class. Data can be either accessible or modifiable, or it can be both or neither.
AP.CSA.5.1.B.3: Instance variables are encapsulated by using the `tttext(private)` access modifier.
AP.CSA.5.1.B.4: The provided accessor and mutator methods in a class allow client code to use and modify data.
AP.CSA.5.2.A: Define instance variables for the attributes to be initialized through the constructors of a class
AP.CSA.5.2.A.1: An object's state refers to its attributes and their values at a given time and is defined by instance variables belonging to the object. This creates a “has-a” relationship between the object and its instance variables.
AP.CSA.5.2.A.2: Constructors are used to set the initial state of an object, which should include initial values for all instance variables.
AP.CSA.5.2.A.3: Constructor parameters are local variables to the constructor and provide data to initialize instance variables.
AP.CSA.5.2.A.4: When a mutable object is a constructor parameter, the instance variable should be initialized with a copy of the referenced object. In this way, the instance variable is not an alias of the original object, and methods are prevented from modifying the state of the original object.
AP.CSA.5.2.A.5: When no constructor is written, Java provides a no-argument constructor, and the instance variables are set to default values.
AP.CSA.5.3.A: Describe the functionality and use of program code through comments.
AP.CSA.5.3.A.1: Comments are ignored by the compiler and are not executed when the program is run.
AP.CSA.5.3.A.2: Three types of comments in Java include `tt(//**)` `tt(**//)`, which generates a block of comments, `tt(////)`, which generates a comment on one line, and `tt(//** **)` `tt(**//)`, which are Javadoc comments and are used to create API documentation.
AP.CSA.5.3.A.3: A precondition is a condition that must be true just prior to the execution of a section of program code in order for the method to behave as expected. There is no expectation that the method will check to ensure preconditions are satisfied.
AP.CSA.5.3.A.4: A postcondition is a condition that must always be true after the execution of a section of program code. Postconditions describe the outcome of the execution in terms of what is being returned or the state of an object.
AP.CSA.5.3.A.5: Programmers write method code to satisfy the postconditions when preconditions are met.
AP.CSA.5.4.A: Define behaviors of an object through non-void methods without parameters written in a class.
AP.CSA.5.4.A.1: An accessor method allows other objects to obtain the value of instance variables or static variables.
AP.CSA.5.4.A.2: A non-void method returns a single value. Its header includes the return type in place of the keyword `tttext(void)`.
AP.CSA.5.4.A.3: In non-void methods, a return expression compatible with the return type is evaluated, and a copy of that value is returned. This is referred to as “return by value.”
AP.CSA.5.4.A.4: When the return expression is a reference to an object, a copy of that reference is returned, not a copy of the object.
AP.CSA.5.4.A.5: The `tttext(return)` keyword is used to return the flow of control to the point immediately following where the method or constructor was called.
AP.CSA.5.4.A.6: The `tttext(toString)` method is an overridden method that is included in classes to provide a description of a specific object. It generally includes what values are stored in the instance data of the object.
AP.CSA.5.4.A.7: If `tttext(System.out.print)` or `tttext(System.out.println)` is passed an object, that object's `tttext(toString)` method is called, and the returned string is printed.
AP.CSA.5.5.A: Define behaviors of an object through void methods with or without parameters written in a class.
AP.CSA.5.5.A.1: A void method does not return a value. Its header contains the keyword `tttext(void)` before the method name.
AP.CSA.5.5.A.2: A mutator (modifier) method is often a void method that changes the values of instance variables or static variables.
AP.CSA.5.6.A: Define behaviors of an object through non-void methods with parameters written in a class.
AP.CSA.5.6.A.1: Methods can only access the private data and methods of a parameter that is a reference to an object when the parameter is the same type as the method's enclosing class.
AP.CSA.5.6.A.2: Non-void methods with parameters receive values through parameters, use those values, and return a computed value of the specified type.
AP.CSA.5.6.A.3: It is good programming practice to not modify mutable objects that are passed as parameters unless required in the specification.
AP.CSA.5.6.A.4: When an actual parameter is a primitive value, the formal parameter is initialized with a copy of that value. Changes to the formal parameter have no effect on the corresponding actual parameter.
AP.CSA.5.6.A.5: When an actual parameter is a reference to an object, the formal parameter is initialized with a copy of that reference, not a copy of the object. If the reference is to a mutable object, the method or constructor can use this reference to alter the state of the object.
AP.CSA.5.6.A.6: Passing a reference parameter results in the formal parameter and the actual parameter being aliases. They both refer to the same object.
AP.CSA.5.7.A: Define behaviors of a class through static methods.
AP.CSA.5.7.A.1: Static methods are associated with the class, not objects of the class.
AP.CSA.5.7.A.2: Static methods include the keyword `tttext(static)` in the header before the method name.
AP.CSA.5.7.A.3: Static methods cannot access or change the values of instance variables.
AP.CSA.5.7.A.4: Static methods can access or change the values of static variables.
AP.CSA.5.7.A.5: Static methods do not have a `tttext(this)` reference and are unable to use the class's instance variables or call non-static methods.
AP.CSA.5.7.B: Define the static variables that belong to the class.
AP.CSA.5.7.B.1: Static variables belong to the class, with all objects of a class sharing a single static variable.
AP.CSA.5.7.B.2: Static variables can be designated as either `tttext(public)` or `tttext(private)` and are designated with the `tttext(static)` keyword before the variable type.
AP.CSA.5.7.B.3: Static variables are used with the class name and the dot operator, since they are associated with a class, not objects of a class.
AP.CSA.5.8.A: Explain where variables can be used in the program code.
AP.CSA.5.8.A.1: Local variables can be declared in the body of constructors and methods. These variables may only be used within the constructor or method and cannot be declared to be `tttext(public)` or `tttext(private)`.
AP.CSA.5.8.A.2: When there is a local variable with the same name as an instance variable, the variable name will refer to the local variable instead of the instance variable.
AP.CSA.5.8.A.3: Formal parameters and variables declared in a method or constructor can only be used within that method or constructor.
AP.CSA.5.8.A.4: Through method decomposition, a programmer breaks down a large problem into smaller subproblems by creating methods to solve each individual subproblem.
AP.CSA.5.9.A: Evaluate object reference expressions that use the keyword `tttext(this)`.
AP.CSA.5.9.A.1: Within a non-static method or a constructor, the keyword `tttext(this)` is a reference to the current object - the object whose method or constructor is being called.
AP.CSA.5.9.A.2: The keyword `tttext(this)` can be used to pass the current object as an actual parameter in a method call.
AP.CSA.5.10: Ethical & Social Implications Of Computing Systems
AP.CSA.5.10.A: Explain the ethical and social implications of computing systems.
AP.CSA.5.10.A.1: System reliability is limited. Programmers should make an effort to maximize system reliability.
AP.CSA.5.10.A.2: Legal issues and intellectual property concerns arise when creating programs.
AP.CSA.5.10.A.3: The creation of programs has impacts on society, economies, and culture. These impacts can be beneficial and/or harmful.
AP.CSA.6.1.A: Represent collections of related primitive or object reference data using one-dimensional (1D) array objects.
AP.CSA.6.1.A.1: The use of array objects allows multiple related items to be represented using a single variable.
AP.CSA.6.1.A.2: The size of an array is established at the time of creation and cannot be changed.
AP.CSA.6.1.A.3: Arrays can store either primitive data or object reference data.
AP.CSA.6.1.A.4: When an array is created using the keyword new, all of its elements are initialized with a specific value based on the type of elements. Elements of type `tttext(int)` are initialized to `0`, elements of type `tttext(double)` are initialized to `0.0`, elements of type `tttext(boolean)` are initialized to `tttext(false)`, and elements of a reference type are initialized to the reference value `tttext(null)` and no objects are automatically created.
AP.CSA.6.1.A.5: Initializer lists can be used to create and initialize arrays.
AP.CSA.6.1.A.6: Square brackets (`tt([` `tt]`) are used to access and modify an element in a 1D array using an index.
AP.CSA.6.1.A.7: The valid index values for an array are `0` through one less than the number of elements in the array, inclusive. Using an index value outside of this range will result in an `tttext(ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)` being thrown.
AP.CSA.6.2.A: Traverse the elements in a 1D array.
AP.CSA.6.2.A.1: Iteration statements can be used to access all the elements in an array. This is called traversing the array.
AP.CSA.6.2.A.2: Traversing an array with an indexed `tttext(for)` loop or `tttext(while)` loop requires elements to be accessed using their indices.
AP.CSA.6.2.A.3: Since the indices for an array start at `tt(0)` and end at the number of elements `tt(-1)`, “off by one” errors are easy to make when traversing an array, resulting in an `tttext(ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)` being thrown.
AP.CSA.6.3.A: Traverse the elements in a 1D array object using an enhanced `tttext(for)` loop.
AP.CSA.6.3.A.1: An enhanced `tttext(for)` loop header includes a variable, referred to as the enhanced for loop variable.
AP.CSA.6.3.A.2: For each iteration of the enhanced `tttext(for)` loop, the enhanced `tttext(for)` loop variable is assigned a copy of an element without using its index.
AP.CSA.6.3.A.3: Assigning a new value to the enhanced `tttext(for)` loop variable does not change the value stored in the array.
AP.CSA.6.3.A.4: Program code written using an enhanced for loop to traverse and access elements in an array can be rewritten using an indexed `tttext(for)` loop or a `tttext(while)` loop.
AP.CSA.6.4.A: For algorithms in the context of a particular specification that requires the use of array traversals, identify standard algorithms, modify standard algorithms, and develop an algorithm.
AP.CSA.6.4.A.1: There are standard algorithms that utilize array traversals to determine a minimum or maximum value, compute a sum, average, or mode, determine if at least one element has a particular property, determine if all elements have a particular property, access all consecutive pairs of elements, determine the presence or absence of duplicate elements, and determine the number of elements meeting specific criteria.
AP.CSA.6.4.A.2: There are standard array algorithms that utilize traversals to shift or rotate elements left or right and reverse the order of the elements.
AP.CSA.7.1.A: Represent collections of related object reference data using `tttext(ArrayList)` objects.
AP.CSA.7.1.A.1: An `tttext(ArrayList)` object is mutable and contains object references.
AP.CSA.7.1.A.2: The `tttext(ArrayList)` constructor `tt(text(ArrayList)())` constructs an empty list.
AP.CSA.7.1.A.3: Java allows the generic type `tt(text(ArrayList)<text(E)>)`, where the generic type `tttext(E)` specifies the type of the elements.
AP.CSA.7.1.A.4: When `tt(text(ArrayList)<text(E)>)` is specified, the types of the reference parameters and return type when using the methods are type `tttext(E)`.
AP.CSA.7.1.A.5: `tt(text(ArrayList)<text(E)>)` is preferred over `tttext(ArrayList)` because it allows the compiler to find errors that would otherwise be found at run-time.
AP.CSA.7.2.A: Represent collections of related object reference data using `tttext(ArrayList)` objects.
AP.CSA.7.2.A.1: The `tttext(ArrayList)` class is part of the `tttext(java.util)` package. An import statement can be used to make this class available for use in the program.
AP.CSA.7.2.A.2: The following `tttext(ArrayList)` methods - including what they do and when they are used - are part of the Java Quick Reference:
AP.CSA.7.2.A.2.a: `tt(text(int size)())` - Returns the number of elements in the list.
AP.CSA.7.2.A.2.b: `tt(text(boolean add)(text(E obj)))` - Appends `tttext(obj)` to end of list; returns `tttext(true)`.
AP.CSA.7.2.A.2.c: `tt(text(void add)(text(int index),text(E obj)))` - Inserts `tttext(obj)` at position `tttext(index)` (`tt(0< =text(index)< =text(size))`), moving elements at position `tttext(index)` and higher to the right (adds `1` to their indices) and adds `1` to size.
AP.CSA.7.2.A.2.d: `tt(text(E get)(text(int index)))` - Returns the element at position `tttext(index)` in the list.
AP.CSA.7.2.A.2.e: `tt(text(E set)(text(int index),text(E obj)))` - Replaces the element at position `tttext(index)` with `tttext(obj)`; returns the element formerly at position `tttext(index)`.
AP.CSA.7.2.A.2.f: `tt(text(E remove)(text(int index)))` - Removes element from position `tttext(index)`, moving elements at position `tt(text(index)+1)` and higher to the left (subtracts `1` from their indices) and subtracts `1` from size; returns the element formerly at position `tttext(index)`.
AP.CSA.7.3.A: For `tttext(ArrayList)` objects, traverse using a for or `tttext(while)` loop and traverse using an enhanced `tttext(for)` loop.
AP.CSA.7.3.A.1: Iteration statements can be used to access all the elements in an `tttext(ArrayList)`. This is called traversing the `tttext(ArrayList)`.
AP.CSA.7.3.A.2: Deleting elements during a traversal of an `tttext(ArrayList)` requires using special techniques to avoid skipping elements.
AP.CSA.7.3.A.3: Since the indices for an `tttext(ArrayList)` start at `tt(0)` and end at the number of elements `tt(-1)`, accessing an index value outside of this range will result in an `tttext(ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)` being thrown.
AP.CSA.7.3.A.4: Changing the size of an `tttext(ArrayList)` while traversing it using an enhanced `tttext(for)` loop can result in a `tttext(ConcurrentModificationException)` being thrown. Therefore, when using an enhanced `tttext(for)` loop to traverse an `tttext(ArrayList)`, you should not add or remove elements.
AP.CSA.7.4.A: For algorithms in the context of a particular specification that requires the use of `tttext(ArrayList)` traversals, identify standard algorithms, modify standard algorithms, and develop an algorithm.
AP.CSA.7.4.A.1: There are standard `tttext(ArrayList)` algorithms that utilize traversals to insert elements, delete elements, and apply the same standard algorithms that are used with 1D arrays.
AP.CSA.7.4.A.2: Some algorithms require multiple `tttext(String)`, array, or `tttext(ArrayList)` objects to be traversed simultaneously.
AP.CSA.7.5.A: Apply sequential/linear search algorithms to search for specific information in array or `tttext(ArrayList)` objects.
AP.CSA.7.5.A.1: There are standard algorithms for searching.
AP.CSA.7.5.A.2: Sequential/linear search algorithms check each element in order until the desired value is found or all elements in the array or `tttext(ArrayList)` have been checked.
AP.CSA.7.6.A: Apply selection sort and insertion sort algorithms to sort the elements of array or `tttext(ArrayList)` objects.
AP.CSA.7.6.A.1: Selection sort and insertion sort are iterative sorting algorithms that can be used to sort elements in an array or `tttext(ArrayList)`.
AP.CSA.7.6.B: Compute statement execution counts and informal run-time comparison of sorting algorithms.
AP.CSA.7.6.B.1: Informal run-time comparisons of program code segments can be made using statement execution counts.
AP.CSA.7.7.A: Explain the risks to privacy from collecting and storing personal data on computer systems.
AP.CSA.7.7.A.1: When using the computer, personal privacy is at risk. Programmers should attempt to safeguard personal privacy.
AP.CSA.7.7.A.2: Computer use and the creation of programs have an impact on personal security. These impacts can be beneficial and/or harmful.
AP.CSA.8.1.A: Represent collections of related primitive or object reference data using two-dimensional (2D) array objects.
AP.CSA.8.1.A.1: 2D arrays are stored as arrays of arrays. Therefore, the way 2D arrays are created and indexed is similar to 1D array objects.
AP.CSA.8.1.A.2: For the purposes of the exam, when accessing the element at `tt(text(arr)[text(first)][text(second)])`, the first index is used for rows, the second index is used for columns.
AP.CSA.8.1.A.3: The initializer list used to create and initialize a 2D array consists of initializer lists that represent 1D arrays.
AP.CSA.8.1.A.4: The square brackets `tt([text(row)][text(col)])` are used to access and modify an element in a 2D array.
AP.CSA.8.1.A.5: “Row-major order” refers to an ordering of 2D array elements where traversal occurs across each row, while “column-major order” traversal occurs down each column.
AP.CSA.8.2.A: For 2D array objects, traverse using nested `tttext(for)` loops and traverse using nested enhanced `tttext(for)` loops.
AP.CSA.8.2.A.1: Nested iteration statements are used to traverse and access all elements in a 2D array. Since 2D arrays are stored as arrays of arrays, the way 2D arrays are traversed using for loops and enhanced for loops is similar to 1D array objects.
AP.CSA.8.2.A.2: Nested iteration statements can be written to traverse the 2D array in “row-major order” or “column-major order.”
AP.CSA.8.2.A.3: The outer loop of a nested enhanced for loop used to traverse a 2D array traverses the rows. Therefore, the enhanced for loop variable must be the type of each row, which is a 1D array. The inner loop traverses a single row. Therefore, the inner enhanced for loop variable must be the same type as the elements stored in the 1D array.
AP.CSA.8.2.B: For algorithms in the context of a particular specification that requires the use of 2D array traversals, identify standard algorithms, modify standard algorithms, and develop an algorithm.
AP.CSA.8.2.B.1: When applying sequential/linear search algorithms to 2D arrays, each row must be accessed then sequential/linear search applied to each row of a 2D array.
AP.CSA.8.2.B.2: All standard 1D array algorithms can be applied to 2D array objects.
AP.CSA.9.1.A: Create an inheritance relationship from a subclass to the superclass.
AP.CSA.9.1.A.1: A class hierarchy can be developed by putting common attributes and behaviors of related classes into a single class called a superclass.
AP.CSA.9.1.A.2: Classes that extend a superclass, called subclasses, can draw upon the existing attributes and behaviors of the superclass without repeating these in the code.
AP.CSA.9.1.A.3: Extending a subclass from a superclass creates an “is-a” relationship from the subclass to the superclass.
AP.CSA.9.1.A.4: The keyword `tttext(extends)` is used to establish an inheritance relationship between a subclass and a superclass. A class can extend only one superclass.
AP.CSA.9.2.A: Create an inheritance relationship from a subclass to the superclass.
AP.CSA.9.2.A.2: The superclass constructor can be called from the first line of a subclass constructor by using the keyword `tttext(super)` and passing appropriate parameters.
AP.CSA.9.2.A.3: The actual parameters passed in the call to the superclass constructor provide values that the constructor can use to initialize the object's instance variables.
AP.CSA.9.2.A.4: When a subclass's constructor does not explicitly call a superclass's constructor using super, Java inserts a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor.
AP.CSA.9.2.A.5: Regardless of whether the superclass constructor is called implicitly or explicitly, the process of calling superclass constructors continues until the `tttext(Object)` constructor is called. At this point, all of the constructors within the hierarchy execute beginning with the `tttext(Object)` constructor.
AP.CSA.9.3.A: Create an inheritance relationship from a subclass to the superclass.
AP.CSA.9.3.A.1: Method overriding occurs when a public method in a subclass has the same method signature as a public method in the superclass.
AP.CSA.9.3.A.2: Any method that is called must be defined within its own class or its superclass.
AP.CSA.9.3.A.3: A subclass is usually designed to have modified (overridden) or additional methods or instance variables.
AP.CSA.9.3.A.4: A subclass will inherit all public methods from the superclass; these methods remain public in the subclass.
AP.CSA.9.4.A: Create an inheritance relationship from a subclass to the superclass.
AP.CSA.9.4.A.1: The keyword `tttext(super)` can be used to call a superclass's constructors and methods.
AP.CSA.9.4.A.2: The superclass method can be called in a subclass by using the keyword `tttext(super)` with the method name and passing appropriate parameters.
AP.CSA.9.5.A: Define reference variables of a superclass to be assigned to an object of a subclass in the same hierarchy.
AP.CSA.9.5.A.1: When a class `tt(S)` “is-a” class `tt(T)`, `tt(T)` is referred to as a superclass, and `tt(S)` is referred to as a subclass.
AP.CSA.9.5.A.2: If `tt(S)` is a subclass of `tt(T)`, then assigning an object of type `tt(S)` to a reference of type `tt(T)` facilitates polymorphism.
AP.CSA.9.5.A.3: If `tt(S)` is a subclass of `tt(T)`, then a reference of type `tt(T)` can be used to refer to an object of type `tt(T)` or `tt(S)`.
AP.CSA.9.5.A.4: Declaring references of type `tt(T)`, when `tt(S)` is a subclass of `tt(T)`, is useful in the following declarations: formal method parameters and arrays - `tt(T[] text(var ArrayList)<T> text(var))`.
AP.CSA.9.6.A: Call methods in an inheritance relationship.
AP.CSA.9.6.A.2: At compile time, methods in or inherited by the declared type determine the correctness of a non-static method call.
AP.CSA.9.6.A.3: At run-time, the method in the actual object type is executed for a non-static method call.
AP.CSA.9.7.A.1: The `tttext(Object)` class is the superclass of all other classes in Java.
AP.CSA.9.7.A.2: The `tttext(Object)` class is part of the `tttext(java.lang)` package.
AP.CSA.9.7.A.3: The following `tttext(Object)` class methods and constructors - including what they do and when they are used - are part of the Java Quick Reference:
AP.CSA.9.7.A.4: Subclasses of `tttext(Object)` often override the `tttext(equals)` and `tttext(toString)` methods with class-specific implementations.
AP.CSA.10.1.A: Determine the result of executing recursive methods.
AP.CSA.10.1.A.1: A recursive method is a method that calls itself.
AP.CSA.10.1.A.2: Recursive methods contain at least one base case, which halts the recursion, and at least one recursive call.
AP.CSA.10.1.A.3: Each recursive call has its own set of local variables, including the formal parameters.
AP.CSA.10.1.A.4: Parameter values capture the progress of a recursive process, much like loop control variable values capture the progress of a loop.
AP.CSA.10.1.A.5: Any recursive solution can be replicated through the use of an iterative approach.
AP.CSA.10.1.A.6: Recursion can be used to traverse `tttext(String)`, array, and `tttext(ArrayList)` objects.
AP.CSA.10.2.A: Apply recursive search algorithms to information in `tttext(String)`, 1D array, or `tttext(ArrayList)` objects.
AP.CSA.10.2.A.1: Data must be in sorted order to use the binary search algorithm.
AP.CSA.10.2.A.2: The binary search algorithm starts at the middle of a sorted array or `tttext(ArrayList)` and eliminates half of the array or `tttext(ArrayList)` in each iteration until the desired value is found or all elements have been eliminated.
AP.CSA.10.2.A.3: Binary search can be more efficient than sequential/linear search.
AP.CSA.10.2.A.4: The binary search algorithm can be written either iteratively or recursively.
AP.CSA.10.2.B: Apply recursive algorithms to sort elements of array or `tttext(ArrayList)` objects.
AP.CSA.10.2.B.1: Merge sort is a recursive sorting algorithm that can be used to sort elements in an array or `tttext(ArrayList)`.
AP.CSP.1.1.A: Explain how computing innovations are improved through collaboration.
AP.CSP.1.1.A.1: A computing innovation includes a program as an integral part of its function.
AP.CSP.1.1.A.2: A computing innovation can be physical (e.g., self-driving car), nonphysical computing software (e.g., picture editing software), or a nonphysical computing concept (e.g., e-commerce).
AP.CSP.1.1.A.3: Effective collaboration produces a computing innovation that reflects the diversity of talents and perspectives of those who designed it.
AP.CSP.1.1.A.4: Collaboration that includes diverse perspectives helps avoid bias in the development of computing innovations.
AP.CSP.1.1.A.5: Consultation and communication with users are important aspects of the development of computing innovations.
AP.CSP.1.1.A.6: Information gathered from potential users can be used to understand the purpose of a program from diverse perspectives and to develop a program that fully incorporates these perspectives.
AP.CSP.1.1.B: Explain how computing innovations are developed by groups of people.
AP.CSP.1.1.B.1: Online tools support collaboration by allowing programmers to share and provide feedback on ideas and documents.
AP.CSP.1.1.B.2: Common models such as pair programming exist to facilitate collaboration.
AP.CSP.1.1.C: Demonstrate effective interpersonal skills during collaboration.
Effective collaborative teams practice interpersonal skills, including but not limited to communication, consensus building, conflict resolution, and negotiation.
AP.CSP.1.2.A: Describe the purpose of a computing innovation.
AP.CSP.1.2.A.1: The purpose of computing innovations is to solve problems or to pursue interests through creative expression.
AP.CSP.1.2.A.2: An understanding of the purpose of a computing innovation provides developers with an improved ability to develop that computing innovation.
AP.CSP.1.2.B: Explain how a program or code segment functions.
AP.CSP.1.2.B.1: A program is a collection of program statements that performs a specific task when run by a computer. A program is often referred to as software.
AP.CSP.1.2.B.2: A code segment is a collection of program statements that is part of a program.
AP.CSP.1.2.B.3: A program needs to work for a variety of inputs and situations.
AP.CSP.1.2.B.4: The behavior of a program is how a program functions during execution and is often described by how a user interacts with it.
AP.CSP.1.2.B.5: A program can be described broadly by what it does, or in more detail by both what the program does and how the program statements accomplish this function.
AP.CSP.1.2.C.1: Program inputs are data sent to a computer for processing by a program. Input can come in a variety of forms, such as tactile, audio, visual, or text.
AP.CSP.1.2.C.2: An event is associated with an action and supplies input data to a program.
AP.CSP.1.2.C.3: Events can be generated when a key is pressed, a mouse is clicked, a program is started, or any other defined action occurs that affects the flow of execution.
AP.CSP.1.2.C.4: Inputs usually affect the output produced by a program.
AP.CSP.1.2.C.5: In event-driven programming, program statements are executed when triggered rather than through the sequential flow of control.
AP.CSP.1.2.C.6: Input can come from a user or other programs.
AP.CSP.1.2.D: Identify output(s) produced by a program.
AP.CSP.1.2.D.1: Program outputs are any data sent from a program to a device. Program output can come in a variety of forms, such as tactile, audio, visual, or text.
AP.CSP.1.2.D.2: Program output is usually based on a program's input or prior state (e.g., internal values).
AP.CSP.1.3.A: Develop a program using a development process.
AP.CSP.1.3.A.1: A development process can be ordered and intentional, or exploratory in nature.
AP.CSP.1.3.A.2: There are multiple development processes. The following phases are commonly used when developing a program: investigating and reflecting, designing, prototyping, and testing.
AP.CSP.1.3.A.3: A development process that is iterative requires refinement and revision based on feedback, testing, or reflection throughout the process. This may require revisiting earlier phases of the process.
AP.CSP.1.3.A.4: A development process that is incremental is one that breaks the problem into smaller pieces and makes sure each piece works before adding it to the whole.
AP.CSP.1.3.B: Design a program and its user interface.
AP.CSP.1.3.B.1: The design of a program incorporates investigation to determine its requirements.
AP.CSP.1.3.B.2: Investigation in a development process is useful for understanding and identifying the program constraints, as well as the concerns and interests of the people who will use the program.
AP.CSP.1.3.B.3: Some ways investigation can be performed are as follows: collecting data through surveys, user testing, interviews, and direct observations.
AP.CSP.1.3.B.4: Program requirements describe how a program functions and may include a description of user interactions that a program must provide.
AP.CSP.1.3.B.5: A program's specification defines the requirements for the program.
AP.CSP.1.3.B.6: In a development process, the design phase outlines how to accomplish a given program specification.
AP.CSP.1.3.B.7: The design phase of a program may include brainstorming, planning and storyboarding, organizing the program into modules and functional components, creation of diagrams that represent the layouts of the user interface, and development of a testing strategy for the program.
AP.CSP.1.3.C: Describe the purpose of a code segment or program by writing documentation.
AP.CSP.1.3.C.1: Program documentation is a written description of the function of a code segment, event, procedure, or program and how it was developed.
AP.CSP.1.3.C.2: Comments are a form of program documentation written into the program to be read by people and do not affect how a program runs.
AP.CSP.1.3.C.3: Programmers should document a program throughout its development.
AP.CSP.1.3.C.4: Program documentation helps in developing and maintaining correct programs when working individually or in collaborative programming environments.
AP.CSP.1.3.C.5: Not all programming environments support comments, so other methods of documentation may be required.
AP.CSP.1.3.D: Acknowledge code segments used from other sources.
AP.CSP.1.3.D.1: It is important to acknowledge any code segments that were developed collaboratively or by another source.
AP.CSP.1.3.D.2: Acknowledgement of a code segment(s) written by someone else and used in a program can be in the program documentation. The acknowledgement should include the origin or original author's name.
AP.CSP.1.4.A: For errors in an algorithm or program, identify the error and correct the error.
AP.CSP.1.4.A.1: A logic error is a mistake in the algorithm or program that causes it to behave incorrectly or unexpectedly.
AP.CSP.1.4.A.2: A syntax error is a mistake in the program where the rules of the programming language are not followed.
AP.CSP.1.4.A.3: A run-time error is a mistake in the program that occurs during the execution of a program. Programming languages define their own run-time errors.
AP.CSP.1.4.A.4: An overflow error is an error that occurs when a computer attempts to handle a number that is outside of the defined range of values.
AP.CSP.1.4.A.5: The following are effective ways to find and correct errors: test cases, hand tracing, visualizations, debuggers, and adding extra output statement(s).
AP.CSP.1.4.B: Identify inputs and corresponding expected outputs or behaviors that can be used to check the correctness of an algorithm or program.
AP.CSP.1.4.B.1: In the development process, testing uses defined inputs to ensure that an algorithm or program is producing the expected outcomes. Programmers use the results from testing to revise their algorithms or programs.
AP.CSP.1.4.B.2: Defined inputs used to test a program should demonstrate the different expected outcomes that are at or just beyond the extremes (minimum and maximum) of input data.
AP.CSP.1.4.B.3: Program requirements are needed to identify appropriate defined inputs for testing.
AP.CSP.2.1.A: Explain how data can be represented using bits.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.1: Data values can be stored in variables, lists of items, or standalone constants and can be passed as input to (or output from) procedures.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.2: Computing devices represent data digitally, meaning that the lowest-level components of any value are bits.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.3: Bit is shorthand for binary digit and is either `tt(0)` or `tt(1)`.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.5: Abstraction is the process of reducing complexity by focusing on the main idea. By hiding details irrelevant to the question at hand and bringing together related and useful details, abstraction reduces complexity and allows one to focus on the idea.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.6: Bits are grouped to represent abstractions. These abstractions include, but are not limited to, numbers, characters, and color.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.7: The same sequence of bits may represent different types of data in different contexts.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.8: Analog data have values that change smoothly, rather than in discrete intervals, over time. Some examples of analog data include pitch and volume of music, colors of a painting, or position of a sprinter during a race.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.9: The use of digital data to approximate real-world analog data is an example of abstraction.
AP.CSP.2.1.A.10: Analog data can be closely approximated digitally using a sampling technique, which means measuring values of the analog signal at regular intervals called samples. The samples are measured to figure out the exact bits required to store each sample.
AP.CSP.2.1.B: Explain the consequences of using bits to represent data.
AP.CSP.2.1.B.1: In many programming languages, integers are represented by a fixed number of bits, which limits the range of integer values and mathematical operations on those values. This limitation can result in overflow or other errors.
AP.CSP.2.1.B.2: Other programming languages provide an abstraction through which the size of representable integers is limited only by the size of the computer's memory; this is the case for the language defined in the exam reference sheet.
AP.CSP.2.1.B.3: In programming languages, the fixed number of bits used to represent real numbers limits the range and mathematical operations on these values; this limitation can result in round-off and other errors. Some real numbers are represented as approximations in computer storage.
AP.CSP.2.1.C: For binary numbers, calculate the binary (base `2`) equivalent of a positive integer (base `10`) and vice versa and compare and order binary numbers.
AP.CSP.2.1.C.1: Number bases, including binary and decimal, are used to represent data.
AP.CSP.2.1.C.2: Binary (base 2) uses only combinations of the digits zero and one.
AP.CSP.2.1.C.3: Decimal (base 10) uses only combinations of the digits `tt(0-9)`.
AP.CSP.2.1.C.4: As with decimal, a digit's position in the binary sequence determines its numeric value. The numeric value is equal to the bit's value (0 or 1) multiplied by the place value of its position.
AP.CSP.2.1.C.5: The place value of each position is determined by the base raised to the power of the position. Positions are numbered starting at the rightmost position with `tt(0)` and increasing by `tt(1)` for each subsequent position to the left.
AP.CSP.2.2.A: Compare data compression algorithms to determine which is best in a particular context.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.1: Data compression can reduce the size (number of bits) of transmitted or stored data.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.2: Fewer bits does not necessarily mean less information.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.3: The amount of size reduction from compression depends on both the amount of redundancy in the original data representation and the compression algorithm applied.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.4: Lossless data compression algorithms can usually reduce the number of bits stored or transmitted while guaranteeing complete reconstruction of the original data.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.5: Lossy data compression algorithms can significantly reduce the number of bits stored or transmitted but only allow reconstruction of an approximation of the original data.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.6: Lossy data compression algorithms can usually reduce the number of bits stored or transmitted more than lossless compression algorithms.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.7: In situations where quality or ability to reconstruct the original is maximally important, lossless compression algorithms are typically chosen.
AP.CSP.2.2.A.8: In situations where minimizing data size or transmission time is maximally important, lossy compression algorithms are typically chosen.
AP.CSP.2.3.A: Describe what information can be extracted from data.
AP.CSP.2.3.A.1: Information is the collection of facts and patterns extracted from data.
AP.CSP.2.3.A.2: Data provide opportunities for identifying trends, making connections, and addressing problems.
AP.CSP.2.3.A.3: Digitally processed data may show correlation between variables. A correlation found in data does not necessarily indicate that a causal relationship exists. Additional research is needed to understand the exact nature of the relationship.
AP.CSP.2.3.A.4: Often, a single source does not contain the data needed to draw a conclusion. It may be necessary to combine data from a variety of sources to formulate a conclusion.
AP.CSP.2.3.B: Describe what information can be extracted from metadata.
AP.CSP.2.3.B.1: Metadata are data about data. For example, the piece of data may be an image, while the metadata may include the date of creation or the file size of the image.
AP.CSP.2.3.B.2: Changes and deletions made to metadata do not change the primary data.
AP.CSP.2.3.B.3: Metadata are used for finding, organizing, and managing information.
AP.CSP.2.3.B.4: Metadata can increase the effective use of data or data sets by providing additional information.
AP.CSP.2.3.B.5: Metadata allow data to be structured and organized.
AP.CSP.2.3.C: Identify the challenges associated with processing data.
AP.CSP.2.3.C.1: The ability to process data depends on the capabilities of the users and their tools.
AP.CSP.2.3.C.2: Data sets pose challenges regardless of size, such as the need to clean data, incomplete data, invalid data, and the need to combine data sources.
AP.CSP.2.3.C.3: Depending on how data were collected, they may not be uniform. For example, if users enter data into an open field, the way they choose to abbreviate, spell, or capitalize something may vary from user to user.
AP.CSP.2.3.C.4: Cleaning data is a process that makes the data uniform without changing their meaning (e.g., replacing all equivalent abbreviations, spellings, and capitalizations with the same word).
AP.CSP.2.3.C.5: Problems of bias are often created by the type or source of data being collected. Bias is not eliminated by simply collecting more data.
AP.CSP.2.3.C.6: The size of a data set affects the amount of information that can be extracted from it.
AP.CSP.2.3.C.7: Large data sets are difficult to process using a single computer and may require parallel systems.
AP.CSP.2.3.C.8: Scalability of systems is an important consideration when working with data sets, as the computational capacity of a system affects how data sets can be processed and stored.
AP.CSP.2.4.A: Extract information from data using a program.
AP.CSP.2.4.A.1: Programs can be used to process data to acquire information.
AP.CSP.2.4.A.2: Tables, diagrams, text, and other visual tools can be used to communicate insight and knowledge gained from data.
AP.CSP.2.4.A.3: Search tools are useful for efficiently finding information.
AP.CSP.2.4.A.4: Data filtering systems are important tools for finding information and recognizing patterns in data.
AP.CSP.2.4.A.5: Programs such as spreadsheets help efficiently organize and find trends in information.
AP.CSP.2.4.A.6: Some processes that can be used to extract or modify information from data include the following: transforming every element of a data set, such as doubling every element in a list, or adding a parent's email to every student record,  filtering a data set, such as keeping only the positive numbers from a list, or keeping only students who signed up for band from a record of all the students, combining or comparing data in some way, such as adding up a list of numbers, or finding the student who has the highest GPA, and visualizing a data set through a chart, graph, or other visual representation
AP.CSP.2.4.B: Explain how programs can be used to gain insight and knowledge from data.
AP.CSP.2.4.B.1: Programs are used in an iterative and interactive way when processing information to allow users to gain insight and knowledge about data.
AP.CSP.2.4.B.2: Programmers can use programs to filter and clean digital data, thereby gaining insight and knowledge.
AP.CSP.2.4.B.3: Combining data sources, clustering data, and classifying data are parts of the process of using programs to gain insight and knowledge from data.
AP.CSP.2.4.B.4: Insight and knowledge can be obtained from translating and transforming digitally represented information.
AP.CSP.2.4.B.5: Patterns can emerge when data are transformed using programs.
AP.CSP.3.1.A: Represent a value with a variable.
AP.CSP.3.1.A.1: A variable is an abstraction inside a program that can hold a value. Each variable has associated data storage that represents one value at a time, but that value can be a list or other collection that in turn contains multiple values.
AP.CSP.3.1.A.2: Using meaningful variable names helps with the readability of program code and understanding of what values are represented by the variables.
AP.CSP.3.1.A.3: Some programming languages provide types to represent data, which are referenced using variables. These types include numbers, Booleans, lists, and strings.
AP.CSP.3.1.A.4: Some values are better suited to representation using one type of datum rather than another.
AP.CSP.3.1.B: Determine the value of a variable as a result of an assignment.
AP.CSP.3.1.B.1: The assignment operator allows a program to change the value represented by a variable.
AP.CSP.3.1.B.2: The exam reference sheet provides the “tt(larr)” operator to use for assignment. For example, `tt(text(a)larrtext(expression))` evaluates `tttext(expression)` and then assigns a copy of the result to the variable `tt(a).
AP.CSP.3.1.B.3: The value stored in a variable will be the most recent value assigned. For example: `tt(text(a)larr1)`; `tt(text(b)larrtext(a))`; `tt(text(a)larr2)`; `tt(text(display)(text(b)))` still displays `tt(1)`.
AP.CSP.3.2.A: Represent a list or string using a variable.
AP.CSP.3.2.A.1: A list is an ordered sequence of elements. For example, `tt([text(value1),text(value2),text(value3),...])` describes a list where `tttext(value1)` is the first element, `tttext(value2)` is the second element, `tttext(value3)` is the third element, and so on.
AP.CSP.3.2.A.2: An element is an individual value in a list that is assigned a unique index.
AP.CSP.3.2.A.3: An index is a common method for referencing the elements in a list or string using natural numbers.
AP.CSP.3.2.A.4: A string is an ordered sequence of characters.
AP.CSP.3.2.B: For data abstraction, develop data abstraction using lists to store multiple elements and explain how the use of data abstraction manages complexity in program code.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.1: Data abstraction provides a separation between the abstract properties of a data type and the concrete details of its representation.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.2: Data abstractions manage complexity in programs by giving a collection of data a name without referencing the specific details of the representation.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.3: Data abstractions can be created using lists.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.4: Developing a data abstraction to implement in a program can result in a program that is easier to develop and maintain.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.5: Data abstractions often contain different types of elements.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.6: The use of lists allows multiple related items to be treated as a single value. Lists are referred to by different names, such as array, depending on the programming language.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.7: The exam reference sheet provides the notation `tt([text(value1,value2,value3,...)])` to create a list with those values as the first, second, third, and so on items.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.7.a: `tt(text(aList)larr[text(value1),text(value2),text(value3),...])` creates a new list that contains the values `tttext(value1)`, `tttext(value2)`, `tttext(value3)`, and `tt(...)` at indices `tt(1)`, `tt(2)`, `tt(3)`, and `tt(...)` respectively and assigns it to `tttext(aList)`.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.7.b: `tt(text(aList)larr[])` creates a new empty list and assigns it to `tttext(aList)`.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.7.c: `tt(text(aList)larrtext(bList))` assigns a copy of the list `tttext(bList)` to the list `tttext(aList)`. For example, if `tttext(bList)` contains `tt([text(20,40,60)])`, then `tttext(aList)` will also contain `tt([text(20,40,60)])` after the assignment.
AP.CSP.3.2.B.8: The exam reference sheet describes a list structure whose index values are 1 through the number of elements in the list, inclusive. For all list operations, if a list index is less than 1 or greater than the length of the list, an error message is produced and the program will terminate.
AP.CSP.3.3.A: Express an algorithm that uses sequencing without using a programming language.
AP.CSP.3.3.A.1: An algorithm is a finite set of instructions that accomplish a specific task.
AP.CSP.3.3.A.2: Beyond visual and textual programming languages, algorithms can be expressed in a variety of ways, such as natural language, diagrams, and pseudocode.
AP.CSP.3.3.A.3: Algorithms executed by programs are implemented using programming languages.
AP.CSP.3.3.A.4: Every algorithm can be constructed using combinations of sequencing, selection, and iteration.
AP.CSP.3.3.B: Represent a step-by-step algorithmic process using sequential code statements.
AP.CSP.3.3.B.1: Sequencing is the application of each step of an algorithm in the order in which the code statements are given.
AP.CSP.3.3.B.2: A code statement is a part of program code that expresses an action to be carried out.
AP.CSP.3.3.B.3: An expression can consist of a value, a variable, an operator, or a procedure call that returns a value.
AP.CSP.3.3.B.4: Expressions are evaluated to produce a single value.
AP.CSP.3.3.B.5: The evaluation of expressions follows a set order of operations defined by the programming language.
AP.CSP.3.3.B.6: Sequential statements execute in the order they appear in the code segment.
AP.CSP.3.3.B.7: Clarity and readability are important considerations when expressing an algorithm in a programming language.
AP.CSP.3.3.C: Evaluate expressions that use arithmetic operators.
AP.CSP.3.3.C.1: Arithmetic operators are part of most programming languages and include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus operators.
AP.CSP.3.3.C.2: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text( MOD )b)`, which evaluates to the remainder when `tt(a)` is divided by `tt(b)`. Assume that `tt(a)` is an integer greater than or equal to `tt(0)` and `tt(b)` is an integer greater than `tt(0)`. For example, `tt(17text( MOD )5)` evaluates to `tt(2)`.
AP.CSP.3.3.C.3: The exam reference sheet provides the arithmetic operators `tt(+)`, `tt(-)`, `tt(**)`, `tt(//)`, and `tttext(MOD)`: `tt(text(a)+text(b))`, `tt(text(a)-text(b))`, `tt(text(a)**text(b))`, `tt(text(a)//text(b))`, and `tttext(a MOD b)`. These are used to perform arithmetic on a and b. For example, `tt(17//5)` evaluates to `tt(3.4)`.
AP.CSP.3.3.C.4: The order of operations used in mathematics applies when evaluating expressions. The `tttext(MOD)` operator has the same precedence as the `**` and `//` operators.
AP.CSP.3.4.A.1: String concatenation joins together two or more strings end-to-end to make a new string.
AP.CSP.3.4.A.2: A substring is part of an existing string.
AP.CSP.3.5.A: For relationships between two variables, expressions, or values, write expressions using relational operators and evaluate expressions that use relational operators.
AP.CSP.3.5.A.1: A Boolean value is either true or false.
AP.CSP.3.5.A.2: The exam reference sheet provides the following relational operators: `tt(=)`, `tt(!=)`, `tt(>)`, `tt(<)`, `tt(>=)`, and `tt(<=)`: `tt(text(a)=text(b))`, `tt(text(a)!=text(b))`, `tt(text(a)>text(b))`, `tt(text(a)<text(b))`, `tt(text(a)>=text(b))`, and `tt(text(a)<=text(b))`. These are used to test the relationship between two variables, expressions, or values. A comparison using a relational operator evaluates to a Boolean value. For example, `tt(text(a)=text(b))` evaluates to `tttext(true)` if `tt(a)` and `tt(b)` are equal; otherwise, it evaluates to `tttext(false)`.
AP.CSP.3.5.B: For relationships between Boolean values, write expressions using logical operators and evaluate expressions that use logic operators.
AP.CSP.3.5.B.1: The exam reference sheet provides the logical operators `tttext(NOT)`, `tttext(AND)`, and `tttext(OR)`, which evaluate to a Boolean value.
AP.CSP.3.5.B.2: The exam reference sheet provides `tttext(NOT condition)` which evaluates to `tttext(true)` if `tttext(condition)` is `tttext(false)`; otherwise it evaluates to `tttext(false)`.
AP.CSP.3.5.B.3: The exam reference sheet provides `tttext(condition1 AND condition2)` which evaluates to `tttext(true)` if both `tttext(condition1)` and `tttext(condition2)` are `tttext(true)`; otherwise it evaluates to `tttext(false)`.
AP.CSP.3.5.B.4: The exam reference sheet provides `tttext(condition1 OR condition2)` which evaluates to `tttext(true)` if `tttext(condition1)` is `tttext(true)` or if `tttext(condition2)` is `tttext(true)` or if both `tttext(condition1)` and `tttext(condition2)` are `tttext(true)`; otherwise it evaluates to `tttext(false)`.
AP.CSP.3.5.B.5: The operand for a logical operator is either a Boolean expression or a single Boolean value.
AP.CSP.3.6.A: Express an algorithm that uses selection without using a programming language.
AP.CSP.3.6.A.1: Selection determines which parts of an algorithm are executed based on a condition being `tttext(true)` or `tttext(false)`.
AP.CSP.3.6.B: For selection, write conditional statements and determine the result of conditional statements.
AP.CSP.3.6.B.1: Conditional statements, or “if-statements,” affect the sequential flow of control by executing different statements based on the value of a Boolean expression.
AP.CSP.3.6.B.2: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(IF)(text(condition)) { <text(block of statements)> })` in which the code in `tttext(block of statements)` is executed if the Boolean expression `tttext(condition)` evaluates to `tttext(true)`; no action is taken if `tttext(condition)` evaluates to `tttext(false)`.
AP.CSP.3.6.B.3: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(IF)(text(condition)) { <text(first block of statements)> }; text(ELSE) { <text(second block of statements)> })` in which the code in `tttext(first block of statements)` is executed if the Boolean expression `tttext(condition)` evaluates to `tttext(true)`; otherwise, the code in `tttext(second block of statements)` is executed.
AP.CSP.3.7.A: For nested selection, write nested conditional statements and determine the result of nested conditional statements.
AP.CSP.3.7.A.1: Nested conditional statements consist of conditional statements within conditional statements.
AP.CSP.3.8.A: Express an algorithm that uses iteration without using a programming language.
AP.CSP.3.8.A.1: Iteration is a repeating portion of an algorithm. Iteration repeats a specified number of times or until a given condition is met.
AP.CSP.3.8.B: For iteration, write iteration statements and determine the result or side effect of iteration statements.
AP.CSP.3.8.B.1: Iteration statements change the sequential flow of control by repeating a set of statements zero or more times, until a stopping condition is met.
AP.CSP.3.8.B.2: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(REPEAT n TIMES) { <text(block of statements)> })` in which the `tttext(block of statements)` is executed `tttext(n)` times.
AP.CSP.3.8.B.3: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(REPEAT UNTIL)(text(condition)) { <text(block of statements)> })` in which the code in `tttext(block of statements)` is repeated until the Boolean expression `tttext(condition)` evaluates to `tttext(true)`.
AP.CSP.3.8.B.4: In `tt(text(REPEAT UNTIL)(text(condition)))` iteration, an infinite loop occurs when the ending condition will never evaluate to `tttext(true)`.
AP.CSP.3.8.B.5: In `tt(text(REPEAT UNTIL)(text(condition)))` iteration, if the conditional evaluates to `tttext(true)` initially, the loop body is not executed at all, due to the condition being checked before the loop.
AP.CSP.3.9.A: Compare multiple algorithms to determine if they yield the same side effect or result.
AP.CSP.3.9.A.1: Algorithms can be written in different ways and still accomplish the same tasks.
AP.CSP.3.9.A.2: Algorithms that appear similar can yield different side effects or results.
AP.CSP.3.9.A.3: Some conditional statements can be written as equivalent Boolean expressions.
AP.CSP.3.9.A.4: Some Boolean expressions can be written as equivalent conditional statements.
AP.CSP.3.9.A.5: Different algorithms can be developed or used to solve the same problem.
AP.CSP.3.9.B: For algorithms, create algorithms and combine and modify existing algorithms.
AP.CSP.3.9.B.1: Algorithms can be created from an idea, by combining existing algorithms, or by modifying existing algorithms.
AP.CSP.3.9.B.2: Knowledge of existing algorithms can help in constructing new ones. Some existing algorithms include determining the maximum or minimum value of two or more numbers, computing the sum or average of two or more numbers, identifying if an integer is or is not evenly divisible by another integer, and determining a robot's path through a maze.
AP.CSP.3.9.B.3: Using existing correct algorithms as building blocks for constructing another algorithm has benefits such as reducing development time, reducing testing, and simplifying the identification of errors.
AP.CSP.3.10.A: For list operations, write expressions that use list indexing and list procedures and evaluate expressions that use list indexing and list procedures.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1: The exam reference sheet provides basic operations on lists, including:
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1.a: Accessing an element by index. `tt(text(aList)[text(i)])` accesses the element of `tttext(aList)` at index `tttext(i)`. The first element of `tttext(aList)` is at index `tt(1)` and is accessed using the notation `tt(text(aList)[1])`.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1.b: Assigning a value of an element of a list to a variable. `tt(text(x)larrtext(aList)[text(i)])` assigns the value of `tt(text(aList)[text(i)])` to the variable `tttext(x)`.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1.c: Assigning a value to an element of a list. `tt(text(aList)[text(i)]larrtext(x))` assigns the value of `tttext(x)` to `tt(text(aList)[text(i)])` and `tt(text(aList)[text(i)]larrtext(aList)[text(j)])` assigns the value of `tt(text(aList)[text(j)])` to `tt(text(aList)[text(i)])`.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1.d: Inserting elements at a given index. `tt(text(INSERT)(text(aList),text(i),text(value)))` shifts to the right any values in `tttext(aList)` at indices greater than or equal to `tttext(i)`. The length of the list is increased by `tt(1)`, and `tttext(value)` is placed at index `tttext(i)` in `tttext(aList)`.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1.e: Adding elements to the end of the list. `tt(text(APPEND)(text(aList),text(value)))` increases the length of `tttext(aList)` by `tt(1)`, and `tttext(value)` is placed at the end of `tttext(aList)`.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1.f: Removing elements. `tt(text(REMOVE)(text(aList),text(i)))` removes the item at index `tttext(i)` in `tttext(aList)` and shifts to the left any values at indices greater than `tttext(i)`. The length of `tttext(aList)` is decreased by `tt(1)`.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.1.g: Determining the length of a list. `tt(text(LENGTH)(text(aList)))` evaluates to the number of elements currently in `tttext(aList)`.
AP.CSP.3.10.A.2: List procedures are implemented in accordance with the syntax rules of the programming language.
AP.CSP.3.10.B: For algorithms involving elements of a list, write iteration statements to traverse a list and determine the result of an algorithm that includes list traversals.
AP.CSP.3.10.B.1: Traversing a list can be a complete traversal, where all elements in the list are accessed, or a partial traversal, where only a portion of elements are accessed.
AP.CSP.3.10.B.2: Iteration statements can be used to traverse a list.
AP.CSP.3.10.B.3: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(FOR EACH item IN aList) { <text(block of statements)> })`. The variable `tttext(item)` is assigned the value of each element of `tttext(aList)` sequentially, in order, from the first element to the last element. The code in `tttext(block of statements)` is executed once for each assignment of `tttext(item)`.
AP.CSP.3.10.B.4: Knowledge of existing algorithms that use iteration can help in constructing new algorithms. Some examples of existing algorithms that are often used with lists include determining a minimum or maximum value in a list and computing a sum or average of a list of numbers.
AP.CSP.3.10.B.5: Linear search or sequential search algorithms check each element of a list, in order, until the desired value is found or all elements in the list have been checked.
