AP.CSP.3.11.A: For binary search algorithms, determine the number of iterations required to find a value in a data set and explain the requirements necessary to complete a binary search.
AP.CSP.3.11.A.1: The binary search algorithm starts at the middle of a sorted data set of numbers and eliminates half of the data; this process repeats until the desired value is found or all elements have been eliminated.
AP.CSP.3.11.A.2: Data must be in sorted order to use the binary search algorithm.
AP.CSP.3.11.A.3: Binary search is often more efficient than sequential/linear search when applied to sorted data.
AP.CSP.3.12.A: For procedure calls, write statements to call procedures and determine the result or effect of a procedure call.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.1: A procedure is a named group of programming instructions that may have parameters and return values.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.2: Procedures are referred to by different names, such as method or function, depending on the programming language.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.3: Parameters are input variables of a procedure. Arguments specify the values of the parameters when a procedure is called.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.4: A procedure call interrupts the sequential execution of statements, causing the program to execute the statements within the procedure before continuing. Once the last statement in the procedure (or a return statement) has executed, flow of control is returned to the point immediately following where the procedure was called.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.5: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(procName)(text(arg1),text(arg2),...))` as a way to call `tt(text(PROCEDURE procName)(text(parameter1),text(parameter2),...) { <text(block of statements)> })` which takes zero or more arguments; `tttext(arg1)` is assigned to `tttext(parameter1)`, `tttext(arg2)` is assigned to `tttext(parameter2)`, and so on.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.6: The exam reference sheet provides the procedure `tt(text(DISPLAY)(text(expression)))` to display the value of `tttext(expression)`, followed by a space.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.7: The exam reference sheet provides the `tt(text(RETURN)(text(expression)))` statement, which is used to return the flow of control to the point where the procedure was called and to return the value of `tttext(expression)`.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.8: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(result procName)(text(arg1),text(arg2),...))` to assign to `tttext(result)` the “value of the procedure” being returned by calling `tt(text(PROCEDURE procName)(text(parameter1),text(parameter2),...) { <text(block of statements)>; text(RETURN)(text(expression)) })`.
AP.CSP.3.12.A.9: The exam reference sheet provides procedure `tt(text(INPUT)())` which accepts a value from the user and returns the input value.
AP.CSP.3.13.A: Explain how the use of procedural abstraction manages complexity in a program.
AP.CSP.3.13.A.1: One common type of abstraction is procedural abstraction, which provides a name for a process and allows a procedure to be used only knowing what it does, not how it does it.
AP.CSP.3.13.A.2: Procedural abstraction allows a solution to a large problem to be based on the solutions of smaller subproblems. This is accomplished by creating procedures to solve each of the subproblems.
AP.CSP.3.13.A.3: The subdivision of a computer program into separate subprograms is called modularity.
AP.CSP.3.13.A.4: A procedural abstraction may extract shared features to generalize functionality instead of duplicating code. This allows for program code reuse, which helps manage complexity.
AP.CSP.3.13.A.5: Using parameters allows procedures to be generalized, enabling the procedures to be reused with a range of input values or arguments.
AP.CSP.3.13.A.6: Using procedural abstraction helps improve code readability.
AP.CSP.3.13.A.7: Using procedural abstraction in a program allows programmers to change the internals of the procedure (to make it faster, more efficient, use less storage, etc.) without needing to notify users of the change as long as what the procedure does is preserved.
AP.CSP.3.13.B: Develop procedural abstractions to manage complexity in a program by writing procedures.
AP.CSP.3.13.B.1: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(PROCEDURE procName)(text(parameter1),text(parameter2),...) { <text(block of statements)> })` which is used to define a procedure that takes zero or more arguments. The procedure contains `tttext(block of statements)`.
AP.CSP.3.13.B.2: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(PROCEDURE procName)(text(parameter1),text(parameter2),...) { <text(block of statements)>; text(RETURN)(text(expression)) })` which is used to define a procedure that takes zero or more arguments. The procedure contains `tttext(block of statements)` and returns the value of `tttext(expression)`. The `tttext(RETURN)` statement may appear at any point inside the procedure and causes an immediate return from the procedure back to the calling statement.
AP.CSP.3.14.A: Select appropriate libraries or existing code segments to use in creating new programs
AP.CSP.3.14.A.1: A software library contains procedures that may be used in creating new programs.
AP.CSP.3.14.A.2: Existing code segments can come from internal or external sources, such as libraries or previously written code.
AP.CSP.3.14.A.3: The use of libraries simplifies the task of creating complex programs.
AP.CSP.3.14.A.4: Application program interfaces (APIs) are specifications for how the procedures in a library behave and can be used.
AP.CSP.3.14.A.5: Documentation for an API/library is necessary in understanding the behaviors provided by the API/library and how to use them.
AP.CSP.3.15.A: For generating random values, write expressions to generate possible values and evaluate expressions to determine the possible results.
AP.CSP.3.15.A.1: The exam reference sheet provides `tt(text(RANDOM)(text(a),text(b)))` which generates and returns a random integer from `tt(a)` to `tt(b)`, inclusive. Each result is equally likely to occur. For example, `tt(text(RANDOM)(1,3))` could return `tt(1)`, `tt(2)`, or `tt(3)`.
AP.CSP.3.15.A.2: Using random number generation in a program means each execution may produce a different result.
AP.CSP.3.16.A: For simulations, explain how computers can be used to represent real-world phenomena or outcomes and compare simulations with real-world contexts.
AP.CSP.3.16.A.1: Simulations are abstractions of more complex objects or phenomena for a specific purpose.
AP.CSP.3.16.A.2: A simulation is a representation that uses varying sets of values to reflect the changing state of a phenomenon.
AP.CSP.3.16.A.3: Simulations often mimic real-world events with the purpose of drawing inferences, allowing investigation of a phenomenon without the constraints of the real world.
AP.CSP.3.16.A.4: The process of developing an abstract simulation involves removing specific details or simplifying functionality.
AP.CSP.3.16.A.5: Simulations can contain bias derived from the choices of real-world elements that were included or excluded.
AP.CSP.3.16.A.6: Simulations are most useful when real-world events are impractical for experiments (e.g., too big, too small, too fast, too slow, too expensive, or too dangerous).
AP.CSP.3.16.A.7: Simulations facilitate the formulation and refinement of hypotheses related to the objects or phenomena under consideration.
AP.CSP.3.16.A.8: Random number generators can be used to simulate the variability that exists in the real world.
AP.CSP.3.17.A: For determining the efficiency of an algorithm, explain the difference between algorithms that run in reasonable time and those that do not and identify situations where a heuristic solution may be more appropriate.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.1: A problem is a general description of a task that can (or cannot) be solved algorithmically. An instance of a problem also includes specific input. For example, sorting is a problem; sorting the list (`2`,`3`,`1`,`7`) is an instance of the problem.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.2: A decision problem is a problem with a yes/no answer (e.g., is there a path from A to B?). An optimization problem is a problem with the goal of finding the “best” solution among many (e.g., what is the shortest path from A to B?).
AP.CSP.3.17.A.3: Efficiency is an estimation of the amount of computational resources used by an algorithm. Efficiency is typically expressed as a function of the size of the input.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.4: An algorithm's efficiency is determined through formal or mathematical reasoning.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.5: An algorithm's efficiency can be informally measured by determining the number of times a statement or group of statements executes.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.6: Different correct algorithms for the same problem can have different efficiencies.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.7: Algorithms with a polynomial efficiency or slower (constant, linear, square, cube, etc.) are said to run in a reasonable amount of time. Algorithms with exponential or factorial efficiencies are examples of algorithms that run in an unreasonable amount of time.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.8: Some problems cannot be solved in a reasonable amount of time because there is no efficient algorithm for solving them. In these cases, approximate solutions are sought.
AP.CSP.3.17.A.9: A heuristic is an approach to a problem that produces a solution that is not guaranteed to be optimal but may be used when techniques that are guaranteed to always find an optimal solution are impractical.
AP.CSP.3.18.A: Explain the existence of undecidable problems in computer science.
AP.CSP.3.18.A.1: A decidable problem is a decision problem for which an algorithm can be written to produce a correct output for all inputs (e.g., “Is the number even?”).
AP.CSP.3.18.A.2: An undecidable problem is one for which no algorithm can be constructed that is always capable of providing a correct yes-or-no answer.
AP.CSP.3.18.A.3: An undecidable problem may have some instances that have an algorithmic solution, but there is no algorithmic solution that could solve all instances of the problem.
AP.CSP.4.1.A: Explain how computing devices work together in a network.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.1: A computing device is a physical artifact that can run a program. Some examples include computers, tablets, servers, routers, and smart sensors.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.2: A computing system is a group of computing devices and programs working together for a common purpose.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.3: A computer network is a group of interconnected computing devices capable of sending or receiving data.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.4: A computer network is a type of computing system.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.5: A path between two computing devices on a computer network (a sender and a receiver) is a sequence of directly connected computing devices that begins at the sender and ends at the receiver.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.6: Routing is the process of finding a path from sender to receiver.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.7: The bandwidth of a computer network is the maximum amount of data that can be sent in a fixed amount of time.
AP.CSP.4.1.A.8: Bandwidth is usually measured in bits per second.
AP.CSP.4.1.B.1: The Internet is a computer network consisting of interconnected networks that use standardized, open (nonproprietary) communication protocols.
AP.CSP.4.1.B.2: Access to the Internet depends on the ability to connect a computing device to an Internet-connected device.
AP.CSP.4.1.B.3: A protocol is an agreed-upon set of rules that specify the behavior of a system.
AP.CSP.4.1.B.4: The protocols used in the Internet are open, which allows users to easily connect additional computing devices to the Internet.
AP.CSP.4.1.B.5: Routing on the Internet is usually dynamic; it is not specified in advance.
AP.CSP.4.1.B.6: The scalability of a system is the capacity for the system to change in size and scale to meet new demands.
AP.CSP.4.1.B.7: The Internet was designed to be scalable.
AP.CSP.4.1.C: Explain how data are sent through the Internet via packets.
AP.CSP.4.1.C.1: Information is passed through the Internet as a data stream. Data streams contain chunks of data, which are encapsulated in packets.
AP.CSP.4.1.C.2: Packets contain a chunk of data and metadata used for routing the packet between the origin and the destination on the Internet, as well as for data reassembly.
AP.CSP.4.1.C.3: Packets may arrive at the destination in order, out of order, or not at all.
AP.CSP.4.1.C.4: IP, TCP, and UDP are common protocols used on the Internet.
AP.CSP.4.1.D: Describe the differences between the Internet and the World Wide Web.
AP.CSP.4.1.D.1: The World Wide Web is a system of linked pages, programs, and files.
AP.CSP.4.1.D.2: HTTP is a protocol used by the World Wide Web.
AP.CSP.4.1.D.3: The World Wide Web uses the Internet.
AP.CSP.4.2.A: For fault-tolerant systems, like the Internet, describe the benefits of fault tolerance, explain how a given system is fault-tolerant, and identify vulnerabilities to failure in a system.
AP.CSP.4.2.A.1: The Internet has been engineered to be fault-tolerant, with abstractions for routing and transmitting data.
AP.CSP.4.2.A.2: Redundancy is the inclusion of extra components that can be used to mitigate failure of a system if other components fail.
AP.CSP.4.2.A.3: One way to accomplish network redundancy is by having more than one path between any two connected devices.
AP.CSP.4.2.A.4: If a particular device or connection on the Internet fails, subsequent data will be sent via a different route, if possible.
AP.CSP.4.2.A.5: When a system can support failures and still continue to function, it is called fault-tolerant. This is important because elements of complex systems fail at unexpected times, often in groups, and fault tolerance allows users to continue to use the network.
AP.CSP.4.2.A.6: Redundancy within a system often requires additional resources but can provide the benefit of fault tolerance.
AP.CSP.4.2.A.7: The redundancy of routing options between two points increases the reliability of the Internet and helps it scale to more devices and more people.
AP.CSP.4.3.A: For sequential, parallel, and distributed computing, compare problem solutions and determine the efficiency of solutions.
AP.CSP.4.3.A.1: Sequential computing is a computational model in which operations are performed in order one at a time.
AP.CSP.4.3.A.2: Parallel computing is a computational model where the program is broken into multiple smaller sequential computing operations, some of which are performed simultaneously.
AP.CSP.4.3.A.3: Distributed computing is a computational model in which multiple devices are used to run a program.
AP.CSP.4.3.A.4: Comparing efficiency of solutions can be done by comparing the time it takes them to perform the same task.
AP.CSP.4.3.A.5: A sequential solution takes as long as the sum of all of its steps.
AP.CSP.4.3.A.6: A parallel computing solution takes as long as its sequential tasks plus the longest of its parallel tasks.
AP.CSP.4.3.A.7: The “speedup” of a parallel solution is measured in the time it took to complete the task sequentially divided by the time it took to complete the task when done in parallel.
AP.CSP.4.3.B: Describe benefits and challenges of parallel and distributed computing.
AP.CSP.4.3.B.1: Parallel computing consists of a parallel portion and a sequential portion.
AP.CSP.4.3.B.2: Solutions that use parallel computing can scale more effectively than solutions that use sequential computing.
AP.CSP.4.3.B.3: Distributed computing allows problems to be solved that could not be solved on a single computer because of either the processing time or storage needs involved.
AP.CSP.4.3.B.4: Distributed computing allows much larger problems to be solved quicker than they could be solved using a single computer.
AP.CSP.4.3.B.5: When increasing the use of parallel computing in a solution, the efficiency of the solution is still limited by the sequential portion. This means that at some point, adding parallel portions will no longer meaningfully increase efficiency.
AP.CSP.5.1.A: Explain how an effect of a computing innovation can be both beneficial and harmful.
AP.CSP.5.1.A.2: The way people complete tasks often changes to incorporate new computing innovations.
AP.CSP.5.1.A.3: Not every effect of a computing innovation is anticipated in advance.
AP.CSP.5.1.A.4: A single effect can be viewed as both beneficial and harmful by different people, or even by the same person.
AP.CSP.5.1.A.5: Advances in computing have generated and increased creativity in other fields, such as medicine, engineering, communications, and the arts.
AP.CSP.5.1.B: Explain how a computing innovation can have an impact beyond its intended purpose.
AP.CSP.5.1.B.1: Computing innovations can be used in ways that their creators had not originally intended: the World Wide Web was originally intended only for rapid and easy exchange of information within the scientific community, targeted advertising is used to help businesses, but it can be misused at both individual and aggregate levels, and machine learning and data mining have enabled innovation in medicine, business, and science, but information discovered in this way has also been used to discriminate against groups of individuals.
AP.CSP.5.1.B.2: Some of the ways computing innovations can be used may have a harmful impact on society, the economy, or culture.
AP.CSP.5.1.B.3: Responsible programmers try to consider the unintended ways their computing innovations can be used and the potential beneficial and harmful effects of these new uses.
AP.CSP.5.1.B.4: It is not possible for a programmer to consider all the ways a computing innovation can be used.
AP.CSP.5.1.B.5: Computing innovations have often had unintended beneficial effects by leading to advances in other fields.
AP.CSP.5.1.B.6: Rapid sharing of a program or running a program with a large number of users can result in significant impacts beyond the intended purpose or control of the programmer.
AP.CSP.5.2.A: Describe issues that contribute to the digital divide.
AP.CSP.5.2.A.1: Internet access varies between socioeconomic, geographic, and demographic characteristics, as well as between countries.
AP.CSP.5.2.A.2: The “digital divide” refers to differing access to computing devices and the Internet, based on socioeconomic, geographic, or demographic characteristics.
AP.CSP.5.2.A.3: The digital divide can affect both groups and individuals.
AP.CSP.5.2.A.4: The digital divide raises issues of equity, access, and influence, both globally and locally.
AP.CSP.5.2.A.5: The digital divide is affected by the actions of individuals, organizations, and governments.
AP.CSP.5.3.A: Explain how bias exists in computing innovations.
AP.CSP.5.3.A.1: Computing innovations can reflect existing human biases because of biases written into the algorithms or biases in the data used by the innovation.
AP.CSP.5.3.A.2: Programmers should take action to reduce bias in algorithms used for computing innovations as a way of combating existing human biases.
AP.CSP.5.3.A.3: Biases can be embedded at all levels of software development.
AP.CSP.5.4.A: Explain how people participate in problem-solving processes at scale.
AP.CSP.5.4.A.1: Widespread access to information and public data facilitates the identification of problems, development of solutions, and dissemination of results.
AP.CSP.5.4.A.2: Science has been affected by using distributed and “citizen science” to solve scientific problems.
AP.CSP.5.4.A.3: Citizen science is scientific research conducted in whole or part by distributed individuals, many of whom may not be scientists, who contribute relevant data to research using their own computing devices.
AP.CSP.5.4.A.4: Crowdsourcing is the practice of obtaining input or information from a large number of people via the Internet.
AP.CSP.5.4.A.5: Human capabilities can be enhanced by collaboration via computing.
AP.CSP.5.4.A.6: Crowdsourcing offers new models for collaboration, such as connecting businesses or social causes with funding.
AP.CSP.5.5.A: Explain how the use of computing can raise legal and ethical concerns.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.1: Material created on a computer is the intellectual property of the creator or an organization.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.2: Ease of access and distribution of digitized information raises intellectual property concerns regarding ownership, value, and use.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.3: Measures should be taken to safeguard intellectual property.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.4: The use of material created by someone else without permission and presented as one's own is plagiarism and may have legal consequences.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.5: Some examples of legal ways to use materials created by someone else include Creative Commons - a public copyright license that enables the free distribution of an otherwise copyrighted work. This is used when the content creator wants to give others the right to share, use, and build upon the work they have created, open source - programs that are made §freely available and may be redistributed and modified, and open access - online research output free of any and all restrictions on access and free of many restrictions on use, such as copyright
AP.CSP.5.5.A.6: The use of material created by someone other than you should always be cited.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.7: Creative Commons, open source, and open access have enabled broad access to digital information.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.8: As with any technology or medium, using computing to harm individuals or groups of people raises legal and ethical concerns.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.9: Computing can play a role in social and political issues, which in turn often raises legal and ethical concerns.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.10: The digital divide raises ethical concerns around computing.
AP.CSP.5.5.A.11: Computing innovations can raise legal and ethical concerns. Some examples of these include the development of software that allows access to digital media downloads and streaming, the development of algorithms that include bias, the existence of computing devices that collect and analyze data by continuously monitoring activities.
AP.CSP.5.6.A: Describe the risks to privacy from collecting and storing personal data on a computer system.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.1: Personally identifiable information (PII) is information about an individual that identifies, links, relates, or describes them. Examples of PII include Social Security number, age, race, phone number(s), medical information, financial information, and biometric data.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.2: Search engines can record and maintain a history of searches made by users.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.3: Websites can record and maintain a history of individuals who have viewed their pages.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.4: Devices, websites, and networks can collect information about a user's location.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.5: Technology enables the collection, use, and exploitation of information about, by, and for individuals, groups, and institutions.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.6: Search engines can use search history to suggest websites or for targeted marketing.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.7: Disparate personal data, such as geolocation, cookies, and browsing history, can be aggregated to create knowledge about an individual.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.8: PII and other information placed online can be used to enhance a user's online experiences.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.9: PII stored online can be used to simplify making online purchases.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.10: Commercial and governmental curation of information may be exploited if privacy and other protections are ignored.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.11: Information placed online can be used in ways that were not intended and that may have a harmful impact. For example, an email message may be forwarded, tweets can be retweeted, and social media posts can be viewed by potential employers.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.12: PII can be used to stalk or steal the identity of a person or to aid in the planning of other criminal acts.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.13: Once information is placed online, it is difficult to delete.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.14: Programs can collect your location and record where you have been, how you got there, and how long you were at a given location.
AP.CSP.5.6.A.15: Information posted to social media services can be used by others. Combining information posted on social media and other sources can be used to deduce private information about you.
AP.CSP.5.6.B: Explain how computing resources can be protected and can be misused.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.1: Authentication measures protect devices and information from unauthorized access. Examples of authentication measures include strong passwords and multifactor authentication.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.2: A strong password is something that is easy for a user to remember but would be difficult for someone else to guess based on knowledge of that user.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.3: Multifactor authentication is a method of computer access control in which a user is only granted access after successfully presenting several separate pieces of evidence to an authentication mechanism, typically in at least two of the following categories: knowledge (something they know), possession (something they have), and inherence (something they are).
AP.CSP.5.6.B.4: Multifactor authentication requires at least two steps to unlock protected information; each step adds a new layer of security that must be broken to gain unauthorized access.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.5: Encryption is the process of encoding data to prevent unauthorized access. Decryption is the process of decoding the data. Two common encryption approaches are symmetric key encryption involves one key for both encryption and decryption and public key encryption pairs a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption. The sender does not need the receiver's private key to encrypt a message, but the receiver's private key is required to decrypt the message.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.6: Certificate authorities issue digital certificates that validate the ownership of encryption keys used in secure communications and are based on a trust model.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.7: Computer virus and malware scanning software can help protect a computing system against infection.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.8: A computer virus is a malicious program that can copy itself and gain access to a computer in an unauthorized way. Computer viruses often attach themselves to legitimate programs and start running independently on a computer.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.9: Malware is software intended to damage a computing system or to take partial control over its operation.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.10: All real-world systems have errors or design flaws that can be exploited to compromise them. Regular software updates help fix errors that could compromise a computing system.
AP.CSP.5.6.B.11: Users can control the permissions programs have for collecting user information. Users should review the permission settings of programs to protect their privacy.
AP.CSP.5.6.C: Explain how unauthorized access to computing resources is gained.
AP.CSP.5.6.C.1: Phishing is a technique that attempts to trick a user into providing personal information. That personal information can then be used to access sensitive online resources, such as bank accounts and emails.
AP.CSP.5.6.C.2: Keylogging is the use of a program to record every keystroke made by a computer user in order to gain fraudulent access to passwords and other confidential information.
AP.CSP.5.6.C.3: Data sent over public networks can be intercepted, analyzed, and modified. One way that this can happen is through a rogue access point.
AP.CSP.5.6.C.4: A rogue access point is a wireless access point that gives unauthorized access to secure networks.
AP.CSP.5.6.C.5: A malicious link can be disguised on a web page or in an email message.
AP.CSP.5.6.C.6: Unsolicited emails, attachments, links, and forms in emails can be used to compromise the security of a computing system. These can come from unknown senders or from known senders whose security has been compromised.
AP.CSP.5.6.C.7: Untrustworthy (often free) downloads from freeware or shareware sites can contain malware.
AP.EH.1.1.A: Explain the context in which the Renaissance and Age of Discovery developed.
AP.EH.1.1.A.1: The rediscovery of works from ancient Greece and Rome and observation of the natural world changed many Europeans' view of their world.
AP.EH.1.1.A.1.i: A revival of classical texts led to new methods of scholarship and new values in both society and religion.
AP.EH.1.1.A.1.ii: The visual arts incorporated the new ideas of the Renaissance and were used to promote personal, political, and religious goals.
AP.EH.1.1.A.2: Europeans explored and settled overseas territories, encountering and interacting with indigenous populations.
AP.EH.1.1.A.2.i: European nations were driven by commercial and religious motives to explore overseas territories and establish colonies.
AP.EH.1.1.A.3: European society and the experiences of everyday life were increasingly shaped by commercial and agricultural capitalism, notwithstanding the continued existence of medieval social and economic structures.
AP.EH.1.1.A.3.i: Economic change produced new social patterns, while traditions of hierarchy and status continued.
AP.EH.1.1.A.3.ii: Most Europeans derived their livelihood from agriculture and oriented their lives around the seasons, the village, or the manor, although economic changes began to alter rural production and power.
AP.EH.1.1.A.4: The struggle for sovereignty within and among states resulted in varying degrees of political centralization.
AP.EH.1.1.A.4.i: The new concept of the sovereign state and secular systems of law played a central role in the creation of new political institutions.
AP.EH.1.2.A: Explain how the revival of classical texts contributed to the development of the Renaissance in Italy.
AP.EH.1.2.A.1: Italian Renaissance humanists, including Petrarch, promoted a revival in classical literature and created new philological approaches to ancient texts. Some Renaissance humanists furthered the values of secularism and individualism.
AP.EH.1.2.B: Explain the political, intellectual, and cultural effects of the Italian Renaissance.
AP.EH.1.2.B.1: Humanist revival of Greek and Roman texts, spread by the printing press, challenged the institutional power of universities and the Catholic Church. This shifted education away from a primary focus on theological writings toward classical texts and new methods of scientific inquiry.
AP.EH.1.2.B.2: Admiration for Greek and Roman political institutions supported a revival of civic humanist culture in the Italian city-states and produced secular models for individual and political behavior.
AP.EH.1.2.B.3: In the Italian Renaissance, rulers and popes concerned with enhancing their prestige commissioned paintings and architectural works based on classical styles, the developing “naturalism” in the artistic world, and often the newly invented technique of geometric perspective.
AP.EH.1.3.A: Explain how Renaissance ideas were developed, maintained, and changed as the Renaissance spread to northern Europe.
AP.EH.1.3.A.1: The Northern Renaissance retained a more religious focus, which resulted in more human-centered naturalism that considered individuals and everyday life appropriate objects of artistic representation.
AP.EH.1.3.A.2: Christian humanism, embodied in the writings of Erasmus, employed Renaissance learning in the service of religious reform.
AP.EH.1.4.A: Explain the influence of the printing press on cultural and intellectual developments in modern European history.
AP.EH.1.4.A.1: The invention of printing promoted the dissemination of new ideas.
AP.EH.1.4.A.1.i: The invention of the printing press in the `text(1450s)` helped spread the Renaissance beyond Italy and encouraged the growth of vernacular literature, which would eventually contribute to the development of national cultures.
AP.EH.1.5.A: Explain the causes and effects of the development of political institutions from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.1.5.A.1: Monarchs and princes, including the English rulers Henry VIII and Elizabeth I, initiated religious reform from the top down in an effort to exercise greater control over religious life and morality.
AP.EH.1.5.A.2: New monarchies laid the foundation for the centralized modern state by establishing monopolies on tax collection, employing military force, dispensing justice, and gaining the right to determine the religion of their subjects.
AP.EH.1.5.A.3: Across Europe, commercial and professional groups gained in power and played a greater role in political affairs.
AP.EH.1.5.A.4: Continued political fragmentation in Renaissance Italy provided a background for the development of new concepts of the secular state.
AP.EH.1.6: Technological Advances & The Age Of Exploration
AP.EH.1.6.A: Explain the technological factors that facilitated European exploration and expansion from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.1.6.A.1: Advances in navigation, cartography, and military technology enabled Europeans to establish overseas colonies and empires.
AP.EH.1.6.B: Explain the motivations for and effects of European exploration and expansion from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.1.6.B.1: European states sought direct access to gold, spices, and luxury goods to enhance personal wealth and state power.
AP.EH.1.6.B.2: The rise of mercantilism gave the state a newrole in promoting commercial development and the acquisition of colonies overseas.
AP.EH.1.6.B.3: Christianity was a stimulus for exploration as governments and religious authorities sought to spread the faith, and for some it served as a justification for the subjugation of indigenous civilizations.
AP.EH.1.7.A: Explain how and why trading networks and colonial expansion affected relations between and among European states.
AP.EH.1.7.A.1: Europeans established overseas empires and trade networks through coercion and negotiation.
AP.EH.1.7.A.1.i: The Spanish established colonies across the Americas, the Caribbean, and the Pacific, which made Spain a dominant state in Europe in the 16th century.
AP.EH.1.7.A.1.ii: The Atlantic nations of France, England, and the Netherlands followed by establishing their own colonies and trading networks to compete with Portuguese and Spanish dominance in the 17th century.
AP.EH.1.7.A.1.iii: The competition for trade led to conflicts and rivalries among European powers in the 17th and 18th centuries.
AP.EH.1.8.A: Explain the economic impact of European colonial expansion and development of trade networks.
AP.EH.1.8.A.1: The Portuguese established a commercial network along the African coast, in South and East Asia, and in South America in the late 15th and throughout the 16th centuries.
AP.EH.1.8.A.2: Europe's colonial expansion led to a global exchange of goods, flora, and fauna; a shift toward European dominance; and the expansion of the trade in enslaved persons.
AP.EH.1.8.A.3: The exchange of goods shifted the center of economic power in Europe from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic states and brought the latter into an expanding world economy.
AP.EH.1.8.A.4: The exchange of new plants, animals, and diseases-the Columbian Exchange-created economic opportunities for Europeans.
AP.EH.1.8.B: Explain the social and cultural impact of European colonial expansion and development of trade networks.
AP.EH.1.8.B.1: Europe's colonial expansion led to a global exchange of goods, flora, fauna, cultural practices, and diseases, resulting in the destruction of some indigenous civilizations, a shift toward European dominance, and the expansion of the trade in enslaved persons.
AP.EH.1.8.B.2: The exchange of new plants, animals, and diseases - the Columbian Exchange - in some cases facilitated European subjugation and destruction of indigenous peoples, particularly in the Americas.
AP.EH.1.9.A: Explain the causes for and the development of the slave trade.
AP.EH.1.9.A.1: Europeans expanded the trade of enslaved Africans in response to the establishment of a plantation economy in the Americas and demographic catastrophes among indigenous peoples.
AP.EH.1.10.A: Explain European commercial and agricultural developments and their economic effects from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.1.10.A.1: Innovations in banking and finance promoted the growth of urban financial centers and a money economy.
AP.EH.1.10.A.2: Most Europeans derived their livelihood from agriculture and oriented their lives around the seasons, the village, or the manor, although economic changes began to alter rural production and power.
AP.EH.1.10.A.2.i: Subsistence agriculture was the rule in most areas, with three-crop field rotation in the north and two-crop rotation in the Mediterranean; in many cases, farmers paid rent and labor services for their lands.
AP.EH.1.10.A.2.ii: The price revolution contributed to the accumulation of capital and the expansion of the market economy through the commercialization of agriculture, which benefited large landowners in western Europe.
AP.EH.1.10.A.2.iii: Population recovered to its pre-Great Plague level in the 16th century, and continuing population pressures contributed to uneven price increases; agricultural commodities increased more sharply than wages, reducing living standards for some.
AP.EH.1.10.B: Explain European commercial and agricultural developments and their social effects from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.1.10.B.1: Economic change produced new social patterns, while traditions of hierarchy and status continued.
AP.EH.1.10.B.1.i: The growth of commerce produced a new economic elite, which related to traditional land-holding elites in different ways in Europe's various geographic regions.
AP.EH.1.10.B.2: As western Europe moved toward a free peasantry and commercial agriculture, serfdom was codified in the east, where nobles continued to dominate economic life on large estates.
AP.EH.1.10.B.3: The attempts of landlords to increase their revenues by restricting or abolishing the traditional rights of peasants led to revolt.
AP.EH.1.10.B.4: Migrants to the cities challenged the ability of merchant elites and craft guilds to govern, and strained resources.
AP.EH.1.10.B.5: From the late 16th century on, Europeans responded to economic and environmental challenges, such as the Little Ice Age, by delaying marriage and childbearing. This European marriage pattern restrained population growth and ultimately improved the economic condition of families.
AP.EH.1.11: Causation In The Renaissance & Age of Discovery
AP.EH.1.11.A: Explain the causes and consequences of the Renaissance and Age of Discovery.
AP.EH.1.11.A.1: The rediscovery of works from ancient Greece and Rome and observation of the natural world changed many Europeans' view of their world.
AP.EH.1.11.A.1.i: A revival of classical texts led to new methods of scholarship and new values in both society and religion.
AP.EH.1.11.A.1.ii: The visual arts incorporated the new ideas of the Renaissance and were used to promote personal, political, and religious goals.
AP.EH.1.11.A.2: Europeans explored and settled overseas territories, encountering and interacting with indigenous populations.
AP.EH.1.11.A.2.i: European nations were driven by commercial and religious motives to explore overseas territories and establish colonies.
AP.EH.1.11.A.3: European society and the experiences of everyday life were increasingly shaped by commercial and agricultural capitalism, notwithstanding the continued existence of medieval social and economic structures.
AP.EH.1.11.A.3.i: Economic change produced new social patterns, while traditions of hierarchy and status continued.
AP.EH.1.11.A.3.ii: Most Europeans derived their livelihood from agriculture and oriented their lives around the seasons, the village, or the manor, although economic changes began to alter rural production and power.
AP.EH.1.11.A.4: The struggle for sovereignty within and among states resulted in varying degrees of political centralization.
AP.EH.1.11.A.4.i: The new concept of the sovereign state and secular systems of law played a central role in the creation of new political institutions.
AP.EH.2.1.A: Explain the context in which the religious, political, and cultural developments of the 16th and 17th centuries took place.
AP.EH.2.1.A.1: Religious pluralism challenged the concept of a unified Europe.
AP.EH.2.1.A.1.i: The Protestant and Catholic reformations fundamentally changed theology, religious institutions, culture, and attitudes toward wealth and prosperity.
AP.EH.2.1.A.1.ii: Religious reform both increased state control of religious institutions and provided justifications for challenging state authority.
AP.EH.2.1.A.1.iii: Conflicts among religious groups overlapped with political and economic competition within and among states.
AP.EH.2.1.A.2: European society and the experiences of everyday life were increasingly shaped by commercial and agricultural capitalism, notwithstanding the continued existence of medieval social and economic structures.
AP.EH.2.1.A.2.i: Population shifts and growing commerce caused the expansion of cities, which often placed stress on their traditional political and social structures.
AP.EH.2.1.A.2.ii: The family remained the primary social and economic institution of early modern Europe and took several forms, including the nuclear family.
AP.EH.2.1.A.2.iii: Popular culture, leisure activities, and rituals reflecting the continued popularity of folk ideas reinforced and sometimes challenged communal ties and norms.
AP.EH.2.1.A.3: The struggle for sovereignty within and among states resulted in varying degrees of political centralization.
AP.EH.2.1.A.3.i: The new concept of the sovereign state and secular systems of law played a central role in the creation of new political institutions.
AP.EH.2.2.A: Explain how and why religious belief and practices changed from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.2.2.A.1: Reformers Martin Luther and John Calvin criticized Catholic abuses and established new interpretations of Christian doctrine and practice. Responses to Luther and Calvin included religious radicals, including the Anabaptists, and other groups, such as German peasants.
AP.EH.2.2.A.2: Some Protestant groups sanctioned the notion that wealth accumulation was a sign of God's favor and a reward for hard work.
AP.EH.2.3.A: Explain how and why religious belief and practices changed from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.2.3.A.1: Protestant reformers used the printing press to disseminate their ideas, which spurred religious reform and helped it to become widely established.
AP.EH.2.3.A.2: Some Protestants, including Calvin and the Anabaptists, refused to recognize the subordination of the church to the secular state.
AP.EH.2.3.A.3: Religious conflicts became a basis for challenging the monarchs' control of religious institutions.
AP.EH.2.4.A: Explain how matters of religion influenced and were influenced by political factors from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.2.4.A.1: Issues of religious reform exacerbated conflicts between the monarchy and the nobility, as in the French wars of religion.
AP.EH.2.4.A.2: Habsburg rulers confronted an expanded Ottoman Empire while attempting unsuccessfully to restore Catholic unity across Europe.
AP.EH.2.4.A.3: States exploited religious conflicts to promote political and economic interests.
AP.EH.2.4.A.4: A few states, such as France with the Edict of Nantes, allowed religious pluralism in order to maintain domestic peace.
AP.EH.2.4.A.5: The Peace of Westphalia (1648), which marked the effective end of the medieval ideal of universal Christendom, accelerated the decline of the Holy Roman Empire by granting princes, bishops, and other local leaders control over religion.
AP.EH.2.5.A: Explain the continuities and changes in the role of the Catholic Church from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.2.5.A.1: The Catholic Reformation, exemplified by the Jesuit Order and the Council of Trent, revived the church but cemented division within Christianity.
AP.EH.2.6.A: Explain how economic and intellectual developments from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)` affected social norms and hierarchies.
AP.EH.2.6.A.1: Established hierarchies of class, religion, and gender continued to define social status and perceptions in rural and urban settings.
AP.EH.2.6.A.2: Rural and urban households worked as units, with men and women engaged in separate but complementary tasks.
AP.EH.2.6.A.3: The Renaissance and Reformation raised debates about female education and women's roles in the family, church, and society.
AP.EH.2.6.A.4: Social dislocation, coupled with the shifting authority of religious institutions during the Reformation, left city governments with the task of regulating public morals.
AP.EH.2.6.A.5: Leisure activities continued to be organized according to the religious calendar and the agricultural cycle, and remained communal in nature.
AP.EH.2.6.A.6: Local and church authorities continued to enforce communal norms through rituals of public humiliation.
AP.EH.2.6.A.7: Reflecting folk ideas and social and economic upheaval, accusations of witchcraft peaked between 1580 and 1650.
AP.EH.2.7: Art Of The 16th Century: Mannerism & Baroque Art
AP.EH.2.7.A: Explain how and why artistic expression changed from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.2.7.A.1: Mannerist and Baroque artists employed distortion, drama, and illusion in their work. Monarchies, city-states, and the church commissioned these works as a means of promoting their own stature and power.
AP.EH.2.8: Causation In The Age Of Reformation & The Wars Of Religion
AP.EH.2.8.A: Explain how the religious, political, and cultural developments of the 16th and 17th centuries affected European society from `text(1450)` to `text(1648)`.
AP.EH.2.8.A.1: Religious pluralism challenged the concept of a unified Europe.
AP.EH.2.8.A.1.i: The Protestant and Catholic reformations fundamentally changed theology, religious institutions, culture, and attitudes toward wealth and prosperity.
AP.EH.2.8.A.1.ii: Religious reform both increased state control of religious institutions and provided justifications for challenging state authority.
AP.EH.2.8.A.1.iii: Conflicts among religious groups overlapped with political and economic competition within and among states.
AP.EH.2.8.A.2: European society and the experiences of everyday life were increasingly shaped by commercial and agricultural capitalism, notwithstanding the continued existence of medieval social and economic structures.
AP.EH.2.8.A.2.i: Population shifts and growing commerce caused the expansion of cities, which often placed stress on their traditional political and social structures.
AP.EH.2.8.A.2.ii: The family remained the primary social and economic institution of early modern Europe and took several forms, including the nuclear family.
AP.EH.2.8.A.2.iii: Popular culture, leisure activities, and rituals reflecting the continued popularity of folk ideas reinforced and sometimes challenged communal ties and norms.
AP.EH.2.8.A.3: The struggle for sovereignty within and among states resulted in varying degrees of political centralization.
AP.EH.2.8.A.3.i: The new concept of the sovereign state and secular systems of law played a central role in the creation of new political institutions.
AP.EH.3.1.A: Explain the context in which different forms of political power developed from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.3.1.A.1: The struggle for sovereignty within and among states resulted in varying degrees of political centralization.
AP.EH.3.1.A.1.i: The new concept of the sovereign state and secular systems of law played a central role in the creation of new political institutions.
AP.EH.3.1.A.1.ii: The competition for power between monarchs and corporate and minority language groups produced different distributions of governmental authority in European states.
AP.EH.3.1.A.1.iii: Monarchies seeking enhanced power faced challenges from nobles who wished to retain traditional forms of shared governance and regional autonomy.
AP.EH.3.1.A.1.iv: Within states, minority local and regional identities based on language and culture led to resistance against the dominant national group.
AP.EH.3.1.A.2: Different models of political sovereignty affected the relationship among states and between states and individuals.
AP.EH.3.1.A.2.i: In much of Europe, absolute monarchy was established over the course of the 17th and 18th centuries.
AP.EH.3.1.A.2.ii: Challenges to absolutism resulted in alternative political systems.
AP.EH.3.2: The English Civil War & The Glorious Revolution
AP.EH.3.2.A: Explain the causes and consequences of the English Civil War.
AP.EH.3.2.A.1: The English Civil War - a conflict among the monarchy, Parliament, and other elites over their respective roles in the political structure - exemplified the competition for power among monarchs and competing groups.
AP.EH.3.2.A.2: The outcome of the English Civil War and the Glorious Revolution protected the rights of gentry and aristocracy from absolutism through assertions of the rights of Parliament.
AP.EH.3.3: Continuities & Changes To Economic Practice & Development
AP.EH.3.3.A: Explain the continuities and changes in commercial and economic developments from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.3.3.A.1: The Agricultural Revolution raised productivity and increased the supply of food and other agricultural products.
AP.EH.3.3.A.2: The importation and transplantation of agricultural products from the Americas contributed to an increase in the food supply in Europe.
AP.EH.3.3.A.3: Labor and trade in commodities were increasingly freed from traditional restrictions imposed by governments and corporate entities.
AP.EH.3.3.A.4: The putting-out system, or cottage industry, expanded as increasing numbers of laborers in homes or workshops produced for markets through merchant intermediaries or workshop owners.
AP.EH.3.3.A.5: The development of the market economy led to new financial practices and institutions.
AP.EH.3.3.A.6: Early modern Europe developed a market economy that provided the foundation for its global role.
AP.EH.3.4.A: Explain the continuities and changes in commercial and economic developments from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.3.4.A.1: The European-dominated worldwide economic network contributed to the agricultural, industrial, and consumer revolutions in Europe.
AP.EH.3.4.A.1.i: European states followed mercantilist policies by drawing resources from colonies in the New World and elsewhere.
AP.EH.3.4.A.1.ii: The transatlantic slave-labor system expanded in the 17th and 18th centuries as demand for New World products increased.
AP.EH.3.4.A.1.iii: Overseas products and influences contributed to the development of a consumer culture in Europe.
AP.EH.3.4.A.1.iv: The importation and transplantation of agricultural products from the Americas contributed to an increase in the food supply in Europe.
AP.EH.3.4.A.1.v: Foreign lands provided raw materials, finished goods, laborers, and markets for the commercial and industrial enterprises in Europe.
AP.EH.3.5.A: Explain the factors that contributed to the development of the Dutch Republic.
AP.EH.3.5.A.1: The Dutch Republic, established by a Protestant revolt against the Habsburg monarchy, developed an oligarchy of urban gentry and rural landholders to promote trade and protect traditional rights.
AP.EH.3.6.A: Explain how European states attempted to establish and maintain a balance of power on the continent throughout the period from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.3.6.A.1: The competitive state system led to new patterns of diplomacy and new forms of warfare.
AP.EH.3.6.A.1.i: Following the Peace of Westphalia, religion declined in importance as a cause for warfare among European states; the concept of the balance of power played an important role in structuring diplomatic and military objectives.
AP.EH.3.6.A.2: The inability of the Polish monarchy to consolidate its authority over the nobility led to Poland's partition by Prussia, Russia, and Austria, and its disappearance from the map of Europe.
AP.EH.3.6.A.3: After `text(1648)`, dynastic and state interests, along with Europe's expanding colonial empires, influenced the diplomacy of European states and frequently led to war.
AP.EH.3.6.A.3.i: After the Austrian defeat of the Turks in `text(1683)` at the Battle of Vienna, the Ottomans ceased their westward expansion.
AP.EH.3.6.A.3.ii: Louis XIV's nearly continuous wars, pursuing both dynastic and state interests, provoked a coalition of European powers opposing him.
AP.EH.3.6.B: Explain how advances in technology contributed to a developing balance of power on the continent throughout the period from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.3.6.B.1: Advances in military technology led to new forms of warfare, including greater reliance on infantry, firearms, mobile cannon, and more elaborate fortifications, all financed by heavier taxation and requiring a larger bureaucracy. New military techniques and institutions (i.e., the military revolution) tipped the balance of power toward states able to marshal sufficient resources for the new military environment.
AP.EH.3.7.A: Explain how absolutist forms of rule affected social and political development from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.3.7.A.1: Absolute monarchies limited the nobility's participation in governance but preserved the aristocracy's social position and legal privileges.
AP.EH.3.7.A.2: Louis XIV and his finance minister, Jean- Baptiste Colbert, extended the administrative, financial, military, and religious control of the central state over the French population.
AP.EH.3.7.A.3: Peter the Great “westernized” the Russian state and society, transforming political, religious, and cultural institutions; Catherine the Great continued this process.
AP.EH.3.8: Comparison In The Age Of Absolutism & Constitutionalism
AP.EH.3.8.A: Compare the different forms of political power that developed in Europe from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.3.8.A.1: The struggle for sovereignty within and among states resulted in varying degrees of political centralization.
AP.EH.3.8.A.1.i: The new concept of the sovereign state and secular systems of law played a central role in the creation of new political institutions.
AP.EH.3.8.A.1.ii: The competition for power between monarchs and corporate and minority language groups produced different distributions of governmental authority in European states.
AP.EH.3.8.A.1.iii: Monarchies seeking enhanced power faced challenges from nobles who wished to retain traditional forms of shared governance and regional autonomy.
AP.EH.3.8.A.1.iv: Within states, minority local and regional identities based on language and culture led to resistance against the dominant national group.
AP.EH.3.8.A.2: Different models of political sovereignty affected the relationship among states and between states and individuals.
AP.EH.3.8.A.2.i: In much of Europe, absolute monarchy was established over the course of the 17th and 18th centuries.
AP.EH.3.8.A.2.ii: Challenges to absolutism resulted in alternative political systems.
AP.EH.3.8.A.3: The expansion of European commerce accelerated the growth of a worldwide economic network.
AP.EH.3.8.A.3.i: Early modern Europe developed a market economy that provided the foundation for its global role.
AP.EH.3.8.A.3.ii: The European-dominated worldwide economic network contributed to the agricultural, industrial, and consumer revolutions in Europe.
AP.EH.4.1: Contextualizing The Scientific Revolution & The Enlightenment
AP.EH.4.1.A: Explain the context in which the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment developed in Europe.
AP.EH.4.1.A.1: The rediscovery of works from ancient Greece and Rome and observation of the natural world changed many Europeans' view of their world.
AP.EH.4.1.A.1.i: New ideas in science based on observation, experimentation, and mathematics challenged classical views of the cosmos, nature, and the human body, although existing traditions of knowledge and the universe continued.
AP.EH.4.1.A.2: The spread of Scientific Revolution concepts and practices and the Enlightenment's application of these concepts and practices to political, social, and ethical issues led to an increased but not unchallenged emphasis on reason in European culture.
AP.EH.4.1.A.2.i: Enlightenment thought, which focused on concepts such as empiricism, skepticism, human reason, rationalism, and classical sources of knowledge, challenged the prevailing patterns of thought with respect to social order, institutions of government, and the role of faith.
AP.EH.4.1.A.2.ii: New public venues and print media popularized Enlightenment ideas.
AP.EH.4.1.A.2.iii: New political and economic theories challenged absolutism and mercantilism.
AP.EH.4.1.A.2.iv: During the Enlightenment, the rational analysis of religious practices led to natural religion and the demand for religious toleration.
AP.EH.4.1.A.3: The experiences of everyday life were shaped by demographic, environmental, medical, and technological changes.
AP.EH.4.1.A.3.i: By the 18th century, family and private life reflected new demographic patterns and the effects of the commercial revolution.
AP.EH.4.2.A: Explain how understanding of the natural world developed and changed during the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment.
AP.EH.4.2.A.1: New ideas and methods in astronomy led individuals, including Copernicus, Galileo, and Newton, to question the authority of the ancients and traditional knowledge, and to develop a heliocentric view of the cosmos.
AP.EH.4.2.A.2: Anatomical and medical discoveries by physicians, including William Harvey, presented the body as an integrated system, challenging the traditional humoral theory of the body and of disease espoused by Galen.
AP.EH.4.2.A.3: Francis Bacon and René Descartes defined inductive and deductive reasoning and promoted experimentation and the use of mathematics, which would ultimately shape the scientific method.
AP.EH.4.2.A.4: Alchemy and astrology continued to appeal to elites and some natural philosophers, in part because they shared with the new science the notion of a predictable and knowable universe. At the same time, many people continued to believe that the cosmos was governed by spiritual forces.
AP.EH.4.3.A: Explain the causes and consequences of Enlightenment thought on European society from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.4.3.A.1: Intellectuals, including Voltaire and Diderot, began to apply the principles of the Scientific Revolution to society and human institutions.
AP.EH.4.3.A.2: Locke and Rousseau developed new political models based on the concept of natural rights and the social contract.
AP.EH.4.3.A.3: Despite the principles of equality espoused by the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, intellectuals such as Rousseau offered controversial arguments for the exclusion of women from political life.
AP.EH.4.3.B: Explain the influence of Enlightenment thought on European intellectual development from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.4.3.B.1: A variety of institutions, including salons, explored and disseminated Enlightenment culture.
AP.EH.4.3.B.2: Political theories, including John Locke's, conceived of society as composed of individuals driven by self-interest and argued that the state originated in the consent of the governed (i.e., a social contract) rather than in divine right or tradition.
AP.EH.4.3.B.3: Mercantilist theory and practice were challenged by new economic ideas, including Adam Smith's, which espoused free trade and a free market.
AP.EH.4.3.B.4: Enlightenment thought, which focused on concepts such as empiricism, skepticism, human reason, rationalism, and classical sources of knowledge, challenged the prevailing patterns of thought with respect to social order, institutions of government, and the role of faith.
AP.EH.4.3.B.5: Intellectuals, including Voltaire and Diderot, developed new philosophies of deism, skepticism, and atheism.
AP.EH.4.3.B.6: Religion was viewed increasingly as a matter of private rather than public concern.
AP.EH.4.4.A: Explain the factors contributing to and the consequences of demographic changes from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.4.4.A.1: In the 17th century, small landholdings, low-productivity agricultural practices, poor transportation, and adverse weather limited and disrupted the food supply, causing periodic famines. By the 18th century, the balance between population and the food supply stabilized, resulting in steady population growth.
AP.EH.4.4.A.1.i: By the middle of the 18th century, higher agricultural productivity and improved transportation increased the food supply, allowing populations to grow and reducing the number of demographic crises (a process known as the Agricultural Revolution).
AP.EH.4.4.A.1.ii: In the 18th century, plague disappeared as a major epidemic disease, and inoculation reduced smallpox mortality.
AP.EH.4.4.A.2: Although the rate of illegitimate births increased in the 18th century, population growth was limited by the European marriage pattern, and in some areas by various birth control methods.
AP.EH.4.4.A.3: As infant and child mortality decreased, and commercial wealth increased, families dedicated more space and resources to children and child-rearing, as well as private life and comfort.
AP.EH.4.4.A.4: Cities offered economic opportunities, which attracted increasing migration from rural areas, transforming urban life and creating challenges for the new urbanites and their families.
AP.EH.4.4.A.4.i: The Agricultural Revolution produced more food using fewer workers; as a result, people migrated from rural areas to the cities in search of work.
AP.EH.4.4.A.4.ii: The growth of cities eroded traditional communal values, and city governments strained to provide protection and a healthy environment.
AP.EH.4.4.A.4.iii: The concentration of the poor in cities led to a greater awareness of poverty, crime, and prostitution as social problems, and prompted increased efforts to police marginal groups.
AP.EH.4.5.A: Explain how European cultural and intellectual life was maintained and changed throughout the period from 1648 to 1815.
AP.EH.4.5.A.1: Despite censorship, increasingly numerous and varied printed materials served a growing literate public and led to the development of public opinion.
AP.EH.4.5.A.2: Natural sciences, literature, and popular culture increasingly exposed Europeans to representations of peoples outside Europe and, on occasion, challenges to accepted social norms.
AP.EH.4.5.A.3: The arts moved from the celebration of religious themes and royal power to an emphasis on private life and the public good.
AP.EH.4.5.A.3.i: Until about `text(1750)`, Baroque art and music promoted religious feeling and was employed by monarchs to illustrate state power.
AP.EH.4.5.A.3.ii: 18th-century art and literature increasingly reflected the outlook and values of commercial and bourgeois society. Neoclassicism expressed new Enlightenment ideals of citizenship and political participation.
AP.EH.4.5.A.4: The consumer revolution of the 18th century was shaped by a new concern for privacy, encouraged the purchase of new goods for homes, and created new venues for leisure activities.
AP.EH.4.6.A: Explain how different forms of political power were influenced by Enlightenment thought from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.4.6.A.1: In the 18th century, a number of states in eastern and central Europe experimented with enlightened absolutism.
AP.EH.4.6.A.2: By `text(1800)`, most governments in western and central Europe had extended toleration to Christian minorities and, in some states, civil equality to Jews.
AP.EH.4.6.B: Explain how and why political and religious developments challenged or reinforced the idea of a unified Europe from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.4.6.B.1: As a result of the Holy Roman Empire's limitation of sovereignty in the Peace of Westphalia, Prussia rose to power, and the Habsburgs, centered in Austria, shifted their empire eastward.
AP.EH.4.7: Causation In The Age Of The Scientific Revolution & The Enlightenment
AP.EH.4.7.A: Explain how and why the Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment challenged the existing European order and understanding of the world.
AP.EH.4.7.A.1: The rediscovery of works from ancient Greece and Rome and observation of the natural world changed many Europeans' view of their world.
AP.EH.4.7.A.1.i: New ideas in science based on observation, experimentation, and mathematics challenged classical views of the cosmos, nature, and the human body, although existing traditions of knowledge and the universe continued.
AP.EH.4.7.A.2: The spread of Scientific Revolution concepts and practices and the Enlightenment's application of these concepts and practices to political, social, and ethical issues led to an increased but not unchallenged emphasis on reason in European culture.
AP.EH.4.7.A.2.i: Enlightenment thought, which focused on concepts such as empiricism, skepticism, human reason, rationalism, and classical sources of knowledge, challenged the prevailing patterns of thought with respect to social order, institutions of government, and the role of faith.
AP.EH.4.7.A.2.ii: New public venues and print media popularized Enlightenment ideas.
AP.EH.4.7.A.2.iii: New political and economic theories challenged absolutism and mercantilism.
AP.EH.4.7.A.2.iv: During the Enlightenment, the rational analysis of religious practices led to natural religion and the demand for religious toleration.
AP.EH.4.7.A.3: The experiences of everyday life were shaped by demographic, environmental, medical, and technological changes.
AP.EH.4.7.A.3.i: By the 18th century, family and private life reflected new demographic patterns and the effects of the commercial revolution.
AP.EH.5.1.A: Explain the context in which the European states experienced crisis and conflict from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.5.1.A.1: Different models of political sovereignty affected the relationship among states and between states and individuals.
AP.EH.5.1.A.1.i: The French Revolution posed a fundamental challenge to Europe's existing political and social order.
AP.EH.5.1.A.1.ii: Claiming to defend the ideals of the French Revolution, Napoleon Bonaparte imposed French control over much of the European continent, which eventually provoked a nationalistic reaction.
AP.EH.5.1.A.2: The expansion of European commerce accelerated the growth of a worldwide economic network.
AP.EH.5.1.A.2.i: Commercial rivalries influenced diplomacy and warfare among European states in the early modern era.
AP.EH.5.1.A.3: The spread of Scientific Revolution concepts and practices and the Enlightenment's application of these concepts and practices to political, social, and ethical issues led to an increased but not unchallenged emphasis on reason in European culture.
AP.EH.5.1.A.3.i: While Enlightenment values dominated the world of European ideas and culture, they were challenged by the revival of public expression of emotions and feeling.
AP.EH.5.1.A.3.ii: Revolution, war and rebellion demonstrated the emotional power of mass politics and nationalism.
AP.EH.5.2.A: Explain the causes and consequences of European maritime competition from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.5.2.A.1: The expansion of European commerce accelerated the growth of a worldwide economic network.
AP.EH.5.2.A.1.i: Commercial rivalries influenced diplomacy and warfare among European states in the early modern era.
AP.EH.5.2.A.1.ii: European sea powers vied for Atlantic influence throughout the 18th century.
AP.EH.5.2.A.1.iii: Portuguese, Dutch, French, and British rivalries in Asia culminated in British domination in India and Dutch control of the East Indies.
AP.EH.5.3.A: Explain the economic and political consequences of the rivalry between Britain and France from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.5.3.A.1: Rivalry between Britain and France resulted in world wars fought both in Europe and in the colonies, with Britain supplanting France as the greatest European power.
AP.EH.5.4.A: Explain the causes, events, and consequences of the French Revolution.
AP.EH.5.4.A.1: The French Revolution resulted from a combination of long-term social and political causes, as well as Enlightenment ideas, exacerbated by short-term fiscal and economic crises.
AP.EH.5.4.A.2: The first, or liberal, phase of the French Revolution established a constitutional monarchy, increased popular participation, nationalized the Catholic Church, and abolished hereditary privileges.
AP.EH.5.4.A.3: After the execution of Louis XVI, the radical Jacobin republic led by Robespierre responded to opposition at home and war abroad by instituting the Reign of Terror, fixing prices and wages, and pursuing a policy of de-Christianization.
AP.EH.5.4.A.4: Revolutionary armies, raised by mass conscription, sought to bring the changes initiated in France to the rest of Europe.
AP.EH.5.4.A.5: Women enthusiastically participated in the early phases of the revolution; however, while there were brief improvements in the legal status of women, citizenship in the republic was soon restricted to men.
AP.EH.5.5.A: Explain how the events and developments of the French Revolution influenced political and social ideas from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.5.5.A.1: Revolutionary ideals inspired a revolt of enslaved people led by Toussaint L'Ouverture in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, which became the independent nation of Haiti in `text(1804)`.
AP.EH.5.5.A.2: While many were inspired by the revolution's emphasis on equality and human rights, others condemned its violence and disregard for traditional authority.
AP.EH.5.6.A: Explain the effects of Napoleon's rule on European social, economic, and political life.
AP.EH.5.6.A.1: As first consul and emperor, Napoleon undertook a number of enduring domestic reforms while often curtailing some rights and manipulating popular impulses behind a façade of representative institutions.
AP.EH.5.6.A.2: Napoleon's new military tactics allowed him to exert direct or indirect control over much of the European continent, spreading the ideals of the French Revolution across Europe.
AP.EH.5.6.B: Explain the nationalist responses to Napoleon's rule in Europe.
AP.EH.5.6.B.1: Napoleon's expanding empire created nationalist responses throughout Europe.
AP.EH.5.7.A: Explain how states responded to Napoleonic rule in Europe and the consequences of the response.
AP.EH.5.7.A.1: After the defeat of Napoleon by a coalition of European powers, the Congress of Vienna (`text(1814)-text(1815)`) attempted to restore the balance of power in Europe and contain the danger of revolutionary or nationalistic upheavals in the future.
AP.EH.5.8.A: Explain how and why the Romantic Movement and religious revival challenged Enlightenment thought from `text(1648)` to `text(1815)`.
AP.EH.5.8.A.1: Rousseau questioned the exclusive reliance. on reason and emphasized the role of emotions in the moral improvement of self and society.
AP.EH.5.8.A.2: Romanticism emerged as a challenge to Enlightenment rationality.
AP.EH.5.8.A.3: Consistent with the Romantic Movement, religious revival occurred in Europe and included notable movements such as Methodism, founded by John Wesley.
AP.EH.5.8.A.4: Revolution, war, and rebellion demonstrated the emotional power of mass politics and nationalism.
AP.EH.5.9.A: Explain how the developments and challenges to the political order resulted in change in the period from 1648 to 1815.
AP.EH.5.9.A.1: Different models of political sovereignty affected the relationship among states and between states and individuals.
AP.EH.5.9.A.1.i: The French Revolution posed a fundamental challenge to Europe's existing political and social order.
AP.EH.5.9.A.1.ii: Claiming to defend the ideals of the French Revolution, Napoleon Bonaparte imposed French control over much of the European continent, which eventually provoked a nationalistic reaction.
AP.EH.5.9.A.2: The expansion of European commerce accelerated the growth of a worldwide economic network.
AP.EH.5.9.A.2.i: Commercial rivalries influenced diplomacy and warfare among European states in the early modern era.
AP.EH.5.9.A.3: The spread of Scientific Revolution concepts and practices and the Enlightenment's application of these concepts and practices to political, social, and ethical issues led to an increased but not unchallenged emphasis on reason in European culture.
AP.EH.5.9.A.3.i: While Enlightenment values dominated the world of European ideas and culture, they were challenged by the revival of public expression of emotions and feeling.
AP.EH.5.9.A.3.ii: Revolution, war and rebellion demonstrated the emotional power of mass politics and nationalism.
AP.EH.6.1.A: Explain the context in which industrialization originated, developed, and spread in Europe.
AP.EH.6.1.A.1: The Industrial Revolution spread from Great Britain to the continent, where the state played a greater role in promoting industry.
AP.EH.6.1.A.1.i: Great Britain established its industrial dominance through the mechanization of textile production, iron and steel production, and new transportation systems in conjunction with uniquely favorable political and social climates.
AP.EH.6.1.A.1.ii: Following the British example, industrialization took root in continental Europe, sometimes with state sponsorship.
AP.EH.6.1.A.2: The experiences of everyday life were shaped by industrialization, depending on the level of industrial development in a particular location.
AP.EH.6.1.A.2.i: Industrialization promoted the development of new classes in the industrial regions of Europe.
AP.EH.6.1.A.2.ii: Europe experienced rapid population growth and urbanization, leading to social dislocations.
AP.EH.6.1.A.2.iii: Over time, the Industrial Revolution altered the family structure and relations for bourgeois and working-class families.
AP.EH.6.1.A.3: Political revolutions and the complications resulting from industrialization triggered a range of ideological, governmental, and collective responses.
AP.EH.6.1.A.3.i: Ideologies developed and took root throughout society as a response to industrial and political revolutions.
AP.EH.6.1.A.3.ii: Governments, at times based on the pressure of political or social organizations, responded to problems created or exacerbated by industrialization.
AP.EH.6.2: The Spread Of Industry Throughout Europe
AP.EH.6.2.A: Explain the factors that influenced the development of industrialization in Europe from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.2.A.1: Britain's ready supplies of coal, iron ore, and other essential raw materials promoted industrial growth.
AP.EH.6.2.A.2: Great Britain established its industrial dominance through the mechanization of textile production, iron and steel production, and new transportation systems in conjunction with uniquely favorable political and social climates.
AP.EH.6.2.A.3: Economic institutions and human capital such as engineers, inventors, and capitalists helped Britain lead the process of industrialization, largely through private initiative.
AP.EH.6.2.A.4: Britain's parliamentary government promoted commercial and industrial interests because those interests were represented in Parliament.
AP.EH.6.2.A.5: France moved toward industrialization at a more gradual pace than Great Britain, with government support and with less dislocation of traditional methods of production.
AP.EH.6.2.A.6: A combination of factors, including geography, lack of resources, the dominance of traditional landed elites, the persistence of serfdom in some areas, and inadequate government sponsorship, accounted for eastern and southern Europe's lag in industrial development.
AP.EH.6.2.A.7: Because of the continued existence of more primitive agricultural practices and land-owning patterns, some areas of Europe lagged in industrialization while facing famine, debt, and land shortages.
AP.EH.6.3.A: Explain how innovations and advances in technology during the Industrial Revolutions led to economic and social change.
AP.EH.6.3.A.1: Mechanization and the factory system became the predominant modes of production by `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.3.A.2: New technologies and means of communication and transportation - including railroads - resulted in more fully integrated national economies, a higher level of urbanization, and a truly global economic network.
AP.EH.6.3.A.3: New, efficient methods of transportation and other innovations created new industries, improved the distribution of goods, increased consumerism, and enhanced quality of life.
AP.EH.6.3.B: Explain how industrialization influenced economic and political development throughout the period from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.3.B.1: During the second industrial revolution (c. `text(1870)-text(1914)`), more areas of Europe experienced industrial activity, and industrial processes increased in scale and complexity.
AP.EH.6.3.B.1.i: Volatile business cycles in the last quarter of the 19th century led corporations and governments to try to manage the market through a variety of methods, including monopolies, banking practices, and tariffs.
AP.EH.6.3.B.2: Along with better harvests caused in part by the commercialization of agriculture, industrialization promoted population growth, longer life expectancy, and lowered infant mortality.
AP.EH.6.3.B.3: A heightened consumerism developed as a result of the second industrial revolution.
AP.EH.6.3.B.3.i: Industrialization and mass marketing increased both the production and demand for a new range of consumer goods - including clothing, processed foods, and labor-saving devices - and created more leisure opportunities.
AP.EH.6.3.B.3.ii: Industrialization in Prussia allowed that state to become the leader of a unified Germany, which subsequently underwent rapid industrialization under government sponsorship.
AP.EH.6.4.A: Explain the causes and consequences of social developments resulting from industrialization.
AP.EH.6.4.A.1: In industrialized areas of Europe (i.e., western and northern Europe), socioeconomic changes created divisions of labor that led to the development of self-conscious classes, including the proletariat and the bourgeoisie.
AP.EH.6.4.A.2: In some of the less industrialized areas of Europe, the dominance of agricultural elites continued into the 20th century.
AP.EH.6.4.A.3: Class identity developed and was reinforced through participation in philanthropic, political, and social associations among the middle classes, and in mutual aid societies and trade unions among the working classes.
AP.EH.6.4.A.4: With migration from rural to urban areas in industrialized regions, cities experienced overcrowding, while affected rural areas suffered declines in available labor as well as weakened communities.
AP.EH.6.4.A.5: Bourgeois families became focused on the nuclear family and the cult of domesticity, with distinct gender roles for men and women.
AP.EH.6.4.A.6: By the end of the century, higher wages, laws restricting the labor of children and women, social welfare programs, improved diet, and increased access to birth control affected the quality of life for the working class.
AP.EH.6.4.A.7: Economic motivations for marriage, while still important for all classes, diminished as the middle-class notion of companionate marriage began to be adopted by the working classes.
AP.EH.6.4.A.8: Leisure time centered increasingly on the family or small groups, concurrent with the development of activities and spaces to use that time.
AP.EH.6.5: The Concert Of Europe & European Conservatism
AP.EH.6.5.A: Explain how the European political order was maintained and challenged from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.5.A.1: Conservatives developed a new ideology in support of traditional political and religious authorities, which was based on the idea that human nature was not perfectible.
AP.EH.6.5.A.2: The Concert of Europe (or Congress System) sought to maintain the status quo through collective action and adherence to conservatism.
