AP.EH.6.5.A.2.i: Metternich, architect of the Concert of Europe, used it to suppress nationalist and liberal revolutions.
AP.EH.6.5.A.2.ii: Conservatives reestablished control in many European states and attempted to suppress movements for change and, in some areas, to strengthen adherence to religious authorities.
AP.EH.6.6.A: Explain how and why various groups reacted against the existing order from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.6.A.1: In the first half of the 19th century, revolutionaries attempted to destroy the status quo.
AP.EH.6.6.A.2: The revolutions of `text(1848)`, triggered by economic hardship and discontent with the political status quo, challenged conservative politicians and governments and led to the breakdown of the Concert of Europe.
AP.EH.6.6.A.3: In Russia, autocratic leaders pushed through a program of reform and modernization, including the emancipation of the serfs, which gave rise to revolutionary movements and eventually the Russian Revolution of `text(1905)`.
AP.EH.6.7.A: Explain how and why different intellectual developments challenged the political and social order from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.7.A.1: Liberals emphasized popular sovereignty, individual rights, and enlightened self-interest but debated the extent to which all groups in society should actively participate in its governance.
AP.EH.6.7.A.2: Radicals in Britain and republicans on the continent demanded universal male suffrage and full citizenship without regard to wealth and property ownership; some argued that such rights should be extended to women.
AP.EH.6.7.A.3: Socialists called for the redistribution of society's resources and wealth and evolved from a utopian to a Marxist scientific critique of capitalism.
AP.EH.6.7.A.4: Marx's scientific socialism provided a systematic critique of capitalism and a deterministic analysis of society and historical evolution.
AP.EH.6.7.A.5: Anarchists asserted that all forms of governmental authority were unnecessary and should be overthrown and replaced with a society based on voluntary cooperation.
AP.EH.6.8.A: Explain the various movements and calls for social reform that resulted from intellectual developments from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.8.A.1: Political movements and social organizations responded to problems of industrialization.
AP.EH.6.8.A.1.i: Mass-based political parties emerged as sophisticated vehicles for social, economic, and political reform.
AP.EH.6.8.A.1.ii: Workers established labor unions and movements promoting social and economic reforms that also developed into political parties.
AP.EH.6.8.A.1.iii: Feminists pressed for legal, economic, and political rights for women as well as improved working conditions.
AP.EH.6.8.A.1.iv: Various nongovernmental reform amovements, many of them religious, assisted the poor and worked to end serfdom and slavery.
AP.EH.6.9.A: Explain how and why governments and other institutions responded to challenges resulting from industrialization.
AP.EH.6.9.A.1: Liberalism shifted from laissez-faire to interventionist economic and social policies in response to the challenges of industrialization.
AP.EH.6.9.A.2: Reforms transformed unhealthy and overcrowded cities by modernizing infrastructure, regulating public health, reforming prisons, and establishing modern police forces. The reforms were enacted by governments motivated by such forces as public opinion, prominent individuals, and charity organizations.
AP.EH.6.9.A.3: Reformers promoted compulsory public education to advance the goals of public order, nationalism, and economic growth.
AP.EH.6.10: Causation In The Age Of Industrialization
AP.EH.6.10.A: Explain the influence of innovations and technological developments in Europe from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.6.10.A.1: The Industrial Revolution spread from Great Britain to the continent, where the state played a greater role in promoting industry.
AP.EH.6.10.A.1.i: Great Britain established its industrial dominance through the mechanization of textile production, iron and steel production, and new transportation systems in conjunction with uniquely favorable political and social climates.
AP.EH.6.10.A.1.ii: Following the British example, industrialization took root in continental Europe, sometimes with state sponsorship.
AP.EH.6.10.A.2: The experiences of everyday life were shaped by industrialization, depending on the level of industrial development in a particular location.
AP.EH.6.10.A.2.i: Industrialization promoted the development of new classes in the industrial regions of Europe.
AP.EH.6.10.A.2.ii: Europe experienced rapid population growth and urbanization, leading to social dislocations.
AP.EH.6.10.A.2.iii: Over time, the Industrial Revolution altered the family structure and relations for bourgeois and working-class families.
AP.EH.6.10.A.3: Political revolutions and the complications resulting from industrialization triggered a range of ideological, governmental, and collective responses.
AP.EH.6.10.A.3.i: Ideologies developed and took root throughout society as a response to industrial and political revolutions.
AP.EH.6.10.A.3.ii: Governments, at times based on the pressure of political or social organizations, responded to problems created or exacerbated by industrialization.
AP.EH.7.1.A: Explain the context in which nationalistic and imperialistic sentiments developed in Europe from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.1.A.1: European states struggled to maintain international stability in an age of nationalism and revolutions.
AP.EH.7.1.A.1.i: The breakdown of the Concert of Europe opened the door for movements of national unification in Italy and Germany as well as liberal reforms elsewhere.
AP.EH.7.1.A.1.ii: The unification of Italy and Germany transformed the European balance of power and led to efforts to construct a new diplomatic order.
AP.EH.7.1.A.2: A variety of motives and methods led to the intensification of European global control and increased tensions among the Great Powers.
AP.EH.7.1.A.2.i: Industrial and technological developments (e.g., the second industrial revolution) facilitated European control of global empires.
AP.EH.7.1.A.3: European ideas and culture expressed a tension between objectivity and scientific realism on one hand, and subjectivity and individual expression on the other.
AP.EH.7.1.A.3.i: Following the revolutions of `text(1848)`, Europe turned toward a realist and materialist worldview.
AP.EH.7.2.A: Explain how the development and spread of nationalism affected Europe from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.2.A.1: Nationalists encouraged loyalty to the nation in a variety of ways, including romantic idealism, liberal reform, political unification, racialism with a concomitant anti-Semitism, and chauvinism justifying national aggrandizement.
AP.EH.7.2.A.2: While during the 19th century western European Jews became more socially and politically acculturated, Zionism, a form of Jewish nationalism, developed late in the century as a response to growing anti-Semitism throughout Europe.
AP.EH.7.2.A.3: A new generation of conservative leaders, including Napoleon III, Cavour, and Bismarck, used popular nationalism to create or strengthen the state.
AP.EH.7.2.A.4: The creation of the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, which recognized the political power of the largest ethnic minority, was an attempt to stabilize the state by reconfiguring national unity.
AP.EH.7.3.A: Explain the factors that resulted in Italian unification and German unification.
AP.EH.7.3.A.1: The Crimean War demonstrated the weakness of the Ottoman Empire and contributed to the breakdown of the Concert of Europe, thereby creating the conditions in which Italy and Germany could be unified after centuries of fragmentation.
AP.EH.7.3.A.2: Cavour's diplomatic strategies, combined with the popular Garibaldi's military campaigns, led to the unification of Italy.
AP.EH.7.3.A.3: Bismarck used Realpolitik, employing diplomacy, industrialized warfare, weaponry, and the manipulation of democratic mechanisms to unify Germany.
AP.EH.7.3.B: Explain how nationalist sentiment and political alliances led to tension between and among European powers from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.3.B.1: After `text(1871)`, Bismarck attempted to maintain the balance of power through a complex system of alliances directed at isolating France.
AP.EH.7.3.B.2: Bismarck's dismissal in `text(1890)` eventually led to a system of mutually antagonistic alliances and heightened international tensions.
AP.EH.7.3.B.3: Nationalist tensions in the Balkans drew the Great Powers into a series of crises, leading up to World War I.
AP.EH.7.4.A: Explain how Darwin's theories influenced scientific and social developments from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.4.A.1: Charles Darwin provided a scientific and material account of biological change and the development of human beings as a species, and inadvertently, a justification for racialist theories that became known as Social Darwinism.
AP.EH.7.5.A: Explain how science and other intellectual disciplines developed and changed throughout the period from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.5.A.1: Positivism, or the philosophy that science alone provides knowledge, emphasized the rational and scientific analysis of nature and human affairs.
AP.EH.7.5.A.2: In the later 19th century, a new relativism in values and the loss of confidence in the objectivity of knowledge led to modernism in intellectual and cultural life.
AP.EH.7.5.A.2.i: Philosophy largely moved from rational interpretations of nature and human society to an emphasis on irrationality and impulse, a view that contributed to the belief that conflict and struggle led to progress.
AP.EH.7.5.A.2.ii: Freudian psychology offered a new account of human nature that emphasized the role of the irrational and the struggle between the conscious and subconscious.
AP.EH.7.5.A.2.iii: Developments in the natural sciences, such as quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory of relativity, undermined the primacy of Newtonian physics as an objective description of nature.
AP.EH.7.6.A: Explain the motivations that led to European imperialism in the period from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.6.A.1: European nations were driven by economic, political, and cultural motivations in their new imperial ventures in Asia and Africa.
AP.EH.7.6.A.1.i: European national rivalries and strategic concerns fostered imperial expansion and competition for colonies.
AP.EH.7.6.A.1.ii: The search for raw materials and markets for manufactured goods, as well as strategic and nationalistic considerations, drove Europeans to colonize Africa and Asia, even as European colonies in the Americas broke free politically, if not economically.
AP.EH.7.6.A.1.iii: European imperialists justified overseas expansion and rule by claiming cultural and racial superiority.
AP.EH.7.6.B: Explain how technological advances enabled European imperialism from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.6.B.1: The development of advanced weaponry ensured the military advantage of Europeans over colonized areas.
AP.EH.7.6.B.2: Communication and transportation technologies facilitated the creation and expansion of European empires.
AP.EH.7.6.B.3: Advances in medicine enabled European survival in Africa and Asia.
AP.EH.7.7.A: Explain how European imperialism affected both European and non-European societies.
AP.EH.7.7.A.1: Imperial endeavors significantly affected society, diplomacy, and culture in Europe and created resistance to foreign control abroad.
AP.EH.7.7.A.1.i: Imperialism created diplomatic tensions among European states that strained alliance systems.
AP.EH.7.7.A.1.ii: Imperial encounters with non-European peoples influenced the styles and subject matter of artists and writers and provoked debate over the acquisition of colonies.
AP.EH.7.7.A.1.iii: Especially as non-Europeans became educated in Western values, they challenged European imperialism through nationalist movements and by modernizing local economies and societies.
AP.EH.7.8.A: Explain the continuities and changes in European artistic expression from `text(1815)` to `text(1914)`.
AP.EH.7.8.A.1: Romanticism broke with Neoclassical forms of artistic representation and with rationalism, placing more emphasis on intuition and emotion.
AP.EH.7.8.A.2: Romantic artists and composers broke from classical artistic forms to emphasize emotion, nature, individuality, intuition, the supernatural, and national histories in their works.
AP.EH.7.8.A.3: Romantic writers expressed similar themes while responding to the Industrial Revolution and to various political revolutions.
AP.EH.7.8.A.4: Realist and materialist themes and attitudes influenced art and literature as painters and writers depicted the lives of ordinary people and drew attention to social problems.
AP.EH.7.8.A.5: Modern art, including Impressionism, Post-Impressionism, and Cubism, moved beyond the representational to the subjective, abstract, and expressive and often provoked audiences that believed that art should reflect shared and idealized values, including beauty and patriotism.
AP.EH.7.9.A: Explain the influence of nationalist and imperialist movements on European and global stability.
AP.EH.7.9.A.1: European states struggled to maintain international stability in an age of nationalism and revolutions.
AP.EH.7.9.A.1.i: The breakdown of the Concert of Europe opened the door for movements of national unification in Italy and Germany as well as liberal reforms elsewhere.
AP.EH.7.9.A.1.ii: The unification of Italy and Germany transformed the European balance of power and led to efforts to construct a new diplomatic order.
AP.EH.7.9.A.2: A variety of motives and methods led to the intensification of European global control and increased tensions among the Great Powers.
AP.EH.7.9.A.2.i: Industrial and technological developments (e.g., the second industrial revolution) facilitated European control of global empires.
AP.EH.7.9.A.3: European ideas and culture expressed a tension between objectivity and scientific realism on one hand, and subjectivity and individual expression on the other.
AP.EH.7.9.A.3.i: Following the revolutions of 1848, Europe turned toward a realist and materialist worldview.
AP.EH.8.1.A: Explain the context in which global conflict developed in the 20th century.
AP.EH.8.1.A.1: Total war and political instability in the first half of the 20th century gave way to a polarized state order during the Cold War and eventually to efforts at transnational union.
AP.EH.8.1.A.1.i: World War I, caused by a complex interaction of long- and short-term factors, resulted in immense losses and disruptions for both victors and vanquished.
AP.EH.8.1.A.1.ii: The conflicting goals of the peace negotiators in Paris pitted diplomatic idealism against the desire to punish Germany, producing a settlement that satisfied few.
AP.EH.8.1.A.1.iii: In the interwar period, fascism, extreme nationalism, racist ideologies, and the failure of appeasement resulted in the catastrophe of World War II, presenting a grave challenge to European civilization.
AP.EH.8.1.A.2: The stresses of economic collapse and total war engendered internal conflicts within European states and created conflicting conceptions of the relationship between the individual and the state, as demonstrated in the ideological battle between and among democracy, communism, and fascism.
AP.EH.8.1.A.3: During the 20th century, diverse intellectual and cultural movements questioned the existence of objective knowledge, the ability of reason to arrive at truth, and the role of religion in determining moral standards.
AP.EH.8.1.A.3.i: Science and technology yielded impressive material benefits but also caused immense destruction and posed challenges to objective knowledge.
AP.EH.8.1.A.4: Demographic changes, economic growth, total war, disruptions of traditional social patterns, and competing definitions of freedom and justice altered the experiences of everyday life.
AP.EH.8.1.A.4.i: The 20th century was characterized by large-scale suffering brought on by warfare and genocide, but also by tremendous improvements in the standard of living.
AP.EH.8.2.A: Explain the causes and effects of World War I.
AP.EH.8.2.A.1: World War I, caused by a complex interaction of long- and short-term factors, resulted in immense losses and disruptions for both victors and vanquished.
AP.EH.8.2.A.1.i: A variety of factors-including nationalism, military plans, the alliance system, and imperial competition-turned a regional dispute in the Balkans into World War I.
AP.EH.8.2.B: Explain how new technology altered the conduct of World War I.
AP.EH.8.2.B.1: New technologies confounded traditional military strategies and led to trench warfare and massive troop losses.
AP.EH.8.2.C: Explain how the developments of World War I changed political and diplomatic interactions between and among nations.
AP.EH.8.2.C.1: The effects of military stalemate, national mobilization, and total war led to protest and insurrection in the belligerent nations and eventually to revolutions that changed the international balance of power.
AP.EH.8.2.C.2: The war in Europe quickly spread to non-European theaters, transforming the war into a global conflict.
AP.EH.8.2.C.3: The relationship of Europe to the world shifted significantly with the globalization of the conflict, the emergence of the United States as a world power, and the overthrow of European empires.
AP.EH.8.3.A: Explain the causes and effects of the Russian Revolution.
AP.EH.8.3.A.1: The Russian Revolution created a regime based on Marxist-Leninist theory.
AP.EH.8.3.A.1.i: In Russia, World War I exacerbated long-term problems of political stagnation, social inequality, incomplete industrialization, and food and land distribution, all while creating support for revolutionary change.
AP.EH.8.3.A.1.ii: Military and worker insurrections, aided by the revived Soviets, undermined the Provisional Government and set the stage for Lenin's long-planned Bolshevik Revolution and establishment of a communist state.
AP.EH.8.3.A.1.iii: The Bolshevik takeover prompted a protracted civil war between communist forces and their opponents, who were aided by foreign powers.
AP.EH.8.3.A.1.iv: In order to improve economic performance, Lenin compromised communist principles and employed some free-market principles under the New Economic Policy.
AP.EH.8.4.A: Explain how and why the settlement of World War I failed to effectively resolve the political, economic, and diplomatic challenges of the early 20th century.
AP.EH.8.4.A.1: The conflicting goals of the peace negotiators in Paris pitted diplomatic idealism against the desire to punish Germany, producing a settlement that satisfied few.
AP.EH.8.4.A.1.i: Wilsonian idealism clashed with postwar realities in both the victorious and the defeated states. Democratic successor states emerged from former empires and eventually succumbed to significant political, economic, and diplomatic crises.
AP.EH.8.4.A.1.ii: The League of Nations, created to prevent future wars, was weakened from the outset by the nonparticipation of major powers, including the U.S., Germany, and the Soviet Union.
AP.EH.8.4.A.1.iii: The Versailles settlement, particularly its provisions on the assignment of guilt and reparations for the war, hindered the German Weimar Republic's ability to establish a stable and legitimate political and economic system.
AP.EH.8.4.A.2: The League of Nations distributed former German and Ottoman possessions to France and Great Britain through the mandate system, thereby altering the imperial balance of power and creating a strategic interest in the Middle East and its oil.
AP.EH.8.5.A: Explain the causes and effects of the global economic crisis in the `yrcy(1920s)` and `yrcy(1930s)`.
AP.EH.8.5.A.1: The Great Depression, caused by weaknesses in international trade and monetary theories and practices, undermined Western European democracies and fomented radical political responses throughout Europe.
AP.EH.8.5.A.1.i: World War I debt, nationalistic tariff policies, overproduction, depreciated currencies, disrupted trade patterns, and speculation created weaknesses in economies worldwide.
AP.EH.8.5.A.1.ii: Dependence on post-World War I American investment capital led to financial collapse when, following the `text(1929)` stock market crash, the United States cut off capital flows to Europe.
AP.EH.8.5.A.1.iii: Despite attempts to rethink economic theories and policies and forge political alliances, Western democracies failed to overcome the Great Depression and were weakened by extremist movements.
AP.EH.8.6.A: Explain the factors that led to the development of fascist and totalitarian regimes in the aftermath of World War I.
AP.EH.8.6.A.1: The ideology of fascism, with roots in the pre-World War I era, gained popularity in an environment of postwar bitterness, the rise of communism, uncertain transitions to democracy, and economic instability.
AP.EH.8.6.A.1.i: Fascist dictatorships used modern technology and propaganda that rejected democratic institutions, promoted charismatic leaders, and glorified war and nationalism to attract the disillusioned.
AP.EH.8.6.A.1.ii: Mussolini and Hitler rose to power by exploiting postwar bitterness and economic instability, using terror, and manipulating the fledgling and unpopular democracies in their countries.
AP.EH.8.6.A.1.iii: Franco's alliance with Italian and German fascists in the Spanish Civil War - in which the Western democracies did not intervene - represented a testing ground for World War II and resulted in authoritarian rule in Spain from `text(1936)` to the `text(mid-1970s)`.
AP.EH.8.6.A.1.iv: After failures to establish functioning democracies, authoritarian dictatorships took power in central and eastern Europe during the interwar period.
AP.EH.8.6.B: Explain the consequences of Stalin's economic policies and totalitarian rule in the Soviet Union.
AP.EH.8.6.B.1: After Lenin's death, Stalin undertook a centralized program of rapid economic modernization, often with severe repercussions for the population.
AP.EH.8.6.B.2: Stalin's economic modernization of the Soviet Union came at a high price, including the liquidation of the kulaks (the land-owning peasantry) and other perceived enemies of the state, devastating famine in the Ukraine, purges of political rivals, and, ultimately, the creation of an oppressive political system.
AP.EH.8.7.A: Explain how and why various political and ideological factors resulted in the catastrophe of World War II.
AP.EH.8.7.A.1: French and British fears of another war, American isolationism, and deep distrust between Western democratic, capitalist nations and the authoritarian, communist Soviet Union allowed fascist states to rearm and expand their territory.
AP.EH.8.7.A.2: In the interwar period, fascism, extreme nationalism, racist ideologies, and the failure of appeasement resulted in the catastrophe of World War II, presenting a grave challenge to European civilization.
AP.EH.8.8.A: Explain how technology and innovation affected the course of World War II and the 20th century.
AP.EH.8.8.A.1: Germany's Blitzkrieg warfare in Europe, combined with Japan's attacks in Asia and the Pacific, brought the Axis powers early victories.
AP.EH.8.8.A.2: American and British industrial, scientific, and technological power, cooperative military efforts under the strong leadership of individuals such as Winston Churchill, the resistance of civilians, and the all-out military commitment of the USSR contributed critically to the Allied victories.
AP.EH.8.8.A.3: Military technologies made possible industrialized warfare, genocide, nuclear proliferation, and the risk of global nuclear war.
AP.EH.8.9.A: Explain how and why cultural and national identities were affected by war and the rise of fascist/totalitarian powers in the period from `text(1914)` to the present.
AP.EH.8.9.A.1: Fueled by racism and anti-Semitism, Nazi Germany - with the cooperation of some of the other Axis powers and collaborationist governments - sought to establish a “new racial order” in Europe, which culminated with the Holocaust.
AP.EH.8.9.A.2: World War II decimated a generation of Russian and German men; virtually destroyed European Jewry; resulted in the murder of millions in other groups targeted by the Nazis including Roma, homosexuals, people with disabilities, and others; forced large-scale migrations; and undermined prewar class hierarchies.
AP.EH.8.10.A: Explain how the events of the first half of the 20th century challenged existing social, cultural, and intellectual understandings.
AP.EH.8.10.A.1: The widely held belief in progress characteristic of much of 19th-century thought began to break down before World War I.
AP.EH.8.10.A.2: When World War I began, Europeans were generally confident in the ability of science and technology to address human needs and problems despite the uncertainty created by the new scientific theories and psychology.
AP.EH.8.10.A.3: The challenge to the certainties of the Newtonian universe in physics opened the door to uncertainty in other fields by undermining faith in objective knowledge while also providing the knowledge necessary for the development of nuclear weapons and power.
AP.EH.8.10.A.4: World War I created a “lost generation” and fostered disillusionment and cynicism, while it transformed the lives of women, and democratized societies.
AP.EH.8.10.A.5: During the world wars, women became increasingly involved in military and political mobilization, as well as in economic production.
AP.EH.8.11: Continuity & Changes In An Age Of Global Conflict
AP.EH.8.11.A: Explain how economic challenges and ideological beliefs influenced prior conceptions about the relationship between the individual and the state.
AP.EH.8.11.A.1: Total war and political instability in the first half of the 20th century gave way to a polarized state order during the Cold War and eventually to efforts at transnational union.
AP.EH.8.11.A.1.i: World War I, caused by a complex interaction of long- and short-term factors, resulted in immense losses and disruptions for both victors and vanquished.
AP.EH.8.11.A.1.ii: The conflicting goals of the peace negotiators in Paris pitted diplomatic idealism against the desire to punish Germany, producing a settlement that satisfied few.
AP.EH.8.11.A.1.iii: In the interwar period, fascism, extreme nationalism, racist ideologies, and the failure of appeasement resulted in the catastrophe of World War II, presenting a grave challenge to European civilization.
AP.EH.8.11.A.2: The stresses of economic collapse and total war engendered internal conflicts within European states and created conflicting conceptions of the relationship between the individual and the state, as demonstrated in the ideological battle between and among democracy, communism, and fascism.
AP.EH.8.11.A.3: During the 20th century, diverse intellectual and cultural movements questioned the existence of objective knowledge, the ability of reason to arrive at truth, and the role of religion in determining moral standards.
AP.EH.8.11.A.3.i: Science and technology yielded impressive material benefits but also caused immense destruction and posed challenges to objective knowledge.
AP.EH.8.11.A.4: Demographic changes, economic growth, total war, disruptions of traditional social patterns, and competing definitions of freedom and justice altered the experiences of everyday life.
AP.EH.8.11.A.4.i: The 20th century was characterized by large-scale suffering brought on by warfare and genocide, but also by tremendous improvements in the standard of living.
AP.EH.9.1.A: Explain the context in which the Cold War developed, spread, and ended in Europe.
AP.EH.9.1.A.1: Total war and political instability in the first half of the 20th century gave way to a polarized state order during the Cold War and eventually to efforts at transnational union.
AP.EH.9.1.A.1.i: As World War II ended, a Cold War between the liberal democratic West and the communist East began, lasting nearly half a century.
AP.EH.9.1.A.2: The stresses of economic collapse and total war engendered internal conflicts within European states and created conflicting conceptions of the relationship between the individual and the state, as demonstrated in the ideological battle between and among democracy, communism, and fascism.
AP.EH.9.1.A.3: During the 20th century, diverse intellectual and cultural movements questioned the existence of objective knowledge, the ability of reason to arrive at truth, and the role of religion in determining moral standards.
AP.EH.9.1.A.3.i: The experience of war intensified a sense of anxiety that permeated many facets of thought and culture, giving way by the century's end to a plurality of intellectual frameworks.
AP.EH.9.1.A.4: Demographic changes, economic growth, total war, disruptions of traditional social patterns, and competing definitions of freedom and justice altered the experiences of everyday life.
AP.EH.9.1.A.4.i: New voices gained prominence in political, intellectual, and social discourse.
AP.EH.9.2.A: Explain how economic developments resulted in economic, political, and cultural change in the period after World War II.
AP.EH.9.2.A.1: Marshall Plan funds from the United States financed an extensive reconstruction of industry and infrastructure and stimulated an extended period of growth in Western and Central Europe, often referred to as an “economic miracle,” which increased the economic and cultural importance of consumerism.
AP.EH.9.3.A: Explain the causes, events, and effects of the Cold War in the period following World War II.
AP.EH.9.3.A.1: Despite efforts to maintain international cooperation through the newly created United Nations, deep-seated tensions between the USSR and the West led to the division of Europe, which was referred to in the West as the Iron Curtain.
AP.EH.9.3.A.2: The Cold War played out on a global stage and involved propaganda campaigns; covert actions; limited “hot wars” in Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the Caribbean; and an arms race, with the threat of a nuclear war.
AP.EH.9.4.A: Explain the economic and political consequences of the Cold War for Europe.
AP.EH.9.4.A.1: The United States exerted a strong military, political, and economic influence in Western Europe, leading to the creation of world monetary and trade systems and geopolitical alliances, including NATO.
AP.EH.9.4.A.2: Countries east of the Iron Curtain came under the military, political, and economic domination of the Soviet Union within the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (COMECON) and the Warsaw Pact.
AP.EH.9.4.A.3: Central and Eastern European nations within the Soviet bloc followed an economic model based on central planning, extensive social welfare, and specialized production among bloc members. This brought with it the restriction of individual rights and freedoms, suppression of dissent, and constraint of emigration for the various populations within the Soviet bloc.
AP.EH.9.4.A.4: Eastern European nations were bound by their relationships with the Soviet Union, which oscillated between repression and limited reform, until the collapse of communist governments in Eastern Europe and the fall of the Soviet Union.
AP.EH.9.4.A.4.i: After `text(1956)`, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev's de-Stalinization policies failed to meet their economic goals within the Soviet Union; combined with reactions to existing limitations on individual rights, this prompted revolts in Eastern Europe, which ended with a reimposition of Soviet rule and repressive totalitarian regimes.
AP.EH.9.4.A.5: The rise of new nationalisms in Central and Eastern Europe brought peaceful revolution in most countries but resulted in instability in some former Soviet republics.
AP.EH.9.5.A: Explain the causes and effects of mass atrocities in the period following World War II to the present.
AP.EH.9.5.A.1: Nationalist and separatist movements, along with ethnic conflict and ethnic cleansing, periodically disrupted the post-World War II peace.
AP.EH.9.5.A.1.i: New nationalisms in central and eastern Europe resulted in war and genocide in the Balkans.
AP.EH.9.6.A: Explain state-based economic developments following World War II and the responses to these developments.
AP.EH.9.6.A.1: Postwar economic growth supported an increase in welfare benefits; however, subsequent economic stagnation led to criticism and limitation of the welfare state.
AP.EH.9.6.A.1.i: The expansion of cradle-to-grave social welfare programs in the aftermath of World War II, accompanied by high taxes, became a contentious domestic political issue as the budgets of European nations came under pressure in the late 20th century.
AP.EH.9.7.A: Explain the causes and effects of the end of the Cold War.
AP.EH.9.7.A.1: Following a long period of economic stagnation, Mikhail Gorbachev's internal reforms of perestroika and glasnost, designed to make the Soviet system more flexible, failed to stave off the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of its hegemonic control over Eastern and Central European satellites.
AP.EH.9.7.A.2: The collapse of the USSR in `text(1991)` ended the Cold War and led to the establishment of capitalist economies throughout Eastern Europe. Germany was reunited, the Czechs and the Slovaks parted, Yugoslavia dissolved, and the European Union was enlarged through the admission of former Eastern bloc countries.
AP.EH.9.8.A: Explain how women's roles and status developed and changed throughout the 20th and 21st centuries.
AP.EH.9.8.A.1: The lives of women were defined by family and work responsibilities, economic changes, and feminism.
AP.EH.9.8.A.1.i: In Western Europe through the efforts of feminists, and in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union through government policy, women finally gained the vote, greater educational opportunities, and access to professional careers, even while continuing to face social inequalities.
AP.EH.9.8.A.1.ii: New modes of marriage, partnership, motherhood, divorce, and reproduction gave women more options in their personal lives.
AP.EH.9.8.A.1.iii: Women attained high political office and increased their representation in legislative bodies in many nations.
AP.EH.9.9.A: Explain the various ways in which colonial groups around the world sought independence from colonizers in the 20th and 21st centuries.
AP.EH.9.9.A.1: The process of decolonization occurred over the course of the century with varying degrees of cooperation, interference, or resistance from European imperialist states.
AP.EH.9.9.A.1.i: At the end of World War I, U.S. President Woodrow Wilson's principle of national self-determination raised expectations in the non-European world for new policies and freedoms.
AP.EH.9.9.A.1.ii: Despite indigenous nationalist movements, independence for many African and Asian territories was delayed until the mid- and even late 20th century by the imperial powers' reluctance to relinquish control, threats of interference from other nations, unstable economic and political systems, and Cold War strategic alignments.
AP.EH.9.10.A: Explain how the formation and existence of the European Union influenced economic developments throughout the period following World War II to the present.
AP.EH.9.10.A.1: European states began to set aside nationalist rivalries in favor of economic and political integration, forming a series of transnational unions that grew in size and scope over the second half of the 20th century.
AP.EH.9.10.A.1.i: As the economic alliance known as the European Coal and Steel Community, envisioned as a means to spur postwar economic recovery, developed into the European Economic Community (EEC or Common Market) and the European Union (EU), Europe experienced increasing economic and political integration and efforts to establish a shared European identity.
AP.EH.9.10.B: Explain how the European Union affected national and European identity throughout the period following World War II to the present.
AP.EH.9.10.B.1: EU member nations continue to balance questions of national sovereignty with the responsibilities of membership in an economic and political union.
AP.EH.9.11.A: Explain the causes and effects of changes to migration within and immigration to Europe throughout the period following World War II to the present.
AP.EH.9.11.A.1: Increased immigration into Europe altered Europe's religious makeup, causing debate and conflict over the role of religion in social and political life.
AP.EH.9.11.A.2: Because of the economic growth of the `text(1950s)` and `text(1960s)`, migrant workers from southern Europe, Asia, and Africa immigrated to western and central Europe; however, after the economic downturn of the `text(1970s)`, these workers and their families often became targets of anti-immigrant agitation and extreme nationalist political parties.
AP.EH.9.12.A: Explain how innovation and advances in technology influenced cultural and intellectual developments in the period 1914 to the present.
AP.EH.9.12.A.1: Medical theories and technologies extended life but posed social and moral questions that eluded consensus and crossed religious, political, and philosophical perspectives.
AP.EH.9.13.A: Explain the technological and cultural causes and consequences of increasing European globalization in the period from `text(1914)` to the present.
AP.EH.9.13.A.1: Increased imports of U.S. technology and popular culture after World War II generated both enthusiasm and criticism.
AP.EH.9.13.A.2: New communication and transportation technologies multiplied the connections across space and time, transforming daily life and contributing to the proliferation of ideas and to globalization.
AP.EH.9.13.A.3: Green parties in Western and Central Europe challenged consumerism, urged sustainable development, and, by the late 20th century, cautioned against globalization.
AP.EH.9.14.A: Explain how and why European culture changed from the period following World War II to the present.
AP.EH.9.14.A.1: The effects of world war and economic depression undermined this confidence in science and human reason, giving impetus to existentialism and producing postmodernism in the `text(post-1945)` period.
AP.EH.9.14.A.2: Organized religion continued to play a role in European social and cultural life despite the challenges of military and ideological conflict, modern secularism, and rapid social changes.
AP.EH.9.14.A.2.i: The challenges of totalitarianism and communism in central and eastern Europe brought mixed responses from the Christian churches.
AP.EH.9.14.A.2.ii: Reform in the Catholic Church found expression in the Second Vatican Council, which redefined the church's doctrine and practices and started to redefine its relations with other religious communities.
AP.EH.9.14.A.3: During the 20th century, the arts were defined by experimentation, self-expression, subjectivity, and the increasing influence of the United States in both elite and popular culture.
AP.EH.9.14.A.3.i: New movements in the visual arts, architecture, and music radically shifted existing aesthetic standards, explored subconscious and subjective states, and satirized Western society and its values.
AP.EH.9.14.A.3.ii: Throughout the century, a number of writers challenged traditional literary conventions, questioned Western values, and addressed controversial social and political issues.
AP.EH.9.14.A.4: Mass production, new food technologies, and industrial efficiency increased disposable income and created a consumer culture in which greater domestic comforts such as electricity, indoor plumbing, plastics, and synthetic fibers became available.
AP.EH.9.14.A.5: With economic recovery after World War II, the birth rate increased dramatically (the baby boom), often promoted by government policies.
AP.EH.9.14.A.6: Various movements, including women's movements, political and social movements, gay and lesbian movements, and others, worked for expanded civil rights, in some cases obtaining the goals they sought, and in others facing strong opposition.
AP.EH.9.14.A.7: Intellectuals and youth reacted against perceived bourgeois materialism and decadence, most significantly with the revolts of `text(1968)`.
AP.EH.9.15.A: Explain how the challenges of the 20th century influenced what it means to be European.
AP.EH.9.15.A.1: Total war and political instability in the first half of the 20th century gave way to a polarized state order during the Cold War and eventually to efforts at transnational union.
AP.EH.9.15.A.1.i: As World War II ended, a Cold War between the liberal democratic West and the communist East began, lasting nearly half a century.
AP.EH.9.15.A.1.ii: Nationalist and separatist movements, along with ethnic conflict and ethnic cleansing, periodically disrupted the post-World War II peace.
AP.EH.9.15.A.2: The stresses of economic collapse and total war engendered internal conflicts within European states and created conflicting conceptions of the relationship between the individual and the state, as demonstrated in the ideological battle between and among democracy, communism, and fascism.
AP.EH.9.15.A.3: During the 20th century, diverse intellectual and cultural movements questioned the existence of objective knowledge, the ability of reason to arrive at truth, and the role of religion in determining moral standards.
AP.EH.9.15.A.3.i: The experience of war intensified a sense of anxiety that permeated many facets of thought and culture, giving way by the century's end to a plurality of intellectual frameworks.
AP.EH.9.15.A.4: Demographic changes, economic growth, total war, disruptions of traditional social patterns, and competing definitions of freedom and justice altered the experiences of everyday life.
AP.EH.9.15.A.4.i: New voices gained prominence in political, intellectual, and social discourse.
AP.ELaC.1.1: Individuals write within a particular situation and make strategic writing choices based on that situation.
AP.ELaC.1.1.A: The rhetorical situation of a text collectively refers to the exigence, purpose, audience, writer, context, and message.
AP.ELaC.1.1.B: The exigence is the part of a rhetorical situation that inspires, stimulates, provokes, or prompts writers to create a text.
AP.ELaC.1.1.C: The purpose of a text is what the writer hopes to accomplish with it. Writers may have more than one purpose in a text.
AP.ELaC.1.1.D: An audience of a text has shared as well as individual beliefs, values, needs, and backgrounds.
AP.ELaC.1.1.E: Writers create texts within a particular context that includes the time, place, and occasion.
AP.ELaC.1.2: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.1.2.A: Writers convey their positions through one or more claims that require a defense.
AP.ELaC.1.2.B: Writers defend their claims with evidence and/or reasoning.
AP.ELaC.1.2.C: Types of evidence may include facts, anecdotes, analogies, statistics, examples, details, illustrations, expert opinions, personal observations, personal experiences, testimonies, or experiments.
AP.ELaC.1.2.D: Effective claims provoke interest and require a defense, rather than simply stating an obvious, known fact that requires no defense or justification.
AP.ELaC.1.2.E: Writers relate source material to their own argument by syntactically embedding particular quoted, paraphrased, or summarized information from one or more sources into their own ideas.
AP.ELaC.2.1: Individuals write within a particular situation and make strategic writing choices based on that situation.
AP.ELaC.2.1.A: Writers' perceptions of an audience's values, beliefs, needs, and background guide the choices they make.
AP.ELaC.2.1.B: To achieve a purpose, writers make choices in an attempt to relate to an intended audience's emotions and values.
AP.ELaC.2.1.C: Arguments seek to persuade or motivate action through appeals-the modes of persuasion.
AP.ELaC.2.2: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.2.2.A: Writers use evidence strategically and purposefully to illustrate, clarify, set a mood, exemplify, associate, or amplify a point.
AP.ELaC.2.2.B: Strategically selected evidence strengthens the validity and reasoning of the argument, relates to an audience's emotions and values, and increases a writer's credibility.
AP.ELaC.2.2.C: An effective argument contains sufficient evidence; evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality provide apt support for the argument.
AP.ELaC.2.3: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.2.3.A: A thesis is the main, overarching claim a writer is seeking to defend or prove by using reasoning supported by evidence.
AP.ELaC.2.3.B: A writer's thesis is not necessarily a single sentence or an explicit statement and may require a thorough reading of the text to identify, but when a thesis is directly expressed, it is called a thesis statement.
AP.ELaC.3.1: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.3.1.A: Effective use of evidence uses commentary to establish a logical relationship between the evidence and the claim it supports.
AP.ELaC.3.1.B: Writers introduce source material by using commentary to properly integrate it into their line of reasoning.
AP.ELaC.3.1.C: Synthesis requires consideration, explanation, and integration of others' arguments into one's own argument.
AP.ELaC.3.1.D: Writers must acknowledge words, ideas, images, texts, and other intellectual property of others through attribution, citation, or reference.
AP.ELaC.3.2: Writers guide understanding of a text's lines of reasoning and claims through that text's organization and integration of evidence.
AP.ELaC.3.2.A: Writers may lead readers through a line of reasoning and then arrive at a thesis.
AP.ELaC.3.2.B: Writers may express a claim and then develop a line of reasoning to justify the claim.
AP.ELaC.3.2.C: Writers explain their reasoning through commentary that connects chosen evidence to a claim.
AP.ELaC.3.2.D: Commentary explains the significance and relevance of evidence in relation to the line of reasoning.
AP.ELaC.3.2.E: The sequence of paragraphs in a text reveals the argument's line of reasoning.
AP.ELaC.3.2.F: Flaws in a line of reasoning may render an argument specious or illogical.
AP.ELaC.3.3: Writers guide understanding of a text's lines of reasoning and claims through that text's organization and integration of evidence.
AP.ELaC.3.3.A: Methods of development are common approaches writers frequently use to develop and organize the reasoning of their arguments. A method of development provides an audience with the means to trace a writer's reasoning in an argument.
AP.ELaC.3.3.B: Some typical methods of development are narration, cause- effect, comparison-contrast, definition, and description.
AP.ELaC.3.3.C: When developing ideas through narration, writers offer details about real-life experiences and offer reflections and insights on the significance of those experiences.
AP.ELaC.3.3.D: When developing ideas through cause-effect, writers present a cause, assert effects or consequences of that cause, or present a series of causes and the subsequent effect(s).
AP.ELaC.4.1: Individuals write within a particular situation and make strategic writing choices based on that situation.
AP.ELaC.4.1.A: The introduction of an argument introduces the subject and/or writer of the argument to the audience. An introduction may present the argument's thesis. An introduction may orient, engage, and/or focus the audience by presenting quotations, intriguing statements, anecdotes, questions, statistics, data, contextualized information, or a scenario.
AP.ELaC.4.1.B: The conclusion of an argument brings the argument to a unified end. A conclusion may present the argument's thesis. It may engage and/or focus the audience by explaining the significance of the argument within a broader context, making connections, calling the audience to act, suggesting a change in behavior or attitude, proposing a solution, leaving the audience with a compelling image, explaining implications, summarizing the argument, or connecting to the introduction.
AP.ELaC.4.2: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.4.2.A: A thesis statement may preview the line of reasoning of an argument. This is not to say that a thesis statement must list the points of an argument, aspects to be analyzed, or specific evidence to be used in an argument.
AP.ELaC.4.3: Writers guide understanding of a text's lines of reasoning and claims through that text's organization and integration of evidence.
AP.ELaC.4.3.A: Methods of development are common approaches writers frequently use to develop and organize the reasoning of their arguments. A method of development provides an audience with the means to trace a writer's reasoning in an argument.
AP.ELaC.4.3.B: When developing ideas through comparison-contrast, writers present a category of comparison and then examine the similarities and/or differences between the objects of the comparison. When analyzing similarities and/or differences, like categories of comparison must be used.
AP.ELaC.4.3.C: When developing ideas through a definition or description, writers relate the characteristics, features, or sensory details of an object or idea, sometimes using examples or illustrations.
AP.ELaC.5.1: Writers guide understanding of a text's lines of reasoning and claims through that text's organization and integration of evidence.
AP.ELaC.5.1.A: The body paragraphs of a written argument make claims, support them with evidence, and provide commentary that explains how the paragraph contributes to the reasoning of the argument.
AP.ELaC.5.2: Writers guide understanding of a text's lines of reasoning and claims through that text's organization and integration of evidence.
AP.ELaC.5.2.A: Coherence occurs at different levels in a piece of writing. In a sentence, the idea in one clause logically links to an idea in the next. In a paragraph, the idea in one sentence logically links to an idea in the next. In a text, the ideas in one paragraph logically link to the ideas in the next.
AP.ELaC.5.2.B: Repetition, synonyms, pronoun references, and parallel structure may indicate or develop a relationship between elements of a text.
AP.ELaC.5.2.C: Transitional elements are words or other elements (phrases, clauses, sentences, or paragraphs) that assist in creating coherence among sentences, paragraphs, or sections in a text by showing relationships among ideas.
AP.ELaC.5.2.D: Transitional elements can be used to introduce evidence or to indicate its relationship to other ideas or evidence in that paragraph or in the text as a whole.
AP.ELaC.5.3: The rhetorical situation informs the strategic stylistic choices that writers make.
AP.ELaC.5.3.A: Words have both connotative and denotative meanings.
AP.ELaC.5.3.B: Descriptive words, such as adjectives and adverbs, not only qualify or modify the things they describe but also convey a perspective toward those things.
AP.ELaC.5.3.C: Precise word choice reduces confusion and may help the audience perceive the writer's perspective.
AP.ELaC.6.1: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.6.1.A: When synthesizing, writers draw upon arguments from multiple sources, strategically select the most relevant information, and combine apt and specific source material as part of their own argument.
AP.ELaC.6.1.B: A source provides information for an argument, and some sources are more reliable or credible than others.
AP.ELaC.6.1.C: A position and a perspective are different. Sources may have the same position on a subject, yet each comes from a different perspective based on their background, interests, and expertise.
AP.ELaC.6.1.D: When incorporating evidence or sources into an argument, the strongest arguments recognize and acknowledge the biases and limitations of the material and account for those limitations in their reasoning.
AP.ELaC.6.1.E: The degree to which a source does or does not consider other positions reflects the degree to which that source is biased.
AP.ELaC.6.2: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.6.2.A: Consideration and use of new evidence may require revision of the thesis statement and/or changes to the line of reasoning.
AP.ELaC.6.3: The rhetorical situation informs the strategic stylistic choices that writers make.
AP.ELaC.6.3.A: A writer's tone is the writer's attitude or feeling about a subject, conveyed through word choice and writing style.
AP.ELaC.6.3.B: Readers infer a writer's tone from the writer's word choice, and especially the positive, negative, or other connotations of those words.
AP.ELaC.6.3.C: A writer's shifts in tone from one part of a text to another may suggest the writer's qualification, refinement, or reconsideration of their perspective on a subject.
AP.ELaC.7.1: Individuals write within a particular situation and make strategic writing choices based on that situation.
AP.ELaC.7.1.A: The introduction of an argument introduces the subject and/or writer of the argument to the audience. An introduction may present the argument's thesis. An introduction may orient, engage, and/or focus the audience by presenting quotations, intriguing statements, anecdotes, questions, statistics, data, contextualized information, or a scenario.
AP.ELaC.7.1.B: The conclusion of an argument brings the argument to a unified end. A conclusion may present the argument's thesis. It may engage and/or focus the audience by explaining the significance of the argument within a broader context, making connections, calling the audience to act, suggesting a change in behavior or attitude, proposing a solution, leaving the audience with a compelling image, explaining implications, summarizing the argument, or connecting to the introduction.
AP.ELaC.7.2: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.7.2.A: A lack of understanding of the complexities of a subject or an issue can lead to oversimplification or generalizations.
AP.ELaC.7.2.B: Because arguments are usually part of ongoing discourse, effective arguments often avoid expressing claims, reasoning, and evidence in absolute terms.
AP.ELaC.7.2.C: Writers may strategically use words, phrases, and clauses as modifiers to qualify or limit the scope of an argument.
AP.ELaC.7.3: The rhetorical situation informs the strategic stylistic choices that writers make.
AP.ELaC.7.3.A: Writers express ideas in sentences. Sentences are made up of clauses, at least one of which must be independent.
AP.ELaC.7.3.B: The arrangement of sentences in a text can emphasize particular ideas.
AP.ELaC.7.3.C: Subordination and coordination are used to express the intended relationship between ideas in a sentence.
AP.ELaC.7.3.D: Writers frequently use coordination to illustrate a balance or equality between ideas.
AP.ELaC.7.3.E: Writers frequently use subordination to illustrate an imbalance or inequality between ideas.
AP.ELaC.7.3.F: The arrangement of clauses, phrases, and words in a sentence can emphasize ideas.
AP.ELaC.7.4: The rhetorical situation informs the strategic stylistic choices that writers make.
AP.ELaC.7.4.A: Grammar and mechanics that follow established conventions of language enable clear communication.
AP.ELaC.7.4.B: Writers use punctuation strategically to demonstrate the relationships among ideas in a sentence.
AP.ELaC.7.4.C: Punctuation (commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, hyphens, parentheses, quotation marks, or end marks) advances a writer's purpose by clarifying, organizing, emphasizing, indicating purpose, supplementing information, or contributing to tone.
AP.ELaC.7.4.D: Some design features, such as italics or boldface, create emphasis.
AP.ELaC.8.1: Individuals write within a particular situation and make strategic writing choices based on that situation.
AP.ELaC.8.1.A: Writers may make comparisons (e.g., similes, metaphors, analogies, or anecdotes) in an attempt to relate to an audience. Effective comparisons must be shared and understood by the audience to advance the writer's purpose.
AP.ELaC.8.1.B: Writers' choices regarding syntax and diction influence how the writer is perceived by an audience and may influence the degree to which an audience accepts an argument.
AP.ELaC.8.1.C: Word choice may reflect writers' biases and may affect their credibility with a particular audience.
AP.ELaC.8.1.D: Because audiences are unique and dynamic, writers must consider the perspectives, contexts, and needs of the intended audience when making choices of evidence, organization, and language in an argument.
AP.ELaC.8.2: The rhetorical situation informs the strategic stylistic choices that writers make.
AP.ELaC.8.2.A: A writer's style is made up of the mix of word choice, syntax, and conventions employed by that writer.
AP.ELaC.8.2.B: Writers may signal a complex or ironic perspective through stylistic choices. Irony may emerge from the differences between an argument and the readers' expectations or values.
AP.ELaC.8.3: The rhetorical situation informs the strategic stylistic choices that writers make.
AP.ELaC.8.3.A: Modifiers-including words, phrases, or clauses-qualify, clarify, or specify information about the thing with which they are associated. To reduce ambiguity, modifiers should be placed closest to the word, phrase, or clause that they are meant to modify.
AP.ELaC.8.3.B: Parenthetical elements-though not essential to understanding what they are describing-interrupt sentences to provide additional information that may address an audience's needs and/or advance a writer's purpose.
AP.ELaC.9.1: Writers make claims about subjects, rely on evidence that supports the reasoning that justifies the claim, and often acknowledge or respond to other, possibly opposing, arguments.
AP.ELaC.9.1.A: Effectively entering into an ongoing conversation about a subject means engaging the positions that have already been considered and argued about.
AP.ELaC.9.1.B: Evidence and sources will either support, complement, or contradict a writer's thesis.
AP.ELaC.9.1.C: Writers enhance their credibility when they refute, rebut, or concede opposing arguments and contradictory evidence.
AP.ELaC.9.1.D: When writers concede, they accept all or a portion of a competing position or claim as correct, agree that the competing position or claim is correct under a different set of circumstances, or acknowledge the limitations of their own argument.
AP.ELaC.9.1.E: When writers rebut, they offer a contrasting perspective on an argument and its evidence or provide alternative evidence to propose that all or a portion of a competing position or claim is invalid.
AP.ELaC.9.1.F: When writers refute, they demonstrate, using evidence, that all or a portion of a competing position or claim is invalid.
AP.ELaC.9.1.G: Transitions may be used to introduce counterarguments.
AP.ELaC.9.1.H: Not all arguments explicitly address a counterargument.
AP.ELiC.1.1: Characters in literature allow readers to study and explore a range of values, beliefs, assumptions, biases, and cultural norms represented by those characters.
AP.ELiC.1.1.A: Description, dialogue, and behavior reveal characters to readers.
AP.ELiC.1.1.B: Descriptions of characters may come from a speaker, narrator, other characters, or the characters themselves.
AP.ELiC.1.1.C: Perspective is how narrators, characters, or speakers understand their circumstances, and is informed by background, personality traits, biases, and relationships.
AP.ELiC.1.1.D: A character's perspective is both shaped and revealed by relationships with other characters, the environment, the events of the plot, and the ideas expressed in the text.
AP.ELiC.1.2: Setting and the details associated with it not only depict a time and place, but also convey values associated with that setting.
AP.ELiC.1.2.A: Setting includes the time and place during which the events of the text occur.
AP.ELiC.1.3: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.1.3.A: Plot is the sequence of events in a narrative; events throughout a narrative are connected, with each event building on the others, often with a cause-and-effect relationship.
AP.ELiC.1.3.B: The dramatic situation of a narrative includes the setting and action of the plot and how that narrative develops to place characters in conflict(s), and often involves the rising or falling fortunes of a main character or set of characters.
AP.ELiC.1.3.C: Plot and the exposition that accompanies it focus readers' attention on the parts of the narrative that matter most to its development, including characters, their relationships, and their roles in the narrative, as well as setting and the relationship between characters and setting.
AP.ELiC.1.4: A narrator's or speaker's perspective controls the details and emphases that affect how readers experience and interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.1.4.A: Narrators or speakers relate accounts to readers and establish a relationship between the text and the reader.
AP.ELiC.1.4.B: Perspective refers to how narrators, characters, or speakers see their circumstances, while point of view refers to the position from which a narrator or speaker relates the events of a narrative.
AP.ELiC.1.4.C: A speaker or narrator is not necessarily the author.
AP.ELiC.1.4.D: The point of view contributes to what narrators, characters, or speakers can and cannot provide in a text based on their level of involvement and intimacy with the details, events, or characters.
AP.ELiC.1.4.E: Narrators may also be characters, and their role as characters may influence their perspective.
AP.ELiC.1.4.F: First-person narrators are involved in the narrative; their relationship to the events of the plot and the other characters shapes their perspective.
AP.ELiC.1.4.H: Third-person narrators' knowledge about events and characters may range from observational to all-knowing, which shapes their perspective.
AP.ELiC.1.4.I: The outside perspective of third-person narrators may not be affected by the events of the narrative.
AP.ELiC.1.5: Readers establish and communicate their interpretations of literature through arguments supported by textual evidence.
AP.ELiC.1.5.A: In literary analysis, writers read a text closely to identify details that, in combination, enable them to make and defend a claim about an aspect of the text.
AP.ELiC.1.5.B: A claim is a statement that requires defense with evidence from the text.
AP.ELiC.1.5.C: In literary analysis, the initial components of a paragraph are the claim and textual evidence that defends the claim.
AP.ELiC.2.1: Characters in literature allow readers to study and explore a range of values, beliefs, assumptions, biases, and cultural norms represented by those characters.
AP.ELiC.2.1.A: Characters reveal their perspectives and biases through the words they use, the details they provide in the text, the organization of their thinking, the decisions they make, and the actions they take.
AP.ELiC.2.2: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.2.2.A: Line and stanza breaks contribute to the development and relationship of ideas in a poem.
AP.ELiC.2.2.B: The arrangement of lines and stanzas contributes to the development and relationship of ideas in a poem.
AP.ELiC.2.2.C: A text's structure affects readers' reactions and expectations by presenting the relationships among the ideas of the text via their relative positions and their placement within the text as a whole.
AP.ELiC.2.2.D: Contrast can be introduced through focus; tone; point of view; character, narrator, or speaker perspective; dramatic situation or moment; settings or time; or imagery.
AP.ELiC.2.2.E: Contrasts are the result of shifts or juxtapositions or both.
AP.ELiC.2.2.F: Shifts may be signaled by a word, a structural convention, or punctuation.
AP.ELiC.2.2.G: Shifts may emphasize contrasts between particular segments of a text.
AP.ELiC.2.3: Comparisons, representations, and associations shift meaning from the literal to the figurative and invite readers to interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.2.3.A: An antecedent is a word, phrase, or clause that precedes its referent. Referents may include pronouns, nouns, phrases, or clauses.
AP.ELiC.2.3.B: Referents are ambiguous if they can refer to more than one antecedent, which affects interpretation.
AP.ELiC.2.3.C: Words or phrases may be repeated to emphasize ideas or associations.
AP.ELiC.2.3.D: Alliteration is the repetition of the same letter sound at the beginning of adjacent or nearby words to emphasize those words and their associations or representations.
AP.ELiC.2.3.E: A simile uses the words “like” or “as” to liken two objects or concepts to each other.
AP.ELiC.2.3.F: Similes liken two different things to transfer the traits or qualities of one to the other.
AP.ELiC.2.3.G: In a simile, the thing being compared is the main subject; the thing to which it is being compared is the comparison subject.
AP.ELiC.2.3.H: A metaphor implies similarities between two (usually unrelated) concepts or objects in order to reveal or emphasize one or more things about one of them, though the differences between the two may also be revealing.
AP.ELiC.2.3.I: In a metaphor, as in a simile, the thing being compared is the main subject; the thing to which it is being compared is the comparison subject.
AP.ELiC.2.3.J: Comparisons between objects or concepts draw on the experiences and associations readers already have with those objects and concepts.
AP.ELiC.2.3.K: Interpretation of a metaphor may depend on the context of its use; that is, what is happening in a text may determine what is transferred in the comparison.
AP.ELiC.2.4: Readers establish and communicate their interpretations of literature through arguments supported by textual evidence.
AP.ELiC.2.4.A: In literary analysis, writers read a text closely to identify details that, in combination, enable them to make and defend a claim about an aspect of the text.
AP.ELiC.2.4.B: A claim is a statement that requires defense with evidence from the text.
AP.ELiC.2.4.C: In literary analysis, the initial components of a paragraph are the claim and textual evidence that defends the claim.
AP.ELiC.3.1: Characters in literature allow readers to study and explore a range of values, beliefs, assumptions, biases, and cultural norms represented by those characters.
AP.ELiC.3.1.A: The description of a character creates certain expectations for that character's behaviors; how a character does or does not meet those expectations affects a reader's interpretation of that character.
AP.ELiC.3.1.B: Details associated with a character and/or used to describe a character contribute to a reader's interpretation of that character.
AP.ELiC.3.1.C: Readers' understanding of a character's perspective may depend on the perspective of the narrator or speaker.
AP.ELiC.3.1.D: A character's perspective may shift during the course of a narrative.
AP.ELiC.3.1.E: When narrators, characters, or speakers compare another character to something or someone else, they reveal their perspective on the compared character and may also reveal something innate about the compared character.
AP.ELiC.3.1.F: Readers can infer a character's motives from that character's actions or inactions.
AP.ELiC.3.1.G: A dynamic character who develops over the course of the narrative often makes choices that directly or indirectly affect the climax and/or the resolution of that narrative.
AP.ELiC.3.1.H: Character changes can be visible and external, such as changes to health or wealth, or can be internal, psychological, or emotional changes; external changes can lead to internal changes, and vice versa.
AP.ELiC.3.1.I: Some characters remain unchanged or are largely unaffected by the events of the narrative.
AP.ELiC.3.2: Setting and the details associated with it not only depict a time and place, but also convey values associated with that setting.
AP.ELiC.3.2.A: Setting includes the social, cultural, and historical situation during which the events of the text occur.
AP.ELiC.3.3: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.3.3.A: A story, or narrative, is delivered through a series of events that relate to a conflict.
AP.ELiC.3.3.B: Events include episodes, encounters, and scenes in a narrative that can introduce and develop a plot.
AP.ELiC.3.3.C: The significance of an event depends on its relationship to the narrative, the conflict, and the development of characters.
AP.ELiC.3.3.D: Conflict is tension between competing values either within a character, known as internal or psychological conflict, or with outside forces that obstruct a character in some way, known as external conflict.
AP.ELiC.3.3.E: A text may contain multiple conflicts. Often two or more conflicts in a text intersect.
AP.ELiC.3.3.F: A primary conflict can be heightened by the presence of additional conflicts that intersect with it.
AP.ELiC.3.3.G: Inconsistencies in a text may create contrasts that represent conflicts of values or perspectives.
AP.ELiC.3.4: Readers establish and communicate their interpretations of literature through arguments supported by textual evidence.
AP.ELiC.3.4.A: In literary analysis, writers read a text closely to identify details that, in combination, enable them to make and defend a claim about an aspect of the text.
AP.ELiC.3.4.B: A claim is a statement that requires defense with evidence from the text.
AP.ELiC.3.4.C: In literary analysis, the initial components of a paragraph are the claim and textual evidence that defends the claim.
AP.ELiC.3.4.D: A thesis statement expresses an interpretation of a literary text and requires a defense through use of textual evidence and a line of reasoning, both of which are explained in an essay through commentary.
AP.ELiC.3.4.E: A thesis statement may preview the development or line of reasoning of an interpretation. This is not to say that a thesis statement must list the points of an interpretation, literary elements to be analyzed, or specific evidence to be used in the argument.
AP.ELiC.3.4.F: A line of reasoning is the logical sequence of claims that work together to defend the overarching thesis statement.
AP.ELiC.3.4.G: A line of reasoning is communicated through commentary that explains the logical relationship between the overarching thesis statement and the claims/evidence within the body of an essay.
AP.ELiC.3.4.H: Writers use evidence strategically and purposefully to illustrate, clarify, exemplify, associate, amplify, or qualify a point.
AP.ELiC.3.4.I: Evidence is effective when the writer of the essay uses commentary to explain a logical relationship between the evidence and the claim.
AP.ELiC.3.4.J: Evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality provide apt support for the line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.3.4.K: Developing and supporting an interpretation of a text is a recursive process; an interpretation can emerge from analyzing evidence and then forming a line of reasoning, or the interpretation can emerge from forming a line of reasoning and then identifying relevant evidence to support that line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.3.4.L: Grammar and mechanics that follow established conventions of language allow writers to clearly communicate their interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.4.1: Characters in literature allow readers to study and explore a range of values, beliefs, assumptions, biases, and cultural norms represented by those characters.
AP.ELiC.4.1.A: The significance of characters is often revealed through their agency and through nuanced descriptions.
AP.ELiC.4.1.B: Characters' choices - in speech, action, and inaction - reveal what they value.
AP.ELiC.4.1.C: The main character in a narrative is the protagonist; the antagonist in the narrative opposes the protagonist and may be another character, the internal conflicts of the protagonist, a collective (such as society), or nature.
AP.ELiC.4.1.D: Protagonists and antagonists may represent contrasting values.
AP.ELiC.4.1.E: Conflict among characters often arises from tensions generated by their different value systems.
AP.ELiC.4.2: Setting and the details associated with it not only depict a time and place, but also convey values associated with that setting.
AP.ELiC.4.2.A: A setting may help establish the mood and atmosphere of a narrative.
AP.ELiC.4.2.B: The environment a character inhabits provides information about that character.
AP.ELiC.4.3: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.4.3.A: Some patterns in dramatic situations are so common that they are considered archetypes, and these archetypes create certain expectations for how the dramatic situations will progress and be resolved.
AP.ELiC.4.3.B: The differences highlighted by a contrast emphasize the particular traits, aspects, or characteristics important for comparison of the things being contrasted.
AP.ELiC.4.3.C: Contrasts often represent conflicts in values related to character, narrator, or speaker perspectives on ideas represented by a text.
AP.ELiC.4.4: A narrator's or speaker's perspective controls the details and emphases that affect how readers experience and interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.4.4.A: Narrators may function as characters in the narrative who directly address readers and either recall events or describe them as they occur.
AP.ELiC.4.4.B: Narrative distance refers to the physical distance, chronological distance, relationships, or emotional investment of the narrator to the events or characters of the narrative.
AP.ELiC.4.4.C: Stream of consciousness is a type of narration in which a character's thoughts are related through a continuous dialogue or description.
AP.ELiC.4.4.D: The narrators', characters', or speakers' backgrounds and perspectives shape the tone they convey about subjects or events in the text.
AP.ELiC.4.4.E: Descriptive words, such as adjectives and adverbs, not only qualify or modify the things they describe but also convey a perspective toward those things.
AP.ELiC.4.4.F: The attitude of narrators, characters, or speakers toward an idea, character, or situation emerges from their perspective and may be referred to as tone.
AP.ELiC.4.5: Readers establish and communicate their interpretations of literature through arguments supported by textual evidence.
AP.ELiC.4.5.A: A thesis statement expresses an interpretation of a literary text, and requires a defense, through use of textual evidence and a line of reasoning, both of which are explained in an essay through commentary.
AP.ELiC.4.5.B: A thesis statement may preview the development or line of reasoning of an interpretation. This is not to say that a thesis statement must list the points of an interpretation, literary elements to be analyzed, or specific evidence to be used in the argument.
AP.ELiC.4.5.C: A line of reasoning is the logical sequence of claims that work together to defend the overarching thesis statement.
AP.ELiC.4.5.D: A line of reasoning is communicated through commentary that explains the logical relationship between the overarching thesis statement and the claims/evidence within the body of an essay.
AP.ELiC.4.5.E: The body paragraphs of a written argument develop the reasoning and justify claims using evidence and providing commentary that links the evidence to the overall thesis.
AP.ELiC.4.5.F: Effective paragraphs are cohesive and often use topic sentences to state a claim and explain the reasoning that connects the various claims and evidence that make up the body of an essay.
AP.ELiC.4.5.G: Writers use evidence strategically and purposefully to illustrate, clarify, exemplify, associate, amplify, or qualify a point.
AP.ELiC.4.5.H: Evidence is effective when the writer of the essay uses commentary to explain a logical relationship between the evidence and the claim.
AP.ELiC.4.5.I: Evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality provide apt support for the line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.4.5.J: Developing and supporting an interpretation of a text is a recursive process; an interpretation can emerge from analyzing evidence and then forming a line of reasoning, or the interpretation can emerge from forming a line of reasoning and then identifying relevant evidence to support that line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.4.5.K: Coherence occurs at different levels in a piece of writing. In a sentence, the idea in one clause logically links to an idea in the next. In a paragraph, the idea in one sentence logically links to an idea in the next. In a text, the ideas in one paragraph logically link to the ideas in the next.
AP.ELiC.4.5.L: Writers achieve coherence when the arrangement and organization of reasons, evidence, ideas, or details is logical. Writers may use transitions, repetition, synonyms, pronoun references, or parallel structure to indicate relationships between and among those reasons, evidence, ideas, or details.
AP.ELiC.5.1: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.5.1.A: Closed forms of poetry include predictable patterns in the structure of lines, stanzas, meter, and rhyme, which develop relationships among ideas in the poem. Note: The AP Exam will not require students to label or identify specific rhyme schemes, metrical patterns, or forms of poetry.
AP.ELiC.5.1.B: Open forms of poetry may not follow expected or predictable patterns in the structure of their lines or stanzas, but they may still have structures that develop relationships between ideas in the poem.
AP.ELiC.5.1.C: Structures combine in texts to emphasize certain ideas and concepts.
AP.ELiC.5.2: Comparisons, representations, and associations shift meaning from the literal to the figurative and invite readers to interpret a text.
