AP.ELiC.5.2.A: Words with multiple meanings or connotations add nuance or complexity that can contribute to interpretations of a text.
AP.ELiC.5.2.B: Descriptive words, such as adjectives and adverbs, qualify or modify the things they describe and affect readers' interaction with the text.
AP.ELiC.5.2.C: Hyperbole exaggerates while understatement minimizes. Exaggerating or minimizing an aspect of an object focuses attention on that trait and conveys a perspective about the object.
AP.ELiC.5.2.D: Descriptive words, such as adjectives and adverbs, contribute to sensory imagery.
AP.ELiC.5.2.E: An image can be literal or it can be a form of a comparison that represents something in a text through associations with the senses.
AP.ELiC.5.2.F: A collection of images, known as imagery, may emphasize ideas in parts of or throughout a text.
AP.ELiC.5.2.G: Metaphorical comparisons do not focus solely on the objects being compared; they focus on the particular traits, qualities, or characteristics of the things being compared.
AP.ELiC.5.2.H: Comparisons not only communicate literal meaning but may also convey figurative meaning or transmit a perspective.
AP.ELiC.5.2.I: An extended metaphor is created when the comparison of a main subject and comparison subject persists through parts of or an entire text, and when the comparison is expanded through additional details, similes, and images.
AP.ELiC.5.2.J: Interpretation of an extended metaphor may depend on the context of its use; that is, what is happening in a text may determine what is transferred in the comparison.
AP.ELiC.5.2.K: Personification is a type of comparison that assigns a human trait or quality to a nonhuman object, entity, or idea, thus characterizing that object, entity, or idea.
AP.ELiC.5.2.L: Allusions in a text can reference literary works including myths and sacred texts; other works of art including paintings and music; or people, places, or events outside the text.
AP.ELiC.5.3: Readers establish and communicate their interpretations of literature through arguments supported by textual evidence.
AP.ELiC.5.3.A: A thesis statement expresses an interpretation of a literary text, and requires a defense, through use of textual evidence and a line of reasoning, both of which are explained in an essay through commentary.
AP.ELiC.5.3.B: A thesis statement may preview the development or line of reasoning of an interpretation. This is not to say that a thesis statement must list the points of an interpretation, literary elements to be analyzed, or specific evidence to be used in the argument.
AP.ELiC.5.3.C: A line of reasoning is the logical sequence of claims that work together to defend the overarching thesis statement.
AP.ELiC.5.3.D: A line of reasoning is communicated through commentary that explains the logical relationship between the overarching thesis statement and the claims/evidence within the body of an essay.
AP.ELiC.5.3.E: Writers use evidence strategically and purposefully to illustrate, clarify, exemplify, associate, amplify, or qualify a point.
AP.ELiC.5.3.F: Evidence is effective when the writer of the essay uses commentary to explain a logical relationship between the evidence and the claim.
AP.ELiC.5.3.G: Evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality provide apt support for the line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.5.3.H: Developing and supporting an interpretation of a text is a recursive process; an interpretation can emerge from analyzing evidence and then forming a line of reasoning, or the interpretation can emerge from forming a line of reasoning and then identifying relevant evidence to support that line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.5.3.I: Transitional elements are words or other elements (phrases, clauses, sentences, or paragraphs) that assist in creating coherence between sentences and paragraphs by showing relationships between ideas.
AP.ELiC.6.1: Characters in literature allow readers to study and explore a range of values, beliefs, assumptions, biases, and cultural norms represented by those characters.
AP.ELiC.6.1.A: Different character, narrator, or speaker perspectives often reveal different information, develop different attitudes, and influence different interpretations of a text and the ideas in it.
AP.ELiC.6.1.B: Foil characters (foils) serve to illuminate, through contrast, the traits, attributes, or values of another character.
AP.ELiC.6.1.C: Inconsistencies between the private thoughts of characters and their actual behavior reveal tensions and complexities between private and professed values.
AP.ELiC.6.1.D: A character's competing, conflicting, or inconsistent choices or actions contribute to complexity in a text.
AP.ELiC.6.2: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.6.2.A: Some narrative structures interrupt the chronology of a plot; such structures include flashback, foreshadowing, in medias res, and stream of consciousness.
AP.ELiC.6.2.B: Narrative structures that interrupt the chronology of a plot, such as flashback, foreshadowing, in medias res, and stream of consciousness, can directly affect readers' experiences with a text by creating anticipation or suspense or building tension.
AP.ELiC.6.2.C: Contrasts often represent contradictions or inconsistencies that introduce nuance, ambiguity, or contradiction into a text. As a result, contrasts make texts more complex.
AP.ELiC.6.3: A narrator's or speaker's perspective controls the details and emphases that affect how readers experience and interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.6.3.A: The narrator's or speaker's tone toward events or characters in a text influences readers' interpretation of the ideas associated with those things.
AP.ELiC.6.3.B: The syntactical arrangement of phrases and clauses in a sentence can emphasize details or ideas and convey a narrator's or speaker's tone.
AP.ELiC.6.3.C: Information included and/or not included in a text conveys the perspective of characters, narrators, and/or speakers.
AP.ELiC.6.3.D: A narrator's or speaker's perspective may influence the details and amount of detail in a text and may reveal biases, motivations, or understandings.
AP.ELiC.6.3.E: Readers can infer narrators' biases by noting which details they choose to include in a narrative and which they choose to omit.
AP.ELiC.6.3.F: Readers who detect bias in a narrator may find that narrator less reliable.
AP.ELiC.6.3.G: The reliability of a narrator may influence a eader's understanding of a character's motives.
AP.ELiC.6.4: Comparisons, representations, and associations shift meaning from the literal to the figurative and invite readers to interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.6.4.A: When a material object comes to represent, or stand for, an idea or concept, it becomes a symbol.
AP.ELiC.6.4.B: A symbol is an object that represents a meaning, so it is said to be symbolic or representative of that meaning. A symbol can represent different things depending on the experiences of a reader or the context of its use in a text.
AP.ELiC.6.4.C: Certain symbols are so common and recurrent that many readers have associations with them prior to reading a text. Other symbols are more contextualized and only come to represent certain things through their use in a particular text.
AP.ELiC.6.4.D: idea or concept, that character becomes symbolic; some symbolic characters have become so common they are archetypal.
AP.ELiC.6.5: Readers establish and communicate their interpretations of literature through arguments supported by textual evidence.
AP.ELiC.6.5.A: A thesis statement expresses an interpretation of a literary text, and requires a defense, through use of textual evidence and a line of reasoning, both of which are explained in an essay through commentary.

AP.ELiC.6.5.I: Writers convey their ideas in a sentence through strategic selection and placement of phrases and clauses. Writers may use coordination to illustrate a balance or equality between ideas or subordination to illustrate an imbalance or inequality.
AP.ELiC.6.5.J: Writers use words that enhance the clear communication of an interpretation.
AP.ELiC.6.5.K: Punctuation conveys relationships between and among parts of a sentence.
AP.ELiC.7.1: Characters in literature allow readers to study and explore a range of values, beliefs, assumptions, biases, and cultural norms represented by those characters.
AP.ELiC.7.1.A: Often the change in a character emerges directly from a conflict of values represented in the narrative.
AP.ELiC.7.1.B: Changes in a character's circumstances may lead to changes in that character.
AP.ELiC.7.1.C: While characters can change gradually over the course of a narrative, they can also change suddenly as the result of a moment of realization, known as an epiphany. An epiphany allows a character to see things in a new light and is often directly related to a central conflict of the narrative.
AP.ELiC.7.1.D: An epiphany may affect the plot by causing a character to act on his or her sudden realization.
AP.ELiC.7.1.E: A group or force can function as a character.
AP.ELiC.7.1.F: When readers consider a character, they should examine how that character interacts with other characters, groups, or forces and what those interactions may indicate about the character.
AP.ELiC.7.1.G: The relationship between a character and a group, including the inclusion or exclusion of that character, reveals the collective attitude of the group toward that character and possibly the character's attitude toward the group.
AP.ELiC.7.2: Setting and the details associated with it not only depict a time and place, but also convey values associated with that setting.
AP.ELiC.7.2.A: When a setting changes, it may suggest other movements, changes, or shifts in the narrative.
AP.ELiC.7.2.B: Settings may be contrasted in order to establish a conflict of values or ideas associated with those settings.
AP.ELiC.7.2.C: The way characters interact with their surroundings provides insights about those characters and the setting(s) they inhabit.
AP.ELiC.7.2.D: The way characters behave in or describe their surroundings reveals an attitude about those surroundings and contributes to the development of those characters and readers' interpretations of them.
AP.ELiC.7.3: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.7.3.A: Pacing is the manipulation of time in a text. Several factors contribute to the pace of a narrative, including arrangement of details, frequency of events, narrative structures, syntax, the tempo or speed at which events occur, or shifts in tense and chronology in the narrative.
AP.ELiC.7.3.B: Narrative pacing may evoke an emotional reaction in readers by the order in which information is revealed; the relationships between the information, when it is provided, and other parts of the narrative; and the significance of the revealed information to other parts of the narrative.
AP.ELiC.7.4: A narrator's or speaker's perspective controls the details and emphases that affect how readers experience and interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.7.4.A: Some narrators or speakers may provide details and information that others do not or cannot provide. Multiple narrators or speakers may provide contradictory information in a text.
AP.ELiC.7.5: Comparisons, representations, and associations shift meaning from the literal to the figurative and invite readers to interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.7.5.A: A setting may become symbolic when it is, or comes to be, associated with abstractions such as emotions, ideologies, and beliefs.
AP.ELiC.7.5.B: Over time, some settings have developed certain associations such that they almost universally symbolize particular concepts.
AP.ELiC.7.5.C: A motif is a unified pattern of recurring objects or images used to emphasize a significant idea in large parts of or throughout a text.
AP.ELiC.7.5.D: The function of a simile relies on the selection of the objects being compared as well as the traits of the objects.
AP.ELiC.7.5.E: By assigning the qualities of a nonhuman object, entity, or idea to a person or character, the narrator, character, or speaker communicates an attitude about that person or character.
AP.ELiC.7.6: Readers establish and communicate their interpretations of literature through arguments supported by textual evidence.
AP.ELiC.7.6.A: A thesis statement expresses an interpretation of a literary text, and requires a defense, through use of textual evidence and a line of reasoning, both of which are explained in an essay through commentary.
AP.ELiC.7.6.B: A thesis statement may preview the development or line of reasoning of an interpretation. This is not to say that a thesis statement must list the points of an interpretation, literary elements to be analyzed, or specific evidence to be used in the argument.
AP.ELiC.7.6.C: A line of reasoning is the logical sequence of claims that work together to defend the overarching thesis statement.
AP.ELiC.7.6.D: A line of reasoning is communicated through commentary that explains the logical relationship between the overarching thesis statement and the claims/evidence within the body of an essay.
AP.ELiC.7.6.E: More sophisticated literary arguments may explain the significance or relevance of an interpretation within a broader context, discuss alternative interpretations of a text, or use relevant analogies to help an audience better understand an interpretation.
AP.ELiC.7.6.F: Writers use evidence strategically and purposefully to illustrate, clarify, exemplify, associate, amplify, or qualify a point.
AP.ELiC.7.6.G: Evidence is effective when the writer of the essay uses commentary to explain a logical relationship between the evidence and the claim.
AP.ELiC.7.6.H: Evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality provide apt support for the line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.7.6.I: Developing and supporting an interpretation of a text is a recursive process; an interpretation can emerge from analyzing evidence and then forming a line of reasoning, or the interpretation can emerge from forming a line of reasoning and then identifying relevant evidence to support that line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.7.6.J: Textual evidence may require revision to an interpretation and a line of reasoning if the evidence does not sufficiently support the initial interpretation and line of reasoning.
AP.ELiC.8.1: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.8.1.A: Ideas and images in a poem may extend beyond a single line or stanza.
AP.ELiC.8.1.B: Punctuation is often crucial to the understanding of a text.
AP.ELiC.8.1.C: When structural patterns are created in a text, any interruption in the pattern creates a point of emphasis.
AP.ELiC.8.1.D: Juxtaposition may create or demonstrate an antithesis.
AP.ELiC.8.1.E: Situational or verbal irony is created when events or statements in a text are inconsistent with either the expectations readers bring to a text or the expectations established by the text itself.
AP.ELiC.8.1.F: Paradox occurs when seemingly contradictory elements are juxtaposed, but the contradiction - which may or may not be reconciled - can reveal a hidden or unexpected idea.
AP.ELiC.8.2: Comparisons, representations, and associations shift meaning from the literal to the figurative and invite readers to interpret a text.

AP.ELiC.8.3.A: A thesis statement expresses an interpretation of a literary text, and requires a defense, through use of textual evidence and a line of reasoning, both of which are explained in an essay through commentary.

AP.ELiC.8.3.J: Writers must acknowledge words, ideas, images, texts, and other intellectual property of others through attribution, citation, or reference.
AP.ELiC.9.1: Characters in literature allow readers to study and explore a range of values, beliefs, assumptions, biases, and cultural norms represented by those characters.
AP.ELiC.9.1.A: Minor characters often remain unchanged because the narrative doesn't focus on them. They may only be part of the narrative to advance the plot or to interact with major characters.
AP.ELiC.9.1.B: Readers' interpretations of a text are often affected by a character changing - or not - and the meaning conveyed by such changes or lack thereof.
AP.ELiC.9.1.C: A character's responses to the resolution of the narrative - in their words or in their actions - reveal something about that character's own values; these responses may be inconsistent with the previously established behaviors or perspectives of that character.
AP.ELiC.9.1.D: Inconsistencies and unexpected developments in a character affect readers' interpretation of that character; other characters; events in the plot; conflicts; the perspective of the narrator, character, or speaker; and/or setting.
AP.ELiC.9.2: The arrangement of the parts and sections of a text, the relationship of the parts to each other, and the sequence in which the text reveals information are all structural choices made by a writer that contribute to the reader's interpretation of a text.
AP.ELiC.9.2.A: Significant events often illustrate competing value systems that relate to a conflict present in the text.
AP.ELiC.9.2.B: Events in a plot collide and accumulate to create a sense of anticipation and suspense.
AP.ELiC.9.2.C: The resolution of the anticipation, suspense, or central conflicts of a plot may be referred to as the moment of catharsis or emotional release.
AP.ELiC.9.2.D: Sometimes things not actually shown in a narrative, such as an unseen character or a preceding action, may be in conflict with or result in conflict for a character.
AP.ELiC.9.2.E: Although most plots end in resolution of the central conflicts, some have unresolved endings, and the lack of resolution may contribute to interpretations of the text.
AP.ELiC.9.3: A narrator's or speaker's perspective controls the details and emphases that affect how readers experience and interpret a text.
AP.ELiC.9.3.A: Multiple, and even contrasting, perspectives can occur within a single text and contribute to the complexity of the text.
AP.ELiC.9.3.B: A narrator or speaker may change over the course of a text as a result of actions and interactions.
AP.ELiC.9.3.C: Changes and inconsistencies in a narrator's or speaker's perspective may contribute to irony or the complexity of the text.

AP.ES.1.1.A: Explain how the availability of resources influences species interactions.
AP.ES.1.1.A.1: In a predator-prey relationship, the predator is an organism that eats another organism (the prey).
AP.ES.1.1.A.2: Symbiosis is a close and long-term interaction between two species in an ecosystem. Types of symbiosis include mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism.
AP.ES.1.1.A.3: Competition can occur within or between species in an ecosystem where there are limited resources. Resource partitioning - using the resources in different ways, places, or at different times-can reduce the negative impact of competition on survival.
AP.ES.1.2.A: Describe the global distribution and principal environmental aspects of terrestrial biomes.
AP.ES.1.2.A.1: A biome contains characteristic communities of plants and animals that result from, and are adapted to, its climate.
AP.ES.1.2.A.2: Major terrestrial biomes include taiga, temperate rainforests, temperate seasonal forests, tropical rainforests, shrubland, temperate grassland, savanna, desert, and tundra.
AP.ES.1.2.A.3: The global distribution of nonmineral terrestrial natural resources, such as water and trees for lumber, varies because of some combination of climate, geography, latitude and altitude, nutrient availability, and soil.
AP.ES.1.2.A.4: The worldwide distribution of biomes is dynamic; the distribution has changed in the past and may again shift as a result of global climate changes.
AP.ES.1.3.A: Describe the global distribution and principal environmental aspects of aquatic biomes.
AP.ES.1.3.A.1: Freshwater biomes include streams, rivers, ponds, and lakes. These freshwater biomes are a vital resource for drinking water.
AP.ES.1.3.A.2: Marine biomes include oceans, coral reefs, marshland, and estuaries. Algae in marine biomes supply a large portion of the Earth's oxygen, and also take in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
AP.ES.1.3.A.3: The global distribution of nonmineral marine natural resources, such as different types of fish, varies because of some combination of salinity, depth, turbidity, nutrient availability, and temperature.
AP.ES.1.4.A: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the carbon cycle.
AP.ES.1.4.A.1: The carbon cycle is the movement of atoms and molecules containing the element carbon between sources and sinks.
AP.ES.1.4.A.2: Some of the reservoirs in which carbon compounds occur in the carbon cycle hold those compounds for long periods of time, while some hold them for relatively short periods of time.
AP.ES.1.4.A.3: Carbon cycles between photosynthesis and cellular respiration in living things.
AP.ES.1.4.A.4: Plant and animal decomposition have led to the storage of carbon over millions of years. The burning of fossil fuels quickly moves that stored carbon into atmospheric carbon, in the form of carbon dioxide.
AP.ES.1.5.A: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the nitrogen cycle.
AP.ES.1.5.A.1: The nitrogen cycle is the movement of atoms and molecules containing the element nitrogen between sources and sinks.
AP.ES.1.5.A.2: Most of the reservoirs in which nitrogen compounds occur in the nitrogen cycle hold those compounds for relatively short periods of time.
AP.ES.1.5.A.3: Nitrogen fixation is the process in which atmospheric nitrogen is converted into a form of nitrogen (primarily ammonia) that is available for uptake by plants and that can be synthesized into plant tissue.
AP.ES.1.5.A.4: The atmosphere is the major reservoir of nitrogen.
AP.ES.1.6.A: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the phosphorus cycle.
AP.ES.1.6.A.1: The phosphorus cycle is the movement of atoms and molecules containing the element phosphorus between sources and sinks.
AP.ES.1.6.A.2: The major reservoirs of phosphorus in the phosphorus cycle are rock and sediments that contain phosphorus-bearing minerals.
AP.ES.1.6.A.3: There is no atmospheric component in the phosphorus cycle, and the limitations this imposes on the return of phosphorus from the ocean to land make phosphorus naturally scarce in aquatic and many terrestrial ecosystems. In undisturbed ecosystems, phosphorus is the limiting factor in biological systems.
AP.ES.1.7.A: Explain the steps and reservoir interactions in the hydrologic cycle.
AP.ES.1.7.A.1: The hydrologic cycle, which is powered by the sun, is the movement of water in its various solid, liquid, and gaseous phases between sources and sinks.
AP.ES.1.7.A.2: The oceans are the primary reservoir of water at the Earth's surface, with ice caps and groundwater acting as much smaller reservoirs.
AP.ES.1.8.A: Explain how solar energy is acquired and transferred by living organisms.
AP.ES.1.8.A.1: Primary productivity is the rate at which solar energy (sunlight) is converted into organic compounds via photosynthesis over a unit of time.
AP.ES.1.8.A.2: Gross primary productivity is the total rate of photosynthesis in a given area.
AP.ES.1.8.A.3: Net primary productivity is the rate of energy storage by photosynthesizers in a given area, after subtracting the energy lost to respiration.
AP.ES.1.8.A.4: Productivity is measured in units of energy per unit area per unit time (e.g., `text(kcal)//text(m)^2//text(yr)`).
AP.ES.1.8.A.5: Most red light is absorbed in the upper `1text(m)` of water, and blue light only penetrates deeper than `100text(m)` in the clearest water. This affects photosynthesis in aquatic ecosystems, whose photosynthesizers have adapted mechanisms to address the lack of visible light.
AP.ES.1.9.A: Explain how energy flows and matter cycles through trophic levels.
AP.ES.1.9.A.1: All ecosystems depend on a continuous inflow of high-quality energy in order to maintain their structure and function of transferring matter between the environment and organisms via biogeochemical cycles.
AP.ES.1.9.A.2: Biogeochemical cycles are essential for life and each cycle demonstrates the conservation of matter.
AP.ES.1.9.A.3: In terrestrial and near-surface marine communities, energy flows from the sun to producers in the lowest trophic levels and then upward to higher trophic levels.
AP.ES.1.10.A: Determine how the energy decreases as it flows through ecosystems.
AP.ES.1.10.A.1: The `10%` rule approximates that in the transfer of energy from one trophic level to the next, only about `10%` of the energy is passed on.
AP.ES.1.10.A.2: The loss of energy that occurs when energy moves from lower to higher trophic levels can be explained through the laws of thermodynamics.
AP.ES.1.11.A: Describe food chains and food webs, and their constituent members by trophic level.
AP.ES.1.11.A.1: A food web is a model of an interlocking pattern of food chains that depicts the flow of energy and nutrients in two or more food chains.
AP.ES.1.11.A.2: Positive and negative feedback loops can each play a role in food webs. When one species is removed from or added to a specific food web, the rest of the food web can be affected.
AP.ES.2.1.A: Explain levels of biodiversity and their importance to ecosystems.
AP.ES.2.1.A.1: Biodiversity in an ecosystem includes genetic, species, and habitat diversity.
AP.ES.2.1.A.2: The more genetically diverse a population is, the better it can respond to environmental stressors. Additionally, a population bottleneck can lead to a loss of genetic diversity.
AP.ES.2.1.A.3: Ecosystems that have a larger number of species are more likely to recover from disruptions.
AP.ES.2.1.A.4: Loss of habitat leads to a loss of specialist species, followed by a loss of generalist species. It also leads to reduced numbers of species that have large territorial requirements.
AP.ES.2.1.A.5: Species richness refers to the number of different species found in an ecosystem.
AP.ES.2.2.A.1: There are four categories of ecosystem services: provisioning, regulating, cultural, and supporting.
AP.ES.2.2.B: Describe the results of human disruptions to ecosystem services.
AP.ES.2.2.B.1: Anthropogenic activities can disrupt ecosystem services, potentially resulting in economic and ecological consequences.
AP.ES.2.3.A.1: Island biogeography is the study of the ecological relationships and distribution of organisms on islands, and of these organisms' community structures.
AP.ES.2.3.A.2: Islands have been colonized in the past by new species arriving from elsewhere.
AP.ES.2.3.B: Describe the role of island biogeography in evolution.
AP.ES.2.3.B.1: Many island species have evolved to be specialists versus generalists because of the limited resources, such as food and territory, on most islands. The long-term survival of specialists may be jeopardized if and when invasive species, typically generalists, are introduced and outcompete the specialists.
AP.ES.2.4.A.1: Ecological tolerance refers to the range of conditions, such as temperature, salinity, flow rate, and sunlight that an organism can endure before injury or death results.
AP.ES.2.4.A.2: Ecological tolerance can apply to individuals and to species.
AP.ES.2.5.A: Explain how natural disruptions, both short- and long-term, impact an ecosystem.
AP.ES.2.5.A.1: Natural disruptions to ecosystems have environmental consequences that may, for a given occurrence, be as great as, or greater than, many human-made disruptions.
AP.ES.2.5.A.2: Earth system processes operate on a range of scales in terms of time. Processes can be periodic, episodic, or random.
AP.ES.2.5.A.3: Earth's climate has changed over geological time for many reasons.
AP.ES.2.5.A.4: Sea level has varied significantly as a result of changes in the amount of glacial ice on Earth over geological time.
AP.ES.2.5.A.5: Major environmental change or upheaval commonly results in large swathes of habitat changes.
AP.ES.2.5.A.6: Wildlife engages in both short- and long-term migration for a variety of reasons, including natural disruptions.
AP.ES.2.6.A: Describe how organisms adapt to their environment.
AP.ES.2.6.A.1: Organisms adapt to their environment over time, both in short- and long-term scales, via incremental changes at the genetic level.
AP.ES.2.6.A.2: Environmental changes, either sudden or gradual, may threaten a species' survival, requiring individuals to alter behaviors, move, or perish.
AP.ES.2.7.A.1: There are two main types of ecological succession: primary and secondary succession.
AP.ES.2.7.A.2: A keystone species in an ecosystem is a species whose activities have a particularly significant role in determining community structure.
AP.ES.2.7.A.3: An indicator species is a plant or animal that, by its presence, abundance, scarcity, or chemical composition, demonstrates that some distinctive aspect of the character or quality of an ecosystem is present.
AP.ES.2.7.B: Describe the effect of ecological succession on ecosystems.
AP.ES.2.7.B.1: Pioneer members of an early successional species commonly move into unoccupied habitat and over time adapt to its particular conditions, which may result in the origin of new species.
AP.ES.2.7.B.2: Succession in a disturbed ecosystem will affect the total biomass, species richness, and net productivity over time.
AP.ES.3.1.A: Identify differences between generalist and specialist species.
AP.ES.3.1.A.1: Specialist species tend to be advantaged in habitats that remain constant, while generalist species tend to be advantaged in habitats that are changing.
AP.ES.3.2.A: Identify differences between K- and r-selected species.
AP.ES.3.2.A.1: K-selected species tend to be large, have few offspring per reproduction event, live in stable environments, expend significant energy for each offspring, mature after many years of extended youth and parental care, have long life spans/life expectancy, and reproduce more than once in their lifetime. Competition for resources in K-selected species' habitats is usually relatively high.
AP.ES.3.2.A.2: r-selected species tend to be small, have many offspring, expend or invest minimal energy for each offspring, mature early, have short life spans, and may reproduce only once in their lifetime. Competition for resources in r-selected species' habitats is typically relatively low.
AP.ES.3.2.A.3: Biotic potential refers to the maximum reproductive rate of a population in ideal conditions.
AP.ES.3.2.A.4: Many species have reproductive strategies that are not uniquely r-selected or K-selected, or they change in different conditions at different times.
AP.ES.3.2.A.5: K-selected species are typically more adversely affected by invasive species than r-selected species, which are minimally affected by invasive species. Most invasive species are r-selected species.
AP.ES.3.3.A.1: A survivorship curve is a line that displays the relative survival rates of a cohort-a group of individuals of the same age-in a population, from birth to the maximum age reached by any one cohort member. There are Type I, Type II, and Type III curves.
AP.ES.3.3.A.2: Survivorship curves differ for K-selected and r-selected species, with K-selected species typically following a Type I or Type II curve and r-selected species following a Type III curve.
AP.ES.3.4.A.1: When a population exceeds its carrying capacity (carrying capacity can be denoted as K), overshoot occurs. There are environmental impacts of population overshoot, including resource depletion.
AP.ES.3.4.B: Describe the impact of carrying capacity on ecosystems.
AP.ES.3.4.B.1: A major ecological effect of population overshoot is dieback of the population (often severe to catastrophic) because the lack of available resources leads to famine, disease, and/or conflict.
AP.ES.3.5.A: Explain how resource availability affects population growth.
AP.ES.3.5.A.1: Population growth is limited by environmental factors, especially by the available resources and space.
AP.ES.3.5.A.2: Resource availability and the total resource base are limited and finite over all scales of time.
AP.ES.3.5.A.3: When the resources needed by a population for growth are abundant, population growth usually accelerates.
AP.ES.3.5.A.4: When the resource base of a population shrinks, the increased potential for unequal distribution of resources will ultimately result in increased mortality, decreased fecundity, or both, resulting in population growth declining to, or below, carrying capacity.
AP.ES.3.6.A.1: Population growth rates can be interpreted from age structure diagrams by the shape of the structure.
AP.ES.3.6.A.2: A rapidly growing population will, as a rule, have a higher proportion of younger people compared to stable or declining populations.
AP.ES.3.7.A: Explain factors that affect total fertility rate in human populations.
AP.ES.3.7.A.1: Total fertility rate (TFR) is affected by the age at which females have their first child, educational opportunities for females, access to family planning, and government acts and policies.
AP.ES.3.7.A.2: If fertility rate is at replacement levels, a population is considered relatively stable.
AP.ES.3.7.A.3: Factors associated with infant mortality rates include whether mothers have access to good healthcare and nutrition. Changes in these factors can lead to changes in infant mortality rates over time.
AP.ES.3.8.A: Explain how human populations experience growth and decline.
AP.ES.3.8.A.1: Birth rates, infant mortality rates, and overall death rates, access to family planning, access to good nutrition, access to education, and postponement of marriage all affect whether a human population is growing or declining.
AP.ES.3.8.A.2: Factors limiting global human population include the Earth's carrying capacity and the basic factors that limit human population growth as set forth by Malthusian theory.
AP.ES.3.8.A.3: Population growth can be affected by both density-independent factors, such as major storms, fires, heat waves, or droughts, and density-dependent factors, such as access to clean water and air, food availability, disease transmission, or territory size.
AP.ES.3.8.A.4: The rule of `70` states that dividing the number `70` by the percentage population growth rate approximates the population's doubling time.
AP.ES.3.9.A.1: The demographic transition refers to the transition from high to lower birth and death rates in a country or region as development occurs and that country moves from a pre-industrial to an industrialized economic system. This transition is typically demonstrated through a four-stage demographic transition model (DTM).
AP.ES.3.9.A.2: Characteristics of developing countries include higher infant mortality rates and more children in the workforce than developed countries.
AP.ES.4.1.A: Describe the geological changes and events that occur at convergent, divergent, and transform plate boundaries.
AP.ES.4.1.A.1: Convergent boundaries can result in the creation of mountains, island arcs, earthquakes, and volcanoes.
AP.ES.4.1.A.2: Divergent boundaries can result in seafloor spreading, rift valleys, volcanoes, and earthquakes.
AP.ES.4.1.A.3: Transform boundaries can result in earthquakes.
AP.ES.4.1.A.4: Maps that show the global distribution of plate boundaries can be used to determine the location of volcanoes, island arcs, earthquakes, hot spots, and faults.
AP.ES.4.1.A.5: An earthquake occurs when stress overcomes a locked fault, releasing stored energy.
AP.ES.4.2.A: Describe the characteristics and formation of soil.
AP.ES.4.2.A.1: Soils are formed when parent material is weathered, transported, and deposited.
AP.ES.4.2.A.2: Soils are generally categorized by horizons based on their composition and organic material.
AP.ES.4.2.A.3: Soils can be eroded by winds or water. Protecting soils can protect water quality as soils effectively filter and clean water that moves through them.
AP.ES.4.3.A: Describe similarities and differences between properties of different soil types.
AP.ES.4.3.A.1: Water holding capacity-the total amount of water soil can hold-varies with different soil types. Water retention contributes to land productivity and fertility of soils.
AP.ES.4.3.A.2: The particle size and composition of each soil horizon can affect the porosity, permeability, and fertility of the soil.
AP.ES.4.3.A.3: There are a variety of methods to test the chemical, physical, and biological properties of soil that can aid in a variety of decisions, such as irrigation and fertilizer requirements.
AP.ES.4.3.A.4: A soil texture triangle is a diagram that allows for the identification and comparison of soil types based on their percentage of clay, silt, and sand.
AP.ES.4.4.A: Describe the structure and composition of the Earth's atmosphere.
AP.ES.4.4.A.1: The atmosphere is made up of major gases, each with its own relative abundance.
AP.ES.4.4.A.2: The layers of the atmosphere are based on temperature gradients and include the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and exosphere.
AP.ES.4.5.A: Explain how environmental factors can result in atmospheric circulation.
AP.ES.4.5.A.1: Global wind patterns primarily result from the most intense solar radiation arriving at the equator, resulting in density differences and the Coriolis effect.
AP.ES.4.6.A: Describe the characteristics of a watershed.
AP.ES.4.6.A.1: Characteristics of a given watershed include its area, length, slope, soil, vegetation types, and divides with adjoining watersheds.
AP.ES.4.7.A: Explain how the sun's energy affects the Earth's surface.
AP.ES.4.7.A.1: Incoming solar radiation (insolation) is the Earth's main source of energy and is dependent on season and latitude.
AP.ES.4.7.A.2: The angle of the sun's rays determines the intensity of the solar radiation. Due to the shape of the Earth, the latitude that is directly horizontal to the solar radiation receives the most intensity.
AP.ES.4.7.A.3: The highest solar radiation per unit area is received at the equator and decreases toward the poles.
AP.ES.4.7.A.4: The solar radiation received at a location on the Earth's surface varies seasonally, with the most radiation received during the location's longest summer day and the least on the shortest winter day.
AP.ES.4.7.A.5: The tilt of Earth's axis of rotation causes the Earth's seasons and the number of hours of daylight in a particular location on the Earth's surface.
AP.ES.4.8.A: Describe how the Earth's geography affects weather and climate.
AP.ES.4.8.A.1: Weather and climate are affected not only by the sun's energy but by geologic and geographic factors, such as mountains and ocean temperature.
AP.ES.4.8.A.2: A rain shadow is a region of land that has become drier because a higher elevation area blocks precipitation from reaching the land.
AP.ES.4.9.A: Describe the environmental changes and effects that result from El Niño or La Niña events (El Niño-Southern Oscillation).
AP.ES.4.9.A.1: El Niño and La Niña are phenomena associated with changing ocean surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. These phenomena can cause global changes to rainfall, wind, and ocean circulation patterns.
AP.ES.4.9.A.2: El Niño and La Niña are influenced by geological and geographic factors and can affect different locations in different ways.
AP.ES.5.1.A: Explain the concept of the tragedy of the commons.
AP.ES.5.1.A.1: The tragedy of the commons suggests that individuals will use shared resources in their own self-interest rather than in keeping with the common good, thereby depleting the resources.
AP.ES.5.2.A: Describe the effect of clearcutting on forests.
AP.ES.5.2.A.1: Clearcutting can be economically advantageous but leads to soil erosion, increased soil and stream temperatures, and flooding.
AP.ES.5.2.A.2: Forests contain trees that absorb pollutants and store carbon dioxide. The cutting and burning of trees releases carbon dioxide and contributes to climate change.
AP.ES.5.3.A.1: The Green Revolution started a shift to new agricultural strategies and practices in order to increase food production, with both positive and negative results. Some of these strategies and methods are mechanization, genetically modified organisms (GMOs), fertilization, irrigation, and the use of pesticides.
AP.ES.5.3.A.2: Mechanization of farming can increase profits and efficiency for farms. It can also increase reliance on fossil fuels.
AP.ES.5.4.A: Describe agricultural practices that cause environmental damage.
AP.ES.5.4.A.1: Agricultural practices that can cause environmental damage include tilling, slash-and-burn farming, and the use of fertilizers.
AP.ES.5.5.A.1: The largest human use of freshwater is for irrigation (`70%`).
AP.ES.5.5.A.2: Types of irrigation include drip irrigation, flood irrigation, furrow irrigation, drip irrigation, and spray irrigation.
AP.ES.5.5.B: Describe the benefits and drawbacks of different methods of irrigation.
AP.ES.5.5.B.1: Waterlogging occurs when too much water is left to sit in the soil, which raises the water table of groundwater and inhibits plants' ability to absorb oxygen through their roots.
AP.ES.5.5.B.2: Furrow irrigation involves cutting furrows between crop rows and filling them with water. This system is inexpensive, but about `1//3` of the water is lost to evaporation and runoff.
AP.ES.5.5.B.3: Flood irrigation involves flooding an agricultural field with water. This system sees about `20%` of the water lost to evaporation and runoff. This can also lead to waterlogging of the soil.
AP.ES.5.5.B.4: Spray irrigation involves pumping ground water into spray nozzles across an agricultural field. This system is more efficient than flood and furrow irrigation, with only `1//4` or less of the water lost to evaporation or runoff. However, spray systems are more expensive than flood and furrow irrigation, and also requires energy to run.
AP.ES.5.5.B.5: Drip irrigation uses perforated hoses to release small amounts of water to plant roots. This system is the most efficient, with only about `5%` of water lost to evaporation and runoff. However, this system is expensive and so is not often used.
AP.ES.5.5.B.6: Salinization occurs when the salts in groundwater remain in the soil after the water evaporates. Over time, salinization can make soil toxic to plants.
AP.ES.5.5.B.7: Aquifers can be severely depleted if overused for agricultural irrigation, as has happened to the Ogallala Aquifer in the central United States.
AP.ES.5.6.A: Describe the benefits and drawbacks of different methods of pest control.
AP.ES.5.6.A.1: One consequence of using common pest-control methods such as pesticides, herbicides, fungicides, rodenticides, and insecticides is that organisms can become resistant to them through artificial selection. Pest control decreases crop damage by pest and increases crop yields.
AP.ES.5.6.A.2: Crops can be genetically engineered to increase their resistance to pests and diseases. However, using genetically engineered crops in planting or other ways can lead to loss of genetic diversity of that particular crop.
AP.ES.5.7.A: Identify different methods of meat production.
AP.ES.5.7.A.1: Methods of meat production include concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs), also called feedlots, and free-range grazing.
AP.ES.5.7.B: Describe the benefits and drawbacks of different methods of meat production.
AP.ES.5.7.B.1: Meat production is less efficient than agriculture; it takes approximately `20` times more land to produce the same amount of calories from meat as from plants.
AP.ES.5.7.B.2: Concentrated animal feeding operation (CAFOs) are used as a way to quickly get livestock ready for slaughter. They tend to be crowded, and animals are fed grains or feed that are not as suitable as grass. Additionally, feedlots generate a large amount of organic waste, which can contaminate ground and surface water. The use of feedlots are less expensive than other methods, which can keep costs to consumers down.
AP.ES.5.7.B.3: Free range grazing allows animals to graze on grass during their entire lifecycle. Meat from free range animals tends to be free from antibiotics and other chemicals used in feedlots. Organic waste from these animals acts as fertilizer. Free range grazing requires large areas of land and the meat produced is more expensive for consumers.
AP.ES.5.7.B.4: Overgrazing occurs when too many animals feed on a particular area of land. Overgrazing causes loss of vegetation, which leads to soil erosion.
AP.ES.5.7.B.5: Overgrazing can cause desertification. Desertification is the degradation of low precipitation regions toward being increasingly arid until they become deserts.
AP.ES.5.7.B.6: Less consumption of meat could reduce `text(CO)_2`, methane, and `text(N)_2text(O)` emissions; conserve water; reduce the use of antibiotics and growth hormones; and improve topsoil.
AP.ES.5.8.A: Describe causes of and problems related to overfishing.
AP.ES.5.8.A.1: Overfishing has led to the extreme scarcity of some fish species, which can lessen biodiversity in aquatic systems and harm people who depend on fishing for food and commerce.
AP.ES.5.9.A: Describe natural resource extraction through mining.
AP.ES.5.9.A.1: As the more accessible ores are mined to depletion, mining operations are forced to access lower grade ores. Accessing these ores requires increased use of resources that can cause increased waste and pollution.
AP.ES.5.9.A.2: Surface mining is the removal of large portions of soil and rock, called overburden, in order to access the ore underneath. An example is strip mining, which removes the vegetation from an area, making the area more susceptible to erosion.
AP.ES.5.9.B: Describe ecological and economic impacts of natural resource extraction through mining.
AP.ES.5.9.B.1: Mining wastes include the soil and rocks that are moved to gain access to the ore and the waste, called slag and tailings that remain when the minerals have been removed from the ore. Mining helps to provide low cost energy and material necessary to make products. The mining of coal can destroy habitats, contaminate ground water, and release dust particles and methane.
AP.ES.5.9.B.2: As coal reserves get smaller, due to a lack of easily accessible reserves, it becomes necessary to access coal through subsurface mining, which is very expensive.
AP.ES.5.10.A: Describe the effects of urbanization on the environment.
AP.ES.5.10.A.1: Urbanization can lead to depletion of resources and saltwater intrusion in the hydrologic cycle.
AP.ES.5.10.A.2: Urbanization, through the burning of fossil fuels and landfills, affects the carbon cycle by increasing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
AP.ES.5.10.A.3: Impervious surfaces are human-made structures-such as roads, buildings, sidewalks, and parking lots-that do not allow water to reach the soil, leading to flooding.
AP.ES.5.10.A.4: Urban sprawl is the change in population distribution from high population density areas to low density suburbs that spread into rural lands, leading to potential environmental problems.
AP.ES.5.11.A: Explain the variables measured in an ecological footprint.
AP.ES.5.11.A.1: Ecological footprints compare resource demands and waste production required for an individual or a society.
AP.ES.5.12.A.1: Sustainability refers to humans living on Earth and their use of resources without depletion of the resources for future generations. Environmental indicators that can guide humans to sustainability include biological diversity, food production, average global surface temperatures and `text(CO)_2` concentrations, human population, and resource depletion.
AP.ES.5.12.A.2: Sustainable yield is the amount of a renewable resource that can be taken without reducing the available supply.
AP.ES.5.13.A: Describe methods for mitigating problems related to urban runoff.
AP.ES.5.13.A.1: Methods to increase water infiltration include replacing traditional pavement with permeable pavement, planting trees, increased use of public transportation, and building up, not out.
AP.ES.5.14.A.1: Integrated pest management (IPM) is a combination of methods used to effectively control pest species while minimizing the disruption to the environment. These methods include biological, physical, and limited chemical methods such as biocontrol, intercropping, crop rotation, and natural predators of the pests.
AP.ES.5.14.B: Describe the benefits and drawbacks of integrated pest management (IPM).
AP.ES.5.14.B.1: The use of integrated pest management (IPM) reduces the risk that pesticides pose to wildlife, water supplies, and human health.
AP.ES.5.14.B.2: Integrated pest management (IPM) minimizes disruptions to the environment and threats to human health but can be complex and expensive.
AP.ES.5.15.A: Describe sustainable agricultural and food production practices.
AP.ES.5.15.A.1: The goal of soil conservation is to prevent soil erosion. Different methods of soil conservation include contour plowing, windbreaks, perennial crops, terracing, no-till agriculture, and strip cropping.
AP.ES.5.15.A.2: Strategies to improve soil fertility include crop rotation and the addition of green manure and limestone.
AP.ES.5.15.A.3: Rotational grazing is the regular rotation of livestock between different pastures in order to avoid overgrazing in a particular area.
AP.ES.5.16.A: Describe the benefits and drawbacks of aquaculture.
AP.ES.5.16.A.1: Aquaculture has expanded because it is highly efficient, requires only small areas of water, and requires little fuel.
AP.ES.5.16.A.2: Aquaculture can contaminate wastewater, and fish that escape may compete or breed with wild fish. The density of fish in aquaculture can lead to increases in disease incidences, which can be transmitted to wild fish.
AP.ES.5.17.A: Describe methods for mitigating human impact on forests.
AP.ES.5.17.A.1: Some of the methods for mitigating deforestation include reforestation, using and buying wood harvested by ecologically sustainable forestry techniques, and reusing wood.
AP.ES.5.17.A.2: Methods to protect forests from pathogens and insects include integrated pest management (IPM) and the removal of affected trees.
AP.ES.5.17.A.3: Prescribed burn is a method by which forests are set on fire under controlled conditions in order to reduce the occurrence of natural fires.
AP.ES.6.1.A: Identify differences between nonrenewable and renewable energy sources.
AP.ES.6.1.A.1: Nonrenewable energy sources are those that exist in a fixed amount and involve energy transformation that cannot be easily replaced.
AP.ES.6.1.A.2: Renewable energy sources are those that can be replenished naturally, at or near the rate of consumption, and reused.
AP.ES.6.2.A.1: The use of energy resources is not evenly distributed between developed and developing countries.
AP.ES.6.2.A.2: The most widely used sources of energy globally are fossil fuels.
AP.ES.6.2.A.3: As developing countries become more developed, their reliance on fossil fuels for energy increases.
AP.ES.6.2.A.4: As the world becomes more industrialized, the demand for energy increases.
AP.ES.6.2.A.5: Availability, price, and governmental regulations influence which energy sources people use and how they use them.
AP.ES.6.3.A: Identify types of fuels and their uses.
AP.ES.6.3.A.1: Wood is commonly used as fuel in the forms of firewood and charcoal. It is often used in developing countries because it is easily accessible.
AP.ES.6.3.A.2: Peat is partially decomposed organic material that can be burned for fuel.
AP.ES.6.3.A.3: Three types of coal used for fuel are lignite, bituminous, and anthracite. Heat, pressure, and depth of burial contribute to the development of various coal types and their qualities.
AP.ES.6.3.A.4: Natural gas, the cleanest of the fossil fuels, is mostly methane.
AP.ES.6.3.A.5: Crude oil can be recovered from tar sands, which are a combination of clay, sand, water, and bitumen.
AP.ES.6.3.A.6: Fossil fuels can be made into specific fuel types for specialized uses (e.g., in motor vehicles).
AP.ES.6.3.A.7: Cogeneration occurs when a fuel source is used to generate both useful heat and electricity.
AP.ES.6.4.A: Identify where natural energy resources occur.
AP.ES.6.4.A.1: The global distribution of natural energy resources, such as ores, coal, crude oil, and gas, is not uniform and depends on regions' geologic history.
AP.ES.6.5.A: Describe the use and methods of fossil fuels in power generation.
AP.ES.6.5.A.1: The combustion of fossil fuels is a chemical reaction between the fuel and oxygen that yields carbon dioxide and water and releases energy.
AP.ES.6.5.A.2: Energy from fossil fuels is produced by burning those fuels to generate heat, which then turns water into steam. That steam turns a turbine, which generates electricity.
AP.ES.6.5.A.3: Humans use a variety of methods to extract fossil fuels from the earth for energy generation.
AP.ES.6.5.B: Describe the effects of fossil fuels on the environment.
AP.ES.6.5.B.1: Hydrologic fracturing (fracking) can cause groundwater contamination and the release of volatile organic compounds.
AP.ES.6.6.A: Describe the use of nuclear energy in power generation.
AP.ES.6.6.A.1: Nuclear power is generated through fission, where atoms of Uranium-235, which are stored in fuel rods, are split into smaller parts after being struck by a neutron. Nuclear fission releases a large amount of heat, which is used to generate steam, which powers a turbine and generates electricity.
AP.ES.6.6.A.2: Radioactivity occurs when the nucleus of a radioactive isotope loses energy by emitting radiation.
AP.ES.6.6.A.3: Uranium-235 remains radioactive for a long time, which leads to the problems associated with the disposal of nuclear waste.
AP.ES.6.6.A.4: Nuclear power generation is a nonrenewable energy source. Nuclear power is considered a cleaner energy source because it does not produce air pollutants, but it does release thermal pollution and hazardous solid waste.
AP.ES.6.6.B: Describe the effects of the use of nuclear energy on the environment.
AP.ES.6.6.B.1: Three Mile Island, Chernobyl, and Fukushima are three cases where accidents or natural disasters led to the release of radiation. These releases have had short- and long-term impacts on the environment.
AP.ES.6.6.B.2: A radioactive element's half-life can be used to calculate a variety of things, including the rate of decay and the radioactivity level at specific points in time.
AP.ES.6.7.A: Describe the effects of the use of biomass in power generation on the environment.
AP.ES.6.7.A.1: Burning of biomass produces heat for energy at a relatively low cost, but it also produces carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, particulates, and volatile organic compounds. The overharvesting of trees for fuel also causes deforestation.
AP.ES.6.7.A.2: Ethanol can be used as a substitute for gasoline. Burning ethanol does not introduce additional carbon into the atmosphere via combustion, but the energy return on energy investment for ethanol is low.
AP.ES.6.8.A: Describe the use of solar energy in power generation.
AP.ES.6.8.A.1: Photovoltaic solar cells capture light energy from the sun and transform it directly into electrical energy. Their use is limited by the availability of sunlight.
AP.ES.6.8.A.2: Active solar energy systems use solar energy to heat a liquid through mechanical and electric equipment to collect and store the energy captured from the sun.
AP.ES.6.8.A.3: Passive solar energy systems absorb heat directly from the sun without the use of mechanical and electric equipment, and energy cannot be collected or stored.
AP.ES.6.8.B: Describe the effects of the use of solar energy in power generation on the environment.
AP.ES.6.8.B.1: Solar energy systems have low environmental impact and produce clean energy, but they can be expensive. Large solar energy farms may negatively impact desert ecosystems.
AP.ES.6.9.A: Describe the use of hydroelectricity in power generation.
AP.ES.6.9.A.1: Hydroelectric power can be generated in several ways. Dams built across rivers collect water in reservoirs. The moving water can be used to spin a turbine. Turbines can also be placed in small rivers, where the flowing water spins the turbine.
AP.ES.6.9.A.2: Tidal energy uses the energy produced by tidal flows to turn a turbine.
AP.ES.6.9.B: Describe the effects of the use of hydroelectricity in power generation on the environment.
AP.ES.6.9.B.1: Hydroelectric power does not generate air pollution or waste, but construction of the power plants can be expensive, and there may be a loss of or change in habitats following the construction of dams.
AP.ES.6.10.A: Describe the use of geothermal energy in power generation.
AP.ES.6.10.A.1: Geothermal energy is obtained by using the heat stored in the Earth's interior to heat up water, which is brought back to the surface as steam. The steam is used to drive an electric generator.
AP.ES.6.10.B: Describe the effects of the use of geothermal energy in power generation on the environment.
AP.ES.6.10.B.1: The cost of accessing geothermal energy can be prohibitively expensive, as is not easily accessible in many parts of the world. In addition, it can cause the release of hydrogen sulfide.
AP.ES.6.11.A: Describe the use of hydrogen fuel cells in power generation.
AP.ES.6.11.A.1: Hydrogen fuel cells are an alternate to non-renewable fuel sources. They use hydrogen as fuel, combining the hydrogen and oxygen in the air to form water and release energy (electricity) in the process. Water is the product (emission) of a fuel cell.
AP.ES.6.11.B: Describe the effects of the use of hydrogen fuel cells in power generation on the environment.
AP.ES.6.11.B.1: Hydrogen fuel cells have low environmental impact and produce no carbon dioxide when the hydrogen is produced from water. However, the technology is expensive and energy is still needed to create the hydrogen gas used in the fuel cell.
AP.ES.6.12.A: Describe the use of wind energy in power generation.
AP.ES.6.12.A.1: Wind turbines use the kinetic energy of moving air to spin a turbine, which in turn converts the mechanical energy of the turbine into electricity.
AP.ES.6.12.B: Describe the effects of the use of wind energy in power generation on the environment.
AP.ES.6.12.B.1: Wind energy is a renewable, clean source of energy. However, birds and bats may be killed if they fly into the spinning turbine blades.
AP.ES.6.13.A.1: Some of the methods for conserving energy around a home include adjusting the thermostat to reduce the use of heat and air conditioning, conserving water, use of energy-efficient appliances, and conservation landscaping.
AP.ES.6.13.A.2: Methods for conserving energy on a large scale include improving fuel economy for vehicles, using BEVs (battery electric vehicles) and hybrid vehicles, using public transportation, and implementing green building design features.
AP.ES.7.1.A: Identify the sources and effects of air pollutants.
AP.ES.7.1.A.1: Coal combustion releases air pollutants including carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, toxic metals, and particulates.
AP.ES.7.1.A.2: The combustion of fossil fuels releases nitrogen oxides into the atmosphere. They lead to the production of ozone, formation of photochemical smog, and convert to nitric acid in the atmosphere, causing acid rain. Other pollutants produced by fossil fuel combustion include carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, and particulate matter.
AP.ES.7.1.A.3: Air quality can be affected through the release of sulfur dioxide during the burning of fossil fuels, mainly diesel fuels.
AP.ES.7.1.A.4: Through the Clean Air Act, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regulated the use of lead, particularly in fuels, which dramatically decreased the amount of lead in the atmosphere.
AP.ES.7.1.A.5: Air pollutants can be primary or secondary pollutants.
AP.ES.7.2.A: Explain the causes and effects of photochemical smog and methods to reduce it.
AP.ES.7.2.A.1: Photochemical smog is formed when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic hydrocarbons react with heat and sunlight to produce a variety of pollutants.
AP.ES.7.2.A.2: Many environmental factors affect the formation of photochemical smog.
AP.ES.7.2.A.3: Nitrogen oxide is produced early in the day. Ozone concentrations peak in the afternoon and are higher in the summer because ozone is produced by chemical reactions between oxygen and sunlight.
AP.ES.7.2.A.4: Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs), such as formaldehyde and gasoline, evaporate or sublimate at room temperature. Trees are a natural source of VOCs.
AP.ES.7.2.A.5: Photochemical smog often forms in urban areas because of the large number of motor vehicles there.
AP.ES.7.2.A.6: Photochemical smog can be reduced through the reduction of nitrogen oxide and VOCs.
AP.ES.7.2.A.7: Photochemical smog can harm human health in several ways, including causing respiratory problems and eye irritation.
AP.ES.7.3.A: Describe thermal inversion and its relationship with pollution.
AP.ES.7.3.A.1: During a thermal inversion, the normal temperature gradient in the atmosphere is altered as the air temperature at the Earth's surface is cooler than the air at higher altitudes.
AP.ES.7.3.A.2: Thermal inversion traps pollution close to the ground, especially smog and particulates.
AP.ES.7.4.A: Describe natural sources of `text(CO)_2` and particulates.
AP.ES.7.4.A.1: `text(CO)_2` appears naturally in the atmosphere from sources such as respiration, decomposition, and volcanic eruptions.
AP.ES.7.4.A.2: There are a variety of natural sources of particulate matter.
AP.ES.7.5.A.1: Carbon monoxide is an indoor air pollutant that is classified as an asphyxiant.
AP.ES.7.5.A.2: Indoor air pollutants that are classified as particulates include asbestos, dust, and smoke.
AP.ES.7.5.A.3: Indoor air pollutants can come from natural sources, human-made sources, and combustion.
AP.ES.7.5.A.4: Common natural source indoor air pollutants include radon, mold, and dust.
AP.ES.7.5.A.5: Common human-made indoor air pollutants include insulation, Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) from furniture, paneling and carpets; formaldehyde from building materials, furniture, upholstery, and carpeting; and lead from paints.
AP.ES.7.5.A.6: Common combustion air pollutants include carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, particulates, and tobacco smoke.
AP.ES.7.5.A.7: Radon-222 is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that is produced by the decay of uranium found in some rocks and soils.
AP.ES.7.5.B: Describe the effects of indoor air pollutants.
AP.ES.7.5.B.1: Radon gas can infiltrate homes as it moves up through the soil and enters homes via the basement or cracks in the walls or foundation. It is also dissolved in groundwater that enters homes through a well.
AP.ES.7.5.B.2: Exposure to radon gas can lead to radon- induced lung cancer, which is the second leading cause of lung cancer in America.
AP.ES.7.6.A: Explain how air pollutants can be reduced at the source.
AP.ES.7.6.A.1: Methods to reduce air pollutants include regulatory practices, conservation practices, and alternative fuels.
AP.ES.7.6.A.2: A vapor recovery nozzle is an air pollution control device on a gasoline pump that prevents fumes from escaping into the atmosphere when fueling a motor vehicle.
AP.ES.7.6.A.3: A catalytic converter is an air pollution control device for internal combustion engines that converts pollutants (`CO`, `NOx`, and hydrocarbons) in exhaust into less harmful molecules (`text(CO)_2`, `text(N)_2`, `text(O)_2`, and `text(H)_2text(O)`).
AP.ES.7.6.A.4: Wet and dry scrubbers are air pollution control devices that remove particulates and/or gases from industrial exhaust streams.
AP.ES.7.6.A.5: Methods to reduce air pollution from coal- burning power plants include scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators.
AP.ES.7.7.A.1: Acid rain and deposition is due to nitrogen oxides and sulfur oxides from anthropogenic and natural sources in the atmosphere.
AP.ES.7.7.A.2: Nitric oxides that cause acid deposition come from motor vehicles and coal-burning power plants. Sulfur dioxides that cause acid deposition come from coal-burning power plants.
AP.ES.7.7.B: Describe the effects of acid deposition on the environment.
AP.ES.7.7.B.1: Acid deposition mainly affects communities that are downwind from coal-burning power plants.
AP.ES.7.7.B.2: Acid rain and deposition can lead to the acidification of soils and bodies of water and corrosion of human-made structures.
AP.ES.7.7.B.3: Regional differences in soils and bedrock affect the impact that acid deposition has on the region-such as limestone bedrock's ability to neutralize the effect of acid rain on lakes and ponds.
AP.ES.7.8.A: Describe human activities that result in noise pollution and its effects.
AP.ES.7.8.A.1: Noise pollution is sound at levels high enough to cause physiological stress and hearing loss.
AP.ES.7.8.A.2: Sources of noise pollution in urban areas include transportation, construction, and domestic and industrial activity.
AP.ES.7.8.A.3: Some effects of noise pollution on animals in ecological systems include stress, the masking of sounds used to communicate or hunt, damaged hearing, and causing changes to migratory routes.
AP.ES.8.1.A: Identify differences between point and nonpoint sources of pollution.
AP.ES.8.1.A.1: A point source refers to a single, identifiable source of a pollutant, such as a smokestack or waste discharge pipe.
AP.ES.8.1.A.2: Nonpoint sources of pollution are diffused and can therefore be difficult to identify, such as pesticide spraying or urban runoff.
AP.ES.8.2.A: Describe the impacts of human activities on aquatic ecosystems.
AP.ES.8.2.A.1: Organisms have a range of tolerance for various pollutants. Organisms have an optimum range for each factor where they can maintain homeostasis. Outside of this range, organisms may experience physiological stress, limited growth, reduced reproduction, and in extreme cases, death.
AP.ES.8.2.A.2: Coral reefs have been suffering damage due to a variety of factors, including increasing ocean temperature, sediment runoff, and destructive fishing practices.
AP.ES.8.2.A.3: Oil spills in marine waters cause organisms to die from the hydrocarbons in oil. Oil that floats on the surface of water can coat the feathers of birds and fur of marine mammals. Some components of oil sink to the ocean floor, killing some bottom-dwelling organisms.
AP.ES.8.2.A.4: Oil that washes up on the beach can have economic consequences on the fishing and tourism industries.
AP.ES.8.2.A.5: Oceanic dead zones are areas of low oxygen in the world's oceans caused by increased nutrient pollution.
AP.ES.8.2.A.6: An oxygen sag curve is a plot of dissolved oxygen levels versus the distance from a source of pollution, usually excess nutrients and biological refuse.
AP.ES.8.2.A.7: Heavy metals used for industry, especially mining and burning of fossil fuels, can reach the groundwater, impacting the drinking water supply.
AP.ES.8.2.A.8: Litter that reaches aquatic ecosystems, besides being unsightly, can create intestinal blockage and choking hazards for wildlife and introduce toxic substances to the food chain.
AP.ES.8.2.A.9: Increased sediment in waterways can reduce light infiltration, which can affect primary producers and visual predators. Sediment can also settle, disrupting habitats.
AP.ES.8.2.A.10: When elemental sources of mercury enter aquatic environments, bacteria in the water convert it to highly toxic methylmercury.
AP.ES.8.3.A.1: Endocrine disruptors are chemicals that can interfere with the endocrine system of animals.
AP.ES.8.3.B: Describe the effects of endocrine disruptors on ecosystems.
AP.ES.8.3.B.1: Endocrine disruptors can lead to birth defects, developmental disorders, and gender imbalances in fish and other species.
AP.ES.8.4.A: Describe the impacts of human activity on wetlands and mangroves.
AP.ES.8.4.A.1: Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil, either part or all of the time.
AP.ES.8.4.A.2: Wetlands provide a variety of ecological services, including water purification, flood protection, water filtration, and habitat.
AP.ES.8.4.A.3: Threats to wetlands and mangroves include commercial development, dam construction, overfishing, and pollutants from agriculture and industrial waste.
AP.ES.8.5.A: Explain the environmental effects of excessive use of fertilizers and detergents on aquatic ecosystems.
AP.ES.8.5.A.1: Eutrophication occurs when a body of water is enriched in nutrients.
AP.ES.8.5.A.2: The increase in nutrients in eutrophic aquatic environments causes an algal bloom. When the algal bloom dies, microbes digest the algae, along with the oxygen in the water, leading to a decrease in the dissolved oxygen levels in the water. The lack of dissolved oxygen can result in large die-offs of fish and other aquatic organisms.
AP.ES.8.5.A.3: Hypoxic waterways are those bodies of water that are low in dissolved oxygen.
AP.ES.8.5.A.4: Compared to eutrophic waterways, oligotrophic waterways have very low amounts of nutrients, stable algae populations, and high dissolved oxygen.
AP.ES.8.5.A.5: Anthropogenic causes of eutrophication are agricultural runoff and wastewater release.
AP.ES.8.6.A: Describe the effects of thermal pollution on aquatic ecosystems.
AP.ES.8.6.A.1: Thermal pollution occurs when heat released into the water produces negative effects to the organisms in that ecosystem.
AP.ES.8.6.A.2: Variations in water temperature affect the concentration of dissolved oxygen because warm water does not contain as much oxygen as cold water.
AP.ES.8.7.A: Describe the effect of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) on ecosystems.
AP.ES.8.7.A.1: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) do not easily break down in the environment because they are synthetic, carbon-based molecules (such as DDT and PCBs).
AP.ES.8.7.A.2: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) can be toxic to organisms because they are soluble in fat, which allows them to accumulate in organisms' fatty tissues.
AP.ES.8.7.A.3: Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) can travel over long distances via wind and water before being redeposited.
AP.ES.8.8.A.1: Bioaccumulation is the selective absorption and concentration of elements or compounds by cells in a living organism, most commonly fat-soluble compounds.
AP.ES.8.8.A.2: Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of substances per unit of body tissue that occurs in successively higher trophic levels of a food chain or in a food web.
AP.ES.8.8.B: Describe the effects of bioaccumulation and biomagnification.
AP.ES.8.8.B.1: Some effects that can occur in an ecosystem when a persistent substance is biomagnified in a food chain include eggshell thinning and developmental deformities in top carnivores of the higher trophic levels.
AP.ES.8.8.B.2: Humans also experience harmful effects from biomagnification, including issues with the reproductive, nervous, and circulatory systems.
AP.ES.8.8.B.3: DDT, mercury, and PCBs are substances that bioaccumulate and have significant environmental impacts.
AP.ES.8.9.A.1: Solid waste is any discarded material that is not a liquid or gas. It is generated in domestic, industrial, business, and agricultural sectors.
AP.ES.8.9.A.2: Solid waste is most often disposed of in landfills. Landfills can contaminate groundwater and release harmful gases.
AP.ES.8.9.A.3: Electronic waste, or e-waste, is composed of discarded electronic devices including televisions, cell phones, and computers.
AP.ES.8.9.A.4: A sanitary municipal landfill consists of a bottom liner (plastic or clay), a storm water collection system, a leachate collection system, a cap, and a methane collection system.
AP.ES.8.9.B: Describe the effects of solid waste disposal methods.
AP.ES.8.9.B.1: Factors in landfill decomposition include the composition of the trash and conditions needed for microbial decomposition of the waste.
AP.ES.8.9.B.2: Solid waste can also be disposed of through incineration, where waste is burned at high temperatures. This method significantly reduces the volume of solid waste but releases air pollutants.
AP.ES.8.9.B.3: Some items are not accepted in sanitary landfills and may be disposed of illegally, leading to environmental problems. One example is used rubber tires, which when left in piles can become breeding grounds for mosquitoes that can spread disease.
AP.ES.8.9.B.4: Some countries dispose of their waste by dumping it in the ocean. This practice, along with other sources of plastic, has led to large floating islands of trash in the oceans. Additionally, wildlife can become entangled in the waste, as well as ingest it.
AP.ES.8.10.A: Describe changes to current practices that could reduce the amount of generated waste and their associated benefits and drawbacks.
AP.ES.8.10.A.1: Recycling is a process by which certain solid waste materials are processed and converted into new products.
AP.ES.8.10.A.2: Recycling is one way to reduce the current global demand on minerals, but this process is energy-intensive and can be costly.
AP.ES.8.10.A.3: Composting is the process of organic matter such as food scraps, paper, and yard waste decomposing. The product of this decomposition can be used as fertilizer. Drawbacks to composting include odor and rodents.
AP.ES.8.10.A.4: E-waste can be reduced by recycling and reuse. E-wastes may contain hazardous chemicals, including heavy metals such as lead and mercury, which can leach from landfills into groundwater if they are not disposed of properly.
AP.ES.8.10.A.5: Landfill mitigation strategies range from burning waste for energy to restoring habitat on former landfills for use as parks.
AP.ES.8.10.A.6: The combustion of gases produced from decomposition of organic material in landfills can be used to turn turbines and generate electricity. This process reduces landfill volume.
AP.ES.8.11.A: Describe best practices in sewage treatment.
AP.ES.8.11.A.1: Primary treatment of sewage is the physical removal of large objects, often through the use of screens and grates, followed by the settling of solid waste in the bottom of a tank.
AP.ES.8.11.A.2: Secondary treatment is a biological process in which bacteria break down organic matter into carbon dioxide and inorganic sludge, which settles in the bottom of a tank. The tank is aerated to increase the rate at which the bacteria break down the organic matter.
AP.ES.8.11.A.3: Tertiary treatment is the use of ecological or chemical processes to remove any pollutants left in the water after primary and secondary treatment.
AP.ES.8.11.A.4: Prior to discharge, the treated water is exposed to one or more disinfectants (usually, chlorine, ozone, or UV light) to kill bacteria.
AP.ES.8.12.A.1: Lethal dose `50%` (`text(LD)_50`) is the dose of a chemical that is lethal to `50%` of the population of a particular species.
AP.ES.8.13.A.1: A dose response curve describes the effect on an organism or mortality rate in a population based on the dose of a particular toxin or drug.
AP.ES.8.14.A: Identify sources of human health issues that are linked to pollution.
AP.ES.8.14.A.1: It can be difficult to establish a cause and effect between pollutants and human health issues because humans experience exposure to a variety of chemicals and pollutants.
AP.ES.8.14.A.2: Dysentery is caused by untreated sewage in streams and rivers.
AP.ES.8.14.A.3: Mesothelioma is a type of cancer caused mainly by exposure to asbestos.
AP.ES.8.14.A.4: Respiratory problems and overall lung function can be impacted by elevated levels of tropospheric ozone.
AP.ES.8.15.A: Explain human pathogens and their cycling through the environment.
AP.ES.8.15.A.1: Pathogens adapt to take advantage of new opportunities to infect and spread through human populations.
AP.ES.8.15.A.2: Specific pathogens can occur in many environments regardless of the appearance of sanitary conditions.
AP.ES.8.15.A.3: As equatorial-type climate zones spread north and south in to what are currently subtropical and temperate climate zones, pathogens, infectious diseases, and any associated vectors are spreading into these areas where the disease has not previously been known to occur.
AP.ES.8.15.A.4: Poverty-stricken, low-income areas often lack sanitary waste disposal and have contaminated drinking water supplies, leading to havens and opportunities for the spread of infectious diseases.
AP.ES.8.15.A.5: Plague is a disease carried by organisms infected with the plague bacteria. It is transferred to humans via the bite of an infected organism or through contact with contaminated fluids or tissues.
AP.ES.8.15.A.6: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that typically attacks the lungs. It is spread by breathing in the bacteria from the bodily fluids of an infected person.
AP.ES.8.15.A.7: Malaria is a parasitic disease caused by bites from infected mosquitoes. It is most often found in sub-Saharan Africa.
AP.ES.8.15.A.8: West Nile virus is transmitted to humans via bites from infected mosquitoes.
AP.ES.8.15.A.9: Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) is a form of pneumonia. It is transferred by inhaling or touching infected fluids.
AP.ES.8.15.A.10: Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) is a viral respiratory illness that is transferred from animals to humans.
AP.ES.8.15.A.11: Zika is a virus caused by bites from infected mosquitoes. It can be transmitted through sexual contact.
AP.ES.8.15.A.12: Cholera is a bacterial disease that is contracted from infected water.
AP.ES.9.1.A: Explain the importance of stratospheric ozone to life on Earth.
AP.ES.9.1.A.1: The stratospheric ozone layer is important to the evolution of life on Earth and the continued health and survival of life on Earth.
AP.ES.9.1.A.2: Stratospheric ozone depletion is caused by anthropogenic factors, such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), and natural factors, such as the melting of ice crystals in the atmosphere at the beginning of the Antarctic spring.
AP.ES.9.1.A.3: A decrease in stratospheric ozone increases the UV rays that reach the Earth's surface. Exposure to UV rays can lead to skin cancer and cataracts in humans.
AP.ES.9.2.A: Describe chemicals used to substitute for chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
AP.ES.9.2.A.1: Ozone depletion can be mitigated by replacing ozone-depleting chemicals with substitutes that do not deplete the ozone layer. Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) are one such replacement, but some are strong greenhouse gases.
AP.ES.9.3.A.1: The principal greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, nitrous oxide, and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
AP.ES.9.3.A.2: While water vapor is a greenhouse gas, it doesn't contribute significantly to global climate change because it has a short residence time in the atmosphere.
AP.ES.9.3.A.3: The greenhouse effect results in the surface temperature necessary for life on Earth to exist.
AP.ES.9.3.B: Identify the sources and potency of the greenhouse gases.
AP.ES.9.3.B.1: Carbon dioxide, which has a global warming potential (GWP) of `1`, is used as a reference point for the comparison of different greenhouse gases and their impacts on global climate change. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) have the highest GWP, followed by nitrous oxide, then methane.
AP.ES.9.4.A: Identify the threats to human health and the environment posed by an increase in greenhouse gases.
