AP.P.4.3.C.2: The bystander effect demonstrates that situational and attentional variables predict whether someone is likely to help another person.
AP.P.4.4.A: Explain how the psychodynamic theory of personality defines and assesses personality.
AP.P.4.4.A.1: According to the psychodynamic theory of personality, unconscious processes drive personality.
AP.P.4.4.A.2: Ego defense mechanisms (denial, displacement, projection, rationalization, reaction formation, regression, repression, and sublimation) serve to protect the ego unconsciously from threats.
AP.P.4.4.A.3: Psychodynamic personality psychologists assess personality using projective tests that are designed to probe the preconscious and unconscious mind.
AP.P.4.4.B: Explain how the humanistic theory of personality defines and assesses personality.
AP.P.4.4.B.1: According to humanistic psychology, personality focuses on unconditional regard and the self-actualizing tendency as primary motivating factors.
AP.P.4.5.A: Explain how the social-cognitive theory of personality defines and assesses personality.
AP.P.4.5.A.1: According to social-cognitive theory, reciprocal determinism shapes personality. Reciprocal determinism explores self-concept (how one views themselves and in relation to others) and how self-efficacy and self-esteem both contribute to self-concept.
AP.P.4.5.B: Explain how trait theories of personality define and assess personality.
AP.P.4.5.B.1: Trait theories of personality conclude that personality involves a set of enduring characteristics that lead to typical responses to stimuli.
AP.P.4.5.B.2: The Big Five theory of personality proposes that traits of agreeableness, openness to experience, extraversion, conscientiousness, and emotional stability make up one's personality. These traits are measured by specialized personality inventories that use factor analysis to organize item responses.
AP.P.4.6.A: Explain how theories about motivation apply to behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.4.6.A.1: Some theories about motivation focus on behavior and mental processes that seek to address physical needs and desires such as drive-reduction theory and arousal theory. Drive-reduction theory addresses how certain behaviors help maintain homeostasis while arousal theory addresses how people seek an optimal level of arousal when they behave (as demonstrated by the Yerkes-Dodson Law).
AP.P.4.6.A.2: Self-determination theory proposes that people are motivated by intrinsic (internal) or extrinsic (external) motivations. Incentive theory explores the role of rewards (an extrinsic motivation) in motivating behavior.
AP.P.4.6.A.3: Many non-human animals are motivated by instincts (innate, typically fixed patterns of behavior in animals in response to certain stimuli). Humans do not seem to demonstrate instinctual behavior or mental processes.
AP.P.4.6.A.4: Lewin's motivational conflicts theory proposes that choices create conflicts one must resolve as the basis of motivation. The type of conflicts faced include approach-approach, approach-avoidance, and avoidance-avoidance.
AP.P.4.6.A.5: Sensation-seeking theory proposes that one's level of need for varied or novel experiences is the basis of motivation. The types of sensation seeking are experience seeking, thrill or adventure seeking, disinhibition, and boredom susceptibility.
AP.P.4.6.B: Explain how eating and belongingness motivate behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.4.6.B.1: Eating is a complex motivated behavior that demonstrates how physical and mental processes interact.
AP.P.4.6.B.1.i: Hormones, such as ghrelin and leptin (regulated by the hypothalamus via the pituitary gland), regulate feelings of hunger and satiety.
AP.P.4.6.B.1.ii: External factors like the presence of food, time of day, or social gatherings around meals also influence the behavior of eating.
AP.P.4.7.A: Explain how theories of emotion apply to behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.4.7.A.1: Emotion, or affect, is a complex psychological process that is distinguished from reasoning or knowledge. Emotions reflect internal and external factors affecting an individual. Early `20^text(th)` `text(century)` psychological theories of emotion parsed the distinction between the physiological and cognitive experiences of emotion. Some theories proposed that the physiological and cognitive experiences occurred in succession while others proposed that they occurred simultaneously. Other theories emphasize that the cognitive label is required to experience an emotion. The facial-feedback hypothesis suggests that the experience of emotion is influenced by facial expressions, which supports theories that propose the physiological experience of emotion precedes the cognitive appraisal, and research testing this hypothesis has produced mixed results.
AP.P.4.7.A.2: The broaden-and-build theory of emotion proposes that positive emotional experiences tend to broaden awareness and encourage new actions and thoughts. Negative emotions tend to reduce awareness and narrow thinking and action.
AP.P.4.7.B: Explain how social norms and experiences influence the expression of emotions.
AP.P.4.7.B.1: Research has explored whether the expression of emotions is universally common. Some emotions that may be commonly experienced across cultures include anger, disgust, sadness, happiness, surprise, and fear. Research on the universality of emotions shows mixed results.
AP.P.4.7.B.2: Display rules and elicitors for emotional expression can differ among cultures. Display rules and elicitors may regulate how people from different genders, ages, or socioeconomic classes within a culture can display and interpret emotions.
AP.P.5.1.A: Explain how health psychology addresses issues of physical health and wellness as they apply to behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.5.1.B: Explain how stress applies to behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.5.1.B.1: Stress is a factor in heightened susceptibility to disorders and disease. Stress has been linked to physiological issues such as hypertension, headaches, and immune suppression.
AP.P.5.1.B.2: Stressors can be viewed as motivating (eustress) or debilitating (distress). Stressors can be experienced as traumatic or as daily hassles that can build up over time. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are sources of stress that can affect a person throughout the lifespan.
AP.P.5.1.C: Explain how reactions to stress apply to behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.5.1.C.1: The general adaptation syndrome (GAS) describes the process of experiencing stress. Initially, alarm reaction occurs when the stress is encountered (via a fight-flight-freeze response). Then, a resistance phase occurs as the stress is confronted. Finally, an exhaustion phase occurs when the stress subsides, or resources are spent. The greatest susceptibility to illness occurs during the exhaustion phase.
AP.P.5.1.C.2: The tend-and-befriend theory proposes that some people react to stress by tending to their own needs and/or the needs of others and seeking connection with others. This phenomenon seems to occur mostly in women.
AP.P.5.1.D: Explain how the ways that people cope with stress applies to behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.5.1.D.1: Problem-focused coping involves seeing stress as a problem to be solved and working solutions until a solution is found.
AP.P.5.1.D.2: Emotion-focused coping involves managing emotional reactions to stress as a means of coping. Strategies that are emotion-focused may include deep breathing, meditation, or taking medication aimed at reducing stressful emotional responses.
AP.P.5.2.A: Explain how positive psychology approaches the study of behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.5.2.A.1: Positive psychology seeks to identify factors that lead to well-being, resilience, positive emotions, and psychological health.
AP.P.5.2.B: Explain how positive subjective experiences apply to behavior and mental processes.
AP.P.5.2.B.1: Expressing gratitude, a positive subjective experience, increases subjective well-being.
AP.P.5.2.B.2: People who exercise their signature strengths or virtues report higher levels of positive objective experiences such as happiness and subjective well-being. A classification of character strengths has been developed around 6 categories of virtues: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance, and transcendence.
AP.P.5.2.B.3: Posttraumatic growth, a positive subjective experience, may result after the experience of trauma or stress.
AP.P.5.3.A: Describe the approaches used to define behaviors and mental processes as psychological disorders.
AP.P.5.3.A.1: Level of dysfunction, perception of distress, and deviation from the social norm are all factors used to identify psychological disorders.
AP.P.5.3.A.2: Diagnosing or classifying psychological disorders has positive and negative consequences depending on the nature of the disorder, the individual being diagnosed, and the presence of cultural/societal norms, stigma, racism, sexism, ageism, and discrimination.
AP.P.5.3.A.3: Diagnosing psychological disorders requires specialized training and the use of evidence-based diagnostic tools. The American Psychiatric Association developed the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) of Mental Disorders to classify mental disorders. The World Health Organization developed the International Classification of Mental Disorders (ICD) to classify mental disorders. These classification systems are updated regularly to be responsive to new research and practice advances.
AP.P.5.3.B: Explain how psychological perspectives define psychological disorders.
AP.P.5.3.B.1: Most psychologists employ an eclectic approach (using more than one psychological perspective) when diagnosing and treating clients.
AP.P.5.3.B.2: The behavioral perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on maladaptive learned associations between or among responses to stimuli.
AP.P.5.3.B.3: The psychodynamic perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on unconscious thoughts and experiences, often developed during childhood.
AP.P.5.3.B.4: The humanistic perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on a lack of social support and being unable to fulfill one's potential.
AP.P.5.3.B.5: The cognitive perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on maladaptive thoughts, beliefs, attitudes, or emotions.
AP.P.5.3.B.6: The evolutionary perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on behaviors and mental processes that reduce the likelihood of survival.
AP.P.5.3.B.7: The sociocultural perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on maladaptive social and cultural relationships and dynamics.
AP.P.5.3.B.8: The biological perspective proposes that the causes of mental disorders focus on physiological or genetic issues.
AP.P.5.3.C: Explain how interaction models define psychological disorders.
AP.P.5.3.C.1: The biopsychosocial model assumes that any psychological problem potentially involves a combination of biological, psychological, and sociocultural factors.
AP.P.5.3.C.2: The diathesis-stress model assumes that psychological disorders develop due to a genetic vulnerability (diathesis) in combination with stressful life experiences (stress).
AP.P.5.4: Selection Of Categories Of Psychological Disorders
AP.P.5.4.A: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected neurodevelopmental disorders.
AP.P.5.4.A.1: Neurodevelopmental disorders are a group of disorders with onset occurring during the developmental period. Symptoms of neurodevelopmental disorders focus on whether the person is exhibiting behaviors appropriate for their age or maturity range.
AP.P.5.4.A.2: Possible causes of neurodevelopmental disorders may be environmental, physiological, or genetic in nature.
AP.P.5.4.B: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected schizophrenic spectrum disorders.
AP.P.5.4.B.1: Schizophrenic spectrum disorders are characterized by issues in one or more of these five areas: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking or speech, disorganized motor behavior, and negative symptoms. Schizophrenia can be experienced as an acute or chronic condition.
AP.P.5.4.B.1.i: Delusions (false beliefs) are positive symptoms and may manifest in ways such as delusions of persecution or grandeur.
AP.P.5.4.B.1.ii: Hallucinations (false perceptions) are positive symptoms and may involve one or more of the senses.
AP.P.5.4.B.1.iii: Disorganized thinking or speech is a positive symptom and may manifest as speaking in ways such as speaking in a word salad (stringing together words in nonsensical ways).
AP.P.5.4.B.1.iv: Disorganized motor behavior may manifest as catatonia. Catatonia, or disordered movement, may be experienced as excitement (a positive symptom manifestation) or stupor (a negative symptom manifestation).
AP.P.5.4.B.1.v: Negative symptoms present as the lack of a typical behavior, such as the lack of emotional expression (flat affect) or lack of movement (catatonic stupor).
AP.P.5.4.B.2: Possible causes of schizophrenia suggest a genetic or biological link, such as prenatal virus exposure or imbalances with certain neurotransmitters (dopamine hypothesis).
AP.P.5.4.C: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected depressive disorders.
AP.P.5.4.C.1: Depressive disorders are characterized by the presence of sad, empty, or irritable mood along with physical and cognitive changes that affect a person's ability to function.
AP.P.5.4.C.2: Possible causes of depressive disorders focus on biological, genetic, social, cultural, behavioral, or cognitive sources.
AP.P.5.4.D: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected bipolar disorders.
AP.P.5.4.D.1: Bipolar disorders are characterized by periods of mania and periods of depression. Bipolar cycling involves experiencing periods of depression and mania in alternating periods that can last various amounts of time.
AP.P.5.4.D.2: Possible causes of bipolar disorders focus on biological, genetic, social, cultural, behavioral, or cognitive sources.
AP.P.5.4.E: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected anxiety disorders.
AP.P.5.4.E.1: Anxiety disorders are characterized by excessive fear and/or anxiety with related disturbances to behavior.
AP.P.5.4.E.1.i: Specific phobia involves fear or anxiety toward a specific object or situation, such as acrophobia (heights) or arachnophobia (spiders).
AP.P.5.4.E.1.ii: Agoraphobia is intense fear of specific social situations, including using public transportation, being in open spaces, being in enclosed spaces (e.g., shops, theaters, etc.), standing in line or being in a crowd, or being outside of the home alone.
AP.P.5.4.E.1.iii: Panic disorder involves the experience of panic attacks (unanticipated and overwhelming biological, cognitive, and emotional experiences of fear/anxiety). Panic disorder can manifest as a culture-bound anxiety disorder such as ataque de nervios (experienced mainly by people of Caribbean or Iberian descent).
AP.P.5.4.E.1.iv: Social anxiety disorder involves the intense fear of being judged or watched by others. Social anxiety disorder is distinct from but may include agoraphobia. Taijin kyofusho is a culture-bound anxiety disorder experienced mainly by Japanese people in which people fear others are judging their bodies as undesirable, offensive, or unpleasing.
AP.P.5.4.E.1.v: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) involves prolonged experiences of nonspecific anxiety or fear.
AP.P.5.4.E.2: Possible causes of anxiety disorders focus on learned associations between and among stimuli, maladaptive thinking or emotional responses, and biological or genetic sources.
AP.P.5.4.F: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected obsessive-compulsive disorders and related disorders.
AP.P.5.4.F.1: Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders are characterized by the presence of obsessions (intrusive thoughts) and compulsions (intrusive, often repetitive, behaviors intended to address obsessions).
AP.P.5.4.F.2: Possible causes of obsessive-compulsive disorders involve learned associations between and among stimuli, maladaptive thinking or emotional responses, and biological or genetic sources.
AP.P.5.4.G: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected dissociative disorders.
AP.P.5.4.G.1: Dissociative disorders are characterized by dissociations from consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, motor control, and behavior.
AP.P.5.4.G.2: Possible causes of dissociative disorders involve the experience of trauma or stress.
AP.P.5.4.H: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected trauma and stressor-related disorders.
AP.P.5.4.H.1: Trauma and stressor-related disorders are characterized by exposure to a traumatic or stressful event with subsequent psychological distress. Symptoms of trauma and stressor-related disorders may involve hypervigilance, severe anxiety, flashbacks to traumatic or stressful experiences, insomnia, emotional detachment, and hostility.
AP.P.5.4.H.2: Possible causes of trauma and stressor-related disorders involve the experience of trauma or stress.
AP.P.5.4.I: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected feeding and eating disorders.
AP.P.5.4.I.1: Feeding and eating disorders are characterized by altered consumption or absorption of food that impairs health or psychological functioning.
AP.P.5.4.I.2: Possible causes of feeding and eating disorders focus on biological, genetic, social, cultural, behavioral, or cognitive sources.
AP.P.5.4.J: Describe the symptoms and possible causes of selected personality disorders.
AP.P.5.4.J.1: Personality disorders (which fall into three clusters) are characterized by enduring patterns of internal experience and behavior that is deviant from one's culture; is pervasive and inflexible; begins in adolescence or early adulthood; is stable over time; and leads to personal distress or impairment.
AP.P.5.4.J.1.i: Cluster A is the odd or eccentric cluster and includes paranoid, schizoid, and schizotypal personality disorders.
AP.P.5.4.J.1.ii: Cluster B is the dramatic, emotional, or erratic cluster and includes antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic, and borderline personality disorders.
AP.P.5.4.J.1.iii: Cluster C is the anxious or fearful cluster and includes avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders.
AP.P.5.4.J.2: Possible causes of personality disorders focus on biological, genetic, social, cultural, behavioral, or cognitive sources.
AP.P.5.5.A: Describe research and trends in the treatment of psychological disorders.
AP.P.5.5.A.1: Many researchers who have conducted meta-analytic studies of psychotherapy conclude that psychotherapies are generally effective. Many psychologists use evidence-based interventions to develop treatment plans. Therapists should exhibit cultural humility and establish a therapeutic alliance with the client to deliver therapy successfully.
AP.P.5.5.B: Describe research and trends in the treatment of psychological disorders.
AP.P.5.5.B.1: Due to the increased use and effectiveness of psychotropic medication therapy, hospitals and asylums deinstitutionalized massive numbers of people in the late `20^text(th)` `text(century)`. Therapists now prefer to treat in decentralized ways, often with a combination of medication and psychological therapies.
AP.P.5.5.C: Describe ethical principles in the treatment of psychological disorders.
AP.P.5.5.C.1: Psychologists in clinical or therapeutic situations must follow certain ethical principles as established by the APA, including nonmaleficence, fidelity, integrity, and respect for people's rights and dignity.
AP.P.5.5.D: Describe techniques used with psychological therapies.
AP.P.5.5.D.1: Psychodynamic therapies employ free association and dream interpretation to uncover the unconscious mind.
AP.P.5.5.D.2: Cognitive therapies may employ cognitive restructuring or fear hierarchies to combat maladaptive thinking. Cognitive therapy proposes that people should focus on the cognitive triad-negative thoughts about oneself, the world, and the future.
AP.P.5.5.D.3: Applied behavior analysis involves applying principles of conditioning to address mental disorders and developmental disabilities. Exposure therapies (such as systematic desensitization), aversion therapies, and token economies all employ principles of applied behavior analysis. Biofeedback uses principles of conditioning to help clients regulate body systems (such as the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems) that contribute to feelings of anxiety or depression.
AP.P.5.5.D.4: Cognitive-behavioral therapies, such as dialectical behavior therapy and rational-emotive behavior therapy, combine techniques from the cognitive and behavioral perspectives to treat mental and behavioral disorders.
AP.P.5.5.D.5: Therapy from the humanistic perspective, commonly referred to as person-centered therapy, employs active listening and unconditional positive regard.
AP.P.5.5.E: Explain how group therapy is different from individual therapy.
AP.P.5.5.F.1: Hypnosis has shown effectiveness in treating pain and anxiety. Research does not support the use of hypnosis to retrieve accurate memories or regress in age.
AP.P.5.5.G: Describe interventions derived from the biological perspective.
AP.P.5.5.G.1: Psychoactive medications, such as antidepressants, antianxiety drugs, lithium, or antipsychotic medications, interact with specific neurotransmitters in the central nervous system to address possible biochemical causes of mental disorders. Psychoactive medications can have side effects such as tardive dyskinesia (a movement disorder related to the regulation of dopamine in the nervous system).
AP.P.5.5.G.2: Surgical or invasive interventions include psychosurgery (which may involve lesioning), TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation), or electroconvulsive therapy. The lobotomy is a form of psychosurgery that was popular in the mid-`20^text(th)` `text(century)` but is rarely, if ever, performed today.
AP.P1AB.1.1.A: Describe a scalar or vector quantity using magnitude and direction, as appropriate.
AP.P1AB.1.1.A.1: Scalars are quantities described by magnitude only; vectors are quantities described by both magnitude and direction.
AP.P1AB.1.1.A.2: Vectors can be visually modeled as arrows with appropriate direction and lengths proportional to their magnitude.
AP.P1AB.1.1.A.3: Distance and speed are examples of scalar quantities, while position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration are examples of vector quantities.
AP.P1AB.1.1.A.3.i: Vectors are notated with an arrow above the symbol for that quantity. Relevant equation: `vec(v)=vec(v)_0+vec(a)t`.
AP.P1AB.1.1.A.3.ii: Vector notation is not required for vector components along an axis. In one dimension, the sign of the component completely describes the direction of that component. Derived equation: `v_x=v_(x0)+a_xt`.
AP.P1AB.1.1.B: Describe a vector sum in one dimension.
AP.P1AB.1.1.B.1: When determining a vector sum in a given one-dimensional coordinate system, opposite directions are denoted by opposite signs.
AP.P1AB.1.2.A: Describe a change in an object's position.
AP.P1AB.1.2.A.1: When using the object model, the size, shape, and internal configuration are ignored. The object may be treated as a single point with extensive properties such as mass and charge.
AP.P1AB.1.2.A.2: Displacement is the change in an object's position. Relevant equation: `Deltax=x-x_0`.
AP.P1AB.1.2.B: Describe the average velocity and acceleration of an object.
AP.P1AB.1.2.B.1: Averages of velocity and acceleration are calculated considering the initial and final states of an object over an interval of time.
AP.P1AB.1.2.B.2: Average velocity is the displacement of an object divided by the interval of time in which that displacement occurs. Relevant equation: `vec(v)_(text(avg))=(Deltavec(x))/(Deltat)`.
AP.P1AB.1.2.B.3: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the interval of time in which that change in velocity occurs. Relevant equation: `vec(a)_(text(avg))=(Deltavec(v))/(Deltat)`
AP.P1AB.1.2.B.4: An object is accelerating if the magnitude and/or direction of the object's velocity are changing.
AP.P1AB.1.2.B.5: Calculating average velocity or average acceleration over a very small time interval yields a value that is very close to the instantaneous velocity or instantaneous acceleration.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A: Describe the position, velocity, and acceleration of an object using representations of that object's motion.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.1: Motion can be represented by motion diagrams, figures, graphs, equations, and narrative descriptions.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.2: For constant acceleration, three kinematic equations can be used to describe instantaneous linear motion in one dimension: `v_x=v_(x0)+a_xt`, `x=x_0+v_(x0)t+1/2at^2`, and `v_x^2=v_(x0)^2+2a_x(x-x_0)`.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.3: Near the surface of `text(Earth)`, the vertical acceleration caused by the force of gravity is downward, constant, and has a measured value approximately equal to `a_g=g~~10` `text(m)//text(s)^2`.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.4: Graphs of position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time can be used to find the relationships between those quantities.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.4.i: An object's instantaneous velocity is the rate of change of the object's position, which is equal to the slope of a line tangent to a point on a graph of the object's position as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.4.ii: An object's instantaneous acceleration is the rate of change of the object's velocity, which is equal to the slope of a line tangent to a point on a graph of the object's velocity as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.4.iii: The displacement of an object during a time interval is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the object's velocity as a function of time (i.e., the area bounded by the function and the horizontal axis for the appropriate interval).
AP.P1AB.1.3.A.4.iv: The change in velocity of an object during a time interval is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the acceleration of the object as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.1.4.A: Describe the reference frame of a given observer.
AP.P1AB.1.4.A.1: The choice of reference frame will determine the direction and magnitude of quantities measured by an observer in that reference
AP.P1AB.1.4.B: Describe the motion of objects as measured by observers in different inertial reference frames.
AP.P1AB.1.4.B.1: Measurements from a given reference frame may be converted to measurements from another reference frame.
AP.P1AB.1.4.B.2: The observed velocity of an object results from the combination of the object's velocity and the velocity of the observer's reference frame.
AP.P1AB.1.4.B.2.i: Combining the motion of an object and the motion of an observer in a given reference frame involves the addition or subtraction of vectors.
AP.P1AB.1.4.B.2.ii: The acceleration of any object is the same as measured from all inertial reference frames.
AP.P1AB.1.5.A: Describe the perpendicular components of a vector.
AP.P1AB.1.5.A.1: Vectors can be mathematically modeled as the resultant of two perpendicular components.
AP.P1AB.1.5.A.2: Vectors can be resolved into components using a chosen coordinate system.
AP.P1AB.1.5.A.3: Vectors can be resolved into perpendicular components using trigonometric functions and relationships. Relevant equations: `sintheta=a/c`, `costheta=b/c`, `tantheta=a/b`, and `a^2+b^2=c^2`.
AP.P1AB.1.5.B: Describe the motion of an object moving in two dimensions.
AP.P1AB.1.5.B.1: Motion in two dimensions can be analyzed using one-dimensional kinematic relationships if the motion is separated into components.
AP.P1AB.1.5.B.2: Projectile motion is a special case of two-dimensional motion that has zero acceleration in one dimension and constant, nonzero acceleration in the second dimension.
AP.P1AB.2.1.A: Describe the properties and interactions of a system.
AP.P1AB.2.1.A.1: System properties are determined by the interactions between objects within the system.
AP.P1AB.2.1.A.2: If the properties or interactions of the constituent objects within a system are not important in modeling the behavior of the macroscopic system, the system can itself be treated as a single object.
AP.P1AB.2.1.A.3: Systems may allow interactions between constituent parts of the system and the environment, which may result in the transfer of energy or mass.
AP.P1AB.2.1.A.4: Individual objects within a chosen system may behave differently from each other as well as from the system as a whole.
AP.P1AB.2.1.A.5: The internal structure of a system affects the analysis of that system.
AP.P1AB.2.1.A.6: As variables external to a system are changed, the system's substructure may change.
AP.P1AB.2.1.B: Describe the location of a system's center of mass with respect to the system's constituent parts.
AP.P1AB.2.1.B.1: For systems with symmetrical mass distributions, the center of mass is located on lines of symmetry.
AP.P1AB.2.1.B.2: The location of a system's center of mass along a given axis can be calculated using the equation `vec(x)_(text(cm))=(summ_ibar(x)_i)/(summ_i)`.
AP.P1AB.2.1.B.3: A system can be modeled as a singular object that is located at the system's center of mass.
AP.P1AB.2.2.A: Describe a force as an interaction between two objects or systems.
AP.P1AB.2.2.A.1: Forces are vector quantities that describe the interactions between objects or systems.
AP.P1AB.2.2.A.1.i: A force exerted on an object or system is always due to the interaction of that object with another object or system.
AP.P1AB.2.2.A.1.ii: An object or system cannot exert a net force on itself.
AP.P1AB.2.2.A.2: Contact forces describe the interaction of an object or system touching another object or system and are macroscopic effects of interatomic electric forces.
AP.P1AB.2.2.B: Describe the forces exerted on an object or system using a free-body diagram.
AP.P1AB.2.2.B.1: Free-body diagrams are useful tools for visualizing forces being exerted on a single object or system and for determining the equations that represent a physical situation.
AP.P1AB.2.2.B.2: The free-body diagram of an object or system shows each of the forces exerted on the object by the environment.
AP.P1AB.2.2.B.3: Forces exerted on an object or system are represented as vectors originating from the representation of the center of mass, such as a dot. A system is treated as though all of its mass is located at the center of mass.
AP.P1AB.2.2.B.4: A coordinate system with one axis parallel to the direction of acceleration of the object or system simplifies the translation from free-body diagram to algebraic representation. For example, in a free-body diagram of an object on an inclined plane, it is useful to set one axis parallel to the surface of the incline.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A: Describe the interaction of two objects using Newton's third law and a representation of paired forces exerted on each object.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A.1: Newton's third law describes the interaction of two objects in terms of the paired forces that each exerts on the other: `vec(F)_text(A on B)=-vec(F)_text(B on A)`.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A.2: Interactions between objects within a system (internal forces) do not influence the motion of a system's center of mass.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A.3: Tension is the macroscopic net result of forces that segments of a string, cable, chain, or similar system exert on each other in response to an external force.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A.3.i: An ideal string has negligible mass and does not stretch when under tension.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A.3.ii: The tension in an ideal string is the same at all points within the string.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A.3.iii: In a string with nonnegligible mass, tension may not be the same at all points within the string.
AP.P1AB.2.3.A.3.iv: An ideal pulley is a pulley that has negligible mass and rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction.
AP.P1AB.2.4.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's velocity remains constant.
AP.P1AB.2.4.A.1: The net force on a system is the vector sum of all forces exerted on the system.
AP.P1AB.2.4.A.2: Translational equilibrium is a configuration of forces such that the net force exerted on a system is zero. Derived equation: `sum_ivec(F)_i=0`.
AP.P1AB.2.4.A.3: Newton's first law states that if the net force exerted on a system is zero, the velocity of that system will remain constant.
AP.P1AB.2.4.A.4: Forces may be balanced in one dimension but unbalanced in another. The system's velocity will change only in the direction of the unbalanced force.
AP.P1AB.2.4.A.5: An inertial reference frame is one from which an observer would verify Newton's first law of motion.
AP.P1AB.2.5.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's velocity changes.
AP.P1AB.2.5.A.1: Unbalanced forces are a configuration of forces such that the net force exerted on a system is not equal to zero.
AP.P1AB.2.5.A.2: Newton's second law of motion states that the acceleration of a system's center of mass has a magnitude proportional to the magnitude of the net force exerted on the system and is in the same direction as that net force. Relevant equation: `vec(a)_text(sys)=(sumvec(F))/m_text(sys)=vec(F)_text(net)/m_text(sys)`.
AP.P1AB.2.5.A.3: The velocity of a system's center of mass will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A: Describe the gravitational interaction between two objects or systems with mass.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A.1: Newton's law of universal gravitation describes the gravitational force between two objects or systems as directly proportional to each of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the systems' centers of mass. Relevant equation: `abs(vec(F)_g)=G(m_1m_2)/r^2`.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A.1.ii: The gravitational force is always exerted along the line connecting the centers of mass of the two interacting systems.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A.1.iii: The gravitational force on a system can be considered to be exerted on the system's center of mass.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A.2: A field models the effects of a noncontact force exerted on an object at various positions in space.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A.2.i: The magnitude of the gravitational field created by a system of mass `M` at a point in space is equal to the ratio of the gravitational force exerted by the system on a test object of mass `m` to the mass of the test object. Derived equation: `abs(vec(g))=abs(vec(F)_g)/m=GM/r^2`.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A.2.ii: If the gravitational force is the only force exerted on an object, the observed acceleration of the object (in `text(m)//text(s)^2`) is numerically equal to the magnitude of the gravitational field strength (in `text(N)//text(kg)`) at that location.
AP.P1AB.2.6.A.3: The gravitational force exerted by an astronomical body on a relatively small nearby object is called weight. Derived Equation: `text(Weight)=F_g=mg`.
AP.P1AB.2.6.B: Describe situations in which the gravitational force can be considered constant.
AP.P1AB.2.6.B.1: If the gravitational force between two systems' centers of mass has a negligible change as the relative position of the two systems changes, the gravitational force can be considered constant at all points between the initial and final positions of the systems.
AP.P1AB.2.6.B.2: Near the surface of `text(Earth)`, the strength of the gravitational field is `g~~10` `text(N)//text(kg)`.
AP.P1AB.2.6.C: Describe the conditions under which the magnitude of a system's apparent weight is different from the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on that system.
AP.P1AB.2.6.C.1: The magnitude of the apparent weight of a system is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the system.
AP.P1AB.2.6.C.2: If the system is accelerating, the apparent weight of the system is not equal to the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on the system.
AP.P1AB.2.6.C.3: A system appears weightless when there are no forces exerted on the system or when the force of gravity is the only force exerted on the system.
AP.P1AB.2.6.C.4: The equivalence principle states that an observer in a noninertial reference frame is unable to distinguish between an object's apparent weight and the gravitational force exerted on the object by a gravitational field.
AP.P1AB.2.6.D.1: Objects have inertial mass, or inertia, a property that determines how much an object's motion resists changes when interacting with another object.
AP.P1AB.2.6.D.2: Gravitational mass is related to the force of attraction between two systems with mass.
AP.P1AB.2.6.D.3: Inertial mass and gravitational mass have been experimentally verified to be equivalent.
AP.P1AB.2.7.A: Describe kinetic friction between two surfaces.
AP.P1AB.2.7.A.1: Kinetic friction occurs when two surfaces in contact move relative to each other.
AP.P1AB.2.7.A.1.i: The kinetic friction force is exerted in a direction opposite to the motion of each surface relative to the other surface.
AP.P1AB.2.7.A.1.ii: The force of friction between two surfaces does not depend on the size of the surface area of contact.
AP.P1AB.2.7.A.2: The magnitude of the kinetic friction force exerted on an object is the product of the normal force the surface exerts on the object and the coefficient of kinetic friction. Relevant equation: `abs(vec(F)_(f,k))=abs(mu_kvec(F)_n)`.
AP.P1AB.2.7.A.2.i: The coefficient of kinetic friction depends on the material properties of the surfaces that are in contact.
AP.P1AB.2.7.A.2.ii: Normal force is the perpendicular component of the force exerted on an object by the surface with which it is in contact; it is directed away from the surface.
AP.P1AB.2.7.B: Describe static friction between two surfaces.
AP.P1AB.2.7.B.1: Static friction may occur between the contacting surfaces of two objects that are not moving relative to each other.
AP.P1AB.2.7.B.2: Static friction adopts the value and direction required to prevent an object from slipping or sliding on a surface. Relevant equation: `abs(vec(F)_(f,s))<=abs(mu_svec(F)_n)`.
AP.P1AB.2.7.B.2.i: Slipping and sliding refer to situations in which two surfaces are moving relative to each other.
AP.P1AB.2.7.B.2.ii: There exists a maximum value for which static friction will prevent an object from slipping on a given surface. Derived equation: `F_(f,s,text(max))=mu_sF_n`.
AP.P1AB.2.7.B.3: The coefficient of static friction is typically greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction for a given pair of surfaces.
AP.P1AB.2.8.A: Describe the force exerted on an object by an ideal spring.
AP.P1AB.2.8.A.1: An ideal spring has negligible mass and exerts a force that is proportional to the change in its length as measured from its relaxed length.
AP.P1AB.2.8.A.2: The magnitude of the force exerted by an ideal spring on an object is given by Hooke's law: `vec(F)_s=-kDeltavec(x)`.
AP.P1AB.2.8..3: The force exerted on an object by a spring is always directed toward the equilibrium position of the object-spring system.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A: Describe the motion of an object traveling in a circular path.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.1: Centripetal acceleration is the component of an object's acceleration directed toward the center of the object's circular path.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.1.i: The magnitude of centripetal acceleration for an object moving in a circular path is the ratio of the object's tangential speed squared to the radius of the circular path. Relevant equation: `a_c=v^2/r`.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.1.ii: Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the center of an object's circular path.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.2: Centripetal acceleration can result from a single force, more than one force, or components of forces exerted on an object in circular motion.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.2.i: At the top of a vertical, circular loop, an object requires a minimum speed to maintain circular motion. At this point, and with this minimum speed, the gravitational force is the only force that causes the centripetal acceleration. Derived equation: `v=sqrt(gr)`.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.2.ii: Components of the static friction force and the normal force can contribute to the net force producing centripetal acceleration of an object traveling in a circle on a banked surface.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.2.iii: A component of tension contributes to the net force producing centripetal acceleration experienced by a conical pendulum.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.3: Tangential acceleration is the rate at which an object's speed changes and is directed tangent to the object's circular path.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.4: The net acceleration of an object moving in a circle is the vector sum of the centripetal acceleration and tangential acceleration.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.5: The revolution of an object traveling in a circular path at a constant speed (uniform circular motion) can be described using period and frequency.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.5.i: The time to complete one full circular path, one full rotation, or a full cycle of oscillatory motion is defined as period, `T`.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.5.ii: The rate at which an object is completing revolutions is defined as frequency, `f`. Relevant equation: `T=1/f`.
AP.P1AB.2.9.A.5.iii: For an object traveling at a constant speed in a circular path, the period is given by the derived equation `T=(2pir)/v`.
AP.P1AB.2.9.B: Describe circular orbits using Kepler's third law.
AP.P1AB.2.9.B.1: For a satellite in circular orbit around a central body, the satellite's centripetal acceleration is caused only by gravitational attraction. The period and radius of the circular orbit are related to the mass of the central body. Derived equation: `T^2=(4pi^2)/(GM)R^3`.
AP.P1AB.3.1.A: Describe the translational kinetic energy of an object in terms of the object's mass and velocity.
AP.P1AB.3.1.A.1: An object's translational kinetic energy is given by the equation `K=1/2mv^2`.
AP.P1AB.3.1.A.2: Translational kinetic energy is a scalar quantity.
AP.P1AB.3.1.A.3: Different observers may measure different values of the translational kinetic energy of an object, depending on the observer's frame of reference.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A: Describe the work done on an object or system by a given force or collection of forces.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.1: Work is the amount of energy transferred into or out of a system by a force exerted on that system over a distance.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.1.i: The work done by a conservative force exerted on a system is path-independent and only depends on the initial and final configurations of that system.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.1.ii: The work done by a conservative force on a system - or the change in the potential energy of the system - will be zero if the system returns to its initial configuration.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.1.iii: Potential energies are associated only with conservative forces.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.1.iv: The work done by a nonconservative force is path-dependent.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.1.v: Examples of nonconservative forces are friction and air resistance.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.2: Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.3: The amount of work done on a system by a constant force is related to the components of that force and the displacement of the point at which that force is exerted.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.3.i: Only the component of the force exerted on a system that is parallel to the displacement of the point of application of the force will change the system's total energy. Relevant equation: `W=F_(||)d=Fdcostheta`.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.3.ii: The component of the force exerted on a system perpendicular to the direction of the displacement of the system's center of mass can change the direction of the system's motion without changing the system's kinetic energy.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.4: The work-energy theorem states that the change in an object's kinetic energy is equal to the sum of the work (net work) being done by all forces exerted on the object. Relevant equation: `DeltaK=sum_iW_i=sum_iF_(||,i)d`.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.4.i: An external force may change the configuration of a system. The component of the external force parallel to the displacement times the displacement of the point of application of the force gives the change in kinetic energy of the system.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.4.ii: If the system's center of mass and the point of application of the force move the same distance when a force is exerted on a system, then the system may be modeled as an object, and only the system's kinetic energy can change.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.4.iii: The energy dissipated by friction is typically equated to the force of friction times the length of the path over which the force is exerted `DeltaE_text(mech)=F_fdcostheta`.
AP.P1AB.3.2.A.5: Work is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of `F_(||)` as a function of displacement.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A: Describe the potential energy of a system.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.1: A system composed of two or more objects has potential energy if the objects within that system only interact with each other through conservative forces.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.2: Potential energy is a scalar quantity associated with the position of objects within a system.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.3: The definition of zero potential energy for a given system is a decision made by the observer considering the situation to simplify or otherwise assist in analysis.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.4: The potential energy of common physical systems can be described using the physical properties of that system.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.4.i: The elastic potential energy of an ideal spring is given by the following equation, where `Deltax` is the distance the spring has been stretched or compressed from its equilibrium length. Relevant equation: `U_s=1/2k(Deltax)^2`.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.4.ii: The general form for the gravitational potential energy of a system consisting of two approximately spherical distributions of mass (e.g., moons, planets or stars) is given by the equation `U_g=-G(m_1m_2)/r`.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.4.iii: Because the gravitational field near the surface of a planet is nearly constant, the change in gravitational potential energy in a system consisting of an object with mass `m` and a planet with gravitational field of magnitude g when the object is near the surface of the planet may be approximated by the equation `DeltaU_g=mgDeltay`.
AP.P1AB.3.3.A.5: The total potential energy of a system containing more than two objects is the sum of the potential energy of each pair of objects within the system.
AP.P1AB.3.4.A: Describe the energies present in a system.
AP.P1AB.3.4.A.1: A system composed of only a single object can only have kinetic energy.
AP.P1AB.3.4.A.2: A system that contains objects that interact via conservative forces or that can change its shape reversibly may have both kinetic and potential energies.
AP.P1AB.3.4.B: Describe the behavior of a system using conservation of mechanical energy principles.
AP.P1AB.3.4.B.1: Mechanical energy is the sum of a system's kinetic and potential energies.
AP.P1AB.3.4.B.2: Any change to a type of energy within a system must be balanced by an equivalent change of other types of energies within the system or by a transfer of energy between the system and its surroundings.
AP.P1AB.3.4.B.3: A system may be selected so that the total energy of that system is constant.
AP.P1AB.3.4.B.4: If the total energy of a system changes, that change will be equivalent to the energy transferred into or out of the system.
AP.P1AB.3.4.C: Describe how the selection of a system determines whether the energy of that system changes.
AP.P1AB.3.4.C.1: Energy is conserved in all interactions.
AP.P1AB.3.4.C.2: If the work done on a selected system is zero and there are no nonconservative interactions within the system, the total mechanical energy of the system is constant.
AP.P1AB.3.4.C.3: If the work done on a selected system is nonzero, energy is transferred between the system and the environment.
AP.P1AB.3.5.A: Describe the transfer of energy into, out of, or within a system in terms of power.
AP.P1AB.3.5.A.1: Power is the rate at which energy changes with respect to time, either by transfer into or out of a system or by conversion from one type to another within a system.
AP.P1AB.3.5.A.2: Average power is the amount of energy being transferred or converted, divided by the time it took for that transfer or conversion to occur. Relevant equation: `P_text(avg)=(DeltaE)/(Deltat)`.
AP.P1AB.3.5.A.3: Because work is the change in energy of an object or system due to a force, average power is the total work done, divided by the time during which that work was done. Relevant equation: `P_text(avg)=W/(Deltat)`.
AP.P1AB.3.5.A.4: The instantaneous power delivered to an object by the component of a constant force parallel to the object's velocity can be described with the derived equation: `P_text(inst)=F_(||)v=Fvcostheta`.
AP.P1AB.4.1.A: Describe the linear momentum of an object or system.
AP.P1AB.4.1.A.1: Linear momentum is defined by the equation `vec(p)=mvec(v)`.
AP.P1AB.4.1.A.2: Momentum is a vector quantity and has the same direction as the velocity.
AP.P1AB.4.1.A.3: Momentum can be used to analyze collisions and explosions.
AP.P1AB.4.1.A.3.i: A collision is a model for an interaction where the forces exerted between the involved objects in the system are much larger than the net external force exerted on those objects during the interaction.
AP.P1AB.4.1.A.3.ii: As only the initial and final states of a collision are analyzed, the object model may be used to analyze collisions.
AP.P1AB.4.1.A.3.iii: An explosion is a model for an interaction in which forces internal to the system move objects within that system apart.
AP.P1AB.4.2.A: Describe the impulse delivered to an object or system.
AP.P1AB.4.2.A.1: The rate of change of momentum is equal to the net external force exerted on an object or system. Relevant equation: `vec(F)_text(net)=(Deltavec(p))/(Deltat)`.
AP.P1AB.4.2.A.2: Impulse is defined as the product of the average force exerted on a system and the time interval during which that force is exerted on the system. Relevant equation: `vec(J)=vec(F)_text(avg)Deltat`.
AP.P1AB.4.2.A.3: Impulse is a vector quantity and has the same direction as the net force exerted on the system.
AP.P1AB.4.2.A.4: The impulse delivered to a system by a net external force is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the net external force exerted on the system as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.4.2.A.5: The net external force exerted on a system is equal to the slope of a graph of the momentum of the system as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.4.2.B: Describe the relationship between the impulse exerted on an object or a system and the change in momentum of the object or system.
AP.P1AB.4.2.B.1: Change in momentum is the difference between a system's final momentum and its initial momentum. Relevant equation: `Deltavec(p)=vec(p)-vec(p)_0`.
AP.P1AB.4.2.B.2: The impulse-momentum theorem relates the impulse exerted on a system and the system's change in momentum. Relevant equation: `vec(J)=vec(F)_text(avg)Deltat=Deltavec(p)`.
AP.P1AB.4.2.B.3: Newton's second law of motion is a direct result of the impulse-momentum theorem applied to systems with constant mass. Relevant equation: `vec(F)_text(net)=(Deltavec(p))/(Deltat)=mv(Deltavec(v))/(Deltat)=mvec(a)`.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A: Describe the behavior of a system using conservation of linear momentum.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.1: A collection of objects with individual momenta can be described as one system with one center-of-mass velocity.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.1.i: For a collection of objects, the velocity of a system's center of mass can be calculated using the equation `vec(v)_text(cm)=(sumvec(p)_i)/(summ_i)=(summ_ivec(v)_i)/(summ_i)`.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.1.ii: The velocity of a system's center of mass is constant in the absence of a net external force.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.2: The total momentum of a system is the sum of the momenta of the system's constituent parts.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.3: In the absence of net external forces, any change to the momentum of an object within a system must be balanced by an equivalent and opposite change of momentum elsewhere within the system. Any change to the momentum of a system is due to a transfer of momentum between the system and its surroundings.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.3.i: The impulse exerted by one object on a second object is equal and opposite to the impulse exerted by the second object on the first. This is a direct result of Newton's third law.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.3.ii: A system may be selected so that the total momentum of that system is constant.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.3.iii: If the total momentum of a system changes, that change will be equivalent to the impulse exerted on the system. Relevant equation: `vec(J)=Deltavec(p)`.
AP.P1AB.4.3.A.4: Correct application of conservation of momentum can be used to determine the velocity of a system immediately before and immediately after collisions or explosions.
AP.P1AB.4.3.B: Describe how the selection of a system determines whether the momentum of that system changes.
AP.P1AB.4.3.B.1: Momentum is conserved in all interactions.
AP.P1AB.4.3.B.2: If the net external force on the selected system is zero, the total momentum of the system is constant.
AP.P1AB.4.3.B.3: If the net external force on the selected system is nonzero, momentum is transferred between the system and the environment.
AP.P1AB.4.4.A: Describe whether an interaction between objects is elastic or inelastic.
AP.P1AB.4.4.A.1: An elastic collision between objects is one in which the initial kinetic energy of the system is equal to the final kinetic energy of the system.
AP.P1AB.4.4.A.2: In an elastic collision, the final kinetic energies of each of the objects within the system may be different from their initial kinetic energies.
AP.P1AB.4.4.A.3: An inelastic collision between objects is one in which the total kinetic energy of the system decreases.
AP.P1AB.4.4.A.4: In an inelastic collision, some of the initial kinetic energy is not restored to kinetic energy but is transformed by nonconservative forces into other forms of energy.
AP.P1AB.4.4.A.5: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects stick together and move with the same velocity after the collision.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A: Describe the rotation of a system with respect to time using angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.1: Angular displacement is the measurement of the angle, in radians, through which a point on a rigid system rotates about a specified axis. Relevant equation: `Deltatheta=theta-theta_0`.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.1.i: A rigid system is one that holds its shape but in which different points on the system move in different directions during rotation. A rigid system cannot be modeled as an object.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.1.ii: One direction of angular displacement about an axis of rotation - clockwise or counterclockwise - is typically indicated as mathematically positive, with the other direction becoming mathematically negative.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.1.iii: If the rotation of a system about an axis may be well described using the motion of the system's center of mass, the system may be treated as a single object. For example, the rotation of `text(Earth)` about its axis may be considered negligible when considering the revolution of `text(Earth)` about the center of mass of the `text(Earth)`-Sun system.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.2: Average angular velocity is the average rate at which angular position changes with respect to time. Relevant equation: `omega_text(avg)=(Deltatheta)/(Deltat)`.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.3: Average angular acceleration is the average rate at which the angular velocity changes with respect to time. Relevant equation: `alpha_text(avg)=(Deltaomega)/(Deltat)`.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.4: Angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration around one axis are analogous to linear displacement, velocity, and acceleration in one dimension and demonstrate the same mathematical relationships.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.4.i: For constant angular acceleration, the mathematical relationships between angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration can be described with the following equations: `omega=omega_0+alphat`, `theta=theta_0+omega_0t+1/2alphat^2`, and `omega^2=omega_0^2+2alpha(theta-theta_0)`.
AP.P1AB.5.1.A.4.ii: Graphs of angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration as functions of time can be used to find the relationships between those quantities.
AP.P1AB.5.2.A: Describe the linear motion of a point on a rotating rigid system that corresponds to the rotational motion of that point, and vice versa.
AP.P1AB.5.2.A.1: For a point at a distance `r` from a fixed axis of rotation, the linear distance `s` traveled by the point as the system rotates through an angle `Deltatheta` is given by the equation `Deltas=rDeltatheta`.
AP.P1AB.5.2.A.2: Derived relationships of linear velocity and of the tangential component of acceleration to their respective angular quantities are given by the following equations: `s=rtheta`, `v=romega`, and `a_T=ralpha`.
AP.P1AB.5.2.A.3: For a rigid system, all points within that system have the same angular velocity and angular acceleration.
AP.P1AB.5.3.A: Identify the torques exerted on a rigid system.
AP.P1AB.5.3.A.1: Torque results only from the force component perpendicular to the position vector from the axis of rotation to the point of application of the force.
AP.P1AB.5.3.A.2: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the exerted force.
AP.P1AB.5.3.B: Describe the torques exerted on a rigid system.
AP.P1AB.5.3.B.1: Torques can be described using force diagrams.
AP.P1AB.5.3.B.1.i: Force diagrams are similar to free-body diagrams and are used to analyze the torques exerted on a rigid system.
AP.P1AB.5.3.B.1.ii: Similar to free-body diagrams, force diagrams represent the relative magnitude and direction of the forces exerted on a rigid system. Force diagrams also depict the location at which those forces are exerted relative to the axis of rotation.
AP.P1AB.5.3.B.2: The magnitude of the torque exerted on a rigid system by a force is described by the following equation, where `theta` is the angle between the force vector and the position vector from the axis of rotation to the point of application of the force: `tau=rF_(_|_)=rFsintheta`.
AP.P1AB.5.4.A: Describe the rotational inertia of a rigid system relative to a given axis of rotation.
AP.P1AB.5.4.A.1: Rotational inertia measures a rigid system's resistance to changes in rotation and is related to the mass of the system and the distribution of that mass relative to the axis of rotation.
AP.P1AB.5.4.A.2: The rotational inertia of an object rotating a perpendicular distance `r` from an axis is described by the equation: `I=mr^2`.
AP.P1AB.5.4.A.3: The total rotational inertia of a collection of objects about an axis is the sum of the rotational inertias of each object about that axis: `I_text(tot)=sumI_i=summ_ir_i^2`.
AP.P1AB.5.4.B: Describe the rotational inertia of a rigid system rotating about an axis that does not pass through the system's center of mass.
AP.P1AB.5.4.B.1: A rigid system's rotational inertia in a given plane is at a minimum when the rotational axis passes through the system's center of mass.
AP.P1AB.5.4.B.2: The parallel axis theorem uses the following equation to relate the rotational inertia of a rigid system about any axis that is parallel to an axis through its center of mass: `I'=I_text(cm)+Md^2`.
AP.P1AB.5.5: Rotational Equilibrium & Newton's First Law In Rotational Form
AP.P1AB.5.5.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's angular velocity remains constant.
AP.P1AB.5.5.A.1: A system may exhibit rotational equilibrium (constant angular velocity) without being in translational equilibrium, and vice versa.
AP.P1AB.5.5.A.1.i: Free-body and force diagrams describe the nature of the forces and torques exerted on an object or rigid system.
AP.P1AB.5.5.A.1.ii: Rotational equilibrium is a configuration of torques such that the net torque exerted on the system is zero. Relevant equation: `sumtau_i=0`.
AP.P1AB.5.5.A.1.iii: The rotational analog of Newton's first law is that a system will have a constant angular velocity only if the net torque exerted on the system is zero.
AP.P1AB.5.5.A.2: A rotational corollary to Newton's second law states that if the torques exerted on a rigid system are not balanced, the system's angular velocity must be changing.
AP.P1AB.5.6: Newton's Second Law In Rotational Form
AP.P1AB.5.6.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's angular velocity changes.
AP.P1AB.5.6.A.1: Angular velocity changes when the net torque exerted on the object or system is not equal to zero.
AP.P1AB.5.6.A.2: The rate at which the angular velocity of a rigid system changes is directly proportional to the net torque exerted on the rigid system and is in the same direction. The angular acceleration of the rigid system is inversely proportional to the rotational inertia of the rigid system. Relevant equation: `alpha_text(sys)=(sumtau)/I_text(sys)=tau_text(net)/I_text(sys)`.
AP.P1AB.5.6.A.3: To fully describe a rotating rigid system, linear and rotational analyses may need to be performed independently.
AP.P1AB.6.1.A: Describe the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid system in terms of the rotational inertia and angular velocity of that rigid system.
AP.P1AB.6.1.A.1: The rotational kinetic energy of an object or rigid system is related to the rotational inertia and angular velocity of the rigid system and is given by the equation: `K=1/2Iomega^2`.
AP.P1AB.6.1.A.1.i: The rotational inertia of an object about a fixed axis can be used to show that the rotational kinetic energy of that object is equivalent to its translational kinetic energy, which is its total kinetic energy.
AP.P1AB.6.1.A.1.ii: The total kinetic energy of a rigid system is the sum of its rotational kinetic energy due to its rotation about its center of mass and the translational kinetic energy due to the linear motion of its center of mass.
AP.P1AB.6.1.A.2: A rigid system can have rotational kinetic energy while its center of mass is at rest due to the individual points within the rigid system having linear speed and, therefore, kinetic energy.
AP.P1AB.6.1.A.3: Rotational kinetic energy is a scalar quantity.
AP.P1AB.6.2.A: Describe the work done on a rigid system by a given torque or collection of torques.
AP.P1AB.6.2.A.1: A torque can transfer energy into or out of an object or rigid system if the torque is exerted over an angular displacement.
AP.P1AB.6.2.A.2: The amount of work done on a rigid system by a torque is related to the magnitude of that torque and the angular displacement through which the rigid system rotates during the interval in which that torque is exerted. Relevant equation: `W=tauDeltatheta`.
AP.P1AB.6.2.A.3: Work done on a rigid system by a given torque can be found from the area under the curve of a graph of torque as a function of angular position.
AP.P1AB.6.3.A: Describe the angular momentum of an object or rigid system.
AP.P1AB.6.3.A.1: The magnitude of the angular momentum of a rigid system about a specific axis can be described with the equation: `L=Iomega`.
AP.P1AB.6.3.A.2: The magnitude of the angular momentum of an object about a given point is `L=rmvsintheta`.
AP.P1AB.6.3.A.2.i: The selection of the axis about which an object is considered to rotate influences the determination of the angular momentum of that object.
AP.P1AB.6.3.A.2.ii: The measured angular momentum of an object traveling in a straight line depends on the distance between the reference point and the object, the mass of the object, the speed of the object, and the angle between the radial distance and the velocity of the object.
AP.P1AB.6.3.B: Describe the angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system by a torque.
AP.P1AB.6.3.B.1: Angular impulse is defined as the product of the torque exerted on an object or rigid system and the time interval during which the torque is exerted. Relevant equation: `text(angular impulse)=tauDeltat`.
AP.P1AB.6.3.B.2: Angular impulse has the same direction as the torque exerted on the object or system.
AP.P1AB.6.3.B.3: The angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system by a torque can be found from the area under the curve of a graph of the torque as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.6.3.C: Relate the change in angular momentum of an object or rigid system to the angular impulse given to that object or rigid system.
AP.P1AB.6.3.C.1: The magnitude of the change in angular momentum can be described by comparing the magnitudes of the final and initial angular momenta of the object or rigid system: `DeltaL=L-L_0`.
AP.P1AB.6.3.C.2: A rotational form of the impulse-momentum theorem relates the angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system and the change in angular momentum of that object or rigid system.
AP.P1AB.6.3.C.2.i: The angular impulse exerted on an object or rigid system is equal to the change in angular momentum of that object or rigid system. Relevant equation: `DeltaL=tauDeltat`.
AP.P1AB.6.3.C.2.ii: The rotational form of the impulse- momentum theorem is a direct result of the rotational form of Newton's second law of motion for cases in which rotational inertia is constant: `tau_text(net)=(DeltaL)/(Deltat)=I(Deltaomega)/(Deltat)=Ialpha`.
AP.P1AB.6.3.C.3: The net torque exerted on an object is equal to the slope of the graph of the angular momentum of an object as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.6.3.C.4: The angular impulse delivered to an object is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the net external torque exerted on an object as a function of time.
AP.P1AB.6.4.A: Describe the behavior of a system using conservation of angular momentum.
AP.P1AB.6.4.A.1: The total angular momentum of a system about a rotational axis is the sum of the angular momenta of the system's constituent parts about that axis.
AP.P1AB.6.4.A.2: Any change to a system's angular momentum must be due to an interaction between the system and its surroundings.
AP.P1AB.6.4.A.2.i: The angular impulse exerted by one object or system on a second object or system is equal and opposite to the angular impulse exerted by the second object or system on the first. This is a direct result of Newton's third law.
AP.P1AB.6.4.A.2.ii: A system may be selected so that the total angular momentum of that system is constant.
AP.P1AB.6.4.A.2.iii: The angular speed of a nonrigid system may change without the angular momentum of the system changing if the system changes shape by moving mass closer to or further from the rotational axis.
AP.P1AB.6.4.A.2.iv: If the total angular momentum of a system changes, that change will be equivalent to the angular impulse exerted on the system.
AP.P1AB.6.4.B: Describe how the selection of a system determines whether the angular momentum of that system changes.
AP.P1AB.6.4.B.1: Angular momentum is conserved in all interactions.
AP.P1AB.6.4.B.2: If the net external torque exerted on a selected object or rigid system is zero, the total angular momentum of that system is constant.
AP.P1AB.6.4.B.3: If the net external torque exerted on a selected object or rigid system is nonzero, angular momentum is transferred between the system and the environment.
AP.P1AB.6.5.A: Describe the kinetic energy of a system that has translational and rotational motion.
AP.P1AB.6.5.A.1: The total kinetic energy of a system is the sum of the system's translational and rotational kinetic energies. Relevant equation:. `K_text(tot)=K_text(trans)+K_text(rot)`.
AP.P1AB.6.5.B: Describe the motion of a system that is rolling without slipping.
AP.P1AB.6.5.B.1: While rolling without slipping, the translational motion of a system's center of mass is related to the rotational motion of the system itself with the equations: `Deltax_text(cm)=rDeltatheta`, `v_text(cm)=romega`, and `a_text(cm)=ralpha`.
AP.P1AB.6.5.B.2: For ideal cases, rolling without slipping implies that the frictional force does not dissipate any energy from the rolling system.
AP.P1AB.6.5.C: Describe the motion of a system that is rolling while slipping.
AP.P1AB.6.5.C.1: When slipping, the motion of a system's center of mass and the system's rotational motion cannot be directly related.
AP.P1AB.6.5.C.2: When a rotating system is slipping relative to another surface, the point of application of the force of kinetic friction exerted on the system moves with respect to the surface, so the force of kinetic friction will dissipate energy from the system.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A: Describe the motions of a system consisting of two objects interacting only via gravitational forces.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.1: In a system consisting only of a massive central object and an orbiting satellite with mass that is negligible in comparison to the central object's mass, the motion of the central object itself is negligible.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.2: The motion of satellites in orbits is constrained by conservation laws.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.2.i: In circular orbits, the system's total mechanical energy, the system's gravitational potential energy, and the satellite's angular momentum and kinetic energy are constant.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.2.ii: In elliptical orbits, the system's total mechanical energy and the satellite's angular momentum are constant, but the system's gravitational potential energy and the satellite's kinetic energy can each change.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.2.iii: The gravitational potential energy of a system consisting of a satellite and a massive central object is defined to be zero when the satellite is an infinite distance from the central object. Relevant equation: `U_g=-G(m_1m_2)/r`.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.3: The escape velocity of a satellite is the satellite's velocity such that the mechanical energy of the satellite-central-object system is equal to zero.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.3.i: When the only force exerted on a satellite is gravity from a central object, a satellite that reaches escape velocity will move away from the central body until its speed reaches zero at an infinite distance from the central body.
AP.P1AB.6.6.A.3.ii: The escape velocity of a satellite from a central body of mass `M` can be derived using conservation of energy laws. Derived equation: `v_text(esc)=sqrt((2GM)/r)`.
AP.P1AB.7.1.A.1: Simple harmonic motion is a special case of periodic motion.
AP.P1AB.7.1.A.2: SHM results when the magnitude of the restoring force exerted on an object is proportional to that object's displacement from its equilibrium position. Derived equation: `ma_x=-kDeltax`.
AP.P1AB.7.1.A.2.i: A restoring force is a force that is exerted in a direction opposite to the object's displacement from an equilibrium position.
AP.P1AB.7.1.A.2.ii: An equilibrium position is a location at which the net force exerted on an object or system is zero.
AP.P1AB.7.1.A.2.iii: The motion of a pendulum with a small angular displacement can be modeled as simple harmonic motion because the restoring torque is proportional to the angular displacement.
AP.P1AB.7.2.A: Describe the frequency and period of an object exhibiting SHM.
AP.P1AB.7.2.A.1: The period of SHM is related to the frequency `f` of the object's motion by the following equation: `T=1/f`.
AP.P1AB.7.2.A.1.i: The period of an object-ideal-spring oscillator is given by the equation: `T_s=2pisqrt(m/k)`.
AP.P1AB.7.2.A.1.ii: The period of a simple pendulum displaced by a small angle is given by the equation: `T_p=2pisqrt(l/g)`.
AP.P1AB.7.3.A: Describe the displacement, velocity, and acceleration of an object exhibiting SHM.
AP.P1AB.7.3.A.1: For an object exhibiting SHM, the displacement of that object measured from its equilibrium position can be represented by the equations: `x=Acos(2pift)` or `x=Asin(2pift)`.
AP.P1AB.7.3.A.1.i: Minima, maxima, and zeros of displacement, velocity, and acceleration are features of harmonic motion.
AP.P1AB.7.3.A.1.ii: Recognizing the positions or times at which the displacement, velocity, and acceleration for SHM have extrema or zeros can help in qualitatively describing the behavior of the motion.
AP.P1AB.7.3.A.2: Changing the amplitude of a system exhibiting SHM will not change the period of that system.
AP.P1AB.7.3.A.3: Properties of SHM can be determined and analyzed using graphical representations.
AP.P1AB.7.4.A: Describe the mechanical energy of a system exhibiting SHM.
AP.P1AB.7.4.A.1: The total energy of a system exhibiting SHM is the sum of the system's kinetic and potential energies. Relevant equation: `E_text(total)=U+K`.
AP.P1AB.7.4.A.2: Conservation of energy indicates that the total energy of a system exhibiting SHM is constant.
AP.P1AB.7.4.A.3: The kinetic energy of a system exhibiting SHM is at a maximum when the system's potential energy is at a minimum.
AP.P1AB.7.4.A.4: The potential energy of a system exhibiting SHM is at a maximum when the system's kinetic energy is at a minimum.
AP.P1AB.7.4.A.4.i: The minimum kinetic energy of a system exhibiting SHM is zero.
AP.P1AB.7.4.A.4.ii: Changing the amplitude of a system exhibiting SHM will change the maximum potential energy of the system and, therefore, the total energy of the system. Relevant equation for a spring-object system: `E_text(total)=1/2kA^2`.
AP.P1AB.8.1.A: Describe the properties of a fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.1.A.1: Distinguishing properties of solids, liquids, and gases stem from the varying interactions between atoms and molecules.
AP.P1AB.8.1.A.2: A fluid is a substance that has no fixed shape.
AP.P1AB.8.1.A.3: Fluids can be characterized by their density. Density is defined as a ratio of mass to volume. Relevant equation: `rho=m/V`.
AP.P1AB.8.1.A.4: An ideal fluid is incompressible and has no viscosity.
AP.P1AB.8.2.A: Describe the pressure exerted on a surface by a given force.
AP.P1AB.8.2.A.1: Pressure is defined as the magnitude of the perpendicular force component exerted per unit area over a given surface area, as described by the equation: `P=F_(_|_)/A`.
AP.P1AB.8.2.A.3: The volume and density of a given amount of an incompressible fluid is constant regardless of the pressure exerted on that fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.2.B: Describe the pressure exerted by a fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.2.B.1: The pressure exerted by a fluid is the result of the entirety of the interactions between the fluid's constituent particles and the surface with which those particles interact.
AP.P1AB.8.2.B.2: The absolute pressure of a fluid at a given point is equal to the sum of a reference pressure `P_0`, such as the atmospheric pressure `P_text(atm)`, and the gauge pressure `P_text(gauge)`. Relevant equation: `P=P_0+rhogh`.
AP.P1AB.8.2.B.3: The gauge pressure of a vertical column of fluid is described by the equation: `P_text(gauge)=rhogh`.
AP.P1AB.8.3.A: Describe the conditions under which a fluid's velocity changes.
AP.P1AB.8.3.A.1: Newton's laws can be used to describe the motion of particles within a fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.3.A.2: The macroscopic behavior of a fluid is a result of the internal interactions between the fluid's constituent particles and external forces exerted on the fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.3.B: Describe the buoyant force exerted on an object interacting with a fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.3.B.1: The buoyant force is a net upward force exerted on an object by a fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.3.B.2: The buoyant force exerted on an object by a fluid is a result of the collective forces exerted on the object by the particles making up the fluid.
AP.P1AB.8.3.B.3: The magnitude of the buoyant force exerted on an object by a fluid is equivalent to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object. Relevant equation: `F_b=rhoVg`.
AP.P1AB.8.4.A: Describe the flow of an incompressible fluid through a cross-sectional area by using mass conservation.
AP.P1AB.8.4.A.1: A difference in pressure between two locations causes a fluid to flow.
AP.P1AB.8.4.A.1.i: The rate at which matter enters a fluid-filled tube open at both ends must equal the rate at which matter exits the tube.
AP.P1AB.8.4.A.1.ii: The rate at which matter flows into a location is proportional to the cross-sectional area of the flow and the speed at which the fluid flows. Derived equation: `V/t=Av`.
AP.P1AB.8.4.A.2: The continuity equation for fluid flow describes conservation of mass flow rate in incompressible fluids. Relevant equation: `A_1v_1=A_2v_2`.
AP.P1AB.8.4.B: Describe the flow of a fluid as a result of a difference in energy between two locations within the `text(fluid)-text(Earth)` system.
AP.P1AB.8.4.B.1: A difference in gravitational potential energies between two locations in a fluid will result in a difference in kinetic energy and pressure between those two locations that is described by conservation laws.
AP.P1AB.8.4.B.2: Bernoulli's equation describes the conservation of mechanical energy in fluid flow. Relevant equation: `P_1+rhogy_1+1/2rhov_1^2=P_2 +rhogy_2+1/2rhov_2^2`.
AP.P1AB.8.4.B.3: Torricelli's theorem relates the speed of a fluid exiting an opening to the difference in height between the opening and the top surface of the fluid and can be derived from conservation of energy principles. Derived equation: `v=sqrt(2gDeltay)`.
AP.P2AB.9.1.A: Describe the pressure a gas exerts on its container in terms of atomic motion within that gas.
AP.P2AB.9.1.A.1: Atoms in a gas collide with and exert forces on other atoms in the gas and with the container in which the gas is contained.
AP.P2AB.9.1.A.1.i: Collisions involving pairs of atoms or an atom and a fixed object can be described and analyzed using conservation of momentum principles.
AP.P2AB.9.1.A.1.ii: The pressure exerted by a gas on a surface is the ratio of the sum of the magnitudes of the perpendicular components of the forces exerted by the gas's atoms on the surface to the area of the surface. Relevant equation: `P=F_(_|_)/A`.
AP.P2AB.9.1.A.1.iii: Pressure exists throughout the gas itself, not just at the boundary between the gas and the container.
AP.P2AB.9.1.B: Describe the temperature of a system in terms of the atomic motion within that system.
AP.P2AB.9.1.B.1: The temperature of a system is characterized by the average kinetic energy of the atoms within that system.
AP.P2AB.9.1.B.1.i: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution provides a graphical representation of the energies and speeds of atoms at a given temperature.
AP.P2AB.9.1.B.1.ii: The root-mean-square speed corresponding to the average kinetic energy for an ideal gas is related to the temperature of the gas by `K_text(avg)=3/2k_BT=1/2mv_text(rms)^2`.
AP.P2AB.9.2.A: Describe the properties of an ideal gas.
AP.P2AB.9.2.A.1: The classical model of an ideal gas assumes that the instantaneous velocities of atoms are random, the volumes of the atoms are negligible compared to the total volume occupied by the gas, the atoms collide elastically, and the only appreciable forces on the atoms are those that occur during collisions.
AP.P2AB.9.2.A.2: An ideal gas is one in which the relationships between pressure, volume, the number of moles or number of atoms, and temperature of a gas can be modeled using the equation: `PV=nRT-Nk_BT`.
AP.P2AB.9.2.A.3: Graphs modeling the pressure, temperature, and volume of gases can be used to describe or determine properties of that gas.
AP.P2AB.9.2.A.4: A temperature at which an ideal gas has zero pressure can be extrapolated from a graph of pressure as a function of temperature.
AP.P2AB.9.3.A: Describe the transfer of energy between two systems in thermal contact due to temperature differences of those two systems.
AP.P2AB.9.3.A.1: Two systems are in thermal contact if the systems may transfer energy by thermal processes.
AP.P2AB.9.3.A.1.i: Heating is the transfer of energy into a system by thermal processes.
AP.P2AB.9.3.A.1.ii: Cooling is the transfer of energy out of a system by thermal processes.
AP.P2AB.9.3.A.2: The thermal processes by which energy may be transferred between systems at different temperatures are conduction, convection, and radiation.
AP.P2AB.9.3.A.3: Energy is transferred through thermal processes spontaneously from a higher-temperature system to a lower-temperature system.
