AP.PCEM.8.3.A.3.iii: Electric field line diagrams are simplified models of electric field maps and can be used to determine the relative magnitude and direction of the electric field at any position in the diagram.
AP.PCEM.8.3.B: Describe the electric field generated by charged conductors or insulators.
AP.PCEM.8.3.B.1: While in electrostatic equilibrium, the excess charge of a conductor is distributed on the surface of the conductor, and the electric field within the conductor is zero.
AP.PCEM.8.3.B.1.i: At the surface of a charged conductor, the electric field is perpendicular to the surface.
AP.PCEM.8.3.B.1.ii: The electric field outside an isolated sphere with spherically symmetric charge distribution is the same as the electric field due to a point charge with the same net charge as the sphere located at the center of the sphere.
AP.PCEM.8.3.B.2: While in electrostatic equilibrium, the excess charge of an insulator is distributed throughout the interior of the insulator as well as at the surface, and the electric field within the insulator may have a nonzero value.
AP.PCEM.8.4.A: Describe the electric field resulting from a given charge distribution.
AP.PCEM.8.4.A.1: Expressions for the electric field of specified charge distributions can be found using integration and the principle of superposition. Relevant equation: `vec(E)=1/(4piepsilon_0)int(dq)/r^2hat(r)`.
AP.PCEM.8.4.A.2: Symmetry considerations of certain charge distributions can simplify analysis of the electric field resulting from those charge distributions.
AP.PCEM.8.5.A: Describe the electric flux through an arbitrary area or geometric shape.
AP.PCEM.8.5.A.1: Flux describes the amount of a given quantity that passes through a given area.
AP.PCEM.8.5.A.2: For an electric field `vec(E)` that is constant across an area `vec(A)`, the electric flux through the area is defined as `Phi_E=vec(E)*vec(A)`.
AP.PCEM.8.5.A.2.i: The direction of the area vector is defined as perpendicular to the plane of the surface and outward from a closed surface.
AP.PCEM.8.5.A.2.ii: The sign of flux is given by the dot product of the electric field vector and the area vector.
AP.PCEM.8.5.A.3: The total electric flux passing through a surface is defined by the surface integral of the electric field over the surface. Relevant equation: `Phi_E=intvec(E)*dvec(A)`.
AP.PCEM.8.6.A: Describe the properties of a charge distribution by applying Gauss's law.
AP.PCEM.8.6.A.1: Gauss's law relates electric flux through a Gaussian surface to the charge enclosed by that surface. Relevant equations: `Phi_E=q_text(enc)/epsilon_0` and `ointvec(E)*dvec(A)=q_text(enc)/epsilon_0`.
AP.PCEM.8.6.A.2: A Gaussian surface is a three-dimensional, closed surface.
AP.PCEM.8.6.A.3: The total electric flux through a Gaussian surface is independent of the size of the Gaussian surface if the amount of enclosed charge remains constant.
AP.PCEM.8.6.A.4: Gaussian surfaces are typically constructed such that the electric field generated by the enclosed charge is either perpendicular or parallel to different regions of the Gaussian surface, resulting in a simplified surface integral.
AP.PCEM.8.6.A.5: If a function of charge density is given for a charge distribution, the total charge can be determined by integrating the charge density over the length (one dimension), area (two dimensions), or volume (three dimensions) of the charge distribution. For example: `Q_text(total)=intrho(vec(r))dV`.
AP.PCEM.8.6.A.6: Maxwell's equations are the collection of equations that fully describe electromagnetism. Gauss's law is Maxwell's first equation. Relevant equation: `ointvec(E)*dvec(A)=q_text(enc)/epsilon_0`.
AP.PCEM.9.1.A: Describe the electric potential energy of a system.
AP.PCEM.9.1.A.1: The electric potential energy of a system of two point charges equals the amount of work required for an external force to bring the point charges to their current positions from infinitely far away.
AP.PCEM.9.1.A.2: The general form for the electric potential energy between two charged objects is given by the equation: `U_E=1/(4piepsilon_0)(q_1q_2)/r=k(q_1q_2)/r`.
AP.PCEM.9.1.A.3: The total electric potential energy of a system can be determined by finding the sum of the electric potential energies of the individual interactions between each pair of charged objects in the system.
AP.PCEM.9.2.A: Describe the electric potential due to a configuration of charged objects.
AP.PCEM.9.2.A.1: Electric potential describes the electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in space.
AP.PCEM.9.2.A.2: Expressions for the electric potential of charge distributions can be found using integration and the principle of superposition. Relevant equation: `V=1/(4piepsilon_0)int(dq)/r`.
AP.PCEM.9.2.A.2.i: The electric potential for single point charge is `V=q/(4piepsilon_0r)`.
AP.PCEM.9.2.A.2.ii: The electric potential due to multiple point charges can be determined by the principle of scalar superposition of the electric potential due to each of the point charges. Relevant equation: `V=1/(4piepsilon_0)sum_iq_i/r_i`.
AP.PCEM.9.2.A.3: The electric potential difference between two points is the change in electric potential energy per unit charge when a test charge is moved between the two points. Relevant equation: `DeltaV=(DeltaU_E)/q`.
AP.PCEM.9.2.A.4: Electric potential difference may also result from chemical processes that cause positive and negative charges to separate, such as in a battery.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B: Describe the relationship between electric potential and electric field.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B.1: The value of an electric field component in any direction at a given location is equal to the negative of the spatial rate of change in electric potential at that location. Relevant equation: `E_x=-(dV)/(dx)`.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B.2: The change in electric potential between two points can be determined by integrating the dot product of the electric field and the displacement along the path connecting the points. Relevant equation: `DeltaV=V_b-V_a=-int_a^bvec(E)*dvec(r)`.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B.3: Electric field vector maps and equipotential lines are tools to describe the field produced by a charge or configuration of charges and can be used to predict the motion of charged objects in the field.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B.3.i: Equipotential lines represent lines of equal electric potential. These lines are also referred to as isolines of electric potential.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B.3.ii: Isolines are perpendicular to electric field vectors. An isoline map of electric potential can be constructed from an electric field vector map, and an electric field map may be constructed from an isoline map.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B.3.iii: An electric field vector points in the direction of decreasing potential.
AP.PCEM.9.2.B.3.iv: There is no component of an electric field along an isoline.
AP.PCEM.9.3.A: Describe changes in a system due to a difference in electric potential between two locations.
AP.PCEM.9.3.A.1: When a charged object moves between two locations with different electric potentials, the resulting change in the electric potential energy of the object-field system is given by the following equation. Relevant equation: `DeltaU_E=qDeltaV`.
AP.PCEM.9.3.A.2: The movement of a charged object between two points with different electric potentials results in a change in kinetic energy of the object consistent with the conservation of energy.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A: Describe the charge distribution within a conductor.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.1: An ideal conductor is a material in which electrons are able to move freely.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.2: When a conductor is in electrostatic equilibrium, mutual repulsion of excess charge carriers results in those charge carriers residing entirely on the surface of the conductor.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.2.i: In a conductor with a negative net charge, excess electrons reside on the surface of the conductor.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.2.ii: In a conductor with a positive net charge, the surface becomes deficient in electrons, and can be modeled as if positive charge carriers reside on the surface of the conductor.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.3: Excess charges will move to the surface of a conductor to create a state of electrostatic equilibrium within the conductor.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.3.i: The time interval over which charges reach electrostatic equilibrium within a conductor is so short as to be negligible.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.3.ii: When a conductor reaches electrostatic equilibrium, all points on the surface of the conductor have the same electric potential, and the conductor becomes an equipotential surface.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.3.iii: The charge density on the surface of a conductor will be greater where there are points or edges compared to planar areas.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.4: All excess charges reside on the surface of a conductor, which means there is no net charge in the interior of the conductor, and the electric field is zero within the conductor.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.5: The electric field is perpendicular to the outer surface of a conductor.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.6: A conductor can be polarized in the presence of an external electric field. This is a consequence of the conductor remaining an equipotential surface.
AP.PCEM.10.1.A.7: Electrostatic shielding is the process of surrounding an area with a closed, conducting shell to create a region inside the conductor that is free from external electric fields.
AP.PCEM.10.2.A: Describe the movement of charge and the resulting interactions when conductors physically contact each other.
AP.PCEM.10.2.A.1: When conductors are in electrical contact, charges will be redistributed such that the surfaces of each conductor are at the same electric potential.
AP.PCEM.10.2.A.2: Ground is an idealized reference point that has zero electric potential and can absorb or provide an infinite amount of charge without changing its electric potential.
AP.PCEM.10.2.A.3: Charge can be induced on a conductor by grounding the conductor in the presence of an external electric field.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A: Describe the physical properties of a parallel-plate capacitor.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.1: A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two separated parallel conducting surfaces that can hold equal amounts of charge with opposite signs.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.2: Capacitance relates the magnitude of the charge stored on each plate to the electric potential difference created by the separation of those charges. Relevant equation: `C=Q/(DeltaV)`.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.2.i: The capacitance of a capacitor depends only on the physical properties of the capacitor, such as the capacitor's shape and the material used to separate the plates.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.2.ii: The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is proportional to the area of one of its plates and inversely proportional to the distance between its plates. The constant of proportionality is the product of the dielectric constant, `kappa`, of the material between the plates and the electric permittivity of free space, `epsilon_0`. Relevant equation: `C=(kappaepsilon_0A)/d`.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.3: The electric field between two charged parallel plates with uniformly distributed electric charge, such as in a parallel-plate capacitor, is constant in both magnitude and direction, except near the edges of the plates.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.3.i: The magnitude of the electric field between two charged parallel plates, where the plate separation is much smaller than the dimensions of the plates, can be determined by applying Gauss's law and the principle of superposition. Derived equation: `E=Q/(epsilon_0A)`.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.3.ii: The electric field is proportional to the surface charge density on either plate of the capacitor.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.3.iii: A charged particle between two oppositely charged parallel plates undergoes constant acceleration, and therefore its motion shares characteristics with the projectile motion of an object with mass in the gravitational field near Earth's surface.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.4: The electric potential energy stored in a capacitor is equal to the work done by an external force to separate that amount of charge on the capacitor.
AP.PCEM.10.3.A.5: The electric potential energy stored in a capacitor is described by the equation: `U_C=1/2QDeltaV`.
AP.PCEM.10.4.A: Describe how a dielectric inserted between the plates of a capacitor changes the properties of the capacitor.
AP.PCEM.10.4.A.1: In a dielectric material, electric charges are not as free to move as they are in a conductor. Instead, the material becomes polarized in the presence of an external electric field.
AP.PCEM.10.4.A.2: The dielectric constant of a material relates the electric permittivity of that material to the permittivity of free space. Relevant equation: `kappa=epsilon/epsilon_0`.
AP.PCEM.10.4.A.3: The electric field created by a polarized dielectric is opposite in direction to the external field.
AP.PCEM.10.4.A.4: The electric field between the plates of an isolated parallel-plate capacitor decreases when a dielectric is placed between the plates. Derived equation: `kappa=E_0/E`.
AP.PCEM.10.4.A.5: The insertion of a dielectric into a capacitor may change the capacitance of the capacitor. Derived equation: `C=kappaC_0`.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A: Describe the movement of electric charges through a medium.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.1: Current is the rate at which charge passes through a cross-sectional area of a wire. Relevant equation: `I=(dq)/(dt)`.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.1.i: Current within a conductor consists of charge carriers traveling through the conductor with an average drift velocity. Relevant equation: `I=nqv_dA`.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.1.ii: Electric charge moves in a circuit in response to an electric potential difference, sometimes referred to as electromotive force, or emf (`varepsilon`).
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.1.iii: If the current is zero in a section of wire, the net motion of charge carriers in the wire is also zero, although individual charge carriers will not have zero speed.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.2: Current density is the flow of charge per unit area. Relevant equation: `I=intvec(J)*dvec(A)`.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.2.i: Current density is related to the motion of the charge carriers within a conductor. Relevant equation: `vec(J)=nqvec(v)_d`.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.2.ii: Current density is a vector quantity.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.2.iii: A potential difference across a conductor creates an electric field within the conductor that is proportional to the resistivity of the conductor and the current density. Relevant equation: `vec(E)=rhovec(J)`.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.3: If a function of current density is given, the total current can be determined by integrating the current density over the area. Derived equation: `I_text(tot)=intvec(J)(r)*dvec(A)`.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.4: Although current is a scalar quantity, it does have a direction. Because its direction is relative to the current carrier and not space, current does not obey the laws of vector addition and has no vector components.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.4.i: The direction of conventional current is chosen to be the direction in which positive charge would move.
AP.PCEM.11.1.A.4.ii: In common circuits, the current is actually due to the movement of electrons (negative charge carriers).
AP.PCEM.11.2.A: Describe the behavior of a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.1: A circuit is composed of electrical loops, which can include wires, batteries, resistors, lightbulbs, capacitors, inductors, switches, ammeters, and voltmeters.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.2: A closed electrical loop is a closed path through which charges may flow.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.2.i: A closed circuit is one in which charges would be able to flow.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.2.ii: An open circuit is one in which charges would not be able to flow.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.2.iii: A short circuit is one in which charges would be able to flow with no change in potential difference.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.3: A single circuit element may be part of multiple electrical loops.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.4: Circuit schematics are representations used to describe and analyze electric circuits.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.4.i: The properties of an electric circuit are dependent on the physical arrangement of its constituent elements.
AP.PCEM.11.2.A.4.ii: Circuit elements have common symbols that are used to create schematic diagrams. Variable elements are indicated by a diagonal strikethrough arrow across the standard symbol for that element.
AP.PCEM.11.3.A: Describe the resistance of an object using physical properties of that object.
AP.PCEM.11.3.A.1: Resistance is a measure of the degree to which an object opposes the movement of electric charge.
AP.PCEM.11.3.A.2: The resistance of a resistor with uniform geometry is proportional to its resistivity and length and is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area. Relevant equation: `R=(rhol)/A`.
AP.PCEM.11.3.A.2.i: Resistivity is a fundamental property of a material that depends on its atomic and molecular structure and quantifies how strongly the material opposes the motion of electric charge.
AP.PCEM.11.3.A.2.ii: The resistivity of a conductor typically increases with temperature.
AP.PCEM.11.3.A.2.iii: The total resistance of a resistor with uniform geometry, but that is made of a material whose resistivity varies along the length of the resistor, is given by `R=int(rho(l)dl)/A`.
AP.PCEM.11.3.B: Describe the electrical characteristics of elements of a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.3.B.1: Ohm's law relates current, resistance, and potential difference across a conductive element of a circuit. Relevant equation: `I=(DeltaV)/R`.
AP.PCEM.11.3.B.1.i: Materials that obey Ohm's law have constant resistance for all currents and are called ohmic materials.
AP.PCEM.11.3.B.1.ii: The resistivity of an ohmic material is constant regardless of temperature.
AP.PCEM.11.3.B.1.iii: Resistors can also convert electrical energy to thermal energy, which may change the temperature of both the resistor and the resistor's environment.
AP.PCEM.11.3.B.1.iv: The resistance of an ohmic circuit element can be determined from the slope of a graph of the current in the element as a function of the potential difference across the element.
AP.PCEM.11.4.A: Describe the transfer of energy into, out of, or within an electric circuit, in terms of power.
AP.PCEM.11.4.A.1: The rate at which energy is transferred, converted, or dissipated by a circuit element depends on the current in the element and the electric potential difference across it. Relevant equation: `P=IDeltaV`. Derived equation: `P=I^2R=(DeltaV^2)/R`.
AP.PCEM.11.4.A.2: The brightness of a lightbulb increases with power, so power can be used to qualitatively predict the brightness of lightbulbs in a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A: Describe the equivalent resistance of multiple resistors connected in a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A.1: Circuit elements may be connected in series and/or in parallel.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A.1.i: A series connection is one in which any charge passing through one circuit element must proceed through all elements in that connection and has no other path available. The current in each element in series must be the same.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A.1.ii: A parallel connection is one in which charges may pass through one of two or more paths. Across each path, the potential difference is the same.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A.2: A collection of resistors in a circuit may be analyzed as though it were a single resistor with an equivalent resistance `R_text(eq)`.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A.2.i: The equivalent resistance of a set of resistors in series is the sum of the individual resistances. Relevant equation: `R_text(eq,s)=sum_iR_i`.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A.2.ii: The inverse of the equivalent resistance of a set of resistors connected in parallel is equal to the sum of the inverses of the individual resistances. Relevant equation: `1/R_text(eq,p)=sum_i1/R_i`.
AP.PCEM.11.5.A.2.iii: When resistors are connected in parallel, the number of paths available to charges increases, and the equivalent resistance of the group of resistors decreases.
AP.PCEM.11.5.B: Describe a circuit with resistive wires and a battery with internal resistance.
AP.PCEM.11.5.B.1: Ideal batteries have negligible internal resistance. Ideal wires have negligible resistance.
AP.PCEM.11.5.B.1.i: The resistance of wires that are good conductors may normally be neglected, because their resistance is much smaller than that of other elements of a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.5.B.1.ii: The resistance of wires may only be neglected if the circuit contains other elements that do have resistance.
AP.PCEM.11.5.B.1.iii: The potential difference a battery would supply if it were ideal is the potential difference measured across the terminals when there is no current in the battery and is sometimes referred to as its emf (`varepsilon`).
AP.PCEM.11.5.B.2: The internal resistance of a nonideal battery may be treated as the resistance of a resistor in series with an ideal battery and the remainder of the circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.5.B.3: When there is current in a nonideal battery with internal resistance `r`, the potential difference across the terminals of the battery is reduced relative to the potential difference when there is no current in the battery. Derived equation: `DeltaV_text(terminal)=epsilon-Ir`.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C: Describe the measurement of current and potential difference in a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C.1: Ammeters are used to measure current at a specific point in a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C.1.i: Ammeters must be connected in series with the element in which current is being measured.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C.1.ii: Ideal ammeters have zero resistance so that they do not affect the current in the element that they are in series with.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C.2: Voltmeters are used to measure electric potential difference between two points in a circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C.2.i: Voltmeters must be connected in parallel with the element across which potential difference is being measured.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C.2.ii: Ideal voltmeters have infinite resistance so that no charge flows through them.
AP.PCEM.11.5.C.3: Nonideal ammeters and voltmeters will change the properties of the circuit being measured.
AP.PCEM.11.6.A: Describe a circuit or elements of a circuit by applying Kirchhoff's loop rule.
AP.PCEM.11.6.A.1: Energy changes in simple electrical circuits may be represented in terms of charges moving through electric potential differences within circuit elements. Relevant equation: `DeltaU_E=qDeltaV`.
AP.PCEM.11.6.A.2: Kirchhoff's loop rule is a consequence of the conservation of energy.
AP.PCEM.11.6.A.2.i: Kirchhoff's loop rule states that the sum of potential differences across all circuit elements in a single closed loop must equal zero. Relevant equation: `sumDeltaV=0`.
AP.PCEM.11.6.A.2.ii: The values of electric potential at points in a circuit can be represented by a graph of electric potential as a function of position within a loop.
AP.PCEM.11.7.A: Describe a circuit or elements of a circuit by applying Kirchhoff's junction rule.
AP.PCEM.11.7.A.1: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a consequence of the conservation of electric charge.
AP.PCEM.11.7.A.2: Kirchhoff's junction rule states that the total amount of charge entering a junction per unit time must equal the total amount of charge exiting that junction per unit time. Relevant equation: `sumI_text(in)=sumI_text(out)`.
AP.PCEM.11.8.A: Describe the equivalent capacitance of multiple capacitors.
AP.PCEM.11.8.A.1: A collection of capacitors in a circuit may be analyzed as though it was a single capacitor with an equivalent capacitance `C_text(eq)`.
AP.PCEM.11.8.A.1.i: The inverse of the equivalent capacitance of a set of capacitors connected in series is equal to the sum of the inverses of the individual capacitances. Relevant equation: `1/C_text(eq,s)=sum_i1/C_i`.
AP.PCEM.11.8.A.1.ii: The equivalent capacitance of a set of capacitors in series is less than the capacitance of the smallest capacitor.
AP.PCEM.11.8.A.1.iii: The equivalent capacitance of a set of capacitors in parallel is the sum of the individual capacitances. Relevant equation: `C_text(eq,p)=sum_iC_i`.
AP.PCEM.11.8.A.2: As a result of conservation of charge, each of the capacitors in series must have the same magnitude of charge on each plate.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B: Describe the behavior of a circuit containing combinations of resistors and capacitors.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.1: The charge on a capacitor or the current in a resistor in an RC circuit can be described by a fundamental differential equation derived from Kirchhoff's loop rule. Derived equation: `varepsilon=(dq)/(dt)R+q/C`.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.2: The time constant (`tau`) an RC circuit.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.2.i: The time constant of an RC circuit is a measure of how quickly the capacitor will charge or discharge and is defined as `tau=R_text(eq)C_text(eq)`.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.2.ii: For a charging capacitor, the time constant represents the time required for the capacitor's charge to increase from zero to approximately `63` `text(percent)` of its final asymptotic value.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.2.iii: For a discharging capacitor, the time constant represents the time required for the capacitor's charge to decrease from fully charged to approximately `37` `text(percent)` of its initial value.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3: The potential difference across a capacitor and the current in the branch of the circuit containing the capacitor each change over time as the capacitor charges and discharges, but both will reach a steady state after a long time interval.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3.i: Immediately after being placed in a circuit, an uncharged capacitor acts like a wire, and charge can easily flow to or from the plates of the capacitor.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3.ii: As a capacitor charges, changes to the potential difference across the capacitor affect the charge on the plates of the capacitor, the current in the circuit branch in which the capacitor is located, and the electric potential energy stored in the capacitor.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3.iii: The potential difference across a capacitor, the current in the circuit branch in which the capacitor is located, and the electric potential energy stored in the capacitor all change with respect to time and asymptotically approach steady state conditions.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3.iv: After a long time, a charging capacitor approaches a state of being fully charged, reaching a maximum potential difference at which there is zero current in the circuit branch in which the capacitor is located.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3.v: Immediately after a charged capacitor begins discharging, the amount of charge on the capacitor and the energy stored in the capacitor begin to decrease.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3.vi: As a capacitor discharges, the amount of charge on the capacitor, the potential difference across the capacitor, and the current in the circuit branch in which the capacitor is located all decrease until a steady state is reached.
AP.PCEM.11.8.B.3.vii: After either charging or discharging for times much greater than the time constant, the capacitor and the relevant circuit branch may be modeled using steady-state conditions.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A: Describe the properties of a magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A.1: A magnetic field is a vector field that can be used to determine the magnetic force exerted on moving electric charges, electric currents, or magnetic materials.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A.1.i: Magnetic fields can be produced by magnetic dipoles or combinations of dipoles, but never by monopoles.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A.1.ii: Magnetic dipoles have north and south polarity.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A.2: A magnetic field is a vector quantity and can be represented using vector field maps.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A.3: Magnetic field lines must form closed loops, as described by Gauss's law for magnetism.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A.3.i: Maxwell's equations are the collection of equations that fully describe electromagnetism. Gauss's law for magnetism is Maxwell's second equation. Relevant equation: `ointvec(B)*dvec(A)=0`.
AP.PCEM.12.1.A.3.ii: Magnetic fields in a bar magnet form closed loops, with the external magnetic field pointing away from one end (defined as the north pole) and returning to the other end (defined as the south pole).
AP.PCEM.12.1.B: Describe the magnetic behavior of a material as a result of the configuration of magnetic dipoles in the material.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.1: Magnetic dipoles result from the circular or rotational motion of electric charges. In magnetic materials, this can be the motion of electrons.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.1.i: Permanent magnetism and induced magnetism are system properties that both result from the alignment of magnetic dipoles within a system.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.1.ii: No magnetic north pole is ever found in isolation from a south pole. For example, if a bar magnet is broken in half, both halves are magnetic dipoles.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.1.iii: Magnetic poles of the same polarity will repel; magnetic poles of opposite polarity will attract.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.1.iv: The magnitude of the magnetic field from a magnetic dipole decreases with increasing distance from the dipole.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.2: A magnetic dipole, such as a magnetic compass, placed in a magnetic field will tend to align with the magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.3: A material's composition influences its magnetic behavior in the presence of an external magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.3.i: Ferromagnetic materials such as iron, nickel, and cobalt can be permanently magnetized by an external field that causes the alignment of magnetic domains or atomic magnetic dipoles.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.3.ii: Paramagnetic materials such as aluminum, titanium, and magnesium interact weakly with an external magnetic field, in that the magnetic dipoles of the material do not remain aligned after the external field is removed.
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.3.iii: All materials have the property of diamagnetism, in that their electronic structure creates a usually weak alignment of the dipole moments of the material
AP.PCEM.12.1.B.4: Earth's magnetic field may be approximated as a magnetic dipole.
AP.PCEM.12.1.C: Describe the magnetic permeability of a material.
AP.PCEM.12.1.C.1: Magnetic permeability is a measurement of the amount of magnetization in a material in response to an external magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.12.1.C.2: Free space has a constant value of magnetic permeability, known as the vacuum permeability `mu_0`, that appears in equations representing physical relationships.
AP.PCEM.12.1.C.3: The permeability of matter has values different from that of free space and arises from the matter's composition and arrangement. It is not a constant for a material and varies based on many factors, including temperature, orientation, and strength of the external field.
AP.PCEM.12.2.A: Describe the magnetic field produced by moving charged objects.
AP.PCEM.12.2.A.1: A single moving charged object produces a magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.12.2.A.1.i: The magnetic field at a particular point produced by a moving charged object depends on the object's velocity and the distance between the point and the object.
AP.PCEM.12.2.A.1.ii: At a point in space, the direction of the magnetic field produced by a moving charged object is perpendicular to both the velocity of the object and the position vector from the object to that point in space and can be determined using the right-hand rule.
AP.PCEM.12.2.A.1.iii: The magnitude of the magnetic field is a maximum when the velocity vector and the position vector from the object to that point in space are perpendicular.
AP.PCEM.12.2.B: Describe the force exerted on moving charged objects by a magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.12.2.B.1: A magnetic field will exert a force on a charged object moving within that field, with magnitude and direction that depend on the cross-product of the charge's velocity and the magnetic field. Relevant equation: `vec(F)_B=q(vec(v)xxvec(B))`.
AP.PCEM.12.2.B.2: In a region containing both a magnetic field and an electric field, a moving charged object will experience independent forces from each field.
AP.PCEM.12.2.B.3: The Hall effect describes the potential difference created in a conductor by an external magnetic field that has a component perpendicular to the direction of charges moving in the conductor.
AP.PCEM.12.3: Magnetic Fields Of Current-Carrying Wires & The Biot-Savart Law
AP.PCEM.12.3.A: Describe the magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire.
AP.PCEM.12.3.A.1: The Biot-Savart law defines the magnitude and direction of a magnetic field created by an electrical current.Relevant equation: `dvec(B)=mu_0/(4pi)(I(dvec(l)xxhat(r)))/r^2`.
AP.PCEM.12.3.A.2: The magnetic field vectors around a small segment of a current-carrying wire are tangent to concentric circles centered on that wire. The field has no component toward, away from, or parallel to the segment of the current-carrying wire.
AP.PCEM.12.3.A.3: The Biot-Savart law can be used to derive the magnitudes and directions of magnetic fields around segments of current-carrying wires, for example at the center of a circular loop of wire. Derived equation: `B_text(center of loop)=(mu_0I)/(2R)`.
AP.PCEM.12.3.B: Describe the force exerted on current-carrying wires by a magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.12.3.B.1: A magnetic field will exert a force on a current-carrying wire. Relevant equation: `vec(F)_B=intI(dvec(l)xxvec(B))`.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A: Use Ampère's law to describe the magnetic field created by a moving charge carrier.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A.1: Ampère's law relates the magnitude of the magnetic field to the current enclosed by a closed imaginary path called an Amperian loop. Relevant equation: `ointvec(B)*dvec(l)=mu_0I_text(enc)`.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A.1.i: Ampère's law can be used to determine the magnetic field near a long, straight current-carrying wire. Derived equation: `B_text(wire)=mu_0/(2pi)I/r`.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A.1.ii: Unless otherwise stated, all solenoids are assumed to be very long, with uniform magnetic fields inside the solenoids and negligible magnetic fields outside the solenoids.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A.1.iii: Ampère's law can be used to determine the magnetic field inside of a long solenoid. Derived equation: ` B_text(sol)=mu_0nI`.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A.2: An Amperian loop is a closed path around a current-carrying conductor.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A.3: The principle of superposition can be used to determine the net magnetic field at a point in space created by various combinations of current-carrying conductors, or conducting loops, segments, or cylinders.
AP.PCEM.12.4.A.4: Maxwell's equations are the collection of equations that fully describe electromagnetism. Maxwell's fourth equation is Ampère's law with Maxwell's addition; it states that magnetic fields can be generated by electric current (Ampère's law) and that a changing electric field creates a magnetic field, similar to the way a moving charge creates a magnetic field (Maxwell's addition). Relevant equations: `ointvec(B)*dvec(l)=mu_0I+mu_0epsilon_0(dPhi_E)/(dt)`.
AP.PCEM.13.1.A: Describe the magnetic flux through an arbitrary area or geometric shape.
AP.PCEM.13.1.A.1: For a magnetic field `vec(B)` that is constant across an area `vec(A)`, the magnetic flux through the area is defined as `Phi_B=vec(B)*vec(A)`.
AP.PCEM.13.1.A.1.i: The area vector is defined as perpendicular to the plane of the surface and outward from a closed surface.
AP.PCEM.13.1.A.1.ii: The sign of flux is given by the dot product of the magnetic field vector and the area vector.
AP.PCEM.13.1.A.2: The total magnetic flux passing through a surface is defined by the surface integral of the magnetic field over the surface area. Relevant equation: `Phi_B=intvec(B)*dvec(A)`.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A: Describe the induced electric potential difference resulting from a change in magnetic flux.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.1: Faraday's law describes the relationship between changing magnetic flux and the resulting induced emf in a system. Relevant equation: `epsilon=-(dPhi_B)/(dt)=-(d(vec(B)*vec(A)))/(dt)`.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.1.i: When the area of the surface being considered is constant, the induced emf is equal to the area multiplied by the rate of change in the component of the magnetic field perpendicular to the surface.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.1.ii: When the magnetic field is constant, the induced emf is equal to the magnetic field multiplied by the rate of change in area perpendicular to the magnetic field.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.1.iii: When an emf is induced in a long solenoid, the total induced emf is equal to the induced emf in a single loop multiplied by the number of loops in the solenoid. Relevant equation: `abs(epsilon_(sol))=Nabs((dPhi_B)/(dt))`.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.2: Lenz's law is used to determine the direction of an induced emf resulting from a changing magnetic flux.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.2.i: An induced emf generates a current that creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in magnetic flux.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.2.ii: The right-hand rule is used to determine the relationships between current, emf, and magnetic flux.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.3: Maxwell's equations are the collection of equations that fully describe electromagnetism. Maxwell's third equation is Faraday's law of induction, which describes the relationship between a changing magnetic flux and an induced electric field. Relevant equation: `epsilon=ointvec(E)*dvec(l)=-(dPhi_B)/(dt)`.
AP.PCEM.13.2.A.4: Maxwell's equations can be used to show that electric and magnetic fields obey wave equations and that electromagnetic waves travel at a constant speed in free space. Derived equation: `c=1/sqrt(epsilon_0mu_0)`.
AP.PCEM.13.3.A: Describe the force exerted on a conductor due to the interaction between an external magnetic field and an induced current within that conductor.
AP.PCEM.13.3.A.1: When an induced current is created in a conductive loop, the already-present magnetic field will exert a magnetic force on the moving charge carriers within the loop. Relevant equation: `vec(F)_B=int(dvec(l)xxvec(B))`.
AP.PCEM.13.3.A.2: When current is induced in a conducting loop, magnetic forces are only exerted on the segments of the loop that are within the external magnetic field. These magnetic forces may cause translational or rotational acceleration.
AP.PCEM.13.3.A.3: The force on a conducting loop is proportional to the induced current in the loop, which depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux, the resistance of the loop, and the velocity of the loop.
AP.PCEM.13.3.A.4: Newton's second law can be applied to a conducting loop moving in a magnetic field as it experiences an induced emf.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A: Describe the physical and electrical properties of an inductor.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.1: Inductance is the tendency of a conductor to oppose a change in electrical current.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.1.i: Inductance of a conductor depends on the physical properties of the conductor. Straight wires are typically modeled as having zero inductance.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.1.ii: An inductor, such as a solenoid, is a circuit element that has significant inductance.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.1.iii: The inductance of a solenoid is dependent on the total number of turns, the length of the solenoid, the cross-sectional area of the solenoid, and magnetic permeability of the solenoid's core. Relevant equation: `L_text(sol)=(mu_text(core)N^2A)/l`.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.2: Inductors store energy in the magnetic field that is generated by current in the inductor. Relevant equation: `U_L=1/2LI^2`.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.2.i: The energy stored in the magnetic field generated by an inductor in which current is flowing can be dissipated through a resistor or used to charge a capacitor.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.2.ii: The transfer of energy generated in an inductor to other forms of energy obeys conservation laws.
AP.PCEM.13.4.A.3: By applying Faraday's law to an inductor and using the definition of inductance, induced emf can be related to inductance and the rate of change of current. Relevant equation: `epsilon_i=-L(dI)/(dt)`.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A: Describe the physical and electrical properties of a circuit containing a combination of resistors and a single inductor.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.1: A resistor will dissipate energy that was stored in an inductor as the current changes.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.2: Kirchhoff's loop rule can be applied to a series LR circuit with a battery of emf `epsilon`, resulting in a differential equation that describes the current in the loop. Derived equation: `epsilon=IR+L(dI)/(dt)`.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.3: The time constant is a significant feature of the behavior of an LR circuit.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.3.i: The time constant of a circuit is a measure of how quickly an LR circuit will reach a steady state and is described with the equation: `tau=L/R_text(eq)`.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.3.ii: The time constant represents the time an LR circuit would take to reach a steady state if the system continued to change at the initial rate of change.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.3.iii: For an inductor that has zero initial current, the time constant represents the time required for the current in the inductor to reach approximately `63` `text(percent)` of its final asymptotic value.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.3.iv: For an inductor with an initial current, the time constant represents the time required for the current in the inductor to reach approximately `37` `text(percent)` of its initial value.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.4: The electric properties of inductors change during the time interval in which the current in the inductor changes, but will exhibit steady state behavior after a long time interval.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.4.i: When a switch is initially closed or opened in a circuit containing an inductor, the induced emf will be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the applied potential difference across the branch containing the inductor.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.4.ii: The potential difference across an inductor, the current in the inductor, and the energy stored in the inductor are exponential with respect to time and have asymptotes that are determined by the initial conditions of the circuit.
AP.PCEM.13.5.A.4.iii: After a time much greater than the time constant of the circuit, an inductor will behave as a conducting wire with zero resistance.
AP.PCEM.13.6.A: Describe the physical and electrical properties of a circuit containing a combination of capacitors and a single inductor.
AP.PCEM.13.6.A.1: In circuits containing only a charged capacitor and an inductor (LC circuits), the maximum current in the inductor can be determined using conservation of energy within the circuit.
AP.PCEM.13.6.A.2: In LC circuits, the time dependence of the charge stored in the capacitor can be modeled as simple harmonic motion. Derived equation: `(d^2q)/(dt^2)=-1/(LC)q`.
AP.PCEM.13.6.A.3: The angular frequency of an oscillating LC circuit can be derived from the differential equation that describes an LC circuit. Derived equation: `omega=1/sqrt(LC)`.
AP.PCM.1.1.A: Describe a scalar or vector quantity using magnitude and direction, as appropriate.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.1: Scalars are quantities described by magnitude only; vectors are quantities described by both magnitude and direction.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.2: Vectors can be visually modeled as arrows with appropriate direction and lengths proportional to their magnitude.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.3: Distance and speed are examples of scalar quantities, while position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration are examples of vector quantities.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.4: Vectors can be expressed in unit vector notation or as a magnitude and a direction.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.4.i: Unit vector notation can be used to represent vectors as the sum of their constituent components in the `x`-, `y`-, and `z`-directions, denoted by `hat(i)`, `hat(j)`, and `hat(k)`, respectively. Relevant equation: `vec(r)=(Ahat(i)+Bhat(j)+Chat(k))`.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.4.ii: The position vector of a point is given by `vec(r)`, and the unit vector in the direction of the position vector is denoted `hat(r)`.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.4.iii: A resultant vector is the vector sum of the addend vectors' components. Relevant equations: `vec(C)=vec(A)+vec(B)` and `vec(C)=(A_x+B_x)hat(i)+(A_y+B_y)hat(j)`.
AP.PCM.1.1.A.5: In a given one-dimensional coordinate system, opposite directions are denoted by opposite signs.
AP.PCM.1.2.A: Describe a change in an object's position.
AP.PCM.1.2.A.1: When using the object model, the size, shape, and internal configuration are ignored. The object may be treated as a single point with extensive properties such as mass and charge.
AP.PCM.1.2.A.2: Displacement is the change in an object's position. Relevant equation: `Deltax=x-x_0`.
AP.PCM.1.2.B: Describe the average velocity and acceleration of an object.
AP.PCM.1.2.B.1: Averages of velocity and acceleration are calculated considering the initial and final states of an object over an interval of time.
AP.PCM.1.2.B.2: Average velocity is the displacement of an object divided by the interval of time in which that displacement occurs: `vec(v)_text(avg)=(Deltavec(x))/(Deltat)`.
AP.PCM.1.2.B.3: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the interval of time in which that change in velocity occurs: `vec(a)_text(avg)=(Deltavec(v))/(Deltat)`.
AP.PCM.1.2.B.4: An object is accelerating if either the magnitude and/or direction of the object's velocity are changing.
AP.PCM.1.2.B.5: Calculating average velocity or average acceleration over a very small time interval yields a value that is very close to the instantaneous velocity or instantaneous acceleration.
AP.PCM.1.2.C: Describe the instantaneous position, velocity, and acceleration of an object as a function of time.
AP.PCM.1.2.C.1: As the time interval used to calculate the average value of a quantity approaches zero, the average value of that quantity approaches the value of the quantity at that instant, called the instantaneous value.
AP.PCM.1.2.C.1.i: Instantaneous velocity is the rate of change of the object's position, which is equal to the derivative of position with respect to time. Relevant equations: `vec(v)=(dvec(r))/(dt)` and `v_x=(dx)/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.1.2.C.1.ii: Instantaneous acceleration is the rate of change of the object's velocity, which is equal to the derivative of velocity with respect to time. Relevant equations: `vec(a)=(dvec(v))/(dt)` and `a_x=(dv_x)/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.1.2.C.2: Time-dependent functions and instantaneous values of position, velocity, and acceleration can be determined using differentiation and integration.
AP.PCM.1.3.A: Describe the position, velocity, and acceleration of an object using representations of that object's motion.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.1: Motion can be represented by motion diagrams, figures, graphs, equations, and narrative descriptions.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.2: For constant acceleration, three kinematic equations can be used to describe instantaneous linear motion in one dimension: `v_x=v_(x0)+a_xt`, `x=x_0+v_(x0)t+1/2at^2`, and `v_x^2=v_(x0)^2+2a_x(x-x_0)`.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.3: Near the surface of Earth, the vertical acceleration caused by the force of gravity is downward, constant, and has a measured value approximately equal to `a_g=g~~10` `text(m)//text(s)^2`.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.4: Graphs of position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time can be used to find the relationships between those quantities.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.4.i: An object's instantaneous velocity is the rate of change of the object's position, which is equal to the slope of a line tangent to a point on a graph of the object's position as a function of time. Relevant equation: `v_x=(dx)/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.4.ii: An object's instantaneous acceleration is the rate of change of the object's velocity, which is equal to the slope of a line tangent to a point on a graph of the object's velocity as a function of time. Relevant equation: `a_x=(dv_x)/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.4.iii: The displacement of an object during a time interval is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the object's velocity as a function of time (i.e., the area bounded by the function and the horizontal axis for the appropriate interval). Relevant equation: `Deltax=int_(t_1)^(t_2)v_x(t)dt`.
AP.PCM.1.3.A.4.iv: The change in velocity of an object during a time interval is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the acceleration of the object as a function of time. Relevant equation: `Deltav_x=int_(t_1)^(t_2)a_x(t)dt`.
AP.PCM.1.4.A: Describe the reference frame of a given observer.
AP.PCM.1.4.A.1: The choice of reference frame will determine the direction and magnitude of quantities measured by an observer in that reference frame.
AP.PCM.1.4.B: Describe the motion of objects as measured by observers in different inertial reference frames.
AP.PCM.1.4.B.1: Measurements from a given reference frame may be converted to measurements from another reference frame.
AP.PCM.1.4.B.2: The observed velocity of an object results from the combination of the object's velocity and the velocity of the observer's reference frame.
AP.PCM.1.4.B.2.i: Combining the motion of an object and the motion of an observer in a given reference frame involves the addition or subtraction of vectors.
AP.PCM.1.4.B.2.ii: The acceleration of any object is the same as measured from all inertial reference frames.
AP.PCM.1.5: Motion In Two Or Three Dimensions
AP.PCM.1.5.A: Describe the motion of an object moving in two or three dimensions.
AP.PCM.1.5.A.1: Motion in two or three dimensions can be analyzed using one-dimensional kinematic relationships if the motion is separated into components.
AP.PCM.1.5.A.2: Velocity and acceleration may be different in each dimension and may be nonuniform.
AP.PCM.1.5.A.3: Motion in one dimension may be changed without causing a change in a perpendicular dimension.
AP.PCM.1.5.A.4: Projectile motion is a special case of two-dimensional motion that has zero acceleration in one dimension and constant, nonzero acceleration in the second dimension.
AP.PCM.2.1.A: Describe the properties and interactions of a system.
AP.PCM.2.1.A.1: System properties are determined by the interactions between objects within the system.
AP.PCM.2.1.A.2: If the properties or interactions of the constituent objects within a system are not important in modeling the behavior of the macroscopic system, the system can itself be treated as a single object.
AP.PCM.2.1.A.3: Systems may allow interactions between constituent parts of the system and the environment, which may result in the transfer of energy or mass.
AP.PCM.2.1.A.4: Individual objects within a chosen system may behave differently from each other as well as from the system as a whole.
AP.PCM.2.1.A.5: The internal structure of a system affects the analysis of that system.
AP.PCM.2.1.A.6: As variables external to a system are changed, the system's substructure may change.
AP.PCM.2.1.B: Describe the location of a system's center of mass with respect to the system's constituent parts.
AP.PCM.2.1.B.1: For objects or systems with symmetrical mass distributions, the center of mass is located on lines of symmetry.
AP.PCM.2.1.B.2: The location of a system's center of mass along a given axis can be calculated using the equation: `vec(x)_text(cm)=(summ_ivec(x)_i)/(summ_i)`.
AP.PCM.2.1.B.3: For a nonuniform solid that can be considered as a collection of differential masses, `dm`, the solid's center of mass can be calculated using the equation: `vec(r)_text(cm)=(intvec(r)dm)/(intdm)`.
AP.PCM.2.1.B.3.i: The linear mass density of a rod or other linear rigid body is the derivative of the rod's mass with respect to the position of the differential mass element on the rigid body. Relevant equation: `lambda=d/(dl)m(l)`.
AP.PCM.2.1.B.3.ii: If a function of mass density is given for a solid, the total mass can be determined by integrating the mass density over the length (one dimension), area (two dimensions), or volume (three dimensions) of the solid. For example: `M_text(total)=intrho(r)dV`.
AP.PCM.2.1.B.4: A system can be modeled as a singular object that is located at the system's center of mass.
AP.PCM.2.2.A: Describe a force as an interaction between two objects or systems
AP.PCM.2.2.A.1: Forces are vector quantities that describe the interactions between objects or systems.
AP.PCM.2.2.A.1.i: A force exerted on an object or system is always due to the interaction of that object or system with another object or system.
AP.PCM.2.2.A.1.ii: An object or system cannot exert a net force on itself.
AP.PCM.2.2.A.2: Contact forces describe the interaction of an object or system touching another object or system and are macroscopic effects of interatomic electric forces.
AP.PCM.2.2.B: Describe the forces exerted on an object or system using a free-body diagram.
AP.PCM.2.2.B.1: Free-body diagrams are useful tools for visualizing forces being exerted on a single object or system and for determining the equations that represent a physical situation.
AP.PCM.2.2.B.2: The free-body diagram of an object or system shows each of the forces exerted on the object or system by the environment.
AP.PCM.2.2.B.3: Forces exerted on an object or system are represented as vectors originating from the representation of the center of mass, such as a dot. A system is treated as though all of its mass is located at the center of mass.
AP.PCM.2.2.B.4: A coordinate system with one axis parallel to the direction of acceleration of the object or system simplifies the translation from free-body diagram to algebraic representation. For example, in a free-body diagram of an object on an inclined plane, it is useful to set one axis parallel to the surface of the incline.
AP.PCM.2.3.A: Describe the interaction of two objects or systems using Newton's third law and a representation of paired forces exerted on each object or system.
AP.PCM.2.3.A.1: Newton's third law describes the interaction of two objects or systems in terms of the paired forces that each exerts on the other: `vec(F)_text(A on B)=-vec(F)_text(B on A)`.
AP.PCM.2.3.A.2: Interactions between objects within a system (internal forces) do not influence the motion of a system's center of mass.
AP.PCM.2.3.A.3: Tension is the macroscopic net result of forces that infinitesimal segments of a string, cable, chain, or similar system exert on each other in response to an external force.
AP.PCM.2.3.A.3.i: An ideal string has negligible mass and does not stretch when under tension.
AP.PCM.2.3.A.3.ii: The tension in an ideal string is the same at all points within the string.
AP.PCM.2.3.A.3.iii: In a string with nonnegligible mass, tension may not be the same at all points within the string.
AP.PCM.2.3.A.3.iv: An ideal pulley is a pulley that has negligible mass and rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction.
AP.PCM.2.4.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's velocity remains constant.
AP.PCM.2.4.A.1: The net force on a system is the vector sum of all forces exerted on the system.
AP.PCM.2.4.A.2: Translational equilibrium is the configuration of forces such that the net force exerted on a system is zero. Derived equation: `sumvec(F)_i=0`.
AP.PCM.2.4.A.3: Newton's first law states that if the net force exerted on a system is zero, the velocity of that system will remain constant.
AP.PCM.2.4.A.4: Forces may be balanced in one dimension but unbalanced in another. The system's velocity will change only in the direction of the unbalanced force.
AP.PCM.2.4.A.5: An inertial reference frame is one from which an observer would verify Newton's first law of motion.
AP.PCM.2.5.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's velocity changes.
AP.PCM.2.5.A.1: Unbalanced forces are a configuration of forces such that the net force exerted on a system is not equal to zero.
AP.PCM.2.5.A.2: Newton's second law of motion states that the acceleration of a system's center of mass has a magnitude proportional to the magnitude of the net force exerted on the system and is in the same direction as that net force. Relevant equation: `vec(a)_text(sys)=(sumvec(F))/m_text(sys)=vec(F)_text(net)/m_text(sys)`.
AP.PCM.2.5.A.3: The velocity of a system's center of mass will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system.
AP.PCM.2.6.A: Describe the gravitational interaction between two objects or systems with mass.
AP.PCM.2.6.A.1: Newton's law of universal gravitation describes the gravitational force between two objects or systems as directly proportional to each of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the systems' centers of mass. Relevant equation: `abs(vec(F)_g)=G(m_1m_2)/r^2`.
AP.PCM.2.6.A.1.ii: The gravitational force is always exerted along the line connecting the center of mass of the two interacting systems.
AP.PCM.2.6.A.1.iii: The gravitational force on a system can be considered to be exerted on the system's center of mass.
AP.PCM.2.6.A.2: A field models the effects of a noncontact force exerted on an object at various positions in space.
AP.PCM.2.6.A.2.i: The magnitude of the gravitational field created by a system of mass `M` at a point in space is equal to the ratio of the gravitational force exerted by the system on a test object of mass `m` to the mass of the test object. Derived equation: `abs(vec(g))=abs(vec(F)_g)/m=GM/r^2`.
AP.PCM.2.6.A.2.ii: If the gravitational force is the only force exerted on an object, the observed acceleration of the object (in `text(m)//text(s)^2`) is numerically equal to the magnitude of the gravitational field strength (in `text(N)//text(kg)`) at that location.
AP.PCM.2.6.A.3: The gravitational force exerted by an astronomical body on a relatively small nearby object is called weight. Derived equation: `text(Weight)=F_g=mg`
AP.PCM.2.6.B: Describe situations in which the gravitational force can be considered constant.
AP.PCM.2.6.B.1: If the gravitational force between two systems' centers of mass has a negligible change as the relative position of the two systems changes, the gravitational force can be considered constant at all points between the initial and final positions of the systems.
AP.PCM.2.6.B.2: Near the surface of Earth, the strength of the gravitational field is `g~~10` `text(N)//text(kg)`.
AP.PCM.2.6.C: Describe the conditions under which the magnitude of a system's apparent weight is different from the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on that system.
AP.PCM.2.6.C.1: The magnitude of the apparent weight of a system is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the system.
AP.PCM.2.6.C.2: If the system is accelerating, the apparent weight of the system is not equal to the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted on the system.
AP.PCM.2.6.C.3: A system appears weightless when there are no forces exerted on the system or when the force of gravity is the only force exerted on the system.
AP.PCM.2.6.C.4: The equivalence principle states that an observer in a noninertial reference frame is unable to distinguish between an object's apparent weight and the gravitational force exerted on the object by a gravitational field.
AP.PCM.2.6.D.1: Objects have inertial mass, or inertia, a property that determines how much an object's motion resists changes when interacting with another object.
AP.PCM.2.6.D.2: Gravitational mass is related to the force of attraction between two systems with mass.
AP.PCM.2.6.D.3: Inertial mass and gravitational mass have been experimentally verified to be equivalent.
AP.PCM.2.6.E: Describe the gravitational force exerted on an object by a uniform spherical distribution of mass.
AP.PCM.2.6.E.1: The net gravitational force exerted on an object by a uniform spherical distribution of mass is the sum of the individual forces from small differential masses that comprise the distribution.
AP.PCM.2.6.E.2: Newton's shell theorem describes the net gravitational force exerted on an object by a uniform spherical shell of mass.
AP.PCM.2.6.E.2.i: The net gravitational force exerted on an object inside a thin spherical shell is zero.
AP.PCM.2.6.E.2.ii: The net gravitational force exerted on an object outside a thin spherical shell can be determined by treating the shell as a single massive object located at the center of the shell.
AP.PCM.2.6.E.2.iii: An object inside a sphere of uniform density experiences a net gravitational force from only a partial mass of the sphere.
AP.PCM.2.6.E.2.iv: The partial mass of a sphere that contributes to the net gravitational force exerted on an object within that sphere is the portion of the sphere's mass located a distance less than or equal to the object's distance from the center of the sphere and can be calculated using the density of the sphere. Derived equation: `m_text(partial)=rho4/3pi(r_text(partial))^3`.
AP.PCM.2.6.E.3: The gravitational force exerted on an object within a uniform sphere can be shown to be proportional to the object's distance from the sphere's center. Derived equation: `F_text(g,partial)=-kr_text(partial)`.
AP.PCM.2.7.A: Describe kinetic friction between two surfaces.
AP.PCM.2.7.A.1: Kinetic friction occurs when two surfaces in contact move relative to each other.
AP.PCM.2.7.A.1.i: The kinetic friction force is exerted in a direction opposite the motion of each surface relative to the other surface.
AP.PCM.2.7.A.1.ii: The force of friction between two surfaces does not depend on the size of the surface area of contact.
AP.PCM.2.7.A.2: The magnitude of the kinetic friction force exerted on an object is the product of the normal force the surface exerts on the object and the coefficient of kinetic friction. Relevant equation: `abs(vec(F)_(f,k))=abs(mu_kvec(F)_N)`.
AP.PCM.2.7.A.2.i: The coefficient of kinetic friction depends on the material properties of the surfaces that are in contact.
AP.PCM.2.7.A.2.ii: Normal force is the perpendicular component of the force exerted on an object by the surface with which it is in contact; it is directed away from the surface.
AP.PCM.2.7.B: Describe static friction between two surfaces.
AP.PCM.2.7.B.1: Static friction may occur between the contacting surfaces of two objects that are not moving relative to each other.
AP.PCM.2.7.B.2: Static friction adopts the value and direction required to prevent an object from slipping or sliding on a surface. Relevant equation: `abs(vec(F)_(f,s))<=abs(mu_svec(F)_n)`.
AP.PCM.2.7.B.2.i: Slipping and sliding refer to situations in which two surfaces are moving relative to each other.
AP.PCM.2.7.B.2.ii: There exists a maximum value for which static friction will prevent an object from slipping on a given surface. Derived equation: `F_text(f,s,max)=mu_sF_N`.
AP.PCM.2.7.B.3: The coefficient of static friction is typically greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction for a given pair of surfaces.
AP.PCM.2.8.A: Describe the force exerted on an object by an ideal spring.
AP.PCM.2.8.A.1: An ideal spring has negligible mass and exerts a force that is proportional to the change in its length as measured from its relaxed length. A nonideal spring either has nonnegligible mass or exerts a force that is not proportional to the change in its length as measured from its relaxed length.
AP.PCM.2.8.A.2: The magnitude of the force exerted by an ideal spring on an object is given by Hooke's law: `vec(F)_s=-kDeltavec(x)`.
AP.PCM.2.8.A.3: The force exerted on an object by a spring is always directed toward the equilibrium position of the object-spring system.
AP.PCM.2.8.B: Describe the equivalent spring constant of a combination of springs exerting forces on an object.
AP.PCM.2.8.B.1: A collection of springs that exert forces on an object may behave as though they were a single spring with an equivalent spring constant `k_text(eq)`.
AP.PCM.2.8.B.1.i: The inverse of the equivalent spring constant of a set of springs in series is equal to the sum of the inverses of the individual spring constants. Derived equation: `1/k_text(eq,series)=sum1/k_i=1/k_1+1/k_2+...`.
AP.PCM.2.8.B.1.ii: The equivalent spring constant of a set of springs arranged in series is smaller than the smallest constituent spring constant.
AP.PCM.2.8.B.1.iii: The equivalent spring constant of a set of springs arranged in parallel is the sum of the individual spring constants. Derived equation: `k_text(eq,parallel)=sumk_i=k_1+k_2+...`.
AP.PCM.2.9.A: Describe the motion of an object subject to a resistive force.
AP.PCM.2.9.A.1: A resistive force is defined as a velocity-dependent force in the opposite direction of an object's velocity, for example: `vec(F)_r=-kvec(v)`
AP.PCM.2.9.A.2: Applying Newton's second law to an object upon which a resistive force is exerted results in a differential equation for velocity.
AP.PCM.2.9.A.2.i: Using the method of separation of variables, the velocity can be determined by integrating over the proper limits of integration.
AP.PCM.2.9.A.2.ii: The acceleration or position of a moving object that is subject to a velocity-dependent force may be determined using initial conditions of the object and methods of calculus, once a function for velocity is determined.
AP.PCM.2.9.A.2.iii: The position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time of an object under the influence of a resistive force of the form `vec(F)_r=-kvec(v)` are exponential and have asymptotes that are determined by the initial conditions of the object and the forces exerted on the object.
AP.PCM.2.9.A.3: Terminal velocity is defined as the maximum speed achieved by an object moving under the influence of a constant force and a resistive force that are exerted on the object in opposite directions. The terminal condition is reached when the net force exerted on the object is zero.
AP.PCM.2.10.A: Describe the motion of an object traveling in a circular path.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.1: Centripetal acceleration is the component of an object's acceleration directed toward the center of the object's circular path.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.1.i: The magnitude of centripetal acceleration for an object moving in a circular path is the ratio of the object's tangential speed squared to the radius of the circular path. Relevant equation: `a_c=v^2/r`.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.1.ii: Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the center of an object's circular path.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.2: Centripetal acceleration can result from a single force, more than one force, or components of forces that are exerted on an object in circular motion.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.2.i: At the top of a vertical, circular loop, an object requires a minimum speed to maintain circular motion. At this point, and with this minimum velocity, the gravitational force is the only force that causes the centripetal acceleration. Derived equation: `v=sqrt(gr)`.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.2.ii: Components of the static friction force and the normal force can contribute to the net force producing centripetal acceleration of an object traveling in a circle on a banked surface.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.2.iii: A component of tension contributes to the net force producing centripetal acceleration experienced by a conical pendulum.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.3: Tangential acceleration is the rate at which an object's speed changes and is directed tangent to the object's circular path.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.4: The net acceleration of an object moving in a circle is the vector sum of the centripetal acceleration and tangential acceleration.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.5: The revolution of an object traveling in a circular path at a constant speed (uniform circular motion) can be described using period and frequency.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.5.i: The time to complete one full circular path, one full rotation, or a full cycle of oscillatory motion is defined as period, `T`.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.5.ii: The rate at which an object is completing revolutions is defined as frequency, `f`. Relevant equation: `T=1/f`.
AP.PCM.2.10.A.5.iii: For an object traveling at a constant speed in a circular path, the period is given by the derived equation: `T=(2pir)/v`.
AP.PCM.2.10.B: Describe circular orbits using Kepler's third law.
AP.PCM.2.10.B.1: For a satellite in circular orbit around a central body, the satellite's centripetal acceleration is caused only by gravitational attraction. The period and radius of the circular orbit are related to the mass of the central body. Derived equation: `T^2=(4pi^2)/(GM) R^3`.
AP.PCM.3.1.A: Describe the translational kinetic energy of an object in terms of the object's mass and velocity.
AP.PCM.3.1.A.1: An object's translational kinetic energy is given by the equation: `K=1/2mv^2`.
AP.PCM.3.1.A.2: Translational kinetic energy is a scalar quantity.
AP.PCM.3.1.A.3: Different observers may measure different values of the translational kinetic energy of an object, depending on the observer's frame of reference.
AP.PCM.3.2.A: Describe the work done on an object or system by a given force or collection of forces.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.1: Work is the amount of energy transferred into or out of a system by a force exerted on that system over a distance.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.1.i: The work done by a conservative force exerted on a system is path-independent and only depends on the initial and final configurations of that system.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.1.ii: The work done by a conservative force on a system - or the change in the potential energy of the system - will be zero if the system returns to its initial configuration.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.1.iii: Potential energies are associated only with conservative forces.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.1.iv: The work done by a nonconservative force is path-dependent.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.1.v: The most common nonconservative forces are friction and air resistance.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.2: Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.3: The work done on an object by a variable force is calculated using `W=int_a^bvec(F)(r)*dvec(r)`, where the integral is taken over the path from point `a` to point `b`.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.3.i: The dot product between two vectors, `vec(A)` and `vec(B`, results in a scalar quantity of magnitude `vec(A)*vec(B)=ABcostheta`.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.3.ii: Only the component of the force exerted on a system that is parallel to the displacement of the point of application of the force will change the system's total energy.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.3.iii: If the component of the force exerted on a system that is parallel to the displacement is constant, the work done on the system by the force is given by the derived equation `W=F_(||)d=Fdcostheta`.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.3.iv: The component of the force exerted on a system perpendicular to the direction of the displacement of the system's center of mass can change the direction of the system's motion without changing the system's kinetic energy.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.4: The work-energy theorem states that the change in an object's kinetic energy is equal to the sum of the work (net work) being done by all forces exerted on the object. Relevant equation: `DeltaK=sumW_i=sumF_(||,i)d_i`.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.4.i: An external force may change the configuration of a system. The component of the external force parallel to the displacement times the displacement of the point of application of the force gives the change in kinetic energy of the system.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.4.ii: If the system's center of mass and the point of application of the force move the same distance when a force is exerted on a system, then the system may be modeled as an object, and only the system's kinetic energy can change.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.4.iii: The energy dissipated by friction is typically equated to the force of friction times the length of the path over which the force is exerted: `DeltaE_text(mech)=F_fdcostheta`.
AP.PCM.3.2.A.5: Work is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of `F_(||)` as a function of displacement.
AP.PCM.3.3.A: Describe the potential energy of a system.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.1: A system composed of two or more objects has potential energy if the objects within that system only interact with each other through conservative forces.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.2: Potential energy is a scalar quantity associated with the position of objects within a system.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.3: The definition of zero potential energy for a given system is a decision made by the observer considering the situation to simplify or otherwise assist in analysis.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.4: The relationship between conservative forces exerted on a system and the system's potential energy is `DeltaU=-int_a^bvec(F)_(cf)(r)*dvec(r)`.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.5: The conservative forces exerted on a system in a single dimension can be determined using the slope of the system's potential energy with respect to position in that dimension; these forces point in the direction of decreasing potential energy. Relevant equation: `F_x=-(dU(x))/(dx)`.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.6: Graphs of a system's potential energy as a function of its position can be useful in determining physical properties of that system.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.6.i: Stable equilibrium is a location at which a small displacement in an object's position results in a force exerted on the object opposite to the direction of the small displacement, accelerating the object back toward the equilibrium position.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.6.ii: Unstable equilibrium is a location at which a small displacement in an object's position results in a force exerted on the object in the same direction as the small displacement, accelerating the object away from the equilibrium position.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.6.iii: In a given dimension, stable equilibrium positions exist at locations where the potential energy as a function of position in that dimension has a local minimum.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.6.iv: In a given dimension, unstable equilibrium positions occur at locations where the potential energy as a function of position in that dimension has a local maximum.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.7: The potential energy of common physical systems can be described using the physical properties of that system.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.7.i: The elastic potential energy of an ideal spring is given by the following equation, where `Deltax` is the distance the spring has been stretched or compressed from its equilibrium length. Relevant equation: `U_s=1/2k(Deltax)^2`.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.7.ii: The general form for the gravitational potential energy of a system consisting of two approximately spherical distributions of mass (e.g., moons, planets, or stars) is given by the equation: `U_g=- G(m_1m_2)/r`.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.7.iii: Because the gravitational field near the surface of a planet is nearly constant, the change in gravitational potential energy in a system consisting of an object with mass `m` and a planet with gravitational field of magnitude g when the object is near the surface of the planet may be approximated by the equation: `DeltaU_g=mgDeltay`.
AP.PCM.3.3.A.8: The total potential energy of a system containing more than two objects is the sum of the potential energy of each pair of objects within the system.
AP.PCM.3.4.A: Describe the energies present in a system.
AP.PCM.3.4.A.1: A system composed of only a single object can only have kinetic energy.
AP.PCM.3.4.A.2: A system that contains objects that interact via conservative forces or that can change its shape reversibly may have both kinetic and potential energies.
AP.PCM.3.4.B: Describe the behavior of a system using conservation of mechanical energy principles.
AP.PCM.3.4.B.1: Mechanical energy is the sum of a system's kinetic and potential energies.
AP.PCM.3.4.B.2: Any change to a type of energy within a system must be balanced by an equivalent change of other types of energies within the system or by a transfer of energy between the system and its surroundings.
AP.PCM.3.4.B.3: A system may be selected so that the total energy of that system is constant.
AP.PCM.3.4.B.4: If the total energy of a system changes, that change will be equivalent to the energy transferred into or out of the system.
AP.PCM.3.4.C: Describe how the selection of a system determines whether the energy of that system changes.
AP.PCM.3.4.C.1: Energy is conserved in all interactions.
AP.PCM.3.4.C.2: If the work done on a selected system is zero and there are no nonconservative interactions within the system, the total mechanical energy of the system is constant.
AP.PCM.3.4.C.3: If the work done on a selected system is nonzero, energy is transferred between the system and the environment.
AP.PCM.3.5.A: Describe the transfer of energy into, out of, or within a system in terms of power.
AP.PCM.3.5.A.1: Power is the rate at which energy changes with respect to time, either by transfer into or out of a system or by conversion from one type to another within a system.
AP.PCM.3.5.A.2: Average power is the amount of energy being transferred or converted, divided by the time it took for that transfer or conversion to occur. Relevant equation: `P_text(avg)=(DeltaE)/(Deltat)`.
AP.PCM.3.5.A.3: Because work is the change in energy of an object or system due to a force, average power is the total work done, divided by the time during which that work was done. Relevant equation: `P_text(avg)=(W)/(Deltat)`.
AP.PCM.3.5.A.4: The instantaneous power delivered to an object by a force is given by the equation: `P_text(inst)=(dW)/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.3.5.A.5: The instantaneous power delivered to an object by the component of a constant force parallel to the object's velocity can be described with the derived equation: `P_text(inst)=F_(||)v=Fvcostheta`.
AP.PCM.4.1.A: Describe the linear momentum of an object or system.
AP.PCM.4.1.A.1: Linear momentum is defined by the equation: `vec(p)=mvec(v)`.
AP.PCM.4.1.A.2: Momentum is a vector quantity and has the same direction as the velocity.
AP.PCM.4.1.A.3: Momentum can be used to analyze collisions and explosions.
AP.PCM.4.1.A.3.i: A collision is a model for an interaction where the forces exerted between the involved objects in the system are much larger than the net external force exerted on those objects during the interaction.
AP.PCM.4.1.A.3.ii: As only the initial and final states of a collision are analyzed, the object model may be used to analyze collisions.
AP.PCM.4.1.A.3.iii: An explosion is a model for an interaction in which forces internal to the system move objects within that system apart.
AP.PCM.4.2.A: Describe the impulse delivered to an object or system.
AP.PCM.4.2.A.1: The rate of change of a system's momentum is equal to the net external force exerted on that system. Relevant equation: `vec(F)_text(net)=(dvec(p))/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.4.2.A.2: Impulse is defined as the integral of a force exerted on an object or system over a time interval. Relevant equation: `vec(J)=int_(t_1)^(t_2)vec(F)_text(net)(t)dt`.
AP.PCM.4.2.A.3: Impulse is a vector quantity and has the same direction as the net force exerted on the system.
AP.PCM.4.2.A.4: The impulse delivered to a system by a net external force is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the net external force exerted on the system as a function of time.
AP.PCM.4.2..5: The net external force exerted on a system is equal to the slope of a graph of the momentum of the system as a function of time.
AP.PCM.4.2.B: Describe the relationship between the impulse exerted on an object or system and the change in momentum of the object or system.
AP.PCM.4.2.B.1: Change in momentum is the difference between a system's final momentum and its initial momentum. Relevant equation: `Deltavec(p)=vec(p)-vec(p)_0`.
AP.PCM.4.2.B.2: The impulse-momentum theorem relates the impulse delivered to an object and the object's change in momentum.
AP.PCM.4.2.B.2.i: The impulse exerted on an object is equal to the object's change in momentum. Relevant equation: `vec(J)=int_(t_1)^(t_2)vec(F)_text(net)(t)dt=Deltavec(p)`.
AP.PCM.4.2.B.2.ii: Newton's second law of motion is a direct result of the impulse-momentum theorem applied to systems with constant mass: `vec(F)_text(net)=(dvec(p))/(dt)=m(dvec(v))/(dt)=mvec(a)`.
AP.PCM.4.2.B.2.iii: The impulse-momentum theorem also describes the behavior of a system in which the velocity is constant but the mass changes with respect to time: `vec(F)_text(net)=(dvec(p))/(dt)=(dm)/(dt)vec(v)`.
AP.PCM.4.3.A: Describe the behavior of a system using conservation of linear momentum.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.1: A collection of objects with individual momenta can be described as one system with one center-of-mass velocity.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.1.i: For a collection of objects, the velocity of a system's center of mass can be calculated using the equation: `vec(v)_text(cm)=(sumvec(p)_i)/(summ_i)=(sum(m_ivec(v)_i))/(summ_i)`.
