AP.PCM.4.3.A.1.ii: The velocity of a system's center of mass is constant in the absence of a net external force.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.2: The total momentum of a system is the sum of the momenta of the system's constituent parts.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.3: In the absence of net external forces, any change to the momentum of an object within a system must be balanced by an equivalent and opposite change of momentum elsewhere within the system. Any change to the momentum of a system is due to a transfer of momentum between the system and its surroundings.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.3.i: The impulse exerted by one object on a second object is equal and opposite to the impulse exerted by the second object on the first. This is a direct result of Newton's third law.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.3.ii: A system may be selected so that the total momentum of that system is constant.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.3.iii: If the total momentum of a system changes, that change will be equivalent to the impulse exerted on the system. Relevant equation: `vec(J)=Deltavec(p)`.
AP.PCM.4.3.A.4: Correct application of conservation of momentum can be used to determine the velocity of a system immediately before and immediately after collisions or explosions.
AP.PCM.4.3.B: Describe how the selection of a system determines whether the momentum of that system changes.
AP.PCM.4.3.B.1: Momentum is conserved in all interactions.
AP.PCM.4.3.B.2: If the net external force on the selected system is zero, the total momentum of the system is constant.
AP.PCM.4.3.B.3: If the net external force on the selected system is nonzero, momentum is transferred between the system and the environment.
AP.PCM.4.4.A: Describe whether an interaction between objects is elastic or inelastic.
AP.PCM.4.4.A.1: An elastic collision between objects is one in which the initial kinetic energy of the system is equal to the final kinetic energy of the system.
AP.PCM.4.4.A.2: In an elastic collision, the final kinetic energies of each of the objects within the system may be different from their initial kinetic energies.
AP.PCM.4.4.A.3: An inelastic collision between objects is one in which the total kinetic energy of the system decreases.
AP.PCM.4.4.A.4: In an inelastic collision, some of the initial kinetic energy is not restored to kinetic energy but is transformed by nonconservative forces into other forms of energy.
AP.PCM.4.4.A.5: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects stick together and move with the same velocity after the collision.
AP.PCM.5.1.A: Describe the rotation of a system with respect to time using angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.1: Angular displacement is the measurement of the angle, in radians, through which a point on a rigid system rotates about a specified axis. Relevant equation: `Deltatheta=theta-theta_0`.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.1.i: A rigid system is one that holds its shape but in which different points on the system move in different directions during rotation. A rigid system cannot be modeled as an object.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.1.ii: One direction of angular displacement about an axis of rotation - clockwise or counterclockwise - is typically indicated as mathematically positive, with the other direction becoming mathematically negative.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.1.iii: If the rotation of a system about an axis may be well described using the motion of the system's center of mass, the system may be treated as a single object. For example, the rotation of Earth about its axis may be considered negligible when considering the revolution of Earth about the center of mass of the Earth-Sun system.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.2: Angular velocity is the rate at which angular position changes with respect to time. Relevant equation: `omega=(d theta)/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.3: Angular acceleration is the rate at which angular velocity changes with respect to time. Relevant equation: `alpha=(domega)/(dt)`.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.4: Angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration around one axis are analogous to linear displacement, velocity, and acceleration in one dimension and demonstrate the same mathematical relationships.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.4.i: For constant angular acceleration, the mathematical relationships between angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration can be described with the following equations: `omega=omega_0+alphat`, `theta=theta_0+omega_0t+1/2alphat^2`, and `omega^2=omega_0^2+2alpha(theta-theta_0)`.
AP.PCM.5.1.A.4.ii: Graphs of angular displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration as functions of time can be used to find the relationships between those quantities.
AP.PCM.5.2.A: Describe the linear motion of a point on a rotating rigid system that corresponds to the rotational motion of that point, and vice versa.
AP.PCM.5.2.A.1: For a point at a distance `r` from a fixed axis of rotation, the linear distance s traveled by the point as the system rotates through an angle `Deltatheta` is given by the equation: `Deltas=rDeltatheta`.
AP.PCM.5.2.A.2: Derived relationships of linear velocity and of the tangential component of acceleration to their respective angular quantities are given by the following equations: `s=rtheta`, `v=romega`, and `a_T=ralpha`.
AP.PCM.5.2.A.3: For a rigid system, all points within that system have the same angular velocity and angular acceleration.
AP.PCM.5.3.A: Identify the torques exerted on a rigid system.
AP.PCM.5.3.A.1: Torque results only from the force component perpendicular to the position vector from the axis of rotation to the point of application of the force.
AP.PCM.5.3.A.2: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the exerted force.
AP.PCM.5.3.B: Describe the torques exerted on a rigid system.
AP.PCM.5.3.B.1: Torques can be described using force diagrams.
AP.PCM.5.3.B.1.i: Force diagrams are similar to free-body diagrams and are used to analyze the torques exerted on a rigid system.
AP.PCM.5.3.B.1.ii: Similar to free-body diagrams, force diagrams represent the relative magnitude and direction of the forces exerted on a rigid system. Force diagrams also depict the location at which those forces are exerted relative to the axis of rotation.
AP.PCM.5.3.B.2: The torque exerted on a rigid system about a chosen pivot point by a given force is described by `vec(tau)=vec(r)xxvec(F)`.
AP.PCM.5.3.B.2.i: The cross-product between two vectors, `vec(A)` and `vec(B)`, results in a vector quantity of magnitude `vec(A)xxvec(B)=ABsintheta`.
AP.PCM.5.3.B.2.ii: The direction of the vector resulting from the cross-product of vectors `vec(A)` and `vec(B)` is perpendicular to both vectors `vec(A)` and `vec(B)` and therefore is normal to the plane defined by vectors `vec(A)` and `vec(B)`.
AP.PCM.5.3.B.2.iii: The direction of the vector resulting from the cross-product of vectors `vec(A)` and `vec(B)` can be qualitatively determined by applying the appropriate right-hand rule.
AP.PCM.5.4.A: Describe the rotational inertia of a rigid system relative to a given axis of rotation.
AP.PCM.5.4.A.1: Rotational inertia measures a rigid system's resistance to changes in rotation and is related to the mass of the system and the distribution of that mass relative to the axis of rotation.
AP.PCM.5.4.A.2: The rotational inertia of an object rotating a perpendicular distance `r` from an axis is described by the equation: `I=mr^2`.
AP.PCM.5.4.A.3: The total rotational inertia of a collection of objects about an axis is the sum of the rotational inertias of each object about that axis: `I_text(tot)=sumI_i=summ_ir_i^2`.
AP.PCM.5.4.A.4: For a solid that can be considered as a collection of differential masses, `dm`, the solid's rotational inertia can be calculated using the equation `I=intr^2dm`, where `r` is the perpendicular distance from `dm` to the axis of rotation.
AP.PCM.5.4.B: Describe the rotational inertia of a rigid system rotating about an axis that does not pass through the system's center of mass.
AP.PCM.5.4.B.1: A rigid system's rotational inertia in a given plane is at a minimum when the rotational axis passes through the system's center of mass.
AP.PCM.5.4.B.2: The parallel axis theorem uses the following equation to relate the rotational inertia of a rigid system about any axis that is parallel to an axis through its center of mass: `I'=I_text(cm)+Md^2`.
AP.PCM.5.5: Rotational Equilibrium & Newton's First Law In Rotational Form
AP.PCM.5.5.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's angular velocity remains constant.
AP.PCM.5.5.A.1: A system may exhibit rotational equilibrium (constant angular velocity) without being in translational equilibrium, and vice versa.
AP.PCM.5.5.A.1.i: Free-body and force diagrams describe the nature of the forces and torques exerted on an object or rigid system.
AP.PCM.5.5.A.1.ii: Rotational equilibrium is a configuration of torques such that the net torque exerted on the system is zero. Relevant equation: `sumtau_i=0`.
AP.PCM.5.5.A.1.iii: The rotational analog of Newton's first law is that a system will have a constant angular velocity only if the net torque exerted on the system is zero.
AP.PCM.5.5.A.2: A rotational corollary to Newton's second law states that if the torques exerted on a rigid system are not balanced, the system's angular velocity must be changing.
AP.PCM.5.6: Newton's Second Law In Rotational Form
AP.PCM.5.6.A: Describe the conditions under which a system's angular velocity changes.
AP.PCM.5.6.A.1: Angular velocity changes when the net torque exerted on the object or system is not equal to zero.
AP.PCM.5.6.A.2: The rate at which the angular velocity of a rigid system changes is directly proportional to the net torque exerted on the rigid system and is in the same direction. The angular acceleration of the rigid system is inversely proportional to the rotational inertia of the rigid system. Relevant equation: `alpha_text(sys)=(sumtau)/I_text(sys)=tau_text(net)/I_text(sys)`.
AP.PCM.5.6.A.3: To fully describe a rotating rigid system, linear and rotational analyses may need to be performed independently.
AP.PCM.6.1.A: Describe the rotational kinetic energy of a rigid system in terms of the rotational inertia and angular velocity of that rigid system.
AP.PCM.6.1.A.1: The rotational kinetic energy of an object or rigid system is related to the rotational inertia and angular velocity of the rigid system and is given by the equation: `K_text(rot)=1/2Iomega^2`.
AP.PCM.6.1.A.1.i: The rotational inertia of an object about a fixed axis can be used to show that the rotational kinetic energy of that object is equivalent to its translational kinetic energy, which is its total kinetic energy.
AP.PCM.6.1.A.1.ii: The total kinetic energy of a rigid system is the sum of its rotational kinetic energy due to its rotation about its center of mass and the translational kinetic energy due to the linear motion of its center of mass.
AP.PCM.6.1.A.2: A rigid system can have rotational kinetic energy while its center of mass is at rest due to the individual points within the rigid system having linear speed and, therefore, kinetic energy.
AP.PCM.6.1.A.3: Rotational kinetic energy is a scalar quantity.
AP.PCM.6.2.A: Describe the work done on a rigid system by a given torque or collection of torques.
AP.PCM.6.2.A.1: A torque can transfer energy into or out of an object or rigid system if the torque is exerted over an angular displacement.
AP.PCM.6.2.A.2: The amount of work done on a rigid system by a torque is related to the magnitude of that torque and the angular displacement through which the rigid system rotates during the interval in which that torque is exerted. Relevant equation: `W=int_(theta_1)^(theta_2)taud theta`.
AP.PCM.6.2.A.3: Work done on a rigid system by a given torque can be found from the area under the curve of a graph of the torque as a function of angular position.
AP.PCM.6.3.A: Describe the angular momentum of an object or rigid system.
AP.PCM.6.3.A.1: The magnitude of the angular momentum of a rigid system about a specific axis can be described with the equation: `L=Iomega`.
AP.PCM.6.3.A.2: The angular momentum of an object about a given point is `vec(L)=vec(r)xxvec(p)`.
AP.PCM.6.3.A.2.i: The selection of the axis about which an object is considered to rotate influences the determination of the angular momentum of that object.
AP.PCM.6.3.A.2.ii: The measured angular momentum of an object traveling in a straight line depends on the distance between the reference point and the object, the mass of the object, the speed of the object, and the angle between the radial distance and the velocity of the object.
AP.PCM.6.3.B: Describe the angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system by a torque.
AP.PCM.6.3.B.1: Angular impulse is defined as the product of the torque exerted on an object or rigid system and the time interval during which the torque is exerted. Relevant equation: `text(angular impulse)=inttaudt`.
AP.PCM.6.3.B.2: Angular impulse has the same direction as the torque imparting it.
AP.PCM.6.3.B.3: The angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system by a torque can be found from the area under the curve of a graph of the torque as a function of time.
AP.PCM.6.3.C: Relate the change in angular momentum of an object or rigid system to the angular impulse given to that object or rigid system.
AP.PCM.6.3.C.1: The magnitude of the change in angular momentum can be described by comparing the magnitudes of the final and initial momenta of the object or rigid system: `DeltaL=L-L_0`.
AP.PCM.6.3.C.2: A rotational form of the impulse-momentum theorem relates the angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system and the change in angular momentum of that object or rigid system.
AP.PCM.6.3.C.2.i: The angular impulse exerted on an object or rigid system is equal to the change in angular momentum of that object or rigid system. Relevant equation: `DeltaL=int_(t_1)^(t_2)taudt`.
AP.PCM.6.3.C.2.ii: The rotational form of the impulse-momentum theorem is a direct result of Newton's second law of motion for cases in which rotational inertia is constant: `tau_text(net)=(dL)/(dt)=I(domega)/(dt)=Ialpha`.
AP.PCM.6.3.C.3: The net torque exerted on an object or rigid system is equal to the slope of the graph of the angular momentum of an object as a function of time.
AP.PCM.6.3.C.4: The angular impulse delivered to an object or rigid system is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of the net external torque exerted on an object as a function of time.
AP.PCM.6.4.A: Describe the behavior of a system using conservation of angular momentum.
AP.PCM.6.4.A.1: The total angular momentum of a system about a rotational axis is the sum of the angular momenta of the system's constituent parts about that rotational axis.
AP.PCM.6.4.A.2: Any change to a system's angular momentum must be due to an interaction between the system and its surroundings.
AP.PCM.6.4.A.2.i: The angular impulse exerted by one object or system on a second object or system is equal and opposite to the angular impulse exerted by the second object or system on the first. This is a direct result of Newton's third law.
AP.PCM.6.4.A.2.ii: A system may be selected so that the total angular momentum of that system is constant.
AP.PCM.6.4.A.2.iii: The angular speed of a nonrigid system may change without the angular momentum of the system changing if the system changes shape by moving mass closer to or farther from the rotational axis.
AP.PCM.6.4.A.2.iv: If the total angular momentum of a system changes, that change will be equivalent to the angular impulse exerted on the system.
AP.PCM.6.4.B: Describe how the selection of a system determines whether the angular momentum of that system changes.
AP.PCM.6.4.B.1: Angular momentum is conserved in all interactions.
AP.PCM.6.4.B.2: If the net external torque exerted on a selected object or rigid system is zero, the total angular momentum of that system is constant.
AP.PCM.6.4.B.3: If the net external torque exerted on a selected object or rigid system is nonzero, angular momentum is transferred between the system and the environment.
AP.PCM.6.5.A: Describe the kinetic energy of a system that has translational and rotational motion.
AP.PCM.6.5.A.1: The total kinetic energy of a system is the sum of the system's translational and rotational kinetic energies. Relevant equation: `K_text(tot)=K_text(trans)+K_text(rot)`.
AP.PCM.6.5.B: Describe the motion of a system that is rolling without slipping.
AP.PCM.6.5.B.1: While rolling without slipping, the translational motion of a system's center of mass is related to the rotational motion of the system itself with the following equations: `Deltax_text(cm)=rDeltatheta`, `v_text(cm)=romega`, and `a_text(cm)=ralpha`.
AP.PCM.6.5.B.2: For ideal cases, rolling without slipping implies that the frictional force does not dissipate any energy from the rolling system.
AP.PCM.6.5.C: Describe the motion of a system that is rolling while slipping.
AP.PCM.6.5.C.1: When slipping, the motion of a system's center of mass and the system's rotational motion cannot be directly related.
AP.PCM.6.5.C.2: When a rotating system is slipping relative to another surface, the point of application of the force of kinetic friction exerted on the system moves with respect to the surface, so the force of kinetic friction will dissipate energy from the system.
AP.PCM.6.6.A: Describe the motions of a system consisting of two objects or systems interacting only via gravitational forces.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.1: In a system consisting only of a massive central object and an orbiting satellite with mass that is negligible in comparison to the central object's mass, the motion of the central object itself is negligible.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.2: The motion of satellites in orbits is constrained by conservation laws.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.2.i: In circular orbits, the system's total mechanical energy, the system's gravitational potential energy, and the satellite's angular momentum and kinetic energy are constant.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.2.ii: In elliptical orbits, the system's total mechanical energy and the satellite's angular momentum are constant, but the system's gravitational potential energy and the satellite's kinetic energy can each change.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.2.iii: The gravitational potential energy of a system consisting of a satellite and a massive central object is defined to be zero when the satellite is an infinite distance from the central object. Relevant equation: `U_g=-G(m_1m_2)/r`.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.3: The total energy of a system consisting of a satellite orbiting a central object in a circular path can be written in terms of the gravitational potential energy of that system or the kinetic energy of the satellite. Derived equations: `K=-1/2U` and `E_text(total)=1/2U=-(GMm)/(2r)`.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.4: The escape velocity of a satellite is the satellite's velocity such that the mechanical energy of the satellite-central-object system is equal to zero.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.4.i: When the only force exerted on a satellite is gravity from a central object, a satellite that reaches escape velocity will move away from the central body until its speed reaches zero at an infinite distance from the central body.
AP.PCM.6.6.A.4.ii: The escape velocity of a satellite from a central body of mass `M` can be derived using conservation of energy laws. Derived equation: `v_text(esc)=sqrt((2GM)/r)`.
AP.PCM.7.1.A.1: Simple harmonic motion is a special case of periodic motion.
AP.PCM.7.1.A.2: SHM results when the magnitude of the restoring force exerted on an object is proportional to that object's displacement from its equilibrium position. Derived equation: `ma_x=-kDeltax`.
AP.PCM.7.1.A.2.i: A restoring force is a force that is exerted in a direction opposite to the object's displacement from an equilibrium position.
AP.PCM.7.1.A.2.ii: An equilibrium position is a location at which the net force exerted on an object or system is zero.
AP.PCM.7.2.A: Describe the frequency and period of an object exhibiting SHM.
AP.PCM.7.2.A.1: The period of SHM is related to the angular frequency, `omega`, of the object's motion by the following equation: `T=(2pi)/omega=1/f`.
AP.PCM.7.2.A.1.i: The period of an object-ideal-spring oscillator is given by the equation: `T_s=2pisqrt(m/k)`.
AP.PCM.7.2.A.1.ii: The period of a simple pendulum displaced by a small angle is given by the equation: `T_p=2pisqrt(l/g)`.
AP.PCM.7.3.A: Describe the displacement, velocity, and acceleration of an object exhibiting SHM.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.1: For an object exhibiting SHM, the displacement of that object measured from its equilibrium position can be represented by the equations: `x=Acos(2pift)` or `x=Asin(2pift)`.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.1.i: Minima, maxima, and zeros of displacement, velocity, and acceleration are features of harmonic motion.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.1.ii: Recognizing the positions or times at which the displacement, velocity, and acceleration for SHM have extrema or zeros can help in qualitatively describing the behavior of the motion.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.2: The position as a function of time for an object exhibiting SHM is a solution of the second-order differential equation derived from the application of Newton's second law. Derived equation: `(d^2x)/(dt^2)=-omega^2x`.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.3: Characteristics of SHM, such as velocity and acceleration, can be determined by or derived from the equation: `x=Acos(omegat+phi)`.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.3.i: The acceleration of an object exhibiting SHM is related to the object's angular frequency and position. Derived equation: `a=-omega^2x`.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.3.ii: It can be shown that the maximum velocity and acceleration of an object exhibiting SHM are related to the angular frequency of the object's motion. Derived equations: `v_text(max)=Aomega` and `a_text(max)=Aomega^2`.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.4: In the presence of a sinusoidal external force, a system may exhibit resonance.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.4.i: Resonance occurs when an external force is exerted at the natural frequency of an oscillating system.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.4.ii: Resonance increases the amplitude of oscillating motion.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.4.iii: The natural frequency of a system is the frequency at which the system will oscillate when it is displaced from its equilibrium position.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.5: Changing the amplitude of a system exhibiting SHM will not change its period.
AP.PCM.7.3.A.6: Properties of SHM can be determined and analyzed using graphical representations.
AP.PCM.7.4.A: Describe the mechanical energy of a system exhibiting SHM.
AP.PCM.7.4.A.1: The total energy of a system exhibiting SHM is the sum of the system's kinetic and potential energies. Relevant equation: `E_text(total)=U+K`.
AP.PCM.7.4.A.2: Conservation of energy indicates that the total energy of a system exhibiting SHM is constant.
AP.PCM.7.4.A.3: The kinetic energy of a system exhibiting SHM is at a maximum when the system's potential energy is at a minimum.
AP.PCM.7.4.A.4: The potential energy of a system exhibiting SHM is at a maximum when the system's kinetic energy is at a minimum.
AP.PCM.7.4.A.4.i: The minimum kinetic energy of a system exhibiting SHM is zero.
AP.PCM.7.4.A.4.ii: hanging the amplitude of a system exhibiting SHM will change the maximum potential energy of the system and, therefore, the total energy of the system. Relevant equation for a spring-object system: `E_text(total)=1/2kA^2`.
AP.PCM.7.5.A: Describe the properties of a physical pendulum.
AP.PCM.7.5.A.1: A physical pendulum is a rigid body that undergoes oscillation about a fixed axis.
AP.PCM.7.5.A.2: For small amplitudes of motion, the period of a physical pendulum is derived from the application of Newton's second law in rotational form. Relevant equation: `T_text(phys)=2pisqrt(I/(mgd))`.
AP.PCM.7.5.A.2.i: When displaced from equilibrium, the gravitational force exerted on a physical pendulum's center of mass provides a restoring torque. Derived equation: `tau=-mgdsintheta`.
AP.PCM.7.5.A.2.ii: For small amplitudes of motion, the small-angle approximation can be applied to the restoring torque. Derived equation: `sintheta~~theta` and `tau=-mgd theta=Ialpha`.
AP.PCM.7.5.A.2.iii: The small-angle approximation and Newton's second law in rotational form yield a second-order differential equation that describes SHM: `(d^2theta)/(dt^2)=-omega^2theta`.
AP.PCM.7.5.A.3: A simple pendulum is a special case of physical pendulums in which the hanging object can be modeled as a point mass at a distance, `l`, from the pivot point. Relevant equation: `T_p=2pisqrt(l/g)`.
AP.PCM.7.5.A.4: A torsion pendulum is a case of SHM where the restoring torque is proportional to the angular displacement of a rotating system. For example, a horizontal disk that is suspended from a wire attached to its center of mass may undergo rotational oscillations about the wire in the horizontal plane. Derived equation: `Ialpha=-kDeltatheta`.
AP.S.1.1: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn From Data?
AP.S.1.1.A: Identify questions to be answered, based on variation in one-variable data.
AP.S.1.1.A.1: Numbers may convey meaningful information, when placed in context.
AP.S.1.2.A: Identify variables in a set of data.
AP.S.1.2.A.1: A variable is a characteristic that changes from one individual to another.
AP.S.1.2.B.1: A categorical variable takes on values that are category names or group labels.
AP.S.1.2.B.2: A quantitative variable is one that takes on numerical values for a measured or counted quantity.
AP.S.1.3: Representing A Categorical Variable With Tables
AP.S.1.3.A: Represent categorical data using frequency or relative frequency tables.
AP.S.1.3.A.1: A frequency table gives the number of cases falling into each category. A relative frequency table gives the proportion of cases falling into each category.
AP.S.1.3.B: Describe categorical data represented in frequency or relative tables.
AP.S.1.3.B.1: Percentages, relative frequencies, and rates all provide the same information as proportions.
AP.S.1.3.B.2: Counts and relative frequencies of categorical data reveal information that can be used to justify claims about the data in context.
AP.S.1.4: Representing A Categorical Variable With Graphs
AP.S.1.4.A.1: Bar charts (or bar graphs) are used to display frequencies (counts) or relative frequencies (proportions) for categorical data.
AP.S.1.4.A.2: The height or length of each bar in a bar graph corresponds to either the number or proportion of observations falling within each category.
AP.S.1.4.A.3: There are many additional ways to represent frequencies (counts) or relative frequencies (proportions) for categorical data.
AP.S.1.4.B.1: Graphical representations of a categorical variable reveal information that can be used to justify claims about the data in context.
AP.S.1.4.C: Compare multiple sets of categorical data.
AP.S.1.4.C.1: Frequency tables, bar graphs, or other representations can be used to compare two or more data sets in terms of the same categorical variable.
AP.S.1.5: Representing A Quantitative Variable With Graphs
AP.S.1.5.A.1: A discrete variable can take on a countable number of values. The number of values may be finite or countably infinite, as with the counting numbers.
AP.S.1.5.A.2: A continuous variable can take on infinitely many values, but those values cannot be counted. No matter how small the interval between two values of a continuous variable, it is always possible to determine another value between them.
AP.S.1.5.B.1: In a histogram, the height of each bar shows the number or proportion of observations that fall within the interval corresponding to that bar. Altering the interval widths can change the appearance of the histogram.
AP.S.1.5.B.2: In a stem and leaf plot, each data value is split into a “stem” (the first digit or digits) and a “leaf” (usually the last digit).
AP.S.1.5.B.3: A dotplot represents each observation by a dot, with the position on the horizontal axis corresponding to the data value of that observation, with nearly identical values stacked on top of each other.
AP.S.1.5.B.4: A cumulative graph represents the number or proportion of a data set less than or equal to a given number.
AP.S.1.5.B.5: There are many additional ways to graphically represent distributions of quantitative data.
AP.S.1.6: Describing The Distribution Of A Quantitative Variable
AP.S.1.6.A: Describe the characteristics of quantitative data distributions.
AP.S.1.6.A.1: Descriptions of the distribution of quantitative data include shape, center, and variability (spread), as well as any unusual features such as outliers, gaps, clusters, or multiple peaks.
AP.S.1.6.A.2: Outliers for one-variable data are data points that are unusually small or large relative to the rest of the data.
AP.S.1.6.A.3: A distribution is skewed to the right (positive skew) if the right tail is longer than the left. A distribution is skewed to the left (negative skew) if the left tail is longer than the right. A distribution is symmetric if the left half is the mirror image of the right half.
AP.S.1.6.A.4: Univariate graphs with one main peak are known as unimodal. Graphs with two prominent peaks are bimodal. A graph where each bar height is approximately the same (no prominent peaks) is approximately uniform.
AP.S.1.6.A.5: A gap is a region of a distribution between two data values where there are no observed data.
AP.S.1.6.A.6: Clusters are concentrations of data usually separated by gaps.
AP.S.1.6.A.7: Descriptive statistics does not attribute properties of a data set to a larger population, but may provide the basis for conjectures for subsequent testing.
AP.S.1.7: Summary Statistics For A Quantitative Variable
AP.S.1.7.A: Calculate measures of center and position for quantitative data.
AP.S.1.7.A.1: A statistic is a numerical summary of sample data.
AP.S.1.7.A.2: The mean is the sum of all the data values divided by the number of values. For a sample, the mean is denoted by `x`-bar: `bar(x)=1/nsum_(i=1)^nx_i`, where `x_i` represents the `i^text(th)` data point in the sample and `n` represents the number of data values in the sample.
AP.S.1.7.A.3: The median of a data set is the middle value when data are ordered. When the number of data points is even, the median can take on any value between the two middle values. In AP Statistics, the most commonly used value for the median of a data set with an even number of values is the average of the two middle values.
AP.S.1.7.A.4: The first quartile, Q1, is the median of the half of the ordered data set from the minimum to the position of the median. The third quartile, Q3, is the median of the half of the ordered data set from the position of the median to the maximum. Q1 and Q3 form the boundaries for the middle `50%` of values in an ordered data set.
AP.S.1.7.A.5: The `p^text(th)` percentile is interpreted as the value that has `p%` of the data less than or equal to it.
AP.S.1.7.B: Calculate measures of variability for quantitative data.
AP.S.1.7.B.1: Three commonly used measures of variability (or spread) in a distribution are the range, interquartile range, and standard deviation.
AP.S.1.7.B.2: The range is defined as the difference between the maximum data value and the minimum data value. The interquartile range (IQR) is defined as the difference between the third and first quartiles: Q3 - Q1. Both the range and the interquartile range are possible ways of measuring variability of the distribution of a quantitative variable.
AP.S.1.7.B.3: Standard deviation is a way to measure variability of the distribution of a quantitative variable. For a sample, the standard deviation is denoted by `s`: `s_x=sqrt(q/(n-1)sum(x_i-bar(x))^2)`. The square of the sample standard deviation, `s^2`, is called the sample variance.
AP.S.1.7.B.4: Changing units of measurement affects the values of the calculated statistics.
AP.S.1.7.C: Explain the selection of a particular measure of center and/or variability for describing a set of quantitative data.
AP.S.1.7.C.1: There are many methods for determining outliers. Two methods frequently used in this course are:
AP.S.1.7.C.1.i: An outlier is a value greater than `1.5xxIQR` above the third quartile or more than `1.5xxIQR` below the first quartile.
AP.S.1.7.C.1.ii: An outlier is a value located 2 or more standard deviations above, or below, the mean.
AP.S.1.7.C.2: The mean, standard deviation, and range are considered nonresistant (or non-robust) because they are influenced by outliers. The median and IQR are considered resistant (or robust), because outliers do not greatly (if at all) affect their value.
AP.S.1.8.A: Represent summary statistics for quantitative data graphically.
AP.S.1.8.A.1: Taken together, the minimum data value, the first quartile (Q1), the median, the third quartile (Q3), and the maximum data value make up the five-number summary.
AP.S.1.8.A.2: A boxplot is a graphical representation of the five-number summary (minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum). The box represents the middle `50%` of data, with a line at the median and the ends of the box corresponding to the quartiles. Lines (“whiskers”) extend from the quartiles to the most extreme point that is not an outlier, and outliers are indicated by their own symbol beyond this.
AP.S.1.8.B: Describe summary statistics of quantitative data represented graphically.
AP.S.1.8.B.1: Summary statistics of quantitative data, or of sets of quantitative data, can be used to justify claims about the data in context.
AP.S.1.8.B.2: If a distribution is relatively symmetric, then the mean and median are relatively close to one another. If a distribution is skewed right, then the mean is usually to the right of the median. If the distribution is skewed left, then the mean is usually to the left of the median.
AP.S.1.9: Comparing Distributions Of A Quantitative Variable
AP.S.1.9.A: Compare graphical representations for multiple sets of quantitative data.
AP.S.1.9.A.1: Any of the graphical representations, e.g., histograms, side-by-side boxplots, etc., can be used to compare two or more independent samples on center, variability, clusters, gaps, outliers, and other features.
AP.S.1.9.B: Compare summary statistics for multiple sets of quantitative data.
AP.S.1.9.B.1: Any of the numerical summaries (e.g., mean, standard deviation, relative frequency, etc.) can be used to compare two or more independent samples.
AP.S.1.10.A: Compare a data distribution to the normal distribution model.
AP.S.1.10.A.1: A parameter is a numerical summary of a population.
AP.S.1.10.A.2: Some sets of data may be described as approximately normally distributed. A normal curve is mound-shaped and symmetric. The parameters of a normal distribution are the population mean, `mu`, and the population standard deviation, `sigma`.
AP.S.1.10.A.3: For a normal distribution, approximately `68%` of the observations are within `1` standard deviation of the mean, approximately `95%` of observations are within `2` standard deviations of the mean, and approximately `99.7%` of observations are within `3` standard deviations of the mean. This is called the empirical rule.
AP.S.1.10.A.4: Many variables can be modeled by a normal distribution.
AP.S.1.10.B: Determine proportions and percentiles from a normal distribution.
AP.S.1.10.B.1: A standardized score for a particular data value is calculated as (data value - mean)/(standard deviation), and measures the number of standard deviations a data value falls above or below the mean.
AP.S.1.10.B.2: One example of a standardized score is a `ztext(-score)`, which is calculated as `ztext(-score)=((x_i-mu)/sigma)`. A `ztext(-score)` measures how many standard deviations a data value is from the mean.
AP.S.1.10.B.3: Technology, such as a calculator, a standard normal table, or computer-generated output, can be used to find the proportion of data values located on a given interval of a normally distributed random variable.
AP.S.1.10.B.4: Given the area of a region under the graph of the normal distribution curve, it is possible to use technology, such as a calculator, a standard normal table, or computer-generated output, to estimate parameters for some populations.
AP.S.1.10.C: Compare measures of relative position in data sets.
AP.S.1.10.C.1: Percentiles and `z`-scores may be used to compare relative positions of points within a data set or between data sets.
AP.S.2.1.A: Identify questions to be answered about possible relationships in data.
AP.S.2.1.A.1: Apparent patterns and associations in data may be random or not.
AP.S.2.2.A: Compare numerical and graphical representations for two categorical variables.
AP.S.2.2.A.1: Side-by-side bar graphs, segmented bar graphs, and mosaic plots are examples of bar graphs for one categorical variable, broken down by categories of another categorical variable.
AP.S.2.2.A.2: Graphical representations of two categorical variables can be used to compare distributions and/or determine if variables are associated.
AP.S.2.2.A.3: A two-way table, also called a contingency table, is used to summarize two categorical variables. The entries in the cells can be frequency counts or relative frequencies.
AP.S.2.2.A.4: A joint relative frequency is a cell frequency divided by the total for the entire table.
AP.S.2.3.A: Calculate statistics for two categorical variables.
AP.S.2.3.A.1: The marginal relative frequencies are the row and column totals in a two-way table divided by the total for the entire table.
AP.S.2.3.A.2: A conditional relative frequency is a relative frequency for a specific part of the contingency table (e.g., cell frequencies in a row divided by the total for that row).
AP.S.2.3.B: Compare statistics for two categorical variables.
AP.S.2.3.B.1: Summary statistics for two categorical variables can be used to compare distributions and/or determine if variables are associated.
AP.S.2.4: Representing The Relationship Between Two Quantitative Variables
AP.S.2.4.A: Represent bivariate quantitative data using scatterplots.
AP.S.2.4.A.1: A bivariate quantitative data set consists of observations of two different quantitative variables made on individuals in a sample or population.
AP.S.2.4.A.2: A scatterplot shows two numeric values for each observation, one corresponding to the value on the `x`-axis and one corresponding to the value on the `y`-axis.
AP.S.2.4.A.3: An explanatory variable is a variable whose values are used to explain or predict corresponding values for the response variable.
AP.S.2.4.B: Describe the characteristics of a scatter plot.
AP.S.2.4.B.1: A description of a scatter plot includes form, direction, strength, and unusual features.
AP.S.2.4.B.2: The direction of the association shown in a scatterplot, if any, can be described as positive or negative.
AP.S.2.4.B.3: A positive association means that as values of one variable increase, the values of the other variable tend to increase. A negative association means that as values of one variable increase, values of the other variable tend to decrease.
AP.S.2.4.B.4: The form of the association shown in a scatterplot, if any, can be described as linear or non-linear to varying degrees.
AP.S.2.4.B.5: The strength of the association is how closely the individual points follow a specific pattern, e.g., linear, and can be shown in a scatterplot. Strength can be described as strong, moderate, or weak.
AP.S.2.4.B.6: Unusual features of a scatter plot include clusters of points or points with relatively large discrepancies between the value of the response variable and a predicted value for the response variable.
AP.S.2.5.A: Determine the correlation for a linear relationship.
AP.S.2.5.A.1: The correlation, `r`, gives the direction and quantifies the strength of the linear association between two quantitative variables.
AP.S.2.5.A.2: The correlation coefficient can be calculated by: `r=1/(n-1)sum((x_i-bar(x))/s_x)((y_i-bar(y))/s_y)`. However, the most common way to determine `r` is by using technology.
AP.S.2.5.A.3: A correlation coefficient close to `1` or `-1` does not necessarily mean that a linear model is appropriate.
AP.S.2.5.B: Interpret the correlation for a linear relationship.
AP.S.2.5.B.1: The correlation, `r`, is unit-free, and always between `-1` and `1`, inclusive. A value of `r=0` indicates that there is no linear association. A value of `r=1` or `r=-1` indicates that there is a perfect linear association.
AP.S.2.5.B.2: A perceived or real relationship between two variables does not mean that changes in one variable cause changes in the other. That is, correlation does not necessarily imply causation.
AP.S.2.6.A: Calculate a predicted response value using a linear regression model.
AP.S.2.6.A.1: A simple linear regression model is an equation that uses an explanatory variable, `x`, to predict the response variable, `y`.
AP.S.2.6.A.2: The predicted response value, denoted by `hat(y)` , is calculated as `hat(y)=a+bx`, where `a` is the `y`-intercept and `b` is the slope of the regression line, and `x` is the value of the explanatory variable.
AP.S.2.6.A.3: Extrapolation is predicting a response value using a value for the explanatory variable that is beyond the interval of `x`-values used to determine the regression line. The predicted value is less reliable as an estimate the further we extrapolate.
AP.S.2.7.A: Represent differences between measured and predicted responses using residual plots.
AP.S.2.7.A.1: The residual is the difference between the actual value and the predicted value: `text(residual)=y-hat(y)`.
AP.S.2.7.A.2: A residual plot is a plot of residuals versus explanatory variable values or predicted response values.
AP.S.2.7.B: Describe the form of association of bivariate data using residual plots.
AP.S.2.7.B.1: Apparent randomness in a residual plot for a linear model is evidence of a linear form to the association between the variables.
AP.S.2.7.B.2: Residual plots can be used to investigate the appropriateness of a selected model.
AP.S.2.8.A: Estimate parameters for the least-squares regression line model.
AP.S.2.8.A.1: The least-squares regression model minimizes the sum of the squares of the residuals and contains the point `(bar(x),bar(y))`.
AP.S.2.8.A.2: The slope, `b`, of the regression line can be calculated as `b=r(s_y/s_x)` where `r` is the correlation between `x` and `y`, `s_y` is the sample standard deviation of the response variable, `y`, and `s_x` is the sample standard deviation of the explanatory variable, `x`.
AP.S.2.8.A.3: Sometimes, the `y`-intercept of the line does not have a logical interpretation in context.
AP.S.2.8.A.4: In simple linear regression, `r^2` is the square of the correlation, `r`. It is also called the coefficient of determination. `r^2` is the proportion of variation in the response variable that is explained by the explanatory variable in the model.
AP.S.2.8.B: Interpret coefficients for the least-squares regression line model.
AP.S.2.8.B.1: The coefficients of the least-squares regression model are the estimated slope and `y`-intercept.
AP.S.2.8.B.2: The slope is the amount that the predicted `y`-value changes for every unit increase in `x`.
AP.S.2.8.B.3: The `y`-intercept value is the predicted value of the response variable when the explanatory variable is equal to `0` . The formula for the `y`-intercept, `a`, is `a=bar(y)-b bar(x)`.
AP.S.2.9.A.1: An outlier in regression is a point that does not follow the general trend shown in the rest of the data and has a large residual when the Least Squares Regression Line (LSRL) is calculated.
AP.S.2.9.A.2: A high-leverage point in regression has a substantially larger or smaller `x`-value than the other observations have.
AP.S.2.9.A.3: An influential point in regression is any point that, if removed, changes the relationship substantially. Examples include much different slope, `y`-intercept, and/or correlation. Outliers and high leverage points are often influential.
AP.S.2.9.B: Calculate a predicted response using a least-squares regression line for a transformed data set.
AP.S.2.9.B.1: Transformations of variables, such as evaluating the natural logarithm of each value of the response variable or squaring each value of the explanatory variable, can be used to create transformed data sets, which may be more linear in form than the untransformed data.
AP.S.2.9.B.2: Increased randomness in residual plots after transformation of data and/or movement of `r^2` to a value closer to `1` offers evidence that the least-squares regression line for the transformed data is a more appropriate model to use to predict responses to the explanatory variable than the regression line for the untransformed data.
AP.S.3.1: Introducing Statistics: Do The Data We Collected Tell The Truth?
AP.S.3.1.A: Identify questions to be answered about data collection methods.
AP.S.3.1.A.1: Methods for data collection that do not rely on chance result in untrustworthy conclusions.
AP.S.3.2.A: Identify the type of a study.
AP.S.3.2.A.1: A population consists of all items or subjects of interest.
AP.S.3.2.A.2: A sample selected for study is a subset of the population.
AP.S.3.2.A.3: In an observational study, treatments are not imposed. Investigators examine data for a sample of individuals (retrospective) or follow a sample of individuals into the future collecting data (prospective) in order to investigate a topic of interest about the population. A sample survey is a type of observational study that collects data from a sample in an attempt to learn about the population from which the sample was taken.
AP.S.3.2.A.4: In an experiment, different conditions (treatments) are assigned to experimental units (participants or subjects).
AP.S.3.2.B: Identify appropriate generalizations and determinations based on observational studies.
AP.S.3.2.B.1: It is only appropriate to make generalizations about a population based on samples that are randomly selected or otherwise representative of that population.
AP.S.3.2.B.2: A sample is only generalizable to the population from which the sample was selected.
AP.S.3.2.B.3: It is not possible to determine causal relationships between variables using data collected in an observational study.
AP.S.3.3.A: Identify a sampling method, given a description of a study.
AP.S.3.3.A.1: When an item from a population can be selected only once, this is called sampling without replacement. When an item from the population can be selected more than once, this is called sampling with replacement.
AP.S.3.3.A.2: A simple random sample (SRS) is a sample in which every group of a given size has an equal chance of being chosen. This method is the basis for many types of sampling mechanisms. A few examples of mechanisms used to obtain SRSs include numbering individuals and using a random number generator to select which ones to include in the sample, ignoring repeats, using a table of random numbers, or drawing a card from a deck without replacement.
AP.S.3.3.A.3: A stratified random sample involves the division of a population into separate groups, called strata, based on shared attributes or characteristics (homogeneous grouping). Within each stratum a simple random sample is selected, and the selected units are combined to form the sample.
AP.S.3.3.A.4: A cluster sample involves the division of a population into smaller groups, called clusters. Ideally, there is heterogeneity within each cluster, and clusters are similar to one another in their composition. A simple random sample of clusters is selected from the population to form the sample of clusters. Data are collected from all observations in the selected clusters.
AP.S.3.3.A.5: A systematic random sample is a method in which sample members from a population are selected according to a random starting point and a fixed, periodic interval.
AP.S.3.3.A.6: A census selects all items/subjects in a population.
AP.S.3.3.B: Explain why a particular sampling method is or is not appropriate for a given situation.
AP.S.3.3.B.1: There are advantages and disadvantages for each sampling method depending upon the question that is to be answered and the population from which the sample will be drawn.
AP.S.3.4.A: Identify potential sources of bias in sampling methods.
AP.S.3.4.A.1: Bias occurs when certain responses are systematically favored over others.
AP.S.3.4.A.2: When a sample is comprised entirely of volunteers or people who choose to participate, the sample will typically not be representative of the population (voluntary response bias).
AP.S.3.4.A.3: When part of the population has a reduced chance of being included in the sample, the sample will typically not be representative of the population (undercoverage bias).
AP.S.3.4.A.4: Individuals chosen for the sample for whom data cannot be obtained (or who refuse to respond) may differ from those for whom data can be obtained (nonresponse bias).
AP.S.3.4.A.5: Problems in the data gathering instrument or process result in response bias. Examples include questions that are confusing or leading (question wording bias) and self-reported responses.
AP.S.3.4.A.6: Non-random sampling methods (for example, samples chosen by convenience or voluntary response) introduce potential for bias because they do not use chance to select the individuals.
AP.S.3.5.A: Identify the components of an experiment.
AP.S.3.5.A.1: The experimental units are the individuals (which may be people or other objects of study) that are assigned treatments. When experimental units consist of people, they are sometimes referred to as participants or subjects.
AP.S.3.5.A.2: An explanatory variable (or factor) in an experiment is a variable whose levels are manipulated intentionally. The levels or combination of levels of the explanatory variable(s) are called treatments.
AP.S.3.5.A.3: A response variable in an experiment is an outcome from the experimental units that is measured after the treatments have been administered.
AP.S.3.5.A.4: A confounding variable in an experiment is a variable that is related to the explanatory variable and influences the response variable and may create a false perception of association between the two.
AP.S.3.5.B: Describe elements of a well-designed experiment.
AP.S.3.5.B.1: A well-designed experiment should include the following:
AP.S.3.5.B.1.a: Comparisons of at least two treatment groups, one of which could be a control group.
AP.S.3.5.B.1.b: Random assignment/allocation of treatments to experimental units.
AP.S.3.5.B.1.c: Replication (more than one experimental unit in each treatment group).
AP.S.3.5.B.1.d: Control of potential confounding variables where appropriate.
AP.S.3.5.C.1: In a completely randomized design, treatments are assigned to experimental units completely at random. Random assignment tends to balance the effects of uncontrolled (confounding) variables so that differences in responses can be attributed to the treatments.
AP.S.3.5.C.2: Methods for randomly assigning treatments to experimental units in a completely randomized design include using a random number generator, a table of random values, drawing chips without replacement, etc.
AP.S.3.5.C.3: In a single-blind experiment, subjects do not know which treatment they are receiving, but members of the research team do, or vice versa.
AP.S.3.5.C.4: In a double-blind experiment neither the subjects nor the members of the research team who interact with them know which treatment a subject is receiving.
AP.S.3.5.C.5: A control group is a collection of experimental units either not given a treatment of interest or given a treatment with an inactive substance (placebo) in order to determine if the treatment of interest has an effect.
AP.S.3.5.C.6: The placebo effect occurs when experimental units have a response to a placebo.
AP.S.3.5.C.7: For randomized complete block designs, treatments are assigned completely at random within each block.
AP.S.3.5.C.8: Blocking ensures that at the beginning of the experiment the units within each block are similar to each other with respect to at least one blocking variable. A randomized block design helps to separate natural variability from differences due to the blocking variable.
AP.S.3.5.C.9: A matched pairs design is a special case of a randomized block design. Using a blocking variable, subjects (whether they are people or not) are arranged in pairs matched on relevant factors. Matched pairs may be formed naturally or by the experimenter. Every pair receives both treatments by randomly assigning one treatment to one member of the pair and subsequently assigning the remaining treatment to the second member of the pair. Alternately, each subject may get both treatments.
AP.S.3.6.A: Explain why a particular experimental design is appropriate.
AP.S.3.6.A.1: There are advantages and disadvantages for each experimental design depending on the question of interest, the resources available, and the nature of the experimental units.
AP.S.3.7.A: Interpret the results of a well-designed experiment.
AP.S.3.7.A.1: Statistical inference attributes conclusions based on data to the distribution from which the data were collected.
AP.S.3.7.A.2: Random assignment of treatments to experimental units allows researchers to conclude that some observed changes are so large as to be unlikely to have occurred by chance. Such changes are said to be statistically significant.
AP.S.3.7.A.3: Statistically significant differences between or among experimental treatment groups are evidence that the treatments caused the effect.
AP.S.3.7.A.4: If the experimental units used in an experiment are representative of some larger group of units, the results of an experiment can be generalized to the larger group. Random selection of experimental units gives a better chance that the units will be representative.
AP.S.4.1.A: Identify questions suggested by patterns in data.
AP.S.4.1.A.1: Patterns in data do not necessarily mean that variation is not random.
AP.S.4.2.A.1: A random process generates results that are determined by chance.
AP.S.4.2.A.2: An outcome is the result of a trial of a random process.
AP.S.4.2.A.3: An event is a collection of outcomes.
AP.S.4.2.A.4: Simulation is a way to model random events, such that simulated outcomes closely match real-world outcomes. All possible outcomes are associated with a value to be determined by chance. Record the counts of simulated outcomes and the count total.
AP.S.4.2.A.5: The relative frequency of an outcome or event in simulated or empirical data can be used to estimate the probability of that outcome or event.
AP.S.4.2.A.6: The law of large numbers states that simulated (empirical) probabilities tend to get closer to the true probability as the number of trials increases.
AP.S.4.3.A: Calculate probabilities for events and their complements.
AP.S.4.3.A.1: The sample space of a random process is the set of all possible non-overlapping outcomes.
AP.S.4.3.A.2: If all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely, then the probability an event E will occur is defined as the fraction: `text(number of outcomes in event E)/text(total number of outcomes in sample space)`.
AP.S.4.3.A.3: The probability of an event is a number between `0` and `1`, inclusive.
AP.S.4.3.A.4: The probability of the complement of an event `E`, `E'` or `E^C`, (i.e., not `E`) is equal to `1-P(E)`.
AP.S.4.3.B.1: Probabilities of events in repeatable situations can be interpreted as the relative frequency with which the event will occur in the long run.
AP.S.4.4.A: Explain why two events are (or are not) mutually exclusive.
AP.S.4.4.A.1: The probability that events `A` and `B` both will occur, sometimes called the joint probability, is the probability of the intersection of `A` and `B`, denoted `P(AnnB)`.
AP.S.4.4.A.2: Two events are mutually exclusive or disjoint if they cannot occur at the same time. So `P(AnnB)=0`.
AP.S.4.5.A.1: The probability that event `A` will occur given that event `B` has occurred is called a conditional probability and denoted `P(A|B)=(P(AnnB))/(P(B))`.
AP.S.4.5.A.2: The multiplication rule states that the probability that events `A` and `B` both will occur is equal to the probability that event `A` will occur multiplied by the probability that event `B` will occur, given that `A` has occurred. This is denoted `P(AnnB)=P(A)*P(B|A)`.
AP.S.4.6.A: Calculate probabilities for independent events and for the union of two events.
AP.S.4.6.A.1: Events `A` and `B` are independent if, and only if, knowing whether event `A` has occurred (or will occur) does not change the probability that event `B` will occur.
AP.S.4.6.A.2: If, and only if, events `A` and `B` are independent, then `P(A|B)=P(A)`, `P(B|A)=P(B)`, and `P(AnnB)=P(A)*P(B)`.
AP.S.4.6.A.3: The probability that event `A` or event `B` (or both) will occur is the probability of the union of `A` and `B`, denoted `P(AuuB)`.
AP.S.4.6.A.4: The addition rule states that the probability that event `A` or event `B` or both will occur is equal to the probability that event `A` will occur plus the probability that event `B` will occur minus the probability that both events A and B will occur. This is denoted `P(AuuB)=P(A)+P(B)-P(AnnB)`.
AP.S.4.7: Introduction To Random Variables & Probability Distributions
AP.S.4.7.A: Represent the probability distribution for a discrete random variable.
AP.S.4.7.A.1: The values of a random variable are the numerical outcomes of random behavior.
AP.S.4.7.A.2: A discrete random variable is a variable that can only take a countable number of values. Each value has a probability associated with it. The sum of the probabilities over all of the possible values must be `1`.
AP.S.4.7.A.3: A probability distribution can be represented as a graph, table, or function showing the probabilities associated with values of a random variable.
AP.S.4.7.A.4: A cumulative probability distribution can be represented as a table or function showing the probability of being less than or equal to each value of the random variable.
AP.S.4.7.B.1: An interpretation of a probability distribution provides information about the shape, center, and spread of a population and allows one to make conclusions about the population of interest.
AP.S.4.8: Mean & Standard Deviation Of Random Variables
AP.S.4.8.A: Calculate parameters for a discrete random variable.
AP.S.4.8.A.1: A numerical value measuring a characteristic of a population or the distribution of a random variable is known as a parameter, which is a single, fixed value.
AP.S.4.8.A.2: The mean, or expected value, for a discrete random variable `X` is `mu_X=sumx_i*P(x_i)`.
AP.S.4.8.A.3: The standard deviation for a discrete random variable `X` is `sigma_X=sqrt(sum(x_i-mu_X)^2*P(x_i))`.
AP.S.4.8.B: Interpret parameters for a discrete random variable.
AP.S.4.8.B.1: Parameters for a discrete random variable should be interpreted using appropriate units and within the context of a specific population.
AP.S.4.9.A: Calculate parameters for linear combinations of random variables.
AP.S.4.9.A.1: For random variables `X` and `Y` and real numbers a and b, the mean of `aX+bY` is `amu_x+bmu_y`.
AP.S.4.9.A.2: Two random variables are independent if knowing information about one of them does not change the probability distribution of the other.
AP.S.4.9.A.3: For independent random variables `X` and `Y` and real numbers `a` and `b`, the mean of `aX+bY` is `amu_x+bmu_y`, and the variance of `aX+bY` is `a^2sigma_x^2+b^2sigma_y^2`.
AP.S.4.9.B: Describe the effects of linear transformations of parameters of random variables.
AP.S.4.9.B.1: For `Y=a+bX`, the probability distribution of the transformed random variable, `Y`, has the same shape as the probability distribution for `X`, so long as `a>0` and `b>0`. The mean of `Y` is `mu_y=a+bmu_x`. The standard deviation of `Y` is `sigma_y=abs(b)sigma_x`.
AP.S.4.10.A: Estimate probabilities of binomial random variables using data from a simulation.
AP.S.4.10.A.1: A probability distribution can be constructed using the rules of probability or estimated with a simulation using random number generators.
AP.S.4.10.A.2: A binomial random variable, `X`, counts the number of successes in `n` repeated independent trials, each trial having two possible outcomes (success or failure), with the probability of success `p` and the probability of failure `1-p`.
AP.S.4.10.B: Calculate probabilities for a binomial distribution.
AP.S.4.10.B.1: The probability that a binomial random variable, `X`, has exactly `x` successes for `n` independent trials, when the probability of success is `p`, is calculated as `P(X=x)=((n),(x))p^x(1-p)^(n-x)`, `x=0,1,2,...,n`. This is the binomial probability function.
AP.S.4.11.A: Calculate parameters for a binomial distribution.
AP.S.4.11.A.1: If a random variable is binomial, its mean, `mu_x`, is `np` and its standard deviation, `sigma_x`, is `sqrt(np(1-p))`.
AP.S.4.11.B: Interpret probabilities and parameters for a binomial distribution.
AP.S.4.11.B.2: Probabilities and parameters for a binomial distribution should be interpreted using appropriate units and within the context of a specific population or situation.
AP.S.4.12.A: Calculate probabilities for geometric random variables.
AP.S.4.12.A.1: For a sequence of independent trials, a geometric random variable, `X`, gives the number of the trial on which the first success occurs. Each trial has two possible outcomes (success or failure) with the probability of success p and the probability of failure `1-p`.
AP.S.4.12.A.2: The probability that the first success for repeated independent trials with probability of success `p` occurs on trial `x` is calculated as `P(X=x)=(1-p)^(x-1)p`, `x=1,2,3,...`. This is the geometric probability function.
AP.S.4.12.B: Calculate parameters of a geometric distribution.
AP.S.4.12.B.1: If a random variable is geometric, its mean, `mu_x`, is `1/p` and its standard deviation, `sigma_x`, is `(sqrt(1-p))/p`.
AP.S.4.12.C: Interpret probabilities and parameters for a geometric distribution.
AP.S.4.12.C.1: Probabilities and parameters for a geometric distribution should be interpreted using appropriate units and within the context of a specific population or situation.
AP.S.5.1: Introducing Statistics: Why Is My Sample Not Like Yours?
AP.S.5.1.A: Identify questions suggested by variation in statistics for samples collected from the same population.
AP.S.5.1.A.1: Variation in statistics for samples taken from the same population may be random or not.
AP.S.5.2.A: Calculate the probability that a particular value lies in a given interval of a normal distribution.
AP.S.5.2.A.1: A continuous random variable is a variable that can take on any value within a specified domain. Every interval within the domain has a probability associated with it.
AP.S.5.2.A.2: A continuous random variable with a normal distribution is commonly used to describe populations. The distribution of a normal random variable can be described by a normal, or “bell-shaped,” curve.
AP.S.5.2.A.3: The area under a normal curve over a given interval represents the probability that a particular value lies in that interval.
AP.S.5.2.B: Determine the interval associated with a given area in a normal distribution.
AP.S.5.2.B.1: The boundaries of an interval associated with a given area in a normal distribution can be determined using `z`-scores or technology, such as a calculator, a standard normal table, or computer-generated output.
AP.S.5.2.B.2: Intervals associated with a given area in a normal distribution can be determined by assigning appropriate inequalities to the boundaries of the intervals:
AP.S.5.2.B.2.a: `P(X<x_a)=p/100` means that the lowest `p%` of values lie to the left of `x_a`.
AP.S.5.2.B.2.b: `P(x_a<X<x_b)=p/100` means that `p%` of values lie between `x_a` and `x_b`.
AP.S.5.2.B.2.c: `P(X>x_b)=p/100` means that the highest `p%` of values lie to the right of `x_b`.
AP.S.5.2.B.2.d: To determine the most extreme `p%` of values requires dividing the area associated with `p%` into two equal areas on either extreme of the distribution: `P(X<x_a)=1/2p/100` and `P(X>x_b)=1/2p/100` means that half of the `p%` most extreme values lie to the left of `x_a` and half of the `p%` most extreme values lie to the right of `x_b`.
AP.S.5.2.C: Determine the appropriateness of using the normal distribution to approximate probabilities for unknown distributions.
AP.S.5.2.C.1: Normal distributions are symmetrical and “bell-shaped.” As a result, normal distributions can be used to approximate distributions with similar characteristics.
AP.S.5.3.A.1: A sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of values for the statistic for all possible samples of a given size from a given population.
AP.S.5.3.A.2: The central limit theorem (CLT) states that when the sample size is sufficiently large, a sampling distribution of the mean of a random variable will be approximately normally distributed.
AP.S.5.3.A.3: The central limit theorem requires that the sample values are independent of each other and that `n` is sufficiently large.
AP.S.5.3.A.4: A randomization distribution is a collection of statistics generated by simulation assuming known values for the parameters. For a randomized experiment, this means repeatedly randomly reallocating/reassigning the response values to treatment groups.
AP.S.5.3.A.5: The sampling distribution of a statistic can be simulated by generating repeated random samples from a population.
AP.S.5.4.A: Explain why an estimator is or is not unbiased.
AP.S.5.4.A.1: When estimating a population parameter, an estimator is unbiased if, on average, the value of the estimator is equal to the population parameter.
AP.S.5.4.B: Calculate estimates for a population parameter.
AP.S.5.4.B.1: When estimating a population parameter, an estimator exhibits variability that can be modeled using probability.
AP.S.5.4.B.2: A sample statistic is a point estimator of the corresponding population parameter.
AP.S.5.5.A: Determine parameters of a sampling distribution for sample proportions.
AP.S.5.5.A.1: For independent samples (sampling with replacement) of a categorical variable from a population with population proportion, `p`, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion, `hat(p)`, has a mean, `mu_hat(p)=p` and a standard deviation, `sigma_hat(p)=sqrt((p(1-p))/n)`
AP.S.5.5.A.2: If sampling without replacement, the standard deviation of the sample proportion is smaller than what is given by the formula above. If the sample size is less than `10%` of the population size, the difference is negligible.
AP.S.5.5.B: Determine whether a sampling distribution for a sample proportion can be described as approximately normal.
AP.S.5.5.C: Interpret probabilities and parameters for a sampling distribution for a sample proportion.
AP.S.5.5.C.1: Probabilities and parameters for a sampling distribution for a sample proportion should be interpreted using appropriate units and within the context of a specific population.
AP.S.5.6: Sampling Distributions For Differences In Sample Proportions
AP.S.5.6.A: Determine parameters of a sampling distribution for a difference in sample proportions.
AP.S.5.6.A.1: For a categorical variable, when randomly sampling with replacement from two independent populations with population proportions `p_1` and `p_2`, the sampling distribution of the difference in sample proportions `hat(p)_1-hat(p)_2` has mean, `mu_(hat(p)_1-hat(p)_2)=p_1-p_2` and standard deviation `sigma_(hat(p)_1-hat(p)_2)=sqrt((p_1(1-p_1))/n_1+(p_2(1-p_2))/n_2)`
AP.S.5.6.A.2: If sampling without replacement, the standard deviation of the difference in sample proportions is smaller than what is given by the formula above. If the sample sizes are less than `10%` of the population sizes, the difference is negligible.
AP.S.5.6.B: Determine whether a sampling distribution for a difference of sample proportions can be described as approximately normal.
AP.S.5.6.B.1: The sampling distribution of the difference in sample proportions `hat(p)_1-hat(p)_2` will have an approximate normal distribution provided the sample sizes are large enough: `n_1p_1>=10n_1(1-p_1)>=10n_2p_2>=10n_2(1-p_2)>=10`.
AP.S.5.6.C: Interpret probabilities and parameters for a sampling distribution for a difference in proportions.
AP.S.5.6.C.1: Parameters for a sampling distribution for a difference of proportions should be interpreted using appropriate units and within the context of a specific populations.
AP.S.5.7.A: Determine parameters for a sampling distribution for sample means.
AP.S.5.7.A.1: For a numerical variable, when random sampling with replacement from a population with mean `mu` and standard deviation, `sigma`, the sampling distribution of the sample mean has mean `mu_(bar(x))=mu` and standard deviation `sigma_(bar(x))=sigma/sqrt(n)`.
AP.S.5.7.A.2: If sampling without replacement, the standard deviation of the sample mean is smaller than what is given by the formula above. If the sample size is less than `10%` of the population size, the difference is negligible.
AP.S.5.7.B: Determine whether a sampling distribution of a sample mean can be described as approximately normal.
AP.S.5.7.B.1: For a numerical variable, if the population distribution can be modeled with a normal distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean, `bar(x)`, can be modeled with a normal distribution.
AP.S.5.7.B.2: For a numerical variable, if the population distribution cannot be modeled with a normal distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean, `bar(x)`, can be modeled approximately by a normal distribution, provided the sample size is large enough, e.g., greater than or equal to `30`.
AP.S.5.7.C: Interpret probabilities and parameters for a sampling distribution for a sample mean.
AP.S.5.7.C.1: Probabilities and parameters for a sampling distribution for a sample mean should be interpreted using appropriate units and within the context of a specific population.
AP.S.5.8: Sampling Distributions For Differences In Sample Means
AP.S.5.8.A: Determine parameters of a sampling distribution for a difference in sample means.
AP.S.5.8.A.1: For a numerical variable, when randomly sampling with replacement from two independent populations with population means `mu_1` and `mu_2` and population standard deviations `sigma_1` and `sigma_2`, the sampling distribution of the difference in sample means `bar(x)_1-bar(x)_2` has mean `mu_(bar(x)_1-bar(x)_2)=mu_1-mu_2` and standard deviation, `sigma_(bar(x)_1-bar(x)_2)=sqrt(sigma_1^2/n_1+sigma_2^2/n_2)`.
AP.S.5.8.A.2: If sampling without replacement, the standard deviation of the difference in sample means is smaller than what is given by the formula above. If the sample sizes are less than `10%` of the population sizes, the difference is negligible.
AP.S.5.8.B: Determine whether a sampling distribution of a difference in sample means can be described as approximately normal.
AP.S.5.8.B.1: The sampling distribution of the difference in sample means `bar(x)_1-bar(x)_2` can be modeled with a normal distribution if the two population distributions can be modeled with a normal distribution.
AP.S.5.8.B.2: The sampling distribution of the difference in sample means `bar(x)_1-bar(x)_2` can be modeled approximately by a normal distribution if the two population distributions cannot be modeled with a normal distribution but both sample sizes are greater than or equal to `30`.
AP.S.5.8.C: Interpret probabilities and parameters for a sampling distribution for a difference in sample means.
AP.S.5.8.C.1: Probabilities and parameters for a sampling distribution for a difference of sample means should be interpreted using appropriate units and within the context of a specific populations.
AP.S.6.1.A: Identify questions suggested by variation in the shapes of distributions of samples taken from the same population.
AP.S.6.1.A.1: Variation in shapes of data distributions may be random or not.
AP.S.6.2: Constructing A Confidence Interval For A Population Proportion
AP.S.6.2.A: Identify an appropriate confidence interval procedure for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.2.A.1: The appropriate confidence interval procedure for a one-sample proportion for one categorical variable is a one sample `z`-interval for a proportion.
AP.S.6.2.B: Verify the conditions for calculating confidence intervals for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.2.B.1: In order to make assumptions necessary for inference on population proportions, means, and slopes, we must check for independence in data collection methods and for selection of the appropriate sampling distribution.
AP.S.6.2.B.2: In order to calculate a confidence interval to estimate a population proportion, `p`, we must check for independence and that the sampling distribution is approximately normal.
AP.S.6.2.B.2.a.i: Data should be collected using a random sample or a randomized experiment.
AP.S.6.2.B.2.a.ii: When sampling without replacement, check that `n≤10%N`, where `N` is the size of the population.
AP.S.6.2.B.2.b: To check that the sampling distribution of `hat(p)` is approximately normal (shape):
AP.S.6.2.B.2.b.i: For categorical variables, check that both the number of successes, `nhat(p)`, and the number of failures, `n(1-hat(p))` are at least `10` so that the sample size is large enough to support an assumption of normality.
AP.S.6.2.C: Determine the margin of error for a given sample size and an estimate for the sample size that will result in a given margin of error for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.2.C.1: Based on sample data, the standard error of a statistic is an estimate for the standard deviation for the statistic. The standard error of `hat(p)` is `SE_hat(p)=sqrt((hat(p)(1-hat(p)))/n)``
AP.S.6.2.C.2: A margin of error gives how much a value of a sample statistic is likely to vary from the value of the corresponding population parameter.
AP.S.6.2.C.3: For categorical variables, the margin of error is the critical value (`z^(***)`) times the standard error (SE) of the relevant statistic, which equals `z^(***)sqrt((hat(p)(1-hat(p)))/n)` for a one sample proportion.
AP.S.6.2.C.4: The formula for margin of error can be rearranged to solve for `n`, the minimum sample size needed to achieve a given margin of error. For this purpose, use a guess for `hat(p)` or use `hat(p)=0.5` in order to find an upper bound for the sample size that will result in a given margin of error.
AP.S.6.2.D: Calculate an appropriate confidence interval for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.2.D.1: In general, an interval estimate can be constructed as point estimate `+-` (margin of error). For a one-sample proportion, the interval estimate is `hat(p)+-z^(***)sqrt((hat(p)(1-hat(p)))/n)`
AP.S.6.2.D.2: Critical values represent the boundaries encompassing the middle C% of the standard normal distribution, where `C%` is an approximate confidence level for a proportion.
AP.S.6.2.E: Calculate an interval estimate based on a confidence interval for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.2.E.1: Confidence intervals for population proportions can be used to calculate interval estimates with specified units.
AP.S.6.3: Justifying A Claim Based On A Confidence Interval For A Population Proportion
AP.S.6.3.A: Interpret a confidence interval for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.3.A.1: A confidence interval for a population proportion either contains the population proportion or it does not, because each interval is based on random sample data, which varies from sample to sample.
AP.S.6.3.A.2: We are `C%` confident that the confidence interval for a population proportion captures the population proportion.
AP.S.6.3.A.3: In repeated random sampling with the same sample size, approximately `C%` of confidence intervals created will capture the population proportion.
AP.S.6.3.A.4: Interpreting a confidence interval for a one-sample proportion should include a reference to the sample taken and details about the
AP.S.6.3.B: Justify a claim based on a confidence interval for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.3.B.1: A confidence interval for a population proportion provides an interval of values that may provide sufficient evidence to support a particular claim in context.
AP.S.6.3.C: Identify the relationships between sample size, width of a confidence interval, confidence level, and of error for a population proportion.
