AP.S.6.4: Setting Up A Test For A Population Proportion
AP.S.6.4.A: Identify the null and alternative hypotheses for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.4.A.1: The null hypothesis is the situation that is assumed to be correct unless evidence suggests otherwise, and the alternative hypothesis is the situation for which evidence is being collected.
AP.S.6.4.A.2: For hypotheses about parameters, the null hypothesis contains an equality reference `(=,>=,or<=)`, while the alternative hypothesis contains a strict inequality `(<,>,or!=)`. The type of inequality in the alternative hypothesis is based on the question of interest. Alternative hypotheses with `<` or `>` are called one-sided, and alternative hypotheses with `!=` are called two-sided. Although the null hypothesis for a one-sided test may include an inequality symbol, it is still tested at the boundary of equality.
AP.S.6.4.A.3: The null hypothesis for a population proportion is: `H_0:p=p_0`, where `p_0` is the null hypothesized value for the population proportion.
AP.S.6.4.A.4: A one-sided alternative hypothesis for a proportion is either `H_a:p<p_0` or `H_a:p>p_0`. A two-sided alternate hypothesis is `H_a:p_1!=p_2`.
AP.S.6.4.A.5: For a one-sample `z`-test for a population proportion, the null hypothesis specifies a value for the population proportion, usually one indicating no difference or effect.
AP.S.6.4.B: Identify an appropriate testing method for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.4.B.1: For a single categorical variable, the appropriate testing method for a population proportion is a one-sample `z`-test for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.4.C: Verify the conditions for making statistical inferences when testing a population proportion.
AP.S.6.4.C.1: In order to make statistical inferences when testing a population proportion, we must check for independence and that the sampling distribution is approximately normal:
AP.S.6.4.C.1.a.i: Data should be collected using a random sample or a randomized experiment.
AP.S.6.4.C.1.a.ii: When sampling without replacement, check that `10%N`.
AP.S.6.4.C.1.b: To check that the sampling distribution of `hat(p)` is approximately normal (shape):
AP.S.6.4.C.1.b.i: Assuming that `H_0` is true (`p=p_0`), verify that both the number of successes, `np_0`, and the number of failures, `n(1-p_0)` are at least `10` so that that the sample size is large enough to support an assumption of normality.
AP.S.6.5.A: Calculate an appropriate test statistic and `p`-value for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.5.A.1: The distribution of the test statistic assuming the null hypothesis is true (null distribution) can be either a randomization distribution or when a probability model is assumed to be true, a theoretical distribution (`z`).
AP.S.6.5.A.2: When using a `z`-test, the standardized test statistic can be written: `text(test statistic)=text(sample statistic-null value of the parameter)/text(standard deviation of the statistic)`. This is called a `z`-statistic for proportions.
AP.S.6.5.A.3: The test statistic for a population proportion is: `z=(hat(p)-p_0)/sqrt((p_0(1-p_0))/n)`.
AP.S.6.5.A.4: A `p`-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the observed test statistic when the null hypothesis and probability model are assumed to be true. The significance level may be given or determined by the researcher.
AP.S.6.5.B: Interpret the `p`-value of a significance test for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.5.B.1: The `p`-value is the proportion of values for the null distribution that are as extreme or more extreme than the observed value of the test statistic. This is:
AP.S.6.5.B.1.a: The proportion at or above the observed value of the test statistic, if the alternative is `>`.
AP.S.6.5.B.1.b: The proportion at or below the observed value of the test statistic, if the alternative is `<`.
AP.S.6.5.B.1.c: The proportion less than or equal to the negative of the absolute value of the test statistic plus the proportion greater than or equal to the absolute value of the test statistic, if the alternative is `!=`.
AP.S.6.5.B.2: An interpretation of the `p`-value of a significance test for a one-sample proportion should recognize that the `p`-value is computed by assuming that the probability model and null hypothesis are true, i.e., by assuming that the true population proportion is equal to the particular value stated in the null hypothesis.
AP.S.6.6: Concluding A Test For A Population Proportion
AP.S.6.6.A: Justify a claim about the population based on the results of a significance test for a population proportion.
AP.S.6.6.A.1: The significance level, `alpha`, is the predetermined probability of rejecting the null hypothesis given that it is true.
AP.S.6.6.A.2: A formal decision explicitly compares the `p`-value to the significance level, `alpha`. If the `ptext(-value)<=alpha`, reject the null hypothesis. If the `ptext(-value)>alpha`, fail to reject the null hypothesis.
AP.S.6.6.A.3: Rejecting the null hypothesis means there is sufficient statistical evidence to support the alternative hypothesis. Failing to reject the null means there is insufficient statistical evidence to support the alternative hypothesis.
AP.S.6.6.A.4: The conclusion about the alternative hypothesis must be stated in context.
AP.S.6.6.A.5: A significance test can lead to rejecting or not rejecting the null hypothesis, but can never lead to concluding or proving that the null hypothesis is true. Lack of statistical evidence for the alternative hypothesis is not the same as evidence for the null hypothesis.
AP.S.6.6.A.6: Small `p`-values indicate that the observed value of the test statistic would be unusual if the null hypothesis and probability model were true, and so provide evidence for the alternative. The lower the `p`-value, the more convincing the statistical evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
AP.S.6.6.A.7: `p`-values that are not small indicate that the observed value of the test statistic would not be unusual if the null hypothesis and probability model were true, so do not provide convincing statistical evidence for the alternative hypothesis nor do they provide evidence that the null hypothesis is true.
AP.S.6.6.A.8: A formal decision explicitly compares the `p`-value to the significance `alpha`. If the `ptext(-value)<=alpha`, then reject the null hypothesis, `H_0:p=p_0`. If the `ptext(-value)>alpha`, then fail to reject the null hypothesis.
AP.S.6.6.A.9: The results of a significance test for a population proportion can serve as the statistical reasoning to support the answer to a research question about the population that was sampled.
AP.S.6.7.A: Identify Type I and Type II errors.
AP.S.6.7.A.1: A Type I error occurs when the null hypothesis is true and is rejected (false positive).
AP.S.6.7.A.2: A Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is false and is not rejected (false negative).
AP.S.6.7.B: Calculate the probability of a Type I and Type II errors.
AP.S.6.7.B.1: The significance level, `alpha`, is the probability of making a Type I error, if the null hypothesis is true.
AP.S.6.7.B.2: The power of a test is the probability that a test will correctly reject a false null hypothesis.
AP.S.6.7.B.3: The probability of making a Type II error `=1-text(power)`.
AP.S.6.7.C: Identify factors that affect the probability of errors in significance testing.
AP.S.6.7.C.1: The probability of a Type II error decreases when any of the following occurs, provided the others do not change:
AP.S.6.7.C.1.ii: Significance level (`alpha`) of a test increases.
AP.S.6.7.C.1.iv: True parameter value is farther from the null.
AP.S.6.7.D: Interpret Type I and Type II errors.
AP.S.6.7.D.1: Whether a Type I or a Type II error is more consequential depends upon the situation.
AP.S.6.7.D.2: Since the significance level, `alpha`, is the probability of a Type I error, the consequences of a Type I error influence decisions about a significance level.
AP.S.6.8: Confidence Intervals For The Difference Of Two Proportions
AP.S.6.8.A: Identify an appropriate confidence interval procedure for a comparison of population proportions.
AP.S.6.8.A.1: The appropriate confidence interval procedure for a two-sample comparison of proportions for one categorical variable is a two-sample `z`-interval for a difference between population proportions.

AP.S.6.10.A.1: For a two-sample test for a difference of two proportions, the null hypothesis specifies a value of `0` for the difference in population proportions, indicating no difference or effect.
AP.S.6.10.A.2: The null hypothesis for a difference in proportions is: `H_0:p_1=p_2`, or `H_0:p_1-p_2=0`.
AP.S.6.10.A.3: A one-sided alternative hypothesis for a difference in proportions is `H_a:p_1<p_2`, or, `H_a:p_1>p_2`. A two-sided alternative hypothesis for a difference of proportions is `H_a:p_1!=p_2`.

Assuming that `H_0` is true (`p_1-p_2` or `p_1=p_2`), check that `n_1hat(p)_c`, `n_1(1-hat(p)_c)`, `n_2hat(p)_c`, and `n_2(1-hat(p)_c)` are all greater than or equal to some predetermined value, typically either `5` or `10`.

AP.S.6.11.A: Calculate an appropriate test statistic for the difference of two population proportions.
AP.S.6.11.A.1: The test statistic for a difference in proportions is: `z=((hat(p)_1-hat(p)_2)-0)/(sqrt(hat(p)_c(1-hat(p)_c))sqrt(1/n_1+1/n_2))`, where `hat(p)_c=(n_1hat(p)_1+n_2hat(p)_2)/(n_1+n_2)`.

AP.S.7.8.C.1: In order to make statistical inferences when testing a difference between population means, we must check for independence and that the sampling distribution is approximately normal:
AP.S.7.8.C.1.a.i: Data should be collected using simple random samples or a randomized experiment.
AP.S.7.8.C.1.a.ii: When sampling without replacement, check that `n_1<=10%N_1` and `n_2<=10%N_2`.
AP.S.7.8.C.1.b: The sampling distribution of `bar(x)_1-bar(x)_2` should be approximately normal (shape).
AP.S.7.8.C.1.b.i: If the observed distribution is skewed, both `n_1` and `n_2` should be greater than `30`.
AP.S.7.8.C.1.b.ii: If the sample size is less than `30`, the distribution of the sample data should be free from strong skewness and outliers. This should be checked for BOTH samples.
AP.S.7.9: Carrying Out A Test For The Difference Of Two Population Means
AP.S.7.9.A: Calculate an appropriate test statistic for a difference of two means.
AP.S.7.9.A.1: For a single quantitative variable, data collected using independent random samples or a randomized experiment from two populations, each of which can be modeled with a normal distribution, the sampling distribution of `t=((bar(x)_1-bar(x)_2)-(mu_1-mu_2))/sqrt((s_1^2)/n_1+(s_2^2)/n_2)` is an approximate `t`-distribution with degrees of freedom that can be found using technology. The degrees of freedom fall between the smaller of `n_1-1` and `n_2-1` and `n_1+n_2-2`.
AP.S.7.9.B: Interpret the `p`-value of a significance test for a difference of population means.
AP.S.7.9.B.1: An interpretation of the `p`-value of a significance test for a two-sample difference of population means should recognize that the `p`-value is computed by assuming that the null hypothesis is true, i.e., by assuming that the true population means are equal to each other.
AP.S.7.9.C: Justify a claim about the population based on the results of a significance test for a difference of two population means in context.
AP.S.7.9.C.1: A formal decision explicitly compares the `ptext(-value)` to the significance `alpha`. If the `ptext(-value)<=alpha`, then reject the null hypothesis, `H_0:mu_1-mu_2=0`, or `H_0:mu_1=mu_2`. If the `ptext(-value)>alpha`, then fail to reject the null hypothesis.
AP.S.7.9.C.2: The results of a significance test for a two-sample test for a difference between two population means can serve as the statistical reasoning to support the answer to a research question about the populations that were sampled.
AP.S.7.10: Skills Focus: Selecting, Implementing & Communicating Inference Procedures
AP.S.8.1: Introducing Statistics: Are My Results Unexpected?
AP.S.8.1.A: Identify questions suggested by variation between observed and expected counts in categorical data.
AP.S.8.1.A.1: Variation between what we find and what we expect to find may be random or not.
AP.S.8.2: Setting Up A Chi-Square Goodness Of Fit Test
AP.S.8.2.A.1: Expected counts of categorical data are counts consistent with the null hypothesis. In general, an expected count is a sample size times a probability.
AP.S.8.2.A.2: The chi-square statistic measures the distance between observed and expected counts relative to expected counts.
AP.S.8.2.A.3: Chi-square distributions have positive values and are skewed right. Within a family of density curves, the skew becomes less pronounced with increasing degrees of freedom.
AP.S.8.2.B: Identify the null and alternative hypotheses in a test for a distribution of proportions in a set of categorical data.
AP.S.8.2.B.1: For a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, the null hypothesis specifies null proportions for each category, and the alternative hypothesis is that at least one of these proportions is not as specified in the null hypothesis.
AP.S.8.2.C: Identify an appropriate testing method for a distribution of proportions in a set of categorical data.
AP.S.8.2.C.1: When considering a distribution of proportions for one categorical variable, the appropriate test is the chi-square test for goodness of fit.
AP.S.8.2.D: Calculate expected counts for the chi-square test for goodness of fit.
AP.S.8.2.D.1: Expected counts for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test are (sample size) (null proportion).
AP.S.8.2.E: Verify the conditions for making statistical inferences when testing goodness of fit for a chi-square distribution.
AP.S.8.2.E.1: In order to make statistical inferences for a chi-square test for goodness of fit we must check the following:
AP.S.8.2.E.1.a.i: Data should be collected using a random sample or randomized experiment.
AP.S.8.2.E.1.a.ii: When sampling without replacement, check that `n<=10%N`.
AP.S.8.2.E.1.b: The chi-square test for goodness of fit becomes more accurate with more observations, so large counts should be used (shape).
AP.S.8.2.E.1.b.i: A conservative check for large counts is that all expected counts should be greater than `5`.
AP.S.8.3: Carrying Out A Chi-Square Test For Goodness of Fit
AP.S.8.3.A: Calculate the appropriate statistic for the chi-square test for goodness of fit.
AP.S.8.3.A.1: The test statistic for the chi-square test for goodness of fit is `chi^2=sum(text(Observed count)-text(Expected count))^2/text(Expected count)` with `text(degrees of freedom)=text(number of categories)-1`.
AP.S.8.3.A.2: The distribution of the test statistic assuming the null hypothesis is true (null distribution) can be either a randomization distribution or, when a probability model is assumed to be true, a theoretical distribution (chi-square).
AP.S.8.3.B: Determine the `p`-value for chi-square test for goodness of fit significance test.
AP.S.8.3.B.1: The `p`-value for a chi-square test for goodness of fit for a number of degrees of freedom is found using the appropriate table or computer generated output.
AP.S.8.3.C: Interpret the `p`-value for the chi-square test for goodness of fit.
AP.S.8.3.C.1: An interpretation of the `p`-value for the chi-square test for goodness of fit is the probability, given the null hypothesis and probability model are true, of obtaining a test statistic as, or more, extreme than the observed value.
AP.S.8.3.D: Justify a claim about the population based on the results of a chi-square test for goodness of fit.
AP.S.8.3.D.1: A decision to either reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis is based on comparison of the `p`-value to the significance level, `sigma`.
AP.S.8.3.D.2: The results of a chi-square test for goodness of fit can serve as the statistical reasoning to support the answer to a research question about the population that was sampled.
AP.S.8.4.A: Calculate expected counts for two-way tables of categorical data.
AP.S.8.4.A.1: The expected count in a particular cell of a two-way table of categorical data can be calculated using the formula: `text(expected count)=((text(row total))(text(column total)))/(text(table total))`.
AP.S.8.5: Setting Up A Chi-Square Test For Homogeneity Or Independence
AP.S.8.5.A: Identify the null and alternative hypotheses for a chi-square test for homogeneity or independence.
AP.S.8.5.A.1: The appropriate hypotheses for a chi-square test for homogeneity are: `H_0`: There is no difference in distributions of a categorical variable across populations or treatments and  `H_a`: There is a difference in distributions of a categorical variable across populations or treatments.
AP.S.8.5.A.2: The appropriate hypotheses for a chi-square test for independence are: `H_0`: There is no association between two categorical variables in a given population or the two categorical variables are independent and `H_a`: Two categorical variables in a population are associated or dependent.
AP.S.8.5.B: Identify an appropriate testing method for comparing distributions in two-way tables of categorical data.
AP.S.8.5.B.1: When comparing distributions to determine whether proportions in each category for categorical data collected from different populations are the same, the appropriate test is the chi-square test for homogeneity.
AP.S.8.5.B.2: To determine whether row and column variables in a two-way table of categorical data might be associated in the population from which the data were sampled, the appropriate test is the chi-square test for independence.
AP.S.8.5.C: Verify the conditions for making statistical inferences when testing a chi-square distribution for independence or homogeneity.
AP.S.8.5.C.1: In order to make statistical inferences for a chi-square test for two-way tables (homogeneity or independence), we must verify the following:
AP.S.8.5.C.1.a.i: For a test for independence: Data should be collected using a simple random sample.
AP.S.8.5.C.1.a.ii: For a test for homogeneity: Data should be collected using a stratified random sample or randomized experiment.
AP.S.8.5.C.1.a.iii: When sampling without replacement, check that `n<=10%N`.
AP.S.8.5.C.1.b: The chi-square tests for independence and homogeneity become more accurate with more observations, so large counts should be used (shape).
AP.S.8.5.C.1.b.i: A conservative check for large counts is that all expected counts should be greater than `5`.
AP.S.8.6: Carrying Out A Chi-Square Test For Homogeneity Or Independence
AP.S.8.6.A: Calculate the appropriate statistic for a chi-square test for homogeneity or independence.
AP.S.8.6.A.1: The appropriate test statistic for a chi-square test for homogeneity or independence is the chi-square statistic: `chi^2=sum(text(Observed count)-text(Expected count))^2/text(Expected count)` with degrees of freedom equal to: `(text(numbers of rows)-1)(text(numbers of columns)-1)`
AP.S.8.6.B: Determine the `p`-value for a chi-square significance test for independence or homogeneity.
AP.S.8.6.B.1: The `p`-value for a chi-square test for independence or homogeneity for a number of degrees of freedom is found using the appropriate table or technology.
AP.S.8.6.B.2: For a test of independence or homogeneity for a two-way table, the `p`-value is the proportion of values in a chi-square distribution with appropriate degrees of freedom that are equal to or larger than the test statistic.
AP.S.8.6.C: Interpret the `p`-value for the chi-square test for homogeneity or independence.
AP.S.8.6.C.1: An interpretation of the `p`-value for the chi-square test for homogeneity or independence is the probability, given the null hypothesis and probability model are true, of obtaining a test statistic as, or more, extreme than the observed value.
AP.S.8.6.D: Justify a claim about the population based on the results of a chi-square test for homogeneity or independence.
AP.S.8.6.D.1: A decision to either reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis for a chi-square test for homogeneity or independence is based on comparison of the `p`-value to the significance level, `alpha`.
AP.S.8.6.D.2: The results of a chi-square test for homogeneity or independence can serve as the statistical reasoning to support the answer to a research question about the population that was sampled (independence) or the populations that were sampled (homogeneity).
AP.S.8.7: Skills Focus: Selecting An Appropriate Inference Procedure For Categorical Data
AP.S.9.1: Introducing Statistics: Do Those Points Align?
AP.S.9.1.A: Identify questions suggested by variation in scatter plots.
AP.S.9.1.A.1: Variation in points' positions relative to a theoretical line may be random or non-random.
AP.S.9.2: Confidence Intervals For The Slope Of A Regression Model
AP.S.9.2.A: Identify an appropriate confidence interval procedure for a slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.2.A.1: Consider a response variable, `y`, that is linearly related to an explanatory variable, `x`. For a simple random sample of `n` observations, the sample regression line, `hat(y)=a+bx`, is an estimate of the population regression line `mu_y=alpha+betax`. For a particular observation, `(x_i,y_i)`, the residual from the sample regression line, `y_i-hat(y)_i=y_i-(a+bx_i)`, is an estimate of `y_i-(alpha+betax_i)`, the deviation of the response variable from the population regression line. For all points `(x,y)` in the population, the standard deviation of all of the deviations of the response variable from the population regression line, `sigma`, can be estimated by the standard deviation of the residuals from the sample regression line, `s=sqrt((sum(y_i-hat(y)_i)^2)/(n-2))`.
AP.S.9.2.A.2: For a simple random sample of `n` observations, let `b` represent the slope of a sample regression line. Then the mean of the sampling distribution for `b` equals the population slope: `mu_b=beta`. The standard deviation of the sampling distribution for `b` is `sigma_b=sigma/(sigma_xsqrt(n))`, where `sigma_x=sqrt((sum(x_i-bar(x))^2)/n)`.
AP.S.9.2.A.3: The appropriate confidence interval for the slope of a regression model is a `t`-interval for the slope.
AP.S.9.2.B: Verify the conditions to calculate confidence intervals for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.2.B.1: In order to calculate a confidence interval to estimate the slope of a regression line, we must check the following:
AP.S.9.2.B.1.a: The true relationship between `x` and `y` is linear. Analysis of residuals may be used to verify linearity.
AP.S.9.2.B.1.b: The standard deviation for `y`, `sigma_y`, does not vary with `x`. Analysis of residuals may be used to check for approximately equal standard deviations for all `x`.
AP.S.9.2.B.1.c.i: Data should be collected using a random sample or a randomized experiment.
AP.S.9.2.B.1.c.ii: When sampling without replacement, check that `n<=10%N`.
AP.S.9.2.B.1.d: For a particular value of `x`, the responses (`y`-values) are approximately normally distributed. Analysis of graphical representations of residuals may be used to check for normality.
AP.S.9.2.B.1.d.i: If the observed distribution is skewed, `n` should be greater than `30`.
AP.S.9.2.C: Determine the given margin of error for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.2.C.1: For the slope of a regression line, the margin of error is the critical value (`t^(***)`) times the standard error (SE) of the slope.
AP.S.9.2.C.2: The standard error for the slope of a regression line with sample standard deviation, `s`, is `SE=s/(s_xsqrt(n-1))`, where `s` is the estimate of `sigma` and `s_x` is the sample standard deviation of the `x` values.
AP.S.9.2.D: Calculate an appropriate confidence interval for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.2.D.1: The point estimate for the slope of a regression model is the slope of the line of best fit, b.
AP.S.9.2.D.2: For the slope of a regression model, the interval estimate is `b+-t^(***)(SE_b)`.
AP.S.9.3: Justifying A Claim About The Slope Of A Regression Model Based On A Confidence Interval
AP.S.9.3.A: Interpret a confidence interval for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.3.A.1: In repeated random sampling with the same sample size, approximately `C%` of confidence intervals created will capture the slope of the regression model, i.e., the true slope of the population regression model.
AP.S.9.3.A.2: An interpretation for a confidence interval for the slope of a regression line should include a reference to the sample taken and details about the population it represents.
AP.S.9.3.B: Justify a claim based on a confidence interval for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.3.B.1: A confidence interval for the slope of a regression model provides an interval of values that may provide sufficient evidence to support a particular claim in context.
AP.S.9.3.C: Identify the effects of sample size on the width of a confidence interval for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.3.C.1: When all other things remain the same, the width of the confidence interval for the slope of a regression model tends to decrease as the sample size increases.
AP.S.9.4: Setting Up A Test For The Slope Of A Regression Model
AP.S.9.4.A: Identify the appropriate selection of a testing method for a slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.4.A.1: The appropriate test for the slope of a regression model is a `t`-test for a slope.
AP.S.9.4.B: Identify appropriate null and alternative hypotheses for a slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.4.B.1: The null hypothesis for a `t`-test for a slope is: `H_0:beta=beta_0`, where `beta_0` is the hypothesized value from the null hypothesis. The alternative hypothesis is `H_0:beta<beta_0`, or `H_0:beta>beta_0`, or `H_0:beta!=beta_0`.
AP.S.9.4.C: Verify the conditions for the significance test for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.4.C.1: In order to make statistical inferences when testing for the slope of a regression model, we must check the following:
AP.S.9.4.C.1.a: The true relationship between `x` and `y` is linear. Analysis of residuals may be used to verify linearity.
AP.S.9.4.C.1.b: The standard deviation for `y`, `sigma_y`, does not vary with `x`. Analysis of residuals may be used to check for approximately equal standard deviations for all `x`.
AP.S.9.4.C.1.c.i: Data should be collected using a random sample or a randomized experiment.
AP.S.9.4.C.1.c.ii: When sampling without replacement, check that `n<=10%N`.
AP.S.9.4.C.1.d: For a particular value of `x`, the responses (`y`-values) are approximately normally distributed. Analysis of graphical representations of residuals may be used to check for normality.
AP.S.9.4.C.1.d.i: If the observed distribution is skewed, `n` should be greater than `30`.
AP.S.9.4.C.1.d.ii: If the sample size is less than `30`, the distribution of the sample data should be free from strong skewness and outliers.
AP.S.9.5: Carrying Out A Test For the Slope Of A Regression Model
AP.S.9.5.A: Calculate an appropriate test statistic for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.5.A.1: The distribution of the slope of a regression model assuming all conditions are satisfied and the null hypothesis is true (null distribution) is a `t`-distribution.
AP.S.9.5.A.2: For simple linear regression when random sampling from a population for the response that can be modeled with a normal distribution for each value of the explanatory variable, the sampling distribution of `t=(b-beta)/(SE_b)` has a `t`-distribution with degrees of freedom equal to `n-2`. When testing the slope in a simple linear regression model with one parameter, the slope, the test for the slope has `df=n-1`.
AP.S.9.5.B: Interpret the `p`-value of a significance test for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.5.B.1: An interpretation of the `p`-value of a significance test for the slope of a regression model should recognize that the `p`-value is computed by assuming that the null hypothesis is true, i.e., by assuming that the true population slope is equal to the particular value stated in the null hypothesis.
AP.S.9.5.C: Justify a claim about the population based on the results of a significance test for the slope of a regression model.
AP.S.9.5.C.1: A formal decision explicitly compares the `ptext(-value)` to the significance `alpha`. If the `ptext(-value)<=alpha`, then reject the null hypothesis, `H_0:beta=beta_0`. If the `ptext(-value)>alpha`, then fail to reject the null hypothesis.
AP.S.9.5.C.2: The results of a significance test for the slope of a regression model can serve as the statistical reasoning to support the answer to a research question about that sample.
AP.S.9.6: Skills Focus: Selecting An Appropriate Inference Procedure
AP.USGP.1.1.A: Explain how democratic ideals are reflected in the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
AP.USGP.1.1.A.1: The U.S. government is based on the following democratic ideals:
AP.USGP.1.1.A.1.i: Natural rights (all people have certain rights that cannot be taken away).
AP.USGP.1.1.A.1.ii: A social contract (an implicit agreement among the people in a society to give up some freedoms to maintain social order).
AP.USGP.1.1.A.1.iii: Popular sovereignty (all government power comes from the consent of its people).
AP.USGP.1.1.A.1.iv: Limited government (a government's power cannot be absolute).
AP.USGP.1.1.A.2: The ideal of limited government is ensured by the interaction of these principles:
AP.USGP.1.1.A.3: The Declaration of Independence, drafted by Thomas Jefferson (with help from Adams and Franklin), restates the philosophy of natural rights, and provides a foundation for popular sovereignty. The U.S. Constitution, drafted by James Madison at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia that was led by George Washington (with important contributions from Hamilton and members of the “Grand Committee”), is an example of a social contract and establishes a system of limited government. The Constitution provides the blueprint for a unique form of democratic government in the United States.
AP.USGP.1.2.A: Explain how models of representative democracy are visible in major institutions, policies, events, or debates in the U.S.
AP.USGP.1.2.A.1: Representative democracies can take several forms including the following models:
AP.USGP.1.2.A.1.i: Participatory democracy, which emphasizes broad participation in politics and civil society.
AP.USGP.1.2.A.1.ii: Pluralist democracy, which emphasizes group-based activism by nongovernmental interests striving for impact on political decision making.
AP.USGP.1.2.A.1.iii: Elite democracy, which emphasizes limited participation in politics and civil society.
AP.USGP.1.2.A.2: Different aspects of the U.S. Constitution as well as the debate between Federalist No. `10` and Brutus No. `1` reflect the tension between the broad participatory model and the more filtered participation of the pluralist and elite models of representative democracy.
AP.USGP.1.2.A.3: The three models of representative democracy continue to be reflected in contemporary institutions and political behavior.
AP.USGP.1.3.A: Explain Federalist and Anti-Federalist views on central government and democracy.
AP.USGP.1.3.A.1: Federalists supported ratification of the Constitution and a strong central government. Madison's arguments in Federalist No. `10` focused on the superiority of a large republic in controlling the “mischiefs of faction,” delegating authority to elected representatives and dispersing power between the states and national government.
AP.USGP.1.3.A.2: Anti-Federalists opposed the ratification of the Constitution and wanted more power reserved to state governments rather than a strong central government. Anti-Federalist writings, including Brutus No. `1`, adhered to popular democratic theory that emphasized the benefits of a small, decentralized republic while warning of the dangers to personal liberty from a large, centralized government.
AP.USGP.1.4: Challenges Of The Articles Of Confederation
AP.USGP.1.4.A: Explain the relationship between key provisions of the Articles of Confederation, and the debate over granting the federal government greater power formerly reserved to the states.
AP.USGP.1.4.A.1: Specific incidents and legal challenges that highlighted key weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation are represented by the:
AP.USGP.1.4.A.1.i: Lack of centralized military power to address Shays' Rebellion.
AP.USGP.1.4.A.1.ii: Lack of an executive branch to enforce laws, including taxation.
AP.USGP.1.4.A.1.iii: Lack of a national court system.
AP.USGP.1.4.A.1.iv: Lack of power to regulate interstate commerce.
AP.USGP.1.4.A.1.v: Lack of the exclusive power to coin money.
AP.USGP.1.5.A: Explain the impact of political negotiation and compromise at the Constitutional Convention on the development of the constitutional system.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.1: Compromises deemed necessary for ratification of the Constitution included the following:
AP.USGP.1.5.A.1.i: Great (Connecticut) Compromise, which created a dual (bicameral) system of congressional representation with the House of Representatives based on each state's population and the Senate representing each state equall.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.1.ii: Electoral College, which created a system for electing the president by electors from each state rather than by popular vote or by congressional vote.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.1.iii: Three-Fifths Compromise, which provided a formula for calculating a state's enslaved population for purposes of representation in the House and for taxation.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.1.iv: Postponing until `text(1808)` a decision whether to ban the importation of enslaved persons.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.1.v: Agreement to add a Bill of Rights to address concerns of the Anti-Federalists.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.2: Debates about self-government during the drafting of the Constitution necessitated the drafting of an amendment process in Article V that entailed either a `text(two-thirds)` vote in both houses or a proposal from `text(two-thirds)` of the state legislatures, with final ratification determined by `text(three-fourths)` of the states.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.3: The compromises necessary to secure ratification of the Constitution left some matters unresolved that continue to generate discussion and debate today.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.4: The debate over the role of the national government, the powers of state governments, and the rights of individuals remains at the heart of present-day constitutional issues about democracy and governmental power, as represented by:
AP.USGP.1.5.A.4.i: Debates about government surveillance resulting from the federal government's response to the 9/11 attacks.
AP.USGP.1.5.A.4.ii: Debates about the role of government in public school education.
AP.USGP.1.6.A: Explain the constitutional principles of separation of powers and checks and balances.
AP.USGP.1.6.A.1: The specific and separate powers delegated to Congress, the president, and the courts allow each branch to check and balance the power of the other branches, ensuring no one branch becomes too powerful.
AP.USGP.1.6.A.2: Federalist No. `51` explains how constitutional provisions of separation of powers and checks and balances control potential abuses by majorities.
AP.USGP.1.6.B: Explain the effects of separation of powers and checks and balances for the U.S. political system.
AP.USGP.1.6.B.1: Separation of powers and checks and balances creates multiple access points for stakeholders and institutions to influence public policy.
AP.USGP.1.6.B.2: Checks and balances and separation of powers allow legal actions to be taken against public officials deemed to have abused their power. Those legal actions include the process of impeachment (the House formally charges an official with abuse of power or misconduct) and removal (if the official is convicted in a Senate impeachment trial).
AP.USGP.1.7: Relationship Between The States & National Government
AP.USGP.1.7.A: Explain how the constitutional allocation of power between the national and state governments affects society.
AP.USGP.1.7.A.1: Federalism is the system of government in the United States in which power is shared between the national and state governments. The exclusive and concurrent powers of the national and state governments help explain the ongoing debate over the balance of power between the two levels.
AP.USGP.1.7.A.2: Exclusive power is held by only one level of government and includes enumerated powers that are written in the Constitution, and implied powers that are not specifically written in the Constitution but are inferred from the Necessary and Proper Clause.
AP.USGP.1.7.A.3: Reserved powers are those not delegated or enumerated to the national government but are reserved to the states, as stated in the `text(Tenth)` Amendment.
AP.USGP.1.7.A.4: Concurrent powers are shared between both levels of government such as the power to collect taxes, the power to make and enforce laws and the power to build roads.
AP.USGP.1.7.A.5: The distribution of power between national and state governments is demonstrated by:
AP.USGP.1.7.A.5.i: Revenue sharing (national funding with almost no restrictions to the states on its use and is the least used form of funding).
AP.USGP.1.7.A.5.ii: Block grants (national funding with minimal restrictions to the states on its use and is preferred by the states).
AP.USGP.1.7.A.5.iii: Categorical grants (national funding that is restricted to specific categories of expenditures, is preferred by the national government, and is the most commonly used form of funding).
AP.USGP.1.7.A.5.iv: Mandates (requirements by the national government of the states).
AP.USGP.1.8.A: Explain how the balance of power between national and state governments has changed over time based on interpretations of the Supreme Court of the United States.
AP.USGP.1.8.A.1: The Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the `text(Fourteenth)` Amendment give the national government the power to enforce protections for any person against the states, but Supreme Court interpretations can influence the extent of those protections.
AP.USGP.1.8.A.2: The Commerce Clause gives the national government the power to regulate interstate commerce, but Supreme Court interpretations can influence the extent of this power.
AP.USGP.1.8.A.3: The Necessary and Proper Clause gives Congress the power to make laws related to carrying out its enumerated powers, but Supreme Court interpretations can influence the extent of these powers.
AP.USGP.1.8.A.4: The Supremacy Clause gives the national government and its laws general precedence over states' laws, but Supreme Court interpretations may affect when specific actions exceed this constitutional power.
AP.USGP.1.9.A: Explain how the distribution of powers between national and state governments impacts policymaking.
AP.USGP.1.9.A.1: The allocation of powers between national and state governments creates multiple access points for stakeholders and institutions to influence public policy.
AP.USGP.1.9.A.2: National policymaking is constrained by the sharing of concurrent powers with state governments.
AP.USGP.2.1: Congress: The Senate & The House Of Representatives
AP.USGP.2.1.A: Describe the different structures, powers, and functions of each house of Congress.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.1: Republicanism, the democratic principle that the will of the people is reflected in government debates and decisions by their representatives, is shown in the bicameral structure of Congress. The Senate is designed to represent states equally, while the House is designed to represent the people.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.2: Different membership sizes influence the formality of debate in each chamber. Debate in the House, which has `435` members, is more formal than in the Senate, with `100` members.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.3: Interactions in Congress are affected by the two-party system and term-length differences. `text(One-third)` of the Senate is elected every `text(two years)`, creating a continuous legislative body. All House members are elected every `text(two years)`.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.4: The enumerated and implied powers in the Constitution allow Congress to participate in the public policy process by:
AP.USGP.2.1.A.4.i: Passing a federal budget, raising revenue by laying and collecting taxes, borrowing money, and coining money.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.4.ii: Declaring war and providing the funds necessary to maintain the armed forces.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.4.iii: Determining the process for naturalization by which people can become citizens of the U.S.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.4.v: Creating federal courts and their jurisdictions.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.4.vi: Enacting legislation under the authority of the necessary and proper clause.
AP.USGP.2.1.A.4.vii: Conducting oversight of the executive branch, including federal agencies in the bureaucracy.
AP.USGP.2.2.A: Explain how the structure, powers, and functions of both houses of Congress affect the policymaking process.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.1: The structures and powers of the Senate and House are different by design. This difference directly affects the legislative process.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.2: Both chambers refer bills to committees, which conduct hearings and debate and mark up bills with revisions and additions. Leadership in committees is determined by the majority political party.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.3: Chamber-specific rules and procedures affect the legislative process.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.3.i: In the House, the Speaker is elected by a majority of members and presides over the legislative work in the House. All revenue bills must originate in the House. Rules for debate in the House on a bill are established by the Rules Committee. The House can form a Committee of the Whole in order to expedite debate on bills. An individual representative in the House can file a discharge petition to have a bill brought to the floor for debate, but it is rarely done.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.3.ii: In the Senate, bills are typically brought to the floor by unanimous consent, but a Senator may request a hold on a bill to prevent it from getting to the floor for a vote. During debate, a Senator can use the filibuster (a tactic to prolong debate and delay or prevent a vote on a bill) or make a motion for cloture (a procedure to end a debate).
AP.USGP.2.2.A.3.iii: When a bill passed by both chambers on the same topic has variation in its wording, a conference committee meets to reconcile those differences.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.4: Congress must generate a budget that addresses both mandatory and discretionary spending.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.4.i: Mandatory spending is required by law for entitlement programs such as Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.4.ii: Discretionary spending is approved on an annual basis for defense spending, education, and infrastructure. As entitlement costs grow, discretionary spending opportunities will decrease unless tax revenues increase, or the budget deficit increases.
AP.USGP.2.2.A.5: Pork-barrel legislation (funding for a local project in a larger appropriation bill) and logrolling (exchange of political favors amonglegislators, such as trading votes, to gain support for legislation) affect the legislative process in both chambers.
AP.USGP.2.3.A: Explain how congressional behavior is influenced by election processes, partisanship, and divided government.
AP.USGP.2.3.A.1: Congressional behavior and governing effectiveness are influenced by ideological divisions between political parties. Partisan voting (when members of Congress vote based on their political party affiliation) and polarization (when political attitudes move toward ideological extremes) can lead to gridlock (a situation in which no congressional action on legislation can be taken due to a lack of consensus).
AP.USGP.2.3.A.2: Gerrymandering, redistricting, and unequal representation of constituencies have been partially addressed by Supreme Court cases that opened the door for equal protection challenges to redistricting.
AP.USGP.2.3.A.3: Elections that have led to a divided government (when one party controls the presidency and the other party controls at least one of the chambers of Congress) can lead to more intense partisanship. This partisanship can result in members of Congress voting against presidential initiatives and appointments, especially those of a lame duck president.
AP.USGP.2.3.A.4: Accountability to constituents in each chamber is affected by how representatives perceive their roles.
AP.USGP.2.3.A.4.1: A representative who conceives of their role as a trustee will vote on issues based on their own knowledge and judgement.
AP.USGP.2.3.A.4.2: A representative acting as a delegate sees themselves as an agent of those who elected them and will vote on issues based on the interests of their constituents.
AP.USGP.2.3.A.4.3: A politico uses a combination of these role conceptions.
AP.USGP.2.4.A: Explain how the president can implement a policy agenda.
AP.USGP.2.4.A.1: Presidents use powers and perform functions of the office, with support from the Vice-President, Cabinet, and Executive Office of the President, to accomplish a policy agenda.
AP.USGP.2.4.A.2: The powers of the president include both formal and informal powers.
AP.USGP.2.4.A.2.i: Vetoes and pocket vetoes are formal powers that enable the president to check Congress, but vetoes can be overridden with a 2/3 vote while pocket vetoes cannot be overridden with a 2/3 vote.
AP.USGP.2.4.A.2.ii: Foreign policy powers that influence relations with foreign nations are both formal (commander-in-chief and treaties) and informal (executive agreements).
AP.USGP.2.4.A.2.iii: Bargaining and persuasion are informal powers that enable the president to secure congressional action.
AP.USGP.2.4.A.2.iv: Executive orders allow the president to manage the federal government and are implied by the president's vested executive power or by power delegated by Congress.
AP.USGP.2.4.A.2.v: Signing statements are informal powers that inform Congress and the public of thepresident's interpretation of laws passed by Congress and signed by the president.
AP.USGP.2.5.A: Explain how the president's agenda can create tension and frequent confrontations with Congress.
AP.USGP.2.5.A.1: Senate confirmation is an important check on appointment powers but there can be a potential for conflict based on who is chosen by the president for appointments, including:
AP.USGP.2.5.A.1.iii: Some positions within the Executive Office of the President.
AP.USGP.2.5.A.1.i;v: Supreme Court Justices, Court of Appeals judges, and District Court judges.
AP.USGP.2.5.A.2: Senate confirmation is an important check on appointment powers, but the president's longest lasting influence lies in life-tenured judicial appointments.
AP.USGP.2.5.A.3: Policy conflicts with the congressional agenda (the formal list of policies Congress is considering at any given time) can lead the president to use executive orders and directives to the bureaucracy to address the president's own agenda items.
AP.USGP.2.6.A: Explain how presidents have interpreted and justified their use of formal and informal powers.
AP.USGP.2.6.A.1: Federalist No. `70` offers justification for a single executive by arguing a strong executive is “essential to the protection of the country against foreign attacks, to the steady administration of the laws, to the protection of property, and to the security of liberty.”
AP.USGP.2.6.A.2: Passage of the `text(Twenty-Second)` Amendment, which established presidential term limits, demonstrates concern about the expansion of presidential power.
AP.USGP.2.6.A.3: Different perspectives on the presidential role, ranging from a limited to a more expansive interpretation and use of power, continue to be debated in the context of contemporary events.
AP.USGP.2.7.A: Explain how communication technology has changed the president's relationship with the national constituency and the other branches.
AP.USGP.2.7.A.1: The impact of presidential communication has increased with advances in communication technology.
AP.USGP.2.7.A.1.i: Modern technology, such as social media, allows for rapid responses to political issues.
AP.USGP.2.7.A.1.ii: Nationally broadcast State of the Union messages and the president's bully pulpit are tools for agenda setting that use the media to influence public views about which policies are the most important.
AP.USGP.2.8.A: Explain the principle of judicial review and how it checks the power of other branches.
AP.USGP.2.8.A.1: The foundation for powers of the judicial branch and the argument for how its independence checks the power of other branches is set forth in the following documents, respectively:
AP.USGP.2.9: The Role Of The Judicial Branch
AP.USGP.2.9.A: Explain the role of legal precedent in judicial decision making.
AP.USGP.2.9.A.1: Stare decisis (the legal doctrine under which courts follow legal precedents when deciding cases with similar facts) plays an important role in judicial decision making.
AP.USGP.2.9.A.2: Ideological changes in the composition of the Supreme Court due to presidential appointments have led to the Court's establishing new or rejecting existing precedents.
AP.USGP.2.10.A: Explain how life tenure can lead to debate about the Supreme Court's power.
AP.USGP.2.10.A.1: Life tenure for justices allows the court to function independent of the current political climate. As a result of this independence, the Court can deliver controversial or unpopular court decisions, which in turn can lead to debate about the court's power.
AP.USGP.2.11.A: Explain how the exercise of judicial review can lead to debate about the Supreme Court's power.
AP.USGP.2.11.A.1: Political discussion about the Supreme Court's power is illustrated by the ongoing debate over differing interpretations of judicial review.
AP.USGP.2.11.A.1.i: Judicial activism asserts that judicial review allows the courts to overturn current Constitutional and case precedent or invalidate legislative or executive acts.
AP.USGP.2.11.A.1.ii: Judicial restraint asserts that judicial review should be constrained to decisions that adhere to current Constitutional and case precedent.
AP.USGP.2.11.B: Explain how other branches in the government can limit the Supreme Court's power.
AP.USGP.2.11.B.1: Restrictions on the Supreme Court are represented by:
AP.USGP.2.11.B.1.i: Congressional legislation to modify the impact of prior Supreme Court decisions.
AP.USGP.2.11.B.1.iii: Judicial appointments and confirmations which may shift the ideological balance of the court.
AP.USGP.2.11.B.1.iv: The president and states delaying implementation of a Supreme Court decision.
AP.USGP.2.11.B.1.v: Enacting legislation to limit the cases the Supreme Court can hear on appeal by removing the court's jurisdiction over a case.
AP.USGP.2.12.A: Explain how the bureaucracy carries out the responsibilities of the federal government.
AP.USGP.2.12.A.1: The federal bureaucracy is composed of departments, agencies, commissions, and government corporations that implement policy by:
AP.USGP.2.12.A.1.iv: Forming iron triangles (alliances of congressional committees, bureaucratic agencies, and interest groups that are prominent in specific policy areas).
AP.USGP.2.12.A.1.v: Creating issue networks (temporary coalitions that form to promote a common issue or agenda).
AP.USGP.2.12.A.2: The civil service primarily uses a merit system that prioritizes hiring and promotion based on professionalism, specialization, and neutrality, as opposed to political patronage, whereby bureaucratic jobs are politically appointed.
AP.USGP.2.13.A: Explain how the federal bureaucracy uses delegated discretionary authority for rulemaking and implementation.
AP.USGP.2.13.A.1: The federal bureaucracy uses discretionary power as delegated by Congress to interpret and implement policies. Through their rulemaking authority, federal bureaucratic agencies utilize their discretion to create and enforce regulations. Bureaucratic agencies include:
AP.USGP.2.14.A: Explain how Congress uses its oversight power in its relationship with the executive branch.
AP.USGP.2.14.A.1: Congressional oversight of the bureaucracy to ensure that legislation is implemented as intended includes:
AP.USGP.2.14.A.1.i: Review, monitoring, and supervision of bureaucratic agencies.
AP.USGP.2.14.A.1.ii: Investigation and committee hearings of bureaucratic activity.
AP.USGP.2.14.A.1.iii: Power of the purse (the ability of Congress to check the bureaucracy by appropriating or withholding funds).
AP.USGP.2.14.A.2: As a means to curtail the use of presidential power, congressional oversight serves as a check of executive authorization.
AP.USGP.2.14.B: Explain how the president ensures that executive branch agencies and departments carry out their responsibilities in concert with the goals of the administration.
AP.USGP.2.14.B.1: Presidential ideology, authority, and influence affect how executive branch agencies carry out the goals of the administration.
AP.USGP.2.14.B.2: Compliance monitoring ensures that funds are being used properly and regulations are being followed. Compliance monitoring can pose a challenge to policy implementation.
AP.USGP.2.15.A: Explain the extent to which governmental branches can hold the bureaucracy accountable given the competing interests of Congress, the president, and the federal courts.
AP.USGP.2.15.A.1: Formal and informal powers of Congress, the president, and the courts over the bureaucracy are used to maintain its accountability.
AP.USGP.2.15.B: Explain how the distribution of powers among the three branches of government impacts policymaking.
AP.USGP.2.15.B.1: The allocation of powers among the three branches of government creates multiple access points for stakeholders and institutions to influence public policy.
AP.USGP.2.15.B.2: National policymaking is constrained by the sharing of powers between the three branches.
AP.USGP.3.1.A: Explain how the U.S. Constitution protects individual liberties and rights.
AP.USGP.3.1.A.1: The U.S. Constitution includes a Bill of Rights specifically designed to protect individual liberties and rights.
AP.USGP.3.1.A.2: Civil liberties are constitutionally established guarantees and freedoms that protect citizens, opinions, and property against arbitrary government interference.
AP.USGP.3.1.A.3: The application of the Bill of Rights is continuously interpreted by the courts.
AP.USGP.3.1.B: Describe the rights protected in the Bill of Rights.
AP.USGP.3.1.B.1: The Bill of Rights consists of the `text(first ten)` Amendments to the Constitution, which enumerate the liberties and rights of individuals.
AP.USGP.3.2.A: Explain the extent to which the Supreme Court's interpretation of the `text(First)` Amendment reflects a commitment to religious liberty.
AP.USGP.3.2.A.1: The interpretation and application of the `text(First)` Amendment's establishment and free exercise clauses reflect an ongoing tension between government power to make law and an individual's right to religious freedom.
AP.USGP.3.3.A: Explain the extent to which the Supreme Court's interpretation of the `text(First)` Amendment reflects a commitment to free speech.
AP.USGP.3.3.A.1: The Supreme Court has held that speech, including symbolic speech (nonverbal action that communicates an idea or belief), is protected by the `text(First)` Amendment.
AP.USGP.3.3.A.2: Efforts to balance social order and individual freedom are reflected in interpretations of the `text(First)` Amendment that limit speech, including:
AP.USGP.3.3.A.2.i: Time, place, and manner regulations that impose restrictions such as limits on the time of day an event can be held, limits on where an event can be held, and limits on the noise levels at an event.
AP.USGP.3.3.A.2.ii: Limitations on some obscene and offensive communication.
AP.USGP.3.3.A.2.iii: Protections against defamation (language that harms the reputation of another) including libel (written communication) and slander (oral communication).
AP.USGP.3.3.A.2.iv: Restrictions on speech that create a clear and present danger and subsequent interpretations which have refined those restrictions.
AP.USGP.3.4.A: Explain the extent to which the Supreme Court's interpretation of the `text(First)` Amendment reflects a commitment to individual liberty.
AP.USGP.3.4.A.1: The Supreme Court bolstered the freedom of the press, affirming support for a heavy presumption against prior restraint even in cases involving national security.
AP.USGP.3.5.A: Explain the extent to which the Supreme Court's interpretation of the `text(Second)` Amendment reflects a commitment to individual liberty.
AP.USGP.3.5.A.1: The Supreme Court's decisions on the `text(Second)` Amendment rest upon its constitutional interpretation of the right to bear arms.
AP.USGP.3.6: Amendments: Balancing Individual Freedom With Public Order & Safety
AP.USGP.3.6.A: Explain how the Supreme Court has attempted to balance claims of individual freedom with laws and enforcement procedures that promote public order and safety.
AP.USGP.3.6.A.1: Court decisions defining cruel and unusual punishment involve interpretation of the `text(Eighth)` Amendment and its application to death penalty statutes.
AP.USGP.3.6.A.2: The debate about the `text(Second)` and `text(Fourth)` Amendments involves concerns about public safety and whether or not the government regulation of firearms or collection of digital metadata promotes or interferes with public safety and individual rights.
AP.USGP.3.7.A: Explain the implications of the doctrine of selective incorporation.
AP.USGP.3.7.A.1: The doctrine of selective incorporation has imposed limitations on state regulation of civil liberties by extending select protections of the Bill of Rights to the states through the due process clause of the `text(Fourteenth)` Amendment.
AP.USGP.3.8: Amendments: Due Process & The Rights Of The Accused
AP.USGP.3.8.A: Explain the extent to which the government is limited by procedural due process from infringing upon individual rights.
AP.USGP.3.8.A.1: The `text(Fifth)` and `text(Fourteenth)` Amendments include clauses which state that the government may not infringe on a person's right to life, liberty, or property without due process of law. The due process clause in the `text(Fifth)` Amendment applies to the national government and the due process clause in the `text(Fourteenth)` Amendment applies to states. Some government interests may justify the restriction of individual rights; for example, speech can be limited when it is shown to present a danger to public safety.
AP.USGP.3.8.A.2: Procedural due process requires that government officials use methods that are not arbitrary when making and carrying out decisions affecting constitutionally protected rights. These procedural due process protections are reinforced by key protections enshrined in other provisions of the Bill of Rights and key legal doctrines established by the Supreme Court. For example, the Miranda rule requires accused persons to be informed of some procedural protections found in the `text(Fifth)` and `text(Sixth)` Amendments prior to interrogation. However, these procedural protections are not absolute. A public safety exception has been sanctioned by the Court that allows unwarned interrogation to stand as direct evidence in court.
AP.USGP.3.8.A.3: Procedural rights of the accused and the prohibition of unreasonable searches and seizures are intended to ensure that individual liberties are not eclipsed by the need for social order and security, including:
AP.USGP.3.8.A.3.i: The right to legal counsel, speedy and public trial, and an impartial jury.
AP.USGP.3.8.A.3.ii: Protection against warrantless searches of cell phone data under the `text(Fourth)` Amendment.
AP.USGP.3.8.A.3.iii: Limitations placed on bulk collection of telecommunication metadata (Patriot and USA Freedom Acts).
AP.USGP.3.8.A.4: Procedural due process also protects the rights of the accused during a trial. The Bill of Rights guarantees the right to an attorney and protection from unreasonable searches and seizures. The exclusionary rule, as decided by the Supreme Court, stipulates that evidence illegally seized by law enforcement officers in violation of the suspect's `text(Fourth)` Amendment rights (including the right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures) cannot be used against that suspect in criminal prosecution.
AP.USGP.3.9: Amendments: Due Process & The Right To Privacy
AP.USGP.3.9.A: Explain the extent to which the government is limited by substantive due process from infringing upon individual rights.
AP.USGP.3.9.A.1: Over time, the Supreme Court has recognized constitutionally protected rights that are not explicitly listed in the Bill of Rights. These unenumerated rights include the right to privacy. Justices and scholars have drawn on several arguments to defend the existence of unenumerated rights. Some argue that an unenumerated right is implied by certain amendments that assume the existence of such rights. Others argue that the `text(Ninth)` Amendment, which states that individuals have protected rights beyond those listed in the first eight amendments, provides support for the existence of unenumerated rights. In a range of cases, the Supreme Court has used substantive due process to examine whether government laws and actions are arbitrary infringements of individual rights.
AP.USGP.3.9.A.2: While a right to privacy is not explicitly named in the Constitution, the Supreme Court, in Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), interpreted the due process clause to protect the right of privacy from government infringement. In Roe v. Wade (1973), the Supreme Court held that the application of substantive due process further extended the privacy right to abortion. The Supreme Court's decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (`text(2022)`) overturned Roe v. Wade, holding that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, leaving decisions about the regulation of abortion to legislatures. AP.USGP.3.10.A: Explain how constitutional provisions have supported and motivated social movements.
AP.USGP.3.10.A.1: Civil rights protect individuals from discrimination based on characteristics such as race, national origin, religion, and sex; these rights are guaranteed to all persons under the due process and equal protection clauses of the U.S. Constitution, as well as acts of Congress.
AP.USGP.3.10.A.2: The civil rights movement, the women's rights movement, and advocacy for LGBTQ rights are evidence of how the equal protection clause can support and motivate social movements, as represented by:
AP.USGP.3.10.A.2.i: Dr. Martin Luther King's “Letter from a Birmingham Jail” and the civil rights movement of the 1960s.
AP.USGP.3.10.A.2.ii: The National Organization for Women and the women's rights movement.
AP.USGP.3.11.A: Explain how the government has responded to social movements.
AP.USGP.3.11.A.1: The government can respond to social movements through court rulings and/or policies.
AP.USGP.3.11.A.1.i: Supreme Court decisions which declared that race-based school segregation violates the `text(Fourteenth)` Amendment's equal protection clause.
AP.USGP.3.11.A.1.ii: The Civil Rights Act of `text(1964)` prohibits discrimination in public places, provides for the integration of schools and other public facilities, and makes employment discrimination illegal.
AP.USGP.3.11.A.1.iii: Title IX of the Education Amendments Act of `text(1972)` prohibits sex discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.
AP.USGP.3.11.A.1.iv: The Voting Rights Act of `text(1965)` prohibits racial discrimination in voting.
AP.USGP.3.12.A: Explain how the Court has at times allowed the restriction of the civil rights of minority groups and at other times has protected those rights.
AP.USGP.3.12.A.1: Decisions demonstrating that minority rights have been restricted at times and protected at other times include:
AP.USGP.3.12.A.1.i: State laws and Supreme Court holdings based on the “separate but equal” doctrine restricting African American access to the same restaurants, hotels, schools, etc., as the majority white population.
AP.USGP.3.12.A.1.ii: Court decisions declaring that race-based school segregation violates the `text(Fourteenth)` Amendment's equal protection clause.
AP.USGP.3.12.A.1.iii: The Supreme Court upholding the rights of the majority in cases that limit and prohibit majority-minority districting.
AP.USGP.3.13.A: Describe Supreme Court debates about affirmative action policies.
AP.USGP.3.13.A.1: Affirmative action refers to policies intended to address workplace and educational disparities related to race, ethnic origin, gender, disability, and age. Supreme Court debate has focused on whether affirmative action is protected by the equal protection clause of the `text(Fourteenth)` Amendment to the Constitution.
AP.USGP.4.1.A: Explain the relationship between core beliefs of U.S. citizens and attitudes about the role of government.
AP.USGP.4.1.A.1: Different interpretations of core values, including individualism (each person has the ability to shape their life and destiny through the choices they make), equality of opportunity (all people are given an equal chance to compete), free enterprise (the market determines prices, products, and services), and rule of law (every person, even those in power, must follow and is accountable to the same laws that govern all), affect the relationship between citizens and the federal government and that citizens have with each other.
AP.USGP.4.2.A: Explain how cultural factors influence political socialization.
AP.USGP.4.2.A.1: Political socialization refers to the process by which individuals develop political beliefs, values, opinions, and behaviors. Family, schools, peers, media, and social environments (including civic and religious organizations) contribute to the development of an individual's political attitudes and values through the process of political socialization.
AP.USGP.4.2.A.2: U.S. political culture is defined by its democratic ideals, principles, and core values. As a result of globalization, U.S. political culture has both influenced and been influenced by the values of other countries.
AP.USGP.4.3.A: Explain how social factors impact political ideology.
AP.USGP.4.3.A.1: Generational effects (experiences shared by people of a common age) and life cycle effects (experiences a person encounters during different life stages) contribute to the development of a person's political ideology.
AP.USGP.4.4: Influence Of Political Events On Ideology
AP.USGP.4.4.A: Explain how major political events influence political ideology.
AP.USGP.4.4.A.1: Major political events can influence the development of individual political attitudes, which is an example of political socialization. Political socialization, in turn, influences political ideology.
AP.USGP.4.5.A: Describe the elements of a scientific poll.
AP.USGP.4.5.A.1: Public opinion data that can affect elections and policy debates is influenced by different types of scientific polls such as:
AP.USGP.4.5.A.1.i: Opinion polls (measuring public opinion on various issues).
AP.USGP.4.5.A.1.ii: Benchmark polls (creating baseline views of a candidate).
AP.USGP.4.5.A.1.iii: Tracking polls (following how views of a candidate change during a campaign).
AP.USGP.4.5.A.1.iv: Exit polls (collecting data on why people voted the way they did).
AP.USGP.4.5.A.2: Public opinion data that can affect elections and policy debates is influenced by polling methodology. Polling methodology is more precise when it includes:
AP.USGP.4.5.A.2.i: Accurate sampling methods, including calculating a margin of error.
AP.USGP.4.5.A.2.ii: Neutral framing of questions (specific and unbiased wording of questions).
AP.USGP.4.5.A.2.iii: Accurate reporting (clear reporting and conclusions that can be supported by the data).
AP.USGP.4.6.A: Explain the quality and credibility of claims based on public opinion data.
AP.USGP.4.6.A.1: The relationship between scientific polling and elections and policy debates is affected by the:
AP.USGP.4.6.A.1.i: Importance of public opinion as a source of political influence in a given election or policy debate.
AP.USGP.4.6.A.1.ii: Reliability and veracity of public opinion data.
AP.USGP.4.7.A: Explain how ideologies of the two major parties shape policy debates.
AP.USGP.4.7.A.1: The Democratic Party (D or DEM) platforms generally align more closely to liberal ideological positions, and the Republican Party (R or GOP) platforms generally align more closely to conservative ideological positions.
AP.USGP.4.8.A: Explain how U.S. political culture (e.g., democratic ideals, principles, and core values) influences the formation, goals, and implementation of public policy over time.
AP.USGP.4.8.A.1: Because the U.S. is a democracy with a diverse society, public policies generated at any given time reflect the attitudes and beliefs of citizens who choose to participate in politics at that time.
AP.USGP.4.8.A.2: The balancing dynamic of individual liberty and government efforts to promote stability and order has been reflected in policy debates and their outcomes over time.
AP.USGP.4.9.A: Explain how different political ideologies affect the role of government in regulating the marketplace.
AP.USGP.4.9.A.1: Liberal ideologies favor more governmental regulation of the marketplace, conservative ideologies favor fewer regulations, and libertarian ideologies favor little or no regulation of the marketplace beyond the protection of property rights and voluntary trade.
AP.USGP.4.9.B: Explain how fiscal and monetary policy actions influence economic conditions.
AP.USGP.4.9.B.1: Fiscal policy consists of actions taken by Congress and the president to influence economic conditions and includes Keynesian and supply-side positions.
AP.USGP.4.9.B.2: Monetary policy consists of actions taken by the Federal Reserve (the Fed) to influence interest rates which affect broader economic conditions. The Fed is an independent agency which seeks to achieve maximum employment and price stability.
AP.USGP.4.10.A: Explain how political ideologies vary on the role of the government in addressing social issues.
AP.USGP.4.10.A.1: Liberal ideologies generally favor more national government involvement to address some social issues such as education and public health, with less responsibility for these issues left to state governments.
AP.USGP.4.10.A.2: Conservative ideologies generally favor less national government involvement to address some social issues such as education and public health, with more responsibility for these issues left to state governments.
AP.USGP.4.10.A.3: Libertarian ideologies generally favor little national or state government involvement except when national or state government is protecting private property or individual liberty.
AP.USGP.4.10.B: Explain how different ideologies affect policy on social issues.
AP.USGP.4.10.B.1: Policy trends concerning the level of government involvement in social issues reflect the success of conservative or liberal perspectives in political parties.
AP.USGP.5.1: Voting Rights & Models Of Voting Behavior
AP.USGP.5.1.A: Describe the voting rights protections in the Constitution and in legislation.
AP.USGP.5.1.A.1: Expansion of opportunities for political participation are found in the legal protections of the Amendments to the Constitution.
AP.USGP.5.1.A.1.i: The `14^text(th)` Amendment granted citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the U.S., including formerly enslaved people.
AP.USGP.5.1.A.1.ii: The `15^text(th)` Amendment granted African American men the right to vote.
AP.USGP.5.1.A.1.iii: The `17^text(th)` Amendment changed the practice for electing Senators from a vote by state legislatures to a direct vote by the people.
AP.USGP.5.1.A.1.iv: The `19^text(th)` Amendment granted women the right to vote.
AP.USGP.5.1.A.1.v: The `24^text(th)` Amendment eliminated poll taxes, a structural barrier to voting.
AP.USGP.5.1.A.1.vi: The `26^text(th)` Amendment lowered the voting age to `18`.
AP.USGP.5.1.B: Describe different models of voting behavior.
AP.USGP.5.1.B.1: Various political models explain differences in voting behavior.
AP.USGP.5.1.B.1.i: Rational choice voting refers to individuals who base their decisions on what is perceived to be in their best interest.
AP.USGP.5.1.B.1.ii: Retrospective voting refers to individuals who decide whether the party or candidate in power should be reelected based on the recent past.
AP.USGP.5.1.B.1.iii: Prospective voting refers to individuals who vote based on predictions of how a party or candidate will perform in the future.
AP.USGP.5.1.B.1.iv: Straight ticket voting refers to individuals who vote for all of the candidates from one political party on a ballot.
AP.USGP.5.2.A: Explain the roles that individual choice and state laws play in voter turnout in elections.
AP.USGP.5.2.A.1: Structural barriers (such as polling hours, availability of absentee ballots, etc.), political efficacy (the belief that an individual's participation in the political process will make a difference), and demographics can influence differences in voter turnout in the U.S.
AP.USGP.5.2.A.2: The following can influence voter turnout:
AP.USGP.5.2.A.2.i: Differences in state-controlled elections (the hours polls are open, Voter ID laws, variations in funding for polling places and workers, variations in types of voting allowed, such as voting by mail, absentee voting, and early voting).
AP.USGP.5.2.A.2.ii: Variations in voter registration laws and procedures (registering in-person, online, or automatically).
AP.USGP.5.2.A.2.iii: Election type (more turnout for presidential elections than midterm elections).
AP.USGP.5.2.A.3: Demographic characteristics and political efficacy or engagement are used to predict the likelihood of whether an individual will vote.
AP.USGP.5.2.A.4.iv: Religious beliefs or affiliation, age, gender, race and ethnicity, and other demographic characteristics.

AP.USGP.5.3.B: Explain the function and impact of political parties on the electorate and government.
AP.USGP.5.3.B.1: The functions and impact of political parties on the electorate and government are represented by:
AP.USGP.5.3.B.1.iv: Campaign management, including fundraising and media strategy.
AP.USGP.5.3.B.1.v: The committee and party leadership systems in legislatures.
AP.USGP.5.4: How & Why Political Parties Change & Adapt
AP.USGP.5.4.A: Explain why and how political parties change and adapt.
AP.USGP.5.4.A.1: Parties have adapted to candidate-centered campaigns where the public focus is on the characteristics of the candidate and not on the party. The role of parties in nominating candidates has also been weakened.
AP.USGP.5.4.A.2: Parties may adapt their policies and messaging to appeal to various demographic coalitions.
AP.USGP.5.4.A.3: The structure of parties has been influenced by:
AP.USGP.5.4.A.3.i: Critical elections (elections in which there is a realignment of political party support among voters).
AP.USGP.5.4.A.3.iii: Changes in communication and data management technology.
AP.USGP.5.4.A.4: Parties use communication technology and voter data management to disseminate, control, and clarify political messages and enhance outreach and mobilization efforts.
AP.USGP.5.5.A: Explain how structural barriers affect third-party and independent candidate success.
AP.USGP.5.5.A.1: In comparison to proportional systems, winner- take-all voting districts serve as a structural barrier to third-party and independent candidate success. Winner-take-all voting advantages the two-party system in the U.S.
AP.USGP.5.5.A.2: The incorporation of third-party agendas into platforms of major political parties serves as a barrier to third-party and independent candidate success.
AP.USGP.5.6.A: Explain the benefits and potential problems of interest group influence on elections and policymaking.
AP.USGP.5.6.A.1: Interest groups may represent very specific or more general interests, and can educate voters and office holders, conduct lobbying, draft legislation, and mobilize membership to apply pressure on and work with legislators and government agencies. Interest groups may also file an amicus curiae brief (a written document submitted as a “friend of the court” to provide additional information for justices to consider when reviewing a case).
AP.USGP.5.6.A.2: In addition to working within party coalitions, interest groups exert influence through iron triangles and issue networks that help interest groups exert influence across political party coalitions.
AP.USGP.5.6.B: Explain how variation in types of interest groups and the resources interest groups possess affects their ability to influence elections and policymaking.
AP.USGP.5.6.B.1: The inequality of interest group resources affects the amount of influence they may have on the policymaking process.
AP.USGP.5.6.B.1.i: Some interest groups, such as AARP, have large memberships, are able to mobilize those members, and possess access to large financial reserves.
AP.USGP.5.6.B.1.ii: Some interest groups have more direct and more frequent access to important people in the policy process.
AP.USGP.5.6.B.1.iii: Free riders are individuals who benefit from the work of an interest group without providing financial support. Interest groups may deal with this issue by providing selective benefits, goods and services that are only available to members, to encourage more people to join.
AP.USGP.5.7.A: Explain how various political actors influence public policy outcomes.
AP.USGP.5.7.A.1: Single-issue groups, ideological/social movements, and protest movements form with the goal of affecting society and policymaking.
AP.USGP.5.7.A.2: Competing actors such as interest groups, professional organizations, social movements, the military, and bureaucratic agencies influence policymaking, such as the federal budget process, at key stages and to varying degrees.
AP.USGP.5.7.A.3: Elections and political parties are related to major policy shifts or initiatives, occasionally leading to political realignments of voting constituencies.
AP.USGP.5.8.A: Explain how the different processes work in a U.S. presidential election.
AP.USGP.5.8.A.1: The process and outcomes in U.S. presidential elections are affected by:
AP.USGP.5.8.A.1.i: Incumbency advantage phenomenon (benefits current officeholders possess over challengers).
AP.USGP.5.8.A.1.ii: Open and closed primaries (voting processes to elect candidates).
AP.USGP.5.8.A.1.iii: Caucuses (closed meetings of party members to select candidates or decide policy).
AP.USGP.5.8.B: Explain how the Electoral College affects U.S. presidential elections.
AP.USGP.5.8.B.1: States can choose how they allocate their electors; most states use a winner-take-all system. Because the results of the Electoral College vote may not be the same as the popular vote nationwide, there is an ongoing debate over the Electoral College.

AP.USGP.5.9.A.1: The process and outcomes in U.S. congressional elections are affected by:
AP.USGP.5.10.A: Explain how campaign organizations and strategies affect the election process.
AP.USGP.5.10.A.1: The benefits and drawbacks of modern campaigns are represented by:
AP.USGP.5.10.A.1.ii: Rising campaign costs and intensive fundraising efforts.
AP.USGP.5.10.A.1.iv: Impact of and reliance on social media for campaign communication and fundraising.
AP.USGP.5.11.A: Explain how the organization, finance, and strategies of national political campaigns affect the election process.
AP.USGP.5.11.A.1: Federal legislation and case law pertaining to campaign finance demonstrate the ongoing debate over the role of money in political and free speech, as set forth in:
AP.USGP.5.11.A.1.i: The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of `text(2002)`, which was an effort to ban soft money and reduce attack ads with “Stand by Your Ad” provision: “I'm [candidate's name] and I approve this message”.
