CC.E11-12.W.B.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
CC.E11-12.W.B.5: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach, focusing on addressing what is most significant for a specific purpose and audience.
CC.E11-12.W.B.6: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce, publish, and update individual or shared writing products in response to ongoing feedback, including new arguments or information.

CC.E11-12.W.C.8: Gather relevant information from multiple authoritative print and digital sources, using advanced searches effectively; assess the strengths and limitations of each source in terms of the task, purpose, and audience; integrate information into the text selectively to maintain the flow of ideas, avoiding plagiarism and overreliance on any one source and following a standard format for citation.
CC.E11-12.W.C.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

CC.E11-12.W.C.9.b: Apply grades 11-12 Reading standards to literary nonfiction (e.g., “Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including the application of constitutional principles and use of legal reasoning [e.g., in U.S. Supreme Court Case majority opinions and dissents] and the premises, purposes, and arguments in works of public advocacy [e.g., The Federalist, presidential addresses]”).
CC.E11-12.W.D.10: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
CC.E11-12.SL.A.1: Initiate and participate effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grades 11-12 topics, texts, and issues, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.
CC.E11-12.SL.A.1.a: Come to discussions prepared, having read and researched material under study; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence from texts and other research on the topic or issue to stimulate a thoughtful, well-reasoned exchange of ideas.
CC.E11-12.SL.A.1.b: Work with peers to promote civil, democratic discussions and decision-making, set clear goals and deadlines, and establish individual roles as needed.
CC.E11-12.SL.A.1.c: Propel conversations by posing and responding to questions that probe reasoning and evidence; ensure a hearing for a full range of positions on a topic or issue; clarify, verify, or challenge ideas and conclusions; and promote divergent and creative perspectives.
CC.E11-12.SL.A.1.d: Respond thoughtfully to diverse perspectives; synthesize comments, claims, and evidence made on all sides of an issue; resolve contradictions when possible; and determine what additional information or research is required to deepen the investigation or complete the task.
CC.E11-12.SL.A.2: Integrate multiple sources of information presented in diverse formats and media (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally) in order to make informed decisions and solve problems, evaluating the credibility and accuracy of each source and noting any discrepancies among the data.
CC.E11-12.SL.A.3: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric, assessing the stance, premises, links among ideas, word choice, points of emphasis, and tone used.
CC.E11-12.SL.B.4: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence, conveying a clear and distinct perspective, such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning, alternative or opposing perspectives are addressed, and the organization, development, substance, and style are appropriate to purpose, audience, and a range of formal and informal tasks.
CC.E11-12.SL.B.5: Make strategic use of digital media (e.g., textual, graphical, audio, visual, and interactive elements) in presentations to enhance understanding of findings, reasoning, and evidence and to add interest.
CC.E11-12.SL.B.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating a command of formal English when indicated or appropriate. (See grades 11-12 Language standards 1 and 3 on page 54 for specific expectations.)

CC.E11-12.L.A.1.b: Resolve issues of complex or contested usage, consulting references (e.g., Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage, Garner's Modern American Usage) as needed.
CC.E11-12.L.A.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
CC.E11-12.L.B.3: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.
CC.E11-12.L.B.3.a: Vary syntax for effect, consulting references (e.g., Tufte's Artful Sentences) for guidance as needed; apply an understanding of syntax to the study of complex texts when reading.

CC.E11-12.L.C.4.a: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence, paragraph, or text; a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
CC.E11-12.L.C.4.b: Identify and correctly use patterns of word changes that indicate different meanings or parts of speech (e.g., conceive, conception, conceivable).

CC.E11-12.L.C.4.d: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

CC.M9-12.A-SSE.A.1: Interpret expressions that represent a quantity in terms of its context.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.A.1.a: Interpret parts of an expression, such as terms, factors, and coefficients.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.A.1.b: Interpret complicated expressions by viewing one or more of their parts as a single entity.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.A.2: Use the structure of an expression to identify ways to rewrite it.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.B: Write expressions in equivalent forms to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.B.3: Choose and produce an equivalent form of an expression to reveal and explain properties of the quantity represented by the expression.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.B.3.a: Factor a quadratic expression to reveal the zeros of the function it defines.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.B.3.b: Complete the square in a quadratic expression to reveal the maximum or minimum value of the function it defines.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.B.3.c: Use the properties of exponents to transform expressions for exponential functions.
CC.M9-12.A-SSE.B.4: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series (when the common ratio is not `1`), and use the formula to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.A.1: Understand that polynomials form a system analogous to the integers, namely, they are closed under the operations of addition, subtraction, and multiplication; add, subtract, and multiply polynomials.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.B: Understand the relationship between zeros and factors of polynomials.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.B.2: Know and apply the Remainder Theorem: For a polynomial `p(x)` and a number `a`, the remainder on division by `x-a` is `p(a)`, so `p(a)=0` if and only if `(x-a)` is a factor of `p(x)`.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.B.3: Identify zeros of polynomials when suitable factorizations are available, and use the zeros to construct a rough graph of the function defined by the polynomial.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.C: Use polynomial identities to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.C.4: Prove polynomial identities and use them to describe numerical relationships.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.C.5: Know and apply the Binomial Theorem for the expansion of `(x+y)^n` in powers of `xandy` for a positive integer n, where `xandy` are any numbers, with coefficients determined for example by Pascal's Triangle.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.D.6: Rewrite simple rational expressions in different forms; write `(a(x))/(b(x))` in the form `q(x)+(r(x))/(b(x))`, where `a(x),b(x),q(x),andr(x)` are polynomials with the degree of `r(x)` less than the degree of `b(x)`, using inspection, long division, or, for the more complicated examples, a computer algebra system.
CC.M9-12.A-APR.D.7: Understand that rational expressions form a system analogous to the rational numbers, closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by a nonzero rational expression; add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational expressions.
CC.M9-12.A-CED.A: Create equations that describe numbers or relationships.
CC.M9-12.A-CED.A.1: Create equations and inequalities in one variable and use them to solve problems. Include equations arising from linear and quadratic functions, and simple rational and exponential functions.
CC.M9-12.A-CED.A.2: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.
CC.M9-12.A-CED.A.3: Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or non-viable options in a modeling context.
CC.M9-12.A-CED.A.4: Rearrange formulas to highlight a quantity of interest, using the same reasoning as in solving equations.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.A: Understand solving equations as a process of reasoning and explain the reasoning.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.A.1: Explain each step in solving a simple equation as following from the equality of numbers asserted at the previous step, starting from the assumption that the original equation has a solution. Construct a viable argument to justify a solution method.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.A.2: Solve simple rational and radical equations in one variable, and give examples showing how extraneous solutions may arise.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.B: Solve equations and inequalities in one variable.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.B.3: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.B.4: Solve quadratic equations in one variable.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.B.4.a: Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation in `x` into an equation of the form `(x-p)^2=q` that has the same solutions. Derive the quadratic formula from this form.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.B.4.b: Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for `x^2=49`), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation. Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as `a+-bi` for real numbers `aandb`.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.C.5: Prove that, given a system of two equations in two variables, replacing one equation by the sum of that equation and a multiple of the other produces a system with the same solutions.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.C.6: Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.C.7: Solve a simple system consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.C.8: Represent a system of linear equations as a single matrix equation in a vector variable.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.C.9: Find the inverse of a matrix if it exists and use it to solve systems of linear equations (using technology for matrices of dimension `3xx3` or greater).
CC.M9-12.A-REI.D: Represent and solve equations and inequalities graphically.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.D.10: Understand that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions plotted in the coordinate plane, often forming a curve (which could be a line).
CC.M9-12.A-REI.D.11: Explain why the `xtext(-coordinates)` of the points where the graphs of the equations `y=f(x)andy=g(x)` intersect are the solutions of the equation `f(x)=g(x)`; find the solutions approximately, e.g., using technology to graph the functions, make tables of values, or find successive approximations. Include cases where `f(x)` and/or `g(x)` are linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
CC.M9-12.A-REI.D.12: Graph the solutions to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.A: Understand the concept of a function and use function notation.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.A.1: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If `f` is a function and `x` is an element of its domain, then `f(x)` denotes the output of `f` corresponding to the input `x`. The graph of f is the graph of the equation `y=f(x)`.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.A.2: Use function notation, evaluate functions for inputs in their domains, and interpret statements that use function notation in terms of a context.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.A.3: Recognize that sequences are functions, sometimes defined recursively, whose domain is a subset of the integers.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.B: Interpret functions that arise in applications in terms of the context.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.B.4: For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship. Key features include: intercepts; intervals where the function is increasing, decreasing, positive, or negative; relative maximums and minimums; symmetries; end behavior; and periodicity.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.B.5: Relate the domain of a function to its graph and, where applicable, to the quantitative relationship it describes.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.B.6: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.7: Graph functions expressed symbolically and show key features of the graph, by hand in simple cases and using technology for more complicated cases.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.7.a: Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maxima, and minima.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.7.b: Graph square root, cube root, and piecewise-defined functions, including step functions and absolute value functions.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.7.c: Graph polynomial functions, identifying zeros when suitable factorizations are available, and showing end behavior.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.7.d: Graph rational functions, identifying zeros and asymptotes when suitable factorizations are available, and showing end behavior.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.7.e: Graph exponential and logarithmic functions, showing intercepts and end behavior, and trigonometric functions, showing period, midline, and amplitude.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.8: Write a function defined by an expression in different but equivalent forms to reveal and explain different properties of the function.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.8.a: Use the process of factoring and completing the square in a quadratic function to show zeros, extreme values, and symmetry of the graph, and interpret these in terms of a context.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.8.b: Use the properties of exponents to interpret expressions for exponential functions.
CC.M9-12.F-IF.C.9: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
CC.M9-12.F-BF.A: Build a function that models a relationship between two quantities.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.A.1: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.A.1.a: Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.A.1.b: Combine standard function types using arithmetic operations.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.A.2: Write arithmetic and geometric sequences both recursively and with an explicit formula, use them to model situations, and translate between the two forms.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.B: Build new functions from existing functions.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.B.3: Identify the effect on the graph of replacing `f(x)` by `f(x)+k,kf(x),f(kx),andf(x+k)`  for specific values of `k` (both positive and negative); find the value of `k` given the graphs. Experiment with cases and illustrate an explanation of the effects on the graph using technology. Include recognizing even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions for them.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.B.4.a: Solve an equation of the form `f(x)=c` for a simple function f that has an inverse and write an expression for the inverse.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.B.4.b: Verify by composition that one function is the inverse of another.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.B.4.c: Read values of an inverse function from a graph or a table, given that the function has an inverse.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.B.4.d: Produce an invertible function from a non-invertible function by restricting the domain.
CC.M9-12.F-BF.B.5: Understand the inverse relationship between exponents and logarithms and use this relationship to solve problems involving logarithms and exponents.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A.1: Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A.1.a: Prove that linear functions grow by equal differences over equal intervals, and that exponential functions grow by equal factors over equal intervals.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A.1.b: Recognize situations in which one quantity changes at a constant rate per unit interval relative to another.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A.1.c: Recognize situations in which a quantity grows or decays by a constant percent rate per unit interval relative to another.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A.2: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A.3: Observe using graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds a quantity increasing linearly, quadratically, or (more generally) as a polynomial function.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.A.4: For exponential models, express as a logarithm the solution to `ab^(ct)=d` where `a,c,andd` are numbers and the base `b` is `2,10,ore`; evaluate the logarithm using technology.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.B: Interpret expressions for functions in terms of the situation they model.
CC.M9-12.F-LE.B.5: Interpret the parameters in a linear or exponential function in terms of a context.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.A: Extend the domain of trigonometric functions using the unit circle.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.A.1: Understand radian measure of an angle as the length of the arc on the unit circle subtended by the angle.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.A.2: Explain how the unit circle in the coordinate plane enables the extension of trigonometric functions to all real numbers, interpreted as radian measures of angles traversed counterclockwise around the unit circle.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.A.3: Use special triangles to determine geometrically the values of sine, cosine, tangent for `pi/3,pi/4,andpi/6`, and use the unit circle to express the values of sine, cosine, and tangent for `pi-x,pi+x,and2pi-x` in terms of their values for `x`, where `x` is any real number.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.A.4: Use the unit circle to explain symmetry (odd and even) and periodicity of trigonometric functions.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.B: Model periodic phenomena with trigonometric functions.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.B.5: Choose trigonometric functions to model periodic phenomena with specified amplitude, frequency, and midline.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.B.6: Understand that restricting a trigonometric function to a domain on which it is always increasing or always decreasing allows its inverse to be constructed.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.B.7: Use inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations that arise in modeling contexts; evaluate the solutions using technology, and interpret them in terms of the context.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.C.8: Prove the Pythagorean identity `sin^2theta+cos^2theta=1` and use it to find `sintheta,costheta,ortantheta` given `sintheta,costheta,ortantheta` and the quadrant of the angle.
CC.M9-12.F-TF.C.9: Prove the addition and subtraction formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent and use them to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.A: Experiment with transformations in the plane.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.A.1: Know precise definitions of angle, circle, perpendicular line, parallel line, and line segment, based on the undefined notions of point, line, distance along a line, and distance around a circular arc.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.A.2: Represent transformations in the plane using, e.g., transparencies and geometry software; describe transformations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give other points as outputs. Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle to those that do not (e.g., translation versus horizontal stretch).
CC.M9-12.G-CO.A.3: Given a rectangle, parallelogram, trapezoid, or regular polygon, describe the rotations and reflections that carry it onto itself.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.A.4: Develop definitions of rotations, reflections, and translations in terms of angles, circles, perpendicular lines, parallel lines, and line segments.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.A.5: Given a geometric figure and a rotation, reflection, or translation, draw the transformed figure using, e.g., graph paper, tracing paper, or geometry software. Specify a sequence of transformations that will carry a given figure onto another.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.B: Understand congruence in terms of rigid motions.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.B.6: Use geometric descriptions of rigid motions to transform figures and to predict the effect of a given rigid motion on a given figure; given two figures, use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to decide if they are congruent.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.B.7: Use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to show that two triangles are congruent if and only if corresponding pairs of sides and corresponding pairs of angles are congruent.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.B.8: Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.C.9: Prove theorems about lines and angles. Theorems include: vertical angles are congruent; when a transversal crosses parallel lines, alternate interior angles are congruent and corresponding angles are congruent; points on a perpendicular bisector of a line segment are exactly those equidistant from the segment's endpoints.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.C.10: Prove theorems about triangles. Theorems include: measures of interior angles of a triangle sum to `180°`; base angles of isosceles triangles are congruent; the segment joining midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half the length; the medians of a triangle meet at a point.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.C.11: Prove theorems about parallelograms. Theorems include: opposite sides are congruent, opposite angles are congruent, the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, and conversely, rectangles are parallelograms with congruent diagonals.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.D.12: Make formal geometric constructions with a variety of tools and methods (compass and straightedge, string, reflective devices, paper folding, dynamic geometric software, etc.). Copying a segment; copying an angle; bisecting a segment; bisecting an angle; constructing perpendicular lines, including the perpendicular bisector of a line segment; and constructing a line parallel to a given line through a point not on the line.
CC.M9-12.G-CO.D.13: Construct an equilateral triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.A: Understand similarity in terms of similarity transformations.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.A.1: Verify experimentally the properties of dilations given by a center and a scale factor:
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.A.1.a: A dilation takes a line not passing through the center of the dilation to a parallel line, and leaves a line passing through the center unchanged.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.A.1.b: The dilation of a line segment is longer or shorter in the ratio given by the scale factor.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.A.2: Given two figures, use the definition of similarity in terms of similarity transformations to decide if they are similar; explain using similarity transformations the meaning of similarity for triangles as the equality of all corresponding pairs of angles and the proportionality of all corresponding pairs of sides.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.A.3: Use the properties of similarity transformations to establish the AA criterion for two triangles to be similar.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.B.4: Prove theorems about triangles. Theorems include: a line parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two proportionally, and conversely; the Pythagorean Theorem proved using triangle similarity.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.B.5: Use congruence and similarity criteria for triangles to solve problems and to prove relationships in geometric figures.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.C: Define trigonometric ratios and solve problems involving right triangles.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.C.6: Understand that by similarity, side ratios in right triangles are properties of the angles in the triangle, leading to definitions of trigonometric ratios for acute angles.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.C.7: Explain and use the relationship between the sine and cosine of complementary angles.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.C.8: Use trigonometric ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem to solve right triangles in applied problems.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.D.9: Derive the formula `A=1/2a bsin(C)` for the area of a triangle by drawing an auxiliary line from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.D.10: Prove the Laws of Sines and Cosines and use them to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.G-SRT.D.11: Understand and apply the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines to find unknown measurements in right and non-right triangles (e.g., surveying problems, resultant forces).
CC.M9-12.G-C.A: Understand and apply theorems about circles.
CC.M9-12.G-C.A.1: Prove that all circles are similar.
CC.M9-12.G-C.A.2: Identify and describe relationships among inscribed angles, radii, and chords. Include the relationship between central, inscribed, and circumscribed angles; inscribed angles on a diameter are right angles; the radius of a circle is perpendicular to the tangent where the radius intersects the circle.
CC.M9-12.G-C.A.3: Construct the inscribed and circumscribed circles of a triangle, and prove properties of angles for a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle.
CC.M9-12.G-C.A.4: Construct a tangent line from a point outside a given circle to the circle.
CC.M9-12.G-C.B: Find arc lengths and areas of sectors of circles.
CC.M9-12.G-C.B.5: Derive using similarity the fact that the length of the arc intercepted by an angle is proportional to the radius, and define the radian measure of the angle as the constant of proportionality; derive the formula for the area of a sector.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.A: Translate between the geometric description and the equation for a conic section.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.A.1: Derive the equation of a circle of given center and radius using the Pythagorean Theorem; complete the square to find the center and radius of a circle given by an equation.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.A.2: Derive the equation of a parabola given a focus and directrix.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.A.3: Derive the equations of ellipses and hyperbolas given the foci, using the fact that the sum or difference of distances from the foci is constant.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.B: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.B.4: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.B.5: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point).
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.B.6: Find the point on a directed line segment between two given points that partitions the segment in a given ratio.
CC.M9-12.G-GPE.B.7: Use coordinates to compute perimeters of polygons and areas of triangles and rectangles, e.g., using the distance formula.
CC.M9-12.G-GMD.A: Explain volume formulas and use them to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.G-GMD.A.1: Give an informal argument for the formulas for the circumference of a circle, area of a circle, volume of a cylinder, pyramid, and cone. Use dissection arguments, Cavalieri's principle, and informal limit arguments.
CC.M9-12.G-GMD.A.2: Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the formulas for the volume of a sphere and other solid figures.
CC.M9-12.G-GMD.A.3: Use volume formulas for cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.G-GMD.B: Visualize relationships between two-dimensional and three-dimensional objects.
CC.M9-12.G-GMD.B.4: Identify the shapes of two-dimensional cross-sections of three-dimensional objects, and identify three-dimensional objects generated by rotations of two-dimensional objects.
CC.M9-12.G-MG.A: Apply geometric concepts in modeling situations.
CC.M9-12.G-MG.A.1: Use geometric shapes, their measures, and their properties to describe objects (e.g., modeling a tree trunk or a human torso as a cylinder).
CC.M9-12.G-MG.A.2: Apply concepts of density based on area and volume in modeling situations (e.g., `text(persons per square mile),text(BTUs per cubic foot)`).
CC.M9-12.G-MG.A.3: Apply geometric methods to solve design problems (e.g., designing an object or structure to satisfy physical constraints or minimize cost; working with typographic grid systems based on ratios).
CC.M9-12.N-RN.A: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.
CC.M9-12.N-RN.A.1: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents.
CC.M9-12.N-RN.A.2: Rewrite expressions involving radicals and rational exponents using the properties of exponents.
CC.M9-12.N-RN.B: Use properties of rational and irrational numbers.
CC.M9-12.N-RN.B.3: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.
CC.M9-12.N-Q.A: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.N-Q.A.1: Use units as a way to understand problems and to guide the solution of multi-step problems; choose and interpret units consistently in formulas; choose and interpret the scale and the origin in graphs and data displays.
CC.M9-12.N-Q.A.2: Define appropriate quantities for the purpose of descriptive modeling.
CC.M9-12.N-Q.A.3: Choose a level of accuracy appropriate to limitations on measurement when reporting quantities.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.A: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.A.1: Know there is a complex number `i` such that `i^2=-1`, and every complex number has the form `a+bi` with `aandb` real.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.A.2: Use the relation `i^2=-1` and the commutative, associative, and distributive properties to add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.A.3: Find the conjugate of a complex number; use conjugates to find moduli and quotients of complex numbers.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.B: Represent complex numbers and their operations on the complex plane.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.B.4: Represent complex numbers on the complex plane in rectangular and polar form (including real and imaginary numbers), and explain why the rectangular and polar forms of a given complex number represent the same number.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.B.5: Represent addition, subtraction, multiplication, and conjugation of complex numbers geometrically on the complex plane; use properties of this representation for computation.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.B.6: Calculate the distance between numbers in the complex plane as the modulus of the difference, and the midpoint of a segment as the average of the numbers at its endpoints.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.C: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.C.7: Solve quadratic equations with real coefficients that have complex solutions.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.C.8: Extend polynomial identities to the complex numbers.
CC.M9-12.N-CN.C.9: Know the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra; show that it is true for quadratic polynomials.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.A: Represent and model with vector quantities.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.A.1: Recognize vector quantities as having both magnitude and direction. Represent vector quantities by directed line segments, and use appropriate symbols for vectors and their magnitudes (e.g., `bbv, absbbv), norm(bbv), v`).
CC.M9-12.N-VM.A.2: Find the components of a vector by subtracting the coordinates of an initial point from the coordinates of a terminal point.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.A.3: Solve problems involving velocity and other quantities that can be represented by vectors.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.B.4.a: Add vectors end-to-end, component-wise, and by the parallelogram rule. Understand that the magnitude of a sum of two vectors is typically not the sum of the magnitudes.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.B.4.b: Given two vectors in magnitude and direction form, determine the magnitude and direction of their sum.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.B.4.c: Understand vector subtraction `bbv-bbw` as `bbv+(-bbw)`, where -`bbw` is the additive inverse of `bbw`, with the same magnitude as `bbw` and pointing in the opposite direction. Represent vector subtraction graphically by connecting the tips in the appropriate order, and perform vector subtraction component-wise.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.B.5: Multiply a vector by a scalar.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.B.5.a: Represent scalar multiplication graphically by scaling vectors and possibly reversing their direction; perform scalar multiplication component-wise, e.g., as `c(v_x,v_y)=(cv_x,cv_y)`.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.B.5.b: Compute the magnitude of a scalar multiple `cbbv` using `norm(cbbv)=abs(c)v`. Compute the direction of `cbbv` knowing that when `abs(c)!=0`, the direction of `cbbv` is either along `bbv` (for `c>0`) or against `bbv` (for `c<0`).
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C.6: Use matrices to represent and manipulate data, e.g., to represent payoffs or incidence relationships in a network.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C.7: Multiply matrices by scalars to produce new matrices, e.g., as when all of the payoffs in a game are doubled.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C.8: Add, subtract, and multiply matrices of appropriate dimensions.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C.9: Understand that, unlike multiplication of numbers, matrix multiplication for square matrices is not a commutative operation, but still satisfies the associative and distributive properties.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C.10: Understand that the zero and identity matrices play a role in matrix addition and multiplication similar to the role of 0 and 1 in the real numbers. The determinant of a square matrix is nonzero if and only if the matrix has a multiplicative inverse.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C.11: Multiply a vector (regarded as a matrix with one column) by a matrix of suitable dimensions to produce another vector. Work with matrices as transformations of vectors.
CC.M9-12.N-VM.C.12: Work with `2xx2` matrices as transformations of the plane, and interpret the absolute value of the determinant in terms of area.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.A: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.A.1: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots).
CC.M9-12.S-ID.A.2: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more different data sets.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.A.3: Interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).
CC.M9-12.S-ID.A.4: Use the mean and standard deviation of a data set to fit it to a normal distribution and to estimate population percentages. Recognize that there are data sets for which such a procedure is not appropriate. Use calculators, spreadsheets, and tables to estimate areas under the normal curve.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.B: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical and quantitative variables.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.B.5: Summarize categorical data for two categories in two-way frequency tables. Interpret relative frequencies in the context of the data (including joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies). Recognize possible associations and trends in the data.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.B.6: Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.B.6.a: Fit a function to the data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data. Use given functions or choose a function suggested by the context. Emphasize linear, quadratic, and exponential models.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.B.6.b: Informally assess the fit of a function by plotting and analyzing residuals.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.B.6.c: Fit a linear function for a scatter plot that suggests a linear association.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.C.7: Interpret the slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model in the context of the data.
CC.M9-12.S-ID.C.8: Compute (using technology) and interpret the correlation coefficient of a linear fit.
CC.M9-12.S-IC.A: Understand and evaluate random processes underlying statistical experiments.
CC.M9-12.S-IC.A.1: Understand statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters based on a random sample from that population.
CC.M9-12.S-IC.A.2: Decide if a specified model is consistent with results from a given data-generating process, e.g., using simulation.
CC.M9-12.S-IC.B: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments and observational studies.
CC.M9-12.S-IC.B.3: Recognize the purposes of and differences among sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies; explain how randomization relates to each.
CC.M9-12.S-IC.B.4: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean or proportion; develop a margin of error through the use of simulation models for random sampling.
CC.M9-12.S-IC.B.5: Use data from a randomized experiment to compare two treatments; use simulations to decide if differences between parameters are significant.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.A: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.A.1: Describe events as subsets of a sample space (the set of outcomes) using characteristics (or categories) of the outcomes, or as unions, intersections, or complements of other events (“or,” “and,” “not”).
CC.M9-12.S-CP.A.2: Understand that two events `AandB` are independent if the probability of `AandB` occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if they are independent.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.A.3: Understand the conditional probability of `A` given `B` as `(P(AandB))/(P(B))`, and interpret independence of `AandB` as saying that the conditional probability of `A` given `B` is the same as the probability of `A`, and the conditional probability of `B` given `A` is the same as the probability of `B`.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.A.4: Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables of data when two categories are associated with each object being classified. Use the two-way table as a sample space to decide if events are independent and to approximate conditional probabilities.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.A.5: Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability and independence in everyday language and everyday situations.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.B: Use the rules of probability to compute probabilities of compound events in a uniform probability model.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.B.6: Find the conditional probability of `A` given `B` as the fraction of `B`'s outcomes that also belong to `A`, and interpret the answer in terms of the model.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.B.7: Apply the Addition Rule, `P(AorB)=P(A)+P(B)-P(AandB)`, and interpret the answer in terms of the model.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.B.8: Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, `P(AandB)=P(A)P(B|A)=P(B)P(A|B)`, and interpret the answer in terms of the model.
CC.M9-12.S-CP.B.9: Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.A: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.A.1: Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space; graph the corresponding probability distribution using the same graphical displays as for data distributions.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.A.2: Calculate the expected value of a random variable; interpret it as the mean of the probability distribution.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.A.3: Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.A.4: Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which probabilities are assigned empirically; find the expected value.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.B: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.B.5: Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.B.5.a: Find the expected payoff for a game of chance.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.B.5.b: Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values.
CC.M9-12.S-MD.B.6: Use probabilities to make fair decisions (e.g., drawing by lots, using a random number generator).
CC.M9-12.S-MD.B.7: Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game).
CO.EP.1.1: Children comprehend and understand the English language (Receptive Language).
CO.EP.1.1.a: Attend to language during conversations, songs, stories or other learning experiences.
CO.EP.1.1.b: Comprehend increasingly complex and varied vocabulary.
CO.EP.1.2: Children use language to convey thoughts and feelings (Expressive Language).
CO.EP.1.2.a: Participate in conversations of more than three exchanges with peers and adults.
CO.EP.1.2.b: Use language to express ideas and needs.
CO.EP.1.2.c: Use increasingly complex and varied vocabulary.
CO.EP.1.2.d: Understand the difference between a question and a statement.
CO.EP.1.2.e: Practice asking questions and making statements.
CO.EP.1.2.f: Speak in sentences of five or six words.
CO.EP.2.1: Children understand and obtain meaning from stories and information from books and other texts.
CO.EP.2.1.a: Show interest in shared reading experiences and looking at books independently.
CO.EP.2.1.b: Recognize how books are read, such as front-to-back and one page at a time, and recognize basic characteristics, such as title, author, and illustrator.
CO.EP.2.1.c: Ask and answer questions and make comments about print materials.
CO.EP.2.1.d: Demonstrate interest in different kinds of literature, such as fiction and nonfiction books and poetry, on a range of topics.
CO.EP.2.1.e: Begin to identify key features of reality versus fantasy in stories, pictures, and events.
CO.EP.2.1.f: Retell stories or information from books through conversation, artistic works, creative movement, or drama.
CO.EP.2.1.h: Begin to identify key features of reality versus fantasy in stories, pictures, and events.
CO.EP.2.2: Phonological awareness is the building block for understanding language.
CO.EP.2.2.a: Identify and discriminate between words in language.
CO.EP.2.2.b: Identify and discriminate between separate syllables in words.
CO.EP.2.2.c: Identify and discriminate between sounds and phonemes in language, such as attention to beginning and ending sounds of words and recognition that different words begin or end with the same sound.
CO.EP.2.2.d: Recognize patterns of sounds in songs, storytelling, and poetry through interactions and meaningful experiences.
CO.EP.2.3: Print concepts and conventions anchor concepts of early decoding.
CO.EP.2.3.a: Recognize print in everyday life, such as numbers, letters, one's name, words, and familiar logos and signs.
CO.EP.2.3.c: Understand conventions, such as print moves from left to right and top to bottom of a page.
CO.EP.2.3.d: Recognize words as a unit of print and understand that letters are grouped to form words.
CO.EP.2.3.e: Recognize the association between spoken or signed and written words.
CO.EP.2.4: The names and sounds associated with letters makes up alphabetic knowledge.
CO.EP.2.4.a: Recognize that the letters of the alphabet are a special category of visual graphics that can be individually named.
CO.EP.2.4.b: Recognize that letters of the alphabet have distinct sound(s) associated with them.
CO.EP.2.4.c: Attend to the beginning letters and sounds in familiar words.
CO.EP.2.4.d: Identify letters and associate correct sounds with letters, including a minimum of ten letters, preferably including letters in the child's name.
CO.EP.3.1: Familiarity with writing implements, conventions, and emerging skills to communicate through written representations, symbols, and letters.
CO.EP.3.1.a: Experiment with writing tools and materials.
CO.EP.3.1.b: Recognize that writing is a way of communicating for a variety of purposes, such as giving information, sharing stories, or giving an opinion.
CO.EP.3.1.c: Use scribbles, shapes, pictures, and letters to represent objects, stories, experiences, or ideas.
CO.EP.3.1.d: Copy, trace, or independently write letters or words.
CO.EP.4.1: Begin research by asking a question to identify and define a problem and its possible solutions.
CO.EP.4.1.b: Identify problems and search for solutions by asking questions during collaborative explorations of the topic; begin to state facts about the topic.
CO.MP.CC.A: Know number names and the count sequence.
CO.MP.CC.A.1: Count verbally or sign to at least 20 by ones.
CO.MP.CC.B: Recognize the number of objects in a small set.
CO.MP.CC.B.2: Instantly recognize, without counting, small quantities of up to five objects and say or sign the number.
CO.MP.CC.C: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities.
CO.MP.CC.C.3: Say or sign the number names in order when counting, pairing one number word that corresponds with one object, up to at least 10.
CO.MP.CC.C.4: Use the number name of the last object counted to answer “How many?” questions for up to approximately 10 objects.
CO.MP.CC.C.5: Accurately count as many as five objects in a scattered configuration or out of a collection of more than five objects.
CO.MP.CC.C.6: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.
CO.MP.CC.D.7: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is more than, less than or the same as objects in another group for up to at least five objects.
CO.MP.CC.D.8: Identify and use numbers related to order or position from first to fifth.
CO.MP.CC.E: Associate a quantity with written numerals up to `5` and begin to write numbers.
CO.MP.CC.E.9: Associate a number of objects with a written numeral 0-5.
CO.MP.CC.E.10: Recognize and, with support, write some numerals up to 10.
CO.MP.OA.A: Understand addition as adding to and understand subtraction as taking away from.
CO.MP.OA.A.1: Represent addition and subtraction in different ways, such as with fingers, objects, and drawing.
CO.MP.OA.A.2: Solve addition and subtraction problems set in simple contexts. Add and subtract up to at least five to or from a given number to find a sum or difference up to 10.
CO.MP.OA.A.3: With adult assistance, begin to use counting on (adding 1 or 2, for example) from the larger number for addition.
CO.MP.OA.B.4: Fill in missing elements of simple patterns.
CO.MP.OA.B.5: Duplicate simple patterns in a different location than demonstrated, such as making the same alternating color pattern with blocks at a table that was demonstrated on the rug. Extend patterns, such as making an eight-block tower of the same pattern that was demonstrated with four blocks.
CO.MP.OA.B.6: Identify the core unit of sequentially repeating patterns, such as color in a sequence of alternating red and blue blocks.
CO.MP.MD.A: Measure objects by their various attributes using standard and nonstandard measurement and use differences in attributes to make comparisons.
CO.MP.MD.A.1: Use comparative language, such as shortest, heavier, biggest, or later.
CO.MP.MD.A.2: Compare or order up to five objects based on their measurable attributes, such as height or weight.
CO.MP.MD.A.3: Measure using the same unit, such as putting together snap cubes to see how tall a book is.
CO.MP.G.A: Identify, describe, compare, and compose shapes.
CO.MP.G.A.1: Name and describe shapes in terms of length of sides, number of sides, and number of angles/corners.
CO.MP.G.A.2: Correctly name basic shapes (circle, square, rectangle, triangle) regardless of size and orientation.
CO.MP.G.A.3: Analyze, compare, and sort two-and three-dimensional shapes and objects in different sizes. Describe their similarities, differences, and other attributes, such as size and shape.
CO.MP.G.A.4: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes.
CO.MP.G.B: Explore the positions of objects in space.
CO.MP.G.B.5: Understand and use language related to directionality, order, and the position of objects, including up/down and in front/behind.
CO.MP.G.B.6: Correctly follow directions involving their own position in space, such as “Stand up” and “Move forward.”
CO.SP.1.1: Recognize that physical properties of objects and/or materials help us understand the world.
CO.SP.1.1.a: Use senses to explore the properties of objects and materials (e.g., solids, liquids).
CO.SP.1.1.b: Make simple observations, predictions, explanations, and generalizations based on real-life experiences.
CO.SP.1.1.c: Collect, describe, predict and record information using words, drawings, maps, graphs and charts.
CO.SP.1.1.d: Observe, describe, and discuss living things and natural processes.
CO.SP.1.2: Recognize there are cause - and - effect relationships related to matter and energy.
CO.SP.1.2.a: Recognize and investigate cause - and - effect relationships in everyday experiences (pushing, pulling, kicking, rolling or blowing objects).
CO.SP.1.2.c: Observe, describe and discuss properties of materials and transformation of substances.
CO.SP.1.2.d: Seek answers to questions and test predictions using simple experiments.
CO.SP.2.1: Recognize that living things have unique characteristics and basic needs that can be observed and studied.
CO.SP.2.1.a: Observe, describe and discuss living things.
CO.SP.2.1.b: Observe similarities and differences in the needs of living things.
CO.SP.2.1.c: Observe and describe how natural habitats provide for the basic needs of plants and animals with respect to shelter, food, water, air and light.
CO.SP.2.1.d: Ask and pursue questions through simple investigations and observations of living things.
CO.SP.2.1.e: Collect, describe, and record information about living things through discussion, drawings, graphs, technology and charts.
CO.SP.2.1.f: Identify differences between living and nonliving things.
CO.SP.2.2: Recognize that living things develop in predictable patterns.
CO.SP.2.2.a: Identify the common needs such as food, air and water of familiar living things.
CO.SP.2.2.b: Predict, explain and infer patterns based on observations and representations of living things, their needs and life cycles.
CO.SP.2.2.c: Observe and document changes in living things over time using different modalities such as drawing, dramatization, describing or using technology.
CO.SP.2.2.d: Recognize that plants and animals grow and change.
CO.SP.3.1: The acquisition of concepts and facts related to the Earth materials and their uses.
CO.SP.3.1.a: Use senses and tools, including technology, to investigate materials, and observe processes and relationships to gather information and explore the environment.
CO.SP.3.1.b: Inquire about the natural and physical environment.
CO.SP.3.1.c: Observe and discuss common properties, differences and comparisons among objects.
CO.SP.3.1.d: Participate in simple investigations to form hypothesis, gather observations, draw conclusions.
CO.SP.3.1.e: Record observations using words, drawings, maps, graphs and charts.
CO.SP.3.2: The acquisition of concepts and facts related to the natural and physical world and the understanding of naturally occurring relationships.
CO.SP.3.2.a: Predict, explain and infer patterns based on observations and evidence.
CO.SP.3.2.b: Articulate findings through a variety of modalities (e.g., drawings, words, dramatizations).
CO.SP.3.2.c: Recognizes familiar elements of the natural world and demonstrates an understanding that these may change over time (e.g., sun and moon, weather).
CO.SP.3.2.d: Observe and describe patterns observed over the course of a number of days and nights (e.g., differences in the activities or appearance of plants and animals).
CO.SSP.1.1: Recognize change and sequence over time.
CO.SSP.1.1.a: Begin to understand concepts of the past, present, and future.
CO.SSP.1.1.b: Begin to recall family traditions or personal events that happened in the past (this can include immediate past events from that day or week, or longer) and the present, especially as it pertains to diverse backgrounds, such as race, and individual family traditions.
CO.SSP.1.1.c: Begin to understand that previous, current, and future events can have an impact on our daily, weekly, or monthly lives.
CO.SSP.2.1: Develop spatial understanding, perspectives, and connections to the world.
CO.SSP.2.1.a: Identify aspects of their immediate environment, such as areas of their preschool classroom, their own room or house, and/or building and roads, trees, gardens, bodies of water, and land formations.
CO.SSP.2.1.b: Develop an awareness of their own home, classroom, school, neighborhood, and community.
CO.SSP.2.1.c: Develop an awareness of basic, developmentally appropriate spatial concepts such as near and far.
CO.SSP.3.1: Understand that individuals have many wants and must make choices.
CO.SSP.3.1.a: Identify choices that individuals can make to get their needs and wants met.
CO.SSP.3.1.b: Explain how individuals earn money and use it to make choices among their various wants.
CO.SSP.4.1: Understand one's relationship to the family and community and respect differences in others.
CO.SSP.4.1.a: Recognize membership in family, neighborhood, school, team, and various other groups and organizations.
CO.SSP.4.1.b: Understand similarities and respect differences among people of diverse backgrounds within their classroom and community.
CO.SSP.4.1.c: Identify emotions using age-appropriate vocabulary and correlate cause and effect to those emotions.
CO.SSP.4.1.d: Utilize positive social skill methods such as communication, trade-offs, common goals, kind actions, etc. to get positive results for obtaining needs and wants from other individuals, classmates, friends, and adults to empathize with others and begin to solve problems.
CO.SSP.4.1.e: Understand how similarities and differences can make a family, classroom, and community stronger.
CO.SSP.4.2: Understand that rules allow groups to work effectively.
CO.SSP.4.2.a: Understand how rules in the classroom, home, and community keep us safe.
CO.SSP.4.2.b: Show interest in interacting with and developing relationships with others, including those who are African American, Latino, Asian American, Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, Indigenous Peoples, LGBTQ, and religious minorities.
CO.SSP.4.2.c: Recognize that everyone has rights and responsibilities within a group.
CO.SSP.4.2.d: Demonstrate self-regulated behaviors and problem-solving skills when resolving conflicts.
CO.SSP.4.2.e: Follow classroom routines, rules, and expectations.
CO.SSP.5.1.a: Recognize coins and currency as money.
CO.SSP.5.1.b: Identify how money is obtained (e.g., through work or gifts) and how it is used.
CO.SSP.5.1.d: Identify different forms of money and their different values.
CO.EK.1.1: Communicate using verbal and nonverbal language.
CO.EK.1.1.a: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about kindergarten topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
CO.EK.1.1.a.i: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (for example: listening to others and taking turns speaking about the topics and texts under discussion).
CO.EK.1.1.a.ii: Continue a conversation through multiple exchanges.
CO.EK.1.1.b: Confirm understanding of a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media by asking and answering questions about key details and requesting clarification if something is not understood.
CO.EK.1.1.c: Ask and answer questions in order to seek help, get information, or clarify asomething that is not understood.
CO.EK.1.1.d: Listen with comprehension to follow two-step directions.
CO.EK.1.1.e: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts.
CO.EK.1.2: Develop oral communication skills through a language-rich environment.
CO.EK.1.2.a: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events and, with prompting and support, provide additional detail.
CO.EK.1.2.b: Add drawings or other visual displays to descriptions as desired to provide additional detail.
CO.EK.1.2.c: Speak audibly and express thoughts, feelings, and ideas clearly.
CO.EK.1.2.d: Sort common objects into categories (for example: shapes, foods) to gain a sense of the concepts the categories represent.
CO.EK.1.2.e: Demonstrate understanding of frequently occurring verbs and adjectives by relating them to their opposites (antonyms).
CO.EK.1.2.f: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (for example: note places at school that are colorful).
CO.EK.1.2.g: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs describing the same general action (for example: walk, march, strut, prance) by acting out the meanings.
CO.EK.1.2.h: Use new vocabulary that is directly taught through reading, speaking, and listening.
CO.EK.1.2.i: Relate new vocabulary to prior knowledge.
CO.EK.2.1: Develop and apply the concepts of print and comprehension of literary texts.
CO.EK.2.1.a: Use Key Ideas and Details to:
CO.EK.2.1.a.i: With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
CO.EK.2.1.a.ii: With prompting and support, retell familiar stories, including key details.
CO.EK.2.1.a.iii: With prompting and support, identify characters, settings, and major events in a story.
CO.EK.2.1.b.i: Ask and answer questions about unknown words in a text.
CO.EK.2.1.b.ii: Recognize common types of texts (for example: storybooks, poems).
CO.EK.2.1.b.iii: With prompting and support, name the author and illustrator of a story and define the role of each in telling the story.
CO.EK.2.1.c: Use Integration of Knowledge and Ideas to:
CO.EK.2.1.c.i: With prompting and support, describe the relationship between illustrations and the story in which they appear (for example: what moment in a story an illustration depicts).
CO.EK.2.1.c.ii: With prompting and support, compare and contrast the adventures and experiences of characters in familiar stories.
CO.EK.2.1.d: Use Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity to:
CO.EK.2.1.d.i: Actively engage in group reading activities with purpose and understanding.
CO.EK.2.2: Develop and apply the concepts of print and comprehension of informational texts.
CO.EK.2.2.a: Use Key Ideas and Details to:
CO.EK.2.2.a.i: With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
CO.EK.2.2.a.ii: With prompting and support, identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
CO.EK.2.2.a.iii: With prompting and support, describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
CO.EK.2.2.b.i: With prompting and support, ask and answer questions about unknown words in a text.
CO.EK.2.2.b.ii: Identify the front cover, back cover, and title page of a book.
CO.EK.2.2.b.iii: Name the author and illustrator of a text and define the role of each in presenting the ideas or information in a text.
CO.EK.2.2.c: Use Integration of Knowledge and Ideas to:
CO.EK.2.2.c.i: With prompting and support, describe the relationship between illustrations and the text in which they appear (for example: what person, place, thing, or idea in the text an illustration depicts).
CO.EK.2.2.c.ii: With prompting and support, identify the reasons an author gives to support points in a text.
CO.EK.2.2.c.iii: With prompting and support, identify basic similarities in and differences between two texts on the same topic (for example: in illustrations, descriptions, or procedures).
CO.EK.2.2.d: Use Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity to:
CO.EK.2.2.d.i: Actively engage in group reading activities with purpose and understanding.
CO.EK.2.3: Develop basic reading skills through the use of foundational skills.
CO.EK.2.3.a: Demonstrate understanding of the organization and basic features of print.
CO.EK.2.3.a.i: Follow words from left to right, top to bottom, and page by page.
CO.EK.2.3.a.ii: Recognize that spoken words are represented in written language by specific sequences of letters.
CO.EK.2.3.a.iii: Understand that words are separated by spaces in print (concept of word).
CO.EK.2.3.a.iv: Recognize and name all upper- and lowercase letters of the alphabet.
CO.EK.2.3.b: Demonstrate understanding of spoken words, syllables, and sounds (phonemes).
CO.EK.2.3.b.ii: Count, pronounce, blend, and segment syllables in spoken words.
CO.EK.2.3.b.iii: Blend and segment the onset and rime of single-syllable spoken words.
CO.EK.2.3.b.iv: Isolate and pronounce the initial, medial vowel, and final sounds (phonemes) in three-phoneme (consonant-vowel-consonant, or CVC) words.
CO.EK.2.3.b.v: Add or substitute individual sounds (phonemes) in simple, one-syllable words to make new words.
CO.EK.2.3.b.vi: Read text consisting of short sentences comprised of learned sight words and consonant-vowel-consonant (CVC) words.
CO.EK.2.3.c: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
CO.EK.2.3.c.i: Demonstrate basic knowledge of letter-sound correspondences by producing the primary or most frequent sound for each consonant.
CO.EK.2.3.c.ii: Associate the long and short sounds with the common spellings (graphemes) for the five major vowels.
CO.EK.2.3.c.iii: Read common high-frequency words by sight (for example: the, of, to, you, she, my, is, are, do, does).
CO.EK.2.3.c.iv: Distinguish between similarly spelled words by identifying the sounds of the letters that differ.
CO.EK.2.3.d: Read emergent-reader texts with purpose and understanding.
CO.EK.2.3.e: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on kindergarten reading and content.
CO.EK.2.3.e.i: Identify new meanings for familiar words and apply them accurately (for example: knowing duck is a bird and learning the verb to duck).
CO.EK.2.3.e.ii: Use the most frequently occurring inflections and affixes (for example: -ed, -s, re-, un-, pre-, -ful, -less) as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word.
CO.EK.2.3.f.i: Identify and produce groups of words that begin with the same sound (alliteration).
CO.EK.2.3.f.ii: Identify the initial, medial, and final phoneme (speech sound) of spoken words.
CO.EK.3.1: Write opinions using labels, dictation, and drawing.
CO.EK.3.1.a: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose opinion pieces in which they tell a reader the topic or the name of the book they are writing about and state an opinion or preference about the topic or book (for example: My favorite book is...).
CO.EK.3.1.b: With guidance and support from adults, respond to questions and suggestions from peers and add details to strengthen writing as needed.
CO.EK.3.1.c: With guidance and support from adults, explore a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.
CO.EK.3.2: Write informative/explanatory texts on a topic using labels, dictation, and drawing.
CO.EK.3.2.a: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose informative/explanatory texts in which they name what they are writing about and supply some information about the topic.
CO.EK.3.2.b: With guidance and support from adults, respond to questions and suggestions from peers and add details to strengthen writing as needed.
CO.EK.3.2.c: With guidance and support from adults, explore a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.
CO.EK.3.3: Write real or imagined narratives using labels, dictation, and drawing.
CO.EK.3.3.a: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to narrate a single event or several loosely linked events, tell about the events in the order in which they occurred, and provide a reaction to what happened.
CO.EK.3.3.b: With guidance and support from adults, respond to questions and suggestions from peers and add details to strengthen writing as needed.
CO.EK.3.3.c: With guidance and support from adults, explore a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.
CO.EK.3.4: Use appropriate mechanics and conventions when creating simple texts.
CO.EK.3.4.a: Demonstrate command of the conventions of Standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
CO.EK.3.4.a.i: Print many upper- and lowercase letters.
CO.EK.3.4.a.ii: Use frequently occurring nouns and verbs.
CO.EK.3.4.a.iii: Form regular plural nouns orally by adding /s/ or /es/ (for example: dog, dogs; wish, wishes).
CO.EK.3.4.a.iv: Understand and use question words (interrogatives) (for example: who, what, where, when, why, how).
CO.EK.3.4.a.v: Use the most frequently occurring prepositions (for example: to, from, in, out, on, off, for, of, by, with).
CO.EK.3.4.a.vi: Produce and expand complete sentences in shared language activities.
CO.EK.3.4.b: Demonstrate command of the conventions of Standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
CO.EK.3.4.b.i: Capitalize the first word in a sentence and the pronoun I.
CO.EK.3.4.b.iii: Write a letter or letters for most consonant and short-vowel sounds (phonemes).
CO.EK.3.4.b.iv: Spell simple words phonetically, drawing on knowledge of sound-letter relationships.
CO.EK.4.1: Explore the purposes for research and inquiry by accessing resources in collaborative settings.
CO.EK.4.1.a: Participate in shared research and writing projects (for example: explore a number of books by a favorite author and express opinions about them).
CO.EK.4.1.b: Identify a clear purpose for research or inquiry (for example: If the class is learning about trees, is my need to know more about pets related?).
CO.EK.4.1.c: Ask a specific question and gather relevant information from various sources related to that question that inform clarity of purpose and conclusions about research.
CO.EK.4.1.d: Ask primary questions of clarity, significance, relevance, and accuracy to improve quality of thinking.
CO.EK.4.1.e: Use a variety of resources to answer questions of interest through guided inquiry (for example: texts read aloud or viewed, direct observation).
CO.EK.4.1.f: Gather relevant information and check various information sources for accuracy (for example: In a class discussion focused on butterflies, students ask questions related to a butterfly and the life cycle.).
CO.EK.4.1.g: With guidance and support from adults, recall information from experience or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
CO.MK.CC.A: Use number names and the count sequence.
CO.MK.CC.A.1: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
CO.MK.CC.A.2: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).
CO.MK.CC.A.3: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).
CO.MK.CC.B: Count to determine the number of objects.
CO.MK.CC.B.4: Apply the relationship between numbers and quantities and connect counting to cardinality.
CO.MK.CC.B.4.a: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.
CO.MK.CC.B.4.b: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.
CO.MK.CC.B.4.c: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.
CO.MK.CC.B.5: Count to answer “how many?” questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1-20, count out that many objects.
CO.MK.CC.C.6: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.
CO.MK.CC.C.7: Compare two numbers between `1and10` presented as written numerals.
CO.MK.NBT.A: Work with numbers 11-19 to gain foundations for place value.
CO.MK.NBT.A.1: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation (such as 18 = 10 + 8); understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.
CO.MK.OA.A: Model and describe addition as putting together and adding to, and subtraction as taking apart and taking from, using objects or drawings.
CO.MK.OA.A.1: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings (drawings need not show details, but should show the mathematics in the problem), sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
CO.MK.OA.A.2: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.
CO.MK.OA.A.3: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1).
CO.MK.OA.A.4: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation.
CO.MK.MD.A.1: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.
CO.MK.MD.A.2: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has “more of”/“less of” the attribute, and describe the difference.
CO.MK.MD.B: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category.
CO.MK.MD.B.3: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
CO.MK.G.A: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).
CO.MK.G.A.1: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.
CO.MK.G.A.2: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.
CO.MK.G.A.3: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, “flat”) or three-dimensional (“solid”).
CO.MK.G.B: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.
CO.MK.G.B.4: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/“corners”) and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).
CO.MK.G.B.5: Model shapes in the world by building shapes from components (e.g., sticks and clay balls) and drawing shapes.
CO.MK.G.B.6: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes.
CO.SK.1.1: Pushes and pulls can have different strengths and directions, and can change the speed or direction of an object's motion or start or stop it.
CO.SK.1.1.a: Plan and conduct an investigation to compare the effects of different strengths or different directions of pushes and pulls on the motion of an object.
CO.SK.1.1.b: Analyze data to determine if a design solution works as intended to change the speed or direction of an object with a push or a pull.
CO.SK.1.2.a: Make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth's surface.
CO.SK.1.2.b: Use tools and materials to design and build a structure that will reduce the warming effect of sunlight on an area.
CO.SK.2.1: To live and grow, animals obtain food they need from plants or other animals, and plants need water and light.
CO.SK.2.1.a: Use observations to describe patterns of what plants and animals (including humans) need to survive.
CO.SK.3.1: Patterns are observed when measuring the local weather, including how humans and other organisms impact their environment.
CO.SK.3.1.a: Use and share observations of local weather conditions to describe patterns over time.
CO.SK.3.1.b: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how plants and animals (including humans) can change the environment to meet their needs.
CO.SK.3.2: Plants and animals meet their needs in their habitats and impact one another; people can prepare for severe weather.
CO.SK.3.2.a: Use a model to represent the relationship between the needs of different plants or animals (including humans) and the places they live.
CO.SK.3.2.b: Ask questions to obtain information about the purpose of weather forecasting to prepare for, and respond to, severe weather.
CO.SK.3.2.c: Communicate solutions that will reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air and/or other living things in the local environment.
CO.SSK.1.1: Ask questions and discuss ideas about the past.
CO.SSK.1.1.a: Ask questions about the past using question starters.
CO.SSK.1.1.b: Identify information from primary and/or secondary sources that answer questions about the past and contribute to the collective memory.
CO.SSK.1.1.c: Provide rationale about something from the past using statements.
CO.SSK.1.2: Understand that the sequence of events is important when describing the past.
CO.SSK.1.2.a: Explore differences and similarities in the lives of children and families from different time periods by using a variety of sources.
CO.SSK.1.2.c: Explain why knowing the order of events is important.
CO.SSK.2.1: Recognize that geographic tools represent places and spaces.
CO.SSK.2.1.a: Distinguish between a map and a globe as ways to show places people live.
CO.SSK.2.1.b: Use geographic tools to describe places.
CO.SSK.2.2: Identify how the environment influences the way people live.
CO.SSK.2.2.a: Identify ways students' lives are similar and different from those in other communities.
CO.SSK.2.2.b: Identify how the environment, geographic features, and climate impact lifestyles.
CO.SSK.3.1: Explain how individuals make choices based on needs and wants.
CO.SSK.3.1.a: Identify the costs and benefits of a choice an individual makes when acquiring an item.
CO.SSK.3.1.b: Recognize and engage in ways to use another individual's items.
CO.SSK.4.1: Identify ways in which civic participation takes place across multiple groups.
CO.SSK.4.1.a: Differentiate among examples of civic participation.
CO.SSK.4.1.b: Explain the qualities of an informed and engaged citizen.
CO.SSK.4.1.c: Practice citizenship skills when working with others including courtesy, honesty, and fairness.
CO.SSK.4.1.d: Identify the difference between fact and opinion.
CO.SSK.4.2: Participate in making logical decisions using democratic principles.
CO.SSK.4.2.c: Explain how a class rule may promote fairness and resolve conflict and compare against a rule that may not.
CO.SSK.4.2.d: Contribute to making and maintaining class community decisions.
CO.SSK.4.2.e: Explain the difference between democratic decision-making and decisions made by authorities.
CO.SSK.5.1: Describe choices people make about how to use the money they earn.
CO.SSK.5.1.a: Recognize choices people make with their money and explain how financial decisions are made.
CO.SSK.5.1.b: Explain how money gives people the ability to buy goods and services.
CO.SSK.5.1.c: Identify the difference between a want and a need and how that impacts purchasing decisions when resources are limited.
CO.E1.1.1: Communicate using verbal and nonverbal language to express and receive information.
CO.E1.1.1.a: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 1 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
CO.E1.1.1.a.i: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (for example: listening to others with care, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).
CO.E1.1.1.a.ii: Build on others' talk in conversations by responding to the comments of others through multiple exchanges.
CO.E1.1.1.a.iii: Ask questions to clear up any confusion about the topics and texts under discussion.
CO.E1.1.1.b: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.
CO.E1.1.1.c: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to gather additional information or clarify something that is not understood.
CO.E1.1.2: Use multiple strategies to develop and expand oral communication.
CO.E1.1.2.a: Describe people, places, things, and events with relevant details, expressing ideas and feelings clearly.
CO.E1.1.2.b: Add drawings or other visual displays to descriptions when appropriate to clarify ideas, thoughts, and feelings.
CO.E1.1.2.c: Produce complete sentences when appropriate to task and situation.
CO.E1.1.2.d: Give and follow simple two-step directions.
CO.E1.2.1: Apply foundational reading strategies to fluently read and comprehend literary texts.
CO.E1.2.1.a: Use Key Ideas and Details to:
CO.E1.2.1.a.i: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
CO.E1.2.1.a.ii: Retell stories, including key details, and demonstrate understanding of their central message or lesson.
CO.E1.2.1.a.iii: Describe characters, settings, and major events in a story, using key details.
CO.E1.2.1.a.iv: Make predictions about what will happen in the text and explain whether they were confirmed or not and why, providing evidence from the text.
CO.E1.2.1.b.i: Identify words and phrases in stories or poems that suggest feelings or appeal to the senses.
CO.E1.2.1.b.ii: Explain major differences between books that tell stories and books that give information.
CO.E1.2.1.b.iii: Identify who is telling the story at various points in a text.
CO.E1.2.1.b.iv: Follow and replicate patterns in predictable poems.
CO.E1.2.1.c: Use Integration of Knowledge and Ideas to:
CO.E1.2.1.c.i: Use illustrations and details in a story to describe its characters, setting, or events.
CO.E1.2.1.c.ii: Compare and contrast the adventures and experiences of characters in stories.
CO.E1.2.1.d: Use Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity to:
CO.E1.2.1.d.i: With prompting and support, read prose and poetry of appropriate complexity for grade 1.
CO.E1.2.2: Apply foundational reading strategies to fluently read and comprehend informational texts.
CO.E1.2.2.a: Use Key Ideas and Details to:
CO.E1.2.2.a.i: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text.
CO.E1.2.2.a.ii: Identify the main topic and retell key details of a text.
CO.E1.2.2.a.iii: Describe the connection between two individuals, events, ideas, or pieces of information in a text.
