ME.M9-12.SSE.B.3.b: Rewrite a quadratic expression (such as by completing the square) to reveal the maximum or minimum value of the function it defines.
ME.M9-12.SSE.B.3.c: Use the properties of exponents to transform expressions for exponential functions.
ME.M9-12.SSE.B.4: Derive the formula for the sum of a finite geometric series (when the common ratio is not 1), and use the formula to solve problems.
ME.M9-12.APR.A.1: Understand that polynomials form a system analogous to the integers, namely, they are closed under certain operations.
ME.M9-12.APR.A.1.a: Perform operations on polynomial expressions (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division), and compare the system of polynomials to the system of integers.
ME.M9-12.APR.A.1.b: Factor and/or expand polynomial expressions, identify and combine like terms, and apply the Distributive Property.
ME.M9-12.APR.B: Understand the relationship between zeros and factors of polynomials.
ME.M9-12.APR.B.2: Know and apply the Remainder Theorem: For a polynomial `p(x)` and a number `a`, the remainder on division by `x-a` is `p(a)`, so `p(a)=0` if and only if `(x-a)` is a factor of `p(x)`.
ME.M9-12.APR.B.3: Identify zeros of polynomials of degree three or higher when suitable factorizations (in factored form or easily factorable) are available, and use the zeros to construct a rough graph of the function defined by the polynomial.
ME.M9-12.APR.C: Use polynomial identities to solve problems.
ME.M9-12.APR.C.4: Prove polynomial identities and use them to describe numerical relationships.
ME.M9-12.APR.C.5: Know and apply the Binomial Theorem for the expansion of (x + y)n in powers of `xandy` for a positive integer n, where `xandy` are any numbers, with coefficients determined for example by Pascal's Triangle.
ME.M9-12.APR.D.6: Rewrite simple rational expressions in different forms; write `(a(x))/(b(x))` in the form `q(x)+(r(x))/(b(x))`, where `a(x),b(x),q(x),andr(x)` are polynomials with the degree of `r(x)` less than the degree of `b(x)`, using inspection, long division, or, for the more complicated examples, a computer algebra system.
ME.M9-12.APR.D.7: Understand that rational expressions form a system analogous to the rational numbers, closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by a nonzero rational expression; add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational expressions.
ME.M9-12.CED.A: Create equations and/or inequalities that describe numbers or relationships.
ME.M9-12.CED.A.1: Create equations and inequalities in one variable and use them to solve problems. Include equations arising from linear and quadratic functions, and simple rational and exponential functions.
ME.M9-12.CED.A.2: Create equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities; graph equations on coordinate axes with labels and scales.
ME.M9-12.CED.A.3: Represent constraints by equations or inequalities, and by systems of equations and/or inequalities, and interpret solutions as viable or nonviable options in a modeling context.
ME.M9-12.CED.A.4: Rearrange formulas to highlight a quantity of interest, using the same reasoning as in solving equations.
ME.M9-12.REI.A: Understand solving equations as a process of reasoning and explain the reasoning.
ME.M9-12.REI.A.1: Explain each step in solving a simple equation as following from the equality of numbers asserted at the previous step, starting from the assumption that the original equation has a solution. Construct a viable argument to justify or refute a solution method.
ME.M9-12.REI.A.2: Solve simple rational and radical equations in one variable, and give examples showing how extraneous solutions may arise.
ME.M9-12.REI.B: Solve equations and inequalities in one variable.
ME.M9-12.REI.B.3: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including equations with coefficients represented by letters.
ME.M9-12.REI.B.4: Solve quadratic equations in one variable.
ME.M9-12.REI.B.4.a: Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation in `x` into an equation of the form `(x-p)^2=q` that has the same solutions. Derive the quadratic formula from this form.
ME.M9-12.REI.B.4.bi: Solve quadratic equations by inspection (e.g., for x^2= 49), taking square roots, completing the square, the quadratic formula and factoring, as appropriate to the initial form of the equation.
ME.M9-12.REI.B.4.bii: Recognize when the quadratic formula gives complex solutions and write them as a ± bi for real numbers `aandb`.
ME.M9-12.REI.C.5: Prove that, given a system of two equations in two variables, replacing one equation by the sum of that equation and a multiple of the other produces a system with the same solutions.
ME.M9-12.REI.C.6: Solve systems of linear equations exactly and approximately (e.g., with graphs), focusing on pairs of linear equations in two variables.
ME.M9-12.REI.C.7: Solve a simple system consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables algebraically and graphically.
ME.M9-12.REI.C.8: Represent a system of linear equations as a single matrix equation in a vector variable.
ME.M9-12.REI.C.9: Find the inverse of a matrix if it exists and use it to solve systems of linear equations (using technology for matrices of dimension `3xx3` or greater).
ME.M9-12.REI.D: Represent and solve equations and inequalities graphically.
ME.M9-12.REI.D.10: Understand that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions plotted in the coordinate plane, often forming a curve (which could be a line). Show that any point on the graph of an equation in two variables is a solution to the equation.
ME.M9-12.REI.D.11: Explain why the `xtext(-coordinates)` of the points where the graphs of the equations `y=f(x)andy=g(x)` intersect are the solutions of the equation `f(x)=g(x)`; find the solutions approximately, e.g., using technology to graph the functions, make tables of values, or find successive approximations. Include cases where `f(x)` and/or `g(x)` are linear, polynomial, rational, absolute value, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
ME.M9-12.REI.D.12: Graph the solutions of a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane (excluding the boundary in the case of a strict inequality), and graph the solution set of a system of linear inequalities in two variables as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.
ME.M9-12.IF.A: Understand the concept of a function and use function notation.
ME.M9-12.IF.A.1: Understand that a function from one set (called the domain) to another set (called the range) assigns to each element of the domain exactly one element of the range. If `f` is a function and `x` is an element of its domain, then `f(x)` denotes the output of `f` corresponding to the input `x`. The graph of f is the graph of the equation `y=f(x)`.
ME.M9-12.IF.A.2: Use function notation, evaluate functions for inputs in their domains, and interpret statements that use function notation in terms of a context.
ME.M9-12.IF.A.3: Recognize that sequences are functions, sometimes defined recursively, whose domain is a subset of the integers.
ME.M9-12.IF.B: Interpret functions that arise in applications in terms of the context.
ME.M9-12.IF.B.4: For a function that models a relationship between two quantities, interpret key features of graphs and tables in terms of the quantities, and sketch graphs showing key features given a verbal description of the relationship.
ME.M9-12.IF.B.5: Relate the domain of a function to its graph and, where applicable, to the quantitative relationship it describes.
ME.M9-12.IF.B.6: Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function (presented symbolically or as a table) over a specified interval. Estimate the rate of change from a graph.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7: Graph functions expressed symbolically as well as show and describe key features of the graph, by hand in simple cases and using technology for more complicated cases.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7.a: Graph linear and quadratic functions and show intercepts, maxima, and minima.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7.bi: Graph square root and piecewise-defined functions, (including step functions and absolute value functions), as well as show and describe key features of the graph.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7.bii: Graph cube root functions, as well as show and describe key features of the graph.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7.c: Graph polynomial functions of degree three or higher, identifying zeros when suitable factorizations (in factored form or easily factorable) are available, and showing end behavior.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7.d: Graph rational functions, identifying zeros and asymptotes when suitable factorizations are available, and showing end behavior.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7.ei: Graph exponential functions, showing intercepts and end behavior.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.7.eii: Graph logarithmic functions, showing intercepts and end behavior and trigonometric functions, showing period, midline, and amplitude.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.8: Write a function defined by an expression in different but equivalent forms to reveal and explain different properties of the function.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.8.a: Use the process of factoring and completing the square in a quadratic function to show zeros, maximum and minimum values, and symmetry of the graph, and interpret these in terms of a context.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.8.b: Use the properties of exponents to interpret expressions for exponential functions. For example, apply the properties to financial situations such as identifying appreciation and depreciation rate for the value of a house or car sometime after its initial purchase: `V_n=P(1+r)^n`.
ME.M9-12.IF.C.9: Compare properties of two functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
ME.M9-12.BF.A: Build a function that models a relationship between two quantities.
ME.M9-12.BF.A.1: Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities.
ME.M9-12.BF.A.1.a: Determine an explicit expression, a recursive process, or steps for calculation from a context.
ME.M9-12.BF.A.1.b: Combine standard function types using arithmetic operations.
ME.M9-12.BF.A.2: Write arithmetic and geometric sequences both recursively and with an explicit formula, use them to model situations, and translate between the two forms.
ME.M9-12.BF.B: Build new functions from existing functions.
ME.M9-12.BF.B.3: Identify the effect on the graph of replacing `f(x)` by `f(x)+k,kf(x),f(kx),andf(x+k)` for specific values of `k` (both positive and negative); find the value of `k` given the graphs. Experiment with cases and illustrate an explanation of the effects on the graph using technology. Include recognizing even and odd functions from their graphs and algebraic expressions for them.
ME.M9-12.BF.B.4.a: Solve an equation of the form `f(x)=c` (where c represents the output value of the function) for a simple function f that has an inverse and write an expression for the inverse.
ME.M9-12.BF.B.4.b: Verify by composition that one function is the inverse of another.
ME.M9-12.BF.B.4.c: Read values of an inverse function from a graph or a table, given that the function has an inverse.
ME.M9-12.BF.B.4.d: Produce an invertible function from a non-invertible function by restricting the domain.
ME.M9-12.BF.B.5: Understand the inverse relationship between exponents and logarithms and use this relationship to solve problems involving logarithms and exponents.
ME.M9-12.LE.A: Construct and compare linear, quadratic, and exponential models and solve problems.
ME.M9-12.LE.A.1: Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.
ME.M9-12.LE.A.1.a: Prove that linear functions grow by equal differences over equal intervals, and that exponential functions grow by equal factors over equal intervals.
ME.M9-12.LE.A.1.b: Recognize situations in which one quantity changes at a constant rate per unit interval relative to another.
ME.M9-12.LE.A.1.c: Recognize situations in which a quantity grows or decays by a constant percent rate per unit interval relative to another.
ME.M9-12.LE.A.2: Construct linear and exponential functions, including arithmetic and geometric sequences, given a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs (include reading these from a table).
ME.M9-12.LE.A.3: Observe using graphs and tables that a quantity increasing exponentially eventually exceeds a quantity increasing linearly, quadratically, or (more generally) as a polynomial function.
ME.M9-12.LE.A.4: For exponential models, express as a logarithm the solution to `ab^(ct)=d` where `a,c,andd` are numbers and the base `b` is `2,10,ore`; evaluate the logarithm using technology.
ME.M9-12.LE.B: Interpret expressions for function in terms of the situation they model.
ME.M9-12.LE.B.5: Interpret the parameters in a linear or exponential function in terms of a context.
ME.M9-12.TF.A: Extend the domain of trigonometric functions using the unit circle.
ME.M9-12.TF.A.1: Understand radian measure of an angle as the length of the arc on the unit circle subtended by the angle.
ME.M9-12.TF.A.2: Explain how the unit circle in the coordinate plane enables the extension of trigonometric functions to all real numbers, interpreted as radian measures of angles traversed counterclockwise around the unit circle.
ME.M9-12.TF.A.3: Use special triangles to determine geometrically the values of sine, cosine, tangent for `pi/3,pi/4andpi/6`, and use the unit circle to express the values of sine, cosine, and tangent for `x,pi+x,and2pi-x` in terms of their values for `x`, where `x` is any real number.
ME.M9-12.TF.A.4: Use the unit circle to explain symmetry (odd and even) and periodicity of trigonometric functions.
ME.M9-12.TF.B: Model periodic phenomena with trigonometric functions.
ME.M9-12.TF.B.5: Choose trigonometric functions to model periodic phenomena with specified amplitude, frequency, and midline.
ME.M9-12.TF.B.6: Understand that restricting a trigonometric function to a domain on which it is always increasing or always decreasing allows its inverse to be constructed.
ME.M9-12.TF.B.7: Use inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations that arise in modeling contexts; evaluate the solutions using technology, and interpret them in terms of the context.
ME.M9-12.TF.C.8: Prove the Pythagorean identity sin^2(θ) + cos²(θ) = 1 and use it to find sin(θ), cos(θ), or tan(θ) given sin(θ), cos(θ), or tan(θ) and the quadrant of the angle.
ME.M9-12.TF.C.9: Prove the addition and subtraction formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent and use them to solve problems.
ME.M9-12.CO.A: Experiment with transformations in the plane.
ME.M9-12.CO.A.1: Know precise definitions of angle, circle, perpendicular line, parallel line, and line segment, based on the undefined notions of point, line, distance along a line, and distance around a circular arc.
ME.M9-12.CO.A.2: Represent transformations in the plane using, e.g., transparencies and/or geometry software; describe transformations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give other points as outputs. Compare transformations that preserve distance and angle to those that do not (e.g., translation versus horizontal stretch).
ME.M9-12.CO.A.3: Given a rectangle, parallelogram, trapezoid, or regular polygon, describe the rotations and reflections that carry it onto itself.
ME.M9-12.CO.A.4: Develop definitions of rotations, reflections, and translations in terms of angles, circles, perpendicular lines, parallel lines, and line segments.
ME.M9-12.CO.A.5: Given a geometric figure and a rotation, reflection, or translation, draw the transformed figure using, e.g., graph paper, tracing paper, or geometry software. Specify a sequence of transformations that will carry a given figure onto another.
ME.M9-12.CO.B: Understand congruence in terms of rigid motions.
ME.M9-12.CO.B.6: Use geometric descriptions of rigid motions to transform figures and to predict the effect of a given rigid motion on a given figure; given two figures, use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to decide if they are congruent.
ME.M9-12.CO.B.7: Use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to show that two triangles are congruent if and only if corresponding pairs of sides and corresponding pairs of angles are congruent.
ME.M9-12.CO.B.8: Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.
ME.M9-12.CO.C: Prove geometric theorems and when appropriate, the converse of theorems.
ME.M9-12.CO.C.9: Prove theorems about lines and angles.
ME.M9-12.CO.D.12: Make formal geometric constructions with a variety of tools and methods (compass and straightedge, string, reflective devices, paper folding, dynamic geometric software, etc.).
ME.M9-12.CO.D.13: Construct an equilateral triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle.
ME.M9-12.SRT.A: Understand similarity in terms of similarity transformations.
ME.M9-12.SRT.A.1: Verify experimentally the properties of dilations given by a center and a scale factor:
ME.M9-12.SRT.A.1.a: A dilation takes a line not passing through the center of the dilation to a parallel line, and leaves a line passing through the center unchanged.
ME.M9-12.SRT.A.1.b: The dilation of a line segment is longer or shorter in the ratio given by the scale factor.
ME.M9-12.SRT.A.2: Given two figures, use the definition of similarity in terms of similarity transformations to decide if they are similar; explain using similarity transformations the meaning of similarity for triangles as the equality of all corresponding pairs of angles and the proportionality of all corresponding pairs of sides.
ME.M9-12.SRT.A.3: Use the properties of similarity transformations to establish the AA criterion for two triangles to be similar.
ME.M9-12.SRT.B: Prove theorems involving similarity using a variety of ways of writing proofs, showing validity of underlying reasoning.
ME.M9-12.SRT.B.5: Use congruence and similarity criteria for triangles to solve problems and to prove relationships in geometric figures.
ME.M9-12.SRT.C: Define trigonometric ratios and solve problems involving right triangles.
ME.M9-12.SRT.C.6: Understand that by similarity, side ratios in right triangles are properties of the angles in the triangle, leading to definitions of trigonometric ratios for acute angles.
ME.M9-12.SRT.C.7: Explain and use the relationship between the sine and cosine of complementary angles.
ME.M9-12.SRT.C.8: Use trigonometric ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem to solve right triangles in applied problems.
ME.M9-12.SRT.D.9: Derive the formula A = ab(1/2)sin(C) for the area of a triangle by drawing an auxiliary line from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.
ME.M9-12.SRT.D.10: Prove the Laws of Sines and Cosines and use them to solve problems.
ME.M9-12.SRT.D.1: Understand and apply the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines to find unknown measurements in right and non-right triangles (e.g., surveying problems, resultant forces).
ME.M9-12.C.A: Understand and apply theorems about circles.
ME.M9-12.C.A.1: Prove that all circles are similar.
ME.M9-12.C.A.2: Identify and describe relationships among inscribed angles, radii, and chords.
ME.M9-12.C.A.3: Construct the inscribed and circumscribed circles of a triangle and prove properties of angles for a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle.
ME.M9-12.C.A.4: Construct a tangent line from a point outside a given circle to the circle.
ME.M9-12.C.B: Find arc lengths and areas of sectors of circles.
ME.M9-12.C.B.5: Derive using similarity the fact that the length of the arc intercepted by an angle is proportional to the radius and define the radian measure of the angle as the constant of proportionality; derive the formula for the area of a sector.
ME.M9-12.GPE.A: Translate between the geometric description and the equation for a conic section.
ME.M9-12.GPE.A.1: Derive the equation of a circle of given center and radius using the Pythagorean Theorem; complete the square to find the center and radius of a circle given by an equation.
ME.M9-12.GPE.A.2: Derive the equation of a parabola given a focus and directrix.
ME.M9-12.GPE.A.3: Derive the equations of ellipses and hyperbolas given the foci and directrix, using the fact that the sum or difference of distances from the foci is constant.
ME.M9-12.GPE.B: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically.
ME.M9-12.GPE.B.4: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically including the distance formula and its relationship to the Pythagorean Theorem.
ME.M9-12.GPE.B.5: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve geometric problems (e.g., find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line that passes through a given point).
ME.M9-12.GPE.B.6: Find the point on a directed line segment between two given points that partitions the segment in a given ratio.
ME.M9-12.GPE.B.7: Use coordinates to compute perimeters of polygons and areas of triangles and rectangles, e.g., using the distance formula.
ME.M9-12.GMD.A: Explain volume formulas and use them to solve problems.
ME.M9-12.GMD.A.1: Give an informal argument for the formulas for the circumference of a circle, area of a circle, volume of a cylinder, pyramid, and cone.
ME.M9-12.GMD.A.2: Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the formulas for the volume of a sphere and other solid figures.
ME.M9-12.GMD.A.3: Use volume formulas for cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres to solve problems.
ME.M9-12.GMD.B: Visualize relationships between two-dimensional and three-dimensional objects.
ME.M9-12.GMD.B.4: Identify the shapes of two-dimensional cross-sections of three-dimensional objects, and identify three-dimensional objects generated by rotations of two-dimensional objects.
ME.M9-12.MG.A: Apply geometric concepts in modeling situations.
ME.M9-12.MG.A.1: Use geometric shapes, their measures, and their properties to describe objects (e.g., modeling a tree trunk or a human torso as a cylinder).
ME.M9-12.MG.A.2: Apply concepts of density based on area and volume in modeling situations (e.g., `text(persons per square mile),text(BTUs per cubic foot)`).
ME.M9-12.MG.A.3: Apply geometric methods to solve design problems (e.g., designing an object or structure to satisfy physical constraints or minimize cost; working with typographic grid systems based on ratios).
ME.M9-12.ID.A: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable.
ME.M9-12.ID.A.1: Represent data with plots on the real number line (dot plots, histograms, and box plots).
ME.M9-12.ID.A.2: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more different data sets.
ME.M9-12.ID.A.3: Interpret differences in shape, center, and spread in the context of the data sets, accounting for possible effects of extreme data points (outliers).
ME.M9-12.ID.A.4: Use the mean and standard deviation of a data set to fit it to a normal distribution and to estimate population percentages. Recognize that there are data sets for which such a procedure is not appropriate. Use calculators, spreadsheets, and tables to estimate areas under the normal curve.
ME.M9-12.ID.B: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on two categorical variables and two quantitative variables.

MN.E2.1.2: Recount stories, including fables and folktales from diverse cultures, and determine their central message, lesson, or moral.
MN.E2.1.3: Describe how characters in a story respond to major events and challenges.
MN.E2.1.4: Describe how words and phrases (e.g., regular beats, alliteration, rhymes, repeated lines) supply rhythm and meaning in a story, poem, or song.
MN.E2.1.5: Describe the overall structure of a story, including describing how the beginning introduces the story and the ending concludes the action.
MN.E2.1.6: Acknowledge differences in the points of view of characters, including by speaking in a different voice for each character when reading dialogue aloud.
MN.E2.1.7: Use information gained from the illustrations and words in a print or digital text to demonstrate understanding of its characters, setting, or plot.
MN.E2.1.9: Compare and contrast two or more versions of the same story (e.g., Cinderella stories) by different authors or from different cultures, including those by or about Minnesota American Indians.
MN.E2.1.10: By the end of the year, select, read and comprehend literature including stories and poetry for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks, in the grades 2-3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
MN.E2.2.1: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.
MN.E2.2.2: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.
MN.E2.2.3: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.
MN.E2.2.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 2 topic or subject area.
MN.E2.2.5: Know and use various text features (e.g., captions, bold print, subheadings, glossaries, indexes, electronic menus, icons) to locate key facts or information in a text efficiently.
MN.E2.2.6: Identify the main purpose of a text, including what the author wants to answer, explain, or describe.
MN.E2.2.7: Explain how specific images (e.g., a diagram showing how a machine works) contribute to and clarify a text.
MN.E2.2.8: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.
MN.E2.2.9: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.
MN.E2.2.10: By the end of year, select, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2-3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range for personal interest, enjoyment, and academic tasks.
MN.E2.3.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
MN.E2.3.3.a: Distinguish long and short vowels when reading regularly spelled one-syllable words.
MN.E2.3.3.b: Know spelling-sound correspondences for additional common vowel teams.
MN.E2.3.3.c: Decode regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels.
MN.E2.3.3.d: Decode words with common prefixes and suffixes.
MN.E2.3.3.e: Identify words with inconsistent but common spelling-sound correspondences.
MN.E2.3.3.f: Recognize and read grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words, including high-frequency words.
MN.E2.3.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
MN.E2.3.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding to promote oral and silent reading fluency.
MN.E2.3.4.b: Read grade-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
MN.E2.3.4.c: Use context and other cues (e.g., phonics, word recognition skills, prior knowledge) to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.
MN.E2.6.1: Write opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or book they are writing about, state an opinion, supply reasons that support the opinion, use linking words (e.g., because, and, also) to connect opinion and reasons, and provide a concluding statement or section.
MN.E2.6.2: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section.
MN.E2.6.3: Write narratives and other creative texts in which they recount a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events, include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.
MN.E2.6.5: With guidance and support from adults, and peers, focus on a topic and strengthen writing as needed by revising and editing.
MN.E2.6.6: With guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.
MN.E2.6.7: Participate in shared research and writing projects (e.g., read a number of books on a single topic to produce a report; record science observations).
MN.E2.6.8: Recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
MN.E2.8.1: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 2 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
MN.E2.8.1.a: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (e.g., gaining the floor in respectful ways, listening to others with care, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).
MN.E2.8.1.b: Build on others' talk in conversations by linking their comments to the remarks of others.
MN.E2.8.1.c: Ask for clarification and further explanation as needed about the topics and texts under discussion.
MN.E2.8.1.e: Follow two- and three-step oral directions.
MN.E2.8.2: Recount or describe key ideas or details from a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.
MN.E2.8.3: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to clarify comprehension, gather additional information, or deepen understanding of a topic or issues.
MN.E2.8.4: Tell a story or recount an experience with appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details, avoid plagiarism by identifying sources, and speak audibly in coherent sentences.
MN.E2.8.5: Create audio recordings of stories or poems; add drawings or other visual displays to stories or recounts of experiences when appropriate to clarify ideas, thoughts, and feelings.
MN.E2.8.6: Produce complete sentences when appropriate to task and situation in order to provide requested detail or clarification.
MN.E2.8.7: Distinguish, understand, and use different types of print, digital, and multimodal media.
MN.E2.8.7.a: Use tools for locating print and electronic materials appropriate to the purpose.
MN.E2.8.8: With prompting and support, create an individual or shared multimedia work for a specific purpose (e.g., to create or integrate knowledge, to share experiences or information, to persuade, to entertain, or as artistic expression).
MN.E2.8.8.a: With prompting and support, critique each found image under consideration for use in a multimedia project for its appropriateness to purpose, its effectiveness in conveying the message, and its effect on the intended audience and justify its use in the project.
MN.E2.8.8.b: Share the work with an audience.
MN.E2.10.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
MN.E2.10.1.b: Form and use frequently occurring irregular plural nouns (e.g., feet, children, teeth, mice, fish).
MN.E2.10.1.d: Form and use the past tense of frequently occurring irregular verbs (e.g., sat, hid, told).
MN.E2.10.1.e: Use adjectives and adverbs, and choose between them depending on what is to be modified.
MN.E2.10.1.f: Produce, expand, and rearrange complete simple and compound sentences (e.g., The boy watched the movie; The little boy watched the movie; The action movie was watched by the little boy).
MN.E2.10.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
MN.E2.10.2.a: Capitalize holidays, product names, and geographic names.
MN.E2.10.2.b: Use commas in greetings and closings of letters.
MN.E2.10.2.c: Use an apostrophe to form contractions and frequently occurring possessives.
MN.E2.10.2.d: Generalize learned spelling patterns when writing words (e.g., cage → badge; boy → boil).
MN.E2.10.2.e: Consult reference materials, including beginning dictionaries, as needed to check and correct spellings.
MN.E2.10.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
MN.E2.10.3.a: Compare formal and informal uses of English.
MN.E2.10.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 2 reading and content, choosing flexibly from an array of strategies.
MN.E2.10.4.a: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
MN.E2.10.4.b: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known prefix is added to a known word (e.g., happy/unhappy, tell/retell).
MN.E2.10.4.c: Use a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word with the same root (e.g., addition, additional).
MN.E2.10.4.d: Use knowledge of the meaning of individual words to predict the meaning of compound words (e.g., birdhouse, lighthouse, housefly; bookshelf, notebook, bookmark).
MN.E2.10.4.e: Use glossaries and beginning dictionaries, both print and digital, to determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases.
MN.E2.10.5: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings to develop word consciousness.
MN.E2.10.5.a: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., describe foods that are spicy or juicy).
MN.E2.10.5.b: Distinguish shades of meaning among closely related verbs (e.g., toss, throw, hurl) and closely related adjectives (e.g., thin, slender, skinny, scrawny).
MN.E2.10.6: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using adjectives and adverbs to describe (e.g., When other kids are happy that makes me happy).
MN.M2.1.1: Compare and represent whole numbers up to `1000` with an emphasis on place value and equality.
MN.M2.1.1.1: Read, write and represent whole numbers up to `1000`. Representations may include numerals, addition, subtraction, multiplication, words, pictures, tally marks, number lines and manipulatives, such as bundles of sticks and base `10` blocks.
MN.M2.1.1.2: Use place value to describe whole numbers between 10 and 1000 in terms of hundreds, tens and ones. Know that 100 is 10 tens, and 1000 is 10 hundreds.
MN.M2.1.1.3: Find 10 more or 10 less than a given three-digit number. Find 100 more or 100 less than a given three-digit number.
MN.M2.1.1.4: Round numbers up to the nearest 10 and 100 and round numbers down to the nearest 10 and 100.
MN.M2.1.1.5: Compare and order whole numbers up to `1000`.
MN.M2.1.2: Demonstrate mastery of addition and subtraction basic facts; add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers in real-world and mathematical problems.
MN.M2.1.2.1: Use strategies to generate addition and subtraction facts including making tens, fact families, doubles plus or minus one, counting on, counting back, and the commutative and associative properties. Use the relationship between addition and subtraction to generate basic facts.
MN.M2.1.2.2: Demonstrate fluency with basic addition facts and related subtraction facts.
MN.M2.1.2.3: Estimate sums and differences up to 100.
MN.M2.1.2.4: Use mental strategies and algorithms based on knowledge of place value and equality to add and subtract two-digit numbers. Strategies may include decomposition, expanded notation, and partial sums and differences.
MN.M2.1.2.5: Solve real-world and mathematical addition and subtraction problems involving whole numbers with up to 2 digits.
MN.M2.1.2.6: Use addition and subtraction to create and obtain information from tables, bar graphs and tally charts.
MN.M2.2.1: Recognize, create, describe, and use patterns and rules to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
MN.M2.2.1.1: Identify, create and describe simple number patterns involving repeated addition or subtraction, skip counting and arrays of objects such as counters or tiles. Use patterns to solve problems in various contexts.
MN.M2.2.2: Use number sentences involving addition, subtraction and unknowns to represent and solve real-world and mathematical problems; create real-world situations corresponding to number sentences.
MN.M2.2.2.1: Understand how to interpret number sentences involving addition, subtraction and unknowns represented by letters. Use objects and number lines and create real-world situations to represent number sentences.
MN.M2.2.2.2: Use number sentences involving addition, subtraction, and unknowns to represent given problem situations. Use number sense and properties of addition and subtraction to find values for the unknowns that make the number sentences true.
MN.M2.3.1: Identify, describe and compare basic shapes according to their geometric attributes.
MN.M2.3.1.1: Describe, compare, and classify two- and three-dimensional figures according to number and shape of faces, and the number of sides, edges and vertices (corners).
MN.M2.3.1.2: Identify and name basic two- and three-dimensional shapes, such as squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, trapezoids, hexagons, cubes, rectangular prisms, cones, cylinders and spheres.
MN.M2.3.2: Understand length as a measurable attribute; use tools to measure length.
MN.M2.3.2.1: Understand the relationship between the size of the unit of measurement and the number of units needed to measure the length of an object.
MN.M2.3.2.2: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between length and the numbers on a ruler by using a ruler to measure lengths to the nearest centimeter or inch.
MN.M2.3.3: Use time and money in real-world and mathematical situations.
MN.M2.3.3.1: Tell time to the quarter-hour and distinguish between a.m. and p.m.
MN.M2.3.3.2: Identify pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters. Find the value of a group of coins and determine combinations of coins that equal a given amount.
MN.E3.1.1: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
MN.E3.1.2: Recount stories, including fables, folktales, and myths from diverse cultures; determine the central message, lesson, or moral and explain how it is conveyed through key details in the text.
MN.E3.1.3: Describe characters in a story (e.g., their traits, motivations, or feelings) and explain how their actions contribute to the sequence of events.
MN.E3.1.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, distinguishing literal from nonliteral language, including figurative language such as similes.
MN.E3.1.5: Refer to parts of stories, dramas, and poems when writing or speaking about a text, using terms such as chapter, scene, and stanza; describe how each successive part builds on earlier sections.
MN.E3.1.6: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the narrator or those of the characters.
MN.E3.1.7: Explain how specific aspects of a text's illustrations contribute to what is conveyed by the words in a story (e.g., create mood, emphasize aspects of a character or setting).
MN.E3.1.9: Compare and contrast the themes, settings, and plots of stories written by the same author about the same or similar characters (e.g., in books from a series).
MN.E3.1.10: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature and other texts including stories, dramas, and poetry, at the high end of the grades 2-3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
MN.E3.1.10.a: Self-select texts for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E3.2.1: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
MN.E3.2.2: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
MN.E3.2.3: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
MN.E3.2.4: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 3 topic or subject area.
MN.E3.2.5: Use text features and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to locate information relevant to a given topic efficiently.
MN.E3.2.6: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the author of a text.
MN.E3.2.7: Use information gained from illustrations (e.g., maps, photographs) and the words in a text to demonstrate understanding of the text (e.g., where, when, why, and how key events occur).
MN.E3.2.8: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).
MN.E3.2.9: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.
MN.E3.2.10: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 2-3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
MN.E3.2.10.a: Self-select texts for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E3.3.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
MN.E3.3.3.a: Identify and know the meaning of the most common prefixes and derivational suffixes.
MN.E3.3.3.b: Decode words with common Latin suffixes.
MN.E3.3.3.d: Read grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words, including high-frequency words.
MN.E3.3.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
MN.E3.3.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
MN.E3.3.4.b: Read grade-level prose and poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
MN.E3.3.4.c: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.
MN.E3.6.1: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons.
MN.E3.6.1.a: Introduce the topic or text they are writing about, state an opinion, and create an organizational structure that lists reasons.
MN.E3.6.1.b: Provide reasons that support the opinion.
MN.E3.6.1.c: Use linking words and phrases (e.g., because, therefore, since, for example) to connect opinion and reasons.
MN.E3.6.1.d: Provide a concluding statement or section.
MN.E3.6.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
MN.E3.6.2.a: Introduce a topic and group related information together; include illustrations when useful to aiding comprehension.
MN.E3.6.2.b: Develop the topic with facts, definitions, and details.
MN.E3.6.2.c: Use linking words and phrases (e.g., also, another, and, more, but) to connect ideas within categories of information.
MN.E3.6.2.d: Provide a concluding statement or section.
MN.E3.6.3: Write narratives and other creative texts to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
MN.E3.6.3.a: Establish a situation and introduce a narrator and/or characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally.
MN.E3.6.3.b: Use dialogue and descriptions of actions, thoughts, and feelings to develop experiences and events or show the response of characters to situations.
MN.E3.6.3.c: Use temporal words and phrases to signal event order.
MN.E3.6.4: With guidance and support from adults, produce writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task and purpose.
MN.E3.6.5: With guidance and support from peers and adults, use a writing process to develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, drafting, revising, and editing.
MN.E3.6.6: With guidance and support from adults, use technology to produce and publish writing (using keyboarding skills) as well as to interact and collaborate with others.
MN.E3.6.7: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge about a topic.
MN.E3.6.8: Recall information from experiences or gather information from print and digital sources; take brief notes on sources and sort evidence into provided categories.
MN.E3.6.10: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.
MN.E3.6.10.a: Independently select writing topics and formats for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E3.8.1: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 3 topics and texts, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly.
MN.E3.8.1.a: Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation and other information known about the topic to explore ideas under discussion.
MN.E3.8.1.b: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (e.g., gaining the floor in respectful ways, listening to others with care, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).
MN.E3.8.1.c: Ask questions to check understanding of information presented, stay on topic, and link their comments to the remarks of others.
MN.E3.8.1.d: Explain their own ideas and understanding in light of the discussion.
MN.E3.8.1.e: Cooperate and compromise as appropriate for productive group discussion.
MN.E3.8.2: Determine the main ideas and supporting details of a text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.
MN.E3.8.3: Ask and answer questions about information from a speaker, offering appropriate elaboration and detail.
MN.E3.8.4: Report on a topic or text and avoid plagiarism by identifying sources, tell a story, or recount an experience with appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details, speaking clearly at an understandable pace.
MN.E3.8.5: Create engaging audio recordings of stories or poems that demonstrate fluid reading at an understandable pace; add visual displays when appropriate to emphasize or enhance certain facts or details.
MN.E3.8.6: Speak in complete sentences when appropriate to task and situation in order to provide requested detail or clarification.
MN.E3.8.7: Distinguish among, understand, and use different types of print, digital, and multimodal media.
MN.E3.8.7.a: Make informed judgments about messages promoted in the mass media (e.g., film, television, radio, magazines, advertisements, newspapers).
MN.E3.8.7.b: Locate and use information in print, non-print, and digital resources, and identify reasons for choosing information used.
MN.E3.8.7.c: Check for accuracy in pictures and images.
MN.E3.8.7.d: Recognize safe practices in personal media communications.
MN.E3.8.8: With prompting and support, create an individual or shared multimedia work for a specific purpose (e.g., to create or integrate knowledge, to share experiences or information, to persuade, to entertain, or as artistic expression).
MN.E3.8.8.a: With prompting and support, critique each found image under consideration for use in a multimedia project for its appropriateness to purpose, its effectiveness in conveying the message, and its effect on the intended audience and justify its use in the project.
MN.E3.8.8.b: Share the work with an audience.
MN.E3.10.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
MN.E3.10.1.a: Explain the function of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs in general and their functions in particular sentences.
MN.E3.10.1.b: Form and use regular and irregular plural nouns.
MN.E3.10.1.d: Form and use regular and irregular verbs.
MN.E3.10.1.e: Form and use the simple (e.g., I walked; I walk; I will walk) verb tenses.
MN.E3.10.1.g: Form and use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs, and choose between them depending on what is to be modified.
MN.E3.10.1.i: Produce simple, compound, and complex sentences.
MN.E3.10.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
MN.E3.10.2.c: Use commas and quotation marks in dialogue.
MN.E3.10.2.e: Use conventional spelling for high-frequency and other studied words and for adding suffixes to base words (e.g., sitting, smiled, cries, happiness).
MN.E3.10.2.f: Use spelling patterns and generalizations (e.g., word families, position-based spellings, syllable patterns, ending rules, meaningful word parts) in writing words.
MN.E3.10.2.g: Consult reference materials, including beginning dictionaries, as needed to check and correct spellings.
MN.E3.10.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
MN.E3.10.3.a: Choose words and phrases for effect.
MN.E3.10.3.b: Recognize and observe differences between the conventions of spoken and written standard English.
MN.E3.10.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning word and phrases based on grade 3 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
MN.E3.10.4.a: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
MN.E3.10.4.b: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known affix is added to a known word (e.g., agreeable/disagreeable, comfortable/uncomfortable, care/careless, heat/preheat).
MN.E3.10.4.c: Use a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word with the same root (e.g., company, companion).
MN.E3.10.4.d: Use glossaries or beginning dictionaries, both print and digital, to determine or clarify the precise meaning of key words and phrases.
MN.E3.10.5: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings to develop word consciousness.
MN.E3.10.5.a: Distinguish the literal and nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context (e.g., take steps).
MN.E3.10.5.b: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., describe people who are friendly or helpful).
MN.E3.10.5.c: Distinguish shades of meaning among related words that describe states of mind or degrees of certainty (e.g., knew, believed, suspected, heard, wondered).
MN.E3.10.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate conversational, general academic, and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal spatial and temporal relationships (e.g., After dinner that night we went looking for them).
MN.M3.1.1: Compare and represent whole numbers up to `100text(,)000` with an emphasis on place value and equality.
MN.M3.1.1.1: Read, write and represent whole numbers up to `100text(,)000`. Representations may include numerals, expressions with operations, words, pictures, number lines, and manipulatives such as bundles of sticks and base `10` blocks.
MN.M3.1.1.2: Use place value to describe whole numbers between `1000and100text(,)000` in terms of ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
MN.M3.1.1.3: Find `10text(,)000` more or `10text(,)000` less than a given `text(five-digit)` number. Find `1000` more or `1000` less than a given `text(four-orfive-digit)`. Find `100` more or `100` less than a given `text(four-orfive-digit)` number.
MN.M3.1.1.4: Round numbers to the nearest `10text(,)000,1text(,)000,100,and10`. Round up and round down to estimate sums and differences.
MN.M3.1.1.5: Compare and order whole numbers up to `100text(,)000`.
MN.M3.1.2: Add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers; represent multiplication and division in various ways; solve real-world and mathematical problems using arithmetic.
MN.M3.1.2.1: Add and subtract multi-digit numbers, using efficient and generalizable procedures based on knowledge of place value, including standard algorithms.
MN.M3.1.2.2: Use addition and subtraction to solve real-world and mathematical problems involving whole numbers. Use various strategies, including the relationship between addition and subtraction, the use of technology, and the context of the problem to assess the reasonableness of results.
MN.M3.1.2.3: Represent multiplication facts by using a variety of approaches, such as repeated addition, equal-sized groups, arrays, area models, equal jumps on a number line and skip counting. Represent division facts by using a variety of approaches, such as repeated subtraction, equal sharing and forming equal groups. Recognize the relationship between multiplication and division.
MN.M3.1.2.4: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving multiplication and division, including both “how many in each group” and “how many groups” division problems.
MN.M3.1.2.5: Use strategies and algorithms based on knowledge of place value, equality and properties of addition and multiplication to multiply a two- or three-digit number by a one-digit number. Strategies may include mental strategies, partial products, the standard algorithm, and the commutative, associative, and distributive properties.
MN.M3.1.3: Understand meanings and uses of fractions in real-world and mathematical situations.
MN.M3.1.3.1: Read and write fractions with words and symbols. Recognize that fractions can be used to represent parts of a whole, parts of a set, points on a number line, or distances on a number line.
MN.M3.1.3.2: Understand that the size of a fractional part is relative to the size of the whole.
MN.M3.1.3.3: Order and compare unit fractions and fractions with like denominators by using models and an understanding of the concept of numerator and denominator.
MN.M3.2.1: Use single-operation input-output rules to represent patterns and relationships and to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
MN.M3.2.1.1: Create, describe, and apply single-operation input-output rules involving addition, subtraction and multiplication to solve problems in various contexts.
MN.M3.2.2: Use number sentences involving multiplication and division basic facts and unknowns to represent and solve real-world and mathematical problems; create real-world situations corresponding to number sentences.
MN.M3.2.2.1: Understand how to interpret number sentences involving multiplication and division basic facts and unknowns. Create real-world situations to represent number sentences.
MN.M3.2.2.2: Use multiplication and division basic facts to represent a given problem situation using a number sentence. Use number sense and multiplication and division basic facts to find values for the unknowns that make the number sentences true.
MN.M3.3.1: Use geometric attributes to describe and create shapes in various contexts.
MN.M3.3.1.1: Identify parallel and perpendicular lines in various contexts, and use them to describe and create geometric shapes, such as right triangles, rectangles, parallelograms and trapezoids.
MN.M3.3.1.2: Sketch polygons with a given number of sides or vertices (corners), such as pentagons, hexagons and octagons.
MN.M3.3.2: Understand perimeter as a measurable attribute of real-world and mathematical objects. Use various tools to measure distances.
MN.M3.3.2.1: Use half units when measuring distances.
MN.M3.3.2.2: Find the perimeter of a polygon by adding the lengths of the sides.
MN.M3.3.3: Use time, money and temperature to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
MN.M3.3.3.1: Tell time to the minute, using digital and analog clocks. Determine elapsed time to the minute.
MN.M3.3.3.2: Know relationships among units of time.
MN.M3.3.3.3: Make change up to one dollar in several different ways, including with as few coins as possible.
MN.M3.3.3.4: Use an analog thermometer to determine temperature to the nearest degree in Fahrenheit and Celsius.
MN.M3.4.1: Collect, organize, display, and interpret data. Use labels and a variety of scales and units in displays.
MN.M3.4.1.1: Collect, display and interpret data using frequency tables, bar graphs, picture graphs and number line plots having a variety of scales. Use appropriate titles, labels and units.
MN.E4.1.1: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
MN.E4.1.2: Determine a theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text; summarize the text.
MN.E4.1.3: Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text (e.g., a character's thoughts, words, or actions).
MN.E4.1.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including those that allude to significant characters found in mythology (e.g., Herculean).
MN.E4.1.5: Explain major differences between poems, drama, and prose, and refer to the structural elements of poems (e.g., verse, rhythm, meter) and drama (e.g., casts of characters, settings, descriptions, dialogue, stage directions) when writing or speaking about a text.
MN.E4.1.6: Compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrated, including the difference between first- and third-person narrations.
MN.E4.1.7: Make connections between the text of a story or drama and a visual or oral presentation of the text, identifying where each version reflects specific descriptions and directions in the text.
MN.E4.1.9: Compare and contrast the treatment of similar themes and topics (e.g., opposition of good and evil) and patterns of events (e.g., the quest) in stories, myths, and traditional literature from different cultures, including American Indian.
MN.E4.1.10: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature and other texts including stories, drama, and poetry, in the grades 4-5 text complexity band proficiently and independently with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
MN.E4.1.10.a: Self-select texts for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E4.2.1: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
MN.E4.2.2: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
MN.E4.2.3: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
MN.E4.2.4: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases in a text relevant to a grade 4 topic or subject area.
MN.E4.2.5: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in a text or part of a text.
MN.E4.2.6: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account, including those by or about Minnesota American Indians, of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
MN.E4.2.7: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
MN.E4.2.8: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
MN.E4.2.9: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
MN.E4.2.10: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
MN.E4.2.10.a: Self-select texts for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E4.3.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
MN.E4.3.3.a: Use combined knowledge of all letter-sound correspondences, syllabication patterns, and morphology (e.g., roots and affixes) to read accurately unfamiliar multisyllabic words in context and out of context.
MN.E4.3.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
MN.E4.3.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
MN.E4.3.4.b: Read grade-level prose and poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
MN.E4.3.4.c: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.
MN.E4.6.1: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
MN.E4.6.1.a: Introduce a topic or text clearly, state an opinion, and create an organizational structure in which related ideas are grouped to support the writer's purpose.
MN.E4.6.1.b: Provide reasons that are supported by facts and details.
MN.E4.6.1.c: Link opinion and reasons using words and phrases (e.g., for instance, in order to, in addition).
MN.E4.6.1.d: Provide a concluding statement or section related to the opinion presented.
MN.E4.6.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
MN.E4.6.2.a: Introduce a topic clearly and group related information in paragraphs and sections; include formatting (e.g., headings), illustrations, and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.
MN.E4.6.2.b: Develop the topic with facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples related to the topic.
MN.E4.6.2.c: Link ideas within categories of information using words and phrases (e.g., another, for example, also, because).
MN.E4.6.2.d: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
MN.E4.6.2.e: Provide a concluding statement or section related to the information or explanation presented.
MN.E4.6.3: Write narratives and other creative texts to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
MN.E4.6.3.a: Orient the reader by establishing a situation and introducing a narrator and/or characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally.
MN.E4.6.3.b: Use dialogue and description to develop experiences and events or show the responses of characters to situations.
MN.E4.6.3.c: Use a variety of transitional words and phrases to manage the sequence of events.
MN.E4.6.3.d: Use concrete words and phrases and sensory details to convey experiences and events precisely.
MN.E4.6.3.e: Provide a conclusion (when appropriate to the genre) that follows from the narrated experiences or events.
MN.E4.6.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
MN.E4.6.5: With guidance and support from peers and adults, use a writing process to develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, drafting, revising, and editing.
MN.E4.6.6: With some guidance and support from adults, use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of one page in a single sitting.
MN.E4.6.7: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.
MN.E4.6.8: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources; take notes and categorize information, and provide a list of sources.
MN.E4.6.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
MN.E4.6.9.a: Apply grade 4 Reading standards to literature (e.g., “Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text [e.g., a character's thoughts, words, or actions].”).
MN.E4.6.9.b: Apply grade 4 Reading standards to informational texts (e.g., “Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text”).
MN.E4.6.10: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.
MN.E4.6.10.a: Independently select writing topics and formats for personal, enjoyment interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E4.8.1: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 4 topics and texts, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly.
MN.E4.8.1.a: Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation and other information known about the topic to explore ideas under discussion.
MN.E4.8.1.b: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions and carry out assigned roles.
MN.E4.8.1.c: Pose and respond to specific questions to clarify or follow up on information, and make comments that contribute to the discussion and link to the remarks of others.
MN.E4.8.1.d: Review the key ideas expressed and explain their own ideas and understanding in light of the discussion.
MN.E4.8.1.e: Cooperate and problem solve as appropriate for productive group discussion.
MN.E4.8.2: Paraphrase portions of a text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.
MN.E4.8.3: Identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points.
MN.E4.8.4: Report on a topic or text and avoid plagiarism by identifying sources, tell a story, or recount an experience in an organized manner, using appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details to support main ideas or themes; speak clearly at an understandable pace.
MN.E4.8.5: Add audio recordings and visual displays to presentations when appropriate to enhance the development of main ideas or themes.
MN.E4.8.6: Differentiate between contexts that call for formal English (e.g., presenting ideas) and situations where informal discourse is appropriate (e.g., small-group discussion); use formal English when appropriate to task and situation.
MN.E4.8.7: Distinguish among, understand, and use different types of print, digital, and multimodal media.
MN.E4.8.7.a: Make informed judgments about messages promoted in the mass media (e.g., film, television, radio, magazines, advertisements, newspapers).
MN.E4.8.7.b: Locate and use information in print, non-print, and digital resources using a variety of strategies.
MN.E4.8.7.c: Locate and use information in print, non-print, and digital resources using a variety of strategies.
MN.E4.8.7.d: Recognize safe practices in social and personal media communications.
MN.E4.8.8: Create an individual or shared multimedia work for a specific purpose (e.g., to create or integrate knowledge, to share experiences or information, to persuade, to entertain, or as artistic expression).
MN.E4.8.8.a: Evaluate the Fair Use of each visual element or piece of music used in a media work and create a list documenting the source for each found image or piece of music.
MN.E4.8.8.b: Publish the work and share it with an audience.
MN.E4.10.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
MN.E4.10.1.a: Use relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that) and relative adverbs (where, when, why).
MN.E4.10.1.b: Form and use the progressive (e.g., I was walking; I am walking; I will be walking) verb tenses.
MN.E4.10.1.c: Use modal auxiliaries (e.g., can, may, must) to convey various conditions.
MN.E4.10.1.d: Order adjectives within sentences according to conventional patterns (e.g., a small red bag rather than a red small bag).
MN.E4.10.1.f: Produce complete sentences, recognizing and correcting inappropriate fragments and run-ons.
MN.E4.10.1.g: Correctly use frequently confused words (e.g., to, too, two; there, their).
MN.E4.10.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
MN.E4.10.2.b: Use commas and quotation marks to mark direct speech and quotations from a text.
MN.E4.10.2.c: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence.
MN.E4.10.2.d: Spell grade-appropriate words correctly, consulting references as needed.
MN.E4.10.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
MN.E4.10.3.a: Choose words and phrases to convey ideas precisely.
MN.E4.10.3.c: Differentiate between contexts that call for formal English (e.g., presenting ideas) and situations where informal discourse is appropriate (e.g., small-group discussion).
MN.E4.10.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 4 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
MN.E4.10.4.a: Use context (e.g., definitions, examples, or restatements in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
MN.E4.10.4.b: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek and Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., telegraph, photograph, autograph).
MN.E4.10.4.c: Consult reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation and determine or clarify the precise meaning of key words and phrases.
MN.E4.10.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings to develop word consciousness.
MN.E4.10.5.a: Explain the meaning of simple similes and metaphors (e.g., as pretty as a picture) in context.
MN.E4.10.5.b: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.
MN.E4.10.5.c: Demonstrate understanding of words by relating them to their opposites (antonyms) and to words with similar but not identical meanings (synonyms).
MN.E4.10.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal precise actions, emotions, or states of being (e.g., quizzed, whined, stammered) and that are basic to a particular topic (e.g., wildlife, conservation, and endangered when discussing animal preservation).
MN.M4.1.1: Demonstrate mastery of multiplication and division basic facts; multiply multi-digit numbers; solve real-world and mathematical problems using arithmetic.
MN.M4.1.1.1: Demonstrate fluency with multiplication and division facts.
MN.M4.1.1.2: Use an understanding of place value to multiply a number by `10,100,and1000`.
MN.M4.1.1.3: Multiply multi-digit numbers, using efficient and generalizable procedures, based on knowledge of place value, including standard algorithms.
MN.M4.1.1.4: Estimate products and quotients of multi-digit whole numbers by using rounding, benchmarks and place value to assess the reasonableness of results.
MN.M4.1.1.5: Solve multi-step real-world and mathematical problems requiring the use of addition, subtraction and multiplication of multi-digit whole numbers. Use various strategies, including the relationship between operations, the use of technology, and the context of the problem to assess the reasonableness of results.
MN.M4.1.1.6: Use strategies and algorithms based on knowledge of place value, equality and properties of operations to divide multi-digit whole numbers by one- or two-digit numbers. Strategies may include mental strategies, partial quotients, the commutative, associative, and distributive properties and repeated subtraction.
MN.M4.1.2: Represent and compare fractions and decimals in real-world and mathematical situations; use place value to understand how decimals represent quantities.
MN.M4.1.2.1: Represent equivalent fractions using fraction models such as parts of a set, fraction circles, fraction strips, number lines and other manipulatives. Use the models to determine equivalent fractions.
MN.M4.1.2.2: Locate fractions on a number line. Use models to order and compare whole numbers and fractions, including mixed numbers and improper fractions.
MN.M4.1.2.3: Use fraction models to add and subtract fractions with like denominators in real-world and mathematical situations. Develop a rule for addition and subtraction of fractions with like denominators.
MN.M4.1.2.4: Read and write decimals with words and symbols; use place value to describe decimals in terms of thousands, hundreds, tens, ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
MN.M4.1.2.5: Compare and order decimals and whole numbers using place value, a number line and models such as grids and base `10` blocks.
MN.M4.1.2.6: Read and write tenths and hundredths in decimal and fraction notations using words and symbols; know the fraction and decimal equivalents for halves and fourths.
MN.M4.1.2.7: Round decimals to the nearest tenth.
MN.M4.2.1: Use input-output rules, tables and charts to represent patterns and relationships and to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
MN.M4.2.1.1: Create and use input-output rules involving addition, subtraction, multiplication and division to solve problems in various contexts. Record the inputs and outputs in a chart or table.
MN.M4.2.2: Use number sentences involving multiplication, division and unknowns to represent and solve real-world and mathematical problems; create real-world situations corresponding to number sentences.
MN.M4.2.2.1: Understand how to interpret number sentences involving multiplication, division and unknowns. Use real-world situations involving multiplication or division to represent number sentences.
MN.M4.2.2.2: Use multiplication, division and unknowns to represent a given problem situation using a number sentence. Use number sense, properties of multiplication, and the relationship between multiplication and division to find values for the unknowns that make the number sentences true.
MN.M4.3.1: Name, describe, classify and sketch polygons.
MN.M4.3.1.1: Describe, classify and sketch triangles, including equilateral, right, obtuse and acute triangles. Recognize triangles in various contexts.
MN.M4.3.1.2: Describe, classify and draw quadrilaterals, including squares, rectangles, trapezoids, rhombuses, parallelograms and kites. Recognize quadrilaterals in various contexts.
MN.M4.3.2: Understand angle and area as measurable attributes of real-world and mathematical objects. Use various tools to measure angles and areas.
MN.M4.3.2.1: Measure angles in geometric figures and real-world objects with a protractor or angle ruler.
MN.M4.3.2.2: Compare angles according to size. Classify angles as acute, right and obtuse.
MN.M4.3.2.3: Understand that the area of a two-dimensional figure can be found by counting the total number of same size square units that cover a shape without gaps or overlaps. Justify why length and width are multiplied to find the area of a rectangle by breaking the rectangle into one unit by one unit squares and viewing these as grouped into rows and columns.
MN.M4.3.2.4: Find the areas of geometric figures and real-world objects that can be divided into rectangular shapes. Use square units to label area measurements.
MN.M4.3.3: Use translations, reflections and rotations to establish congruency and understand symmetries.
MN.M4.3.3.2: Apply reflections (flips) to figures by reflecting over vertical or horizontal lines and relate reflections to lines of symmetry.
MN.M4.3.3.3: Apply rotations (turns) of 90˚ clockwise or counterclockwise.
MN.M4.3.3.4: Recognize that translations, reflections and rotations preserve congruency and use them to show that two figures are congruent.
MN.M4.4.1: Collect, organize, display and interpret data, including data collected over a period of time and data represented by fractions and decimals.
MN.M4.4.1.1: Use tables, bar graphs, timelines and Venn diagrams to display data sets. The data may include fractions or decimals. Understand that spreadsheet tables and graphs can be used to display data.
MN.E5.1.1: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
MN.E5.1.2: Determine a theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text, including how characters in a story or drama respond to challenges or how the speaker in a poem reflects upon a topic; summarize the text.
MN.E5.1.3: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text (e.g., how characters interact).
MN.E5.1.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative language such as metaphors and similes.
MN.E5.1.5: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to provide the overall structure of a particular story, drama, or poem.
MN.E5.1.6: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described.
MN.E5.1.7: Analyze how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text (e.g., graphic novel, multimedia presentation of fiction, folktale, myth, poem).
MN.E5.1.9: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre (e.g., mysteries and adventure stories) on their approaches to similar themes and topics.
MN.E5.1.10: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature and other texts including stories, dramas, and poetry at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band proficiently and independently.
MN.E5.1.10.a: Self -select texts for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E5.2.1: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
MN.E5.2.2: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
MN.E5.2.3: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
MN.E5.2.4: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
MN.E5.2.5: Compare and contrast the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
MN.E5.2.6: Analyze multiple accounts by various cultures of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
MN.E5.2.7: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
MN.E5.2.8: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
MN.E5.2.9: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
MN.E5.2.10: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4-5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
MN.E5.2.10.a: Self-select texts for personal enjoyment, interest, and academic tasks.
MN.E5.3.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
MN.E5.3.3.a: Use combined knowledge of all letter-sound correspondences, syllabication patterns, and morphology (e.g., roots and affixes) to read accurately unfamiliar multisyllabic words in context and out of context
MN.E5.3.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
MN.E5.3.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
