NE.E8.V.2.a: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., verbal irony, puns) in context.
NE.E8.V.2.b: Determine the relationship between particular words to better understand each of the words.
NE.E8.V.2.c: Distinguish between the connotations of words with similar denotations (e.g., willful, resolute).
NE.E8.W.1: Create grammatically correct multi-paragraph compositions with varied sentence structures.
NE.E8.W.1.a: Apply knowledge of rules for capitalization.
NE.E8.W.1.b: Use punctuation (comma, ellipsis, dashes) to indicate a pause or break and an ellipsis to indicate an omission.
NE.E8.W.1.c: Explain the function of and use different types of verbals in sentences (e.g., gerunds, participles, infinitives).
NE.E8.W.1.d: Distinguish between and use active and passive voice, formal and informal tone, and types of grammatical mood (e.g. indicative, subjunctive, conditional, imperative).
NE.E8.W.1.e: Use appropriate parallel structure in words, phrases, and clauses.
NE.E8.W.1.f: Identify and revise fragment and run-on sentences and inappropriate shifts in verb tense, number, voice, and mood.
NE.E8.W.2: Use a recursive writing process to develop, strengthen, and produce writing appropriate to the audience, purpose, and discipline.
NE.E8.W.2.a: Identify and use resources and inquiry tools to plan, organize, and draft writing.
NE.E8.W.2.b: Adapt writing processes to sustain engagement in short and long-term writing tasks of increasing length and complexity.
NE.E8.W.2.c: Improve and clarify the content, structure, and organization of writing by revising, considering feedback from adults and peers.
NE.E8.W.2.d: Improve and clarify writing by editing and proofreading, considering feedback from adults and peers.
NE.E8.W.2.e: Use appropriate print and digital/multimedia tools to produce, enhance, and/or publish writing individually or in collaboration with peers.
NE.E8.W.3: Write in a variety of literary forms to convey real or imagined experiences or events in which the development and structure are appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience.
NE.E8.W.3.a: Engage and orient the reader by establishing a conflict, situation, or observation, introducing a narrator and/or character(s), and establishing and maintaining point(s) of view; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally and logically.
NE.E8.W.3.b: Use literary techniques (e.g., dialogue, pacing, description, multiple plot lines) to develop experiences, events, characters, and settings.
NE.E8.W.3.c: Use a variety of techniques to sequence events so that they build on one another to create a coherent whole.
NE.E8.W.3.d: Use precise words and phrases, descriptive/sensory details, and figurative language to establish mood and tone and convey a vivid picture.
NE.E8.W.3.e: Provide a conclusion that is clearly related to and reflects upon what is experienced, observed, or left unresolved over the course of the piece.
NE.E8.W.4: Write arguments that develop a perspective with supporting reasons and evidence, organized as appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience.
NE.E8.W.4.a: Develop a structure to sequence ideas appropriately; introduce a clear claim where appropriate.
NE.E8.W.4.b: Introduce claim(s), acknowledge and distinguish the claim(s) from alternate or supporting claims, and develop a structure in which ideas are grouped logically.
NE.E8.W.4.c: Explain and cite relevant evidence from multiple credible sources.
NE.E8.W.4.d: Use words, phrases, and key vocabulary to create cohesion and clarify the relationship between the claim(s) and supporting evidence.
NE.E8.W.4.e: Adapt style and tone appropriate to the norms and conventions of the task and discipline.
NE.E8.W.4.f: Provide a conclusion that follows from and supports the argument(s) presented.
NE.E8.W.5: Write informative/explanatory pieces to clearly convey ideas and information in which the development and structure are appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience.
NE.E8.W.5.a: Introduce a topic clearly and provide a specific focus; organize ideas, concepts, and information into broader categories or sections including text features, illustrations, and/or multimedia elements.
NE.E8.W.5.b: Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, and/or other information and examples.
NE.E8.W.5.c: Use appropriate transitions and domain-specific vocabulary to clarify relationships among ideas and concepts.
NE.E8.W.5.d: Provide a concluding statement or section that follows from the information or explanation(s).
NE.E8.W.6: Gather and use credible evidence from multiple trustworthy sources and assess its relevance in answering the research question(s).
NE.E8.W.6.a: Integrate evidence into writing by quoting or paraphrasing data and conclusions while avoiding plagiarism.
NE.E8.W.6.b: Locate and evaluate the credibility of evidence (e.g., the expertise or motivation of the creator of an information product, potential bias and/or deception) from print and digital sources to generate and answer questions and create new understandings.
NE.E8.W.6.c: Select and use appropriate note-taking formats to collect and organize information.
NE.E8.W.6.d: Demonstrate academic integrity by avoiding overreliance on any one source and citing sources within text (e.g., parenthetical and numerical); provide a list of sources using a standard format.
NE.E8.W.6.e: Practice safe and ethical behaviors when communicating and interacting with others digitally (e.g., safe information to share, utilize appropriate sites and materials, appropriate language use, respect diverse perspectives).
NE.E8.SL.1: Initiate and participate in structured discussions and collaborations about 8th grade topics and texts.
NE.E8.SL.1.a: Ask relevant questions to build on ideas, clarify own ideas, or acquire or confirm information.
NE.E8.SL.1.b: Demonstrate interpretation of verbal and non-verbal messages in a conversation.
NE.E8.SL.1.c: Converse with peers and adults in an all-inclusive manner to foster positive relationships while respecting diverse perspectives.
NE.E8.SL.1.d: Demonstrate active and attentive listening skills (e.g., eye contact, nonverbal cues, taking notes, summarizing, questioning).
NE.E8.SL.1.e: Complete a task following complex, multi-step directions.
NE.E8.SL.2: Present claims and findings, emphasizing key ideas in a focused, coherent manner with relevant descriptions, facts, details, and examples to clarify themes or central ideas.
NE.E8.SL.2.a: Demonstrate and adjust speaking techniques (e.g., appropriate eye contact, pacing, adequate volume, clear pronunciation) for a variety of purposes and situations, including interpreting 8th grade texts.
NE.E8.SL.2.b: Convey a perspective with clear reasoning and valid evidence.
NE.E8.SL.2.c: Analyze the purpose of information being presented and evaluate its motives (e.g., social, commercial, political).
NE.E8.SL.2.d: Demonstrate awareness of and sensitivity to the appropriate use of words (e.g., stereotypes, multiple meanings of words).
NE.E8.SL.2.e: Select and use appropriate visual and/or digital tools to enhance verbal communication and add interest.
NE.M8.N.1: Numeric Relationships: Students will demonstrate, represent, and show relationships among real numbers within the base-ten number system.
NE.M8.N.1.a: Determine subsets of numbers as natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational, or real based on the definitions of these sets of numbers.
NE.M8.N.1.b: Represent numbers with positive and negative exponents and in scientific notation.
NE.M8.N.1.c: Describe the difference between a rational and irrational number.
NE.M8.N.1.d: Approximate, compare, and order real numbers, both rational and irrational, and locate them on the number line.
NE.M8.N.2: Operations: Students will compute with exponents and roots.
NE.M8.N.2.a: Evaluate the square roots of perfect squares less than or equal to 400 and cube roots of perfect cubes less than or equal to 125.
NE.M8.N.2.b: Simplify numerical expressions involving integer exponents, square roots, and cube roots (e.g., 4-2 is the same as 1/16).
NE.M8.N.2.c: Evaluate numerical expressions involving absolute value.
NE.M8.N.2.d: Multiply and divide numbers using scientific notation.
NE.M8.A.1: Algebraic Processes: Students will apply the operational properties when evaluating expressions and solving equations.
NE.M8.A.1.a: Describe single variable equations as having one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions.
NE.M8.A.1.b: Solve multi-step equations involving rational numbers with the same variable appearing on both sides of the equation.
NE.M8.A.1.c: Solve equations of the form x^2= k(k <= 400) and x^3 = k(k <= 125), where k is a positive rational number, using square root and cube root symbols.
NE.M8.A.2: Applications: Students will solve authentic problems involving multi-step equations.
NE.M8.A.2.a: Write multi-step single variable equations from words, tables, and authentic situations.
NE.M8.A.2.b: Determine and describe the rate of change for given situations through the use of tables and graphs.
NE.M8.A.2.c: Graph proportional relationships and interpret the rate of change.
NE.M8.G.1: Attributes: Students will apply properties of angle relationships in triangles and with lines to determine angle measures.
NE.M8.G.1.a: Determine and use the relationships of the interior angles of a triangle to solve for missing measures.
NE.M8.G.1.b: Identify and apply geometric properties of parallel lines cut by a transversal and the resulting corresponding same side interior, alternate interior, and alternate exterior angles to find missing measures.
NE.M8.G.2: Coordinate Geometry: Students will determine location, orientation, and relationships on the coordinate plane.
NE.M8.G.2.a: Perform and describe positions and orientations of shapes under single transformations including rotations in multiples of 90 degrees about the origin, translations, reflections, and dilations on and off the coordinate plane.
NE.M8.G.2.b: Determine if two-dimensional figures are congruent or similar.
NE.M8.G.2.c: Perform and describe positions and orientations of shapes under a sequence of transformations on and off the coordinate plane.
NE.M8.G.3: Measurement: Students will reason with formulas and context to determine and compare length, area, and volume.
NE.M8.G.3.a: Explain a model of the Pythagorean Theorem.
NE.M8.G.3.b: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find side lengths of triangles and to solve authentic problems.
NE.M8.G.3.c: Find the distance between any two points on the coordinate plane using the Pythagorean Theorem.
NE.M8.G.3.d: Determine the volume of cones, cylinders, and spheres and solve authentic problems using volumes.
NE.M8.D.1: Data Collection and Statistical Methods: Students will formulate statistical investigative questions, collect data, and organize data.
NE.M8.D.2: Analyze Data and Interpret Results: Students will represent and analyze the data and interpret the results.
NE.M8.D.2.a: Represent and interpret bivariate data (e.g., ordered pairs) using scatter plots.
NE.M8.D.2.b: Describe patterns such as positive or negative association, linear or nonlinear association, clustering, and outliers when bivariate data is represented on a coordinate plane.
NE.M8.D.2.c: Draw an informal line of best fit based on the closeness of the data points to the line.
NE.M8.D.2.d: Use a linear model to make predictions and interpret the rate of change and `ytext(-intercept)` in context.
NE.M8.D.3: Probability: Students will interpret and apply concepts of probability.
NE.S8.1.1: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of forces and interactions.
NE.S8.1.1.a: Apply Newton's Third Law to design a solution to a problem involving the motion of two colliding objects.
NE.S8.1.1.b: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.
NE.S8.1.1.c: Plan an investigation to provide evidence of Newton's Laws that the change in an object's motion depends on the sum of the forces on the object and the mass of the object.
NE.S8.1.1.d: Ask questions about data to determine the factors that affect the strength of electrical and magnetic forces.
NE.S8.1.1.e: Construct and present arguments using evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on both the mass and distance of interacting objects.
NE.S8.1.1.f: Conduct an investigation and evaluate the experimental design to provide evidence that electrical and magnetic fields exist between objects exerting forces on each other even though the objects are not in contact.
NE.S8.2.2: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of waves and electromagnetic radiation.
NE.S8.2.2.a: Use mathematical representations to describe a simple model for waves that includes how the amplitude of a wave is related to the energy in a wave.
NE.S8.2.2.b: Develop and use a model to describe that Light and mechanical waves are reflected, absorbed, or transmitted through various materials.
NE.S8.2.2.c: Gather and make sense of information to support the claim that the structure of analog and digital signals allows for encoding and transmission of information.
NE.S8.4.3: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of energy.
NE.S8.4.3.a: Construct and interpret graphical displays of data to describe the relationships of kinetic energy to the mass and speed of an object.
NE.S8.4.3.b: Develop a model to describe that when the arrangement of objects interacting at a distance changes, then different amounts of potential energy are stored in the system.
NE.S8.9.4: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of the inheritance and variation of traits.
NE.S8.9.4.a: Develop and use a model to describe why structural changes to genes (mutations) may result in harmful, beneficial, or neutral effects to structure and function of organisms.
NE.S8.9.4.b: Gather and synthesize information about technologies that have changed the way humans influence inheritance of desired traits in organisms.
NE.S8.10.5: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of natural selection and adaptations.
NE.S8.10.5.a: Analyze and interpret data for patterns in the fossil record that document the existence, diversity, extinction, and change of life forms throughout the history of life on Earth under the assumption that natural laws operate today as in the past.
NE.S8.10.5.b: Apply scientific ideas to construct an explanation for the anatomical similarities and differences among and between modern and fossil organisms to infer evolutionary relationships.
NE.S8.10.5.c: Construct an explanation based on evidence that describes how genetic variations of traits in a population increase some individuals' probability of surviving and reproducing in a specific environment.
NE.S8.10.5.d: Use mathematical representations to support explanations of how natural selection may lead to increases and decreases of specific traits in populations over time.
NE.S8.11.6: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of the interactions among bodies in space.
NE.S8.11.6.a: Develop and use a model of the Earth-sun-moon system to describe the cyclic patterns of lunar phases, eclipses of the sun and moon, and seasons.
NE.S8.11.6.b: Develop and use a model to describe the role of gravity in the motions within the galaxy and the solar system.
NE.S8.11.6.c: Analyze and interpret data to determine scale properties of objects in the solar system.
NE.S8.14.7: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence to explain Earth's history.
NE.S8.14.7.a: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence found within rock strata, including index fossils, for how the geologic time scale is used to organize Earth's `4.6text(-billion-year-old)` history.
NE.E9-10.RP.1: Analyze the development of two or more implied or explicit themes over the course of a literary text or texts.
NE.E9-10.RP.2: Analyze how the development of characters, settings, and important events contribute to the meaning of the work as a whole.
NE.E9-10.RP.3: Analyze how the author's choices related to perspective or point of view contribute to the meaning, significance, or aesthetic of a literary text.
NE.E9-10.RP.4: Analyze how an author uses text structure, including the manipulation of time (e.g., foreshadowing, flashbacks) to create literary effects such as mystery, tension, and suspense.
NE.E9-10.RP.5: Analyze how an author draws on and transforms source material in a specific work (e.g., how Shakespeare treats a theme or topic from the Bible).
NE.E9-10.RP.6: Analyze the implied or stated theme(s) in a literary text to draw conclusions, deepen understanding of self and others, and generate questions for further inquiry.
NE.E9-10.RP.7: Analyze multiple perspectives within and across a wide range of literary texts.
NE.E9-10.RP.8: Read and comprehend a wide range of literary texts of appropriate complexity at the high end of the 9-10 grade band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
NE.E9-10.RI.1: Analyze the development of two or more implied or explicit central ideas over the course of an informational text or texts.
NE.E9-10.RI.2: Analyze how the interaction of individuals, important events, and key ideas contribute to the meaning of the work as a whole.
NE.E9-10.RI.3: Analyze an author's perspective or purpose in a text and analyze how an author uses rhetoric to advance that point of view or purpose.
NE.E9-10.RI.4: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or larger portions of a text (e.g., a section or chapter).
NE.E9-10.RI.5: Analyze informational texts of historical and/or cultural significance, including their treatment of related topics and concepts.
NE.E9-10.RI.6: Compare and contrast the development of different arguments on the same topic, evaluating the effectiveness and validity of the claims.
NE.E9-10.RI.7: Analyze how an author or speaker unfolds a series of events, ideas, or perspectives within and across a wide range of informational texts.
NE.E9-10.RI.8: Read and comprehend a wide range of informational texts of appropriate complexity at the high end of the 9- 10 grade band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.
NE.E9-10.V.1: Integrate grade-level academic vocabulary appropriately for a variety of tasks and purposes.
NE.E9-10.V.1.a: Use context clues (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word's position or function in a sentence) to determine the meanings of words and phrases.
NE.E9-10.V.1.b: Identify and correctly use patterns of word changes that indicate different meanings or parts of speech (e.g., analyze, analysis).
NE.E9-10.V.1.c: Consult general and specialized reference materials to determine or clarify the precise meanings, pronunciations, parts of speech, or etymology of words.
NE.E9-10.V.2: Interpret an author's use of figurative, connotative, and technical language in grade-level literary and informational text.
NE.E9-10.V.2.a: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., euphemism, oxymoron) in context and analyze their role in text.
NE.E9-10.V.2.b: Analyze nuances in the meanings of words with similar denotations.
NE.E9-10.W.1: Compose grammatically correct multi-paragraph compositions to convey meaning and add variety, interest, and fluency to written and spoken language.
NE.E9-10.W.1.a: Apply knowledge of rules for capitalization.
NE.E9-10.W.1.b: Use a colon to introduce a quotation, definition, or to expand on information in a sentence; use a semicolon with a conjunctive adverb.
NE.E9-10.W.1.c: Apply knowledge of function and usage to revise personal writing while resolving issues of complex or contested usage, consulting appropriate and reliable reference materials.
NE.E9-10.W.1.d: Select and use verbs with appropriate voice and mood.
NE.E9-10.W.1.e: Identify and revise fragment and run-on sentences and inappropriate shifts in verb tense, number, voice, mood, and parallel structure.
NE.E9-10.W.2: Use a recursive writing process to develop, strengthen, and produce writing appropriate to the audience, purpose, and discipline.
NE.E9-10.W.2.a: Identify and use resources and inquiry tools to plan, organize, and draft writing.
NE.E9-10.W.2.b: Adapt writing processes to sustain engagement in short and long-term writing tasks of increasing length and complexity.
NE.E9-10.W.2.c: Improve and clarify writing by revising, considering feedback from adults and peers to address the needs of a particular audience and enhance the purpose and structure.
NE.E9-10.W.2.d: Improve and clarify writing by editing and proofreading to enhance style appropriate to audience, purpose, and task.
NE.E9-10.W.2.e: Use appropriate print and digital/multimedia tools to produce, enhance, and/or publish writing individually or in collaboration with peers.
NE.E9-10.W.3: Write in a variety of literary forms to convey real or imagined experiences or events, themes, and perspectives in which the development, structure, and style are appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience.
NE.E9-10.W.3.a: Engage and orient the reader by setting out a problem, situation, or observation, establishing multiple points of view, and introducing a narrator and/or characters; create a smooth progression of experiences or events.
NE.E9-10.W.3.b: Use literary techniques, such as dialogue, pacing, description, reflection, and multiple plot lines, to develop experiences, events, settings, and/or characters.
NE.E9-10.W.3.c: Use a variety of techniques to sequence events so that they build on one another to create a coherent whole.
NE.E9-10.W.3.d: Use precise words and phrases, telling details, and sensory language to convey a vivid picture of the experiences, events, setting, and/or characters and to establish mood and tone.
NE.E9-10.W.3.e: Provide a conclusion that follows from and reflects upon what is experienced, observed, resolved or left unresolved, and what new implications or questions are raised over the course of the piece.
NE.E9-10.W.4: Write arguments that develop a perspective with supporting reasons and evidence, organized as appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience.
NE.E9-10.W.4.a: Develop a structure to sequence ideas logically; introduce a clear claim where appropriate, and/or distinguish the claim(s) from alternate or supporting claims.
NE.E9-10.W.4.b: Demonstrate understanding and engagement with multiple viewpoints and sources to create and support nuanced claims as a recursive process of inquiry and exploration.
NE.E9-10.W.4.c: Use words, phrases, key vocabulary, and varied syntax to clarify relationships between claim(s), counterclaim(s), and supporting evidence.
NE.E9-10.W.4.d: Adapt style and tone appropriate to the norms and conventions of the task and discipline.
NE.E9-10.W.4.e: Provide a conclusion that follows from and supports the argument(s) presented.
NE.E9-10.W.5: Write informative/explanatory pieces to clearly convey ideas, information, and concepts in which the development and structure are appropriate to the task, discipline, purpose, and audience.
NE.E9-10.W.5.a: Introduce a topic clearly and provide a specific focus; organize complex ideas, concepts, and information to make clear connections and distinctions including text features, illustrations, and/or multimedia elements.
NE.E9-10.W.5.b: Develop the topic with relevant, sufficient facts, extended definitions, concrete details, quotations, and/or other information and examples.
NE.E9-10.W.5.c: Use appropriate and varied transitions, domain-specific vocabulary, and varied syntax to manage the complexity of the topic.
NE.E9-10.W.5.d: Establish and maintain a formal style and objective tone while attending to the norms and conventions of the discipline.
NE.E9-10.W.5.e: Provide a conclusion that follows from and supports the information or explanations and articulates the implications and/or significance of the topic.
NE.E9-10.W.6: Gather and use credible evidence from multiple authoritative sources and assess its relevance in answering the research question(s).
NE.E9-10.W.6.a: Integrate information and evidence into writing selectively, accurately quoting or paraphrasing data and conclusions to maintain the flow of ideas while avoiding plagiarism.
NE.E9-10.W.6.b: Locate and evaluate the credibility of evidence (e.g., the expertise or motivation of the creator of an information product, potential bias and/or deception, and social, political, and/or historical perspectives) from print and digital sources to generate and answer questions and create new understandings.
NE.E9-10.W.6.c: Select and use appropriate note-taking formats to collect and organize information.
NE.E9-10.W.6.d: Demonstrate academic integrity by avoiding overreliance on any one source; cite sources using a variety of in-text citations to enhance fluency; develop a list of sources that conforms to a style guide appropriate to the discipline (e.g. MLA, APA, Chicago).
NE.E9-10.W.6.e: Practice safe and ethical behaviors when communicating and interacting with others digitally (e.g. safe information to share, utilize appropriate sites and materials, appropriate language use, respect diverse perspectives).

NE.E11-12.W.2.d: Improve and clarify writing by editing and proofreading to enhance style appropriate to audience, purpose, and task.
NE.E11-12.W.2.e: Use appropriate print and digital/multimedia tools to produce, enhance, and/or publish writing individually or in collaboration with peers.
NE.E11-12.W.3: Write in a variety of literary forms to convey real or imagined experiences or events, themes, and perspectives in which the development, structure, and style are appropriate to the task, purpose, and discipline.
NE.E11-12.W.3.a: Engage and orient the reader by setting out a problem, situation, or observation, establishing multiple points of view, and introducing a narrator and/or characters; create a smooth progression of experiences or events.
NE.E11-12.W.3.b: Use literary techniques, such as dialogue, pacing, description, reflection, and multiple plot lines, to develop experiences, events, settings, and/or characters.
NE.E11-12.W.3.c: Use a variety of techniques to sequence events so that they build on one another to create a coherent whole.
NE.E11-12.W.3.d: Use precise words and phrases, telling details, and sensory language to convey a vivid picture of the experiences, events, setting, and/or characters and to set mood and tone.
NE.E11-12.W.3.e: Provide a conclusion that follows from and reflects upon what is experienced, observed, resolved or left unresolved, and what new implications or questions are raised over the course of the piece.
NE.E11-12.W.4: Write arguments that develop a perspective with supporting reasons and evidence, organized as appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience.
NE.E11-12.W.4.a: Develop a structure to sequence ideas logically; introduce a clear claim where appropriate, and/or distinguish the claim(s) from alternate or supporting claims.
NE.E11-12.W.4.b: Demonstrate understanding and engagement with multiple viewpoints and sources to create and support nuanced claims as a recursive process of inquiry and exploration.
NE.E11-12.W.4.c: Use words, phrases, key vocabulary, and varied syntax to clarify relationships between claim(s), counterclaim(s), and supporting evidence.
NE.E11-12.W.4.d: Adapt style and tone appropriate to the norms and conventions of the task and discipline.
NE.E11-12.W.4.e: Provide a conclusion that follows from and supports the argument(s) presented.
NE.E11-12.W.5: Write informative/explanatory pieces to clearly convey ideas, information, and concepts in which the development and structure are appropriate to the task, discipline, purpose, and audience.
NE.E11-12.W.5.a: Introduce a topic clearly and provide a specific focus; organize complex ideas, concepts, and information to make clear connections and distinctions including text features, illustrations, and/or multimedia elements.
NE.E11-12.W.5.b: Develop the topic thoroughly with relevant, sufficient facts, extended definitions, concrete details, quotations, and/or other information and examples.
NE.E11-12.W.5.c: Use appropriate and varied transitions, domain-specific vocabulary, and varied syntax to manage the complexity of the topic.
NE.E11-12.W.5.d: Establish and maintain a formal style and objective tone while attending to the norms and conventions of the discipline.
NE.E11-12.W.5.e: Provide a conclusion that follows from and supports the information or explanations and articulates the implications and/or significance of the topic.
NE.E11-12.W.6: Gather and use credible evidence from multiple authoritative sources, evaluate the strengths and limitations of sources in terms of the task, purpose, and audience, and assess their relevance in answering the research question(s).
NE.E11-12.W.6.a: Integrate information and evidence into writing selectively, accurately quoting or paraphrasing data and conclusions to maintain the flow of ideas while avoiding plagiarism.
NE.E11-12.W.6.b: Locate and evaluate the credibility of evidence (e.g., the expertise or motivation of the creator of an information product, potential bias and/or deception, and social, political, and/or historical perspectives) from print and digital sources to generate and answer questions and create new understandings.
NE.E11-12.W.6.c: Select and use appropriate note-taking formats to collect and organize information.
NE.E11-12.W.6.d: Demonstrate academic integrity by avoiding overreliance on any one source; cite sources using a variety of in-text citations to enhance fluency; develop a list of sources that conforms to a style guide appropriate to the discipline (e.g., MLA, APA, Chicago).
NE.E11-12.W.6.e: Practice safe and ethical behaviors when communicating and interacting with others digitally (e.g. safe information to share, utilize appropriate sites and materials, appropriate language use, respect diverse perspectives).
NE.E11-12.SL.1: Communicate effectively and appropriately in collaborative activities for a variety of tasks, purposes, and audiences to express ideas, share knowledge, and generate new understandings.
NE.E11-12.SL.1.a: Ask relevant questions to build on ideas, clarify own ideas, or acquire or confirm information.
NE.E11-12.SL.1.b: Demonstrate interpretation of verbal and non-verbal messages in a conversation.
NE.E11-12.SL.1.c: Converse with peers and adults in an all-inclusive manner to foster positive relationships while respecting diverse perspectives.
NE.E11-12.SL.1.d: Demonstrate active and attentive listening skills (e.g., eye contact, nonverbal cues, taking notes, summarizing, questioning).
NE.E11-12.SL.1.e: Complete a task following complex, multi-step directions.
NE.E11-12.SL.2: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence effectively and in which the organization, development, and style are appropriate to a variety of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
NE.E11-12.SL.2.a: Demonstrate and adjust speaking techniques (e.g., appropriate eye contact, pacing, nonverbal cues, intonation) for a variety of purposes and situations, including interpreting grade-level texts.
NE.E11-12.SL.2.b: Convey a perspective with clear reasoning and valid evidence.
NE.E11-12.SL.2.c: Evaluate the purpose of information being presented, its motives (e.g., social, commercial, political), and determine its credibility.
NE.E11-12.SL.2.d: Demonstrate awareness of and sensitivity to the appropriate use of words (e.g., stereotypes, multiple meanings of words).
NE.E11-12.SL.2.e: Make strategic use of appropriate visual and/or digital tools to enhance understanding of findings, reasoning, and evidence for specific audiences.
NE.M9-12.N.1: Estimation and Technology: Students will use estimation strategies and technology to reason, to solve problems, and to make connections within mathematics and across disciplines.
NE.M9-12.N.1.a: Select, apply, and explain the method of computation when problem solving using real numbers (e.g., models, mental computation, paper-pencil, technology).
NE.M9-12.N.1.b: Determine if the context of a problem calls for an approximation or an exact value.
NE.M9-12.N.1.c: Determine the rounding convention to be used based on the context of a problem.
NE.M9-12.N.1.d: Estimate a value using the concept of betweenness by bounding above and below (e.g., since log(10) = 1 and log(1,000) = 3 we know log(500) is between 1 and 3).
NE.M9-12.N.1.e: Determine the tolerance interval and percent of error in measurement.
NE.M9-12.N.1.f: Convert equivalent rates (e.g., miles per hour to feet per second).
NE.M9-12.N.1.g: Determine whether extremely large or extremely small quantities can be reasonably represented by a calculator or graphing utility.
NE.M9-12.N.1.h: Use scientific notation to appropriately represent large and small quantities.
NE.M9-12.N.2: Sets and Operations: Students will use number sets and operations to reason and to solve problems.
NE.M9-12.N.2.a: Extend the properties of exponents to rational numbers.
NE.M9-12.N.2.b: Use properties of rational and irrational numbers.
NE.M9-12.N.2.c: Demonstrate, represent, and show relationships among the subsets of real numbers and the complex number system.
NE.M9-12.N.2.d: Compute with subsets of the complex number system including imaginary, rational, irrational, integers, whole, and natural numbers.
NE.M9-12.N.3: Interpretation and Sense Making: Students will reason abstractly and quantitatively using units to solve problems and interpret results in context.
NE.M9-12.N.3.a: Understand roundoff error and why roundoff error accumulates when rounding occurs prior to the last step in a computation.
NE.M9-12.N.3.b: Use estimation methods to check the reasonableness of real number computations and decide if the problem calls for an approximation (including appropriate rounding) or an exact number.
NE.M9-12.N.3.c: Use units to assess the validity of an answer in the context of a problem.
NE.M9-12.N.3.d: Communicate the meaning of an answer in the context of a problem.
NE.M9-12.A.1: Algebraic Relationships: Students will demonstrate and represent relationships with functions.
NE.M9-12.A.1.a: Demonstrate that functions are a well mapped subdomain of relations.
NE.M9-12.A.1.b: Analyze a relation to determine if it is a function given mapping diagrams, function notation (e.g., f(x)=x2), a table, or a graph.
NE.M9-12.A.1.c: Classify a function given its mapping diagram, function notation, table, or graph as a linear, quadratic, absolute value, exponential, or other function.
NE.M9-12.A.1.d: Analyze a function's domain and range to determine if it is one-to-one and has an inverse function both algebraically and graphically.
NE.M9-12.A.1.e: Define, interpret, and analyze linear, quadratic, absolute value, and exponential functions using the points of interest of the functions and graphing technology.
NE.M9-12.A.1.f: Identify, analyze, and apply transformations of existing functions (including translation and dilation).
NE.M9-12.A.1.g: Interpret logarithmic equations as exponential equations.
NE.M9-12.A.1.h: Describe arithmetic sequences using tables of values and functions in explicit and recursive forms.
NE.M9-12.A.1.i: Describe geometric sequences using tables of values and functions in explicit and recursive forms.
NE.M9-12.A.2: Algebraic Processes: Students will apply the operational properties when evaluating rational expressions and solving linear and quadratic equations, and inequalities.
NE.M9-12.A.2.a: Analyze and explain the properties used in solving equations, inequalities, systems of linear equations, systems of linear inequalities, and literal equations.
NE.M9-12.A.2.b: Generate expressions in equivalent forms by using algebraic properties to make different characteristics or features visible.
NE.M9-12.A.2.c: Analyze equations and inequalities to determine and apply efficient methods to solve and use appropriate technology as needed.
NE.M9-12.A.2.d: Calculate the slope (rate of change) of a line given coordinate points, a graph, or a table of values.
NE.M9-12.A.2.e: Write and graph equations of functions (linear, absolute value, quadratic, and exponential) using the points of interest of the function.
NE.M9-12.A.2.f: Given a line, write the equation of a line that is parallel or perpendicular to it.
NE.M9-12.A.2.g: Perform and explain operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and factoring on polynomials.
NE.M9-12.A.2.h: Explain the connection between the factors of a polynomial and the zeros of a polynomial.
NE.M9-12.A.2.i: Combine functions by composition and perform operations on functions.
NE.M9-12.A.3: Applications: Students will solve authentic problems using nonlinear functions.
NE.M9-12.A.3.a: Analyze and model authentic situations using various representations and appropriate technology.
NE.M9-12.A.3.b: Identify, interpret, relate, and graph the factors, `xtext(-intercepts)`, roots, and zeros of polynomial functions using algebraic and graphing methods.
NE.M9-12.A.3.c: Identify and predict appropriate solutions to equations given context and domain/range (e.g., extraneous solutions, imaginary solutions, no solution, infinitely many solutions).
NE.M9-12.G.1: Attributes: Students will identify and describe geometric attributes, apply properties and theorems, and create two-dimensional shapes.
NE.M9-12.G.1.a: Demonstrate that two figures are similar or congruent by using a sequence of rigid motions and dilations that map a figure onto the other in problems both with and without coordinates.
NE.M9-12.G.1.b: Describe symmetries of a figure in terms of rigid motions that map a figure onto itself and make inferences about symmetric figures (e.g., unknown side lengths or angle measures) in problems both with and without coordinates.
NE.M9-12.G.1.c: Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence and similarity (ASA, SAS, AAS, and SSS congruence; AA similarity criterion) follow from the definition of congruence and similarity in terms of corresponding parts.
NE.M9-12.G.1.d: Identify and apply right triangle relationships including converse of the Pythagorean Theorem.
NE.M9-12.G.1.e: Apply side and angle relationships of special right triangles (30 degree-60 degree-90 degree and 45 degree-45 degree-90 degree) to solve geometric problems.
NE.M9-12.G.1.f: Identify and apply right triangle relationships including sine, cosine, and tangent.
NE.M9-12.G.1.g: Apply interior and exterior angle formulas for n-gons and apply to authentic situations.
NE.M9-12.G.1.h: Compare/contrast the properties of quadrilaterals: parallelograms, rectangles, rhombi, squares, kites, trapezoids, and isosceles trapezoids.
NE.M9-12.G.1.i: Use slope and the distance formula to determine the type of quadrilateral.
NE.M9-12.G.1.j: Identify, describe, apply, and reason through properties of central angles, inscribed angles, angles formed by intersecting chords, secants, and/or tangents to find the measures of angles related to the circle, arc lengths, and areas of sectors.
NE.M9-12.G.2: Attributes: Students will identify and describe geometric attributes, apply properties and theorems and create three-dimensional shapes.
NE.M9-12.G.2.a: Convert between various units of volume (e.g., cubic feet to cubic yards).
NE.M9-12.G.2.b: Apply the effect of a scale factor to determine the volume of similar three-dimensional shapes and solids.
NE.M9-12.G.2.c: Determine surface area and volume of pyramids, as well as solids that are composites of pyramids, prisms, spheres, cylinders, and cones, using formulas and appropriate units.
NE.M9-12.G.3: Coordinate Geometry and Transformations: Students will demonstrate and represent location, orientation, and relationships on the coordinate plane.
NE.M9-12.G.3.a: Derive the midpoint formula using the concept of average and apply the midpoint formula to find coordinates.
NE.M9-12.G.3.b: Find the images and preimages of transformations of a point, shape, or a relation on the coordinate plane. Transformations include the following and their compositions: reflections across horizontal and vertical lines and the lines `y=xandy=-x`, rotations about the origin of 90 degrees, dilations about the origin by any positive scale factor, and any translation.
NE.M9-12.G.3.c: Find the equation of a circle given the radius and the center.
NE.M9-12.G.4: Logic and Proof: Students will use geometric definitions and theorems to reason abstractly and quantitatively.
NE.M9-12.G.4.a: Know and use definitions to make deductions in mathematical argumentation (e.g., syllogism, detachment).
NE.M9-12.G.4.b: Evaluate the validity of conditional statements, including biconditional statements (e.g., conditional, converse, contrapositive, inverse).
NE.M9-12.G.4.c: Evaluate the validity of an argument communicated in different ways (e.g., a flow format, two- column, paragraph format).
NE.M9-12.G.4.d: Use coordinate geometry to prove triangles are right, acute, obtuse, isosceles, equilateral, or scalene.
NE.M9-12.G.4.e: Prove and apply geometric properties and theorems regarding triangles, congruence, and similarity using deductive reasoning.
NE.M9-12.G.4.f: Prove and apply geometric theorems about quadrilaterals using deductive reasoning.
NE.M9-12.D.1: Data Collection and Statistical Methods: Students will formulate statistical investigative questions, collect data, and organize data.
NE.M9-12.D.1.a: Formulate multi-variable statistical investigative questions and determine how data can be collected and analyzed to provide an answer.
NE.M9-12.D.1.b: Apply an appropriate data collection plan when collecting primary data for the statistical investigative question of interest.
NE.M9-12.D.1.c: Use appropriate technology, including spreadsheet-based logic, to organize data for analysis.
NE.M9-12.D.1.d: Distinguish between surveys, observational studies, and experiments.
NE.M9-12.D.1.e: Understand what constitutes good practice in designing a sample survey, an experiment, and an observational study.
NE.M9-12.D.1.f: Understand issues of bias and confounding variables in a study and their implications for interpretation.
NE.M9-12.D.2: Analyze Data and Interpret Results: Students will represent and analyze the data and interpret the results.
NE.M9-12.D.3: Probability: Students will interpret and apply concepts of probability.
NE.M9-12.D.3.a: Describe events as subsets of a sample space using characteristics of the outcomes or as unions, intersections, or complements of other events.
NE.M9-12.D.3.b: Explain independent versus dependent probability of an event.
NE.M9-12.D.3.c: Determine when order in counting matters and use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of events accordingly.
NE.M9-12.D.3.d: Determine whether or not events are mutually exclusive (disjoint) and calculate their probabilities in either case.
NE.M9-12.D.3.e: Recognize and explain the concepts of conditional probability in everyday language and everyday situations.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.1: Estimation and Technology: Students will use estimation strategies and technology to reason, to solve problems, and to make connections within mathematics and across disciplines.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.1.a: Use domain and range restrictions to apply an appropriate viewing window while using graphing technology.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.1.b: Compare and contrast radians and degrees as measures of angles and the reason graphing utilities tend to use radians as the default setting.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.2: Sets and Operations: Students will compare and contrast subsets and perform operations with subsets of the complex number system to reason and to solve problems.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.2.a: Perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.2.b: Represent complex numbers and their operations in the complex plane.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.2.c: Use complex numbers in polynomial identities and equations.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.2.d: Represent quantities using bases other than decimal such as binary (base 2) or hexadecimal (base 16) and convert numbers to and from base 10.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.2.e: Explain modular arithmetic and its role in computer programming.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.2.h: Perform operations on matrices and use matrices in applications.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.3: Interpretation and Sense Making: Students will reason abstractly and quantitatively using units to solve problems and interpret results in context.
NE.M9-12.AT.N.3.a: Use vectors to communicate the geometric relationships between complex numbers in the complex plane.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.1: Algebraic Relationships: Students will demonstrate and represent relationships with functions.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.1.a: Analyze and graph nonlinear functions (trigonometric, rational, higher-order polynomials, logarithmic, and piecewise) and relations (conic sections) using their points of interest and graphing technology.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.1.b: Use the unit circle to define the trigonometric functions on multiples of known angles (positive and negative multiples of 30 and 45 degrees or pi/6 and pi/4).
NE.M9-12.AT.A.1.c: Given a function, list the sequence of algebraic transformations that changes a parent function to the given function.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.1.d: Define the radian unit of measure and its relationship with degrees.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.2: Algebraic Processes: Students will apply the operational properties when evaluating nonlinear expressions and solving nonlinear equations and inequalities.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.2.a: Explain symmetry of functions and determine whether a function is odd, even, or neither.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.2.b: Represent, interpret, and analyze inverses of functions algebraically and graphically using domain restrictions when necessary.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.2.c: Write equations of nonlinear functions (trigonometric, rational, higher-order polynomials, logarithmic and piecewise) using points of interest of the function.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.2.d: Convert between radian and degree measures of an angle.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.2.e: Use limits to describe the behavior of a function near its asymptotes and removable discontinuities.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.3: Applications: Students will solve authentic problems using nonlinear functions and relations.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.3.a: Analyze and model authentic situations using various non-linear representations and relations with appropriate technology.
NE.M9-12.AT.A.3.b: Analyze and model authentic application situations using various non-linear representations and relations with appropriate technology.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.1: Attributes: Students will identify and describe geometric attributes, apply properties and theorems, and create two-dimensional shapes.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.1.a: Apply the Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines to find unknown measures in triangles.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.2: Attributes: Students will identify and describe geometric attributes, apply properties and theorems, and create three-dimensional shapes.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.2.a: Determine the three-dimensional object created by rotating or revolving a two-dimensional object about an axis.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.2.b: Determine the shape of a two-dimensional cross-section of a three-dimensional object.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.2.c: Use Cavalieri's Principle to determine volume of three-dimensional figures.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.3: Coordinate Geometry and Transformations: Students will demonstrate and represent location, orientation, and relationships on the coordinate plane.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.3.a: Identify symmetry properties of a function (e.g., axis of symmetry of a parabola) and know the connection between its symmetry properties and specific transformations.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.3.b: Recognize that translations can be described in terms of vectors.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.3.c: Find the images and preimages of transformations of a point, shape, or relation on the coordinate plane, where transformations include the following compositions: reflections about lines of any rational slope passing through the origins, delations about the origin by any positive scale factor, and translations.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.3.d: Explain the focus-directrix construction of a parabola and derive the equation of a parabola from focus and directrix for a parabola whose axis of symmetry is a coordinate axis.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.4: Logic and Proof: Students will use geometric definitions and theorems to reason abstractly and quantitatively.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.4.a: Use known definitions and results in informal argumentation to construct logical arguments.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.4.b: Distinguish between empirical reasoning, examples, and deductive reasoning, as well as informal and formal reasoning.
NE.M9-12.AT.G.4.c: Evaluate the deductive consequences of alternative definitions of known objects (e.g., whether a trapezoid is defined as a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides or defined as at least one pair of parallel sides).
NE.M9-12.AT.D.1: Data Collection and Statistical Methods: Students will formulate statistical investigative questions, collect data, and organize data.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.1.a: Explain what constitutes good practice in designing a sample survey, an experiment, and an observational study.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.1.b: Explain the use of randomization to reduce the influence of confounding or lurking variables.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.1.c: Explain issues of bias and confounding variables in a study and their implications for interpretation.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.1.d: Demonstrate knowledge of the role sampling distributions play in the estimation of an unknown population parameter through the use of appropriate sampling techniques.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.2: Analyze Data and Interpret Results: Students will represent and analyze the data and interpret the results.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.2.a: Determine when a data set can be reasonably said to be normally distributed and draw conclusions about the data from the associated normal distribution.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.2.b: Use technology to develop regression models for linear and non-linear data to predict unobserved outcomes. Apply algebraic transformations to non-linear data to generate a linearized data set and employ linear regression techniques to analyze the non-linear data set.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.3: Probability: Students will interpret and apply concepts of probability.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.3.a: Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values. Interpret the expected value as the mean of a probability distribution.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.3.b: Communicate what constitutes statistical significance. Interpret statistical significance in the context of a situation and answer investigative questions appropriately.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.3.c: Use data to compare two groups, describe sample variability, and decide if differences between parameters are significant based on the statistics.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.3.d: Use probability as a tool for assessing risk and for informed decision making by computing and interpreting P-values.
NE.M9-12.AT.D.3.e: Use confidence intervals to estimate an unknown population parameter.
NE.S9-12.1.1: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of forces and interactions.
NE.S9-12.1.1.a: Analyze data to support the claim that Newton's Second Law of Motion describes the mathematical relationship among the net force on a macroscopic object, its mass, and its acceleration.
NE.S9-12.1.1.b: Use mathematical representations to support the claim that the total momentum of a system of objects is conserved when there is no net force on the system.
NE.S9-12.1.1.c: Apply science and engineering ideas to design, evaluate, and refine a device that minimizes the force on a macroscopic object during a collision.
NE.S9-12.1.1.d: Use mathematical representations of Newton's Law of Gravitation and Coulomb's Law to describe and predict the gravitational and electrostatic forces between objects.
NE.S9-12.1.1.e: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that an electrical current can produce a magnetic field and that a changing magnetic field can produce an electrical current.
NE.S9-12.2.2: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of the interactions of waves.
NE.S9-12.2.2.a: Use mathematical representations to support a claim regarding relationships among the frequency, wavelength, and speed of waves traveling in various media.
NE.S9-12.2.2.b: Evaluate claims about the advantages of digital transmission and storage of information.
NE.S9-12.2.2.c: Evaluate the claims, evidence, and reasoning behind the idea that electromagnetic radiation can be described either by a wave model or a particle model, and that for some situations one model is more useful than the other.
NE.S9-12.2.2.d: Evaluate the validity and reliability of claims in published materials of the effects that different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation have when absorbed by matter.
NE.S9-12.2.2.e: Communicate technical information about how some technological devices use the principles of wave behavior and wave interactions with matter to transmit and capture information and energy.
NE.S9-12.3.3: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of the structure, properties, and interactions of matter.
NE.S9-12.3.3.a: Use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties of elements based on the patterns of electrons in the outermost energy level of atoms.
NE.S9-12.3.3.b: Plan and conduct an investigation to gather evidence to compare the structure of substances at the macro scale to infer the strength of electrical forces between particles.
NE.S9-12.3.3.c: Develop models to illustrate the changes in the composition of the nucleus of the atom and the energy released during the processes of fission, fusion, and radioactive decay.
NE.S9-12.3.3.d: Communicate scientific and technical information about why the molecular-level structure is important in the functioning of designed materials.
NE.S9-12.4.4: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of the interactions of energy.
NE.S9-12.4.4.a: Create a computational model to calculate the change in the energy of one component in a system when the change in energy of the other component(s) and energy flows in and out of the system are known.
NE.S9-12.4.4.b: Develop and use models to illustrate that energy at the macroscopic scale can be accounted for as a combination of energy associated with the motion of particles (objects) and energy associated with the relative positions of particles (objects).
NE.S9-12.4.4.c: Design, build, and refine a device that works within given constraints to convert one form of energy into another form of energy.
NE.S9-12.4.4.d: Analyze a major global challenge to specify qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints for solutions that account for societal needs and wants.
NE.S9-12.4.4.e: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that the transfer of thermal energy when two components of different temperature are combined within a closed system results in a more uniform energy distribution among the components in the system (second law of thermodynamics).
NE.S9-12.4.4.f: Develop and use a model of two objects interacting through electrical or magnetic fields to illustrate the forces between objects and the changes in energy of the objects due to the interaction.
NE.S9-12.5.5: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of chemical reactions.
NE.S9-12.5.5.a: Construct and revise an explanation for the outcome of a simple chemical reaction based on the outermost electron states of atoms, trends in the periodic table, and knowledge of the patterns of chemical properties.
NE.S9-12.5.5.b: Develop a model to illustrate that the release or absorption of energy from a chemical reaction system depends on the changes in total bond energy
NE.S9-12.5.5.c: Apply scientific principles and evidence to provide an explanation about the effects of changing the temperature or concentration of the reacting particles on the rate at which a reaction occurs.
NE.S9-12.5.5.d: Refine the design of a chemical system by specifying a change in conditions that would produce increased amounts of products at equilibrium.
NE.S9-12.5.5.e: Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems that can be solved through engineering.
NE.S9-12.5.5.f: Use mathematical representations to support the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved during a chemical reaction.
NE.S9-12.6.1: Gather, analyze, and communicate evidence of the relationship between structure and function in living things.

NJ.EK.L.RF.1: Demonstrate understanding of the organization and basic features of print.
NJ.EK.L.RF.1.A: Follow words from left to right, top to bottom, and page by page.
NJ.EK.L.RF.1.B: Recognize that spoken words are represented in written language by specific sequences of letters.
NJ.EK.L.RF.1.C: Understand that words are separated by spaces in print.
NJ.EK.L.RF.1.D: Recognize and name all upper- and lowercase letters of the alphabet.

NJ.EK.L.RF.2.C: Blend and segment onsets and rimes of single-syllable spoken words.
NJ.EK.L.RF.2.D: Orally repeat multi-syllable words and pronounce the separate syllables.

NJ.EK.L.RF.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding and encoding words.
NJ.EK.L.RF.3.A: Demonstrate basic knowledge of one-to-one letter-sound correspondences by producing many of the most frequently used sounds of each consonant.
NJ.EK.L.RF.3.B: Associate the long and short sounds with the common spellings (graphemes) for the five major vowels.
NJ.EK.L.RF.3.C: Read high-frequency words and grade level irregular words with automaticity.
NJ.EK.L.RF.3.D: Recognize the parts of high-frequency words that are regular and the parts that are irregular.
NJ.EK.L.RF.3.E: Distinguish between similarly spelled words by identifying the sounds of the letters that differ (e.g., nap and tap; cat and cot).
NJ.EK.L.RF.4: Read emergent-reader texts (decodable texts, including words with one-to-one letter- sound correspondences) orally with sufficient decoding accuracy to support comprehension.
NJ.EK.L.WF.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of writing.
NJ.EK.L.WF.1.B: Write upper and lowercase letters, with reference to a model.
NJ.EK.L.WF.1.C: Write left to right and include a space between words.
NJ.EK.L.WF.1.D: Identify the letters used to represent vowel phonemes and those used to represent consonants, knowing that every syllable has a vowel.
NJ.EK.L.WF.1.E: Write a common grapheme (letter or letter group) for each phoneme.
NJ.EK.L.WF.1.F: Orally segment the phonemes in any single syllable, spoken word.

NJ.EK.L.WF.2.E: Attempting phonetic spellings of unknown words.
NJ.EK.L.WF.2.F: Writing initial and final consonant blends (must, slab, plump).
NJ.EK.L.WF.3: Demonstrate command of the conventions of sentence composition.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.A: Repeat a sentence, identifying how many words are in the sentence.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.C: Capitalize the first word in a sentence, capitalize proper names, and include spaces between words.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.E: Use manipulatives or digital tools to construct complete sentences.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.G: Supply the “who,” “is doing,” “what,” in a subject-verb-object sentence frame.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.H: Match periods, question marks, and exclamation points to statements, questions, commands, and exclamations.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.I: With support, distinguish between a complete sentence and a sentence fragment.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.J: With support, write statements in response to questions, and questions transformed from statements, using conventional word order.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.K: Elaborate a simple subject or simple predicate, in response to questions who, what, where, when, how, or why.
NJ.EK.L.WF.3.L: Use conjunctions appropriately in sentences (e.g., and, but, so, and because).

NJ.EK.L.KL.1.E: Produce and expand complete sentences in shared language activities.

NJ.EK.L.VI.3.B: Demonstrate understanding of frequently occurring verbs and adjectives by relating them to their opposites (antonyms).
NJ.EK.L.VI.3.C: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., note places at school that are colorful).
NJ.EK.L.VI.3.D: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs describing the same general action (e.g., walk, march, strut, prance) by acting out the meanings.

NJ.EK.R.RI.CT.8: With prompting and support, identify basic similarities in and differences between two informational texts on the same topic (e.g., characters, experiences, illustrations, descriptions, or procedures).
NJ.EK.W.AW.1: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose opinion pieces on topics or texts (e.g., My favorite book is...).

NJ.EK.W.NW.3.C: Provide a reaction to the experiences or events.

NJ.EK.W.RW.7: With prompting and support, engage in brief but regular writing and drawing tasks.
NJ.EK.SL.PE.1: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about kindergarten topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.

NJ.EK.SL.PE.1.B: Continue a conversation through multiple exchanges.
NJ.EK.SL.II.2: Confirm understanding of a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media by asking and answering questions about key details and requesting clarification if something is not understood.
NJ.EK.SL.ES.3: Ask and answer questions in order to seek help, get information, or clarify something that is not understood.
NJ.EK.SL.PI.4: Describe familiar people, places, things, and events and, with prompting and support, provide additional detail.
NJ.EK.SL.UM.5: Add drawings or other visual displays to descriptions as desired to provide additional detail.
NJ.EK.SL.AS.6: Speak audibly and express thoughts, feelings, and ideas clearly.
NJ.MK.CC.A: Know number names and the count sequence.

NJ.MK.CC.A.2: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

NJ.MK.CC.B: Count to tell the number of objects.
NJ.MK.CC.B.4: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.
NJ.MK.CC.B.4.a: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.
NJ.MK.CC.B.4.b: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.
NJ.MK.CC.B.4.c: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.
NJ.MK.CC.B.5: Count to answer “how many?” questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1-20, count out that many objects.
NJ.MK.CC.C.6: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.
NJ.MK.CC.C.7: Compare two numbers between `1and10` presented as written numerals.
NJ.MK.OA.A: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
NJ.MK.OA.A.1: Represent addition and subtraction up to 10 with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
NJ.MK.OA.A.2: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.
NJ.MK.OA.A.3: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., and).
NJ.MK.OA.A.4: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation.
NJ.MK.OA.A.5: Demonstrate accuracy and efficiency for addition and subtraction within 5.
NJ.MK.NBT.A: Work with numbers 11-19 to gain foundations for place value.
NJ.MK.NBT.A.6: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g.,); understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones
NJ.MK.MD.A.1: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.

NJ.MK.MD.B: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category.
NJ.MK.MD.B.3: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
NJ.MK.G.A: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).

NJ.MK.G.A.3: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, “flat”) or three-dimensional (“solid”).
NJ.MK.G.B: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.
NJ.MK.G.B.4: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/“corners”) and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).

NJ.MK.G.B.6: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes.
