OK.MHS.G.RL.1.3: Assess the validity of a logical argument and give counterexamples to disprove a statement.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1: Discover, evaluate, and analyze the relationships between lines, angles, and polygons to solve real-world and mathematical problems; express proofs in a form that clearly justifies the reasoning (e.g., two-column proofs, paragraph proofs, flowcharts).
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.1: Use properties of parallel lines cut by a transversal to determine angle relationships and solve problems.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.2: Use the angle relationships formed by lines cut by a transversal to determine if the lines are parallel and verify, using  proofs.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.3: Apply the properties of angles (corresponding, exterior, interior, vertical, complementary, supplementary) to solve problems using mathematical models, algebraic reasoning, and proofs.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.4: Apply theorems involving the interior and exterior angle sums of polygons to solve problems using mathematical models, algebraic reasoning, and proofs.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.5: Apply the properties of special quadrilaterals (square, rectangle, trapezoid, isosceles trapezoid, rhombus, kite, parallelogram) to solve problems involving angle measures and segment lengths using mathematical models, algebraic reasoning, and proofs.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.6: Use coordinate geometry and algebraic reasoning to represent and analyze line segments and polygons, including determining lengths, midpoints, and slopes of line segments.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.7: Apply the properties of polygons, and use them to represent and apply mathematical models involving perimeter and area (e.g., triangles, special quadrilaterals, regular polygons up to `12` sides, composite figures).
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.8: Apply the properties of congruent or similar polygons to solve problems using mathematical models and algebraic and logical reasoning.
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.9: Construct logical arguments to prove triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and HL).
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.10: Construct logical arguments to prove triangle similarity (AA, SSS, SAS).
OK.MHS.G.2D.1.11: Use numeric, graphic, and algebraic representations of transformations in two dimensions (e.g., reflections, translations, dilations, rotations about the origin by multiples of `90 ̊`) to solve problems involving figures on a coordinate plane and identify types of symmetry.
OK.MHS.G.3D.1: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving three-dimensional figures.
OK.MHS.G.3D.1.1: Represent, use, and apply mathematical models and other tools (e.g., nets, measuring devices, formulas) to solve problems involving surface area and volume of three-dimensional figures (prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, spheres, composites of these figures).
OK.MHS.G.3D.1.2: Use ratios derived from similar three-dimensional figures to make conjectures, generalize, and to solve for unknown values such as angles, side lengths, perimeter, and circumference of a face, area of a face, and volume.
OK.MHS.G.C.1: Solve real-world and mathematical problems using the properties of circles.
OK.MHS.G.C.1.1: Apply the properties of circles to solve problems involving circumference and area, using approximate values and in terms of pi, using algebraic and logical reasoning.
OK.MHS.G.C.1.2: Use the distance and midpoint formula, where appropriate, to recognize and write the radius `r`, center `(h,k)`, and standard form of the equation of a circle `(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2` with and without graphs.
OK.MHS.G.C.1.3: Apply the properties of circles and relationships among angles, arcs, and distances in a circle among radii, chords, secants, and tangents to solve problems using algebraic and logical reasoning.
OK.MHS.G.RT.1: Apply mathematical relationships of right triangles and trigonometric ratios to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
OK.MHS.G.RT.1.1: Apply the distance formula, the Pythagorean theorem, and the Pythagorean theorem converse (approximate and exact values, including Pythagorean triples) to solve problems, using algebraic and logical reasoning and mathematical models.
OK.MHS.G.RT.1.2: Verify and apply properties of right triangles, including properties of `text(45-45-90)` and `text(30-60-90)` triangles, to solve problems using algebraic and logical reasoning.
OK.MHS.G.RT.1.3: Use the definition of the trigonometric functions to determine the sine, cosine, and tangent ratio of an acute angle in a right triangle. Apply the inverse trigonometric functions to find the measure of an acute angle in right triangles.
OK.MHS.G.RT.1.4: Apply the trigonometric functions as ratios (sine, cosine, tangent) to find side lengths in right triangles in mathematical models, including the coordinate plane.
OK.MHS.PA.N.1: Read, write, compare, classify, and represent real numbers, and use them to solve problems in various contexts.
OK.MHS.PA.N.1.1: Develop and apply the properties of integer exponents, including `a^0=1` (with `a!=0`), to generate equivalent numerical and algebraic expressions.
OK.MHS.PA.N.1.2: Express and compare approximations of very large and very small numbers using scientific notation.
OK.MHS.PA.N.1.3: Multiply and divide numbers expressed in scientific notation and express the answer in scientific notation.
OK.MHS.PA.N.1.4: Compare and order real numbers; locate real numbers on a number line. Identify the square roots of perfect squares to `400` or, if it is not a perfect square root, locate it as an irrational number between two consecutive positive integers.
OK.MHS.PA.A.1: Explain the concept of function in mathematical situations and distinguish between the concepts of linear and nonlinear functions.
OK.MHS.PA.A.1.1: Recognize that a function is a relationship between an independent variable and a dependent variable in which the value of the independent variable determines the value of the dependent variable.
OK.MHS.PA.A.1.2: Use linear functions to represent and model mathematical situations.
OK.MHS.PA.A.1.3: Identify a function as linear if it can be expressed in the form `y=mx+b` or if its graph is a non-vertical straight line.
OK.MHS.PA.A.2: Identify and justify linear functions using mathematical models and situations; solve problems involving linear functions and interpret results in the original context.
OK.MHS.PA.A.2.1: Represent linear functions with tables, verbal descriptions, symbols, and graphs; translate from one representation to another.
OK.MHS.PA.A.2.2: Identify, describe, and analyze linear relationships between two variables.
OK.MHS.PA.A.2.3: Identify graphical properties of linear functions, including slope and intercepts. Know that the slope equals the rate of change and that the y-intercept is zero when the function represents a proportional relationship.
OK.MHS.PA.A.2.4: Predict the effect on the graph of a linear function when the slope or y-intercept changes. Use appropriate tools to examine these effects.
OK.MHS.PA.A.2.5: Solve problems involving linear functions and interpret results in the original context.
OK.MHS.PA.A.3: Generate equivalent numerical and algebraic expressions and use algebraic properties to evaluate expressions.
OK.MHS.PA.A.3.1: Use substitution to simplify and evaluate algebraic expressions.
OK.MHS.PA.A.3.2: Justify steps in generating equivalent expressions by combining like terms and using order of operations (to include grouping symbols). Identify the properties used, including the properties of operations (associative, commutative, and distributive).
OK.MHS.PA.A.4: Represent and solve problems using mathematical models and situations with equations and inequalities involving linear expressions.
OK.MHS.PA.A.4.1: Solve mathematical problems using linear equations with one variable where there could be one, infinitely many, or no solutions. Represent situations using linear equations and interpret solutions in the original context.
OK.MHS.PA.A.4.2: Represent, write, solve, and graph problems leading to linear inequalities with one variable in the form `px+q>r` and `px+q<r`, where `p`, `q`, and `r` are rational numbers.
OK.MHS.PA.A.4.3: Represent real-world situations using equations and inequalities involving one variable.
OK.MHS.PA.GM.1: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to solve problems involving triangles.
OK.MHS.PA.GM.1.1: Justify the Pythagorean theorem using measurements, diagrams, or dynamic software to solve problems in two dimensions involving right triangles.
OK.MHS.PA.GM.1.2: Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the distance between any two points in a coordinate plane.
OK.MHS.PA.GM.2: Justify and use formulas to calculate surface area and volume of three-dimensional figures.
OK.MHS.PA.GM.2.1: Calculate the surface area of a rectangular prism using decomposition or nets. Use appropriate units (e.g., `text(cm)^2`).
OK.MHS.PA.GM.2.2: Calculate the surface area of a cylinder, in terms of pi (`pi`) and using approximations for pi (`pi`), using decomposition or nets. Use appropriate units (e.g., `text(cm)^2`).
OK.MHS.PA.GM.2.3: Justify why base area (`B`) and height (`h`) in the formula `V=Bh` are multiplied to find the volume of a rectangular prism. Use appropriate units (e.g., `text(cm)^3`).
OK.MHS.PA.GM.2.4: Develop and use the formulas `V=pir^2h` and `V=Bh` to determine the volume of right cylinders, in terms of `pi` and using approximations for pi (`pi`). Justify why base area (`B`) and height (`h`) are multiplied to find the volume of a right cylinder. Use appropriate units (e.g., `text(cm)^3`).
OK.MHS.PA.D.1: Display and interpret data in a variety of ways, including using scatter plots and approximate lines of best fit. Use the line of best fit and average rate of change to make predictions and draw conclusions about data.
OK.MHS.PA.D.1.1: Describe the impact that inserting or deleting a data point has on the mean and the median of a data set. Create data displays using technology to examine this impact.
OK.MHS.PA.D.1.2: Explain how outliers affect measures of center and spread.
OK.MHS.PA.D.1.3: Collect, display, and interpret data using scatter plots. Use the shape of the scatter plot to find the informal line of best fit, make statements about the average rate of change, and make predictions about values not in the original data set. Use appropriate titles, labels, and units.
OK.MHS.PA.D.2: Calculate experimental probabilities and reason about probabilities to model and solve problems.
OK.MHS.PA.D.2.1: Calculate experimental probabilities and represent them as percents, fractions, and decimals between `0` and `1`. Use experimental probabilities to predict relative frequencies when actual probabilities are unknown.
OK.MHS.PA.D.2.2: Determine how samples are chosen (randomness) to draw and support conclusions about generalizing a sample to a population, including identifying limitations and biases.
OK.MHS.PA.D.2.3: Define, compare, and contrast the probabilities of dependent and independent events.
OK.MHS.PC.F.1.1: Interpret characteristics of a function defined by an expression in the context of the situation.
OK.MHS.PC.F.1.2: Sketch the graph of a function that models a relationship between two quantities, identifying key features.
OK.MHS.PC.F.1.3: Interpret characteristics of graphs and tables for a function that models a relationship between two quantities in terms of the quantities.
OK.MHS.PC.F.1.4: Describe end behavior, asymptotic behavior, and points of discontinuity.
OK.MHS.PC.F.1.5: Determine if a function has an inverse. Algebraically and graphically find the inverse or define any restrictions on the domain that meet the requirement for invertibility, and find the inverse on the restricted domain.
OK.MHS.PC.F.2: Build functions to model and validate relationships among functions.
OK.MHS.PC.F.2.1: Model relationships through composition, and attend to the restrictions of the domain.
OK.MHS.PC.F.2.2: Rewrite a function as a composition of functions.
OK.MHS.PC.F.2.3: Interpret the meanings of quantities involving functions and their inverses.
OK.MHS.PC.F.2.4: Verify by analytical methods that one function is the inverse of another.
OK.MHS.PC.F.3: Predict and verify solutions involving functions.
OK.MHS.PC.F.3.1: Predict solutions involving functions that are quadratic, polynomial of higher order, rational, exponential, and logarithmic.
OK.MHS.PC.F.3.2: Graphically verify solutions involving functions that are quadratic, polynomial of higher order, rational, exponential, and logarithmic.
OK.MHS.PC.F.3.3: Algebraically verify solutions involving functions that are quadratic, polynomial of higher order, rational, exponential, and logarithmic.
OK.MHS.PC.CS.1.1: Model real-world situations which involve conic sections.
OK.MHS.PC.CS.1.2: Identify key features of conic sections (foci, directrix, radii, axes, asymptotes, center) graphically and algebraically.
OK.MHS.PC.CS.1.3: Sketch a graph of a conic section using its key features.
OK.MHS.PC.CS.1.4: Write the equation of a conic section given its key features.
OK.MHS.PC.CS.1.5: Given the equation `ax^2+by^2+cx+dy+e=0`, determine if the equation represents a circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1: Make sense of the unit circle and its relationship to the graphs of trigonometric functions.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.1: Draw and recognize angles in standard position using radian measure, and determine the quadrant of the terminal side.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.2: Convert radian measure to degree measure and vice-versa.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.3: Find the length of an arc and the area of a sector on a circle.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.4: Use special triangles to determine geometrically the values of sine, cosine, tangent for `pi/3`, `pi/4`, and `pi/6`, and use the unit circle to express the values of sine, cosine, and tangent for `pi-x`, `pi+x`, and `2pi-x` in terms of their values for `x`, where `x` is any real number.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.5: Use reference angles to determine the terminal point `P(x,y)` on the unit circle for a given angle.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.6: Estimate trigonometric values of any angle.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.7: Apply the properties of a unit circle to explain symmetry (odd and even) and periodicity of trigonometric functions.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.8: Graph all six trigonometric functions, identifying key features.
OK.MHS.PC.T.1.9: Describe and analyze the relationships of the properties of a unit circle.
OK.MHS.PC.T.2: Apply trigonometric concepts beyond the right triangle.
OK.MHS.PC.T.2.1: Create models for situations involving trigonometry.
OK.MHS.PC.T.2.2: Apply the Law of Sines and Law of Cosines to solve problems.
OK.MHS.PC.T.2.3: Use trigonometry to find the area of triangles.
OK.MHS.PC.T.2.4: Use inverse functions to solve trigonometric equations; evaluate the solution and interpret them in terms of context.
OK.MHS.PC.T.3: Verify trigonometric identities and solve equations.
OK.MHS.PC.T.3.1: Algebraically manipulate the structure of a trigonometric expression to identify ways to rewrite it.
OK.MHS.PC.T.3.2: Choose and produce an equivalent form of an expression to explain the properties of the quantity represented by the expression.
OK.MHS.PC.T.3.3: Graphically and algebraically verify solutions to trigonometric equations.
OK.MHS.PC.T.4.1: Use the relation `i^2=-1` and the mathematical properties to add, subtract, and multiply complex numbers.
OK.MHS.PC.T.4.2: Find the conjugate of a complex number in rectangular forms and quotients of complex numbers.
OK.MHS.PC.T.4.3: Solve quadratic equations in one variable that have complex solutions.
OK.MHS.S.Q.1: Understand the distinction between mathematical models and statistical models.
OK.MHS.S.Q.1.1: Distinguish among different sources of variability, including measurement, natural, induced, and sampling variability.
OK.MHS.S.Q.1.2: Formulate meaningful statistical questions to clarify the problem at hand.
OK.MHS.S.Q.2: Distinguish between the distribution of a population, a distribution of sample data, and a sampling distribution.
OK.MHS.S.Q.2.1: Distinguish between sample statistics and population parameters.
OK.MHS.S.Q.2.2: Recognize a population distribution has fixed values of its parameters and that these parameter values are typically unknown.
OK.MHS.S.Q.2.3: Recognize that a sample data distribution is taken from a population distribution, and the data distribution is what is seen in practice.
OK.MHS.S.Q.2.4: Recognize a sampling distribution is the distribution of a sample statistic (e.g., sample mean, sample proportion) obtained from repeated samples.
OK.MHS.S.Q.3: Identify differences between categorical and quantitative data.
OK.MHS.S.Q.3.1: Determine whether categorical or quantitative data is appropriate to answer a statistical question.
OK.MHS.S.Q.3.2: Compare and contrast different potential graphical or visual representations given the same data set.
OK.MHS.S.DC.1: Distinguish among different types of study designs for collecting data, and know the scope of inference for each design type.
OK.MHS.S.DC.1.1: Distinguish among sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies.
OK.MHS.S.DC.1.2: Compare and contrast the benefits of different sampling techniques.
OK.MHS.S.DC.1.3: Determine the appropriate scope of inference for generalizing results.
OK.MHS.S.DC.1.4: Explain how sample size impacts the precision with which generalizations can be made.
OK.MHS.S.DC.1.5: Determine when a cause-and-effect inference can be drawn from an association, based on how the data were collected.
OK.MHS.S.DC.2: Identify common sources of bias and the role of randomization in study design.
OK.MHS.S.DC.2.1: Explain how randomization and sources of bias impact the results of a study.
OK.MHS.S.DC.2.2: Understand the different roles of random selection and random assignment in study design.
OK.MHS.S.DA.1: Use distributions of quantitative and categorical data to identify the key features of the data collected in context.
OK.MHS.S.DA.1.1: Summarize and represent the distribution for univariate quantitative data by describing and analyzing the shape of the distribution, the measures of center for the distribution, the patterns in variability for the distribution, and any outliers, gaps, or other unusual features in the distribution.
OK.MHS.S.DA.1.2: Select and create an appropriate display (e.g., dot plots, histograms, box plots) for univariate data.
OK.MHS.S.DA.1.3: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center and variability of two or more different data sets.
OK.MHS.S.DA.1.4: Describe and analyze the distribution of univariate categorical data.
OK.MHS.S.DA.2: Use the mean and standard deviation of a data set to fit it to a normal distribution and to estimate population percentages.
OK.MHS.S.DA.2.1: Use calculators, computers, or tables to estimate areas under the normal curve. Recognize that there are data sets for which such a procedure is not appropriate.
OK.MHS.S.DA.3: Compare two or more groups by analyzing distributions.
OK.MHS.S.DA.3.1: Construct appropriate parallel graphical displays of distributions.
OK.MHS.S.DA.3.2: Use numerical attributes of distributions to make comparisons between distributions.
OK.MHS.S.DA.4.1: Create two-way tables for bivariate categorical data and analyze for possible associations between the two categories using marginal, joint, and conditional frequencies.
OK.MHS.S.DA.4.2: Make predictions and draw conclusions from regression models (linear, exponential, quadratic) from two-variable quantitative data.
OK.MHS.S.DA.4.3: Analyze scatter plots for patterns, linearity, outliers, and influential points.
OK.MHS.S.DA.4.4: Using technology, compute and interpret the correlation coefficient.
OK.MHS.S.DA.4.5: Understand the implications of extrapolating data to make predictions.
OK.MHS.S.DA.5: Make statistical inferences and evaluate claims from studies.
OK.MHS.S.DA.5.1: Construct and interpret confidence intervals for the mean of a normally distributed population and for a population proportion.
OK.MHS.S.DA.5.2: Explain how a sample statistic and a confidence level are used in the construction of a confidence interval
OK.MHS.S.DA.5.3: Explain how changes in the sample size, confidence level, and standard error affect the margin of error of a confidence interval.
OK.MHS.S.DA.5.4: Construct a confidence interval for the mean of a normally distributed population (with a known standard deviation) and for a population proportion. Use confidence intervals to evaluate claims.
OK.MHS.S.DA.5.5: Use confidence intervals to evaluate claims for a single population parameter.
OK.MHS.S.IR.1: Interpret and communicate the results of a statistical analysis in context.
OK.MHS.S.IR.1.1: Recognize when the difference between two sample proportions or two sample means is due to random variation or if the difference is statistically significant.
OK.MHS.S.IR.1.2: Understand the concept of a confidence interval, including the interpretation of confidence level, margin of error, and statistical significance.
OK.MHS.S.IR.1.3: Develop inferences or predictions to construct resulting decisions or recommendations.
OK.MHS.S.IR.1.4: Create and evaluate recommendations for areas of future research.
OK.MHS.S.IR.2: Evaluate practical implications of statistical significance or lack thereof.
OK.MHS.S.IR.2.1: Develop and critique arguments for practical implications based on statistical significance.
OK.MHS.S.IR.2.2: Identify potential lurking variables which may explain an association between two variables.
OK.MHS.S.IR.3.1: Evaluate strengths and weaknesses in the studies or methods used to generate data.
OK.MHS.S.IR.3.2: Evaluate the statistical validity of claims made.
OK.MHS.S.P.1: Connect basic probability concepts to statistical analysis.
OK.MHS.S.P.1.1: Describe events as subsets of a sample space.
OK.MHS.S.P.1.2: Describe the relationship between theoretical and empirical probabilities using the Law of Large Numbers.
OK.MHS.S.P.1.3: Use counting techniques (e.g., permutations and combinations) to solve mathematical and real-world problems, including determining probabilities of compound events.
OK.MHS.S.P.2: Determine probabilities, including joint probabilities, conditional probabilities, probabilities of independent events, and probabilities of dependent events. Interpret the results.
OK.MHS.S.P.2.1: Understand that two events, `A` and `B`, are independent if the probability of `A` and B occurring together is the product of their probabilities, and use this characterization to determine if two events are independent.
OK.MHS.S.P.2.2: Understand and calculate the conditional probability of `A` given `B` as `P(AandB)//P(B)`.
OK.MHS.S.P.2.3: Interpret independence of `A` and `B` as saying that the conditional probability of `A`, given `B`, is the same as the probability of `A`.
OK.MHS.S.P.3.1: Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts and expected values.
OK.MHS.S.P.3.2: Analyze decisions about statistical significance based on reported p-values.
PA.E3.A-K.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of key ideas and details in literature.
PA.E3.A-K.1.1.1: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
PA.E3.A-K.1.1.2: Recount poems, dramas, or stories, including fables, folktales, and myths from diverse cultures; determine the central message, lesson, or moral and explain how it is conveyed through key details in the text.
PA.E3.A-K.1.1.3: Describe characters in a story (e.g., their traits, motivations, feelings) and explain how their actions contribute to the sequence of events.
PA.E3.A-C.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of craft and structure in literature.
PA.E3.A-C.2.1.1: Explain the point of view from which a story is narrated, including the difference between first- and third-person narrations.
PA.E3.A-C.3.1: Demonstrate understanding of connections within, between, and/or among texts.
PA.E3.A-C.3.1.1: Compare and contrast the themes, settings, and plots of stories written by the same author about the same or similar characters (e.g., in books from a series).
PA.E3.A-V.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of vocabulary and figurative language in literature.
PA.E3.A-V.4.1.1: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 3 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
PA.E3.A-V.4.1.1a: Use context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
PA.E3.A-V.4.1.1b: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known affix is added to a known word (e.g., agreeable/disagreeable, comfortable/uncomfortable, care/careless, heat/preheat).
PA.E3.A-V.4.1.1c: Use a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word with the same root (e.g., company, companion).
PA.E3.A-V.4.1.2: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.
PA.E3.A-V.4.1.2a: Distinguish the literal and nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context (e.g., take steps).
PA.E3.A-V.4.1.2b: Distinguish shades of meaning among related words (e.g., knew, believed, suspected, heard, wondered).
PA.E3.B-K.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of key ideas and details in informational texts.
PA.E3.B-K.1.1.1: Answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.
PA.E3.B-K.1.1.2: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.
PA.E3.B-K.1.1.3: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
PA.E3.B-C.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of craft and structure in informational texts.
PA.E3.B-C.2.1.1: Explain the point of view from which a text is written.
PA.E3.B-C.2.1.2: Use text features (e.g., headings, graphics, charts) and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to efficiently locate information relevant to a given topic.
PA.E3.B-C.3.1: Demonstrate understanding of connections within, between, and/or among informational texts.

PA.E3.B-V.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of vocabulary and figurative language in informational texts.
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.1: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 3 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.1a: Use context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.1b: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known affix is added to a known word (e.g., agreeable/disagreeable, comfortable/uncomfortable, care/careless, heat/preheat).
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.1c: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases used in a text.
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.1d: Use a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word with the same root (e.g., company, companion).
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.2: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.2a: Distinguish the literal and nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context (e.g., take steps).
PA.E3.B-V.4.1.2b: Distinguish shades of meaning among related words (e.g., knew, believed, suspected, heard, wondered).
PA.E3.D.1.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage.
PA.E3.D.1.1.1: Explain the function of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs in general and their functions in particular sentences.
PA.E3.D.1.1.2: Form and use regular and irregular plural nouns.
PA.E3.D.1.1.4: Form and use regular and irregular verbs.
PA.E3.D.1.1.5: Form and use the simple verb tenses (e.g., I walked; I walk; I will walk).
PA.E3.D.1.1.7: Form and use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs, and choose between them depending on what is to be modified.
PA.E3.D.1.1.9: Produce simple, compound, and complex sentences.
PA.E3.D.1.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.
PA.E3.D.1.2.3: Use commas and quotation marks in dialogue.

PA.E3.D.2.1: Use knowledge of language and its conventions.
PA.E3.D.2.1.1: Choose words and phrases for effect.
PA.M3.A-T.1: Use place-value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
PA.M3.A-T.1.1: Apply place-value strategies to solve problems.
PA.M3.A-T.1.1.1: Round two- and three-digit whole numbers to the nearest ten or hundred, respectively.
PA.M3.A-T.1.1.2: Add two- and three-digit whole numbers (limit sums from `100` through `1text(,)000`) and/or subtract two- and three-digit numbers from three-digit whole numbers.
PA.M3.A-T.1.1.3: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by two-digit multiples of `10` (from `10` through `90`).
PA.M3.A-T.1.1.4: Order a set of whole numbers from least to greatest or greatest to least (up through `9text(,)999`, and limit sets to no more than four numbers).
PA.M3.A-F.1: Develop an understanding of fractions as numbers.
PA.M3.A-F.1.1: Develop and apply number theory concepts to compare quantities and magnitudes of fractions and whole numbers.
PA.M3.A-F.1.1.1: Demonstrate that when a whole or set is partitioned into `y` equal parts, the fraction `1/y` represents `1` part of the whole and/or the fraction `x/y` represents `x` equal parts of the whole (limit denominators to `2,3,4,6,and8`; limit numerators to whole numbers less than the denominator; and no simplification necessary).
PA.M3.A-F.1.1.2: Represent fractions on a number line (limit denominators to `2,3,4,6,and8`; limit numerators to whole numbers less than the denominator; and no simplification necessary).
PA.M3.A-F.1.1.3: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions (limit the denominators to `1,2,3,4,6,and8` and limit numerators to whole numbers less than the denominator).
PA.M3.A-F.1.1.4: Express whole numbers as fractions, and/or generate fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers (limit denominators to `1,2,3,4,6,and8`).
PA.M3.A-F.1.1.5: Compare two fractions with the same denominator (limit denominators to `1,2,3,4,6,and8`), using the symbols `>,=,or<`, and/or justify the conclusions.
PA.M3.B-O.1: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.
PA.M3.B-O.1.1: Understand various meanings of multiplication and division.
PA.M3.B-O.1.1.1: Interpret and/or describe products of whole numbers (up to and including `10xx10`).
PA.M3.B-O.1.1.2: Interpret and/or describe whole-number quotients of whole numbers (limit dividends through `50` and limit divisors and quotients through `10`).
PA.M3.B-O.1.2: Solve mathematical and real-world problems using multiplication and division, including determining the missing number in a multiplication and/or division equation.
PA.M3.B-O.1.2.1: Use multiplication (up to and including `10xx10`) and/or division (limit dividends through `50` and limit divisors and quotients through `10`) to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and/or measurement quantities.
PA.M3.B-O.1.2.2: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication (up to and including `10xx10`) or division (limit dividends through `50` and limit divisors and quotients through `10`) equation relating three whole numbers.
PA.M3.B-O.2: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.
PA.M3.B-O.2.1: Use properties to simplify and solve multiplication problems.
PA.M3.B-O.2.1.1: Apply the commutative property of multiplication (not identification or definition of the property).
PA.M3.B-O.2.1.2: Apply the associative property of multiplication (not identification or definition of the property).
PA.M3.B-O.2.2: Relate division to a missing-number multiplication equation.
PA.M3.B-O.2.2.1: Interpret and/or model division as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor.
PA.M3.B-O.3: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.
PA.M3.B-O.3.1: Use operations, patterns, and estimation strategies to solve problems (may include word problems).
PA.M3.B-O.3.1.1: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations (expressions are not explicitly stated). Limit to problems with whole numbers and having whole-number answers.
PA.M3.B-O.3.1.2: Represent two-step word problems using equations with a symbol standing for the unknown quantity. Limit to problems with whole numbers and having whole-number answers.
PA.M3.B-O.3.1.3: Assess the reasonableness of answers. Limit problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers.
PA.M3.B-O.3.1.4: Solve two-step equations using order of operations (equation is explicitly stated with no grouping symbols).
PA.M3.B-O.3.1.5: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table) and/or explain them using properties of operations.
PA.M3.B-O.3.1.6: Create or match a story to a given combination of symbols `(+,-,xx,div,<,>,and=)` and numbers.
PA.M3.B-O.3.1.7: Identify the missing symbol `(+,-,xx,div,<,>,and=)` that makes a number sentence true.
PA.M3.C-G.1: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
PA.M3.C-G.1.1.1: Explain that shapes in different categories may share attributes and that the shared attributes can define a larger category.
PA.M3.C-G.1.1.2: Recognize rhombi, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals and/or draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.
PA.M3.C-G.1.1.3: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
PA.M3.D-M.1: Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, money, liquid volumes, masses, and lengths of objects.
PA.M3.D-M.1.1: Determine or calculate time and elapsed time.
PA.M3.D-M.1.1.1: Tell, show, and/or write time (analog) to the nearest minute.
PA.M3.D-M.1.1.2: Calculate elapsed time to the minute in a given situation (total elapsed time limited to 60 minutes or less).
PA.M3.D-M.1.2: Use the attributes of liquid volume, mass, and length of objects.
PA.M3.D-M.1.2.1: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units (cups [c], pints [pt], quarts [qt], gallons [gal], ounces [oz.], and pounds [lb]) and metric units (liters [l], grams [g], and kilograms [kg]).
PA.M3.D-M.1.2.2: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or liquid volumes that are given in the same units.
PA.M3.D-M.1.2.3: Use a ruler to measure lengths to the nearest quarter inch or centimeter.
PA.M3.D-M.1.3: Count, compare, and make change using a collection of coins and one-dollar bills.
PA.M3.D-M.1.3.1: Compare total values of combinations of coins (penny, nickel, dime, and quarter) and/or dollar bills less than `$5.00`.
PA.M3.D-M.1.3.2: Make change for an amount up to $5.00 with no more than $2.00 change given (penny, nickel, dime, quarter, and dollar).
PA.M3.D-M.1.3.3: Round amounts of money to the nearest dollar.
PA.M3.D-M.2.1: Organize, display, and answer questions based on data.
PA.M3.D-M.2.1.1: Complete a scaled pictograph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories (scales limited to `1,2,5,and10`).
PA.M3.D-M.2.1.2: Solve one- and two-step problems using information to interpret data presented in scaled pictographs and scaled bar graphs (scales limited to `1,2,5,and10`).
PA.M3.D-M.2.1.3: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with `text(halves)andtext(fourths of an inch)`. Display the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked in appropriate units - `text(whole numbers),text(halves),ortext(quarters)`.
PA.M3.D-M.2.1.4: Translate information from one type of display to another. Limit to pictographs, tally charts, bar graphs, and tables.
PA.M3.D-M.3: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.
PA.M3.D-M.3.1: Find the areas of plane figures.
PA.M3.D-M.3.1.1: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in., square ft, and non-standard square units).
PA.M3.D-M.3.1.2: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.
PA.M3.D-M.4: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.
PA.M3.D-M.4.1: Find and use the perimeters of plane figures.
PA.M3.D-M.4.1.1: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas, and exhibiting rectangles with the same area and different perimeters. Use the same units throughout the problem.
PA.E4.A-K.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of key ideas and details in literature.
PA.E4.A-K.1.1.1: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text explicitly says and when drawing inferences from the text.
PA.E4.A-K.1.1.2: Determine a theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text; summarize the text.
PA.E4.A-K.1.1.3: Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story, drama, or poem, drawing on specific details in the text (e.g., a character's thoughts, words, or actions).
PA.E4.A-C.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of craft and structure in literature.
PA.E4.A-C.2.1.1: Compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrated, including the difference between first- and third-person narrations.
PA.E4.A-C.3.1: Demonstrate understanding of connections within, between, and/or among texts.
PA.E4.A-C.3.1.1: Compare and contrast the treatment of similar themes and topics (e.g., opposition of good and evil) and patterns of events (e.g., the quest) in stories, myths, and traditional literature from different cultures.
PA.E4.A-V.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of vocabulary and figurative language in literature.
PA.E4.A-V.4.1.1: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 4 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
PA.E4.A-V.4.1.1a: Use context (e.g., definitions, examples, or restatements in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase, including words or phrases that allude to significant characters found in literature (e.g., Herculean effort).
PA.E4.A-V.4.1.1b: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek and Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., telegraph, photograph, autograph).
PA.E4.A-V.4.1.2: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
PA.E4.A-V.4.1.2a: Explain the meaning of similes and metaphors in context.
PA.E4.A-V.4.1.2b: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.
PA.E4.A-V.4.1.2c: Demonstrate understanding of words by relating them to their antonyms and synonyms.
PA.E4.B-K.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of key ideas and details in informational texts.
PA.E4.B-K.1.1.1: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
PA.E4.B-K.1.1.2: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
PA.E4.B-K.1.1.3: Explain events, procedures, ideas, steps, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
PA.E4.B-C.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of craft and structure in informational texts.
PA.E4.B-C.2.1.1: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
PA.E4.B-C.2.1.2: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information and text features in a text or part of a text.
PA.E4.B-C.3.1: Demonstrate understanding of connections within, between, and/or among informational texts.
PA.E4.B-C.3.1.1: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
PA.E4.B-C.3.1.2: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to demonstrate subject knowledge.
PA.E4.B-C.3.1.3: Interpret text features (e.g., headings, graphics, charts, timelines, diagrams) and/or make connections between text and the content of text features.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of vocabulary and figurative language in informational texts.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.1: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 4 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.1a: Use context (e.g., definitions, examples, or restatements in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.1b: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek and Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., telegraph, photograph, autograph).
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.1c: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases used in a text.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.2: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.2a: Explain the meaning of similes and metaphors in context.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.2b: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.
PA.E4.B-V.4.1.2c: Demonstrate understanding of words by relating them to their antonyms and synonyms.
PA.E4.D.1.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage.
PA.E4.D.1.1.1: Use relative pronouns (e.g., who, whose, whom, which, that) and relative adverbs (e.g., where, when, why).
PA.E4.D.1.1.2: Form and use the progressive verb tenses (e.g., I was walking, I am walking, I will be walking).
PA.E4.D.1.1.3: Use modal auxiliaries (e.g., can, may, must) to convey various conditions.
PA.E4.D.1.1.4: Order adjectives within sentences according to conventional patterns (e.g., a small red bag rather than a red small bag).
PA.E4.D.1.1.6: Produce complete sentences, recognizing and correcting inappropriate fragments and run-on sentences.
PA.E4.D.1.1.7: Correctly use frequently confused words (e.g., to, too, two; there, their, they're).
PA.E4.D.1.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.
PA.E4.D.1.2.2: Use commas and quotation marks to mark direct speech and quotations from a text.
PA.E4.D.1.2.3: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence.
PA.E4.D.2.1: Use knowledge of language and its conventions.
PA.E4.D.2.1.1: Choose words and phrases to convey ideas precisely.
PA.E4.D.2.1.3: Choose words and phrases for effect.
PA.E4.E.1.1: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and/or research.
PA.E4.E.1.1.1: Introduce text(s) for the intended audience, state an opinion and/or topic, establish a situation, and create an organizational structure in which related ideas are logically grouped to support the writer's purpose.
PA.E4.E.1.1.2: Develop the analysis using a variety of evidence from text(s) to support claims, opinions, ideas, and inferences.
PA.E4.E.1.1.3: Link ideas within categories of information using words and phrases (e.g., another, for example, also, because).
PA.E4.E.1.1.4: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic and/or convey the experience and events.
PA.E4.E.1.1.5: Provide a concluding statement or section related to the analysis presented.
PA.M4.A-T.1: Generalize place-value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.
PA.M4.A-T.1.1: Apply place-value strategies to solve problems.
PA.M4.A-T.1.1.1: Demonstrate an understanding that in a multi-digit whole number (through `1text(,)000text(,)000`), a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
PA.M4.A-T.1.1.2: Read and write whole numbers in expanded, standard, and word form through `1text(,)000text(,)000`.
PA.M4.A-T.1.1.3: Compare two multi-digit numbers through `1text(,)000text(,)000` based on meanings of the digits in each place, using `>,=,and<` symbols.
PA.M4.A-T.1.1.4: Round multi-digit whole numbers (through `1text(,)000text(,)000`) to any place.
PA.M4.A-T.2: Use place-value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
PA.M4.A-T.2.1.1: Add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers (limit sums and subtrahends up to and including `1text(,)000text(,)000`).
PA.M4.A-T.2.1.2: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number and multiply `2` `text(two-digit)` numbers.
PA.M4.A-T.2.1.3: Divide up to four-digit dividends by one-digit divisors with answers written as whole-number quotients and remainders.
PA.M4.A-T.2.1.4: Estimate the answer to addition, subtraction, and multiplication problems using whole numbers through six digits (for multiplication, no more than `2` digits`xx1` digit, excluding powers of `10`).
PA.M4.A-F.1: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.
PA.M4.A-F.1.1.2: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`) using the symbols `>,=,or<` and justify the conclusions.
PA.M4.A-F.2: Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers.
PA.M4.A-F.2.1: Solve problems involving fractions and whole numbers (straight computation or word problems).
PA.M4.A-F.2.1.1: Add and subtract fractions with a common denominator (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`; answers do not need to be simplified; and no improper fractions as the final answer).
PA.M4.A-F.2.1.2: Decompose a fraction or a mixed number into a sum of fractions with the same denominator (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`), recording the decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions (e.g., by using a visual fraction model).
PA.M4.A-F.2.1.3: Add and subtract mixed numbers with a common denominator (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`; no regrouping with subtraction; fractions do not need to be simplified; and no improper fractions as the final answers).
PA.M4.A-F.2.1.4: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole or set and having like denominators (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`).
PA.M4.A-F.2.1.5: Multiply a whole number by a unit fraction (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100` and final answers do not need to be simplified or written as a mixed number).
PA.M4.A-F.2.1.6: Multiply a whole number by a non-unit fraction (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100` and final answers do not need to be simplified or written as a mixed number).
PA.M4.A-F.2.1.7: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a whole number by a fraction (denominators limited to `2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,and100`).
PA.M4.A-F.3: Understand decimal notation for fractions and compare decimal fractions.
PA.M4.A-F.3.1: Use operations to solve problems involving decimals, including converting between fractions and decimals (may include word problems).
PA.M4.A-F.3.1.1: Add two fractions with respective denominators `10and100`.
PA.M4.A-F.3.1.2: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators `10or100`.
PA.M4.A-F.3.1.3: Compare two decimals to hundredths using the symbols `>,=,or<`, and justify the conclusions.
PA.M4.B-O.1: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.
PA.M4.B-O.1.1: Use numbers and symbols to model the concepts of expressions and equations.
PA.M4.B-O.1.1.1: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.
PA.M4.B-O.1.1.2: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.
PA.M4.B-O.1.1.3: Solve multi-step word problems posed with whole numbers using the four operations. Answers will be either whole numbers or have remainders that must be interpreted yielding a final answer that is a whole number. Represent these problems using equations with a symbol or letter standing for the unknown quantity.
PA.M4.B-O.1.1.4: Identify the missing symbol `(+,-,xx,div,=,<,and>)` that makes a number sentence true (single-digit divisor only).
PA.M4.B-O.2: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.
PA.M4.B-O.2.1: Develop and apply number theory concepts to represent numbers in various ways.
PA.M4.B-O.2.1.1: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the interval `1` through `100`. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the interval `1` through `100` is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the interval `1` through `100` is prime or composite.
PA.M4.B-O.3.1: Recognize, describe, extend, create, and replicate a variety of patterns.
PA.M4.B-O.3.1.1: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
PA.M4.B-O.3.1.2: Determine the missing elements in a function table (limit to `+,-,orxx` and to whole numbers or money).
PA.M4.B-O.3.1.3: Determine the rule for a function given a table (limit to `+,-,orxx` and to whole numbers).
PA.M4.C-G.1: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.
PA.M4.C-G.1.1: List properties, classify, draw, and identify geometric figures in two dimensions.
PA.M4.C-G.1.1.1: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, and obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.
PA.M4.C-G.1.1.2: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.
PA.M4.C-G.1.1.3: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into mirroring parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry (up to two lines of symmetry).
PA.M4.D-M.1: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.
PA.M4.D-M.1.1: Solve problems involving length, weight (mass), liquid volume, time, area, and perimeter.
PA.M4.D-M.1.1.1: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including standard units (in., ft, yd, mi; oz., lb; and c, pt, qt, gal), metric units (cm, m, km; g, kg; and mL, L), and time (sec, min, hr, day, wk, mo, and yr). Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit.
PA.M4.D-M.1.1.2: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time (such as elapsed time), liquid volumes, masses of objects; money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals; and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit.
PA.M4.D-M.1.1.3: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real-world and mathematical problems (may include finding a missing side length). Whole numbers only.
PA.M4.D-M.1.1.4: Identify time (analog or digital) as the amount of minutes before or after the hour.
PA.M4.D-M.2.1: Organize, display, and answer questions based on data.
PA.M4.D-M.2.1.1: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (e.g., intervals of `1/2,1/4,or1/8`).
PA.M4.D-M.2.1.2: Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots (line plots must be labeled with common denominators, such as `1/4,2/4,3/4`).
PA.M4.D-M.2.1.3: Translate information from one type of display to another (table, chart, bar graph, or pictograph).
PA.M4.D-M.3: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of angle; measure and create angles.
PA.M4.D-M.3.1: Use appropriate tools and units to sketch an angle and determine angle measurements.
PA.M4.D-M.3.1.1: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. With the aid of a protractor, sketch angles of specified measure.
PA.M4.D-M.3.1.2: Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real-world and mathematical problems. (Angles must be adjacent and non-overlapping.)
PA.S4.A.1.1: Identify and explain the application of scientific, environmental, or technological knowledge to possible solutions to problems.
PA.S4.A.1.1.1: Distinguish between a scientific fact and an opinion, providing clear explanations that connect observations and results (e.g., a scientific fact can be supported by making observations).
PA.S4.A.1.1.2: Identify and describe examples of common technological changes past to present in the community (e.g., energy production, transportation, communications, agriculture, packaging materials) that have either positive or negative impacts on society or the environment.
PA.S4.A.1.3: Recognize and describe change in natural or human-made systems and the possible effects of those changes.
PA.S4.A.1.3.1: Observe and record change by using time and measurement.
PA.S4.A.1.3.2: Describe relative size, distance, or motion.
PA.S4.A.1.3.3: Observe and describe the change to objects caused by temperature change or light.
PA.S4.A.1.3.4: Explain what happens to a living organism when its food supply, access to water, shelter, or space is changed (e.g., it might die, migrate, change behavior, eat something else).
PA.S4.A.1.3.5: Provide examples, predict, or describe how everyday human activities (e.g., solid waste production, food production and consumption, transportation, water consumption, energy production and use) may change the environment.
PA.S4.A.2: Processes, Procedures & Tools Of Scientific Investigations
PA.S4.A.2.1: Apply skills necessary to conduct an experiment or design a solution to solve a problem.
PA.S4.A.2.1.1: Generate questions about objects, organisms, or events that can be answered through scientific investigations.
PA.S4.A.2.1.2: Design and describe an investigation (a fair test) to test one variable.
PA.S4.A.2.1.3: Observe a natural phenomenon (e.g., weather changes, length of daylight/night, movement of shadows, animal migrations, growth of plants), record observations, and then make a prediction based on those observations.

PA.M6.A-N.3.2.3: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by plotting points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.
PA.M6.A-R.1: Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.
PA.M6.A-R.1.1: Represent and/or solve real-world and mathematical problems using rates, ratios, and/or percents.

PA.M6.A-R.1.1.5: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate `text(per)` `100` (e.g., `30%` of a quantity means `30/100` times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percentage.

PA.M6.B-E.1.1.4: Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables, including expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems.
PA.M6.B-E.1.1.5: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
PA.M6.B-E.2: Interpret and solve one-variable equations and inequalities.
PA.M6.B-E.2.1: Create, solve, and interpret one-variable equations or inequalities in real-world and mathematical problems.

PA.M6.B-E.2.1.2: Write algebraic expressions to represent real-world or mathematical problems.

PA.M6.B-E.3.1.1: Write an equation to express the relationship between the dependent and independent variables.
PA.M6.B-E.3.1.2: Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables and/or relate these to an equation.

PA.M6.C-G.1.1.3: Determine the volume of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths.

PA.M6.C-G.1.1.5: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made of rectangles and triangles.
PA.M6.C-G.1.1.6: Determine the surface area of triangular and rectangular prisms (including cubes).

PA.E8.A-V.4.1.2: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
PA.E8.A-V.4.1.2a: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., verbal irony, puns) in context.
PA.E8.A-V.4.1.2b: Use the relationship between particular words to better understand each of the words.
PA.E8.A-V.4.1.2c: Distinguish among the connotations (associations) of words with similar denotations (definitions) (e.g., bullheaded, willful, firm, persistent, resolute).
PA.E8.B-K.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of key ideas and details in informational texts.
PA.E8.B-K.1.1.1: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences, conclusions, and/or generalizations drawn from the text.
PA.E8.B-K.1.1.2: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
PA.E8.B-K.1.1.3: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events (e.g., through comparisons, analogies, categories).
PA.E8.B-C.2.1: Demonstrate understanding of craft and structure in informational texts.
PA.E8.B-C.2.1.1: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author acknowledges and responds to conflicting evidence or viewpoints.
PA.E8.B-C.2.1.2: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
PA.E8.B-C.2.1.3: Determine how the author uses the meaning of words or phrases, including figurative, connotative, or technical meanings, in a text; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
PA.E8.B-C.3.1: Demonstrate understanding of connections within, between, and/or among informational texts.
PA.E8.B-C.3.1.1: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient; recognize when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
PA.E8.B-C.3.1.2: Analyze a case in which two or more texts provide conflicting information on the same topic, and identify where the texts disagree on matters of fact or interpretation.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1: Demonstrate understanding of vocabulary and figurative language in informational texts.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.1: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words or phrases based on grade 8 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.1a: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph, a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.1b: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., precede, recede, secede).
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.1c: Determine the meaning of technical words and phrases used in a text.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.2: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.2a: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., verbal irony, puns) in context.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.2b: Use the relationship between particular words to better understand each of the words.
PA.E8.B-V.4.1.2c: Distinguish among the connotations (associations) of words with similar denotations (definitions) (e.g., bullheaded, willful, firm, persistent, resolute).
PA.E8.D.1.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage.
PA.E8.D.1.1.1: Explain the function of verbals (i.e., gerunds, participles, and infinitives) in general and their function in particular sentences.
PA.E8.D.1.1.2: Form and use verbs in the active and passive voice.
PA.E8.D.1.1.3: Form and use verbs in the indicative, imperative, interrogative, conditional, and subjunctive mood.
PA.E8.D.1.1.4: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb voice and mood.
PA.E8.D.1.1.5: Place phrases and clauses within a sentence, recognizing and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers.
PA.E8.D.1.1.6: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in pronoun number and person.
PA.E8.D.1.1.7: Recognize and correct vague pronouns (i.e., ones with unclear or ambiguous antecedents).
PA.E8.D.1.1.8: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense.
PA.E8.D.1.1.9: Produce complete sentences, recognizing and correcting inappropriate fragments and run-on sentences.
PA.E8.D.1.1.10: Correctly use frequently confused words (e.g., to, too, two; there, their, they're).
PA.E8.D.1.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.
PA.E8.D.1.2.1: Use punctuation (i.e., comma, ellipsis, and dash) to indicate a pause or break.
PA.E8.D.1.2.2: Use an ellipsis to indicate an omission.
PA.E8.D.1.2.4: Use punctuation (i.e., commas, parentheses, and dashes) to set off nonrestrictive/parenthetical elements.
PA.E8.D.1.2.5: Use punctuation to separate items in a series.
PA.E8.D.2.1: Use knowledge of language and its conventions.
PA.E8.D.2.1.1: Use verbs in the active and passive voice and in the its conventions. conditional and subjunctive mood to achieve particular effects (e.g., emphasizing the actor or the action, expressing uncertainty, or describing a state contrary to fact).
PA.E8.D.2.1.2: Choose language that expresses ideas precisely and concisely, recognizing and eliminating wordiness and redundancy.
PA.E8.D.2.1.3: Vary sentence patterns for meaning, reader/listener interest, and style.
PA.E8.D.2.1.4: Maintain consistency in style and tone.
PA.E8.D.2.1.6: Choose words and phrases for effect.
PA.E8.E.1.1: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and/or research.
PA.E8.E.1.1.1: Introduce text(s) for the intended audience, state an opinion and/or topic, establish a situation, and create an organizational structure in which ideas are logically grouped to support the writer's purpose.
PA.E8.E.1.1.2: Develop the analysis using relevant evidence from text(s) to support claims, opinions, ideas, and inferences and demonstrating an understanding of the text(s).
PA.E8.E.1.1.3: Use appropriate and varied transitions to create cohesion and clarify the relationships among ideas and concepts.
PA.E8.E.1.1.4: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic and/or convey the experience and events.
PA.E8.E.1.1.5: Establish and maintain a formal style.
PA.E8.E.1.1.6: Provide a concluding section that follows from and supports the analysis presented.
PA.M8.A-N.1: Demonstrate an understanding of rational and irrational numbers.
PA.M8.A-N.1.1: Apply concepts of rational and irrational numbers.
PA.M8.A-N.1.1.1: Determine whether a number is rational or irrational. For rational numbers, show that the decimal expansion terminates or repeats (limit repeating decimals to thousandths).
PA.M8.A-N.1.1.2: Convert a terminating or repeating decimal to a rational number (limit repeating decimals to thousandths).
PA.M8.A-N.1.1.3: Estimate the value of irrational numbers without a calculator (limit whole number radicand to less than 144).
PA.M8.A-N.1.1.4: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare and order irrational numbers.
PA.M8.A-N.1.1.5: Locate/identify rational and irrational numbers at their approximate locations on a number line.
PA.M8.B-E.1: Demonstrate an understanding of expressions and equations with radicals and integer exponents.
PA.M8.B-E.1.1: Represent and use expressions and equations to solve problems involving radicals and integer exponents.
PA.M8.B-E.1.1.1: Apply one or more properties of integer exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions without a calculator (with final answers expressed in exponential form with positive exponents).
PA.M8.B-E.1.1.2: Use square root and cube root symbols to represent solutions to equations of the form `x^2=pandx^3=p`, where `p` is a positive rational number. Evaluate square roots of perfect squares (up to and including `12^2`) and cube roots of perfect cubes (up to and including `5^3`) without a calculator.
PA.M8.B-E.1.1.3: Estimate very large or very small quantities by using numbers expressed in the form of a single digit times an integer power of `10` and express how many times larger or smaller one number is than another.
PA.M8.B-E.1.1.4: Perform operations with numbers expressed in scientific notation, including problems where both decimal and scientific notation are used. Express answers in scientific notation and choose units of appropriate size for measurements of very large or very small quantities (e.g., use `text(millimeters per year)` for seafloor spreading). Interpret scientific notation that has been generated by technology (e.g., interpret `4.7text(EE)9` displayed on a calculator as `4.7xx10^9`).
PA.M8.B-E.2: Understand the connections between proportional relationships, lines, and linear equations.
PA.M8.B-E.2.1: Analyze and describe linear relationships between two variables, using slope.
PA.M8.B-E.2.1.1: Graph proportional relationships, interpreting the unit rate as the slope of the graph. Compare two different proportional relationships represented in different ways.
PA.M8.B-E.2.1.2: Use similar right triangles to show and explain why the slope `m` is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line in the coordinate plane.
PA.M8.B-E.2.1.3: Derive the equation `y=mx` for a line through the origin and the equation `y=mx+b` for a line intercepting the vertical axis at `b`.
PA.M8.B-E.3: Analyze and solve linear equations and pairs of simultaneous linear equations.
PA.M8.B-E.3.1: Write, solve, graph, and interpret linear equations in one or two variables, using various methods.
PA.M8.B-E.3.1.1: Write and identify linear equations in one variable with one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions. Show which of these possibilities is the case by successively transforming the given equation into simpler forms until an equivalent equation of the form `x=a,a=a,ora=b` results (where `aandb` are different numbers).
PA.M8.B-E.3.1.2: Solve linear equations that have rational number coefficients, including equations whose solutions require expanding expressions using the distributive property and collecting like terms.
PA.M8.B-E.3.1.3: Interpret solutions to a system of two linear equations in two variables as points of intersection of their graphs because points of intersection satisfy both equations simultaneously.
PA.M8.B-E.3.1.4: Solve systems of two linear equations in two variables algebraically and estimate solutions by graphing the equations. Solve simple cases by inspection.
PA.M8.B-E.3.1.5: Solve real-world and mathematical problems leading to two linear equations in two variables.
PA.M8.B-F.1.1: Define, evaluate, and compare functions displayed algebraically, graphically, or numerically in tables or by verbal descriptions.
PA.M8.B-F.1.1.1: Determine whether a relation is a function.
PA.M8.B-F.1.1.2: Compare properties of two functions, each represented in a different way (i.e., algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
PA.M8.B-F.1.1.3: Interpret the equation `y=mx+b` as defining a linear function whose graph is a straight line; give examples of functions that are not linear.
PA.M8.B-F.2: Use functions to model relationships between quantities.
PA.M8.B-F.2.1: Represent or interpret functional relationships between quantities using tables, graphs, and descriptions.
PA.M8.B-F.2.1.1: Construct a function to model a linear relationship between two quantities. Determine the rate of change and initial value of the function from a description of a relationship or from two `(x,y)` values, including reading these from a table or from a graph. Interpret the rate of change and initial value of a linear function in terms of the situation it models and in terms of its graph or a table of values.
PA.M8.B-F.2.1.2: Describe qualitatively the functional relationship between two quantities by analyzing a graph (e.g., where the function is increasing or decreasing, linear or nonlinear). Sketch or determine a graph that exhibits the qualitative features of a function that has been described verbally.
PA.M8.C-G.1: Demonstrate an understanding of geometric transformations.
PA.M8.C-G.1.1: Apply properties of geometric transformations to verify congruence or similarity.
PA.M8.C-G.1.1.1: Identify and apply properties of rotations, reflections, and translations.
PA.M8.C-G.1.1.2: Given two congruent figures, describe a sequence of transformations that exhibits the congruence between them.
PA.M8.C-G.1.1.3: Describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.
PA.M8.C-G.1.1.4: Given two similar two-dimensional figures, describe a sequence of transformations that exhibits the similarity between them.
PA.M8.C-G.2: Understand and apply the Pythagorean theorem.
PA.M8.C-G.2.1: Solve problems involving right triangles by applying the Pythagorean theorem.
PA.M8.C-G.2.1.1: Apply the converse of the Pythagorean theorem to show a triangle is a right triangle.
PA.M8.C-G.2.1.2: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.
PA.M8.C-G.2.1.3: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system.
PA.M8.C-G.3: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving volume.
PA.M8.C-G.3.1: Apply volume formulas of cones, cylinders, and spheres.
PA.M8.C-G.3.1.1: Apply formulas for the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
PA.M8.D-S.1: Investigate patterns of association in bivariate data.
PA.M8.D-S.1.1: Analyze and interpret bivariate data displayed in multiple representations.
PA.M8.D-S.1.1.1: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities. Describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative correlation, linear association, and nonlinear association.
PA.M8.D-S.1.1.2: For scatter plots that suggest a linear association, identify a line of best fit by judging the closeness of the data points to the line.
PA.M8.D-S.1.1.3: Use the equation of a linear model to solve problems in the context of bivariate measurement data, interpreting the slope and intercept.
PA.M8.D-S.1.2: Understand that patterns of association can be seen in bivariate categorical data by displaying frequencies and relative frequencies in a two-way table.
PA.M8.D-S.1.2.1: Construct and interpret a two-way table summarizing data on two categorical variables collected from the same subjects. Use relative frequencies calculated for rows or columns to describe possible associations between the two variables.
PA.S8.A.1.1: Explain, interpret, and apply scientific, environmental, or technological knowledge presented in a variety of formats (e.g., visuals, scenarios, graphs).
PA.S8.A.1.1.1: Distinguish between a scientific theory and an opinion, explaining how a theory is supported with evidence, or how new data/information may change existing theories and practices.
PA.S8.A.1.1.2: Use evidence, such as observations or experimental results, to support inferences about a relationship.
PA.S8.A.1.1.3: Distinguish between a scientific fact and an opinion, providing clear explanations that connect observations and results (e.g., a scientific fact can be supported by making observations).
PA.S8.A.1.1.4: Develop descriptions, explanations, predictions, and models using evidence.
PA.S8.A.1.2: Identify and explain the impacts of applying scientific, environmental, or technological knowledge to address solutions to practical problems.
PA.S8.A.1.2.1: Describe the positive and negative, intended and unintended, effects of specific scientific results or technological developments (e.g., air/space travel, genetic engineering, nuclear fission/fusion, artificial intelligence, lasers, organ transplants).
PA.S8.A.1.2.2: Identify environmental issues and explain their potential long-term health effects (e.g., pollution, pest controls, vaccinations).
PA.S8.A.1.2.3: Describe fundamental scientific or technological concepts that could solve practical problems (e.g., Newton's laws of motion, Mendelian genetics).
PA.S8.A.1.2.4: Explain society's standard of living in terms of technological advancements and how these advancements impact on agriculture (e.g., transportation, processing, production, storage).
PA.S8.A.1.3: Identify and analyze evidence that certain variables may have caused measurable changes in natural or human-made systems.
PA.S8.A.1.3.1: Use ratio to describe change (e.g., percents, parts per million, grams per cubic centimeter, mechanical advantage).
PA.S8.A.1.3.2: Use evidence, observations, or explanations to make inferences about change in systems over time (e.g., carrying capacity, succession, population dynamics, loss of mass in chemical reactions, indicator fossils in geologic time scale) and the variables affecting these changes.
PA.S8.A.1.3.3: Examine systems changing over time, identifying the possible variables causing this change, and drawing inferences about how these variables affect this change.
PA.S8.A.1.3.4: Given a scenario, explain how a dynamically changing environment provides for the sustainability of living systems.
PA.S8.A.2: Processes, Procedures & Tools Of Scientific Investigations
PA.S8.A.2.1: Apply knowledge of scientific investigation or technological design in different contexts to make inferences to solve problems.
PA.S8.A.2.1.1: Use evidence, observations, or a variety of scales (e.g., mass, distance, volume, temperature) to describe relationships.
PA.S8.A.2.1.2: Use space/time relationships, define concepts operationally, raise testable questions, or formulate hypotheses.
PA.S8.A.2.1.3: Design a controlled experiment by specifying how the independent variables will be manipulated, how the dependent variable will be measured, and which variables will be held constant.
PA.S8.A.2.1.4: Interpret data/observations; develop relationships among variables based on data/observations to design models as solutions.
PA.S8.A.2.1.5: Use evidence from investigations to clearly communicate and support conclusions.
PA.S8.A.2.1.6: Identify a design flaw in a simple technological system and devise possible working solutions.
PA.S8.A.2.2: Apply appropriate instruments for a specific purpose and describe the information the instrument can provide.
PA.S8.A.2.2.1: Describe the appropriate use of instruments and scales to accurately and safely measure time, mass, distance, volume, or temperature under a variety of conditions.
PA.S8.A.2.2.2: Apply appropriate measurement systems (e.g., time, mass, distance, volume, temperature) to record and interpret observations under varying conditions.
PA.S8.A.2.2.3: Describe ways technology (e.g., microscope, telescope, micrometer, hydraulics, barometer) extends and enhances human abilities for specific purposes.
PA.S8.A.3.1: Explain the parts of a simple system, their roles, and their relationships to the system as a whole.
PA.S8.A.3.1.1: Describe a system (e.g., watershed, circulatory system, heating system, agricultural system) as a group of related parts with specific roles that work together to achieve an observed result.
PA.S8.A.3.1.2: Explain the concept of order in a system [e.g., (first to last: manufacturing steps, trophic levels); (simple to complex: cell, tissue, organ, organ system)].
PA.S8.A.3.1.3: Distinguish among system inputs, system processes, system outputs, and feedback (e.g., physical, ecological, biological, informational).
PA.S8.A.3.1.4: Distinguish between open loop (e.g., energy flow, food web) and closed loop (e.g., materials in the nitrogen and carbon cycles, closed-switch) systems.
PA.S8.A.3.1.5: Explain how components of natural and human-made systems play different roles in a working system.
PA.S8.A.3.2: Apply knowledge of models to make predictions, draw inferences, or explain technological concepts.
PA.S8.A.3.2.1: Describe how scientists use models to explore relationships in natural systems (e.g., an ecosystem, river system, the solar system).
PA.S8.A.3.2.2: Describe how engineers use models to develop new and improved technologies to solve problems.
PA.S8.A.3.2.3: Given a model showing simple cause-and-effect relationships in a natural system, predict results that can be used to test the assumptions in the model (e.g., photosynthesis, water cycle, diffusion, infiltration).
PA.S8.A.3.3: Describe repeated processes or recurring elements in natural, scientific, and technological patterns.
PA.S8.A.3.3.1: Identify and describe patterns as repeated processes or recurring elements in human-made systems (e.g., trusses, hub-and-spoke system in communications and transportation systems, feedback controls in regulated systems).
PA.S8.A.3.3.2: Describe repeating structure patterns in nature (e.g., veins in a leaf, tree rings, crystals, water waves) or periodic patterns (e.g., daily, monthly, annually).
PA.S8.B.1.1: Describe and compare structural and functional similarities and differences that characterize diverse living things.
PA.S8.B.1.1.1: Describe the structures of living things that help them function effectively in specific ways (e.g., adaptations, characteristics).
PA.S8.B.1.1.2: Compare similarities and differences in internal structures of organisms (e.g., invertebrate/vertebrate, vascular/nonvascular, single-celled/multi-celled) and external structures (e.g., appendages, body segments, type of covering, size, shape).
PA.S8.B.1.1.3: Apply knowledge of characteristic structures to identify or categorize organisms (i.e., plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, and protista).
PA.S8.B.1.1.4: Identify the levels of organization from cell to organism and describe how specific structures (parts), which underlie larger systems, enable the system to function as a whole.
PA.S8.B.2.1: Explain the basic concepts of natural selection.
PA.S8.B.2.1.1: Explain how inherited structures or behaviors help organisms survive and reproduce in different environments.
PA.S8.B.2.1.2: Explain how different adaptations in individuals of the same species may affect survivability or reproduction success.
PA.S8.B.2.1.3: Explain that mutations can alter a gene and are the original source of new variations.
PA.S8.B.2.1.4: Describe how selective breeding or biotechnology can change the genetic makeup of organisms.
PA.S8.B.2.1.5: Explain that adaptations are developed over long periods of time and are passed from one generation to another.
PA.S8.B.2.2: Explain how a set of genetic instructions determines inherited traits of organisms.
PA.S8.B.2.2.1: Identify and explain differences between inherited and acquired traits.
PA.S8.B.2.2.2: Recognize that the gene is the basic unit of inheritance, that there are dominant and recessive genes, and that traits are inherited.
PA.S8.B.3.1: Explain the relationships among and between organisms in different ecosystems and their abiotic and biotic components.
PA.S8.B.3.1.1: Explain the flow of energy through an ecosystem (e.g., food chains, food webs).
PA.S8.B.3.1.2: Identify major biomes and describe abiotic and biotic components (e.g., abiotic: different soil types, air, water sunlight; biotic: soil microbes, decomposers).
