WI.MK.RI.2: Share key details from a text.
WI.MK.RI.3: With prompting and support, identify characters, settings, and important events in a story or pieces of information in a text.
WI.MK.RI.4: With prompting and support, identify specific words that express feelings or content- specific words within a text.
WI.MK.RI.6: Define the role of the author and the illustrator in presenting the ideas in a text.
WI.MK.RI.7: With prompting and support, describe the relationship between illustrations and the text.
WI.MK.RI.8: With prompting and support, identify specific information to support ideas in a text.
WI.MK.RI.9: With prompting and support, compare and contrast two texts; recognize that texts reflect one's own and others' culture.
WI.MK.W.1: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose reflective, formal, and creative writing, which may happen simultaneously or independently, for a variety of high-stakes and low-stakes purposes.
WI.MK.W.2: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose text in a variety of modes.
WI.MK.W.2.a: Opinion pieces in which they tell the reader the topic or the name of the book they are writing about and state an opinion or preference about the topic or book.
WI.MK.W.2.b: Informative or explanatory text in which they name what they are writing about and supply some information about the topic.
WI.MK.W.2.c: Convey events, real or imagined and narrate a single event or several loosely linked events, tell about the events in the order in which they occurred, and provide a reaction to what happened.
WI.MK.W.3: Use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose text that utilizes:
WI.MK.W.3.a: Organization: Provide a sense of structure, attempt an introduction.
WI.MK.W.3.b: Word Choice (including domain specific): Use words familiar to the student.
WI.MK.W.4: With guidance and support from adults, use a combination of drawing, dictating, and writing to compose text in which the development and organization are culturally-sustaining and rhetorically authentic to task and purpose.
WI.MK.W.5: With guidance and support from adults, respond to questions and suggestions from peers and add details to strengthen writing as needed.
WI.MK.W.6: With guidance and support from adults, explore a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers. Learn to produce writing through printing (including forming most printed upper- and lower-case letters), cursive, or typing.
WI.MK.W.7: Participate in shared inquiry and writing projects (e.g., explore a number of books by a favorite author and express opinions about them).
WI.MK.W.8: With guidance and support from adults, recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
WI.MK.W.9: With guidance and support from adults, recall facts from literary and informational text to research characters, setting, key detail, specified information, and ideas presented in a text.
WI.MK.SL.1: With guidance and support, participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
WI.MK.SL.1.a: Follow agreed-upon norms and participate by actively listening, taking turns, and staying on topic.
WI.MK.SL.1.b: Participate in a conversation through multiple exchanges.
WI.MK.SL.1.c: Ask questions about the topic or text.
WI.MK.SL.1.d: Consider individual differences when communicating with others.
WI.MK.SL.2: With guidance and support, ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.
WI.MK.SL.3: Ask and answer questions in order to seek help, get information, or clarify something that is not understood.
WI.MK.SL.4: With guidance and support, describe familiar people, places, things, and events.
WI.MK.SL.5: With guidance and support, create an original or utilize existing visual displays to support descriptions.
WI.MK.L.1: Demonstrate an understanding of how language functions in different cultures and contexts; apply this knowledge to comprehend more fully when reading and listening, and make effective choices when composing, creating, and speaking.
WI.MK.L.1.a: Recognize and appreciate the linguistic diversity of peers, teachers, and other members of the school community.
WI.MK.L.2: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases in grade-level reading and content; use context clues, analyze meaningful word parts, consult general and specialized reference materials, and apply word solving strategies (for meaning) as appropriate.
WI.MK.L.2.a: Begin to recognize some words have multiple meanings (e.g., duck, tie).
WI.MK.L.2.b: Use some word prefixes and suffixes as clues to the meaning of unknown words (e.g., un-, -ed).
WI.MK.L.3: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
WI.MK.L.3.a: With guidance and support from adults, ask and answer questions about unknown words.
WI.MK.L.3.b: With guidance and support from adults, sort common objects into categories.
WI.MK.L.3.c: With guidance and support from adults, demonstrate understanding of frequently occurring verbs and their opposites (antonyms).
WI.MK.L.3.d: With guidance and support from adults, connect common words to real life (e.g., colorful).
WI.MK.L.3.e: With guidance and support from adults, act out shades of meanings with verbs (e.g., strut, skip).
WI.MK.L.4: Demonstrate an ability to collaboratively and independently build vocabulary knowledge when encountering unknown words including cultural, general academic, and discipline-specific terms and phrases; use vocabulary appropriate to the context and situation.
WI.MK.L.5: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English grammar and usage when writing or speaking. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.MK.L.5.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with frequently used nouns, verbs, and prepositions.
WI.MK.L.5.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with oral pluralizations of nouns.
WI.MK.L.5.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with question words (who, what, etc.).
WI.MK.L.5.d: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with oral production and expansion of complete sentences.
WI.MK.L.6: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.MK.L.6.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with capitalization of the first word in a sentence.
WI.MK.L.6.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with name frequently used punctuation.
WI.MK.L.6.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with phonetically spell simple words drawing on knowledge of letter-sound relationships.
WI.MK.L.6.d: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with writes letters for most consonant and short vowel sounds (phonemes).
WI.MK.CC.A: Know number names and the count sequence.
WI.MK.CC.A.1: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
WI.MK.CC.A.2: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).
WI.MK.CC.A.3: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).
WI.MK.CC.B.4: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.
WI.MK.CC.B.4.a: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object (one to one correspondence).
WI.MK.CC.B.4.b: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted (cardinality). The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted (number conservation).
WI.MK.CC.B.4.c: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger and the previous number is one smaller (hierarchical inclusion).
WI.MK.CC.B.5: Quickly recognize and name the quantity of up to `5` objects briefly shown in structured or unstructured arrangements without counting (perceptual subitizing).
WI.MK.CC.B.6: Count to answer “how many?” questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1-20, count out that many objects.
WI.MK.CC.C.7: Identify whether the number of objects (up to 10) in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.
WI.MK.CC.C.8: Compare two numbers between `1and10` presented as written numerals using student-generated ways to record the comparison.
WI.MK.OA.A: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.
WI.MK.OA.A.1: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, or numbers. Drawings need not show details but should show the mathematics in the problem.
WI.MK.OA.A.2: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.
WI.MK.OA.A.3.a: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition with drawings or numbers.
WI.MK.OA.A.3.b: Quickly name the quantity of objects briefly shown in structured arrangements anchored to 5 (e.g., fingers, ten frames, math rack/rekenrek) with totals up to 10 without counting by recognizing the arrangement or seeing the quantity in subgroups that are combined (conceptual subitizing).
WI.MK.OA.A.4: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or numbers.
WI.MK.OA.A.5: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 5 using mental images and composing or decomposing numbers up to 5.
WI.MK.NBT.A: Work with numbers 11-19 to gain foundations for place value.
WI.MK.NBT.A.1: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into 10 ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or numbers; understand that these numbers are composed of 10 ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.
WI.MK.MD.A.1: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.
WI.MK.MD.A.2: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has “more of” / “less of” the attribute, and describe the difference.
WI.MK.MD.B: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category.
WI.MK.MD.B.3: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count. Limit category counts to be less than or equal to 10.
WI.MK.G.A: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).
WI.MK.G.A.1: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.
WI.MK.G.A.2: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.
WI.MK.G.A.3: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, “flat”) or three-dimensional (“solid”).
WI.MK.G.B: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.
WI.MK.G.B.4: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/“corners”) and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).
WI.MK.G.B.5: Model shapes in the world by building shapes from components (e.g., sticks and clay balls) and drawing shapes.
WI.MK.G.B.6: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes.
WI.M1.RF.1: Demonstrate understanding of the organization and basic features of print.
WI.M1.RF.1.a: Recognize the distinguishing features of a sentence (e.g., first word, capitalization, ending punctuation).
WI.M1.RF.2: Demonstrate understanding of spoken words, syllables, and sounds (phonemes).
WI.M1.RF.2.a: Distinguish long from short vowel sounds in spoken single-syllable words.
WI.M1.RF.2.b: Orally produce single-syllable words by blending sounds (phonemes), including consonant blends.
WI.M1.RF.2.c: Isolate and pronounce initial, medial vowel, and final sounds (phonemes) in spoken single-syllable words.
WI.M1.RF.2.d: Segment spoken single-syllable words into their complete sequence of individual sounds (phonemes).
WI.M1.RF.2.e: Add, delete, or substitute individual sounds (phonemes) in simple one-syllable words to make new words.
WI.M1.RF.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
WI.M1.RF.3.a: Know the spelling-sound correspondences for common consonant digraphs.
WI.M1.RF.3.b: Decode and encode regularly spelled one-syllable words (e.g., cat, fox, bet, cup, fit, etc.).
WI.M1.RF.3.c: Know final -e and common vowel team conventions for representing long vowel sounds (Examples include but are not limited to: ai, ay, oa, ea, ee, ie, ue, ow).
WI.M1.RF.3.d: Use knowledge that every syllable must have a vowel sound to determine the number of syllables in a printed word.
WI.M1.RF.3.e: Decode two-syllable words following basic (known) patterns by breaking the words into syllables.
WI.M1.RF.3.g: Recognize and read grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words.
WI.M1.RF.4: Read emergent-reader texts with purpose, understanding, and sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
WI.M1.RF.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
WI.M1.RF.4.b: Read grade-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
WI.M1.RF.4.c: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.

WI.M1.RL.2: Identify a main topic or central idea in a text with guidance and support; retell important details.
WI.M1.RL.3: Describe characters, settings, and important events in a story or pieces of information in a text.
WI.M1.RL.4: Identify specific words and phrases that express feeling, appeal to the senses, or content-specific words within a text.
WI.M1.RL.5: Identify a variety of genres and explain major differences between literary texts and informational texts.
WI.M1.RL.6: Describe how illustrations and details support the point of view or purpose of the text.

WI.M1.RI.6: Describe how illustrations and details support the point of view or purpose of the text.

WI.M1.RI.9: Compare and contrast two texts; recognize that texts reflect one's own and others' culture.
WI.M1.W.1: Compose reflective, formal, and creative writing, which may happen simultaneously or independently, for a variety of high-stakes and low-stakes purposes.
WI.M1.W.2: Write text in a variety of modes.
WI.M1.W.2.a: Opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or name the text they are writing about, state an opinion, supply a reason for the opinion, and provide some sense of closure.
WI.M1.W.2.b: Informative or explanatory text in which they name a topic, supply some facts about the topic, and provide some sense of closure.

WI.M1.W.3.b: Transitions: Use simple word transitions and temporal words or pictures that link ideas.
WI.M1.W.3.c: Word Choice (including domain specific): Experiment with descriptive words to describe feelings, events, and images.
WI.M1.W.4: With guidance and support from adults, produce writing in which the development and organization are culturally-sustaining and rhetorically authentic to task and purpose.
WI.M1.W.5: With guidance and support from adults, focus on a topic, respond to questions and suggestions from peers, and add details to strengthen writing as needed.
WI.M1.W.6: With guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers. Learn to produce writing through printing (including forming most printed upper- and lower-case letters), cursive, or typing.
WI.M1.W.7: Participate in shared inquiry and writing projects (e.g., explore a number of “how-to” books on a given topic and use them to write a sequence of instructions).
WI.M1.W.8: With guidance and support from adults, recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
WI.M1.W.9: With guidance and support from adults, recall and use facts from literary and informational text to support reflection and inquiry on characters, setting, key details, specified information, and ideas presented in a text.
WI.M1.SL.1: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
WI.M1.SL.1.a: With guidance and support, follow agreed-upon norms for discussions and participate by actively listening, taking turns, and staying on topic.
WI.M1.SL.1.b: Build on others' talk in conversations by responding to the comments of others through multiple exchanges.
WI.M1.SL.1.c: Ask questions to clear up any confusion about the topics and texts under discussion.
WI.M1.SL.1.d: Consider individual differences when communicating with others.
WI.M1.SL.2: Ask and answer questions about key details in a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.
WI.M1.SL.3: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to gather additional information or clarify something that is not understood.
WI.M1.SL.4: Describe people, places, things, and events with relevant details, expressing ideas clearly.
WI.M1.SL.5: Create an original or utilize existing visual displays to support descriptions to clarify ideas, thoughts, and feelings.
WI.M1.L.1: Demonstrate an understanding of how language functions in different cultures and contexts; apply this knowledge to comprehend more fully when reading and listening; and make effective choices when composing, creating, and speaking.
WI.M1.L.1.a: Recognize and appreciate the linguistic diversity of peers, teachers, and other members of the school community.
WI.M1.L.2: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases in grade-level reading and content; use context clues, analyze meaningful word parts, consult general and specialized reference materials, and apply word solving strategies (for meaning) as appropriate.
WI.M1.L.2.a: Use inflexional forms as clues to the meaning of unknown words (e.g., looks, looked).
WI.M1.L.3: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
WI.M1.L.3.a: With guidance and support from adults, identify words and phrases that suggest feelings or appeal to the senses (e.g., in stories, poems, or conversations).
WI.M1.L.3.b: With guidance and support from adults, explain rationale for sorting words into categories.
WI.M1.L.3.c: With guidance and support from adults, act out or define shades of meanings with verbs of differing manner (e.g., peek, scowl) and adjectives (e.g., gigantic, large).
WI.M1.L.4: Demonstrate an ability to collaboratively and independently build vocabulary knowledge when encountering unknown words including cultural, general academic, and discipline-specific terms and phrases; use vocabulary appropriate to the context and situation. Use frequently occurring conjunctions (e.g., because) to signal simple relationships.
WI.M1.L.5: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English grammar and usage when writing or speaking. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M1.L.5.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with common, proper, and possessive nouns.
WI.M1.L.5.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with nouns/verbs agreement in simple sentences.
WI.M1.L.5.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with frequently occurring pronouns, adjectives, conjunctions, verb tenses, and prepositions.
WI.M1.L.5.d: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with production and expansion of complete sentences in response to prompts.
WI.M1.L.6: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M1.L.6.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with capitalization of dates and names of people.
WI.M1.L.6.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with end punctuation.
WI.M1.L.6.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with commas in dates and simple sets.
WI.M1.L.6.d: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with use conventional spelling for words with common spelling patterns and draw on phonological awareness and spelling conventions to spell other words phonetically.
WI.M1.OA.A: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.
WI.M1.OA.A.1: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
WI.M1.OA.A.2: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
WI.M1.OA.B: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
WI.M1.OA.B.3: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
WI.M1.OA.B.4: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
WI.M1.OA.C.5: Use counting and subitizing strategies to explain addition and subtraction.
WI.M1.OA.C.5.a: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).
WI.M1.OA.C.5.b: Use conceptual subitizing in unstructured arrangements with totals up to 10 and structured arrangements anchored to 5 or 10 (e.g., ten frames, double ten frames, math rack/rekenrek) with totals up to 20 to relate the compositions and decompositions to addition and subtraction.
WI.M1.OA.C.6: Use multiple strategies to add and subtract within 20.
WI.M1.OA.C.6.a: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 10 using strategies that may include mental images and composing and decomposing up to 10.
WI.M1.OA.C.6.b: Add and subtract within 20 using objects, drawings, or equations. Use multiple strategies that may include counting on; making a ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).
WI.M1.OA.D: Work with addition and subtraction equations.
WI.M1.OA.D.7: Understand the meaning of the equal sign as “has the same value or amount as” and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
WI.M1.NBT.A.1: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.
WI.M1.NBT.B.2: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:
WI.M1.NBT.B.2.a: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones-called a “ten.”
WI.M1.NBT.B.2.b: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.
WI.M1.NBT.B.2.c: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).
WI.M1.NBT.B.3: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits and describe the result of the comparison using words and symbols `(>,=,and<)`.
WI.M1.NBT.C: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.
WI.M1.NBT.C.4: Add within `100`, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.
WI.M1.NBT.C.5: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.
WI.M1.NBT.C.6: Subtract multiples of `10` in the range `10-90` from multiples of `10` in the range `10-90` (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.
WI.M1.MD.A: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.
WI.M1.MD.A.1: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.
WI.M1.MD.A.2: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
WI.M1.MD.B.3: Tell and write time in `text(hours)` and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.
WI.M1.MD.C.4: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.
WI.M1.G.A: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
WI.M1.G.A.1: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.
WI.M1.G.A.2: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape. Student use of formal names such as “right rectangular prism” is not expected.
WI.M1.G.A.3: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe and count the shares using the words halves and fourths, and use the phrases half of and fourth of the whole. Describe the whole as being two of the shares, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.
WI.M2.RF.2: Demonstrate understanding of spoken words, syllables, and sounds (phonemes).
WI.M2.RF.2.a: Add, delete, and substitute individual sounds (phonemes) in simple one-syllable words to make new words, including initial, final, medial, consonant blends, short vowel sounds, and long vowel sounds.
WI.M2.RF.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
WI.M2.RF.3.a: Distinguish long and short vowels when reading regularly spelled one-syllable words.
WI.M2.RF.3.b: Know spelling-sound correspondences for additional common vowel teams.
WI.M2.RF.3.c: Decode and encode regularly spelled one, two, and some three syllable CVC pattern words (e.g., 1 syllable: mat, 2 syllable: picnic, 3 syllable: fantastic, etc.).
WI.M2.RF.3.d: Decode words with common prefixes and suffixes.
WI.M2.RF.3.e: Decode regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels. Encode some of these words.
WI.M2.RF.3.e.i: Know when to drop the final e when adding an -ing, -ed endings. (Silent -e vowel pattern base word).
WI.M2.RF.3.e.ii: Know when to double the final consonant when adding a suffix. -ing, -ed.
WI.M2.RF.3.f: Recognize and read grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words.
WI.M2.RF.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
WI.M2.RF.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
WI.M2.RF.4.b: Read grade-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
WI.M2.RF.4.c: Use context to confirm or self- correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.
WI.M2.RL.1: Develop and answer questions to demonstrate an understanding of key ideas and details in a text.
WI.M2.RL.2: Summarize portions of a text in order to identify a main topic or central idea and key details in a text.
WI.M2.RL.3: Describe how characters respond to major events and challenges.
WI.M2.RL.4: Explain how specific words and phrases express feelings, appeal to the senses, or determine the meaning of content-specific words within a text.
WI.M2.RL.5: Describe the overall structure of a text, including describing how the beginning introduces the text and the ending concludes the text.
WI.M2.RL.6: Identify examples of how illustrations, text features, and details support the point of view or purpose of the text.
WI.M2.RL.7: Demonstrate understanding of story elements and/or topics by applying information gained from illustrations or text features.
WI.M2.RL.9: Compare and contrast key points or perspectives presented in two texts; recognize that texts reflect one's own and others' culture.
WI.M2.RI.1: Develop and answer questions to demonstrate an understanding of key ideas and details in a text.
WI.M2.RI.2: Summarize portions of a text in order to identify a main topic or central idea and key details in a text.
WI.M2.RI.3: Describe the connections between ideas, concepts, or a series of events.
WI.M2.RI.4: Explain how specific words and phrases express feelings, appeal to the senses, or determine the meaning of content-specific words within a text.
WI.M2.RI.5: Describe the overall structure of a text, including describing how the beginning introduces the text and the ending concludes the text.
WI.M2.RI.6: Identify examples of how illustrations, text features, and details support the point of view or purpose of the text.
WI.M2.RI.7: Demonstrate understanding of story elements and/or topics by applying information gained from illustrations or text features.
WI.M2.RI.8: Explain how specific points the author or illustrator makes in a text are supported by relevant reasons and evidence.
WI.M2.RI.9: Compare and contrast key points or perspectives presented in two texts; recognize that texts reflect one's own and others' culture.
WI.M2.W.1: Compose reflective, formal, and creative writing, which may happen simultaneously or independently, for a variety of high-stakes and low-stakes purposes.
WI.M2.W.2: Write text in a variety of modes.
WI.M2.W.2.a: Opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or text they are writing about; state an opinion; supply reasons that support the opinion using words for emphasis, addition, contrast, or order to connect opinion and reasons; and provide a concluding statement or section.
WI.M2.W.2.b: Informative or explanatory text in which they introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section.
WI.M2.W.2.c: Convey events, real or imagined, through narratives in which they recount a well elaborated event or short sequence of events; include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings; and use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.
WI.M2.W.3.a: Organization: Provide a beginning, middle and ending that works cohesively to promote the central theme of the text.
WI.M2.W.3.b: Transitions: Use transitions to link and build connections between ideas, text, and events.
WI.M2.W.3.c: Word Choice (including domain specific): Use descriptive words to demonstrate creativity and to provide vivid examples of feelings, events, and images.
WI.M2.W.4: With guidance and support from adults, produce writing in which the development and organization are culturally-sustaining and rhetorically authentic to task and purpose.
WI.M2.W.5: With guidance and support from adults and peers, focus on a topic and strengthen writing as needed by revising and editing.
WI.M2.W.6: With guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers. Learn to produce writing through printing (including forming most printed upper- and lower-case letters), cursive, or typing.
WI.M2.W.7: Participate in shared and independent inquiry and writing projects (e.g., read a number of books on a single topic to produce a report; record science observations).
WI.M2.W.8: Recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.
WI.M2.W.9: With guidance and support from adults and peers, recall and use facts from literary and informational text to support reflection and inquiry on characters, setting, key details, specified information, and ideas presented in a text.
WI.M2.SL.1: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.
WI.M2.SL.1.a: Follow agreed-upon norms for discussions and participate by actively listening, taking turns, gaining the floor in respectful ways, and staying on topic.
WI.M2.SL.1.b: Build on others' talk in conversations by linking their comments to the remarks of others.
WI.M2.SL.1.c: Ask for clarification and further explanation as needed about the topics and texts under discussion.
WI.M2.SL.1.d: Consider individual differences when communicating with others.
WI.M2.SL.2: Recount or describe key ideas or details from a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.
WI.M2.SL.3: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to gather additional information, or clarify something that is not understood, or expand on the topic.
WI.M2.SL.4: Tell a story or recount an experience with descriptive details, expressing ideas clearly.
WI.M2.SL.5: Include digital media and visual displays in presentations to clarify or support ideas, thoughts, and feelings.
WI.M2.L.1: Demonstrate an understanding of how language functions in different cultures and contexts; apply this knowledge to comprehend more fully when reading and listening; and make effective choices when composing, creating, and speaking.
WI.M2.L.1.a: Recognize and appreciate linguistic diversity (e.g., at home, in the community and in peer and professional writing and speaking).
WI.M2.L.1.b: Recognize formal and informal uses of English.
WI.M2.L.2: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases in grade-level reading and content; use context clues, analyze meaningful word parts, consult general and specialized reference materials, and apply word solving strategies (for meaning) as appropriate.
WI.M2.L.2.a: Determine the meaning of a new word when a prefix or suffix is added.
WI.M2.L.2.b: Use a common root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word.
WI.M2.L.2.c: Use individual words to predict meaning of compound words (e.g., birdhouse).
WI.M2.L.2.d: Use resources to clarify meanings of words.
WI.M2.L.3: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
WI.M2.L.3.a: Describe how words and phrases supply rhythm and meaning in a text (e.g., alliteration, rhyme, repeated lines).
WI.M2.L.3.b: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., describe foods that are juicy).
WI.M2.L.3.c: Distinguish shades of meaning among similar verbs (e.g., toss, throw) and adjectives (e.g., happy, pleased).
WI.M2.L.4: Demonstrate an ability to collaboratively and independently build vocabulary knowledge when encountering unknown words including cultural, general academic, and discipline-specific terms and phrases; use vocabulary appropriate to the context and situation. Use adjectives and adverbs to describe (e.g., when other kids are happy, that makes me happy.).
WI.M2.L.5: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English grammar and usage when writing or speaking. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M2.L.5.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with collective nouns, adjectives and adverbs, frequently occurring regular plural nouns, frequently occurring irregular past tense verbs.
WI.M2.L.5.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with production, expansion, and rearrangement of complete simple and compound sentences.
WI.M2.L.6: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M2.L.6.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with capitalization of holidays, products, geographic places.
WI.M2.L.6.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with commas in greetings and closings.
WI.M2.L.6.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with apostrophes in contractions and frequently occurring possessives.
WI.M2.L.6.d: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with use common spelling patterns, phonemic awareness, and basic reference materials to solve words.
WI.M2.OA.A: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.
WI.M2.OA.A.1: Use addition and subtraction within `100` to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
WI.M2.OA.B.2: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within 20 using multiple mental strategies which may include counting on; making ten; decomposing a number leading to a ten; using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).
WI.M2.OA.C: Work with equal groups of objects to gain foundations for multiplication.
WI.M2.OA.C.3: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by twos; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
WI.M2.OA.C.4: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to `5` rows and up to `5` columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.
WI.M2.NBT.A.1: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones; e.g., 706 equals 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones. Understand the following as special cases:
WI.M2.NBT.A.1.a: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens-called a “hundred”.
WI.M2.NBT.A.1.b: The numbers 100,200,300,400,500,600,700,800, 900 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones).
WI.M2.NBT.A.2: Count within `1text(,)000`; skip-count by fives, tens, and hundreds.
WI.M2.NBT.A.3: Read and write numbers to `1text(,)000` using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.
WI.M2.NBT.A.4: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, and describe the result of the comparison using words and symbols `(>,=,and<)`.
WI.M2.NBT.B: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.
WI.M2.NBT.B.5: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within `100` using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction. In Grade 2, subtraction with decomposition is an exception and may include drawings or representations.
WI.M2.NBT.B.6: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.
WI.M2.NBT.B.7: Add and subtract within `1text(,)000`, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method. Understand that in adding or subtracting three digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.
WI.M2.NBT.B.8: Mentally add `10or100` to a given number 100 - 900, and mentally subtract `10or100` from a given number 100 - 900.
WI.M2.NBT.B.9: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations. These explanations may be supported by drawings or objects.
WI.M2.MD.A: Measure and estimate lengths in standard units.
WI.M2.MD.A.1: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.
WI.M2.MD.A.2: Measure the length of an object twice, using length units of different lengths for the two measurements; describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen.
WI.M2.MD.A.3: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.
WI.M2.MD.A.4: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit.
WI.M2.MD.B: Relate addition and subtraction to length.
WI.M2.MD.B.5: Use addition and subtraction within `100` to solve word problems involving lengths that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as number lines) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
WI.M2.MD.B.6: Represent whole numbers as lengths from `0` on a number line with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers 0, 1, 2 ... and represent whole-number sums and differences within `100` on a number line.
WI.M2.MD.C.7: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.
WI.M2.MD.C.8: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately.
WI.M2.MD.D.9: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit, or by making repeated measurements of the same object. Show the measurements by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in whole-number units.
WI.M2.MD.D.10: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.
WI.M2.G.A: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
WI.M2.G.A.1: Recognize and draw shapes having specified attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces. Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes. Sizes are compared directly or visually, not compared by measuring.
WI.M2.G.A.2: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
WI.M2.G.A.3: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares, describe and count the shares using the words halves, thirds, and fourths, and use phrases half of, a third of, and a fourth of the whole. Describe the whole as composed of two halves, three thirds, and four fourths. Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.
WI.M3.RF.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
WI.M3.RF.3.a: Identify and know the meaning of the most common prefixes and derivational suffixes.
WI.M3.RF.3.b: Decode words with common Latin suffixes.
WI.M3.RF.3.c: Decode multi-syllable words that include all learned syllable patterns (see previous grade level standards for specific targets).
WI.M3.RF.3.e.i: Know when to drop the final e when adding endings. (Silent -e vowel pattern base word).
WI.M3.RF.3.e.ii: Know when to double the final consonant when adding a suffix.
WI.M3.RF.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
WI.M3.RF.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
WI.M3.RF.4.b: Read grade-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
WI.M3.RF.4.c: Use context to confirm or self- correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.
WI.M3.RL.1: Develop and answer questions to locate relevant and specific details in a text to support an answer or inference.
WI.M3.RL.2: Summarize portions of a text to determine a theme or central idea and explain how it is supported by key details.
WI.M3.RL.3: Describe a character (traits, motivations, feelings) drawing on specific details from the text.
WI.M3.RL.4: Determine the meaning of words, phrases, figurative language, and academic and content-specific words within a text.
WI.M3.RL.5: Identify parts of stories, dramas, and poems using terms such as chapter, scene, and stanza.
WI.M3.RL.6: Discuss how the reader's point of view or perspective may differ from that of the author, narrator, or characters in a text.
WI.M3.RL.7: Explain how specific illustrations or text features contribute to what is conveyed by the words in a text (e.g., create mood, emphasize character or setting, or determine where, when, why, and how key events occur).
WI.M3.RL.9: Recognize genres and make connections to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, identities, eras, personal events, and situations.
WI.M3.RI.1: Develop and answer questions to locate relevant and specific details in a text to support an answer or inference.
WI.M3.RI.2: Summarize portions of a text to determine a theme or central idea and explain how it is supported by key details.
WI.M3.RI.3: Describe the relationship among a series of events, ideas, concepts, or steps in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.
WI.M3.RI.4: Determine the meaning of words, phrases, figurative language, and academic and content-specific words within a text.
WI.M3.RI.5: Identify and use text features to build comprehension.
WI.M3.RI.6: Discuss how the reader's point of view or perspective may differ from that of the author, narrator, or characters in a text.
WI.M3.RI.7: Explain how specific illustrations or text features contribute to what is conveyed by the words in a text (e.g., create mood, emphasize character or setting, or determine where, when, why, and how key events occur).
WI.M3.RI.8: Explain how claims in a text are supported by relevant reasons and evidence.
WI.M3.RI.9: Recognize genres and make connections to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, identities, eras, personal events, and situations.
WI.M3.W.1: Compose reflective, formal, and creative writing, which may happen simultaneously or independently, for a variety of high-stakes and low-stakes purposes.
WI.M3.W.2: Write text in a variety of modes.
WI.M3.W.2.a: Opinion pieces in which the student supports a point of view about a topic or text they are writing about, state an opinion, list reasons that support the opinion.
WI.M3.W.2.b: Informative or explanatory texts in which they introduce a topic, use facts, definitions, and details to develop points.
WI.M3.W.2.c: Convey events, real or imagined, through narrative or short stories to develop experiences or events using descriptive details and clear event sequences to establish a situation and introduce a narrator or characters. Use dialogue and description of actions, thoughts, and feelings to develop experiences and events or show the responses of characters to situations.
WI.M3.W.3.a: Organization: Include an introduction that establishes a purpose and provides a concluding statement appropriate to the mode of writing.
WI.M3.W.3.b: Transitions: Use prompts, words, and phrases to signal event order and to link and build connections between ideas, text, and events.
WI.M3.W.3.c: Word Choice (including domain specific): Use words familiar to the student for emphasis, addition, contrast, or order to connect categories or information, and to convey meaning.
WI.M3.W.4: With support from adults and peers, produce writing in which the development and organization are culturally-sustaining and rhetorically authentic to task and purpose.
WI.M3.W.5: With guidance and support from adults and peers, respond to questions and suggestions from peers and add details to strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, and editing.
WI.M3.W.6: With guidance and support from adults and peers, use digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers. Learn to produce writing through printing, cursive, or typing.
WI.M3.W.7: Conduct short inquiry projects that build knowledge about a topic.
WI.M3.W.8: Recall information from experiences or gather information from print and digital sources; take brief notes on sources and sort evidence into provided categories.
WI.M3.W.9: Recall facts from literary or informational texts to support reflection and inquiry.
WI.M3.SL.1: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher led) with diverse partners on topics and texts, building on others' ideas and expressing one's thinking clearly.
WI.M3.SL.1.a: Come to discussions prepared, explicitly draw on topics and texts along with personal knowledge and experiences to explore ideas under discussion.
WI.M3.SL.1.b: Follow agreed-upon norms for discussions (e.g., gaining attention in respectful ways, actively listening, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).
WI.M3.SL.1.c: Ask questions to check understanding of information presented, stay on topic, and link their comments to the remarks of others.
WI.M3.SL.1.d: Explain their own ideas and understanding in light of the discussion.
WI.M3.SL.2: Determine main ideas and supporting details of a text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats.
WI.M3.SL.3: Ask and answer questions about information from a speaker, offering elaboration and detail.
WI.M3.SL.4: Report on a topic or text, tell a story, read a poem, or recount an experience with facts and relevant, descriptive details, speaking clearly at an understandable pace.
WI.M3.SL.5: Include digital media and visual displays in presentations to enhance certain facts and details.
WI.M3.L.1: Demonstrate an understanding of how language functions in different cultures, contexts, and disciplines; apply this knowledge to comprehend more fully when reading and listening, and make effective choices when composing, creating, and speaking.
WI.M3.L.1.a: Compare and contrast the ways in which language is used in familiar contexts (e.g., at home, in the community, in peer and professional writing/speaking).
WI.M3.L.1.b: Recognize differences between the conventions of written and spoken English.
WI.M3.L.1.c: Identify key words and phrases that help readers understand a topic; choose words and phrases for effect when writing and speaking.
WI.M3.L.2: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases in grade-level reading and content; use context clues, analyze meaningful word parts, consult general and specialized reference materials, and apply word solving strategies (for meaning) as appropriate.
WI.M3.L.2.a: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
WI.M3.L.2.b: Determine the meaning of new words when a suffix or prefix is added.
WI.M3.L.2.c: Use resources to determine word meanings.
WI.M3.L.3: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
WI.M3.L.3.a: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, distinguishing between literal and non-literal language.
WI.M3.L.3.b: Distinguish shades of meaning among words describing degrees of certainty (e.g., knew, believed, suspected).
WI.M3.L.3.c: Make connections between words and how they are used in real life (i.e., help students build or add on to existing schema when encountering new words).
WI.M3.L.4: Demonstrate an ability to collaboratively and independently build vocabulary knowledge when encountering unknown words including cultural, general academic, and discipline-specific terms and phrases; use vocabulary appropriate to the context and situation.
WI.M3.L.4.a: Identify and use phrases that signal spatial and temporal relationships (e.g., after dinner that night, we went looking for them.).
WI.M3.L.5: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English grammar and usage when writing or speaking. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M3.L.5.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with irregular and regular nouns and verbs.
WI.M3.L.5.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with simple verb tenses.
WI.M3.L.5.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with subject-verb agreement.
WI.M3.L.5.d: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with simple and compound sentences.
WI.M3.L.5.e: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with easily confused words (e.g., to, too, two).
WI.M3.L.6: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M3.L.6.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with titles.
WI.M3.L.6.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with quotation marks for speech.
WI.M3.L.6.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with possessives.
WI.M3.L.6.d: Use spelling patterns and generalizations (e.g., word families, position-based spellings, syllable patterns, ending rules, meaningful word parts) in writing words.
WI.M3.L.6.e: Use conventional spelling for high frequency words.
WI.M3.L.6.f: Use conventional spelling for adding suffixes to basic words.
WI.M3.L.6.g: Use learned syllable patterns and reference materials to solve and write unknown words.
WI.M3.OA.A: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.
WI.M3.OA.A.1: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 x 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
WI.M3.OA.A.2: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret `56-:8` as the number of objects in each share when `56` objects are partitioned equally into `8` shares, or as a number of shares when `56` objects are partitioned into equal shares of `8` objects each.
WI.M3.OA.A.3: Use multiplication and division within `100` to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
WI.M3.OA.B: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.
WI.M3.OA.B.4: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide. Student use of the formal terms for these properties is not necessary.
WI.M3.OA.B.5: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.
WI.M3.OA.C.6: Use multiplicative thinking to multiply and divide within `100`.
WI.M3.OA.C.6.a: Use the meanings of multiplication and division, the relationship between the operations (e.g., knowing that 8 x 5 = 40, one could reason that 40 ÷ 5 = 8), and properties of operations (e.g., the distributive property) to develop and understand strategies to multiply and divide within `100`.
WI.M3.OA.C.6.b: Flexibly and efficiently use strategies, the relationship between the operations, and properties of operations to find products and quotients with multiples of `0,1,2,5,and10` within `100`.
WI.M3.OA.D: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.
WI.M3.OA.D.7: Solve two-step word problems, posed with whole numbers and having whole number answers, using the four operations. Represent these problems using one or two equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. If one equation is used, grouping symbols (i.e. parentheses) may be needed. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.
WI.M3.OA.D.8: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table) and explain them using properties of operations.
WI.M3.NBT.A: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
WI.M3.NBT.A.1: Use place value understanding to generate estimates for problems in real-world situations, with whole numbers within `1text(,)000`, using strategies such as mental math, benchmark numbers, compatible numbers, and rounding. Assess the reasonableness of their estimates (e.g., Is my estimate too low or too high? What degree of precision do I need for this situation?).
WI.M3.NBT.A.2: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract within `1text(,)000` using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
WI.M3.NBT.A.3: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of `10` in the range `10-90` (e.g., `9xx80,5xx60`) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.
WI.M3.NF.A: Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.
WI.M3.NF.A.1: Understand a unit fraction as the quantity formed when a whole is partitioned into equal parts and explain that a unit fraction is one of those parts (e.g., `1/4`). Understand fractions are composed of unit fractions.
WI.M3.NF.A.2: Understand and represent a fraction as a number on the number line.
WI.M3.NF.A.2.a: Understand the whole on a number line is defined as the interval from `0` to `1` and the unit fraction is defined by partitioning the interval into equal parts (i.e., equal-sized lengths).
WI.M3.NF.A.2.b: Represent fractions on a number line by iterating lengths of the unit fraction from `0`. Recognize that the resulting interval represents the size of the fraction and that its endpoint locates the fraction as a number on the number line.
WI.M3.NF.A.3: Explain equivalence of fractions and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.
WI.M3.NF.A.3.a: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size or name the same point on a number line.
WI.M3.NF.A.3.b: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., `1/2=2/4,4/6=2/3`) and explain why the fractions are equivalent by using a visual fraction model (e.g., tape diagram or number line).
WI.M3.NF.A.3.c: Express whole numbers as fractions (3 = 3/1), and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers (4/4 = 1).
WI.M3.NF.A.3.d: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Justify the conclusions by using a visual fraction model (e.g., tape diagram or number line) and describe the result of the comparison using words and symbols `(>,=,and<)`.
WI.M3.MD.A: Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.
WI.M3.MD.A.1: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in `text(minutes)`. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in `text(minutes)`, e.g., by representing the problem on a number line.
WI.M3.MD.A.2: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l), excluding compound units such as `text(cm)^3` and finding the geometric volume of a container. Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem.
WI.M3.MD.B.3: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
WI.M3.MD.B.4: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with `text(halves)andtext(fourths of an inch)`. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units-whole numbers, halves, fourths.
WI.M3.MD.C: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.
WI.M3.MD.C.5: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.
WI.M3.MD.C.6: Measure areas by counting unit squares (`text(square cm),text(square m),text(square in),text(square ft)`., and improvised units).
WI.M3.MD.C.7: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.
WI.M3.MD.C.7.a: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.
WI.M3.MD.C.7.b: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole number side lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.
WI.M3.MD.C.7.c: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths `aandb+c` is the sum of `axxbandaxxc`. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.
WI.M3.MD.C.7.d: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real-world problems.
WI.M3.MD.D: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.
WI.M3.MD.D.8: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.
WI.M3.G.A: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
WI.M3.G.A.1: Understand that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (e.g., quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.
WI.M3.G.A.2: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
WI.M4.RF.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words. Use combined knowledge of all letter-sound correspondences, syllabication patterns, and morphology (e.g., roots and affixes) to read accurately unfamiliar multisyllabic words in context and out of context.
WI.M4.RF.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
WI.M4.RF.4.a: Read grade-level text with purpose and understanding.
WI.M4.RF.4.b: Read grade-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.
WI.M4.RF.4.c: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.
WI.M4.RL.1: Locate and refer to relevant details and evidence when explaining what a text says explicitly or implicitly and make logical inferences.
WI.M4.RL.2: Summarize texts, from a variety of genres, to determine a theme or central idea and explain how it is supported by key details.
WI.M4.RL.3: Describe a character (traits, motivations, feelings), setting, or event, drawing on specific details in the text.
WI.M4.RL.4: Determine the meaning of words, phrases, figurative language, academic, and content-specific words within a text.
WI.M4.RL.5: Identify and analyze structural elements, using terms such as verse, rhythm, meter, characters, settings, dialogue, stage directions.
WI.M4.RL.6: In literary text, compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrated, including the difference between first- and third-person narrations.
WI.M4.RL.7: Explain how text features (e.g., charts, graphs, diagrams, timelines, animations, and illustrations) contribute to an understanding of the text.
WI.M4.RL.9: Recognize genres and make connections to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, identities, eras, personal events, and situations.
WI.M4.RI.1: Locate and refer to relevant details and evidence when explaining what a text says explicitly or implicitly and make logical inferences.
WI.M4.RI.2: Summarize texts, from a variety of genres, to determine a theme or central idea and explain how it is supported by key details.
WI.M4.RI.3: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts, including what happened and why, based on specific evidence from the text.
WI.M4.RI.4: Determine the meaning of words, phrases, figurative language, academic, and content-specific words within a text.
WI.M4.RI.5: Identify the overall structure using terms such as sequence, comparison, cause and effect, and problem and solution.
WI.M4.RI.6: In informational text, compare and contrast a primary and secondary source on the same event or topic.
WI.M4.RI.7: Explain how text features (e.g., charts, graphs, diagrams, timelines, animations, and illustrations) contribute to an understanding of the text.
WI.M4.RI.8: Explain how claims in a text are supported by relevant reasons and evidence.
WI.M4.RI.9: Recognize genres and make connections to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, identities, eras, personal events, and situations.
WI.M4.W.1: Compose reflective, formal, and creative writing, which may happen simultaneously or independently, for a variety of high-stakes and low-stakes purposes.
WI.M4.W.2: Write text in a variety of modes.
WI.M4.W.2.a: Opinion pieces in which the student introduces the topic or text they are writing about, state an opinion and create an organizational structure in which related ideas are grouped to support the writer's purpose. List reasons that support the opinion.
WI.M4.W.2.b: Informative texts in which they clearly introduce a topic, group related information in paragraphs and sections; include formatting (e.g., headings), illustrations, and multimedia when useful to aid comprehension. Use facts, definitions, and details to develop points.
WI.M4.W.2.c: Convey events, real or imagined, through narrative or short stories which orients a reader by establishing a real or imagined situation and introducing a narrator and characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally. Use narrative techniques, such as dialogue, description, and pacing, to develop experiences and events or show the responses of characters to situations.
WI.M4.W.3.a: Organization: Include an introduction that establishes a purpose and provides a concluding statement related to the body of the composition. Structure of text reflects the purpose.
WI.M4.W.3.b: Transitions: Use phrases to signal event order and to link and build connections between ideas, text, and events.
WI.M4.W.3.c: Word Choice (including domain specific): Experiment with words to provide emphasis, addition, contrast, or order to connect themes and ideas.
WI.M4.W.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are culturally-sustaining and rhetorically authentic to task, purpose, and audience.
WI.M4.W.5: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience. Respond to questions and suggestions from peers; and add details to strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, and editing.
WI.M4.W.6: With some guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers. Learn to produce writing through printing, cursive, or typing (with sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of one page in a single sitting).
WI.M4.W.7: Conduct short inquiry projects that build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.
WI.M4.W.8: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources, take notes and categorize information, and provide a list of sources.
WI.M4.W.9: Recall and use facts from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and inquiry.
WI.M4.SL.1: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher led) with diverse partners on topics and texts, building on others' ideas and expressing one's thinking clearly.
WI.M4.SL.1.a: Come to discussions prepared, explicitly draw on topics and texts along with personal knowledge and experiences to explore ideas under discussion.
WI.M4.SL.1.b: Follow agreed-upon norms for discussions (e.g., gaining attention in respectful ways, actively listening, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).
WI.M4.SL.1.c: Pose and respond to specific questions to clarify or follow up on information, and make comments that contribute to the discussion and link to the remarks of others.
WI.M4.SL.1.d: Review the key ideas expressed and explain their own ideas and understanding in light of the discussion.
WI.M4.SL.2: Paraphrase portions of a text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats.
WI.M4.SL.3: Identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points.
WI.M4.SL.4: Report on a topic or text, tell a story, read a poem, or recount an experience in an organized manner, using facts and relevant, descriptive details to support main ideas or themes; speak clearly at an understandable pace. Communicate clearly and in an engaging manner, considering the audience, purpose, and situation.
WI.M4.SL.5: Integrate audio and visual content in presentations to enhance the development of main ideas or themes.
WI.M4.L.1: Demonstrate an understanding of how language functions in different cultures, contexts, and disciplines; apply this knowledge to comprehend more fully when reading and listening, and make effective choices when composing, creating, and speaking.
WI.M4.L.1.a: Compare and contrast the ways in which language is used in familiar and unfamiliar contexts (e.g., at home, outside of their own communities, by diverse authors and speakers).
WI.M4.L.1.b: Determine the language demands of varied writing and speaking situations; respond appropriately (e.g., formal writing and presentations; personal writing and conversations).
WI.M4.L.1.c: Identify examples of precise and concise language when reading; choose words and phrases to convey ideas precisely when writing and speaking.
WI.M4.L.2: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases in grade-level reading and content; use context clues, analyze meaningful word parts, consult general and specialized reference materials, and apply word solving strategies (for meaning) as appropriate.
WI.M4.L.2.a: Use context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
WI.M4.L.2.b: Consult print and digital reference materials for meaning and pronunciation.
WI.M4.L.3: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
WI.M4.L.3.a: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative language such as similes and metaphors.
WI.M4.L.3.c: Understand words by relating them to synonyms and antonyms.
WI.M4.L.3.d: Make connections between words and how they are used in real life (i.e., help students build or add on to existing schema when encountering new words).
WI.M4.L.4: Demonstrate an ability to collaboratively and independently build vocabulary knowledge when encountering unknown words including cultural, general academic, and discipline-specific terms and phrases; use vocabulary appropriate to the context and situation.
WI.M4.L.4.a: Identify and use phrases that signal precise actions, emotions, or states of being (e.g., quizzed, whined, stammered) and that are basic to a particular topic (e.g., wildlife, conservation, and endangered when discussing animal preservation).
WI.M4.L.5: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English grammar and usage when writing or speaking. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M4.L.5.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with relative pronouns and adverbs.
WI.M4.L.5.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with prepositional phrases.
WI.M4.L.5.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with order of adjective.
WI.M4.L.5,d: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with adjectives, adverbs, conjunctions.
WI.M4.L.5.e: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with compound and complex sentences.
WI.M4.L.5.f: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose of language choice with easily confused words (e.g., to, too, two).
WI.M4.L.6: Demonstrate contextually appropriate use of the conventions of standardized English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing. Discern when and where it is appropriate to use standardized English.
WI.M4.L.6.a: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with capitalization.
WI.M4.L.6.b: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with commas and quotation marks for quotations.
WI.M4.L.6.c: Appropriately use and explain the intended purpose in conventions with commas in compound sentences.
WI.M4.L.6.d: Spell grade-level words correctly using reference materials to solve words as needed.
WI.M4.OA.A: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.
WI.M4.OA.A.1: Interpret a multiplication equation as a multiplicative comparison, e.g., interpret `35=5xx7` as a statement that `35` is `5` times as many as `7and7` times as many as `5`. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.
WI.M4.OA.A.2: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.
WI.M4.OA.A.3: Solve multi-step word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.
WI.M4.OA.B: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.
WI.M4.OA.B.4: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range `1-100`. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range `1-100` is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range `1-100` is prime or composite.
WI.M4.OA.B.5: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
WI.M4.OA.D.6: Flexibly and efficiently multiply and divide within `100`, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that `8xx5=40`, one knows `40-:5=8`) or properties of operations [e.g., knowing that 7 x 6 can be thought of as 7 groups of 6 so one could think 5 groups of 6 is 30 and 2 more groups of 6 is 12 and 30 + 12 = 42 (informal use of the distributive property)].
WI.M4.NBT.A: Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.
WI.M4.NBT.A.1: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
WI.M4.NBT.A.2: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place and describe the result of the comparison using words and symbols `(>,=,and<)`.
WI.M4.NBT.A.3: Use place value understanding to generate estimates for real-world problem situations, with multi-digit whole numbers, using strategies such as mental math, benchmark numbers, compatible numbers, and rounding. Assess the reasonableness of their estimates. (e.g., Is my estimate too low or too high? What degree of precision do I need for this situation?)
WI.M4.NBT.B: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
WI.M4.NBT.B.4: Flexibly and efficiently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using strategies or algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
WI.M4.NBT.B.5: Multiply a whole number of up to `text(four digits)` by a `text(one-digit whole number)`, and multiply `text(two two-digit)` numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, or area models.
WI.M4.NBT.B.6: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, or area models.
WI.M4.NF.A: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.
WI.M4.NF.A.1.a: Explain why a fraction is equivalent to another fraction by using visual fraction models (e.g., tape diagrams and number lines), with attention to how the number and the size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size.
WI.M4.NF.A.1.b: Understand and use a general principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions that name the same amount.
WI.M4.NF.A.2: Compare fractions with different numerators and different denominators while recognizing that comparisons are valid only when the fractions refer to the same whole.
